Ingredients:
- 2 cups enriched white rice
- 4 cups water
- 2/3 cup chopped baby carrots
- 1/2 cup frozen green peas
- 2 tablespoons vegetable oil
- 2 eggs
- soy sauce to taste
- sesame oil, to taste (optional)
Directions:
1. In a saucepan, combine rice and water. Bring to a boil. Reduce heat, cover, and simmer for 20 minutes.
2. In a small saucepan, boil carrots in water about 3 to 5 minutes. Drop peas into boiling water, and drain.
3. Heat wok over high heat. Pour in oil, then stir in carrots and peas; cook about 30 seconds. Crack in eggs, stirring quickly to scramble eggs with vegetables. Stir in cooked rice. Shake in soy sauce, and toss rice to coat. Drizzle with sesame oil, and toss again.

Many members of the community insist on referring to FTL as a "roguelike" however we shall forgive this error and judge this pixel-art, trendy, indie puzzle game slash strategy sim for what it is--alright it's a ♥♥♥♥ing roguelike, fine!
FTL: Faster Than Light, the sole offering to date by Subset Games offers a selection of roguelike-worthy challenges well beyond other indie offerings despite eschewing the traditional form of the genre. The game forces strategic foresight and consistency from the macroscopic, character building (in this case ship-building) level down to hyper-tight management during combat encounters. Randomness is similarly introduced into playthroughs on myriad levels. Each game requires pathing through a selection of sectors--think dungeon floors--whose distinct challenges and rewards must be balanced against the particular strengths of the ship. Within each sector the captain meanders her ship as slowly as possible to the exit, staying ahead of the advancing rebel fleet whose ominous advance serves well as an anti-grinding mechanic.
Individual combat encounters are the meat of this game and designers Justin Ma and Matthew Davis have married tactical play and tense timing superbly well. These encounters play out in real time, though the player can (and should) pause as often as is wanted. Though pausing shifts the primary skills from action-oriented to tactical, precise timing remains critical. It is exhilarating to destroy critical systems on an enemy ship with a synchronized volley seconds before they are able to attack. A subtler triumph of the game's combat is each encounter's long-term import. You cannot afford to take a beating every fight: the cost of repairs will hamper the development of a ship capable of tackling the mounting challenges of later sectors.
I judge FTL by the higher standards imposed by its classification as a roguelike and it defiantly impresses on most fronts. However, there are a few relatively minor failings. My most critical criterion for a successful roguelike is that performing the optimal strategy must not be boring. Playing FTL well is mostly just as enjoyable as learning how the game works, but there is some potential for grinding your crew's skills during non-threatening encounters. Employing this strategy provides a small enough advantage that it ought to be ignored but that it is possible irks me. Unlocking the secondary layouts for each ship requires the player to perform two out of three prescribed achievements. Some of these tasks are fairly uninteresting and I would prefer not to have to undertake them.
FTL will stand as an exemplar of indie development for years to come. Players willing to learn the game's unique mechanics will be rewarded with a balanced, intense, and altogether thrilling flight through the galaxy.

If Braid is in your backlog and you're looking for something to do on Saturday afternoon, give it a playthrough.  It will only take a few hours and you won't regret a moment of it.
+ Gameplay - Interesting mechanics executed well.  The game just feels good to play.  I enjoyed it so much that I played through the game a few times so that I could earn the Speed Run achievement.
+ Art - Crisp sprites and nice backgrounds.  Fun sound effects.  This 6 year old game feels like it could have been released today.
+ Music - A calming soundtrack that doesn't get old or annoying as you figure out each level.  The music follows the same timeline as your character (e.g. turn back time and the music plays backwards; speed up time and the music speeds up) which is a great touch that helps with immersion.  The string-heavy soundtrack lends itself well to such temporal manipulations.
+ Level design - Every level feels fresh and interesting.  Some levels are repeated across worlds, but adapated slightly to the unique mechanic of each world.  You might get frustrated once or twice, but every puzzle has a clean and fair solution.
+ Length - Braid feels like the perfect length.  It took me about four hours to complete the first time around and I was satisfied by the depth to which the various mechanics were explored.  It's a nice, bite-sized game.
~ Story - Told through a few short bits of text, the story is not at the forefront of this game.  There is likely symbolism that ties the mechanics of the game to the story, but it isn't really made obvious to the player.

+ Boobs
+ Smaller boobs
+ It is actually a good fighting game
+ Good training mode and combo challenges
+ Beautiful and creative costumes
+ One of those "easy to learn, hard to master" games
- No online lobby
- Overpriced DLC that only you can see (more on this below)
- People can't see past the sexy characters and disregard this game before giving it a chance
- This game for some incomprehensible reason has male characters too
I have that awkward feeling... I don't know who KOEI hates more. Their western audience, or their PC players?
On one hand, we never got that patch for "Dynasty Warriors 7: Empires" that brings additional hair colors, outside of Japan.
On the other hand, their PC ports are often... subpar.
Well, no matter which is the case, it can still be hard to justify purchasing their games, no matter how awesome they are at their core.
So, let's address two elephants in this DoA room. The most glaring issues with this game.
The lack of online lobbies and the overpriced DLC.
The DLC speak for themselves. They are strictly cosmetic, pricey and there's a lot of them. And I wouldn't say it's a huge issue. There are often discounts for them and obviously nobody forces you to buy another bikini for your favorite fighter. However, to me, this is not the issue. The main issue is that you are the only one who will see these costumes. Because yes, unlike the console version (thanks, KOEI, I love you too), there is no "catalogue" patch that allows other people to see the costumes they don't own. Basically, if you buy that gorgeous Helena bikini and wear it (with pure intentions of throwing your opponent off guard only, obviously), your online opponent actually won't see it and your character will default to costume 1 or 2 on their screen. Ouch. So, no showing off these amazing and utterly overpriced costumes to anyone who doesn't play with you locally.
The second issue is more severe. There is no lobby. In a fighting game. I don't know whose brilliant idea this was, but I hope this person is fired (almost typed "fried", which wouldn't be wrong either).
So, basically, when you want to play against your friend, you just both start searching for matches and hope that you find each other and not somebody else. You can filter it by region which helps a little bit, but you still see how this can be frustrating. Thankfully (and I can't believe I'm saying it) this game doesn't seem to have too big of an online player base in my region. Yaaaay...
On a more positive note, you don't have to sit in a menu while you wait for the game to find an opponent for you. There is an option for it to keep searching while you play training or arcade mode. So at least you still get to play the game while you wait.
So then, Simon, you may ask, why the hell are you giving this game a positive review?
Well, it is a great fighting game. Surprised? Yes, there is a game past all those boobs, and the game is amazing.
I am a rather casual player when it comes to fighting games. That is to say, I love them, but I am horrible at them. There are a few exceptions, like, for example, Skullgirls, Arcana Hearts or Tekken where I feel somewhat comfortable, at least comfortable enough to play with friends and to sometimes play online. And that's because these games took time to teach me what they have to offer. Tekken had a great training room, Skullgirls had a very in-depth tutorial. And Dead or Alive is no exception. It has an amazing training room that lets you learn the basic movesets, an extensive tutorial with all of the game mechanics and a "combo challenge" mode that teaches you the some combos characters can pull. All of this makes this game very beginner-friendly.
The combat itself feels way more fluent and therefore looks somewhat more realistic than, say, Tekken, and definitely than most of the 2D fighters. When you are playing in company of friends, especially non-gamer friends, it's very important because it lets them watch it as if it was a spectacle and not just a set of mechanics.
And speaking of spectacle, the costumes - DLC ones, of course, but even many default ones - are fantastic. And I'm not just talking about skimpy outfits (btw, nothing wrong with them, accept and embrace the sexiness!). If there's one thing I can give KOEI credit for - it's costume originality. I mean, look at Dynasty Warriors, they are re-releasing that game so much that we're expecting it's 9 installment at the time of this review, and never once did they re-use the same costume for a character, while still maintaining that character's unique features. Dead or Alive is no exception and the costumes are actually amazing.
So, in the end I want to say this:
If you want to play locally with your friends, but don't have a console, buy this game. It is a no-brainer. It is an amazing fighting game and is a lot of fun in a room full of friends.
If you want to play solo, in arcade mode, survival, time challenge, finish the story mode (which is meh, imo, but is still an option), buy this game. It's a great fighting game and will teach you everything you need to know about it, and some of its training transfers well into other fighting games.
If you want to play online with strangers, it's still a fine purchase. The player base isn't huge, but I have never had troubles finding a few different opponents per play session. Plus, once again, you still can play arcade while you're searching, so you won't get bored.
If, however, you want to play online with your friends. Then this is a tough sell. You need to decide for yourself if the chore of trying to find each other is worth it. Personally, I still play with friends online occasionally. But every time before playing we're like "Ugh... Do we really want to play DoA THIS much?".
Oh, and when I say "buy it", I do mean "buy it", because free to play version is just not worth the space. It's basically just there as a demo and I simply can't recommend it. The full game though, in my opinion, is worth it even at full price, but definitely at a discount.
Most importantly, please, PLEASE, don't disregard this game just because it has sexy women and men in skimpy clothes. Yes, it is part of this game, but first of all - it's nothing to be ashamed of, as sexual attractiveness is a natural part of this world. Secondly, there are plenty of costumes that cover skin. And last, but not least - I'll say once more that there is a great fighting game behind all the skimpiness, and it would just be a shame to miss it simply because of its looks.

Forget all you know about statistics - XCOM is the game that will teach you that 30% to hit is as good as zero, and will get your entire squad killed somehow or another.  10/10 would get screwed over by Chryssalids again.
Seriously, though, this is a good game.  Sometimes frustrating, yes, and depending on what difficulty you set it at, you probably deserve feeling like you're gonna get screwed no matter what you do.  And there are a few flaws and bugs here and there that you'll run into; sometimes the grenade aiming mechanism is annoyingly sensitive, and on a few occasions enemies might inexplicably bug and warp to another position on the map.  But overall, this is a great turn-based tactical game that really captures the "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ aliens!" panic and the struggle to keep up against an overwhelmingly superior force - at least until you max out your research and get a few good soldiers trained up.  And if you're not a savescummer, it'll make it hurt that much more when your colonel misses a 95% shot and gets wrecked.
One last thing:  don't do Ironman Mode without taking proper precautions.  Sometimes the save files get corrupted, and you lose days of hard effort and badass warriors you trained up from green rookies.

Quake III is a classic game. It's simplified the weapon roster from previous Quake games, and refined movement systems and map design, and it was an instant hit. Every weapon had its advantages and disadvantages, and it was easy enough to pick up and play without ruining the competitive scene too.
Quake Live, when it first came out in 2009, basically took that and re-tweaked some of the damage output for the meta, changed the UI, and stuck the Quake Live logo in every level. The original Free-2-Play model worked well for it; several dozen maps were available for free, and anyone can play them, but for $4 a month, players can access nearly four times as many maps, have access to several game modes, and can have set up clan systems.
A few things had changed before the big jump. Bethesda had bought Id in that time, and updates to Quake Live were on the weird side. The game originally was an in-browser game, and it had then been migrated to Steam, but still retaining the web UI on the main menu. Players could also join premium servers and play alongside pro players, but they couldn't host it themselves.
On the 27th of October 2015, Bethesda announced that the game had now completely migrated to Steam. The UI is much better, the game now uses Steam profiles directly, and has Valve Anti-Cheat incorporated. They also got rid of the premium model, so now everyone can do everything in the game. And finally, Steamworks integration now allows 16 years of map making history to be shared and developed easily across the community.
Everyone is peeved though that Bethesda never mentioned anywhere that the game would now not be a Free-2-Play game. It now costs $10 to those who had never played it before. Yes, that is a bit of shoddy business practice, but it doesn't ruin the game in any way. In fact, I think it improves it. Rather than paying $4 a month, the $10 up front gets you full access to all the content all the time. And there's definitely more than 2 and a half months worth of content up for grabs. There's nearly 150 maps in deathmatch alone, and Steam Workshop support keeps upping that number with quality and interesting maps.
The rest of this review is more an evaluation of the game itself.
Quake Live has about 15 weapons on offer, and all of them have their strengths and weaknesses. Like any classic Id game, they're designed to be superior in different map scenarios, and maps are designed in a way to showcase all of them. My favourites are the plasma gun which fires slower moving huge balls of plasma, dishing up massive damage per hit, but it's tricky damaging people from a distance. The rocket launcher is a classic weapon with its large-ish splash radius, and the ability to do rocket jumps everywhere.
Players also move around very quickly, which encourages skillful aiming and finesse with timing weapon shots. There's a lot of emphasis on moving fast and trying to outsmart your opponent while landing hits of your own. Rocket jumps are easy to execute, and provide a risky outtage to any fight, encouraging learning map layouts, hotzones, and power-up locations.
And it all comes together really nicely. Fight for a bit, try to restock on supplies, and then find another fight. Dying is a quick second break until you get thrown back in. Every game mode revolves around this simple draw the enemy concept. Maps aren't huge, so it's never difficult to find some action.
Quake III is a bit of an old game, so the visuals are a little here and there. Particle and lighting effects are still quite well done, and new textures on maps keep a good amount of visual variety. The model detail is a little lacking in some cases, but the overall level of visual fidelity is quite low, which means you can run this game on almost any computer you own.
Sound design is also a bit here and there. The music shows its age a little bit, and isn't available on every map, which leaves a bit of an awkward silence. Weapons make some pretty characteristic sound effects though, and it's always satisfying to hear that little blip sound every time you deal damage to an enemy. The new main menu music they added in the recent update sounds exactly like the menu music from Doom 3 BFG, and it just seems out of place, especially since all demonic imagery from Quake 3 was removed.
Don't be deterred if you see negative reviews or posts about this game though. It runs flawlessly on any hardware from the past ten years, it's fun, fast, frantic, and is ridiculously easy for both new and pro players to play together. With a bazillion maps and game modes on offer, a great community, and lots more free updates coming along, Quake Live is an excellent game that everyone should try out, even if you're not a big FPS fan.
Just buy it.

Battlefleet Gothic: Armada. First things first, do I recommend it? Wholeheartedly yes!
Now that's out of the way, on to my thoughts about this game. I will be say that I've decided to base my review on the feel and atmosphere of this game, it's faithfulness to the feel of the Warhammer 40k universe, especially with an eye to past 40k games. I won't be reviewing it on the gameplay in depth simply because I do not play enough RTSes to feel qualified to make an assessment either way.
Is this game faithful to the 40k universe? Very much so I feel. One of the most striking things personally was listening to the soundtrack, the background music, the dialogue, and finding a welcome familiarity about it. It's as if the people in charge of the music at Tindalos Interactive had sat down to listen to all of Dawn of War II's music and dialogue. Some of those ship captains sound like they could be voiced by the Lord General in DoW2: Retribution. The music, with long mournful organ notes and soaring choral performances, is eerily reminiscent of DoW2: Retribution too. This helps the game feel a strong connection with previous 40k titles from Relic.
Set against the backdrop of the 12th Black Crusade, the story thrusts you into a pivotal role in fighting against the various enemies of mankind. The weight of expectations lends a tension to each mission, even though mission types are picked from a standardised set. Despite that you do feel a sense of progression and each battle feels unique. The levelling up of ships and your admiral, and the amount of combinations for ship builds, gives you that additional sense of progression, and the motivation to want to win every single battle. Add in epic clashes involving ships of tremendous infamy such as the Terminus Est, and you feel a firm sense that you're right at the heart of the 12th Black Crusade.
I personally also love the difficulty scaling. I think it's perfect. Easy is just about right for casual players like me, normal is challenging, and hard and heroic are perfect for those who're bored easily if they're not juggling 9 chainsaws on fire. Something for everyone, just the way inclusive gaming should be.
Conclusion: for any 40k fan who's been bemoaning the lack of any serious 40k titles over the last few years, this is the answer to your prayers to the God-Emperor/Ruinous Powers/Gork & Mork/Greater Good or whoever it is you pray to... heretic. I would recommend it even at its full price, and I hope that more content is to come. The foundations are there for this to be the big spiritual successor to DoW2, and I hope Tindalos Interactive seizes that opportunity with both hands!

This game has huge potential - I don't recommend never buying it, but I wish I had waited to buy it, and I recommend you hold off on buying until the game-breaking issues are fixed (assuming they will be).
Most of the users recommending this game excused its flaws by pointing out the fact that it's in early access. While this is true, there is a difference between "buggy and needs work" and "unplayable". This game unfortunately falls under the latter category.
Single Player mode works beautifully with very few issues, but the moment you go into PvE or PvP:
There are devestating issues with de-syncing of both players and creatures. This renders combat nearly impossible, especially in PvP - it's pretty difficult to hit a target that's teleporting around while you're teleporting as well. The combat in this game is simply not viable. Creatures that are meant to aggro you don't necessarily. They will sometimes stand there, not realizing they're being stabbed to death. When they do aggro, they will teleport around (sometimes into the air if they are a creature that has jumping capabilities), and your hits will miss the majority of the time unless you use ranged weapons. Harvesting their corpses is even worse. They will appear to be in one location on your screen but due to the de-syncing could be anywhere, which means when you're trying to harvest you have to swing blindly hoping you'll hit the creature, wherever it may be. Because of this, the bigger creatures are much easier to harvest (you're more likely to hit them) while the small creatures like rabbits and sheep are usually impossible.
Combat against players is worse. You can stand point blank in front of someone and both swing punches or swords repeatedly (on a pvp/Knight server) and take/deal zero damage.
Creatures and other players are no threat currently.
I haven't even attempted taming yet, so I don't have any input on that.
Gathering from resources (trees, rocks, plants) can be problematic as well. You gather very slowly, perhaps obtaining 1 item every 5 to 10 hits, whereas in single player, each hit gives resources.
All of these problems do improve when you move away from the spawn points and towns, but they're still very much there.
I would call the game nearly unplayable in its current state, unfortunately. I had high hopes for this, as someone who thoroughly enjoyed Ark Survival. These issues need to be fixed.
Other cons:
- forced 3rd person mode - this is a matter of personal preference. I greatly prefer first person view in games like this. The scenery is so beautiful, but it is cheapened by the awkward, somewhat jerky, odd animations. I feel that the character models don't fit in completely with the style and look of the terrain so it looks a bit strange and displaced. The characters move somewhat stiffly and I'd very much enjoy a good view of everything in front of me instead of always seeing my character off to the side. Camera angles also seem a bit weird.
- Some of the sound effects (I played as a human female) are just atrocious. The 'dehydrated' sound effect is a constant spamming of a horrendous groan. When hungry, your stomach rumbles continuously. I think the sound effects need to be less spammy and some of them just need to be completely redone.
- You can drink water from anywhere, including the sea, with no repurcussions. This was the case in Ark as well. This isn't a huge deal, but it really cheapens the "survival" aspect when you can drink salt water for hydration or get your hydration instantly filled from rainfall...why not introduce some sort of water filtering system & rain barrels?
- I had heard that the map for this game is huge - bigger than Ark's. I don't know whether that was an official statement or not, but regardless, it's not true. I was greatly disappointed when I realized that. The map is around the same size as the maps in Ark, if not smaller. It's still an okay size, but when you have a lot of people playing, land-grabbing with pillars/foundations, and building huge houses and castles, you run out of room quick (and the game lags much much more). On PvE, there's no room to build. Already. I had to go far from town to even find a place to set down my campfire.
On a more positive note:
- The game is beautiful; exploration is marvelous!
- Building is quite good. It works similarly to Ark and has similar issues with placement - sometimes it's a struggle to put a ceiling in, for example, and you have to keep moving around to get it to snap. But overall, the buildings look nice, and it's very enjoyable
I haven't given up on this game. Almost all of the issues with it can be fixed. I hope that they are fixed sooner than later. I would hate to see this game turn out to be like Conan Exiles.
If you want to play this game single player only, I'd say go ahead and get it now!
**EDIT/UPDATE:
According to several comments (I have not tried myself), servers with very small player bases also work fine. It seems that official or private servers with moderate to large player bases cannot handle the load. This needs to be addressed and hopefully remedied!
End of Update**
If you want to do PvE or PvP, just hold off for now. Wait and see what the Devs do about all of these problems. I can't recommend the game to anyone hoping to PvE or PvP right now. I truly hope that changes soon.

If every gaming news source and their dog are to be believed, Braid is a flawless masterpiece of a puzzle platformer that shows exactly what indie game developers should all strive to create. I don’t know of any other game I have ever gone into with such high expectations with equally high cynicism.
While I think it’s a beautiful work of art, I don’t think Braid can live up to the enshrinement the community generally places it in. The platforming is tight and precise, the time manipulation mechanics are really well designed, the art is undeniably some of the best gaming has to offer and the writing really connected with me at times in a way not many games ever could. In the end though, it is just another indie puzzle platformer. It’s a majestically fantastic puzzle platformer with the polish and care you don’t often see many designers put into games, but it’s still an indie puzzle platformer.
I think Braid is wonderful, and if you’re into the genre this is a great piece to add to your collection. However, this awe inspiring masterpiece that everyone describes seems to be more of a case of reviews following a hype train rather than the product actually being perfect.

Gameplay:
Incredibly fluid and fun parkour system. Assassin's Creed + Mirror's Edge + Zombies = Dying Light
Graphics:
They hold up really well. I think they look very nice (although, there are slight lag spikes every once in a while).
Story:
Completely non-exsistent. Boring characters, boring plot-lines, just all boring. If I reviewed Dying Light just on story, it would be a 0/10.
Extra Stuff:
There is a weapon durability system in the same way as Dead Island, but same as Dead Island, there are a lot of weapons pretty much everywhere. (In fact there is a skill you can get which means durability goes down slower).
Progression is pretty nice in this game. As you go through the game you get better loot and experience for 4 skill trees;
Survivor, Agility, Power & Legend, (+ Driver in The Following).
You really feel like you've worked for your sweet gear seeing as early game you can't even kill a fly.
If you want an action-packed parkour-em'-up zombie sandbox with a intricate story in the vain of Walking Dead, you won't find it here.
But if you just want an action-packed parkour-em'-up zombie sandbox, this will be a good way to kill some time.
*NOTE: I highly recommend you play online/with friends because singleplayer is... well, it isn't very good.*

Braid has lots of really innovative game design elements but, put together, I don't know if they work really well.
When I play a puzzle game, I like to be able to quickly iterate possible solutions and once I know how to solve it that's it, bring me the next puzzle. In Braid, you can't be really sure if your hypothesis is wrong or if it's just the timing in your jumps/movement. In games like Portal or Limbo, once you know how to solve the puzzle, executing the solution is pretty straightforward and even if you fail it doesn't feel that tedious.
In a traditional platformer like Mario, when you make a mistake you die or have to try the whole part again, but when you execute it right and you see the character gracefully "flow" from platform to platform it feels awesome, and you feel agency, and different people may have different play styles. The most skilled ones might quickly recover from what would've been a fatal mistake to a newbie.
In Braid, it feels like you have to move the character exactly in the way Blow intended, going back and forward in time until you get the timing exactly right(while the music tortures you by also playing back and forward).
Overall, it feels like playing chess, but there is only one sequence of moves that will make you win the match and you have to rewind every time you think you made a mistake, which may have been five or six moves ago. Oh, and each time you want to capture a piece you have to win a fencing match.
I think Jonathan Blow is a genius programmer and he really created something different and innovative, but I'm not sure if all the elements combined make for a game that's actually fun to play.

I have been thinking for a while whether this game should get a thumbs up or a thumbs down from me. In the end, I'm going with a reluctant thumbs up, though I'd recommend waiting for a sale.
NEO Scavenger is a post-apocalyptic roguelike survivalist game that is also often dubbed a hobo simulator. For good reason: you start the game waking up in a facility with nothing but a hospital gown, a wrist strap and a strange talisman. Once you start playing and get to look at your inventory screen, you will notice that you do not actually have any inventory space. This game does not give you an abstract bag to store your items in. You can carry whatever you carry around in your hand - if you want more, you will need to scavenge a cardboard box or a plastic shopping bag to carry your stuff in (the former you have to carry in your hand, the latter can be used as a backpack). If you are good enough at scavenging, you may eventually be able to find something better, such as a children's backpack - a legit travelling backpack is a luxury you'll have to search a lot for, and either way, even these backpacks will be extremely limiting, so you do have to carefully pick and choose what to carry with you. Eventually, you can get a much bigger inventory by finding an abandoned shopping cart or other similar vehicle you can lug your items around in, but that makes it harder to run away if you get into trouble (unless you ditch the cart and just run for your life).
Anyway, there are strict inventory constraints and you also have to deal with rapid wear and tear on your equipment - some shoddy stuff (hand-crafted weapons, sandals) might fall apart after just a short period of use. You also have to deal with finding food and water - and beyond that, you have to make sure the food is edible, the water is not contaminated, and beyond that, to find a same place to sleep, to find a pair of shoes (that don't give you blisters when you walk in them), and to survive all the encounters out there. All this makes for a very gritty and tough survivalist game and this is actually the strong point of NEO Scavenger. The 'feel' is really good and the challenges of this game are rather unique - not many games have you struggle for basic necessities like this one. Death is permanent - no reloads.
There are three major weak points, though, which you should be aware of. One of them would not be enough to spoil the game, but the three of them together do, or at least get close to doing so... it is up to you to decide if they are big enough red flags for you.
First: NEO Scavenger's survivalism is based around an extensive crafting system. You need to craft in order to ensure your water is not infected (drinking all the water you find makes things much harder, though it's actually possible to survive with the constant diarrhea and other illnesses you get from doing so if you are lucky enough), to light fires for warmth and cooking, to craft primitive weapons and more. The crafting system is quite cumbersome, though, which is a major problem when it is so necessary to use it. It is hard to get into at first, hard to understand all the different options you have, and the interface is a bit unwieldy in general.
Second: The developers originally started programming this game in Flash, which (according to their own admission, even) turned out to be a pretty bad idea, but they never rebuilt it in a more suitable environment. This means that the game has a few quirks and a few very nasty bugs. Saves seem to have a tendency to get corrupted every now and then, and while there is an autosave option, that introduces other problems in turn (I had my minimap data get wiped while autosave was on).
[Note: apparently some autosave bugs were just recently fixed a few days after writing this review. So there's that.]
Third: despite being a roguelike, this game lacks something most roguelikes have, which is extensive replayability. Unlike in most RLs, there is no leveling or character development - your guy doesn't get any stronger or weaker throughout the game (aside from illnesses/injuries and other temporary buffs/debuffs), so the progression in the game stems solely from you exploring newer areas and finding stronger enemies. There is also only one start (no races/classes, no different starting scenarios) so if you've completed the game once, you've seen it all... aside from any optional areas you might have missed the first time around. Further, quite a few of the challenges in the game don't even stem from poor scavenging strategy or combat - sometimes you just get a brief "choose your own adventure" segment where you have to click on various options and hope that you aren't instakilled. Common sense and caution can generally get you through these encounters, but still, this doesn't help replayability. Further, though it takes a while to learn how to survive early on, the game is not actually that hard later on once you're set and since it is easy to just run away from the majority of foes (plus there's little reason to fight them when you can't get XP or essential loot from them - you can get everything you need from just scavenging), you just need to learn what options to click (or not to click) in the choose-your-own-adventure segments and you know how to win.
Well, NEO Scavenger is a good hobo simulator, but not a very good roguelike. So I guess that whether you should buy the game depends on whether you're looking for the former or the latter. It's a fun little game with an interesting story (and you'll have some interesting stories of your own to tell on the forum after you play), but it just isn't something that will keep you occupied for hundreds of hours, replaying it again and again. Its hobo simulator aspect is good enough for me to barely justify a recommendation, however.

I love the 40k universe and this game presents is spectacularly. The art design nails the cartoonishly grim feel of the universe and the campaign presents it in a similar way as Dawn of War II (in all the right ways). The actual gameplay feels like a refined version of the naval battles from Rome total war, and the additional abilities and general number of ships you're commanding at any given time makes it generally more enjoyable and more of a tactical experience. The developers basically nailed the amount of persistence and customization to give the ships, both making you feel invested in upgrading ships and miserable when you make a mistake and let one of your prized battlecruisers go up in flames, while still maintaining some amount of balance for players who are just beginning the game. The factions are very assymmetric and this leads to some favored matchups depending on which mission is being played. While the basic cruiser clash is quite balanced, things like convoy missions are much easier with the Eldar than say the Imperium, due to differences in ship speed and strength. This is still being worked on by the developers and in a few patches I think it will be really quite good, but even as is, the slight imbalances act more as quirks to work your strategy around, rather than straight up flaws that make the game unenjoyable.
While there are complaints about the 2d layout of this space game, it does make sense from its tabletop origins and after several matches I stopped questioning why my mile-long flying-space-cathedral had a design that was somewhere between Admiral nelsons flagship and a roman ram ship. You will often hear people whining that there aren't more factions, do not take this as a foul cry against this game, but rather know that people love this universe deeply and want to see their favorite races in the game. However when they do come out with the (I hope) inevitable dlc that includes the Necrons, Tau, tyrannids, and other factions, I will be buying that without a second thought.
This game is fun. It's very niche and has a bit of a learning curve, but it is thoroughly and completely enjoyable to play and I'll give props to the developers for letting me ram space cathedrals into floating ork rustbuckets. Do them the favor and give them your money, they've earned it.

Beautifully calming. While the game isn't particularly engaging, it is definitely nice on the eyes, with several, all very cute creatures to play as. A few are gated by the purchase of other games by the same developers, but the games in question are all very great themselves, and more than worth the small price tag they have.
You can't directly communicate with anyone, only through emotes provided to you. At first, you only have a few, but you can unlock others through playing normally. The game encourages socialization and grouping together through obelisks, unique rocks that require a certain number, or type, of animals nearby. The obelisks provide you with puzzle pieces, which are used to unlock new animals, or a skin/emote for the animal you're currently using at the time. Puzzle pieces can also be found randomly lying around, if unfortunately, you can't find anyone to travel with. The world itself is quite large as far as I can tell, with four different "biomes", one for each season, as well as expansive underground caves.
I've enjoyed it so far. I'm sure once I've unlocked everything, the game will start to grow stale, but I doubt that will be any time soon, as there are a good number of animals and customization options for each. For $3, it is more than worth the price.

Braid was such an important Puzzle-Platformer of it's time. What looked like a fancy Super Mario Bros on the surface, turned out to have an immesurably deep story, with a multitude of real-world analogies.
The time-based mechanics were the first of their kind, and exciting in their variety. They called on you to really flex your brain, teaching you to think in brand new ways. Creating localised spots with slower time in one world, and another where the mere action of walking left or right makes time move backwards or forwards.
The protagonist, Tim, isn't your standard hero. He's facing regret, which you learn through the books left open at the start of each world. This regret pushes him forward to atone for his mistakes, while in search for the princess he lost long ago.
Braid is also a bit self-aware of it's foundations, with some subtle and not-so-subtle references to Super Mario Bros (goombas, princesses in another castle).
Like some of it's mechanics, this game is timeless. It won't age, because it stands up on its own.

The game makes it look like difficult in the beginning, but through the first few planets the player feels safe. Now after a few sectors the game becomes pretty hard, with enemy crew teleporting into your ship, or turning your ship on fire. The travelling between planets is incredibly well done, it let's you make decisions which are usually repeating but not in a boring way. Sometimes it's a kind of moral question, sometimes a trap, or a strategic decision.
The strategy part is really good, if you've ever played with any turn based game and you liked it then you'll like this one too. It lets you pause between actions, but idoing an action while paused doesn't consume any kind of action points. It's supposed to be a real time strategy, or at least when you are fighting with the enemy, but the game doesn't force you into thinking real time, and the pausing ability really makes the game more flexible.

Dead or Alive 5 Last Round, a spectacle brawler / fighting game. Game has that unique attention to martial arts (to an extent) and female beauty.
Dead or Alive game on PC, what else could you wish for? Console fanboys might be picky about this, but PC gamers of all ages will love this. I don't care if it's PS3 or PS4 port, on videos they look identical. I could care less about some missing stages (if any), because that's not relevant. There's no Online mode yet, but it's in the works. I'm not even going to bother saying anything about "Soft Engine", don't really care personally. Sure it would be great if you could rebind buttons and such, but that "could" be added later down the line, but in no shape or form makes it harder to play.
Game looks great in my opinion, with decent textures on basic, destructible environment and great detail on characters. Movement and attacks are responsive and easy to use even if you just mash the keys. It's even fine playing on keyboard, and not that challenging if you go through Training stages (and there are a lot of those, and then some).
You can play many different fighting modes; from 1 on 1 versus mode; two character tag teams; survival games where you try and defeat as many enemies as you can one by one or 8 on 8 elimination matches, and more. There's a story mode available, for those who like a bit of lore, it's basic with not much in terms of dialogue and voice acting depth, but it's enjoyable and funny.
Each game can be customized to your liking, where you can adjust AI, health amount, clock, outfits, stages, hair styles, character details and more. Apart from training tutorial mode, you can practice combos, do a combo challenge rounds, save / play match replays with additional tool that lets you capture the screen shot of exact frame and angle you want from the match (no doubt you will find many funny and disturbing images on community site already).
Like majority of fighting games, you have a decent roster of characters available, with their own strengths and weaknesses. Each have their own set of attacks and moves you can combo into devastating chains (there are a lot of combinations). Main aspect of the game for many people is their character, and to beat the life bar out of your opponents. But that's not all, it's equally important to have INAPPROPRIATE attire to the boot, so why not! You have  insane amount of costumes available for every character, and if you want more, there are always paid DLC's you can get to boost that wardrobe.
Game has decent audio soundtrack, that will keep you going for a while. I admit, game has some light mature element to it, as you tend to unlock more and more skimpier outfits, but nothing completely nude (no sensitive parts). So I don't advise to play this under the age limit, but who am I kidding, just make sure door is closed at least, so people don't get any wrong ideas walking by your room. Other than that, it's fun fighting game to waste some time, and not get completely bored in process, as your eyes will get plenty of "candy". Personally I enjoyed it (from a completely normal gaming standpoint) more than games like Mortal Kombat, Injustice or Super Street Fighter.
Enjoy.

This is my review of the Ardennes Assault DLC.
They could have at least added a few skins to the multiplayer with this release. Maybe even a few commanders. There are rangers, but there is no way to use them in the multiplayer. Obviously they will milk it and release them as a paid DLC.
The campaign itself feels unpolished. Some of the voice acting is really bad, which is very un-Relic. But then again some of the characters are really quite well acted (like the airborne Lieutenant), and also have quite a lot of character.
I'm also not a fan of the 1v1 type missions. I think the campaign does a much better job when it gives you "cinematic" sequences like those in the Soviet campaign. Especially when the gameplay in these missions just ends up in you chasing around enemy units with your death blob around the map. They are really really easy and even someone who has never played a CoH game could finish them on the hardest difficulty no problem.
You can also just charge your guys into the enemy base, kill the flak emplacements and steal them. Using this tactic you can finish any mission just AFK'ing since the flak will kill any infantry that spawns. and you can cap the entire map and wait for the points to tick down. Obviously they didn't play test the campaign enough.
Leave the 1v1 style gameplay to the skirmish mode. It just feels lazy coming from Relic, and really does feel like padding.
Overall it's quite overpriced for what it is. If it had Western Front Armies bundled in with it, and if you didn't already owned this it would be worth it then I think, otherwise maybe wait for a sale, or just skip it. I wish I had.

This is an "okay" port of DOA5 for the PC. Derived from the arcade version, which also runs on Windows, it can be seen as lacking visually compared to current generation consoles.
Graphics are OK nonetheless, equivalent to those of the PlayStation 3 version, but looking a bit nicer when rendered in 1080p and higher resolutions.
However I do believe that, as generally current gaming PCs are more powerful than even the current generation consoles, they can do better than that. This is quite a letdown, considering graphics are pretty much this franchise's main selling point.
Performance-wise, the game can run well on machines that do not meet the stated minimum requirements. I'm running it on an old Core 2 Quad Q9300 at stock clock (2.5 GHz) with a GeForce GTX 650 Ti, and it runs smoothly at constant 60 fps, in 1920x1080 resolution with FXAA and maximum shadow resolution.
For 1920x1080, 1 GB of VRAM minimum is a must, and looking at the CPU usage behavior (Core #0 is stuck at 100% at all times while playing, while other cores see a much lower usage, around 20-30%) I'd say it might run well on a 2.66 GHz Core 2 Duo.
That Core #0 stays stuck at 100% shows signs of an unoptimized program though. It does the same on a more powerful machine I run the game on (a Core i5 3570K at 4.6 GHz). The dropping of the "yawaraka engine" (which adds realism to graphics on current-gen consoles) might have something to do with this; just speculation on my part though.
The game currently lacks an online play mode, which is set to be released in a patch three months from the game's release date. While I'm not much of an online fighter, this may turn down many players. Those who like to play online might want to wait until then. Other play modes are identical to the PlayStation 3 version, except that the photo viewer is gone - the game uses Steam's built-in screenshot viewer for the photo viewer feature. I think that's good though.
In-game, it plays much like its PlayStation 3 counterpart. Effective use of holds is key, and the timing of commands may take a good while to master. Gameplay flows quite OK but I prefer the likes of Tekken and Soul Calibur when it comes to 3D fighter gameplay - a matter of personal preference, though. Playing with a PC keyboard could be somewhat iffy, however doable. I'd recommend using a XInput-compatible gamepad, those seem to work the best.
To wrap it up:
console gaming coming to the PC, good fighting action, and the franchise's traditional nice ladies ;-)
Apparently rushed port, downgraded graphics, sub-optimal performance, no online (for now)
: 6/10. This port is passable, but could be much better. I hope the devs get the hang of how the PC ecosystem works and bring us better quality ports in the future. Recommended - not for everyone though, but for those who like the franchise and/or want more games coming from console to PC. Those who have a current-gen console and the respective version of the game may want to stick to it though.

Stick to or go and get CoH 1 and download the multitudes of amazing mods available for it. Three that spring to mind are the Eastern Front mod, Blitzkrieg Mod, and Modern Combat. A zombie mod is on its way as well. (Looks f&%king fantastic!)
- Coming in at the #2 fault is the "Politically unbiased" campaign. I won't even speak of it, look it up on Youtube and you'll see what I mean.
- Relic's servers (at least for me) are about as reliable and problem-free as a retiree's erection.

Dawn of War 1 is an amazing game, plain and simple
Take Starcraft 1, but remember how annoying it is to keep re-building one or two lost units so that you have a full army? Well this game solves that. You build squads of soldiers (save a few special units and vehicles) and then if you lose one or two, you can rebuild. Many vehicles and squads have weapon choices, allowing squads to be vehicle/building focused, infantry focused, heavy infantry focused, or anti-moral focused.
You might be thinking, "What's moral?" well moral is everything in Warhammer dawn of war 1. If your troops are getting slammed by artillery or are getting ripped apart or constantly on the front lines, they'll lose moral, which makes them underperform significantly if their moral fully breaks. You can focus on breaking enemy moral (if the troops aren't vehicles) and they will still lose even if your units are a little worse. This system, in combination with other moral restoring abilities makes army clashes much more intense than many army v army battle games.
Some folks may be wondering about differences in this game versus other RTS's. One, base building is a thing. You have a main base but also other buildings to build a lot of your units and to get access to upgrades (think of a barracks versus an armory). There are defences you can erect to assist in battle, but they are limited (8 or so powerful turrets). The game also forces a lot of movement around the battlefield since there isn't a good way to turtle. If you turtle, not only do capture points (which you need) degrade over time (long long term) but also your enemy now has those points and way more requisition to put to buying units. So movement of armies, quickly around the battlefield is useful. That combined with the wide array of unit types, you get a lot of ways you can try to beat an opponent. Do you try to sneak past their defences and raid their base while they slowly try to stop you? Do you pummel their defences with wave after wave until they break?  Do you build up a perfectly tuned army that is balanced against what you will fight perfectly and crush? Or will you hassle them with artillery until they are forced to fight you on your terms?
All options in Warhammer 40k dawn of war 1.

Company of Heroes 2 focuses on events of the infamous Eastern Front during World War 2. Players get to play as Soviet troops from the start of Operation Barbarossa in June 1941 and finishing at final operation of capturing Reichstag during Berlin Offensive in April-May 1945. Campaign is focused on one of the officers that atrocities committed by Red Army have turned anti-war. That's where the problem starts.
Many players say that CoH 2 is Anti-Russian because it mainly focuses on what war crimes Soviets committed, while German crimes are just mentioned. Although many things shown in the game are true (such as Soviets killing Polish Resistance Fighters), some were reported as evil but in fact were necessary to win the war.
But let's focus back on the game. Game's graphics are very good, and the game is very realistic. Morale of your troops is an important factor (if it's too low they run away), which is affected by the training quality of your troops (such as Soviet Recruits won't take as much as for example Soviet Guard Army Troops) and the things going on around them. Game has plenty of detail there and there.
To conclude:
Positives
+ Good graphics
+ Very good realism
+ Units carefully replicated
+ Eastern Front is shown as it was
Negatives
- Some arguments of the main character are badly explained and thought of
Score: 8/10

Having bought the original Metro 2033 a few years back, I have to say that I'm very impressed with the improvements 4A has made. There really are too many improvements to list off here, but this was definitely a good purchase in my opinion. I'm using the MSI GTX 970 4GB. When I first set up the graphics options, I was getting some terrible stuttering. As it turns out, I had the "in game" SR settings maxed out COMBINED with my GPUs DSR ( Dynamic Super Resolution) seettings maxxed out as well. Basically, this game has the DSR option just as Nvidia GPUs have as well. MAKE SURE you're not using both at max settings (unless you have a monster mamba-jamba machine). I have trieed using the in game DSR options on with GPU options off, and reverse, and I dont seee one performing better than the other. But I havee to say, I love the DSR settings. With the DSR turned up, you really dont need any Anti Alliasing, and your screen resolution increases dramatically.
This is a great story and a great game made even better now. If you haven't read the book "Metro 2033", you're missing out. A lot of things in the game will make a lot more sense, and you'll find yourself unlocking more achievements if you try to "go by the book" in the game.

Took 3 arrows but won the fight...i don't take them out cause I figure it'll make the wound worse. Limped back to base. Fought off a dog on the way. Boil up some clean rags, notice that my wounds have stopped bleeding.♥♥♥♥♥♥this is going to hurt.
Takes out an arrow, bandages (wow, I'll survive this!)
Takes out another arrow, bandages (Damn right!)
Takes out third arrow, everything goes fine! I'm going to live! Arrow in 'hand,' move cursor to place arrow on ground, click, not enough room to place. Game decides "oops, gotta put this arrow somewhere, but there's no room on the ground..."
Game inserts arrow back into my gushing chest, slicing the pulmonary, kills me instantly.
Fucing...hell....
All because the game designers ♥♥♥♥ed up the item movement system. (FIX THIS!!!)
So yeah.
Otherwise, it's a pretty fun game, just lacks on content. I know, shocking...but I believe this. The big problem is how do you survive? Once you figure this out...not much left to do. The main storyline is pretty short all things considered (and not really deep or logical when you really try to make sense of it) and there's not terribly many 'random'/'lesser' encounters to keep you busy along the way. None of the guys that walks around ever talks to you, they just try to kill you or run away.
Overall the impression you are left with is that you are fighting a wave of death. This is really cool. But shallow after about 5 hours because everything is so in depth that you are left wondering, "why isn't the human side of things as complex?"
There should be people who are traders. There should be non-combat entities walking around on the map, trying to accomplish their own goals (secure a campsite like you...hunt deer or creatures for their faction). Desperates who are sort of lost, running away that you can interact with. You should be able to form a band of followers, be able to discuss their roles in your little band of survivors and start relationships etc... I feel like other games already do this but that people developing a game pick one main theme to go after then stop, instead of diversifying and branching out and growing.
At the moment there are some 'encounters' that happen randomly when you enter a square...and these are great!...but there aren't enough. This is sort of like a 'first step' towards humanizing the game.
There should be an alliance 'system,' so that if a guy with the 'trapper' skill settles down 20 hexes from you and makes that his base, you can go approach him, offer to trade, and develop a relationship. Now you can approach more freely etc...
Here's another idea: Instead of adding human-centric 'content' in the form of side quests and dialogue trees, try and think of some ways you can mix it up. Be innovative. If you can add something that completely shocks people because they don't expect it from a video game, they'll love you forever and your game will be remembered.
What I think is funny is that the devs tried to hook a story onto the game without any of the above 'humanization'. You get a thrill from uncovering the story but the SECOND you know what happens, you stop caring. The devs should hire some literacy major who just graduated and is working at BK (this would cost next to nothing) to take a look at their game and write some story in for them. Might even do it for free for the resume.
So my advice:
1) Add some more 'systems' (like the allegience, like seriously expanded dialogue, like other NOT-PLAYER CENTERED characters etc.). Every system you add on top of what you've got will expand the scope, audience, and profit of the game geometrically.
2) Hire someone who knows how to write a story and populate a world with characters. If you're going to end the story like you did (and hint at a sequel like you did), you need to have a reason for us to follow the guy we play as. For the audience to care, you need a good characterization and some intriguing humanization. Try engendering endearment with non-life threatening consequences (severing of relationships, loss of 'honor' or something else your guy values).
3) Don't give up. You've made something really great here, but it seems like you've stopped. Don't do that.
4) With every step you take, ask if someone has done it before. If you can, try to make your solution unique.

Wow. I'm glad to say that the tone of the game is very true to the dark 40k universe, and in particular the well documented struggle in the Gothic Sector. The portaits, voices and attitudes of the characters are some of the best I've seen for a 40k game.
The single player campaign appears well balanced, missions are hard and mistakes are punished. Upgrading and deploying ships is a joy, which adds an RPG element to the game. You'll find yourself caring about ships under your command in the interesting and varied battles. Ships can be customised for particular roles as well.
Combat itself is a lot of fun. After the first few struggles you'll begin to get the hang of handling the fleet. Having a genuine tactic appears to pay off, which is nice. Some missions may seem impossible until you hit on the correct tactic.
Graphically the game is beautiful. You don't quite get the sense that the ships are as big as they are however. Probably because you'll be zoomed out a wee bit most of the time.
If you like strategy games or 40k, this is a must.

I REALLY wanted to like this game, but ultimately really didn't.
From the start, I love the idea.  I love everything 40k and I'm pretty into naval simulators and anything ship-to-ship combat related.  For me this was a win-win.
I played the game through the beta for awhile and enjoyed myself briefly, but in my opinion that's about most people are going to get from it.  It looks good initially, but as you progress and fleet sizes grow (both in single player and multiplayer) you start to realize how much of a mess it is.
As far as the "good" parts of the game go, the game looks good and it more or less captures the feel and flavor of 40k.  I do feel like I'm part of that universe playing and the ships all do their part to draw you in.  In the beginning of the game, when you're playing smaller ships and smaller fleet sizes, you really do get the feeling that you're engaging in naval/space combat.  Your ships trade broadsides with the enemies, you line up torpedo salvos, boarding actions etc...it all feels really good.
As you progress in the game, however, it becomes less and less fun.  You start to equip your ships with active abilities and upgrades and these essentially take over the entire game.  Battle becomes less and less about positioning, maneuvering and trading gunfire, and more and more about spamming and trying to land/avoid abilities.  The main offenders here, of course, are "bombs" that you teleport into space and which blow up after a brief timer.  The blast radius for these bombs is large and do enormous damage, lock your ships in place via stasis or disable all ships' shields in the AoE.  These abilities can be devastating when they land and I'm not exaggerating at ALL when I say they're spammed.  This becomes painfully clear later on against the AI in the single player campaign where you will encounter (upon initial contact with the enemy) a giant minefield of bombs that your enemy instantly teleports against you and which you often have literally no chance to avoid.  The games regularly end up being decided in these brief moments of bomb trading/avoiding and it ends up looking and feeling really silly.
Additionally, the game is VERY heavily tilted towards RNG.  A "crit" in this game usually disables a vital ship system and it's basic dice-rolling that determines whether or not it happens.  It's not a system where after a certain amount of damage your engines or generator will be destroyed - it's almost completely random.  There will be games where you basically win right off the start because the first torpedo you land destroys the enemy ships shield generator, or games you lose from the start because a max range boarding cannon (the orks shoot dudes into your ship out of a cannon...) disables your engines on a lucky first shot.  These instances aren't particularly fun when they go in your favor (which they often do) but they're beyond frustrating when they happen to you.
My final complaint, and probably one of the biggest, is how bad the mission design is in the game.  While it's usually nice to have a wide variety of missions, it's far more important to make sure that these missions are "fun".  Certain missions, unfortunately, are so lopsided for certain races that the outcome is almost pre-determined.  The newest mission type, "Planetary Assault" has your fleet (if you're the attacker) attempting to navigate towards randomly spawning objectives (within a specific time limit) to bombard points on the planet.  To give you an idea on how much competent thought went into designing this game mode, imagine how fun it is to be required to reach map objectives when they regularly spawn so far away that you could never reach them in time even under ideal circumstances where you're not even fighting anyone.  I've found the most reliable way to win this mission is to ignore the formal objectives in single-player and try to destroy all of the enemy's ships instead (which still awards victory). Actually achieving the stated objectives is a random roll of the dice entirely dependant on where they spawn.  It's THAT bad right now.
To summarize, I want to say that I don't hate this game.  I think there are some neat ideas behind it and it could have been better had the devs focused on a more slow and deliberate style of game awhile back, but for whatever reason they opted for a clunky, confusing and overly luck-based mess.

TL;DR - Great game for those who would appreciate a fairly realistic, though basic racing sim. This is not for somebody looking for an arcade racer, "car porn", amazing graphics, or any kind of satisfying progression like a career mode. The racing experience is all that you get, and for some people that will be more than enough. If this is what you want, the price is incredible value (I paid $3.99).
I grew up playing a lot of console games, including racers like Gran Turismo 1 and 2 (both of which I absolutely love). Nowadays my limited free time has made me more of a casual gamer, but I still get the intense craving to play a good racing game once in awhile. For that purpose, this game is perfect.
First off, this game is not nearly as "fun" as something like Gran Turismo, nor will it satisfy any craving for "car porn". In GT, a lot of the fun is in the window shopping and building up your garage with your dream cars. On the plus side though, for a casual gamer, Race 07 doesn't require you to spend any time painfully working yourself up to the nice, fast, expensive cars. Nor does it require you to spend time earning licenses in order to drive in the more difficult races. This game allows you to satisfy your racing craving right away, with fairly realistic physics and great, challenging tracks. You don't even need to tweak your car's setup to become competitive, though I'm sure it would help if you knew what you were doing. As a partial result of this quick satisfaction though, there is no real "progression" in this game. What you get in race 1 is basically what you will get in race 150. For some people, the racing experience will be enough. For others looking for something more typically "fun" or amazing graphics, you might want to find another racer.
You will definitely want at least a 360 controller for this game, though if you play on the "pro" settings with driver aids turned off (ABS, traction/stability control, etc), I imagine a wheel/pedal setup would be much better. Keyboard controls would be a nightmare in this game. This is definitely not an arcade-style racer. If you miss your braking point, you're off the track. If you come on the gas too quickly, you may spin out. If you miss an apex and get off the racing line, there's a good chance you will be passed. If you decide to drive recklessly, chances are you'll end up with a DNF or something like a damaged suspension that will constantly pull the car to one side. That said, there are "novice" and "semi-pro" settings that are much more forgiving to those, like myself, who appreciate the racing sim experience but don't have the skills (or the time to build those skills) to handle a powerful race car with no driving aids.

So lets start by making a decent review of a game that could have had everything to be a great game and instead is a disgrace of a Space RTS that offends even the most casual of player's eyes and brains.
I am a hardcore fan of the War40K series, i used to play the tabletop, bought the few games that came out ( yes even turds like this one) and i can proudly say i have almost every book that the Black Library brought out to date.
Does this make me a Pro Reviewer or some authority in what comes to appreciation of games? No. But i do have an extensive background in IT ranging from programming and having been involved in some titles to currently being a sort of Specialist for companies with problems.. yes i identify and sort out problems in exchange for money. ( yes im a capitalist pig and i enjoy every second of it )
So without more preamble my opinion on this game...
... its CRAP.
The UE4 engine is a beautifull engine, only that Tindalos is a very ugly dev team, dont get me wrong the game in itself is interesting in some aspects, small details like ship textures and animations are well made, the only problem is that the maps are rubbish, and by saying they are rubbish i mean imagine yourself a A4 piece of paper with some colourfull background imprinted on it, then smack a white gride accross that lovely piece of paper and start placing figurines of ships moving in a 2D environment, yep you got it, thats BFG Armada for you, repeated every single mission, every map is more or less the same, recycled with some objects to make it look diferent but very much the same with the same elements and the same background, in other words, this dev team hasn't put an ounce of imagination and effort to make the game in itself appealing and pleasing to the eye.
The game modes are pretty much the same you can expect from the maps, you are either a defender or attacker and face Orks, Elder, Chaos, seditious forces and have besides of the fact of choice which force you want to take on to keep the campaign rolling in your favour not much else to help you with.
Bear in mind that the campaign was balanced around the awfull extended Beta phase Multiplayer bringing all the unbalance, bugs, quirks and issues along with it.
As game modes you have,
- Assassination - which works pretty ok
- Convoy - God help you if you face Eldar or Orks whatever position you are
- Siege - Meh...
- Cruiser clash - smack figurines against figurines against one another over the A4 paper and start roling dice
- Retrieve data - God help you again...
Probably theres one mode im forgetting but then again its nothing you are missing out on since the game revolves around the rinse and repeat mechanism i explained above.
The races, well fellow Imperial loyalists , you dream of bringing the Emperor's light to the galaxy? Crush Chaos and the Xenos assailing the imperium with your mighty fleets?
Think again, while the Emperium is the jack of all trades its also the most difficult race to achieve anything with, the Imperials lack speed, range, adequate tools and get beat by amout everything else in the game, yes even in the campaign, remember this game was balanced around multiplayer.
Chaos - Long range, favours of the dark gods, crush Imperium die to everyone else. ( and its also a load of rubbish the way they were implemented lorewise, Table Top they make sense, but book wise, well its an offence )
Orks - WAAAAAGH!!! ... errr no. You do have tractor beams, can boost your ships in a similar way that the eldar do and are deadly are close range. The issue is getting in range with them, once you get to grips on a ship you can pretty much anihilate it but then again not all of us want to play the same thing over and over again.. or play Orks for that matter, Orks remain the only race where i believe people with brains can actually succeed in MP, which in itself is good and ultimately sad at the same moment. If you like lotsa guns and a funky gameplay style of grabbing people, ramming and shooting then Orks are your race.
Eldar - the swiss knife of MP and the bane of Tindalos, or a bucket of idiocy on display. Eldar are like a sniper riding a motorbike zapping you from range and peeling away before you can do anything, its one of the races that needed a profound balance work but never got to because Tindalos cant keep deadlines and sorta rushed eldar out .
These guys are the long range of long range fighters in the game and no one can catch them except for a good ork player with brains and even then its not a garanteed win for the Ork while for the Eldar player its more or less of a FU and IWIN in 90% of the fights kinda sign.
I have played the Multiplayer, while the Imperium revolves around spamming Nova canons and doing not much else and every other race doing what i described above the game doesnt bring anything else new, you pick a race, win renown, build up your ships and get splattered with 300 points game modes where you cant bring anything meaningfull to the table.. or get into 600 gp games and get anihilated by people with already countless hours and every excel spreadsheet available just to get a garanteed win.
Also a word of caution, if you think someone is cheating, it probably is, other than finding the odd 6 battleship player ( which i encountered quite a few times ) , there is the player using one Battlecruiser that somehow just does not die to anything, or the player with perma invis ships, yes there is alot of polish work to be done by Tindalos.
The game is,
-Prone to freeze and ensures you a reboot
-Prone to crash out of nowhere
-Prone to consume insane ammounts of resources over nothing ( and i have 2 good rigs )
- Filled with bugs.
There is one good point about this game and its the fact you can use Renown to equip your ships and customise them, only you cant always use them when you need and just because you have a good strat rolling unless you use the flavour of the month race you cant do jack.
Another point, the descriptions for the guns, modules, ships and about everything are an aberration, so be prepared to go trough countless spread sheets and grow a Korean accent.
This game is not about fleet fights also, its about micro management where who clicks the fastest wins, forget the Cogitator mode , you want to win? Get yourself some Korean finger enhancements and start clicking away.
Conclusion:
I am of the option that games should catter to everyone, to some more then others naturally but they should grant this feeling of joy and satisfaction, provide you immersion in a alternative world where you can have fun and forget your wife and worries for a good couple of hours. Battlefleet Gothic fails at providing fun, its buggy, its unfinished, its unbalanced in all aspects and lacks the depth and respect that a Warhammer 40K title should have.
Tindalos proved to me at least that they are not up to the task of programming games, perhaps a calculator or a rudimentary solitaire game in Pascal or qBasic but not something of this dimension.
Remember this launch was delayed to iron out bugs and bring out balance, instead it came out with all the old problems and some more attached.
If you are a hardcore 40K fan then this game might appeal to you for the sake of having another WAR40k title in your library, if not spare yourself the money and the trouble and keep away from every game Tindalos develops.
PS. Why does Games Workshop grant licenses to such midgets that cant even hammer a nail on a wall without breaking the house is a question that bogles even the mightiest of minds on this planet, but alas, perhaps we can see a gem like DoWII somewhere in the future.

The game makes it look like difficult in the beginning, but through the first few planets the player feels safe. Now after a few sectors the game becomes pretty hard, with enemy crew teleporting into your ship, or turning your ship on fire. The travelling between planets is incredibly well done, it let's you make decisions which are usually repeating but not in a boring way. Sometimes it's a kind of moral question, sometimes a trap, or a strategic decision.
The strategy part is really good, if you've ever played with any turn based game and you liked it then you'll like this one too. It lets you pause between actions, but idoing an action while paused doesn't consume any kind of action points. It's supposed to be a real time strategy, or at least when you are fighting with the enemy, but the game doesn't force you into thinking real time, and the pausing ability really makes the game more flexible.
Still a great game , especially considering its 7 years old. Would recommend :)

A game like no other, Braid impresses its players with charming graphics, lovely musical scores and unique gameplay mechanics. However, the star of the show is a fascinating take on game design. In order to proceed through this platforming game, you will have to manipulate the flow of time and space, often both at the same time. The puzzles and sceneries of Braid are unique, often prompting the gamer himself to question his role as a participant in game's rich lore. Some of the challenges are supposed to be mind-bending, and can’t be solved by usual reflexive process of a common gamer. In certain cases, it seems like the authors want you to go online and seek for solutions, counting that as a part of experience the Braid delivers. You will be amazed many times by wit and originality of this game.
The way Braid's story is told is equally original. Like a reflection in the muddled window, the game doesn't intend to deliver a straightforward tale with beginning and the end. Through a very loveable interpretation of Super Mario mythos, the authors actually build their narrative around the main character's mental states and how he responds to the impulses from the "outside". The plot-twist comes when these are countered with the actions and beliefs of other characters, but we won't spoil the fun of discovering the ending.
It is a very brave experiment for storytelling in games, but fundamentally, it leads to certain issues. Sometimes, it seems that authors simply didn't want to be understood, their message lost in the confusing amount of quotations and touches of symbolism. But who knows, maybe it is another feature of Braid? Maybe this game wants to leave you puzzled, yet under impression for days to come after finishing it. What did this mean? Why did this happen? Were we asked a question by its authors? Or were we given an answer to questions we had?
A mighty addition to your library, indeed.

First of all, the bad points - the costume pack DLC is insanely priced (£90 for 2 packs), 2 stages have been left out from the PS4 version (and could be sold to us later, judging by the day one DLC) and there's no soft engine.
However, the graphics look (as far as I am concerned) far better than the PS4 version due to the higher resolution and using tools like SweetFX can help improve them further. The DLC is purely cosmetic, so far, so it is not necessary to purchase for the gaming experience. The game runs smoothly and the characters are all gorgeous (backgrounds not so much).
DOA 5 is easily the best fighting game on any platform, with a huge array of moves, 34 characters and multi-level, destructible stages. It has loads to unlock, great training modes to teach the commands and combos for each character. It has arcade mode, time attack, survival, team mode (7 on 7) as well as the story mode.
The story is ridiculous, but who cares? It's fun to play through.
I am hoping the soft engine gets added before the new DLC is added, with clothes that can tear - the port to PC has certainly left out a few features that should have been added and there's no excuse to not add them. If these are added with free DLC, then the game will be perfect.
As for the current DLC, I recommend not buying it because developers cannot come to believe it is ok to charge this amount for costumes - if the DLC was £3-£5 per pack, loads of people would buy it and they'd probably make a lot more. I believe the £40 and £50 price tags will simply encourage piracy.

Before I start this review, I have been playing Dead or Alive since the PS2 version.
Dead or Alive 5 Last Round PC Edition is an interesting beast. On the one hand it has the largest character roster in DOA history, and a huge amount of unlockables, but on the other the DLC is insane (not in a good way), and there is currently no online mode.

Windows 7 64 bit Professional
Intel Core i5 2400 at 3.1GHz
AMD Radeon R9 270X 2GB
16GB DDR3 RAM
(So nothing absolutely insane)
Gameplay: Absolutely no slowdown. Extremely responsive controls using an Xbox One pad (Pause button is clicking the Right Stick for some weird reason...).
Sound: Same as the Console Versions.
DLC and Online: OK, kinda sucks no Online, but the AI is still a competent alternative until it comes out. DLC on the other hand, my problem isn't that it exists, or how much it is, it is just that I would have liked the packs to have been split like on PSN. Maybe wait until a Steam Sale for these.
