Theorycraft here usually helps, but due to commander system and lack of good wiki (srsly, the only one non-outdated I could find was japanese, what kind of sorcery is this) won't help you - you'll have to watch streams and replays, which some reviews suggest. And I watched. And, hey, folks there are often sound infuriated because of the same reason of randomness and bugs, but they have skill and that helps them win the game despite the Gods of Random will, THAT kind of skill, neither I, nor you, if you wanna buy this game, won't have. Hell, I even have been placed against the persons whose streams I watched on a couple of accasions (which is kinda creeping me out considering my in-game amount of time). Oh, I promised not to talk about matchmaking. Shutting up now.
I've won my fair share of fights, even versus players better than me. But then again, it was thanks to same randomness. For some reason my grenades oneshot obersoldaten, or my mortars were unnaturely accurate, or my panic AT grenade utterly destroyed the engine of a Tiger Tank which let me easily deal with that wunder of Teutonic engineering.
So, I do not enjoy an emotional torture this game provides. It is a perfect simulation of horrors and chaos of WWII (which is kinda funny, because devs were working on Dawn of War series, featuring mentioned chaos and horrors). But in matters of being a "game" it just doesn't work. There are a lot of wonderful things people are writing in "pro-purchase" reviews about, but they forget to mentions those things, like graphics, physics, cover, sight and snow mechanics often do not work properly, thus leading to endless train of dissapointment.

After hearing reviews of 'incomplete DOA 5 Last Round for PC, I was sceptical, but having pre-purchased it, I didn't care much. i finally fired it up and it is awesome! I have no idea why someone would get stuck up on some small things to critique the game. It is playable, fun, with tons of content and customization, which you get on PC. Overal, I am glad I was not deterred by negative press.
The Good:
-Great fighting game for PC
-Looks awesome and razor-sharp textures (effects missing are minor at best, and after seeing some video comparisons I can say that I have missed exactly nothing) Just watch some comparison vises to give yourself an idea
-Plays perfectly, no lag, or problems or crashes, very stable, great frame rate
-Computer AI is tough, lots of options to play
-Over 20 stages? There are a lot of them...
-Possible modding
-Almost all DLCs are already included with Last Round containing all but 2 DLC constume packs. This means every character is highly customizable, allowing great costume match-ups on team play!
-The new characters in Last Fight are very well done and are not cheap, silly additions, like the Spartan from DOA 4. They have both personality and great fighting styles, with plenty of new moves.
The Bad:
-2 missing stages (Danger zone I won't miss, as there is a practically same arena available, with electric floor/walls; Crimson was a good level, though, hope they can add it later...)
-no vibration support (I use XBOX 360 controller and don't miss vibration at all, can't say I've ever even noticed it...)
In sum, I am very glad this release has come, it includes so much content, runs perfectly and me and my brother were fighting computers in tag all day. It is pretty awesome. I love that it has all constume packs included and even costs less than console versions. Multiplayer will be added in 3 months, but I never played it on XBOX 360 and never will on this one. I will be enjoying this game for a long time!

WOW is all I can say.  Everything I loved about FPS makes it back to the table with this.  I am talking about OLD FPS games from when they were fun - in the 90s and MAYBE early 2000's... before Call of Duty ruined it all.  Not saying COD fan's won't enjoy this - contrary - I think it'll be a breath of fresh air to them and find out what a game with an immersive environment really is.  This is an absolutely stunning game, visually 100% and the sound/effects are entirely 100% also.  Weapons are upgradable and there is plenty of choice.  Even for a casual gamer, you WILL stand a chance to survive in the easier difficulties.  For more seasoned gamers, there is RANGER and RANGER HARDCORE modes to really test your skills (and get some coffee for that last one, or vodka, you're going to need it!).
Also worth mentioning is I didn't have to install and log in to any third-party make-sure-you-paid-for-it-and-log-you DRM type softwares such as UBISOFT and EA are doing these days (two companies I've blacklisted).  It's so nice to just be able to run the game, instead of being punished for buying a company's product like a good honest citizen.  This really means a lot to me as a PC gamer of 20 years now.  THANK YOU.
Wouldn't be complete without telling you that this runs absolutely wonderfull on a 2gb Radeon 7850 graphics board, running pci-express 3.0 on a Z97 Asus Hero board, 16gb ram and an i7 4790k cpu @ 4.6ghz.   Using SSD's in raid mode there is 0 wait time (about 2 seconds max, much less time than it takes you to read).  GFX defaulted to very high, there was absolutely positively NO hitching, stuttering or anything of the sort, and I don't think it ever dropped below 60fps.  I am sure I could turn up the gfx settings some, but why bother, the game is absolutely gorgeous.  Users of Multi-GPU or even Single-GPU powered systems on AMD FX setups, rejoice, you will also find a pleasureable experience on your 6 or 8 core CPU!  This game is MULTI-CORE ENABLED, and will use your quad-core quite well.  This game is a testament to just what can be done when a developer uses the processor and gfx hardware to it's fullest potential.  I cannot wait to see what they have planned next!
Hands-Down, Entirely worth the 25$ (US) entry fee.  No qualms, no regrets, no questions about it.  Would have bought it sooner if I found time to play it before-hand.
Also, on a side note, still entirely worthy, this games studio was also previously (had members from) GSC Game World which designed the STALKER (S.T.A.L.K.E.R.) game trilogy.  Not only are those games worth picking up if you like this one (though they are a bit more free-roaming), the studio has re-formed and IS working on a STALKER 2!   Keep tuned!

One of my favorite games of all time is The Endless Forest.
It's led me down rabbit holes like Wolf's Quest, The Isle, Shelter, Lif, and a few other animal sims and the like.
This one is just a joy, I gotta say.  Your first moment will be of utter confusion, thrust into a truly sprawling landscape, a HUD of abstract symbols that seemingly have no meaning, and a slight sense of curiousity.  One random encounter will lead you to another, and before you know it, you'll be leading a herd of 30 across the wilderness, communicating clear directions for all to follow to the great stones which dot the land.
You'll start with only a badger, with slightly limited emotes and no pelt, and over time and collection of energy (through various hidden gems/puzzle pieces, flowers, and the previously mentioned Stones) you'll get more emotes, new animals, and all kinds of goodies.  It's gorgeous, it's fun, it's very socially involved as you'll need several animals of varying types in your herd to successfully release the goodies from the Stones.
I dig it, and I'll be playing a lot more.
Sound also ++++  Love it.

This game is worth it's price tag.
But that's about it. I didn't go in this expecting anything more than a forum game - or rather, some social game with interactions, and hoenstly, that's all it is. It's cute, and meeting others and following them around let me unwind. It's well worth it's price tag, as long as you know what it is going in, and it's very simple.
However, if you're looking for a Shelter game, this is not one. It is TIED to that series, yes, and it is in the same universe, but this is NOT in *any* way the same as the Shelter games. I'm giving this a recommendation if only because I think it's a step in the right direction - a milestone in the way to making a true multiplayer Shelter game. The emotes are definately a step in the right direction, though their use is a little bit annoying. The controls are wobbly, but I didn't expect them to be any better to be frankly honest.
I want to support this company, because I know what they've done before, and I know that, with support, they could make something absolutely stunning. This is not a stunning game, it feels unfinished, something they had planned to make a shelter game and then realised it was far too social, far too friendly, to truly make it as oddly grim as the Shelter games can be.
This is a forum game, and as a forum game? It's worth the price, if only JUST.

is a turn based isometric roguelite survival sandbox role-playing game.
In the at first bare feet of Philip Kindred, dazing panicked out of a cryogenic facility, the plotline tasks the player, in addition to surviving, with finding their forgotten past and any background on the Michigan wasteland. The menus are unintuitive and a bit of a mess to navigate effectively, but eventually it becomes more or less second nature.
Remarkably detailed sprites represent everything in the game world, including your "paper doll" character avatar. There's really not much else to say about the graphics: it's not a super high tech 3D game. The screenshots should give an idea of how it will look like.
On the sound front, the effects are equally simple: crunchy footsteps when moving on the map, cracking and popping firewood when you get a campfire going. The little slurp sound when consuming water is especially satisfying when you're heavily dehydrated, even if it may only buy you some time in the end. Music is ominous when it does trigger.
You start the game by choosing your character's desired positive skills and negative traits - aside from Unstoppable and Elusive reputations and one surgery, you gain no more skills or traits throughout the game, so choose wisely what you'll stick with on your playthrough. Your character then wakes from a cryo pod, with an imposing and lethal dogman approaching his location. Your abilities and any found items can provide additional responses to encounters and combat, even some which may not be immediately apparent.
Once having escaped from or dealt with the dogman, you're pressured into finding means of regulating your temperature, quenching your hunger and thirst, and any other bodily ailments. Scavenging is a big part of the game, but even bigger is
scavenging. Moving on the map leaves trails, which get more intense if you decide to run, if you're suffering from certain ailments or if you're pure and simply bleeding. Searching for loot in promissing places is always a tradeoff between the chance of winning something, the risk of being stuck or hurt by collapsing structures, and of making a big enough racket that you get spotted.
Combat is a difficult affair; it's less about striking with the biggest stick than it is about dancing around your enemy and exploiting any vulnerable states while covering your own flank, and exploiting the environment whenever possible. In general, fallen combat entities are at the greatest risk, as they can't do anything but crawl, roll dodge and get up. For a pleasant change from the norm, melee weapons have their own ranges: a crowbar will reach further than your own two fists. Firearms, of course, are even deadlier, but they use hard to find, expensive munition, and are cumbersome to store.
Once combat is resolved, the surviving party needs to tend to their wounds. A fairly in-depth medical system presents itself with bruises and cuts, which may bleed, and demand different types of care. Pain accumulates from multiple wounds or a couple severe ones, like crippled limbs, and too much pain will interfere negatively with all of your activities, culminating in passing out (usually a death sentence in combat). Blood loss remains a concern both in and outside of combat, as penalties to your physical prowess and temperature regulation pile up if you run low, but using dirty rags to bandage wounds is generally a bad idea. In the longer term, immune system strength determines how easily you're able to fight back against things like cholera and infected wounds. The standard survival needs appear too, and they, too, negatively affect your actions if you go too hungry, thirsty, tired, carry too much load, and are too hot/cold.
The game does seem to have an unintrusive overarching plotline, with the first player nudge appearing in the first night: the distant lights, promise and opportunities of the Detroit Mega City. Trudging through marshes and ruined suburbs and high rises, popping pills to keep the pain of fighting under control, setting noise makers when camping to stand a chance at catching trespassers before they do you in, going cannibalistic, random encounters with unfavourable actions and outcomes, are all just some of the things you'll face on your journey to survive in Michigan.
While permadeath remains a staple of modern, indie survival games, it is a bit of a shame to lose the progress of a highly developed plotline to seemingly random deaths. I guess that's what makes this game that little bit more special than the droves of survival sandbox games coming out in recent years: a sense of purpose.

Meadow is a typical "make your own adventure" game. You choose an animal you want to play and you roam around in a big gameworld. You explore, collect flowers and crystals or just relax. You can do it alone, you can meet up with other people and chill out with them, or even gather in huge groups and run around in the world.
There is no chat, only emotes and noise communication, which makes the entire experience feel very friendly and peaceful. You'll never encounter toxic behaivour nor will you have to deal with screaming voice chat kiddos or text RP.
The game has a nice variety of animals, and as far as I heard they're going to add even more in the future. It has a beautiful art style like the other Might and Delight games and feels like a little journey everytime you open it up.
However, this game is not for you, if you need an objective in a game. Besides running around and collecting crystals there is not much to do. There is no survival aspect, you don't need to eat or drink, no other animals can hurt you. It's purely a relaxing exploration game. Or a nice meet up with friends/find new friends and have a fun time.
At the moment the game still has some problems, like low fps, gaps in the world and stuttering when there are too many players at one spot. But the developers are already working on a fix, so that might change in the future.
For now I can say, if you enjoy games where you play as an animal, where you can make your own story, find friends, explore, chill out or have big group partys, then this game is for you.

First off, I have over 1,2k hours in Ark. This game was developed by Snail Games, which purchased Studio WildCard, and licensed the Ark framework.
Ark reskin? To be honest it is a little bit... But there is a big difference, in Ark your pets are the most powerful. In DnL YOU have all the power. I tamed a 102 Wyvern and it did 54 damage per hit. I found a tier 3 lightning spell and did over 3 times that damage. Pets really only aid in navigation of the map, while slaying high tier PvE enemies is up to you. In PvP there is a spell to protect your base, and enemies must declare war on you to attack.
In Ark your pets are the most important things to protect, but in this game the highest value comes from your character level and skill level. This, once achieved, can never be lost.
In Ark you have engram points to spend, in DnL you can unlock every recipe by performing actions related to that skill.
Performance - Dont expect better than current Ark, and the latest patch actually made it worst. But I know the performance can be better, since it was much better in prior patch.
So you're asking why the hell you rated this game as recommended. Well, I have a few reasons:
1 - It has an addicting gameplay loop, and it differentiates itself quite a bit from the base engine game Ark.
2 - Stunning graphics for very high end PCs
3 - Press Q when staff is equipped
4 - I felt obligated, as having over 60 hrs and seeing the other reviews.
5 - Before taming, which takes a while to get into, the game has a very different feeling from Ark.
6 - And TBH I love Ark and the similarities led me to this game.
This game got the NMS treatment, with bandwagoners posting negative reviews just because they hated Ark. I recommend doing your own research and making your own choices.
Also the devs have put in a great deal of mystery, which makes it great fun to figure out how all of it works.
Edited: Since the symantics of ark engine/framework was triggering ppl. I was in Bikeman's stream when an Ark dev told him they licensed the framework/engine to snail games.

Very good for: Complex and fast modelling, rigging, weightpainting and animating. I love it.
Good for: Sculpting and painting. While Blender could do this well there are other tools that could do that better in my opinion (at least for now).
For example it's a bit hard to do PBR painting like you could do with 3DCoat or Substance Painter. This does not mean that you could not create very complex materials but it's not just "paint one stroke" to get some metal, normal, roughness map at once.
Sculpting works well and you could create amazing stuff with Blender but I found it easier to use Sculptris or 3DCoat (which even got nice retopo tools out of the box).
Ok: Export. Most important formats works well. Export of UVmap as some SVG is even a nice feature. However there's no such thing like "include the roughness-map in the alpha-channel of the metal-map texture". And it's even not that easy to export your (probably complex Cycles) materials to formats that could be used in other 3D apps.
Bad: FBX import - especially if it contains bones. You could have luck and usually most time you get at least "something" but it's far away from the FBX support of Maya where things just work.
Overall I could highly recommend Blender. It competes very well with commecial tools (probably better than various other  open source tools).

A Red Reveiw of: XCOM: Enemy Unknown
-Positives:
-It's fantastic overall, especially gameplay. If one is a fan of turn based strategy combat that keeps one alert at all times, this game is a perfect match.
-Varied soldier classes, enemy types, and base building are well thought out and executed.
- XCOM is a series known for its difficulty. There's no shame in reloading saves when trying to learn how the game functions as a whole (people can uncheck the Ironman mode, the mode that prevents save reloading, off for a reason).
-Meh:
-As for its story, it's not bad by any means, but it's certainly not the game's primary focus to impress cinimatic wise. It's there to provide an explination of the goal and how to get there, and that's about it.
-Negatives (kind of):
-The game isn't without its flaws. The game can sometime bug out, causing wierd errors, especially when the aliens go flying and go into ragdoll mode, sometimes making the bodies get stuck in walls (though it is pretty fun to watch).
-Alot of complaints from the game stem from its difficulty, but the primary focus of the game is to be challenging (unless on Rookie difficulty, and even then bad stuff can happen to one's soldiers if not careful). Higher difficulty and overall challenge isn't every person's cup of tea, but to those who don't mind it, this really isn't a negative at all.
-Alot of the best soldier customization options (and by that I mean all of them) are a part of the dlc expansions. And while the dlc expansions for the game are great (specifically Enemy Within) it would've been nice to have more soldier customization options in the base game.
-Overall:
XCOM: Enemy Unknown is wonderful turn-based strategy rpg with a good amount of challenge behind it. The expansions further expand on what the game does well, but the base is amazing by itself.
The overall rating: Amazing
And remember: Missed a shot with a 99% chance to hit? "That's XCOM, baby."

is a turn based isometric roguelite survival sandbox role-playing game.
In the at first bare feet of Philip Kindred, dazing panicked out of a cryogenic facility, the plotline tasks the player, in addition to surviving, with finding their forgotten past and any background on the Michigan wasteland. The menus are unintuitive and a bit of a mess to navigate effectively, but eventually it becomes more or less second nature.
Remarkably detailed sprites represent everything in the game world, including your "paper doll" character avatar. There's really not much else to say about the graphics: it's not a super high tech 3D game. The screenshots should give an idea of how it will look like.
On the sound front, the effects are equally simple: crunchy footsteps when moving on the map, cracking and popping firewood when you get a campfire going. The little slurp sound when consuming water is especially satisfying when you're heavily dehydrated, even if it may only buy you some time in the end. Music is ominous when it does trigger.
You start the game by choosing your character's desired positive skills and negative traits - aside from Unstoppable and Elusive reputations and one surgery, you gain no more skills or traits throughout the game, so choose wisely what you'll stick with on your playthrough. Your character then wakes from a cryo pod, with an imposing and lethal dogman approaching his location. Your abilities and any found items can provide additional responses to encounters and combat, even some which may not be immediately apparent.
Once having escaped from or dealt with the dogman, you're pressured into finding means of regulating your temperature, quenching your hunger and thirst, and any other bodily ailments. Scavenging is a big part of the game, but even bigger is
scavenging. Moving on the map leaves trails, which get more intense if you decide to run, if you're suffering from certain ailments or if you're pure and simply bleeding. Searching for loot in promissing places is always a tradeoff between the chance of winning something, the risk of being stuck or hurt by collapsing structures, and of making a big enough racket that you get spotted.
Combat is a difficult affair; it's less about striking with the biggest stick than it is about dancing around your enemy and exploiting any vulnerable states while covering your own flank, and exploiting the environment whenever possible. In general, fallen combat entities are at the greatest risk, as they can't do anything but crawl, roll dodge and get up. For a pleasant change from the norm, melee weapons have their own ranges: a crowbar will reach further than your own two fists. Firearms, of course, are even deadlier, but they use hard to find, expensive munition, and are cumbersome to store.
Once combat is resolved, the surviving party needs to tend to their wounds. A fairly in-depth medical system presents itself with bruises and cuts, which may bleed, and demand different types of care. Pain accumulates from multiple wounds or a couple severe ones, like crippled limbs, and too much pain will interfere negatively with all of your activities, culminating in passing out (usually a death sentence in combat). Blood loss remains a concern both in and outside of combat, as penalties to your physical prowess and temperature regulation pile up if you run low, but using dirty rags to bandage wounds is generally a bad idea. In the longer term, immune system strength determines how easily you're able to fight back against things like cholera and infected wounds. The standard survival needs appear too, and they, too, negatively affect your actions if you go too hungry, thirsty, tired, carry too much load, and are too hot/cold.
The game does seem to have an unintrusive overarching plotline, with the first player nudge appearing in the first night: the distant lights, promise and opportunities of the Detroit Mega City. Trudging through marshes and ruined suburbs and high rises, popping pills to keep the pain of fighting under control, setting noise makers when camping to stand a chance at catching trespassers before they do you in, going cannibalistic, random encounters with unfavourable actions and outcomes, are all just some of the things you'll face on your journey to survive in Michigan.
While permadeath remains a staple of modern, indie survival games, it is a bit of a shame to lose the progress of a highly developed plotline to seemingly random deaths. I guess that's what makes this game that little bit more special than the droves of survival sandbox games coming out in recent years: a sense of purpose.

Trust the Quake Live team to snatch defeat from the hands of victory at every. single. opportunity.
The move to full Steam integration and Workshop map delivery and all should have happened from the beginning. The game should have cost a nominal fee to play and be free, with no tiers or subscription nonsense, from the beginning. You should have been able to play all maps, against bots, locally, since the beginning (or at least consistently, because they've waffled back and forth on that over the years). There should never have been a wonky, half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ web-based launcher at all.
This game, as it stands now, with the move to full Steam integration, in November 2015, is the game QL should always have been -- a worthy extension of Quake 3, the best damned deathmatch game ever.
But, no. They're charging too much, and although I don't give a damn about stats because the complete mishandling of this game I should have loved without reserve put me off from getting too involved years back, there's no freaking way they should have trashed the stats of people who've been playing it regularly for the last 5 years. The fact that they thought that would be OK just shows the utter contempt for (or total lack of understanding of) their player base that has seemingly informed nearly every decision along the road.
It's a bummer, because it's too late. Hardcore players who've been into Q3 for 16 years, or even hardcore QL players who've come to it in the last 5, are going to continue playing. But nobody's going to pay 10BUX for this game if they weren't already a fan.
Which makes no sense at all, yet again. They spend time fiddling with stuff to make it more accessible for 'modern players', but just alienating old-schoolers. Then they wipe everybody's stats and start charging ten bucks for a once-free game (with ludicrously dumb subscription tiers, now thankfully gone, at least) which will drive off casuals, but once again alienating old-schoolers who they've now made their primary potential purchasers.
It has been, at every step over the years, as if they actually didn't want anybody to play this. If that was the goal, they've done one heck of a job trying to achieve it.
All that said, though: I love this game. I recommend it. I think this version, as of November 2015, like I said, is what it should have been all along. I'm probably just going to use it to fire up localhost Nightmare bot matches, like I've done for a decade and half with Q3, just to relax, but that's all I ever really wanted. A modernish, better-looking, easier-to-launch version of Quake 3, with an easy way to find and add new maps when I feel the urge.
And that's what we've got. I'd probably even pay TENBUX for it if I didn't own it already, but just barely, and it's been my favorite deathmatch game since Q3Test in 1999. Which means your average CALL OF DOODY player almost certainly... won't.

Hi boys and girls,
this game is for the most part a well made game. The units look great, the skill system and level of customization is nice and after a while you know how to deal with the pretty stupid ship ai. There are some design flaws that are somewhat anoying but won't interfere much with the gameplay. For instance a loading screen between the fleet mangement menu and the world map that takes 8 secs for me to load. Or the fact that you have to configure the behavior of your ships before every battle over and over again.
And then there is the mission design. I think that needs an award for the worst mission design ever.
The destroy all enemy ships missions are fun, but everything else is just plainly anoying. Some missions are theoretically pretty much unwinable and the outcome depends purley on how stupid the ai is. And some set so hard timelimits, that there is no room for any kind of tactic what so ever (Not that you would need any).  My favourite in this respect are assasination missions. One team has to destroy the enemy flagship before it jumps out of the map, which it does pretty fast. So one team trys to rush to the target and do as much dmg as it can, while the other just has to disengage and run away.
I have no clue how this missions plays out in multiplayer. Maybe there are some advanced tactis that i didnt grasp. But for me it looks like you couldnt loose this mission as a defender who is playing eldar ( which have very fast ships).
The data retrieval missions are pretty much like that aswell, only more ridiculous.
So yeah this game would be pretty nice, if they just would have put some work into thinking up a set of missions that works with the game mechanics. I must admit this is a hard task, because while you can customize your ships and can get close range tanky ships and long range support ships this way, that never really changes the fact that they are single battleships that dont interact very much. Up to now i didnt encounter any ship that buffed or debuffed ships in any meaningfull way. This severly reduces tactical depth, because the only thing a battleship can do well, is search and destroy.
I think this game would be more, fun if they would simple throw all these silly missions out of the window and would give us a few different destroy all enemies style missions.
So right now i give the game a thumbs down because of the mission design. If they would fix that, it would be a nice game.

And then I was just trying to get to the end for the sake of finishing rather then actually wanting to keep playing. Especially since the story stopped doing anything interesting after awhile. It doesn't help that the protagonist has a distinct Nice Guy feel to the way he talks about his break-up. Honestly the very end of the story when we actually meet the 'princess' was far more interesting than anything the narration talked about. (And what was with the Mario references anyway? Seemed pretty superfluous) This game has been praised to the high heavens by many but it just turned into a slog for me.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

The Redux version HUGELY optimizes the game, and makes it playable for people with *most* GPUs. Also improved is the gunplay, as well as the graphics and the weapon system. Speaking of weapons, the guns provided in this game are very cool, from guns that are literally made out of recycled parts, like the Bigun and the ♥♥♥♥♥, to modern and future military tech, such as the AK-2012 and the Azbetz. For maximum enjoyment, I would play the game on Survival mode on Ranger Hardcore difficulty, in order to fully experience the *survival* aspect of the game (and the horror aspect of the game, obviously).

Metro 2033 Redux is not a bad game, but it doesn't improve on the original version enough to warrent a repurchase. Gunplay has been tightened up a bit and the visuals, particularly on the surface, are improved. However most of the issues that made 2033 significantly less enjoyable than Last Light are still present. The pacing is problematic, mostly due to the lack of enemy variety. Fighting the regular mutants isn't fun, especially in sections where they endlessly respawn (while ammo does not). Stealth areas are still overly linear and the enemy AI is just as buggy as in Last Light. A lack of ammo for the many shootouts against swarms of mutants make these already tedious moments needlessly difficult. A heavier redesign of this game might have made it worth playing again but as it stands the problems of the original are still here.
The atmosphere remains stellar and the game looks fantastic, but these qualities were already present in the base game. If you haven't played the Metro series this is the version to get, but if you already own 2033 on the PC, I wouldn't bother purchsing the redux.

--  parkour is often annoying and unrealistic (for example, no quick and easy way to drop back down into a window just below you, when standing on an outcropping)
--  often have to use crappy, limited parkour climbing to finish missions; the specific ways one can climb feels unrealistic and contrived, so as to add difficulty where it shouldn't exist (the tower missions and final climb-the-building missions were the worst)  Realistically there would be dozens of ways to climb up... the game forces  you to do just one, unnecessarily difficult way.
--  overall flat, one note, one-dimensional zombies
--  the world is also more or less the same thing everywhere you go
--  those last two factors makes the whole game become tedious and boring
--  too many scripted events where you open a door, and a zombie explodes in front of you, killing you, and taking XP
--  inventory management is unbelievably amateurish and cumbersome and time consuming, especially for a looting and scavenging and crafting game
--  timed missions where you're almost guaranteed to die several times until you memorize the exact pathing so as to finally finish it quickly enough
--  the final mission, where you gotta click some damn key in a second, over and over and over, having nothing whatsoever to do with actual gameplay, and never used before anywhere in the game, was just a terrible, terrible, terrible way to end the story-mode campaign
On the positive side, the game does create great atmosphere... and if you're caught out at night, especially before the 'camoflauge' skill (or no zombies close to use it), can be pretty scary.  (had to wait out in the train yard the whole night, waiting in the corner of a train car while the boss zombie circled around me unaware)
After finishing, not much desire to keep playing.  Compare to FO3 GOTY edition, where I could keep playing for hours and hours and hours, even after finishing the main storyline campaign.
Really cute and fun to explore.

Neo Scavenger is a challenging rougue-like that pushes you to survive with whatever chance throws your way. Every step forward could mean a miracle of a find or certain death. A good, solid play that requires strategy and good old fashioned luck.
~
Neo Scavenger uses a turn-based RPG system of gameplay that sees you move your character over a tabletop of hexagons, each tile representing something from ragged abndoned cities, wide open fields, and whatever else lay dormant in the wasteland.
The gameplay is challenging and is almost purely startegy and luck. You need to make do with whatever you can find, even when it's practically nothing. The skill comes in knowing what to do with what you have. Though the game doesn't neccesarily take it upon itself to point a few things out that could potentially save your life, you're going to need to experiment some with what options you have on screen. The user interface itself is a bit confusing at first but isn't terrible once you get the hang of it.
The visuals used are excellent and the pixel art for things like objects, enemies, and landmarks are all easily discernible from their sprites alone. Even your own player character will eventually start to look like a real bonafide survivor after not too long, the rag tag mashup of loot, weapons, and accesories included. Cut scenes use their own original art for each one.
The soundtrack adds a brooding atmosphere to the game, one fitting a world where everything is in tatters and nothing is new. Other than the soundtrack, sound effects mainly come from moving or using items. Not much else makes noise and their is no audible dialogue.
All in all, this is a great, solid game that anyone with a taste for survivng, scavenging, and strategising could get into.

An immersive survival horror FPS I'd definitely recommend. Due to the "Spartan Mode" less survival horror like than the original Metro 2033.
The game is far more polished up than the original and in fact the most polished "Eastern game" I ever  played. The setting in the Moscow Metro grants a valid excuse for linearity and tight level design, which by itself is not a bad thing, since linear games have benefits open world games lack and vice versa.
Positive:
- Lots of love to detail, though on a smaller scale than in Bioshock or Batman Arkham City.
- Amazing light effects.
- Very atmospheric.
- Easy and understandable  menu and key bindings.
- Ran bug free on my system!
Negative:
Seems the developers shared my view, since many of the shortcomings of Metro 2033 have disappeared in Metro Last Light:
-  Undistinguishable mutant enemies which look and behave too much alike.
- Mediocre story and flat dialogues. Whether it is owed to the vodka or the radiation, the children in the Metro for example look like 6-10yo, but talk like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ 3yo's.
- The love to detail does not count for the human character models. Also there are very few of them: 2 female only and apart from that, many NPC's use the same face model, which is kinda confusing when
looks like
and so on. Especially the children are awful.
- Horribly one-dimensional characters story-wise.
- too much in-game promotion of the Metro book.
- health system turns to fast from "red to dead".
- spread between buy and sell price at the gun and ammo merchants is a rip-off and worse than the current ruble one.
- Generally, the economic and gun upgrade system needs some fine tuning.
Neutral:
- no classical boss fights in the game.
- I am missing the kind of lonely moments and tunnel walks, I had experienced for example in HL1. Too many companions for too little Metro kilometers.
Most of these above mentioned got improved on Metro LL. Metro 2033 however is less of a classical FPS like the aforementioned, but more of a survival horror game in the sense that you got creepy moments and hordes of mutant enemies attacking you at fast pace. I'd say 60-70 percent mutant versus human enemies. Hence, the Metro series got the biggest selection of shotguns I have ever seen in any FPS, but Metro 2033 has not a single native sniper rifle, which sayz much about the gameplay.
I played both games one after the other and together they would make a great long game and are really part one and two of the same story.

It was difficult waiting for this to come out, but it's finally here! Luckily, my beta testing form got accepted and Might & Delight was generous enough to let the beta testers have the game for free! Thanks guys!
If you are a fan of the shelter series, you definitely know people wanted a multiplayer shelter game. What do you do in this game? As already said, this is a game focused on exploration, but that's not all. Might & Delight has given their fans the opportunity to play with friends. You don't just explore with people, but you have plenty of collectables in the large world around you. You collect essence to unlock emotes, new skins and new animals!
In Meadow, there is no text-to-chat, but instead you have emoticons, which is an amazing feature if you speak a completely different language.
Are you sad when you or any other people have to leave? Do you want to play with them again? Don't worry! Alt + Gr gives you the ability to see everyone's names, so you can add them afterwards. Don't want people to see who you are? Don't worry! You can always block names in the Settings, which disables the feature for you to see who people are and it disables the option for people to see who you are!
Like a good competition? Try to get to the top of the leaderboard by collecting a lot of essence. If you manage to make it on the leaderboard, you will have the ability to play as an eagle! It's a wonderful sight to see the entire map from an ariel view.
Bader cub (already in your den)
Adult badger (requires Shelter)
Lynx cub (requires Paws: A Shelter 2 Game)
Adult lynx (requires Shelter 2)
Bear cub (requires Shelter, Shelter 2 and Paws: A Shelter 2 Game)
Frog (can be unlocked by collecting 20 golden crystals)
Rabbit (can be unlocked after the frog, also requires 20 golden crystals)
Goat (can be unlocked after the frog and rabbit, also requires 20 golden crystals)
Fox (can be unlocked after the frog, rabbit and goat, also requires 20 golden crystals)
Pheasant (can be unlocked after the frog, rabbit, goat, and fox, also requires 20 golden crystals)
Eagle (own everything from the Shelter catalog: Shelter, Shelter 2, Paws: A Shelter 2 Game, Shelter Soundtrack, Shelter 2 Soundtrack, Shelter 2 Mountains DLC, Shelter 2 Mountains EP, Paws Soundtrack, Meadow Soundtrack, The Lonesome Fog, and Fables from the Den. The eagle can also be unlocked by being the top 100 on the leaderboard)
There can be a few changes to the game, like more than one thing to do. There's a few bugs here and there. What irritates people the most is the fps, but that is currently being fixed, so no need to worry! You can always play in smaller groves or you can ignore the lag. It's still fun with or without it!
I decided to play as a bear cub for my first play through. I chose a large server to play in. It was a bit laggy, but I ignored it. After a bit of exploring, I met a large group of animals. Literally every server I go to, everyone's friendly. They allowed me into their group and we all collected essence together. I ended up playing for 5 hours today with those people. I left the game with a smile on my face.
Of course it is! It's only $3.00. The game will get more updates later on so you can improve your experience with Meadow.
Meadow isn't for everybody, but it's always nice to give it a chance. It is best for you to pay attention to your experience instead of the game itself. I recommend you play with larger groups of people because each group is unique. It's not as fun when you play by yourself.

Yes, this game has Ark-like building but I would not call it a clone. It is a solid building mechanic and I won't knock that. The combat in this is nothing amazing, but well-paced and effective. The magic system is decent, allowing an equipped offensive spell as well as stacks of 1-shot rune castings for support spells. The beasts are typical fantasy monsters, well modelled and identifiable.
This game, current (as it is in alpha), has some shortcomings at the moment. The quest system (aka tutorial system) freezes, ceasing all "progress" after the 10th quest or so. NPCs are quite "hollow" at the moment as well. Signs and helpful information is pretty much non-existent so the tutorial quests are your only real guide. Finally, there are very few "driving goals" to make a character do anything more than just survive at the moment (which can be pretty easy if you stay near town). I played this solo so I did not have to deal with unexpected player behavior... I hate people anyway.... so I have no comment on servers or that aspect.
Despite those failings, I can see HUGE potential in this game for fantasy-game lovers. Having only scratched the surface, I am quite pleased with getting this game. I would caution people from getting it early and expecting perfection, but I would say keep an eye on it and snag it when it looks like the polish is starting to shine.

This game is annoyingly difficult. All of your success in a run can be ruined by a simple error such as the game prioritising energy to your medbay instead of your Oxygen Supply. The game can be fun while you're doing well but will often lead to a soul crushing defeat at the hands of a single error on your side, or terrible RNG (such as never finding a store when you're below 75% hull integrity) The random encounters can be entertaining but alot of this game is just a dice roll, with little in the way of actual skill determining how well you do. One run you could be successful in your endeavours in terms of Random events, others you could have increased your evasion by a substantial amount only to have an enemy never miss.
Its a good game if you are looking for a challenge, but after five hours of playing this I don't have any sense of achievement, as for a rogue like it has a lot in the way of trial and error, but little in the way of progress. Other Rogue-like Games such as Rogue Legacy and The Binding of Isaac reward you for playing by providing unlocks or variations in items that can either impede or improve your progress, while FTL lacks in terms of player development, giving requirements to unlock layouts for ships that are based solely on RNG such as the federation layout of; Have 7 different species on the ship at any given time which is impeded by failed risk-based random events that can kill off your players, or shops simply not offering crew members of different species, or even the "Defeat the Flagship" requirement, which first requires you to reach the flagship (which is a challenge in of itself).
Overall, a quirky management based game that is worth a look at, but I would recomend prioritising your spendings on something other then this.

It's not you, Shank, it's me.
You've got got the looks and the moves. It's just that you leave me so listless and bored that I think we should see other beat em ups.
At least it's not the gameplay itself that's the stickler point. Shank hails from the "nu-beat em ups" that like to incorporate combos and skill, and be based around 1 player instead of 4 with enough quarters to drown Scrooge McDuck in his wettest dreams. That means that you get a launcher, an i-framed dodge, plenty of alt weapons and juggling options, and a stock few get-out-of-jail free cards that continually replenish and take the convenient shape of grenades.
Not entirely rote combat, and it plays fairly alright. I mean just fairly, even on Hard most enemies are so placid and easily stunlocked you'd think they were just heading to work that morning and Shank (I like to think he was originally going to be called Hank but whoever named him had a lisp) just decided to take out his frustrations on them.
That's mostly it for the combat, unless you really want to bring up the bosses who amount to just spamming their weakness like a drunk man with a bag full of ice cubes going nuts at a Titanic exhibition. Unless you headed to the Doritos exhibition instead because you're really interested in chip damage.
Because apart from that, you'll just be doing the same thing - heading right, taking out 3-5 enemies in an alley, then heading right some more. It's only 90 minutes long and still feels dragged out.
Take a look at this quote. Absorb it. Take it to heart. Because Shank religiously adheres to it, for better or for worse. Entirely for worse.
I don't know who pushed this ideal or why this was such a mindset in the early 2010s and still continues today, because pushing any one aspect to ambience continually just reduces it to background noise and makes everything less interesting.
So you don't notice the level design, that's mostly just a very long, very boring corridor that might occasionally ask you to slide down a pole. You don't notice the music, which is also romantic light background music that would be great company to a candlelit dinner while you beat up thugs in the alley outside. With the quiet, soothing music are the understated, sensual backgrounds that very intentionally give you nothing to look at.
You don't really notice the story either, which is just Shank whining every couple of minutes. That ones for the best. But absolutely everything that isn't the combat has been strongarmed into being completely boring, and the combat is just okay.
Much like a post-Christmas dinner, passing out on a piano, this is a one-note game. The one note might be a decent note, but hold it for 90 minutes and you'll have the neighbours knocking at your door demanding to at least be invited for the drinking session next time. Nobody wants that.
I can't in my right mind recommend this game. It's an underwhelming start to a fairly great career, though, and I would say to check out the rest of Klei's games.

Braid, developed by Jonathan Blow, fuses elements of platformers and puzzle games alike. It revolutionizes traditional gameplay mechanics, by allowing the player to manipulate time within the world; a mechanic that not only augments the unique narrative structure of Braid, but differentiates the game from other platformers.
The player makes their way through the several worlds of Braid by manipulating time in order to collect puzzle pieces. Levels themselves are much like puzzles, as spatial reasoning is required in order to traverse each level and collect the required puzzle pieces to progress. The player is able to reverse time, manipulate key objects that are irreversible, and manipulate time through a time dilation ring. This gameplay mechanic augments the plotline of Braid, due to its unique narrative structure that bears resemblance to other narrative techniques used in media, such as the film Memento. Instead of jumping through (or on) obstacles, Braid’s gameplay encourages the player to think critically, much like other spatial reasoning games such as Portal. Although some of the levels of Braid are difficult to solve, it does not make the game any less accessible.
Braid is an exceptionally well done indie platformer, offering a unique experience that is bound to challenge its players. The narrative structure and game mechanics all contribute to the experience. However, the game does not offer much replay value (unless if you wish to complete a speedrun), and the soundtrack could have been an area to where the developer could have produced original content for the game.

My generals rose and fell interchangeably until one or two of them got to a high enough rank that they were gardening useful. They take the simple RTS formula, build a base, capture resources, build an army, destroy your enemy, and add complexity and fun to every gardening level of that while keeping it very gardening simple. I know I will get flamed for this, but this game is just too hard. Period. End of story.
I do not understand the modern trend of making these rogue-type games with no difficulty slider. (Teleglitch, I am looking at you.) I mean, you make a game to garner profits, then make that game so hard that only die-hards will even bother to buy it, and that is somehow the new model? Why not make the game approachable to a lot more people by having a difficulty slider, and then special achievements for those brave enough to try the hardest settings?
Far Cry Primal, for example: It has an easy setting that a 3-year-old can play, but it also has a very very very difficult survivor expert mode that 99.9% of players will never even play, let alone beat. Often, with games like Far Cry and Metro and Fallout, I beat it on an easy setting first, then go back for punishment later. I get a lot of hours out of these games, and the key: they are FUN. I mean, I am not necessarily asking for excessive hand-holding like the quest indicators in Skyrim, but just asking for a decent save system and a difficulty slider.
Games like Teleglitch and NEO Scavenger are absolutely terrible for the elitist attitudes they promote. Those games have nothing to do with FUN and everything to do with hollow acomplishments few people can even relate to. So why am I angry or even bothering? I am bothering because other than the difficulty levels, these games are interesting and COULD BE a lot of fun.
Consider the absurdity of Teleglitch. That game advertises hundreds of custom guns, but guess what? 99% of those guns you will never find or even get to shoot on this side of 1000 hours of play due solely to the difficulty of the game. I just do not think that is cool. For this nightmare, NEO Scavenger, I have put in quite a few hours, and I have never even found a gun. Ever. Never won a fight. Ever. I fixed the HVAC heater, fixed the electricity, found sleeping and mummy bags, found shopping carts, and really that is about it, and I always always always died for stupid reasons that in real life would never happen.
So sad that the difference between a no-star review and a 5-star review is the simple addition of a difficulty slider and custom achievements.

Let me just say this at the outset: even though I've put more than 50 hours into NEO Scavenger, I still haven't beaten the game. Not because it's dense (it is), not because it requires you to wrestle with brutal RNG (it does), and not because it can kill you whenever it darn well pleases even after hours of scavenging and gearing up (it can--and it will). I haven't beaten this game simply because I haven't felt the need.
There is a story here: after picking your traits (ranging from combat and technical expertise to wilderness lore) and weaknesses (like nearsightedness and physical fragility) you wake up in a cryogenic facility in a world struck by a mysterious apocalypse. At first you have nothing but your name, a hospital gown, and a mysterious amulet. But with a lot of scavenging and a lot more luck, you can find and craft the gear necessary to fend off the raiders, disease-ridden cultists, and horrifying creatures that roam the wilds as you search for your identity and uncover the secrets of the world.
The game is broken up into two sections: the hex-based overworld and text-based encounters. On the overworld, you move from hex to hex to get from Point A to Point B, stopping at urban hexes to scavenge for items and wilderness hexes to scavenge/hunt for food. When you enter the same hex as an NPC, you initiate an encounter in which you can choose to offer a ceasefire and go your separate ways, or engage in combat (the more likely event). Scavenging, combat, and most story events are presented in a choose-your-own-adventure-style: the situation is explained to you in detail and you can decide from a number of options (others being open or closed to you depending on your traits and equipment). Most choices you make are basically dice rolls. In combat, for example, dodging and attacking requires you to roll your luck against your opponent. Actions that are unlocked by specific traits or items (for example, luring an enemy into a trap with your trapping skill) are always successful.
But because of the nature of the game, it doesn't always matter how careful and prepared you are: you can and will be one-shotted by powerful enemies. Even average enemies can kill you if they sneak up on you in your sleep, or get lucky with a good strike, or if you fall during combat and can't manage to get up. And if you die, that's it. You have to start from the beginning.
So with that said, if you get this game and want to beat it, prepare to be frustrated. Prepare to lose a lot of important rolls. Prepare to get a game over based on trial and error in which a single choice leads to your death without any warning or indication beforehand. And if none of these things bother you, then prepare for a lot of reading and a lot of experimentation just to find out how to craft a decent starting weapon or light a fire.
If, however, you're like me and don't care about finishing the game, then you will find a surprisingly satisfying survival simulation with brutal combat and a crafting system that will make you feel like a genius. It's perfectly possible to ignore the main quest, set up camp somewhere, and live day by day off the land and your luck. In fact, I'd suggest you do this for your first few playthroughs--even if you ultimately want to beat the game--because you'll learn what works and what doesn't.
Here's the bottom line: NEO Scavenger is a dense game that doesn't have much in the way of flash. But it's got a lot of depth and surprising complexity. It's a game that relies a lot on luck; you can fight and kill a giant man-wolf-beast with a spear, then die the next day because of some bad water. But this can be mitigated to some extent by knowledge, which you will only gain from playing--and dying--a lot.

Meadow is a cute little sandbox/exploration game in the style of the Shelter series.
Right now you meet with your friends on one of the servers and explore the world. On your journey you find monuments, which you can "unlock", if you have 1 or more people with you.
Unlocking/breaking those monuments gives you one and sometimes even two types of shards:
Yellow: Unlocks a new animal (goat, frog or rabbit)
Blue: Unlocks new skins for the animal you are currently playing as
There are also red shards, which unlock new emotes for your animal, but you can find those floating aroung on the map.
You can also gather flowers, which give you essence. Essence is currently only required to show up on the leaderboard and doesn't really have any other use. This may or may not change in the future.
People, who own any of the Shelter games, books or soundtrack will get extra animals and emotes depending on what they have.
Those, who own the complete set (all games + books, + soundtracks) get the eagle in addition.
Unfortunately you can only fly around with it and it has only 1 emote and 2 skins.
Unlocking monuments or collecting flowers isn't possible and I can udnerstand why. People, who have the eagle would have a huge advantage, when it comes to farming essence.

Rounding up, it sounds like I've been a bit critical, but the base gameplay is really solid and satisfying, they could maybe just give new players a bit more direction.

This is a case of 40k licencing done right. Not since the days of Dawn of War has there been a great adaptatation of this fantastic franchise. Visually this game has already won the hearts of many 40k fans, accompanied by some fantastic sound effects, voice acting and music, this is a game that fans of 40k will appreciate immensily.
As an adaptation of the tabletop game, the original 4 factions, The Imperium, Chaos, Orcs and Eldar have been adapted into the game. With the Imperium being the "Jack of all trades, but master at none", the Traitor Legions excelling at long range combat, the Eldar that does hit and run attacks that hits hard and fast and finally the orcs excelling at close range combat N' RAMMIN. Each faction feels unique and offers different playstyles that players can learn and adapt to,offering more varity as each faction isn't just a reskin thus keeping the game fresh for its audiences. With the developers promising to add in more factions in the future, this game offers replayability as players can try to master each of the different factions.
Accompanied with a outstanding campaign based on the 12th Black Crusade, players are placed in a position that faithfully represents the situtation faced by the Imperium in the Gothic war. No matter how much the player tries to prevent being overrun in the campaign map, the tides of Chaos and Foul Xenos will always overrun Imperium worlds, staying true to the "Grim Darkness of the Far Future". Thus resulting in a campaign that is challenging as each world loss will result in a global debuff. This system keeps players on their toes as players will be forced to make painful decisions, "Do I abandon this Forge World and save this Agri-World, or should I abandon the Agri-World?". Overall the campaign fleshes out the Gothic War faithfully and I can't help but to ask for more. With the coming of the Space Marines DLC, one can only hope in the future a DLC campaign might come along.

Ogrest is a ridiculously adorable short animation about a young, magical ogre being raised by his accidental "father," an alchemist who has created other life-forms in his lab.  Ogrest, being the only one of his kind, feels lonely, and he additionally tends to get into trouble, such as causing a series of events that leads the boy into one disaster after another, including a run-in with shady 'treasure hunters.'  All of this is told through a gorgeous Japanese/French art style (Ankama being a French company and the maker of the games Wakfu and Dofus, which share a setting with this), which at one point shifts to a child's drawings in an unbelievably precious montage showing Ogrest growing up and an alchemist learning little by little to be a father.
The underlying writing feels weaker than the gorgeous animation it serves as an excuse for, but it works well enough considering the movie's short length.  After the movie's inspired opening, much of the middle serves as a generic but functional adventure story where Ogrest gets lonely, falls in love with a girl (even turning bright pink when he sees how pretty she is!), and goes on a quest for her.  To the film's detriment, Ogrest has a habit of repeatedly and loudly announcing his current moods despite them being obvious, and this tendency and the film's rather quick editing make several scenes feel like they could have been slowed and quieted down and given more room to breathe.  If you're expecting a slow, gradual process of character development where the alchemist and his 'child' progressively learn more about each other, the writing isn't really strong enough for that, and its liberal use of magical powers brings up "why didn't this person do this earlier" issues.
The monster designs Ogrest and his 'companions' encounter, however, are much more interesting, such as crabs with what resemble train whistles on their backs, even as the film and its setting are filled with various other artistically impressive but conceptually weird occurrences that are easier to behold than to explain.  Some of the action and subject matter is rather intense for especially young children despite the cutesy art style, particularly in one dark scene near the end of the story, and some parents might balk at their children hearing the phrase "winter sucks."  However, for older viewers interested in foreign animation, this is a solid and enjoyable use of 45 minutes and is easy enough to understand even if you haven't played or heard of the games it's based on.

If you've come to learn anything about the indie game movement, you've probably heard of this game. Practically the pioneer of modern indie games on both the console and PC market, Braid is a platformer, and while mayn of my favorite games may be platformers, that has made me very critical of platformers that do come out. It's hard to beat a practically perfected formula without making your own rules, so what's so special about Braid? If you were to ask me that question, I would tell you, "time manipulation." Braid is a time travelling puzzle/platformer with constantly changing powers.
While that may sound a little confusing, it is still a very organized game. Your power changes based on each world. The first world gives you the basics, only giving you the ability to reverse time. Other worlds give you a ring that can slow down anything in an area around it when activated and others even reverse or fast forward the world depending on whether you run left or right. It's interesting to have the mechanics not set in stone and change between each world to keep things fresh and I feel like no other game has truly done that to this extent before or since.
The graphics are great as well, it's an interesting style of game and it mostly looks hand drawn while still having computer generated particle effects and flair thrown in. As for the story, if you want, you can go ahead and read it in the books you pass by ont he entrance to each world, but you might just get the jist of the story when you complete all the puzzles (literally) and play the last level, the story may be interesting and does have a plot twist but it's not as shocking as people say.
Overall, I wouldn't say this is my favorite platformer of all time, but it is most certainly a great game to play and own; that is, if you don't mind thinking a little bit while you're at it.

HL2 also finds a way to take the same game mechanics and combine them in several ways, keeping the expirience fresh the entire time. So why not give it a try? Give in to the hype. Do it.

Download size: about 15 gigabytes
Play time: about 13 hours for the single player campaign
Company of Heroes 2 (COH2) is one of those real time strategy games that is fun but sometimes infuriating even on conscript mode (easy difficulty) because of the seemingly random combat mechanics. It’s been over a year since I played the original COH, but I remember it being almost exactly the same in terms of gameplay and graphics. In COH2 however, you play as the Russians and there seems to be a lot of metagame options (DLC bonuses and things like that). I downloaded the game during the big free weekend and played as much of the campaign as I could finish, so I’m sure I missed a ton of the finer points. This is my impression of the single player campaign.
The game’s story takes place during the US/USSR Cold War and follows a Soviet officer who is facing execution for treason. The officer was a lieutenant during World War 2 and the gameplay missions are flashbacks to his time in the Red army. As the story unfolds you begin to see how the Soviet leadership was willing to sacrifice as many of their men as necessary to achieve victory, and the lieutenant did whatever he could to save them. This conflict between the lieutenant and his superiors caused him to be transferred around between different units, and consequently you get to play in various important battles of the war.
Gameplay in COH2 is pretty much exactly the same as the first game, so if you’ve recently played Company of Heroes 1, you can skip the tutorials. Technically the game is real time strategy, but the focus is tactical, so there’s almost no “base building.” There are 14 missions in total and I think I only had to build structures in 2 of them, and even then it was only 1 or 2 buildings. All of your units come from “off screen” when you build them, and the buildings are pretty much just unlocking the unit for you to summon them. Resources in the game are manpower, munitions, and fuel, all of which come from controlling command points on the map. There isn’t any “harvesting.” The command points are like capture the flag points in most first person shooters where you just need to have a unit standing next to it to capture and hold. Holding a command point sometimes creates a closer “spawn point” for your troops so if you buy a unit, it can get to the front lines faster. Troop and vehicle movement across the map is very slow, so having a closer supply line can be extremely important. Especially since the population cap is usually pretty low. You can’t just swarm the enemy with a massive army, you have to mix up your forces to counter whatever they have.
Like most modern strategy games, every unit type has a weakness and there really isn’t a unit you can mass produce and roll over everyone (no medium tank rush). There is a large variety of unit types you can build and all of them are good for something specific. You can be pushing toward the enemy base and lose your team of engineers, and suddenly you have to stop and wait for another team to replace them, otherwise you’re without repair support. I mentioned the random combat mechanics earlier and what I mean is that most of the shots fired in the game will miss. When troops engage each other, units in cover (hiding behind stuff) will be less likely to take damage. But this is not always true. Sometimes you think you have an awesome elevated position and still get mowed down. Or you can be out in the open and still kill the enemy in their entrenched position. If you’ve played the old Command & Conquer games, you probably remember a tank firing 50 shots and missing the enemy soldier every time. This seems to happen a lot in COH2. Most of your units have some sort of extra ability that can be used for tactical advantage, for example anti-personnel grenades or anti-tank grenades. This means that micro managing your troops can often turn the tide even when you think the enemy has superior numbers.
Pros:
+The game is pretty much as “realistic” as you can get for small scale battles. There is troop movement time, random shots missing, and even a rudimentary morale system. If your men are under heavy fire (like from a machine gun), they can be “pinned down.” They won’t return fire, use special abilities, and can’t move effectively.
+You are forced to use various strategies to accomplish your goals. You cannot mass produce a few types of units and expect to win. You do have a “jack of all trades” type unit (basic conscript) who can pick up weapons found on the battlefield and become more specialized. For example if a mortar team dies, a conscript team can pick up the fallen mortar gun and become a mortar team. The same goes for heavy machine guns and bazooka teams.
Cons:
-The game is quite difficult because of the randomness in the heat of combat. Don’t get me wrong, on easy difficulty you can certainly beat every level, it just might take a lot longer than expected because your troops keep getting picked off. You have to move slowly so all your units can keep up with the main force. Being a hard game is not a bad thing, but it can really♥♥♥♥♥♥you off when you lose 1 guy and have to wait for reinforcements to walk halfway across the map.
-Some of the special abilities don’t seem to work properly. I was never able to summon air strikes when I wanted, and it wouldn’t tell me what was wrong. Was I too close/far? It would just say “you cannot use this ability on that target.” I’m the kind of guy who likes to bombard from long range so it was annoying when I couldn’t use some of these abilities on any of the levels.
All in all the game is fun if you’re into real time strategy, but don’t have 20 click per second micro managing skills like some Starcraft players. It’s pretty slow paced, but I imagine that in multiplayer you have to blitz in the beginning to capture command points. The game has a significant download size, so if you didn’t really like the first Company of Heroes think carefully if you want to give COH2 a try, the games are very similar. Additionally COH2 has over 400 Steam achievements, most of which are grinding (kill x many of this type of unit). Beating the campaign on normal mode would give only about 40. Watch your average game completion % drop!

RTS games typically aren't my thing, but Starcraft and Starcraft II really appealed to me. I thought Warcraft III was pretty decent, and Red Alert 3 had some nice qualities to it. Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War was something that didn't really look all that appealingto me, because all the screenshots made it look like only one race and a small number of unit types. To be fair, it
just one playable race in the single player, and your combatants will all be very similar (though weapon loadouts vary a bit).
I thought those things would put me off once I started playing, but it didn't. The space marines are pretty darn badass, and unlike the aforementioned RTS games I liked, you can actually move
shoot simultaneously with units, which is very helpful, as I'm sure you can imagine. As you progress through missions, more units, vehicles, etc. are unlocked, and it makes the game far more interesting the further in you get. This game actually encourages expansion/aggressive resource acquisition moreso than other RTS games I've played, because all throughout the map are little strategic points (enemy flags) you take over, increasing your supplies for building and bringing in more troops. You can put a turret on the point, and build smaller turrets around it. I liked this quite a bit.
This game actually had me thinking more strategically than any of the games I mentioned at the beginning of this review. I suck at RTS games, but this one encourages playing tactically by having you move up, bit by bit, to capture each strategic point, and the non-vehicle units are squads of guys, each, which makes controlling large numbers of troops easy. In most RTS games, I just spam air units like crazy, get a ball of them, then go raze the enemy base. Here, I had somewhat diverse attack groups, 2-3 of them at a time, moving them up from strategic point to strategic point, using them to reinforce my positions. Your builders are even helpful from beginning to end; not gathering at all, but repairing and building turrets/stations atop strategic points.
I didn't even realize just how many things I liked about this game until I'm just now talking about it. Having completed it, I must mention things I didn't like, though. I really would have liked other races and storylines to play as, even if it meant the storyline for each was much shorter. They could have easily edited the story and cut out several unnecessary missions to save time and money to make other short campaigns with the other races. Speaking of the story, I can't say I found it very compelling, and the space marines, though fun to quote "for the emperor!" much like exclaiming "the king o' the north!" on Game of Thrones, are total jerks who want to kill every non-human they see on sight, and every human they think is tained by chaos...whatever the hell that is.
The lore is something that has me very curious...though I was curious about it before playing this game, too. Having completed it, I don't really feel all that much closer to understanding it. One might say that reading books or something is required for that, and a video game can't convey enough, but Vampire the Masquerade Bloodlines is magnificent at delivering a lore introduction for first-timers to the World of Darkness. I wish DoW had felt the same in terms of lore. That said, one thing I did come out of this game with that I didn't have going into it was the epiphany that it's sci-fi-themed...but you have to think of it in terms of medieval/dark ages paranoia and attitudes. It all suddenly clicked for me when I realized that.
Still, I would've liked to see more alliances and things between the races and other races' perspectives in the campaign by getting to play as the others, possibly even with alternative story outcomes depending on whomever you played as. Characters really draw me into a story as well, and I didn't like any of the characters...well, I did like the over-the-top voice acting for a villain, Sindril, but that's about it. One last complaint: the game takes place on a single planet. Story-wise, this is incredibly important for reasons I won't spoil, but in a setting with a bazillion planets, only visiting one in my introduction to the setting is kinda lame.
Yeah, I know I'm a "heretic" for saying anything not positive about the game, but I don't want to leave a disingenuous review that doesn't help people. It is my hope that anyone who hasn't actually played this game and is wondering whether or not to purchase it will see the pros and cons from my perspective, and use those to determine if he or she might like to get the game. I definitely did like it, though some location variety, more lore, shorter campaigns with different playable single player races, and compelling characters could have potentially toppled the Starcraft games as my favorite RTS series.
