What can be said that haven't already in the reviews? The graphics are amazing, the revamped levels are really nice and overall the content is just better compared to Metro 2033. However there are a few things that bothered me.
FIrst of all the reload animations in survival mode is done sloppy. Instead of having a unique reload animation 4A have slowed down the reload speed making it look like the main character suddenly suffered a stroke. This problem however isn't true for all weapons, some weapon animations look really bad because of it and others are barely noticable.
Second the difficulty in survival mode is unfair. The trick to pull of a game that is good but still difficult is to introduce a good balance, if a death is unjustified its more akin to being unfair than difficult. As an example during the trolley combat you were pretty much forced to repeatedly try to abuse knowing where everything were or else you couldn't complete it (artifical difficulty). The whole design around the trolley combat level was poorly executed and could have been improved significantly (it was already bad in Metro 2033). Another thing is that fighting the librarians was also very unfair, being killed in one hit would have been understandable if you could actually hear the footsteps when it ran. Kiting it around the enviornment without knowing how far or close the beast was is just unfair. It feels like the survival mode was taken to an extreme that only hurt the experience instead of improving it, you die overall way to easy. They managed to struck a perfect balance in the original game, why couldn't they in redux?
Third some changes to both the level design and characters was unneeded. Many times it often felt like having high resolution characters instead of just replacing them would be better. During the opening chapter the NPCs that was roaming the area felt for some reason out of place, like the character design and atmosphere became more Last Light removing much of original games identity (this is just an opinion though). Lastly the level design felt cluttered at times. No having a♥♥♥♥♥♥load of boxes everywhere doesn't feel authentic, it feels just cluttered. There were way to few levels that was open without clutter and that took away a bit from the experience, having open areas can sometimes be breathtaking and work better when fighting. This however can just be a opinion, but it felt very cluttered compared to the original game.
I strongly recommend new players to buy this game at the current price, however if you are a veteran of the series rethink it once or twice. It is not worth 19.99 euro, just slightly less than that.

A fantastic RTS experience that offers a promising base to build from.
At present the game offers an interesting single player campaign as the imperial navy, on a large scale world map (think dawn of war soulstorm). Unlike so many recent RTS games the AI will beat you! I have lost a number of missions on the harder difficulty settings. Instead of this resulting in a game over and thus encouraging 'save scumming' the story line evolves, building your defeat into the narrative and leading to a more nuanced and engaging single player experience. While the story line itself isnt going to win any oscars, and the twists can be a bit telegraphed the way in which it incorporates your defeats makes up for this.
The battles themselves are smaller, personal affairs - think company of heros but with spaceship. With you controlling from 2 - 6 ships in fast paced, ship to ship engagements where facing, positioning and appropirate use of abilities is key. An active "pause" button allows you to slow down time both in single player and mutliplayer ensuring that players of all abilities have the time to effectively micro (and also to appriciative the graphics and explosions).
Multiplayer involves 4 races that each play very differently. Everyone will find a race that appeals to their play styles but you will need to be adaptably as there is always a race that will hard counter your advantages - so adaptability is key. Games last from 3 - 10 minutes, with a hard 20 min time limit. Mission structures are a little hit and miss, particularly convoy missions that involve transport defence BUT this is NOT an e-sport. Games are short, you can easily get in 10 in an hour. Much like a game like hearthstone, you will lose just as regularly as you win but the fast pace and short game time negates any hard feelings.
Balance is being continuely worked on - with patches in the BETA coming regularly.
While the game is a great stand alone product - providing hours of enjoyment (30 hours and still going for me) I am most excited for its post launch dlc and potenial as a platform for further expansion.
The introduction of new fleets, the potenial for extended single player campaigns, the potenial for an army painter introduction. All these offer exciting opportunities to extend the life of this game. While only the former is confirmed this game has a huge ammount of potenial for further development. More importantly none of these things are currently in the game and hidden behind a pay wall. It is clear that the developer is actively working on expanding the experience post launch and for this reason I would be happy to pay for DLC to cover the costs for the time and effort in creating these. UNLIKE WARHAMMER TOTAL WAR where races are being INTENTIONALLY locked off despite being in the game! The only pity is that mod support is not inbuilt - think Xcom 1 rather than Xcom 2.
My advice - buy it and try it. The game provides both bite sized RTS single / multiplayer missions for when you only have 30 minutes to spare AND a lengthy single player campaign / mutiplayer ship development for those with more time.
Anyway enough typing - I am off to play and forge a narrative for my mutiplayer fleet. DEATH TO THE HERETIC! FULL AHEAD AND BRACE FOR RAMMING!

Dying Light was fun. I enjoyed it immensely. The combat system is awesome. My only issue with combat is the QTE forced mid combat. If the game is going to force you into QTE in combat, the least it could do would be to make it either optional or constructive.
A QTE that does not add to gameplay makes it unnecessarily annoying. Like a reload animation that takes forever and for which you can not escape.
The QTE for unlocking boxes I understood. Those made sense. A QTE for dodging an attack though, I didn't understand and it didn't add to the gameplay. It seemed constructed for the purpose of progressing dialogue without allowing the player to deviate from the script. Since the game seems to ride around on the concept of choice, it seems a QTE in dialogue would be the antithesis of choice.
Perhaps it was intended as an artistic expression on the illusion of choice where it does not really exist.
Overall, I loved it. The game was fun, engaging and it stands alone for its combat alone. The parkour is fun and thrilling once you're on a roll.

At the present time I can't recommend this game for a number of reasons as noted below:
- There are a number of bugs that have carried over from the Beta into the game. Although these may get fixed, some of them are really annoying. Examples include UI errors, key binding problems and crashes that occur. A particular favourite crash seems to be when I go over the number of ships "allowed" by beaming in reinforcements using a particular favour.
- There is an interesting single player campaign, but on normal there are insane difficulty spikes. A good example is a mission defending a crippled ship from waves of other ships. Unless you resort to "pin ball" (more later) it is very hard to win with proper tactics.
- "Pin ball" revolves around using high energy turns and thrusters to ram other ships and keep ramming them. The AI is poor at avoiding this tactic, so for example in the aforementioned mission, a cruiser with the 50% ram upgrade was able to take out most of their LCs leaving the crippled ship over 75% HP before it warped out. Without this pin-ball attempt, I was failing it badly. This tactic works in MP as well, although some players are skillful enough now to try and avoid it.
- The graphics are great, but there are problems. Despite having 'Epic settings', I need to Micro my dual graphics cards to smooth out rough edges and deal with zoom problems. Maybe it's my config, but don't normally have to do this.
- The skirmish is limited to 700 points. For those who aren't yet aware, this means a handful (4 to 6 ships). When you try and team up with a friend or AI, this is reduced to 350 points each which in extreme means one capital ship and a tiny escort each.
- Missions in MP and Skirmish include horrors such as "Assassination" or "Data Retrieval" which against a few of the factions (looking at the Point Ears here) are very hard. They are much faster and you have to board their ship to try and win. Kiting Imperial or Ork becomes easy.
Overall, this game reminds me of Star Fleet Command and Star Fleet Command 2, but with less features. Those older games, while set in a different universe offered all the same tricks (bombs, shuttles, high energy turns, cloaking, ship design, etc) while also offering a 6 player multiverse for persistent fights. There were also better modes for MP (e.g. start in a tiny ship and progress upwards as destroyed) that rewarded skill more than BFG. Although BFG is now very far ahead graphically, there is no gameplay innovation, so this is a purchase for people who like the universe (or who don't like Star Trek).
Finally, the MP and Skirmish is poor. 2 v 2 is the max, and you can't matchmake with friends, so it's allways randoms.

What a cracking little gem this game is. Brutal and unforgiving though it is is does manage that rarest of feats in providing an emergent story. The moment you get cocky you're toast. Complaints against the RNG element are not without basis, but then survival is like that. I'm not a massive rogue-like fan and would usually prefer the ability to save, but I realised this game had something special when I died after a 6 hour solid playthrough and smiled rather than rage-quit. The graphics are abysmal, the menus somewhat clunky and I come from an era that had to live through low res graphics and don't find them charming and rretro. But never has a game drawn so heavily on the imagination, and never have I experienced a game that manages to bring a crappy low res hex to life.
The combat is what sets it apart from Project Zomboid, apart from the deep joy of not having to deal with ***king zombies. Whilst somewhat barebones it does make you very careful about how you go about it. In addition there doesn't come a time when easy mobs are trivial bore to swat away. That feral dog can still trouble an unfortunate or over-confident veteran. Every encounter has the potential to send you into a downward spiral if not handled with care.
The luck cuts both ways, I had a very fortunate shot with a sling that set me up nicely with very useful loot, which I lost because I thought it made me king of the hill.
In short if you really want a zombie free realistic survival experience and you have the imagination to paint the picture in your mind rather than have it rendered in technicolor for yo,u then this game is a must buy. The dev deserves high praise for this little cracker and whilst it is by no means perfect and regularly kicks you in the nads there's something special about this one that spectacularly succeeds in  being greater than the sum of its parts.

I am a huge fan of the Dead or Alive series, and can legitimately say it has gameplay loads more fun and accessable then more "serious" fighters like Tekken or Street Fighter as there are interactive environments and you can pull off long combos with ease.  Dead or Alive 5 was my very favorite game in the series to the point where I was willing to shell out large amounts of money for  both of its glorified expansions.  I am very disappointed however in the quality of the PC port of DOA5 Last Round.  The graphics look last gen, online play is unavailable for the first couple of months upon release, and there are as of yet no achievements.  I didn't know this going in as I preordered it soon after finding out about it as my PC is the only system I have that can play "next gen" titles.  This does not ruin the fact that the core gameplay is very fun, but it is a disappointment, and seemingly a result of rushed and sloppy porting.  There are a massive amount of costumes, levels and characters in this verion and even an extra move or two.  Some of the costumes are quite nice, such as the casual, halloween, and ninja outfits, but some seem incredibly similar (I get that fanservice has always been a part of the appeal to many, but how many different bikinis do you really need?)  Overall, If you haven't played DOA offline yet, it may warrant purchasing as of now, but for those wanting the full experience off the get go, I would highly recommend waiting a couple of months or buying the PS4 or XBONE version (last gen consoles' online communities are probably very dead).  9/10 for the gameplay, 6/10 for the port quality.

Shank is a bad game.
There's not much story here.  Your woman is killed and you're looking for revenge.  End of story.
This is a beat'em up game.  You options are a weak attack, heavy attack, shoot, jump, grapple, throw grenades, block and dodge.  You'll find occasional pickups like health and extra grenades.  There are new weapons you'll find along the way.  The guns are distinct but I have absolutely no idea if any of the various new heavy weapons you find actually do anything different from one another.  When you run into enemies, the camera usually traps you in that area until you finishing killing all the enemies.  There's some variety in enemies but not a whole lot.  Normal enemies mainly come in 3 forms, those who focus on melee, shooting, or both.  There are larger enemies who you can't grapple.  These enemies sometimes wield miniguns, grenade launchers, shields, or sometimes just charge through the fight area and hurt you if they run into you.  There are bosses as well, most of them follow the same exact recipe.  Discover weakness, exploit weakness over and over and over until they die.  The game occasionally throws in platforming sections for no reason, I would guess for the purpose of artificially extending the game as it's quite short (Took me about 2 ½ - 3 hours on normal).
I really don't have much positive to say about this game, I suppose the graphics are nice and somewhat distinct.
So let's hit the many negatives.  The game is too easy on normal and too annoying on hard (note I did not say hard).  Normal has checkpoints all over the place so dying places you pretty much wherever you were at.  Hard has no checkpoints, so if you die, you go back to the beginning of the stage and get the joy of fighting all the same enemies over again.  Bosses have their own stages, so dying on a boss  puts you back at the start of the boss fight.
Hard is annoying for 3 reasons.  1. You don't really get better as you play through this game as there's not much to get better at, so you won't necessarily do any better fighting enemies you've already fought before.  2.  Some of the later levels have random crap you have to deal with. One level has an enemy shooting grenades at you through part of the level.  The board after that has a guy who shoots rockets at you pretty much throughout the whole stage.  Both the grenade launcher guy and rocket guy do significant damage if they do happen to hit you and it'll mostly be luck whether they hit you or not.  Also they shoot at you during some of the platforming sections while you're over insta death pits.  The next to last level has you in some cavern or something and rocks start falling from the ceiling.  All these levels suffer from the same problem, the camera is too zoomed in on you, so you barely have time to react to the grenades/rockets/rocks until it's too late, especially if you're running forward or have already jumped somewhere.  The biggest problem though is reason number 3.
3.  The game is full of cheapshots that on normal are survivable but are not survivable on hard since you take more damage.  Usually you can sit there and combo enemies over and over until they die, but sometimes they randomly attack and hit you through your combo.  I have no idea how the game decides when it's going to happen but it's very annoying.  Nothing like slicing through enemies and suddenly a dog is randomly on top of you biting you somehow.  I've had guys somehow have time to pull out guns and shoot me while in between stabbings.  Somehow had an uzi chick unload her clip into me point blank while I was stabbing her.  Especially cool is when the larger enemies decide to randomly attack you through your combo and start comboing you for a ton of damage.  If you're killing enemies up against the edge of the screen, new enemies can come in from there and start attacking you from off screen.  Especially cool is when large enemies spawn out there and start hitting you for a bunch of damage or decide to run in and just run you over with you having no way to react to them.
The game has cutscenes that occur in a small box in the upper right while you're playing.  The problem is that they like to pop these up during parts where you're fighting enemies.  I'm not sure if the developers are aware of this, but A. I'd like to watch these cutscenes and B. It's physically impossible to both watch the cutscenes and successfully fight a bunch of enemies at the same time.  I have no idea why some idiot decided they didn't want to have the cutscenes occur during parts where you're not fighting enemies.  The voice acting and dialogue are really bad too.
The first time you see a pit, you have no idea if it's safe or not to go down, so you might decide to explore and find out.  The first one is empty, the second one has a health pickup.  So naturally you'd assume you're going to be rewarded for exploring pits.  Get further into the level, see a third pit, decide to hop down into it to see if there's anything cool in it.  Oh, there's something cool in it alright, insta death.  So the game teaches you to check pits but then throws in insta kill pits..... and there's absolutely no way to distinguish whether a pit is insta death or not.  Great game design guys.  Also of note is that if you're near full life and find a health pickup, you might leave it behind to pick up later.  Sometimes the game lets you move backwards to get it, other times it won't let you move back at all, and there's no way to tell which one it'll do.  Again, nice game design guys, way to be consistent.
The game has QTEs that happen throughout the game.  The problem is that instead of showing you the corresponding button, they show you a small picture of an action associated with a button.  The pictures are really small so it's hard to distinguish details, several of them look very similiar, and you don't get a lot of time to react to them.  So you'll often takes hits because of this and you'll often be pausing the game to go into the controls to see what the hell action the picture is associated with.
The controls are really, really bad.  This is a beat'em up, so it's pretty important not only for the block/dodge buttons to have a high priority but also for them to actually work.  You'll be attacking enemies, see an enemy is getting ready to attack you and press the block/dodge button but your character continues throwing attacks for another 2 seconds instead of blocking/dodging.  Even worse is that dodging quite often doesn't work correctly.  I've watched enemies hit me while my guy is flashing white (dodge animation) and watched quite often as bullets I'm attempting to dodge still hit and damage me.  So I'm not sure if dodge is actually suppose to prevent damage or not.  Using grenades is an aggravating task.  If you're standing still Shank will toss it right in front of himself, but if you happen to be moving or turning at all and throw one, he tosses it across the length of the screen, and he does this at a height that it will go over the top of every enemy until it bounces off the far side of the camera, even if they're 3 feet in front of him.  The grapple controls are also pretty poor.  When you grapple, Shank lunges at the enemy but if you're too close, he'll just go flying right through them, so occasionally you go flying through enemies off ledges to your death or into something that'll hurt you.
On a personal note, Shank's wrists really bother me every time I look at them.  They look like they should snap in half if someone would touch them.  Anyway, this game is bad.  Don't play it.

I wanted to like Braid. It's a game that begs to be liked: beautiful, painting-like art, soothing soundtrack, and ingeniously crafted puzzles. It has a complex, well-written storyline that requires a series of intelligent inferences to follow, as well as a whole horde of subtext and interpretation articles written by people far more intelligent than me. It's an intimidating game, too: a game that birthed an entire genre and has become a sort of initiation into indie gaming for many players out there. It's one of those games that, when you're having a conversation about small developer teams and the rise in indie gaming, you just can't ignore.
A lot of people make the mistake of equating an industry changing game with a good game, and while Braid is, in truth, a work of art, I struggle to qualify it at as a truly enjoyable experience as a game. The mechanics of Braid revolve around the idea of time-manipulation as a core gameplay element. When your character moves forward, time moves forward. If your character moves backwards, time moves backward. But what starts as a relatively simple and unique method of creative puzzle solving turns into something grotesquely twisted and almost indecipherably complicated. Hard puzzles in a game should never be a bad thing, but puzzles that are so far out of the realm of my thinking that they become nigh unsolvable aren't fun, they're incredibly off-putting.
On top of the intensely challenging puzzle-solving aspect of Braid, the game also identifies as a platformer that often tests the reflexes and timing of the player holding the controller. As the game progresses the player must become more and more precise with their control of the main character. Unfortunately, this, in combination with the difficult puzzles, made for a game that I could only play half of—any of the puzzles that weren't too farfetched for me to understand were instead doubly frustrating because they required a precision and sense of timing that my fumbling hands just couldn't seem to fathom.
Altogether, Braid's the kind of game whose phenomenal story is somewhat ruined by its gameplay for me. It's the sort of game that I would rather watch someone play through on YouTube and then read about it on the wiki afterwards than sit down with the controller myself. It's a summary game—the kind of thing that when you step back and look at it as a whole, it's a wonderfully enlightening experience, but that experience is drowned out by an incredibly steep learning curve and absurdly convoluted puzzle solutions. Playing Braid is an uphill climb and while the view at the top of that mountain is pretty great, it's not quite worth the struggle to get to it in the first place.

Shank is a side scrolling beat em up with a battle system highly reminiscient of something like Devil May Cry. As far as combat mechanics go, it's top notch,with plenty of depth for fansofvery technical action games (I did play with a key board and didn't have too much trouble after rebinding the keys to something more comfortable than the terrible defaults, although it doesn't replace a controller if you're looking to chase astupidly high combo.
You have plenty of weapons at your disposal to gruesomely dispatch your enemies,including a chainsaw, machetes, a shotgun, and more. It's worth noting that even though the game is very violent, with a gorgeous art style that reminds me a lot of Samurai Jack, there's not really any gore, so even though there's loads of blood, there's no visible damage on the bodies of the enemies. Switching weapons on the fly and getting a high combo is utterly satisfying and makes you feel like a badass. There are some cool action set pieces as well, like running through a collapsing mine or dodging rockets on the roof of a church.
The story, though, is perfunctory at best. Shank is on a quest for revenge against some people who wronged him, but none of the characters have any real development or anything. It's a shame that the writing doesn't live up to the production values, because this could have been something special otherwise.
Still, it's an enjoyable, if short, ride that's worth a look if you can get it on sale or have ten bucks burning a hole in your pocket.

Dawn of War is a bespoke strategy game based on the Warhammer 40k mythology.
Four races (Space Marines, Chaos Space Marines, Orks, and Eldar) are playable in the ‘Skirmish’ mode, with their own quirks and mechanics. The game involves several innovations (for its time), such as:
Cover: infantry take less damage in these areas
Requisition and strategic points: resource gathering does not involve mining, hooray!, and
Morale: A squad with high morale can continue fighting at full health for ages, whilst a squad with low morale would ‘break’ and scatter
I thought the Campaign was actually a real gem. The story was interesting and the characters surprisingly deep for a RTS game. I enjoyed the twists and the clever way in which the player could play against the three other races through the storyline. Props go to the voice actors for the Chaos Lord Bale (hilariously evil) and Sorcerer Sindri (devious and manipulating both friends and enemies). I also thought some of the missions were incredibly fulfilling.
The game itself was pretty much exactly how I imagined a Warhammer 40k game to be. The Space Marines were suitably heroic, the Chaos Space Marines were like dark reflections of their Loyalist Brothers, the Orks were brutal and all about numbers, and the Eldar were mysterious and difficult to pin down.
Standout units included:
The Dreadnought, which can smash infantry out of the way, or even impale them on its arm and execute it brutally by spinning them around and flinging them away.
The Whirlwind, which I used to hold a Control Point from multiple points of ingress. Their huge range and infantry-scattering abilities meant I could break enemy charges from afar.
The Chaos Obliterator, which trumps even the Terminator as the ultimate heavy infantry. Those lascannons!
This game is awesome in both Campaign and Skirmish mode. Play it!

Dawn of War was an absolute sensation when it first came out.  It shook up the RTS genre with a ton of innovations:
*  Players had to take and hold territory to gain the resources they needed to make units.  This practically eliminated rushing and forced players out of their bases.
*  You trained squads, not individual units.  This made managing large armies much easier.
*  You could reinforce your squads in the field, rather than wait for new units to come from your base.
*  You only had you to eliminate the enemy's main fortress to defeat them.
All of these changes produced a visceral, fast-paced game rather than the staid, hour-long grinds of previous RTS games.  Couple this with the amazing Warhammer 40,000 universe and an excellent campaign with some amazing voice acting and you've got an RTS for the ages, despite its flaws.
Flaws?  Oh, yes.  Nothing is perfect.  The pathfinding can be quite bad at times, especially when your army gets large.  And when you do get a large army, you're going to wish you could zoom out the camera just a little bit more to help you manage it.  The base game and the Winter Assault addon only run in 4:3 resolutions and they don't support multi-monitor well (though both of these problems were fixed in the Dark Crusade and Soulstorm addons).
But honestly, there is still nothing quite like firing this game up and making glorious war in the name of the Emperor, or causing a wake of destruction in service to Khorne, or crumping some heads as part of the Ork WAAAGH!
Oh, and the Eldar are in there as well, but I never play them.  Stupid pointy-headed space elves...

The game is actually a really good RTS.  Runs fine on my 750ti and AMDFX6300 at Epic settings. The ships themselves are really well made, although I feel the textures aren't as good as what I saw in the preview videos on YouTube.
I'm enjoying the campaign, it feels like an actual campaign and not just something tacked on. I also like how some missions are designed to have you be defeated which is great as lets be honest we've had far too many campaigns in games where you win every battle.
Great thing though is that defeat doesn't end the campaign nor does it make you restart the battle.  The campaign continues regardless.
Victory however is really well rewarded.  You can get upgrades for your ships, favours from different factions which gives ships different bonuses, abilities and awesome paint jobs.
In short the campaign is probably one of the best I've played in a long time.  One thing I would have liked to have seen is a campaign for different races as not everyone is a fan of the imperial navy.
In terms of gameplay its a solid and complex RTS. I don't want to cover everything here, but lets just say you have a lot of control over how your fleet moves, how and what it attacks and so on. This is the first time I've seen an RTS have mechanics like this and they are a welcomed addition and I hope other RTS games implement these types of mechanics.
Battlefleet Gothic Armarda is a solid RTS with robust mechanics and a great campaign mode. If you've played games such as Empire At War or are a W40k fan then you have no excuse to not get this game.

FTL is a game that challenges your multi-tasking ability and emotionality stability while being thoroughly entertaining even in utter defeat.
Few games that I can remember leave me overjoyed at my prospects of success one minute to staring at the GAMEOVER screen in shocked disbelief at my inability to adapt.
Simple, creative, rock solid and tantalizingly hopeful, FTL is a game that can challenge you with meaningless badges or achievements. After hours of grueling game play and shrewd decision making, every jump to a new sector will have your pulse pounding when you release the mouse button.
While I sometimes feel, I am cursed or the game hates me, I keep coming back for more. Not because the CPU players change the rules, cheats or somehow does the impossible, no - that would be too simple. FTL makes you weigh each decision, every chance and if you want more challenge the game will beat you down as you wish.
Highly recommended to everyone but never accept the easy path, go for the harder ships and settings. Feel the panic, the heat of the flames and rename all your characters so their deaths are more crushing.
Live, hope, jump and play FTL until they pull your hands from the keyboard.

Cons*
Unlockables that you cannot change little control over unlocks.

Example if you're a frog and you spot 3 Pillars of essense (used to upgrade animals), and the whole point of moving in a large group. They all need various combinations of Animals, players are using in the game.
So you're a Frog you're at the middle back of the group, you can call out that you spot a Pillar(essense) all day long. Unfortunatly more often then not, the group will ignore you, and follow the Goat player. Even if that player is blindly leading the group around in circles, and eventually does nothing but jumps off the end of the level, over and over, after wasting your time on a wild goose chase.
Performance*
very bad optimization somehow (such simple objects,textures) low FPS reported from most users.
End point*
In the end of the day I recomend everyone atleast try it out. Needs a better way of tagging points of interest for large hoards to find.

First Impressions:
Combat is easy to use, hard to master with a wide variety of combos utilizing several different melee and shooting weapons, light attacks, heavy attacks, grapples, dodges, juggles, and jumps. Most enemy attacks can be dodged, blocked, or inturrupted. I rarely felt like i was forced to take damage which is a huge plus. Health on the normal difficulty is plentiful and respawn points are forgiving. In most situations, you can go left to gather health and other drops you didn't collect earlier. Combat is a bit repetative, but the constantly changing enemy variations/combinations and environments keep it engaging so far. The story is told with beautiful art which would be enough for the price of admission, even if the story didn't have me hooked to see what's next.
Final Thoughts:
While i enjoyed my time with this game, i couldn't honestly recommend it to anyone looking for anything other than a pleasent time waster. The story is cliche and tiresome and the combat is very samy towards the end where bosses are damage sponges that you repeat the same 3-6 hit combo over a dozen times. The biggest detractor is missing out on a large portion of the story without multiplayer. 6/10, an enjoyable pocket sized time sink, buy on sale.
Criticisms:
No training room- Early difficulty is simple enough, but i firmly believe that ALL fighing games should have a room with an immortal enemy/ infinate respawning enemies that you can practice all your moves on and expiriment.
Multiplayer campagin is a seperate story from the single player. To some this is a plus, but without anyone to play it with, i'll have to go to youtube to see it.
Dogs are an enemy type. I'm not a big fan of animal violence but understand that in the universe this game takes place in, using attack dogs is not to be unexpected.
Every QTE i have encountered uses some symbol with a red background. I instinctually press the red B button on my 360 controller, but every time it is in vain. From the multiplayer mode, i know that the game can recognize different controlers. It's a shame that it can't customize the input symbol for the controller. As i play more the sybols will be more easily identafiable, but it's hard to overwrite years of twitch muscle memory as simple as "Red Button=B"
Game features full button remapping, but doing so with a controller alone is either impossible or so obtuse that i am unable to figure it out. This interface could be greatly improved.

I oftentimes find myself reading the reviews for a game and seeing them start with "Well, if there was a neutral choice I'd choose it!"
I myself have a lifestyle of "meh you're alrite but you're also pretty sh
te." I could consider myself the personification of passivity. I also think a "neutral" decision on a game is redundant and counter-productive. What I'm going to say INSTEAD is that you should pick this up when it's heavily discounted.
Klei is a developer that has never ceased to amaze me with games such as Mark of the Ninja and Don't Starve/DST. Shank was one of their first games and also arguably their worst (I have not played their newest project, Shank's sequel, or Invisible Inc.)
The story is fine and gets its point across, and it's pleasant in its own self-aware intentionally-cliche Kill Bill-esque plot. I feel it's somewhat rushed/not really explained that well but it was a small indie project by a small company at the time and it's easy to piece together once you're a decent way into it.
For a beat 'em up the combat is fairly simplisitc, and it doesn't HAVE to be complex. I see this weird trend among games like Shank and Castle Crashers where people really, REALLY like to b
tch about the simple take on combat. Not every game needs a combat system with 50 combos, 20 items, and 10 ways to approach a situation. Shank knows what its combat system details, and it does it well.
Mechanic-wise the free-running minimal-interaction parkour is pretty nice. The Meat District is easily the most parkour-based level and it's decent, the slow-down effect is helpful, yet not annoying. The weapon variety you eventually get is nice and actually does allow you to set up combos nicely, albeit simplistic ones (for my opinion on that, refer to the above paragraph). Although I will say whoever's idea it was to bind the pick-up-healing-item button to the same button you use to do a normal knife attack is daft and I have ZERO idea as to what they were thinking.
Difficulty-wise the game's somewhat alrite.The hand-holding on the boss fights is insanely frustrating however. If I die to a boss ONCE you don't have to give me a f
cking pop-up telling me the trick to defeating him/her. On that subject, some of the bosses are hot garbage. The ATV's attacks are insanely inconsistant and nearly undodgable. Toro is a reskin of the fake Butcher, for instance. Also Angelo sucks. Both the fight itself and the garbage villa level thing before him.
My main problem with this game's difficulty is the hard mode. It basically removes checkpoints and makes a boss' prompt insanely fast. This is particularly present in the Cassandra boss fight. She has an attack that you have to react to in a second, maybe less, and that attack does about a quarter of your health. She has no tells either. Tie this in with the fact that somebody decided to bind normal melee and pick-up to the same button (resulting in you oftentimes accidently using one of the two healing items in the boss area) and you get an absolute dumpster-fire of a fight that made me uninstall the game.

This game is something else. If you aren't good at making your own fun, if you require a more linear game, if you hate exploring or gathering or could care less about being social, this game is not for you. The other Shelter games (including Paws, which doesn't have 'Shelter' in the title but is included in the lineup) are singleplayer and fairly linear (even Shelter 2 has a beginning and an end) so you'll be perfectly satisfied. This game is not a cheaper version of the other Shelter games. Honestly, if you want a beautiful, emotional, mothering game then PLEASE buy one of the other games, they are amazing and worth the money. This game is a reward for fans of the Shelter series who already own the other games and you can get the fullest out of it if you buy the others, see it as a reward for fans of the series and less as a 'pay-to-win' game.
This game is for fans of the animals, graphics and lovely music of the Shelter games that long for something quiet, relaxing and social. It's for people who are tired of swearing and bullying in multiplayer games and just want to have fun with other people in a very simple, rudimentary way. It's for the people who can enjoy something simple, something special, who can enjoy a game of puffball soccer or who-can-pop-the-most-puff-mushrooms, or who just want to unwind after work.
It is said that this game lacks features, and that's totally untrue. There's a big, beautiful world to explore, there are TONS of emotes and skins to unlock (for each animal, too), there are lots of animals to choose from, there is a rudimentary but pleasing form of communication (little animal pictograms) and there are people to play with. If you use what's given to you instead of complaining about everything this game isn't, then you will have a good time. Relax, and enjoy: you don't need to keep looking over your shoulder to see if that eagle is going to murder you or your loved ones.
9/10, fully recommended but it's not for everyone.
Note: I haven't experienced a grain of lag in this game, and my computer isn't particularly high-end (just a Mac desktop). Your computer might, but they are trying to fix the lag so it's your choice to either risk it or wait and see if it's fixed.

I've been part of the Beta since day one, and have been playing the campaign since it was released. I must say I'm very, very pleased about what I've bough, and I highly recommend it not only to every fan of Warhammer 40,000, but to anyone who likes tactical RTS games, naval games, spaceship games, and sci-fi in general. Let me list the reasons.
- A great port of the tabletop game to the RTS genre. It is highly based on the rules of the original game, namely ship positioning, fire arcs, manouvering, space hazards, special orders... while at the same time adding new functionalities.
- A beautiful depiction of the inmensely rich Warhammer 40,000 universe. Attention to detail is everywhere: descriptions, UI, voice quotes... It represents the setting as no game has done since the original Dawn of War, about 10 years ago.
- Graphics and sound are just impressive. You will see shields rippling from impacts, chunks flying off hulls, destroyed parts of the ships' hulls (which also means losing equipment on the ships: yes, you can target specific ship systems), gorgeous space landscapes, boarding parties boring into ships...
- Gameplay is deep and can be quite competitive. Make no mistake: this is a Tactical RTS game, which means lots of micromanagement, and where each ships' position and orientation is key, not to mention the abilities. It takes some time to learn, but it's quite intuitive once you do. Also, by pressing spacebar, you can slow down the game's pace to a crawl, which can help you to react to very complex situations if you need it. This feature is also available in Multiplayer, although with a time restriction to avoid trolling.
- The single-player campaign is lengthy and rich as well. You will have to defend a whole sector (star cluster) against several enemies: the Chaos forces, local rebellions, and Ork and Eldar pirate attacks. You decisions will matter. Those players who prefer playing campaigns over MP will enjoy it a lot.
- Both in SP and MP you will be the admiral of a fleet. There is a progression system: you start as a lowly new admiral, but as you earn renown, you will get more ships and upgrades for your ships. You won't lose ships permanently (unless in super-hard mode in the campaign), but destroyed ships will not be available for 2 games unless spending points on priority repairs. Personally I like this mechanic, as it forces you to think like an admiral. Is it worth losing your entire fleet if the enemy overwhelms you? No! Better warp out: you will earn points by losing as well. This also means you should carefully select your upgrades, and which ships to bring to each battle depending on the objectives. It encourages tactical thinking, and I appreciate that.
- The support the developers (and even the publishers!) have given to their game during the Beta stage (and before that)  has been enormous. They have worked really hard to make the game as good as possible for release. They've listened to the players' issues, both technical and of gameplay, and have updated the game many times before release. Such dedication to their playerbase and the game they've created is much respectable, and something sadly unusual these days. Rest assured that their support will continue: in their own words, "release is not the end, but the beginning". They will be adding more races and factions from the W40k universe via DLCs, and I'd say they also want to add more campagins.
- To continue the previous point, just have a look at the Early Adopters program. By buying the game within 2 moths after release (or having pre-ordered it), you will get the 2 first faction DLCs (Space Marines and a yet-unveiled 6th faction) for FREE once they are released. How cool is that?! Oh and by the way...
- ... that 6th faction was not originally devised to be free too. It was once the devs/publishers realised they couldn't meet the original release date (March 23rd) without releasing a half-baked game. So they swallowed up and postponed release a month later, extending the Early Adopters program to the 6th faction as well. How many game developers of today would do that? How many would see it would be better to push back release to improve the game? I say, only a few.
So that's it for my review, for now. Again I say: I highly recommend this game.
NOTE: make sure you buy the game either on Steam or at the official webpage. Some people are having issues with being elligible to the Early Adopters rewards when buying from 3rd party websites like GMG. If you want to buy it from those, make sure they do include those rewards before buying!
Edit: after a series of patches and updates, it is now possible to play with friends, competitive MP with no progression (full fleet from the start), among more functionalities.

Don't let my hours fool you.
I've been working with this application on and off for the last 10 years. I just added this thing via Steam so I could leave a review.
I've probably got around 20,000 hours on it. At least.
I use this application for my job as a 3D artist. This application right now is giving me an income, I owe it thanks.
Lets look at some of the features:
- Free!
- One of the best 3D modelling tools available, commercial or otherwise, with N-Gon support
- Comes with 2 rendering engines, the Blender Internal scanline renderer and Cycles, a photorealistic pathtracer, with CPU and GPU support, in viewport previews, flexible powerful node based material editor, etc
- Powerful rigging tools, even automatic rig generators, flexible bones, weight/rigging mirroring, etc.
- 2D and 3D Animation, things like automated walk cycles along paths, NLA editor, IK, sound syncing, almost every property can be animated, etc
- 3D Sculpting, Dynamic topology, mirrored sculpting, texture based brushes
- UV unwrapping tools, different kinds of UV projections, alignment tools, etc
- Texture painting in viewport directly onto meshes.
- Node based compositor for renders, colour management, many filter effects and camera effects, etc
- Video editor, Camera and Object tracking, etc
- Nearly everything is multithreaded and has GPU acceleration available, including rendering, compositing, subsurf, physics, hair, etc.
- Powerful simulation tools for: fluid, smoke, hair (with 'combing' tools), cloth, fire, rigid bodies, soft bodies, particles
- Powerful particle animation system with support for fluid/boid/swarm/other kinds of particles.
- A built in game engine and ability to export interactive applications, with Bullet physics, 3D audio, normal mapping, etc.
- Multiwindow/Multipanel highly customisable user interface
- Completely free and open source.
On top of this there are more plugins available than you can count, the developers regularly add new features, improve the UI, add speed optimisations, fix bugs, expand file support, there's a huge active passionate community around Blender, and there are free P2P Blender render farms for rendering large animations even. And it's free!
There are other applications out there which can do one function or another better than Blender in specific areas, but few applications have such a broad scope of functionality all in one little neat package. There's very little this application can't do!

Yes!  After a couple months of Beta it has finally launched!  Having played the tabletop, this game holds an extremely sentimental place in my heart.  They did a great job of staying true to the core of the tabletop game while also converting it to a RTS.   Perhaps the best part of the game is that feeling of the Warhammer world.  The races are portrayed in all their glory.   Of course Orks is Best! :-D
So far the reviews hold at a "Very Positive", which is exactly what I would give the game.  A complete recommend.  If you've never played a Warhammer 40k game, this is a fantastic intro, as they do such a great job replicating the ambience of the Warhammer world.  A Grim dark future of War.
What takes some getting used to is the massive amount of micro-management of your fleet.  The game moves just quick enough to keep you on your toes.  You can always engage the "Tactical Cogitators" which slows the game down to a crawl.  However, between ship facing, torpedoes, lining up shots, squadrons, ramming, bombs, mines, asteroids, and people who have no soul that play Eldar... there is always something to react to.  As you continue through the ranks, you can field a larger fleet and it gets more intense (obviously).
Besides that, which is needed, the game plays phenomenally well.  The graphics are incredible.  Looking around the battlefield is picturesque.  The celestial bodies encircle your grand engagement as spectators to the death of thousands.  Your mile long ships unleashing a hell storm of destruction upon your worthy foes.  The terrible realization that, despite your best attempts, your ship has suffered a mortal blow and explosions rip through space sending the souls of the damned to their maker.  The fleet management reflects this with repair times, so each vessel holds importance.  A loss is not permanent, but it can be crippling to your fleet.
Guide your vessels with courage, Lock on with your mighty weapons of war, and pray to the Emperor that you live to see the next day for this is Battlefleet Gothic Armada and the universe is vast and no one will miss you.

This is my very favorite MMO.
It's unlike any other I've played because there's no combat, no quests, and no main goal of any kind. You can run around as animals and collect flowers and shards for points and unlocks, or just lounge around by other players with no need to rush. Playing as different animals is fantastic- this game is a definite one for animal enthsiasts.
The visuals for both the world and its creatures are unique and made up of colored shapes fitting together like puzzle pieces, which really fits the chill nature of the game. The music and sound effects are nature-y and calm (except the annoying but amusing goat and lynx calls. You know which ones I'm talking about).
Meadow highly encourages cooperation and camaraderie. There's no text chat at all, so the usual spam, rage, and "selling this this this this this this and this" copy pasted 50 times is gone. That's not to say that you have to greet other people, you can ignore them and teleport back to the main tree or your set home if another player is bothering you (plus there are angry and goodbye emotes).
The greatest thing about this communication is how it breaks the language barrier. I've seen tons of usernames in different languages, but with emotes we all speak the same tongue.
Next is the obelisks. Obelisks can only be opened by multiple players and contain the colorful shards that unlock more emotes (red), skins (blue), and new animals (yellow). It was brilliant to add these, and even better that everyone gets the same amount of shards instead of forcing a greedy rush to be the person that grabs them. This incentive to play in groups has led to many of the best moments with other people and the greatest explorations of the game world.
And man do I love the game world, you'll learn quickly when you play that it's split into beautiful areas like the western winter plain and southern fall forests. Although there's no in-game map, this adds a bit of mystery and excitement when you explore places you've never seen (if you ever get really lost, there are player-made maps too). And once you learn landmarks it feels great to know your way around - you get really immersed in the world.
Finally is the community: I don't think I've ever been encouraged to help a community more than this one. Because of Meadow I made the first guide I've ever done and spent lots of time in game getting the info I needed. Despite playing solo for that, it was also one of the most memorable times as well (and I learned the map really well in the process). There's no race to the top unless you want the highest essence score, but for once in a game it's worth taking tmore time to help others.
Because of the recent summer sale the game has grown, and I really want to see it keep growing. I can see several more animals in the future and new mechanics as well, so here's to this game's future. No matter when it dies (which, as an online game, it will eventually), I'll never forget Meadow.

FTL is by far, one of my favorite games, even after looking at the fact that everything ends up comming down to RNG and that the flagship definetly has an advantage over you.
First off, I have only beaten the game 8 times during my aproximate 400 runs and it can get a little frustrating. (Especially when runing into a star or pulsar star early.) However, since a decent run can take up quite some time, frustration can die off easily. Keep in mind, this game is supposed to be hard.
I've seen people complain how the random nature of the game tends to throw strategy out the window and I do not agree with this at all. The randomness ends up brings its own kind of strategy. You end up having to adapt to what the game throws at you. Got stuck in a Mantis sector? Upgrade your doors. Need to pass through a Rock sector? Upgrade your engines. Zoltans destroying you with lasers? Upgrade your sheilds. Everything in the end has some sort of counter to it. Even if it seems pointless to upgrade something to deal with one enemy just keep in mind that the final boss has more or less everything to throw at you.
Then there is the random loot. This is what I'm guessing to be the biggest, or atleast bigger complaint. You can end up going whole runs without cloaking or missile weapons or ion weapons or really anything that isn't normaly on your ship. You more or less have to deal with what you get. You can adapt to this in some ways, such as getting more dodge to compensate for lack of cloaking, but most of these tend to be sold in shops as well, meaning you might not even get anything to help against high level shields. The chances of this happening is not too low and can be improved during gameplay. (Spending more time searching for stores rather than looting) In all, your first few stores might not have what you need, but the farther you get the more opportunities will arise for you to finally get what you need.
Even though this game is very random at times, I still find it fun. I can deal with the mild frustration at times and the seemingly impossible boss at the end. In the end, all that matters is what decisions you make and what you do when life gives you limes instead of lemons.

Edit: As of 12/11/17 I have been made aware of multiple severe bugs that can prevent you from progressing far into the game. Hopefully these will be fixed in a timely manner, so more people can enjoy a bug free experience.

As a game, this is an admirable failure.  As an artistic experience, it succeeds, but not in a way that makes for a playable video game.  The bottom line, however, is that you almost certainly should not play it.
The writing is excellent, and not just by video game standards.  The dev could write good sci-fi fiction.
The game has permadeath.  The core game loop is good, but clunky.  Progress is punishing.  It takes 10 real life minutes to make a bunch of arrows, which aren't particularly effective, but they're what you get.  I recommend the sling.  Even taking all precautions, you can die instantly because a dogman or blue frog pops up at close proximity or in your sleep and kills you in one round.  You realize that there's nothing you could have done, and often there's nothing you can learn from to prevent it in the future.
Because getting a character into survival state, which allows exploring the story, takes several hours, the clunkiness becomes an insane ping-pong of clicks (left screen, right screen, ten ping-pong clicks to sleep; seven to scavenge a single building; repeat until you die or quit, then repeat some more).  I view this as an artistic statement about life that, like the sudden and unpreventable deaths, cannot be understood until wearily experienced.
The problem is that the game breaks into choose-your-own-adventure encounters that are both the reason to play the game and what breaks it.  A majority of the options in these encounters will instantly end your game.  Single encounters will have branching choices, the majority of which will end your game.  They cannot be predicted.  Because of their branching nature and the immense real life time to get to the point where you see them, you cannot realistically finish the game.  Further, the game hard-limits your exploration; you get X number of choices, then time's up.  The internet is full of gnashing and wailing, true believers who spent over 100 hours on the game begging the dev to release the text files of the end-game, which he basically did by telling people what to search for in the XML files.
If you do buy it, some guy made a batch file that acts as a save-game manager.  Get it.

Shank is a lot of fun. It's a sidescrolling beat 'em up released in 2010 with an over the top, violent graphic novel aesthetic. It has a bunch of different weapons, some costume unlocks and moves along at a very fast pace.
It is however, not without issues. Although the movement and combat is mostly pretty fluid and feels great, there's some platforming sections that feel unresponsive. Not to the point of frustration but I imagine if you're playing on hard (where there are no checkpoints), dying here would be pretty damn infuriating. It's also extremely short at about 2.5 hours. It has local co-op but that requires friends and I haven't met any of those yet, so if you're expecting a game with a tonne of replay value you're definitely looking in the wrong place. I also don't really like how similar a lot of the "counter buttons" look, as most of them just have Shank standing or doing a pose and there were 2 that are barely different but require a completely different button to counter with.
All in all though, I think Shank is a pretty good game. It has flaws but they're not glaring or extremely off-putting. It's short, fun and fast-paced. The story is cheesy and has pretty mediocre voice acting but it's such a small focus of the game that it really doesn't change my opinion on it. The actual gameplay and feel of it is quite good even 7 years after release. Get it on sale, it's worth a playthrough.

Battlefront II is a pretty damn good game. It ranks incredibly highly on my favorite games of all time, and I still think it is one of the best FPS games ever made. Even despite the awful first experience of not being able to play the game, once I figured out how it was like playing with some of your old child toys again. The nostalga was real with this game. Honestly  I don't like the prequels at all (along with most people with half a brain) but I think most people agree that at least two really good things came out of the prequels, a) the musical score by John Williams b) the games. Battlefront II is no exception to that. The clone wars era battles are just as fun as the galactic civil war battles, and it truly disgusts me whenever I hear about people who like the new 'Battlefront'. Ten years prior and there is still at least a thousands times more content and replayability than Battlefront EA. This game is by no means perfect, but goddamnit if it isn't close. The singleplayer feels a bit on the short side but it's still more entertaining than most FPS singleplayer campaigns today. The space battles can get a bit repetitive if not spaced out more (get it), especially in galactic conquest. Galactic Conquest is quite a bit of fun but can also get really repetitive if you are constantly fighting over the same two planets over and over again. I feel like they should have spaced out the planets a bit more, and taking a planet really should have provided better benefits than just credits. For example, taking (insert planet here) could have given you added bonuses every other turn or so. Taking Geonosis or Kamino wierdly enough doesn't halt production of battle droids and clones respectivly. There also should have been a better reason to build more fleets, I did an entire campaign as the rebels with one fleet but maybe that's just because I'm fairly good at the game having played it so many years ago. It's honestly a better investment to buy bonuses and train units than it is to have several fleets across the galaxy. Small things in my opinion but I feel like they would have improved galactic conquest quite a bit. Also the bots AI is not particularly good. It's not god-awful but it really could have been better. I'd recommend playing at least galactic conquset on Elite difficulty, singleplayer on Elite can be a bit frustrating though, the Coruscant level especially. Battlefront II however is still absolutly incredible to play. Although unless you're pretty hardcore with this game, I'd recommend playing in hourly bursts (at least for Galactic Conquest). I will give this game a recommendation even though it can be a hassle to play. Sadly it seems we may never get another great star wars game like thsi ever again with EA holding onto the license. Kiss your star wars games good night and tell 'em how much you love them, because these old star wars games from the early 2000's are really all we star wars videogame fans have left.

meadow is a game for niche players who only want aesthetic collectibles to show off their virtual prowess.
there is no goal besides collecting flowers / rocks / essense, which give you emotes and skins and new animals (which you need to collect more flowers and rocks for... to get more skins and emotes...).
the 'forum in games clothing' claim is honestly a lie. 10 emotes and a couple directional symbols barely add up to being the kind of diction comparable to a forum. none of the creatures on when i played used it for anything close to that purpose, either. emotes were used primarily just to spam (along with jumping and the animal noise button), and directional symbols were used to say 'over here / this way' and nothing much else.
i like the visuals of the game in theory, but in motion its unclear and not that great to stare at. ALL of the textures are busy, and repeated, busy textures on low poly EVERYTHING is bad. the still images for the collectables were just as textured, but being STILL IMAGES, they actually looked good and had a good feel to them--i really do like the emote pictures as well.
sound design wasnt terrible, but every animal seemed to only have one call noise (from what i could tell from people spamming it). there seemed to only be one or two BGM songs, one of which had a very action-y tempo that didnt fit the mood at all.
gameplay also wasnt too bad. i ran around in a pack for a bit as a frog and a badger. the whole being-in-a-pack thing made my game lag pretty bad (which it shouldnt!!! my computer can definitely handle a bunch of low-poly animals). the camera is probably the worst aspect of the game. i tried both the freelook and locked version, despite there being an almost indiscernable difference between the two, and at random either the animal i was playing or the camera would decide to turn extremely slow. it was annoying to deal with it the entirety of the time i played.
id suggest trying The Endless Forest before even considering buying Meadow. theyre basically the same save for one having more animal choices than the other. TEF gives you more unique choices for the skins you can wear (not JUST busy textures), and theyre a lot easier to get. TEFs visuals, while a bit older than Meadows, are much more natural and less of a pain to look at. Also, TEF is free.

tl;dr You have 2 months to buy in before the free DLC thing expires, wait it out, there's tons of balance and content that needs added.
This thing needs massive work and balance.
Campaign/Single Player:  Little more than a chain of AI skirmish missions with voice over and a few movies and scripted special missions, and a fleet building and upgrade system that will leave many new players utterly confused. Ship balance from tabletop did not transition well to RTS, and the mechanics are not balanced to make up for this. Expecting almost a fleet style FTL experience of having to scrap by, and pooling as much resources as possible with risks and rewards, and it's not remotely as enjoyable. Losses snowball into more losses which slows your renown gain to the point of losing time and time again.
Sound/Music: Fine, pretty 40k themed, at least Imperial wise. Only a few tracks you'll hear a dozen times before muting forever. Sound of things is pretty well done too. Voice acting from the campaign is done well, but it doesn't make up for the gameplay. Captains and their little voice responses to your commands will quickly get old, but I suppose that's any RTS where you micro everything to death.
Graphics: Beautiful. A shame really, as this game feels like it has a lot of potential to be interesting and an enjoyable naval game in space churches. There's a template for what feels like a really gorgeous space opera battle here, but a lot of work is needed to flesh the game out and make it more enjoyable for all.
MUTIPLAYER: The real beast, balance is beyond borked with bugs and utterly overpowered setups available to some factions. Tindalos has a very knee jerk reaction to their balancing, often met with huge backlash from their community on their almost randomly gamebreaking ideas of how to "fix" anything. At one point they considered letting the Imperial Navy be faster than Chaos, a true heresy if I ever heard one. Other balance ideas would outright take an overpowered ability down to making it unusable for anyone, and several factions have had key parts hit with the nerf bat so hard they still haven't recovered. Eldar don't have Pulsars as much as space flashlights that beam out ridiculous amounts of burst damage, though the last patch made them noticably more fragile. Matchups range from a breeze to insultingly tedious, to the point I would really recommend dodging whatever faction you know gives you the worst trouble. Game types are identical to single player, except again balance has some very favored by some Factions. Eldar again in particular are so mobile that data recovery and assassination are basically free wins cause no one except other Eldar can keep up with you.
Maybe like 5/10. Wait a month or two, you won't miss anything. The multiplayer population will probably die out by then too (remember Space Marine? DoW2?) and you won't of missed anything anyways.

I want to recommend this game. I really do.
One one hand, it's the best Star Trek game never made. Not literally of course, its not the same IP, but just in terms of how the game FEELS when you play  it. From the tactical combat which involves re-routing limited power to numerous systems and directing your own attacks at key enemy systems to cripple them in a fight, to strategic management of resources as you upgrade you ships systems and acquire new weapons and mods for your ship, it does a good job of making you feel like a starship captain. You'll find yourself saying, "Quick! Emergency Power to the shields!" More than once to save yourself in the nick of time from an intense enemy laser barrage.
You might then, be wondering, why I don't recommend this game. Roguelikes are inherently difficult, and part of that difficulty comes from the random aspect. This game is no exception, but here its been poorly executed. Even knowing the system so well that you have a general familiarity with the events that can happen to your ship, ultimately the game is pushing more towards luck than skill. Be it your evasion chance, which is just a percentage, or how much scrap and weaponry you can get your hands on, you'll find certain playthroughs vastly easier than other playthroughs despite your relative experience at the game not really changing. You might find that five events in a row all end positively and you have an excess of scrap and your ship and crew is healthy, or those same five events might arbitrarily kill half your crew, rip a hole in your hull and set your engines on fire. Same events, same decisions, five different outcomes.
This isn't to imply there is NO skill involved. I would never say that. In any roguelike there is some elements of luck and some elements of skill. This is to say, however, this game for your average user ends up feeling a little too much like dice rolling than tactics and resource management. Ultimately, if you really love Sci-Fi, particularly Star Trek, you'll probably get a kick out of the game, but the amount of sheer luck which the came is based upon will ultimately leave you feeling unfulfilled even if you win - because you'll ultimately know that nothing you did really earned that win. The game gave it to you. And next time you play even with the same ship, you're probably not going to do as well.

Blender is the best free 3d application on the market, and capable of providing most features of even the highest end commercial applications. It may be surprising but it is also one of the oldest 3D applications on the market as well, though it has been totally overhauled in recent years from it's legacy as a proprietary product.
While arguments can certainly be made for the superiority of various other applications to cover some of the things it can do, very few commercial packages come close to it's full capability, and all have extremely high cost in terms of licensing, equipment and expertise needed to use them. As such, currently Blender is a one-stop shop for:
3D modelling
3D sculpting
2D & 3D animation
Rigging
Rigid Body Physics,
Hair, Cloth, Liquid, Smoke, Particle Simulation
UV unwrapping
UV texturing
Compositing, Image and Video
Video Editing
Camera tracking and stabilizatoin
Pre-Viz, simulation analysis
Direct output to a sample game engine
Support (through plugins) to export assets to Unity and UE game engines.
On top of that impressive list, plugins provide even more functionality and Blender is constantly being updated by a huge community of programmers constantly pushing for a more unified approach and better access to cutting edge technologies.

Race 07 is an excellent entry-level simulator for the PC. It does require you to use some sort of controller other than a keyboard and mouse, but can easily be controlled with the stuff you probably already own, like a Dualshock III or Xbox controller.
The expansion packs are worth it, especially GTR Evolution for us who need a bit more speed than what touring cars can offer.
The community creates a lot of free tracks and cars that are excellent for making the game last a lot longer.
On the downside of things, the force feedback in this game compared to earlier Simbin titles like GTR2 is horrible. You don't get that distinct feel of lack of grip when understeering, a vital thing in a game with mostly FWD cars.
The graphics are very dated by now, and no mod seems to freshen them up properly. Creating your own skins do help a bit though, something I do a lot.
All in all, for its age, Race07 is around an 8/10 because of the lack of proper FFB and lack of "fast" racing cars. GTR2 is better.

NOTE: This review includes notes on expansions aswell.
With 800+ Hours played, I think it's safe to say that this game and it's expansions is one that will last the test of time.
It may not have the following of other racing simulators like rFactor or iRacing, but this is easily up there with some/all of the best.
It has a great racing community if you find a relaxed group of racers (RaceDepartment are great for clean racing and no lock-in racing series). The choice of cars across all the expansions is perfect for online racing.
There really is something for everyone, from slow and nimble Mini Coopers, to high powered open wheel racers, to classic and modern muscle cars (Race On expansion).
My favorite part of this game though is it's single player section though. It's ability to play and create championships makes this a great single player game, along with the fact that the AI is actually rather smart to race against compared to other games.
Modding is also fairly popular with this game as is evident by sites like NoGripRacing and RaceDepartment, with various add-on cars and tracks all waiting to be played.
Since this is a racing simulation, it is definitely a greater experience to use a wheel. I highly recommend getting yourself a wheel if you don't have one yet as it will change your experience entirely.
If you don't play racing games that often it's more than acceptable to use a gamepad, it's still good fun but not as good as with a wheel. The game is drivable with a keyboard as well, but that's a last resort.
In short, it's definitely worth getting the whole package: Race Injection, GTR Evo and Race On. It's perfect to me...
For games as a whole, it's easily 8/10.
For racing sims, it's 9/10.

FTL has you take charge of a ship (of your choice) in the Federation fleet to take on the Rebels and defeat their flagship. FTL is all about managing your ship and your crew effectively in order to make your ship powerful enough to fight the boss (good luck with that one).

+Several different races, each with their own specialities and backstories
+Lots of customisation options for ships
+Different ships suit different playstyles
+Plenty of different enemy ship types
+Extremely replayable
+Some really good mods, especially FTL Infinite, and the game is simple to mod
+/-The boss is extremely hard to beat, I still haven't beaten it at the time of writing this review but it doesn't really matter because playing through the game and unlocking new ships is where the fun comes from
-Some of the ships are extremely difficult to unlock
-It has in-game achievements but no Steam achievements
Verdict:
9.5

My experience with this game can be summed as thus: every update I found myself testing the changes, nodding in satisfaction, then quitting the game to await the next update.
Arkane knows how to make a good game. No question. But if you film an Oscar-worthy movie and the lens is smudged while filming, you can't judge what's underneath without acknowledging what's been marring your experience the entire time.
=============================
PERFORMANCE
Everyone is aware of the performance issues, and these still persist to this day. It runs much better than at launch, where it was literally unplayable, but that's because the game looks worse than before - the most noticeable change being the extremely aggressive LOD scaling. Out of the corner of your eye you notice the shapes of window frames and posters on distant buildings morphing in shape, or the furniture at the opposite end of a long hallway suddenly blinking into existence. FPS dropped to 15 when stabbing a gravehound, so they simply removed the inky visual effect that was causing the problem instead of optimizing it.
Also, Denuvo authentication is one of the longest "loading screens" of the game. Around half a minute to a full minute or more every startup.
=============================
GAMEPLAY
For the most part, gameplay is excellent and is Dishonored's strongest suit.
Dark Vision was changed to a blurry short range sonar so unlike Dishonored 1 you aren't constantly seeing blue and yellow because you had no reason not to
AI is much smarter
Nonlethal combat options are a blast
Bonecharm crafting system allows for player flexibility and "builds"
Each level feels lived-in while maintaining the duality of directive flow and open options that made the first game so good.
Emily and Corvo have distinct animations and final weapon upgrades. The animations are supremely cool.
Each level is fairly distinct, some with extremely interesting central "gimmicks." I do, however, wish the game relied less on them and had more "regular" areas.
However, under the hood lie other problems. Most of them are quality-of-life issues:
Gone are the hotkeys for journal, inventory, bonecharms, powers. Only one "journal" exists now, despite still having separate subsections.
It took months for the power wheel to be fixed. It took almost a full second after activating to pop up and be usable, breaking flow so badly I almost never used it in the first place. It's finally fixed now, but this issue was glaring and it took so long to be addressed most of us played through without it fixed.
Thrown objects don't always go exactly where your crosshair is. While this adds a layer of difficulty, it feels noticeably more clunky than in the first game.
Mana regen is pitifully slow. From using a power to fully regenerating, Dishonored 1's time is 4.7 seconds -> 3.1 seconds with Spiritual Pool. Dishonored 2's time with 4x Spiritual Pool is 6.3s -> 5.5s. The devs said they fixed this effect, but it was only made worse.
Bugs. Street speakers not playing. Dying after possessing gravehounds. An arc pylon never shutting down after pulling out its power, leaving it to either be dangerous to you to dangerous to your nonlethal playthrough. Some of these still aren't fixed.
=============================
STORY AND ATMOSPHERE
Reactivity
Great. My favorite part of Dishonored. You need to hide from a gang member to access a certain black market shop, and there are different scenarios and dialogue for if you hide, if you run into him outside, kill him outside, or kill him inside.
Emily and Corvo
Emily and Corvo are voiced. And... they don't talk enough. It's good that they're silent for most of the game, but there are times when you come across a portrait or photograph with an "Inspect" prompt. I'd love to hear Emily's thoughts on the High Overseer as see how that compares to Corvo's, or if it changes based on whether or not you accept the Outsider's Mark. Instead, all I get is the protagonist muttering the name of the person pictured. What's the point? Might as well keep them silent.
It made sense to me to play Emily first, but her story felt lackluster, like people at every turn were saying "check your royal privilege" despite my efforts to resolve everyone's problems without drawing blood. Corvo's is MUCH more interesting as a veteran of Dishonored 1.
The Outsider and The Void
I hate the new Outsider and his new voice. He felt threatening and malicious in the first game due to how calm and composed he was, and the Void felt like a strange and otherworldly place. The vignettes of Dunwall made it feel both unnatural and unnerving yet fundamentally woven into the universe. In Dishonored 2, it's just smoky blackness and sharp rocks. The Outsider is much jollier and moves around erratically, making grandiose hand gestures. They actually had a plot plot that could explain this change, but it was never addressed, so it just seems like a pointless retcon to me.
Main Plot
Dishonored's worldbuilding was always one of its appeals, and that remains true in Dishonored 2. However, the villains felt lackluster. Only the main villain has a real presence throughout the game, whereas everyone else feels introduced abruptly only to fall by your hand, all within the same mission. In Dishonored 1 everything felt personal and real. Perhaps it was because of the long intro where you interacted with most of them, or the Hound Pits's cast of characters all having different connections to your targets.
=============================
As you can see, I've played this game a LOT and have put a lot of thought into it. It was definitely worth all those hours and all that money, but the condition it was at launch and the sluggish drip-feed of support we barely get now is unacceptable. To set a precedent for future games, I can't recommend buying this unless they manage to fix all the performance issues and bugs, which doesn't seem to be happening anytime soon.
