NEO Scavenger is a great roguelike survival RPG. Playing it, you really get the impression that the experience of surviving (or not surviving, probably) in a post-apocalyptic future would be this difficult. I recommend it with a few warnings:
- It's a Flash game. That fact annoyed me for some reason when I learned it. Probably because there's no animation and it feels kind of "cheap." It creates the impression of a big, hex-based board game. Also, I'm not sure if it's because of the Flash-based game engine, but I lost all of my "map" progress when the game failed to save properly once.
- The pixelated, retro-style graphics work, but they don't cover up the fact that the game is rather ugly--and not because of the apocalyptic setting.
- There is some groan-inducing writing. Most of the writing is nice, though. It's not anything that detracts from the experience.
- The game is random to a fault sometimes. You're going to come across things that can instantly kill you. Or they'll come across you while you're sleeping. It's not fun to lose hours of progress when a thug caves in your head with a monkey wrench because you picked a poor campsite...or RNGesus didn't give you his blessing.
- Despite the game's randnomness, certain events never change. When you die, you're going to have to redo certain key events to be able to have a decent chance of advancing to the real progression. This can become monotonous after a few new games.
- There are no save slots. This is unconditionally an ironman-mode game. That wouldn't be a problem if there wasn't the occasional corrupted save file.
If you're interested in the genre and you understand that this is a game you might never complete because it's just so damned unforgiving, you can get a lot of fulfilling hours out of this.

First and foremost, this game has been the victim of bad PR. Most of the negative reviews on here are being drama queens. I'll try to give as unbiased a review as possible, both for people who are new, and for the ones that already have the game.
+ System requirements are lower than what you'd expect
+ Stable port, which means it runs very smoothly during gameplay
+ Nice visuals, superior to all console versions in many (but not all) ways
+ Diverse fighting styles
+ DIverse characters
+ Has a story mode which is above average for fighting game standards
+ Three VF Characters available
+ First full 3D fighting game on PC
+ Fighting mechanics are quite deep
+ Save replays
+ Training mode can display frame data and other details
+ Tutorial can help new players
+ Interactive stages
+ Has support for Xbox 360 controllers (Haven't tested others)
- Can't map keyboard buttons
- Although visually superior, the game is missing the Soft Engine and particle engine of the PS4/XB1 version. These engines would allow for ripped cloths, better 'boob physics' and more particle effects. Has no influence on gameplay though.
- Misses two stages from the PS4/XB1 version
- Online is missing for now. This was announced a long while before the game was released. It will be patched in within three months.
- Limited character customization in terms of cloths etc (mods remedy this obviously)
- Additional costumes are overpriced, being almost twice the price of the game itself
- Changing your Steam name makes you lose your saves
- No achievements
- No steam cloud
- No controller rumble
If you like fighting games, and don't have an XB1 or PS4, this is a must buy. The cons are there, but they are not game breaking. Most of them fall under the 'nice to have' category, rather than being mandatory. And the online, which is a must to have, will be patched in soon enough. The 10% discount will be removed after online is patched in, so I'd buy it now if you can.
The system requirements seem a bit steep, but it's not that bad. Your CPU is quite important because the game is quite CPU bound, so don't expect to run it if you have an old Core2Duo. Graphically, older GPUs should do fine. I can run the game at 1080p/60fps with my HD 6850 with SSAA2x and 2048x2048 shadows. This is almost max settings.

Not sure what to put here so have recipe for Welsh gingerbread
Ingredients
Makes 12 squares
350g self-raising flour
3 tsp ground ginger (optional)
100g unsalted butter, diced
150g demerara sugar
50g mixed candied peel, chopped
50g black treacle
80g honey
150ml milk
Method
You'll need a 27 x 20cm baking tin (or tin with similar dimensions)
Heat the oven to 170°C/Gas 3. Grease and line a 27 x 20cm baking tin (or tin with similar dimensions).
Sift the flour into a large bowl with the ginger, if using. Add the butter and rub it in with your fingertips until the mixture resembles fine breadcrumbs. Stir in the sugar and candied peel.
Put the treacle, honey and milk in a saucepan and heat gently, stirring, until the treacle and honey have melted into the milk. Pour onto the dry ingredients and mix thoroughly.
Pour the mixture into the prepared baking tin and bake for 30–40 minutes, until a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean.
Leave to cool completely, then cut into squares. Store in an airtight tin. The gingerbread will mature and become stickier with keeping.

In the missions, the weather mechanic makes for an interesting game. In multiplayer, it is an irritating game mechanic that makes the game somewhat... unabalanced.
Here's the thing- like in CoH, the Germans have excellent armor. Russia is supposed to counter this by having excellent artillery and cheaper, more easily spammable infantry.
In theory, this creates asymetrical balance.
In practice, it means that the Germans tend to curbstomp the Russians on snow maps, because the winter effect hurts infantry and Russian armor can't compete with that of the Germans.
If you liked CoH, you'll probably like this. Just don't expect any real development. I enjoyed it, though I don't know that it was worth full price.

You know those usually rare heart racing moments that happen only in the most atmospheric and engrossing games, where you can hear the terrors or monsters that you know you'll need to kill or get past but you can't see them, and you genuinely don't want to move because you're experiencing a strangely comfortable, uncomfortable feeling?........throughout this game there are many times i felt like that.
There have only been a few games in my life that have made me feel genuinely on edge or as though i really don't know what to expect next (and am kind of hesitant to find out but want to anyway), the first couple of Resident Evil games on the playstation, Silent Hill when it first came out, and of course there was the 'We don't go to Ravenholm' section in Half Life 2. Metro redux 2033 beats them all in my opinion.
It really is a great experience and the game really draws you in. The amazing graphics, atmospheric sounds (from water dripping in tunnels to howling in the distance or the wind blowing) and feeling of both hope for your character and hopelessness of the situations you often find yourself in all combine to generate that rare feeling of realism that you want from a game. I love how the story progresses for your main character and others involved and the way in which you can find occasional notes hidden in the game to provide you with context with regards the world you find yourself in, but there aren't too many of them to bother you or distract you from the game at all.
I would recommend this game to anybody, and for those of you who like myself read reviews to not only try and understand what the game offers in terms of content, I can also tell you that i had absolutely no issues with performance at all. I didn't experience a single crash, there was never any lag and i can't recall a single bug or glitch in the game.
It truly feels like a finely polished masterpiece, and it takes a lot for a game to impress me the way that this game has. Occasionally games come along that I get incredible enjoyment out of and can really immerse myself in, Fallout, Skyrim, Dragon Age etc, and Metro 2033 Redux is now definitely right up there with the best of them.
I strongly suggest getting this game, it's worth every penny and you will wonder where the hell the last few hours of your life have gone! Enjoy your heart racing!

TL;DR - If you like 40K and want to manage a space battle, buy this game. If you don't know what 40K is or you're one of those insufferable people that demands a video game play exactly like its board-game inspiration, skip this.
1] The game oozes 40K. If you like the 40K theme, the developers did a very good job staying true to the source material. Tech priests, commissars, and navigators have voice recordings that feel right. The ships are all very pretty. The developers can recite the Imperial Hymnal, and it shows...
2] There is an amazing amount of depth to upgrading and managing your fleet. Understanding your own play-style is key to doing this well because you simply will not be able to upgrade each ship in your fleet to do everything. Opportunity cost is everywhere.
3] The game makes you feel the impact of your decisions. Fail a mission? You get less reknown for a mission. Reknown is used to upgrade your ships. Choose poorly in upgrading your ships/fleet, you will feel the impact of those choices in upcoming battles. Lose a ship in battle, and you lose access to it for a number of rounds. Although you can recover from any mistakes, it takes time and reknown to correct those mistakes.
4] The game difficulty scales reasonably well, (1-4). On 4, I win about half of the time. On 3, I win about 80% of the time. Easier difficulties and you can feel like a tactical genius. You can play at whatever difficulty suits you.
5] The game is 2D naval combat metaphor, and not 3D space combat. People will whine about this, in a post-Homeworld space RTS world. However, there are enough other things going for this game, that I'm willing to overlook that aspect of the game.
6] The detail and pretty videos you see on YouTube are great... except, I don't really spend any time managing my fleet zoomed in like that. It's a perfect way to lose my battle. In a sad/unfortunate way, so much wonderful detail gets lost/ignored when playing the game.
7] The game runs well on my 6th gen Core i7 with Nvidia 970M gfx, which is saying it runs well on the latest and greatest laptop with discrete gfx. It was barely playable on a laptop that is 3 years old.
[updated review]
I've seen a few complaints from other reviewers that are worth addressing.
8] Reviewers that write, "It's too hard. [faction] is too hard on [mission] types," are not playing correctly. If the Chaos Space Marines are outrunning your Imperial ships in an assassination mission, stop using large and slow capital ships and use light cruisers. If the Orks keep destroying all of your Imperial defense platforms, then properly group your ships into a massive clump concentrate fire on a single ship at a time so that at least one platform survives. If the Eldar keep destroying your fleet, then use light cruisers with lots of frigates. Every complaint about the game being too hard is due to the player not understanding the victory conditions, their ships strengths/weaknesses, or their enemies' strengths/weaknesses.
9] Reviewers that write, "the mission types get boring/repetitive" do have a point. There are only a handful of mission types: cruiser clash, assassination, convoy, breakthrough, and data acquisition. That's a meager 9 basic mission types, when you factor that victory conditions for attackers and defenders are different, and the tactics used to win are often different between attacker/defender. And if you choose to include faction permutations, that's roughly 27 mission types. There's some reasonable diversity there, but I would agree that it could benefit from more single player campaign missions that are scripted. This is something that Warcraft3 and Starcraft2 franchises did and it does make the missions more engaging.

This review is for the Redux version, but it basically applies to regular Metro: 2033 as well.
Metro 2033 Redux, which is the precise game this is for, is like the original with all the DLC thrown in, plus some features from Metro: Last Light (like wiping the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off your mask). All in all it is an excellent game and I've grown fond of it - probably because it's similar (sort-of) to the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series, and indeed some of S.T.A.L.K.E.R.S. dev's did join 4A when making it. The game is
a free-roam game like S.T.A.L.K.E.R. was, it is linear - but it does allow some off-route exploration and such, like finding safes to open, which in turn require finding the key to that safe, which usually have money (military-grade bullets) in them. Ammo is semi-limited, less so if you just go out and kill everone. If you decide to take a Stealth route - there is less ammo, but you also shoot less people thus, it's not a big issue really.
The monsters in this game are what kinda♥♥♥♥♥♥me off. It's not that I hate them, of course I do but not because they're in the game, but because sometimes you have zero ammo and♥♥♥♥♥♥is still coming for you! I've never been able to take the stealth-route around the monsters, which is why I kill everyone for their ammo - of course maybe I'm playing wrong when I try to sneak around monsters? I don't know.
Anyways, as the title implies, most of the game takes place in the Russian Metro tunnels, however you do go to the surface sometimes. The game does take place after a nuclear-apocalypse so people living in Metro tunnels does make sense, of course. I probably should of mentioned this first - but I write my reviews as I go, so meh.
Some of the other cool features I DO like about this game are things such as your Gas Mask, you need it in some areas because they're irradiated. Your watch tells the actual time that your PC is set to, except when wearing these Gas Masks, in which case it counts down until you need to switch mask filters, which I found pretty cool. Filters, at least when I played - which was NOT in any hardcore mode, were plentiful, however that may only be different when playing in Ranger or Hardcore modes. Other than that you shoot stuff, blows stuff up, and all-in-all try to help one faction while fighting others plus the monsters/mutants or whatever they may be.
The difference between the Redux versions and the regular versions of Metro, is that they run on a new higher-end, fancier-looking game engine. In addition they have some extra in-game features as well as all the DLC and such standard. If you own both regular Metro games, the Redux Version is something like 50% off the regular price.
Would I recommend buying the Metro Redux games if you already own the originals? Well if you want prettier graphics, all the DLC, and extra in-game features (like Metro 2033 shares features from Last Light and such) then, yes I would. If you could care less because they're essentially the same game and you still don't wanna spend $25 or $20 bucks, then no I wouldn't. However I do recommend them in-general regardless.

Do you remember how you learned to play tag? For me it feels like we always knew. But that can't be right, can it? That's not something a child innately knows. So that must mean we learned how to play it. Learned the rules. Played it with kids who must have taught us, and in turn shared the game with others. Soon we reached a point where everyone we met could start up a game without question. Tag became something we just knew.
Meadow recaptures that experience in a gorgeously simple fashion. You spawn in the world at the base of a massive tree as a Badger Cub. Slow, clumsy, and generally awkward. As you gain your bearings you quickly figure out you can perform a limited, but varied number of actions: walk, run, jump, yelp, and, most importantly, emote. Soon, you notice other slow, clumsy, and generally awkward Badger Cubs. After flashing a few emotes at one another you figure out these crude pictographs can actually be used to communicate with each other. Other Badger Cubs amble over and your group very quickly swells in numbers. But it's not just other Badgers. Among you now walks a couple Lynxes, a rabbit, and a frog. They can do everything you do. The yipping of badgers transforms into a chorus of croaks, meows, and chirps.
Satisfied with your group's sizable numbers, you venture out from under the tree into the wild. You might end up in any number of locations: a snowy mountain range, grassy knolls, wooded hills flush with the color of autumn. Wherever your travels take you, you will encounter a series of black stone obelisks. They vary in size, ranging from small to very large, and will break apart when a certain number and type of animals gather around it. Inside is contained Essence, a stat that unlocks different animals, skins, and emotes the higher it gets.
Upgrades in Meadow consist of these three different Essence unlocks, which can drastically affect how you play the game. However, it is all directed towards a singular objective: finding the obelisks. Following that central design philosophy, the animals vary greatly in terms of movement. A rabbit will be quick on land whereas a frog will swim far better, while an Eagle can overcome any obstacle and fly with complete freedom.
So your ragtag band of animals has gathered together and decided to explore the landscape. Despite your limited number of actions and ways to interact with the world, the game is still incredibly engaging. You work with other players towards a common goal by utilizing the same rules, much like tag. At some point when you are playing Meadow, everything just clicks and you are utterly focused on the game. You are an eagle, soaring ahead of the pack searching for an obelisk, while your rabbit friend is wrangling up the slower animals in a combined exploration effort.
Meadow is strangely nostalgic of not just having fun playing games as a kid, but learning how to do it. There's a simple joy in figuring out the world around you, a mood that it captures quite well. At $3 it's a great price for such an amazing game. There really isn't much to it, but what it does it does extremely well. Hope to see you in game!

I started my computer and began my journey. My badger pup had spawned into a grassy meadow and far in the distance I saw a lynx. I attempted to communicate through yelps and jumps, but he seemed to ignore my plea of friendship. After numerous failed attempts, he simply walked off into the distance, leaving me to wonder what to do next. That was my introduction to Meadow.
Further along the road, I met some fellow badger pups. We jumped and yelped and ran around, not really understanding each other, but still enjoying the company. Later, a red goat appeared (red due to a bug, now fixed). We gathered around it, and marveled at its speed and agility. The goat asked us if we would like to travel with it and we gladly accepted.
And so our band of three badger pups and a goat was formed. We didn't really get far before many of us began to spam the question mark button. We had no clue as to where we were going. Then I saw it, a lake. It wasn't a big lake, but it was the first source of water I had seen in the game. The others saw it too, and began to race towards it. A pressing matter in the real word put me at last place, but I was first to see our new friend, and eagle.
All of the pups gathered around it like children, me included. It squawked at us and then broke a rock, revealing a collectible! After some time of chasing the eagle, the goat caught our attention again. He wanted us to follow him into the water and to a small island. We did, and were greeted with the goat sleeping since badger pups are so slow at swimming. Thinking we were all going to take a nap, I spawned a small fire on the island. The goat jerked up and ran into the water, saying he was surprised at the same time.
Later on, I tried spawning a fire while swimming and it worked (please fix)! The fire sat directly on top of the water, making it seem like the water was solid. The goat, whom we were following exclaimed again and continued to swim in front of us.
In the end, the eagle brought us to multiple collectibles and the goat tagged along for the ride. Communication was minimal and often confusing, but it was still fun. Considering that I'm a fan of the Shelter games, I quite enjoyed this, even though there was no point but exploration.
8/10, It's a great game to play and simply relax in. There's an abundance of new content regularly uploaded byt the devs which make it that more enjoyable. Buy it, play it. If it isn't your thing, ask for a refund.

I don't think this is a bad a game per se, I think it is a game that suffers from poor design choices that make it a lot less fun than it could be with just a little more thought and understanding of what makes a game fun. The basic premise is promising - post-apocalyptic survivor wakes up with nothing and is left to fend for themselves.
Unfortunately, you are totally at the mercy of the RNG in this game, meaning that one bad result = game over. Given how almost all mechanics apart from crafting in the game are RNG-based, that means a lot of die rolls and a lot of potential for that one unlucky roll to come up. This is particularly evident in combat, where one lucky roll/critical hit means game over. You can mitigate this somewhat by trying to avoid combat. But you will not be entirely able to avoid combat and retreating is, you guessed it, RNG-based.
Now of course, RNG-based games always feature bad luck - it's what the R stands for after all. What separates the wheat from the chaff (and where NEO Scavenger desperately falls short) is whether you can recover from "bad luck", i.e. to what extent you are at the mercy of factors outside of your control. Good games always give the player a sense of control over their own destiny – even if the RNG is brutal. When I play something like nethack and die, I normally think, "had I done XYZ differently, I might have survived ".
NEO Scavenger is far too unforgiving in this respect. A single hit can one-shot you. An unlucky stumble in combat can mean game over. However much you can hedge your bets, the nature of a RNG means that at some point you
be unlucky. When I die in NEO Scavenger I think, “had the RNG been kinder, I might have survived”. That's a bad sign.
This is a real shame, because the combat in itself is interesting and tactical enough to be engaging initially. But a few games in, and combat no longer interests me. Why not just throw a die at the start and see if I get one-shotted and save me the hassle of trying to be tactical/retreat? This sums up my core problem with NEO Scavenger: it feels like the game is a single dice throw that simply determines how and when you will die; not whether you will die. And that's why it’s not fun.
Other ways to die include dying of hypothermia (= the RNG didn’t spawn enough clothes in the first ~10 turns), infected wounds (=the RNG didn’t spawn a fire-proof canister for boiling water; or alcohol) etc. It’s essentially a glorified version of Snakes & Ladders or Ludo, games determined purely by luck of the dice.
There are a number of other obvious flaws that would be forgivable if the game itself was fun: Flash is a terrible choice of platform, there are several bugs still in the game (e.g. the act of changing, not wearing, footwear gives you blisters; visual glitches) and the interface (particularly crafting) is clunky to say the least. But none of this would matter if the core game was actually fun.
This game strikes an ammazing balance between simpllicity and depth.

DISCLAIMER: This review is specifically for RACE Injection (and not RACE '07). The reason why I wrote it here is because everytime you run RACE Injection, Steam misinterprets it as RACE '07. Likewise, my total gameplay for this game is supposedly 1 minute (I actually played it for 9 frickin' hours).
Fix this♥♥♥♥♥♥right away, Steam.
[BEGIN REVIEW]
RACE Injection is pretty much like RACE '07 (because that's exactly what it is). What makes RACE Injection different from the series is that this game comes bundled with other expansion packs for the RACE series such as the WTCC Expansion, the STCC Expansion, the Formula RaceRoom Expansion, Retro Maxx Expansions as well as other expansions that exists in the Sim-Bin racing verse.
Although not much good can be said about this game, there isn't really anything bad about RACE Injection. The game retains its sim-ish gameplay, along with various vehicles and teams to choose from as well as various tracks that still exist till today. Players can either join a singleplayer game and battle with a couple of offline bots in a race for pole position, or they can simply do the same thing in the multiplayer world, where things get slightly out of hand as the onlineverse of RACE Injection is littered with pros, amateurs, road rage drivers and those who just can't drive as well.
The variety of cars listed is a lot, and I mean a lot. Players can assume any car in any team in more than 14 different classes, ranging from the tame and puny like the Formula BMW and other Touring Cars to the much faster and wild cars like the Formula RaceRoom and the GT Touring Pro Series. What's good about this game is that this game lets you install any mods that you download online into your RACE '07 folder, pretty much like rFactor. Which means that as long as the modding community keeps making mods for this game, players will keep themselves glued to their seats as they test and enjoy every single mod the community has to offer.
As for the gameplay, RACE Injection counts as a sim-ish game, due to its availability of driving anaesthetics, its complex driving system and the overall realism that is implemented in the game. The features such as ABS, TCS, damage sensitivity, tire wear and all the little itsy bitsy details can be configured to the player's liking, either by turning it up a notch and removing the driving aids to increase the difficulty of driving in the game and thus increasing the challenge of placing in the podium finish, or nerfing the difficulty down a little and activating the ABS and TCS to ease the driving. Either way, even though the gameplay can be a little hard to master, the game does appeal to both realism addicts and casual drivers.
Since the game is quite dated, it's no surprise that this game isn't as realistic as Assetto Corsa, nor does it have shiny graphics like Need For Speed Rivals. But if you're the type of gamer who has a lackluster system who wants to enjoy a slightly less serious racing sim game, RACE Injection is definitely for you.
And the others? Well, it's a safe bet that they may not want to drive in RACE Injection. Unless they don't mind the shoddy graphics and slightly-less-serious racing physics.

I struggle with roguelikes. I want to like them. They sound so cool, so edgy. But in practice, after a few hours, the start/restart feels like a grind. An algorithmically generated grind, but a grind nonetheless.
But not FTL. FTL hits a beautiful sweet spot between chance and skill. Casinos wish they had it figured out this good. Each time I boot it up, I have no idea what I'm going to encounter. I could be completely screwed over in the first system. I could coast by conflict-free. I might find a game-changing weapon salvaging an old, dilapidated ship, or it could break apart and kill one of my crew.
Through all of this, there's a sense that you're slowly getting better. You've got to mix, match, and weave around what luck gives you to make the best of it. And after many, many failures, you get more efficient, more ruthless, more calculating. You start planning several moves ahead, even as you have no idea what's going to happen the next time you make a jump.
Great game, super unforgiving and super rewarding. Play it already.

Despite the lower playtime shown on Steam, I am an older player of Quake Live before the game went on Steam. I decided to just now convert my QL account to Steam since the external launcher will be discontinued, even though the Steam version of QL launched quite a while ago. I started my account on December 21, 2009 with a total of 3:04:18:51 Ranked time and 13:19 Unranked time. In addition I have amassed several Awards over the course of my QL playtime.
Quake Live is basically the free to play version of Quake 3 Arena. That's all there really is to it. This is not a bad thing at all, because Q3A and by extension QL both have the one unique and strong point of the game: the gameplay. A true fast paced arena shooter, Quake Live lends itself to quality competitive gameplay relying not just on reflexes but also timing and positioning. Knowing how and when to use multiple weapons for the right situation along with mastery of movement options such as strafe jumping are key to high level play. Item timing is also crucial, leading to the necessary map knowledge across Quake's varied map designs. Most of the competitive play is set in Duel, but more casual modes such as Deathmatch and Capture the Flag also exist. A personal favorite is Clan Arena, granting all players all the weapons and full health and armor, perfect for practicing techniques in a team based gamemode. Whatever gamemode you pick, the gameplay is refined yet complex with many options available at your disposal.
Since Quake Live is pretty much a reskinned Quake 3 Arena, it looks and sounds much like its predecessor too. The graphics have not been updated too much, looking like an early 2000s game. I find that the graphics aged well and that it's not terribly ugly, while still maintaining clean visual clarity for competitive situations. The sounds are still good quality, and it is important to know what is happening in the middle of a fight with unique sounds for everything. While music is not a very important thing in a competitive title, Quake 3 Arena's soundtrack is quite nice. It's a bit dated electronic music, but still holds up for a good listen outside of the game.
Quake Live is one of the best competitive FPS games around. It is essentially a repackaging of Quake 3 Arena, but it has all the solid competitive gameplay that still plays great along with a strong community around it. The game overall has been more streamlined for a modern, smooth, and great experience. While the changes from the developers might scare some, they shouldn't since at its core, Quake Live has the unique gameplay that holds up strongly for a rewarding and competitive game.

Where do I start. First off, this is one of the best games I have ever played. It's like Dead Island, except better in every possible way. Graphics are great, facial animations are great, and just overall a great atmostphere. You really feel as if you are actually in the game, it pulls you in and doesn't let go.
The parkour aspect is top notch. It feels genuine, and not like some arcadey junk. Running across rooftops, climbing fences, and running away from volatiles at night really gets your blood going.
Combat system is great. Most of the weapons you will use are melee weapons (one handed and two handed), but there are also guns (pistols, assault rifles, shotguns, smgs), a bow with different arrow types and a crossbow thrown into the mix once you start the following. There are a ton of collectible blueprints scattered around the map, and some you can get from completing missions, that you can use to enhance your melee weapon with different effects like Toxic, Electric, Fire, and Impact. More advanced blueprints let you put two effects on one weapon. It is so damn staisfying chopping off heads with a machete and bashing in zombie skulls with a sledgehammer.
The story is alright, not going to dive into any spoilers, but it does its job in keeping everything flowing smoothly. I have completed the main story twice now, and all of the side quests as well.
You get two different maps in the base game, Slums and Old Town, that I think are very detailed and do a good job of rewarding exploration. Each one has a very different feel to it, and that helps add to the overall atmostphere of the game.
This is one of the few games where I have found/completed most of the easter eggs, and collected most if not all of the developer blueprints. No other game has made me want to come back and throughly collect and explore as much as Dying Light. I love going around and exploring every little nook and cranny, just to make sure there's nothing that I missed. The biggest thing I have accomplished is grinding for about 12 hours or so, getting around 9k disater relief packages to reach max legend level at 250. I don't believe any other game will pull me back in as much as this one.
To sum it up, Dying Light is one of the best games I have and I think I will ever play. Everything from the graphics, the animations, the combat, the parkour and the story, feels very very solid and well done. And as much fun as it is to play it alone, playing with your friends is an absolute blast. Techland nailed this one. 10/10

First and foremost, this game has been the victim of bad PR. Most of the negative reviews on here are being drama queens. I'll try to give as unbiased a review as possible, both for people who are new, and for the ones that already have the game.
+ System requirements are lower than what you'd expect
+ Stable port, which means it runs very smoothly during gameplay
+ Nice visuals, superior to all console versions in many (but not all) ways
+ Diverse fighting styles
+ DIverse characters
+ Has a story mode which is above average for fighting game standards
+ Three VF Characters available
+ First full 3D fighting game on PC
+ Fighting mechanics are quite deep
+ Save replays
+ Training mode can display frame data and other details
+ Tutorial can help new players
+ Interactive stages
+ Has support for Xbox 360 controllers (Haven't tested others)
- Can't map keyboard buttons
- Although visually superior, the game is missing the Soft Engine and particle engine of the PS4/XB1 version. These engines would allow for ripped cloths, better 'boob physics' and more particle effects. Has no influence on gameplay though.
- Misses two stages from the PS4/XB1 version
- Online is missing for now. This was announced a long while before the game was released. It will be patched in within three months.
- Limited character customization in terms of cloths etc (mods remedy this obviously)
- Additional costumes are overpriced, being almost twice the price of the game itself
- Changing your Steam name makes you lose your saves
- No achievements
- No steam cloud

What an awesome change of pace from traditional city building games!
Tropico games combine city building with world history, with a lot of special Tropico-flavored PG-13 humor. You are a corrupt Presidente of the Caribbean. The level of your corruption, what you fight for, who you ally with, and how happy your people truly are is all up to you.
It takes a little bit of getting used to. There are missions as well as a sandbox mode with customizable conditions. The missions are sometimes a little serious, usually very goofy (including one about a hiccup disease), and will often leave you scrambling to keep your city going while whatever morals you determine for yourself are constantly at odds with the rest of the world.
The building tools aren't as sophisticated as in other games, and you won't be able to do everything exactly the way you want. Many buildings you might expect to have don't exist in the game, and it can be confusing at first to figure out how to get certain buildings or upgrades you want. Much of the islands cannot be built on, and you are often forced into a small area while many of the buildings have large footprints. My advice is to have several construction offices and really focus on getting your economy going as quickly as possible (with farms, mines, or whatever).
I love this game when I want to do some city building without having to think too hard. It's a great way to relax and enjoy a bit of humor and that satisfaction of watching a poor, angry town turn into a modern tourist haven, or whatever floats your boat.
Highly recommended.

Braid is an example of minimalism in game design. Each level has a different twist to it, all based on time manipulation, none long enough to be tedious. One sample twist: the ability to rewind time at will, which mans that jumps which would be absurdly difficult in a 'real' platformer become an interesting puzzle to solve. And that's a meta-twist: The game is not one that needs reflexes to solve. If you ever find yourself thinking "I'm just not fast enough/skilled enough" you need to take a step back and think rather than react.
Speaking of thinking, the story line is thought-provoking. If you are the type that likes a backstory that hinted at rather than spelled out, Braid will give you ample fodder to ponder and/or discuss.
Braid was one of the forerunners of what is now the Indie revolution. Its fame is deserved.

This game is an absolute classic. This was my first REAL forray into a REAL RTS game, and it was definitely the RTS for me as I am a big fan of the Warhammer 40k universe. Firstly, there is loads of replay value because there are a lot of different difficulty settings, and there is the extremely fun Skirmish mode for multiplayer, but you can also play against the computer, the game even goes as far as letting you have 4 different opposing forces in skirmish mode. It allows you to put the 4 different factions against eachother, and also lets you double up and have the same faction as enemies, and it allows you to ally whatever factions you want together. Then there is the Army Painter, which allows you to give whatever chapter you want of your faction a custom look(the difference in chapters of each faction however, is unfortunately completely cosmetic.)
The level of strategy involved is certainly palatable to someone who has never really played an RTS game before and is looking to start, however there is definitely more strategy than say, Aliens vs. Predator: Extinction, which is an RTS game with no strategy whatsoever, that was all about how many units you could have on screen at once.
With all that said, the action, and the different types of units(for space marine at least, who I am most familiar with) is VERY cool. You can build armies of Space Marines, jetpack marines who can 'jump' or jet pack short distances, you can build excellent tanks, (there are not a large variety of flying vehicles though, there is the land speeder which can fly short distances however with the 'jump' option.) There are deep-striking Dreadnoughts, terrifying mech warriors who you can deploy anywhere on the battlefield where the fog of war has been lifted, orbital bombardments, and of course, Warhammer 40k's signature Terminators.(All of these available provided you have built the orbital relay building of course.)
The multiplayer is about as dead as you'd expect for a game from 2004, however I do believe there is still support for it if you have a friend who plays it.
The only actual fault I have with the game is that, when you are trying to train yourself to be good at multiplayer, if you set the A.I. on the harder difficulty settings it cheats when it comes to resources and spams you with units instead of it actually improving it's strategy. I suppose that helps train you for multiplayer battles, but it makes the skirmish mode a lot less fun to play honestly. A flaw the game could do without. If only the A.I. was a little smarter on each A.I. setting instead.

DISCLAIMER: When I first bought this game on Steam I couldn't start a single mission without the game crashing to desktop. I googled it and it seems lots of people suffer this same problem. I don't actually know if any other versions work properly, ie. a disk version maybe, but I can say even though this is a FPS, I'd actually recommend a PS2 version or even maybe the PSN version on th PS3 (provided that works, I honestly have no idea, but whatever you do, do not buy the PSP version as it is nearly as stripped down as the new EA Battlefront). I have found work-arounds for the crashing on google but most of them are incredibly complicated. I managed to finnaly get the game working by just plugging a pair of headphones into my mic jack before starting the game from steam. I know this sounds stupid and unbelievable but it actually worked for me. However, just because it worked for me does not mean it will work for you. If you are determined to get a PC version of this game I can't stop you. But please purchase at your own risk. Or just get a refund.
Battlefront II is a pretty damn good game. It ranks incredibly highly on my favorite games of all time, and I still think it is one of the best FPS games ever made. Even despite the awful first experience of not being able to play the game, once I figured out how it was like playing with some of your old child toys again. The nostalga was real with this game. Honestly  I don't like the prequels at all (along with most people with half a brain) but I think most people agree that at least two really good things came out of the prequels, a) the musical score by John Williams b) the games. Battlefront II is no exception to that. The clone wars era battles are just as fun as the galactic civil war battles, and it truly disgusts me whenever I hear about people who like the new 'Battlefront'. Ten years prior and there is still at least a thousands times more content and replayability than Battlefront EA. This game is by no means perfect, but goddamnit if it isn't close. The singleplayer feels a bit on the short side but it's still more entertaining than most FPS singleplayer campaigns today. The space battles can get a bit repetitive if not spaced out more (get it), especially in galactic conquest. Galactic Conquest is quite a bit of fun but can also get really repetitive if you are constantly fighting over the same two planets over and over again. I feel like they should have spaced out the planets a bit more, and taking a planet really should have provided better benefits than just credits. For example, taking (insert planet here) could have given you added bonuses every other turn or so. Taking Geonosis or Kamino wierdly enough doesn't halt production of battle droids and clones respectivly. There also should have been a better reason to build more fleets, I did an entire campaign as the rebels with one fleet but maybe that's just because I'm fairly good at the game having played it so many years ago. It's honestly a better investment to buy bonuses and train units than it is to have several fleets across the galaxy. Small things in my opinion but I feel like they would have improved galactic conquest quite a bit. Also the bots AI is not particularly good. It's not god-awful but it really could have been better. I'd recommend playing at least galactic conquset on Elite difficulty, singleplayer on Elite can be a bit frustrating though, the Coruscant level especially. Battlefront II however is still absolutly incredible to play. Although unless you're pretty hardcore with this game, I'd recommend playing in hourly bursts (at least for Galactic Conquest). I will give this game a recommendation even though it can be a hassle to play. Sadly it seems we may never get another great star wars game like thsi ever again with EA holding onto the license. Kiss your star wars games good night and tell 'em how much you love them, because these old star wars games from the early 2000's are really all we star wars videogame fans have left.
Seriously there is actually no reason for you not to own this game; It takes up almost no space, It will run on a potato and still get over 60fps and it's stupidly fun.

This review is for the Redux version, but it basically applies to regular Metro: 2033 as well.
Metro 2033 Redux, which is the precise game this is for, is like the original with all the DLC thrown in, plus some features from Metro: Last Light (like wiping the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off your mask). All in all it is an excellent game and I've grown fond of it - probably because it's similar (sort-of) to the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series, and indeed some of S.T.A.L.K.E.R.S. dev's did join 4A when making it. The game is
a free-roam game like S.T.A.L.K.E.R. was, it is linear - but it does allow some off-route exploration and such, like finding safes to open, which in turn require finding the key to that safe, which usually have money (military-grade bullets) in them. Ammo is semi-limited, less so if you just go out and kill everone. If you decide to take a Stealth route - there is less ammo, but you also shoot less people thus, it's not a big issue really.
The monsters in this game are what kinda♥♥♥♥♥♥me off. It's not that I hate them, of course I do but not because they're in the game, but because sometimes you have zero ammo and♥♥♥♥♥♥is still coming for you! I've never been able to take the stealth-route around the monsters, which is why I kill everyone for their ammo - of course maybe I'm playing wrong when I try to sneak around monsters? I don't know.
Anyways, as the title implies, most of the game takes place in the Russian Metro tunnels, however you do go to the surface sometimes. The game does take place after a nuclear-apocalypse so people living in Metro tunnels does make sense, of course. I probably should of mentioned this first - but I write my reviews as I go, so meh.
Some of the other cool features I DO like about this game are things such as your Gas Mask, you need it in some areas because they're irradiated. Your watch tells the actual time that your PC is set to, except when wearing these Gas Masks, in which case it counts down until you need to switch mask filters, which I found pretty cool. Filters, at least when I played - which was NOT in any hardcore mode, were plentiful, however that may only be different when playing in Ranger or Hardcore modes. Other than that you shoot stuff, blows stuff up, and all-in-all try to help one faction while fighting others plus the monsters/mutants or whatever they may be.
The difference between the Redux versions and the regular versions of Metro, is that they run on a new higher-end, fancier-looking game engine. In addition they have some extra in-game features as well as all the DLC and such standard. If you own both regular Metro games, the Redux Version is something like 50% off the regular price.
Would I recommend buying the Metro Redux games if you already own the originals? Well if you want prettier graphics, all the DLC, and extra in-game features (like Metro 2033 shares features from Last Light and such) then, yes I would. If you could care less because they're essentially the same game and you still don't wanna spend $25 or $20 bucks, then no I wouldn't. However I do recommend them in-general regardless.

The main focuses of the game are exploring and being social with other players. If you like doing those things in games, and/or you've enjoyed any of the other Shelter games, I'd say this is definitely worth a buy.
The art style takes some getting used to, but once you do you can see a sort of beauty in the landscapes. Controls, as in other Shelter games are a bit awkward and hard to use at first, but you learn to get yourself pointed where you need to be after some practice.
The game throws you in without much of a tutorial atm, so if you haven't read too much into the store page, or any guides or anything, you start with kind of a loss of what to do. If you wander around a bit, players will usually come over and offer to run around with you and you can start to pick up on game mechanics.
There's not a whole super lot to do in the game. I don't know how much they're planning on changing or adding, but right now all you can do is team up with other players and run around finding obelisk things, which give you new animals, skins, and emotes. And find some flowers and stuff. It is enjoyable though, learning to stick together and communicate with your companions without typing, just actions, animal calls and emotes.
I own a few of the other Shelter games, so I started with some animals that I don't think you can obtain if you haven't bought the games. I dunno if that was the wisest choice, since it seems like a move to try and get people to buy their other games.. but it makes a little bit of sense I guess. You can certainly play the game without owning any of the others though, it just depends on if you want an animal that comes with another game or not.
All in all I'd definitely recommend it if these types of games are your thing, and for 3 bucks its not a bad deal at all. I've already spent a good couple of enjoyable hours in game, and I find it relaxing, so I plan on playing some more when I need some down time.

Love it. I was very critical of the original, mostly due to technical issues. My computer was able to play Last light seemlessly (with the PhysX) but struggled with 2033. With this new edition the FPS drops below 50 occasionally but it's not enough to effect gameplay (still a resource hog if you're playing on an older computer). Another complaint was that the character models looked awkward and cartoonish. The monsters have been vastly improved with only a couple awkward attack animations left to remind us how awful they were originally, and the humans have seen a similar improvement, but sadly the eyes and eyebrows still have little to know movement as though they were painted on, and the mostly awful voice acting  has carried over.
A lot of people are criticizing the higher lighting level; true enough, even at the lowest gamma setting everything is clearly visible in the dark. THIS ONLY EFFECTS THE FIRST THIRD OF THE GAME, after that for some reason the darks get much darker, and you'll have night vision anyway.
The enemy AI has been vastly improved meaning that it's actually possible to take a stealth approach to many of the levels. Personally, I found this alone completely changed the game and made it worth the extra play though. That said; the levels aren't exactly designed for stealth (lot's of enemies hudled around a camp fire for instance, the games very oriented around scavenging so ignoring them puts you at a disadvantage) and enemies are much too easily alerted to you presence. For instance you'll alert everyone close to you by taking a single step while not crouched. The stealth is more enjoyable, but it's far easier to go in guns blazing which takes away the fun.
One unfortunate effect of the Redux is the game is really easy now. With the exceptions of (a lot) of cheap deaths, I hardly had to worry about dying at all, and even when I did the checkpoint system was so forgiving that there did not seem to be any incentive to not die.

Not sure what to put here so have recipe for Welsh gingerbread
Ingredients
Makes 12 squares
350g self-raising flour
3 tsp ground ginger (optional)
100g unsalted butter, diced
150g demerara sugar
50g mixed candied peel, chopped
50g black treacle
80g honey
150ml milk
Method
You'll need a 27 x 20cm baking tin (or tin with similar dimensions)
Heat the oven to 170°C/Gas 3. Grease and line a 27 x 20cm baking tin (or tin with similar dimensions).
Sift the flour into a large bowl with the ginger, if using. Add the butter and rub it in with your fingertips until the mixture resembles fine breadcrumbs. Stir in the sugar and candied peel.
Put the treacle, honey and milk in a saucepan and heat gently, stirring, until the treacle and honey have melted into the milk. Pour onto the dry ingredients and mix thoroughly.
Pour the mixture into the prepared baking tin and bake for 30–40 minutes, until a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean.
Leave to cool completely, then cut into squares. Store in an airtight tin. The gingerbread will mature and become stickier with keeping.

being someone who jumped in on the Shelter series with the release of Meadow, i can pretty safely say you don’t need to know anything about Shelter to be able to easily grasp the premise of the game.
your main objective in the game is to collect flowers and puzzle pieces to raise your overall score, or essense as it’s called in game.  the puzzle pieces also are what you need to work your way towards unlocking other animals, as well as fur skins and emotes for the animal you’re currently playing as.
in order to get many of these puzzle pieces, however, you have to explore and navigate your way through the environment that’s been laid out, often times checking every nook and cranny you lay eyes on.  but there are also these pseudo-puzzles in the form of what i personally call singing stones.  how you extract the pieces from these stones, is you need to cooperate with at least one other player, often times more, gathering around and literally screaming at the singing stones with your animals’ calls.  this obviously puts a huge emphasis of cooperation into the game if you want to earn unlockables at a faster pace.
but, as stated above, you do have to unlock other animals to play as, and in turn you start off as a badger cub, (unless you own any combination of the Shelter games on Steam) which seems to be the most basic of the animals you can play as; a slow movement speed in comparison to others, standard jump height, small stature.  to me, this is an ingenius idea, because it is immediately putting you into the shoes of the ‘runt of the litter’, making you the easiest for your pack to shrug off and ignore, heading to puzzle pieces and singing stones more quickly.
however, i find that most players don’t actually just cut and run from those who take longer to catch up, and actively try to have the group slow down so that they can catch up.  this gives newer players a sense of acceptence from those who have put more time into the game, and in turn, makes it easier for them to understand and be more patient with those who may take more time to rejoin the pack.
it gives the game a very strong sense of being a close-knit group, despite most people you encounter being complete strangers, and creates a very pleasant and joyful experience to the game, which i feel is much needed in today’s multiplayer genre.

I struggle with roguelikes. I want to like them. They sound so cool, so edgy. But in practice, after a few hours, the start/restart feels like a grind. An algorithmically generated grind, but a grind nonetheless.

I could be completely screwed over in the first system. I could coast by conflict-free. I might find a game-changing weapon salvaging an old, dilapidated ship, or it could break apart and kill one of my crew.
Through all of this, there's a sense that you're slowly getting better. You've got to mix, match, and weave around what luck gives you to make the best of it. And after many, many failures, you get more efficient, more ruthless, more calculating. You start planning several moves ahead, even as you have no idea what's going to happen the next time you make a jump.
Great game, super unforgiving and super rewarding. Play it already.

I was connected to North American servers several times, and, being an Australian, had lag issues on a scale the world has never seen. Rockets actually appearing to fire thirty seconds behind actually firing, lightning guns that didn't hit, the players I was shooting being thirty seconds in the future. Latency problems aside, the game is Quake 3. Now, don't get me wrong, Quake 3 is awesome, but Live adds new features that have brought the rage and hatred of veterans.
A change I didn't like was picking your starter weapon.
Now, I cannot comprehend why they would do such a thing, as part of the fun in Quake 3 was scrambling to find a weapon more powerful than your starting maching gun, and for me, it was trying to find the rocket launcher before anyone else, but here, it just gives you a rocket launcher. Now, I both love and hate this, partially because new players can spawn with an instagib weapon immediately, and partially that I can spawn in with a rocket launcher, ready to confuse and juggle anyone with the poor judgement to enter my line of sight.
So, one thing to make Quake Live better is to have better matchmaking, taking location into account, so Australians and other people who live in countries far, far away from where the main servers are, can get into a decent game that doesn't cause a temporal anomaly, and maybe reduce the starter weapon pool to weaker versions of the guns.
(i.e a mini-rocket launcher that has rockets do less damage, and have a smaller blast radius.)
Until then, however, this game is a no-go from me.

>>Do not buy this game unless you really want to have the pc version. It misses key features that the consoles do have. You pay the same amount of money as you would for the console, but for missing features on the pc.<<
The biggest gamebreaker is to wait for online to come in 3 months, but I think that was obvious for people looking to buy this. Just incase people looking to buy this game and reading this. Now you know.
I think the DOA franchise is pretty fun and one of my favorite, but this time KT gave the pc community the shaft by not porting over several features and making it essentially a PS3™ port. A last generation port in some aspects, because they are too lazy?
Missing features include: The Soft Engine (makes characters look better), which as Silconera explained last year, makes skin appear more natural, has been dropped, 2 stages and PS4™ equivalent particle effects are NOT included.
Some aspect ratios are missing as well. It supports 4k which is neat, but it misses a number of key resolutions. For example, 1920x1200. The best resolution you can get with 16:10 is 1680x1050 which is not really that great if you wish to have a higher res for 16:10 for that kickass monitor you have.
KT pretty much tells the modders community to not mod anything naughty. Before you port a game over the pc, obviously someone might do that. KT pretty much tells people how to mod this game, whats allowed and are limiting the modding communities freedom to do so or else they will refrain from porting another DOA to pc.
Now back to the game. The graphics and missing features bring me to this question. Why would you port over the DOA 5: last round game to the pc if it's essentially going to be a PS3™ version with less features than what you can get if you buy it on the PS4™ console? The background doesn't look as great since the textures quality isn't that great either on this port.
This only makes the consumers wanting to buy the console version instead of the pc one. Atleast i do, after i came to know about the missing features and graphical effects equivalent to the PS3™ version. It makes me really dissapointed that important features are missing. It doesn't have full controller support which is strange for a fighting game and keys are not rebindable, which makes no sense. If you use a fight stick it won't work properly unless you fiddle around with it somehow by rebinding start and select buttons.
Another aspect that has caught my attention. Pc gamers are forced to buy a bundle of dlc instead of individual character outfits. Console gamers can buy one outfit per character. Dlc is expensive on steam as it stands now. It is even more expensive than the game itself, so wait for a sale.
Another con: Found out that senran kagura outfits are not for sale on pc as dlc. For those who do not know. They have a special gimmick that the outfit gets torn when damaged enough. Might be updated or not, depending on KT.
The only positive side of the pc port is that it's stable, has modding support, resolution options and etc (like shadows). But thats it in my opinion. The game will just not look as good as it would on a next gen console which brings me to the fact that i can't recommend it in it's current state.
Only things that would get someone to buy this game  or make me recommend it is. If you are a huge pc fan, if you use a controller, if you can live with the PS3 graphics, bad texture quality in backgrounds and if you can wait for online in 3 months then yes it would be something for you.

Ok, I have not played a single DOA title since numbers 1 and 2 on the original playstation and arcade machines. That should tell you how old I am. So when I found out that DOA 5 was headed to the PC market, I didn't hesitate to pre-order myself a copy. I'm glad I did.
A couple things that many people will find disappointing. 1: No "Soft Engine" and PS3 particle effects and shaders, as well as no day-one multiplayer support. I can see where that would irk some. However, the game looks beautiful and runs great on my machine.
The character models are very well rendered and animated, and the hair system looks good with collision detections and very minor noticible clipping through the shoulders, I'd say hardly at all. The beads of sweat on the body and dripping down their faces after a match is a very nice touch and looks great.
Characters animate how you'd expect them to: Women are lithe and agile, and the muscle-bound men feel like they have a pressence even though they are all animated at the same speed.
Ok so no multiplayer for three months. You have PLENTY to do in the meantime. The story is pretty good so far at the point I'm in, and there are tutorials that you can master and get bonuses as well as a series of combo challenges.
The controls are great, haven't played it on a keyboard since I've been using an XBox 360 gamepad. My only complaint is that the analog stick for movement has a high latency in this game and really requires you to jam it all the way forward or back just to move, so I suggest using the D-pad.
Speaking of controls, they are very easy and intuitive to pick up even if you've never played a single DOA title in your life. All characters (and it's a pretty big roster) share countless moves with each other which means you don't have to lean every single move of a character. And each character has individual moves unique to them for you to master.
As I said about the story, it's not bad. Each chapter is filled with a few single round fights relating to that character and each chapter is a new character. I don't know if the game gets progressively harder the further you progress, or if that is just me playing characters I haven't trained with.
There are music tracks to unlock (and can be set to a certain theme for individual characters and such) as well as costumes for characters.
There are several modes of fighting outside of the story mode. Time attack, Survival, Versus (tag or solo) and arcade (also tag or solo matches) with multiple difficulties ranging from the easiest to one that will test even the best players.
A couple of things I want to note about the engine this game uses. And is practically manditory to mention in the DOA games. The breast jigglage has been toned down in this game versus previous games to a more realistic physics model.
Also, even if it is on the ps3 engine, like I said earlier, that game is just beautiful to see in motion.
My last comment in my review are about the stages. There is a good selection of stages, all unique and varying, and many of them are multi-tiered fighting rings with multiple environmental hazards ranging from electric fences to exploding cars and even a tiger jumping through a flaming ring to maul your opponent.
I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who enjoys fighting games, as there are not enough top quality fighting games on the pc besides Street Fighter 4, Street Fighter x Tekken, and Mugen.

Sometimes, when watching a film or reading a novel, you feel a burn of emotion deep inside your chest. Something that affects you so profoundly that it moves beyond being just a form of media. It is internalized and remembered forever.
Braid is one of those things. But it isn't just an example of art in gaming, it's a game full of pure genius as well.
The game, at first, comes off as a platformer. There are relatively little instances of hardcore platforming in the game, and they usually only serve as a medium to allow you to interact with the puzzle that you're dealing with. Make no mistake, this is a puzzle game at heart.
The puzzles here are incredibly good, and very well scaled from level to level. The first two levels are relatively easy and will only take you a few minutes, the third is a bit harder, and the last puzzles will make you feel like your brain is deflated. The amount of time that you'll have to put into each puzzle may be debilitating for some, but the sheer joy and pleasure of solving one overcomes any sense of stress that staring at your screen racking your brain may cause. These aren't just run of the mill puzzles, either. There are a number that are, in my mind, some of the best puzzles that I've ever seen in a game.
The art direction is beautiful. The backgrounds are watercolor constructed, they're vibrant and bright, and dark and brooding. The soundtrack is perfectly placed and flooded with beautiful violin work. Each are augmented by an incredibly written preface that comes prior to starting each level. The story is written so broadly and so metaphorically that it can literally be translated to represent whatever the player would like it to. The ending represents one of the epic twists in video game history, and does so in game -- a puzzle in itself.
I literally cannot think of one thing that I dislike about this game. It could be longer, but length can't really be expected from a game that costs so little.
There is so much value stuffed into the 10ish hours that you'll spend playing this game, it's hard to put it into words any other way than just to spout off the cliche of "buy it and experience it yourself". It's an experience to be had, and it's one of the most artistically beautiful exhibits in gaming history that is guaranteed to affect you in a most profound way.

It's early access, and we all know what that means. Expect bugs, lack of optimization, etc...but the core gameplay is great.  Assuming the developers are responsive to the community (and based on the first patch and discussions on preventing offline raiding things are good so far), there's a lot of opportunity here.  The game itself plays like a mix between ARK and Skyrim.  The survival aspects are real, but not too punishing, and it feels a lot less grindy that ARK.  Your character matters a lot, and as you level up your character through general experience gains, you also level up individual skills by doing tasks that pretain to that skill, which is a lot of fun.
The core mechanics are solid, although the game seems to run better on private servers than the public ones...but just like ARK, I tended to avoid the pubilc cheating/exploiting/hacking garbage than tends to ruin public servers anyway.
All in all, if you're looking for a great cross-over between an RPG and an open-world survival game, D&L is it.

Braid is a refreshing independant release, cleverly mixing puzzle and platform games. Using time-travel based mechanisms, the player has to make his way through very short levels, where he will encounter goons and bosses to kill, and enigmas to solve in order to get some mysterious puzzle pieces. One of the most interesting aspect of the gameplay is that the "rules" of time-travel evolve, and change in each chapters, forcing the player to adapt permanently.
Aside from the fact that mixing time-travel with a Supermario-like adventure is sometime quite surprising, as it breaks a few common rules of platform games, Braid is a very aesthetically pleasing game. The soundtrack, using classical instruments, is beautiful, and the painting-style animation is superb. The icing on the cake is that Braid also contains a original and deep story, told in a very unusual way.
One of its only drawbacks is that the lifespan is quite short (it takes an average person about 6 hours to complete the game). But given its low price, and the fact that the player will go for it again, just to enjoy the unique atmopshere, or to try to figure out the part of the plot he missed, that lifespan is satisfactory.

EA...  Uh oh.... what did I get myself into?
Klei.   Wait a second... that'.... that's a pretty good developer right?
Yes ... yes it is.  Klei is the same developer of some of my favorite games.  Don't starve, and Mask of the Ninja are two of my favorites.   And as for Shank?
Well I'll say it's another hit with a small caveat.    It's a fantastic side scrolling fighter where the player is given a shank (of course) a chainsaw, and pistols and has to fight through hundreds of enemies for a revenge story.  The story is actually pretty good, if a little strange.  The player's family was murdered and now he's out to kill "the butcher" and from there... well a lot happens, and he has to fight his way through many many enemies to get that revenge.
The gameplay is pretty simple, but you do have a number of attacks, you get a shank attack (weak but easy to hit with) a chainsaw (a strong attack but slow) and the guns (a range attack but... actually over powered as hell)  and from there you have a lot of enemies.  But in addition there's a pounce attack, a grapple, a grenade attack and of course a block/dodge move.  And really all of these together make the player field either really powerful or really weak.  If you take away the block and dodge move, the player will easily get over whelmed, there are some attacks that might not be dodgeable, but most of the game, those are the key to winning.  The game compensates by through four or five enemies at you, and most of these guys don't know the rule about attacking one at a time.  And of course that's a good thing.
The player has to take on a variety of enemies including larger enemies that can't be grappled easily, and can't be pouced at all, and each encounter feels fresh, even though most of the time you will be fighting the same enemies.  There's a few moves that are just "win" buttons until you find the enemies that can handle it, or you get swarmed by enough enemies to make it challenging, and that's a good feeling.  The player feels both strong, and weak at almost the same time.
The negative for this game though is that it's short.... Not very short, but I was able to run through it in 4 hours.  There's a hard mode, but I wasn't compelled to play it (No checkpoints would make this game brutally hard).  There's apparently a co-op mode with a different set of levels and enemies, and I'd love to tackle that but I didn't have a partner.   So there is ways to length the game especially if you have someone else who wants to play the game, but realize the base single player game is shortish.
However overall this is a great game, it's very stylized.  The game sounds like it's going to be bloody, and there's some blood in cutscenes, but surprisingly less bloody than I expect from a game called Shank.   It is violent, but not overly so.  Personally I think this is a gem of a game, that missed out on a little celebrity.  I've heard the combat called a touch simple, but.... it's a 2d brawler, it's far more complex than similar games, so to me, this is just right.  Doesn't overstay its welcome and provides a fantastic experience.

This awesome RTS has so much more to offer than what appears at face value. I am writing this with 1 hour of game play in because I am so excited and will return to update it when I have a few notches on my belt. The game play is more than solid. The graphics are comparable to any other triple (A) RTS of the time. It's the lore behind Warhammer that gets me excited. It is really no wonder Warhammer is a house hold name.
Some games can't get the basics right, like controls. Dawn of War is not a game like that. moving units is not a tedious chore. It is smooth, fluid, and simple to grasp. the build and research menu is simple enough and if you have experience with these types of games you should have no problem knowing were to find what your looking for in a timely manner. This allows building to be constant. Building and research  time management is important, as it should be with any true RTS. It was a nice breath of fresh air, to play a game that had the controls, mechanics and over all functions of the game flushed out.
The graphics are not the greatest of all time, But they hold up strong against similar games of the time. You would have the ability to zoom in rotate, pan or other wise manipulate the camera in away you feel. In Warhammer you wont really have the time to be creating cinematic scenes while in game. This is a good thing. It basically means you won't be so bored that you will be zoomed in on your favorite unit's attack for hours on end.
Not only was the game play its self well executed and the graphics, suitable for the purpose. The reason I bought Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War was because of the lore and deep story driven universe behind it all. Just by looking at the Warhammer series on a whole, it was clear I had missed something. Warhammer began as a physical  table top strategy game in the late 80's. Fans of warhammer have been following along for 20-30 years. On one hand, I thought it was to late for me. Until, someone said this to me "its ok if you don't understand Warhammer, you can just jump in anywhere and eventually, you will" I would definitely recommend you at least check out Warhammer and its universe if you have not yet. Don't let another 20 years go by with this amazing game in your back log.

Wehrmacht is marching into the Soviet Union. It's 1941 and one of the largest military campaigns in the history of warfare is about to begin. Company of Heroes 2, makes no qualms about how desperate and costly the conflict on the Eastern Front was for both sides.
Fourteen large missions make up the Company of Heroes 2's campaign mode. They follow Lieutenant Lev Abramovich Isakovich, a Soviet Officer who now resides in a Siberian gulag. Presented as flashbacks, this tried and true method of storytelling follows Isakovich and his superior, as they discuss the war and the Lieutenant's disgust at the atrocities committed by his comrades.
The campaign is pretty massive and it begins with Operation Barbarossa in 1941 and ends in the conquest of Berlin. Missions are varied presenting new challenges along the way & each mission also has two or three phases, which are added as older ones are completed. This really adds to the gameplay and makes the game that much better.

Big boys toys are vast and varied throughout the game too. You will find both mechanical and human to enjoy. There are, what almost feels like, limitless tanks, artillery, jeeps and soldiers to play with. Many of which can be upgraded with new abilities or, in the case of the soldiers, scavenge new weapons left scattered on the battlefield.
The games physics and graphics give the game a more realistic feel too. Smoke from explosions will block a sniper's field of view, walls are smashed down by indomitable tanks, artillery bombardments dent the ground with craters which can be used by infantry for cover and buildings are consumed by raging fires; as flamethrower-wielding engineers attempt to barbeque hiding foes.

One thing I really like in Company of Heroes 2 is, the weather component. It gives the players one more thing to manage during missions, but yet never seems to be overbearing on the mission at hand. Thanks to the changing weather, it does make for some fun additional challenge and does not seem to get tiresome.
You should also be careful not to leave troops out of cover, or they might find themselves freezing to death. Body temperature represented by a small, blue meter & when it turns into a tiny skull, they will stop and eventually collapse, never to fight again. Units can also walk or drive over frozen rivers, but be wary, the ice can also be their end. Ice can crack from heavy vehicles (Ever seen Ice Road Truckers) sending soldiers to a very cold and very wet grave. It is also a tactic that can and should be exploited by you but remember, AI forces will use this tactic too.
Playing through the campaign wasn't as challenging as expected either. It was a compelling and story-driven campaign, but still not as challenging as I had anticipated in my mind. Some possible reasons for this could be that despite the contrary, troops are almost a "throwaway" item, enemies make poor use of the environment and ambushes are fairly rare also. Perhaps a patch down the road will bring better campaign AI, for now though, the enemy AI seems a little "dense" at times.

That said, other gameplay options are available:
The "Theatre of War" mode is a series of one-off missions that are noticeably harder than the campaign. Some are single player, some are co-op, some are AI skirmishes.
"Victory Point" and "Annihilation" Multiplayer Modes. Here is where the fun happens. Both MP modes have thirteen maps available to them and both are very different from each other. Victory Point is effectively a "Domination" style mode where players gun to to hold key points and the side with the least amount of points slowly loses points until their total reaches zero. At which point the other team wins.

"Annihilation" mode is a deathmatch scenario. Unfortunately, it does somewhat, lack imagination however I still found it to be fun. Playing Multiplayer requires tact and planning. Human enemies certainly offer a much harder game (in most cases anyway) which means using all of your skills is now more paramount than ever.

coh2 02Company of Heroes 2 kind of gives off the feeling that perhaps it is just one massive expansion pack for the original, in saying that, it is probably not a bad thing. The foundation from the original game can still be felt in this sequel, but a reinvention it is not. In the world of RTS, I must say that this is certainly one of the strongest games I have played in a while, even with it's few shortcomings. New players will find the ease of the campaign an excellent introduction to the franchise and the returning veterans should find plenty to like about the addition of hostile weather and the expanded multiplayer component.

If you liked the original Company of Heroes, you will surely like Company of Heros 2. RTS fans in general will enjoy this game. Like I said, apart from a few shortfalls, this is still one of the best RTS games I have gotten my hands on for a long time.
