The Pro's of this Program are that one may produce something very complex fairly fast,
with the use of shortcuts as well as easy and attainable modeling workflow.
For 'creative' or more hobbyist activities in the 3D world I'd recommend sticking with Blender,
because it promises a very fast learning courve to anything that you can do in it :
(Modeling, Animation, or even 3D printing mechanical things, industrial CAD or (industrial) prototyping and more)
But for more professional VFX animations ike fluid/smoke/fire simulations, cloth, destruction, physics, particles,
there are other programs like 3Ds max that can handle it better. (But you will be fine with Blender , too, if you learn optimal workflows.
The only big negative thing about blender is outside of the program itself, and even tough Blender is by no means worse than the industry standards like Max, Maya, or Modo etc. , its not being used by 'professional' studios, or most smaller ones. There are some Indie - type  game developers or Animation studios that use Blender, but the problem is from what I have catched, that its not applyable to these big companies because of the constant Updates and no "final" version.
I would still recommend learning as much as I did in Blender, for like a year intensified, or more.But if you really want to get into the Industry as a job , most require to use Max, and Maya for animation studios.
There are some cases in which they dont necessarily ask for you to work in Max etc. , but just make good Artwork,
and thats what it is about, after all.
CONCLUSION:
Use Blender for an enry into the 3D Industry, and keep using it if you want to work for yourself (freelance, Indie, Hobbyist)
And you can get very professional and make very stunning work in it , too. (You are not limited, after all )
But the problem is that its still not accepted as an industry standard, so take into consideration and research about what programs to learn in future , if the 3D career is truly for you.
PS:
sorry for having the review a bit negative sided, but I guess most of the reviews dont mention the points I brought forward. ;) I really love using Blender, tho.  And sorry for the language mistakes as its not my mother tounge

Race’07 is simply a must to any real sim racer’s library. It is quite simply the best touring car experience out there. I've put hundreds of hours into this sim, most of which doing competitive league and championship racing at
. The features and details this sim has to offer, especially at the time of its release, were second to none. Comprehensive tire model, very rich setup with (most) cars responding very well to the setup changes, best FWD touring car or similar experience to date, windscreen and visor bug splats/mud with helmets having tear-offs, lots of good add-ons (particularly Retro Expansion!) which gave a variety of cars and more tracks such as the entire Green Hell and a barrage of GT1 - GT3 content with the GTREvo expansion.
The GT car physics are sub-par, I'll be honest. GTR2 was much better for these and GTRE fails to exploit the same GT experience. The formula cars are kind of a hit and miss. You really need to dive into the setup to get these feeling correctly, but the FMaster and FRR are really fun when you do. Unfortunately the Formula cars in this game use GT car brakes! Grand Prix length events with the FRR, even with full brake duct and lower pressure, will overheat and destroy the brakes. Because they overheat at 600C like the GT brakes, instead of overheating at the F1 range of 1000C, which they can easily reach with higher ambient temperature and heavy brake-load circuits. Unfortunately having my brakes fail in two Grands Prix cost me a very prestigious drivers championship at R2P so I remain bitter about that flaw.
But all-in-all the setup depth and complexity and telemetry coming off the car, the amount of cars and the detail put into the individual physics for each (even model-by-model in classes!) is amazing, the detail of the tracks including the bumps and undulations of the surface make driving a F1 or GT1 car on the edge in league racing incredibly intense, and just.. yeah. It's a sim, not an arcade game. If you take the time to learn how to setup each car, push yourself to be consistent and drive it like a sim - drive it like you would a real car - setup your FFB to really feel the front suspension weight transfers this is a driving sim experience like no other!

Wow. I don't know what to say, really.
I opened Steam, which takes me to the store page. And while I put the charger in my phone, I saw this going by on the slideshow.
My first thought was; Huh, a new Shelter game? I've heard about them, but never played them. I saw it was extremely cheap, which made me check the game's page.
I look at some of the reviews, and from what I could gather it was an open world Shelter game, online no less. I instantly bought it, frankly because I was bored, but I was also very curious.
I launch the game and start off as a badger cub. I walk around for a bit, not seeing a single soul. I eventually meet another badger cub, and I use one of the emotes to say hi. He responds with a big X, and I took that as a sign to ♥♥♥♥ off. I searched for more animals, and before I knew it, I was in a huge pack of animals, including other badger cubs, bear cubs, a goat and lynxes. And I had a surprising amount of fun.
What's the objective? Well, shortly explained, you walk around searching for crystals and flowers. All of these give you points, which dictates your spot on the game's leaderboards. The crystals have an extra benefit, though.
Gold: Progression to new animal.
Blue: New fur.
Red: New emotes.
Every animal have their own individual blue and red crystal progression. It works like puzzle pieces, so when you get enough, you unlock a new emote/fur/animal.
Red and blue crystals can be found in the wild, while gold can only be found inside monoliths, as far as I know. Blue can also be found in these. There are circles on said monoliths, which indicate how many different players need to make noise for it to break. Some monoliths also require a certain species of animal. This basically means that, you cannot progress the game alone. Unless you don't mind wandering around at your own leisure.
There is no voice or text chat. Communication is purely through emotes and body language. It seems weird at first, but it works really well. Pretty much everyone is willing to make parties, so say hi to everyone you meet!
That being said, it's not a competitive game at all. You explore at your own (or your pack of strangers') pace. The game is not fun, unless you make it fun.
I enjoyed it way more than I thought I would, and I'll still be playing this.
P.S. I write this on my phone in a car ride, so there might be spelling errors. I'll proof-read when I get home.

I was really looking forward to this, but I cannot recommend this in its current state. It's going to need some big changes to improve, changes I don't see them moving to make. The 2 big problems are micromanagement and grind.
Micro management hell:
In order to give it the RPG elements that seem mandatory in every game these days, each ship can be upgraded with tons of special abilities, all of which have their own separate hot key and button. It's common to see ships with a DOZEN ability buttons each. Many of these are ridiculously powerful (nova cannon, stasis bomb) and tend to overshadow the basic guns. The game ends up resembling an MMO style ability cooldown management experience rather than a naval maneuvering game. It doesn't feel like you're fighting with ships so much as you're controlling dueling space wizards casting spells. It would be one thing if all these special abilities were limited to support style ships, but EVERY ship gets the SAME "spells". A light cruiser can "cast" the exact same stasis bomb as a battleship.
Speaking of the upgrades in general, there is no strategy to choosing them because a couple are obviously useless (+5 degrees/sec turn speed when instant turn maneuvering thrusters are already practically free?) while a couple are obviously better (almost any of the damage/gunnery skills). You end up seeing fleet with 90% the same skills (oh hey another stasis bomb).
All of this is made worse by the default speed being way too fast. WAY too fast to be managing what amounts to controlling 2-6 individual MMO characters. You can activate a "bullet time" mode (tactical cogitators) which effectively pauses the game, but it's jarring having to do this constantly. If you really want to be serious about your micro, you'll rarely let it run at default speed for more than one second at a time, having the announcer scream "TACTICAL COGITATORS ONLINE!" every single time you pause (holy hell will you get sick of hearing that).
The speed also causes large groups of ships to crash into each other constantly. In the tabletop, it assumed the distance between ships in space was big enough that collisions were only possible if one ship was intentionally trying to ram. In this game you're going to have ships constantly bumping off each other like pinballs unless you use your annoying and precious pause time to avoid it.
The grind:
Holy hell the grind. You start off only being able to use a single light cruiser and a couple of the smallest escort ships. It is very boring playing with just these. To unlock more, you must grind battle after battle to gradually earn xp until you're "allowed" to use whatever ships you want in a battle. It's so slow and obnoxious that it feels like a F2P unlock model designed to make you go "screw this" and fork over cash to skip the grind, except this is a full price retail game you already paid for. This unlock model would be fine in the single player campaign which plays out like a long term RPG experience, but for skirmish and multiplayer? Completely unacceptable. It's going to take 10-15 hours to unlock every unit for a race, and you must repeat this for every...single...race. If that wasn't enough, you must repeat the grind again for every...single...difficulty level. Spend 40 hours unlocking everything on normal and want more of a challenge? That will be 40 more hours to unlock everything on hard, please. Totally unacceptable.
This isn't even getting into the horrible mechanic where fleeing or losing a ship means you cannot use it for X number of battles. This would be fine for the single player campaign but it carries over into skirmish and multiplayer Ridiculous. Imagine playing a Warhammer game and having someone take away your models if they die. "You can have them back at the end of the day." Whether it's laziness or insanity, the developers are obsessed with carrying over all the campaign mechanics to the skirmish or multiplayer modes, regardless of how badly it doesn't work. Some insane people will defend it saying, "It gives your ships value!" All it does is promote overly cautious play where people give up at the first sign of losing and run away. Some battles start with players retreating right away because they don't have their good ships and are just trying to "grind" X number of battle to get them back again. Ridiculous.
I realize you can’t make it an RTS and have it be a perfect conversion of the table top game, but they screwed up so many of the core concepts. In the table top, you got ONE special order per turn and had to roll to see if you could carry it out or risk losing control. Many special orders had drawbacks (full speed wouldn’t let you turn, brace for impact cut your firepower in half, etc). It was a risk vs reward setup. In BFG Armada, everything is just a free MMO cooldown ability. All movement is no longer tied to special orders but a stupid boost gauge. There is no drawback to any of the special orders (other than waiting for the cooldown) and the movement stuff is free. Carriers no longer need to use the Reload order between launches and can use just as much extra speed boost as other ships. The result is boring, overly long games of chasing endlessly kiting ships around.
There’s the whole damage model. In the TT, the point of manuevering was to “cross the T” like old naval battles since it gave you the best chance to hit. In this version, heading does not matter. 90% of maneuvering is just getting into range of the MMO spells and trying to keep ships from bouncing off each other like drunken bumper cars.
The campaign? I thought this would save the game. A longterm campaign with strategic decisions to make inbetween battles? Sadly, no. The only choice you're presented with every turn is "choose one of two systems to fight for and you'll lose the other one". That's it. It's like an XCOM game with nothing but terror missiosn but dumbed down even more.
Special mention really must be made how awful the sound design is. You're supposed to be firing massive thirty FOOT shells and 100 meter long torpedos and other outlandishly massive weaponry, but all you hear tinny fart noises that have all the impact of a pea shooter. Your ears should be blown away every time these shots land. Contrast this to World of Warships where weapons 2% the size have 100 times the aural impract and you hold your breath when torpedos are about to hit. You know what's even worse about the sound? While your massive cannons pack the sonic punch of a baby's burb, your crew shouting will shatter your eardrums with TACTICAL COGITATORS ONLINE! FULL SPEED A-ALL STOP-FULL SP-RESUMING NORMAL SPEED TACTICAL COGITATORS ONLINE RESUMING NORMAL FUNC-TACTICAL COGITATORS O-RESUM-TACTICAL COG-RESUMING NORMAL FUNCTION! If they took half the effort they put into having your crew constantly scream at you into making the weapons sound halfway decent...
If it was just the over use of MMO cooldown abilities and too fastly paced combat, I say maybe get it and hope that they improve it. However, that in combination with the insane F2P grind model and ship loss penalty push this into an emphatic thumbs down. If you're interested, check the updates and only purchase it if they fix 2 out of 3 of these things.

(me at age 6!) it was the 2000's kids version of something like the Tiger electronic games, or like the game packages for your Imac or windows XP! in the sense that, they were cheap (in this case free) and everyone had them!, they were milked to death! sites were dedicated to keeping thousands of these free games up and running with cheap monetization tactics like having a page with nothing but an add show up before sending you to the URL where the game runs, on top of having adds seconds before the game loads, as well as ADS cover up the whole page, SLOWING DOWN THE ♥♥♥♥ING GAME!  as well as an ad that surrounded lower resolution games, making them harder to play!
Out of the thousands of free games that we used to play, only about 8% are actually worth remembering. Dino run belongs in that 8% of alright to good games, and for browser litter game standards, the original version is a masterpiece.
Its an okay game, not one you would want to invest your free time to modding to perfection or to make a speed run for world record, its just a simple platforming game that gets early internet era kids such as me in a nostalgic mood.
I say play it first on browser if you want, consider downloading it later on steam for the novelty of extra content to a game that doesn't really cry for more than what it already offers for free.
Its a novelty, a gift shop trinket, but it has a charm that few browser games have mannaged to keep through the years.

I have played several Simbin games. All of them including this one are very realistic with excellent steering wheel and force feedback handling.

Tip for beginners:
Many people recommend beginners to use driving aids in sim games.
I do not.
If you are, say in your forties and an experienced driver in real life, go for the most realistic, just choose cars in the beginning that are similar to cars you have driven for real.
When practicing, go for better time than your last, but don't try to be an ace. Otherwise you might make to many mistakes, get disappointed and loose interest in the game..

I've played through a few chapters of the campaign and run a few skrimishes as the non-Imperial races and so far I feel the game is pretty good. One of the stumbling blocks for me getting started was expecting the game to play at roughly the same difficulty as most RTS I've played through in the past, but in Battlefleet Gothic you really can't just mass your ships and just point them at the enemy and hope to win most of the time. Positioning and knowing how your ships perform compared to the enemy are really important to the point where you might breeze through the first few missions only to find yourself losing mission after mission until you adjust your fleet comp and tactics based on your foe and the objectives.
So, I guess if you're looking for a C&C type RTS this probably isn't it, but if you're looking for something more micro intensive with a bit of a learning curve this might be the game for you, That said, if you're into multiplayer I can't make any recommendation on that yet as I haven't delved into that part of the game at all.

Shank is an action-packed brawler with a lot of humour and gore.
The artwork and graphics of Shank are brilliant. The vividly drawn and animated eye-catchers are numerous, not only in the cut scenes but throughout the game. Admittedly, you have to be a fan of violent and gory titles to fully enjoy the cartoon graphics.
Another very positive aspect is the sound and the music: Both are varied and atmospheric.
This is also true for the gameplay. You can seamlessly and without much effort combine your moves to create lunatic, wicked combos of melee and gun action.
I would have given the game an even higher score, if two problems would not spoil the fun a little. When you play the game in hard diffculty, the last level before the end boss can be quite a nuisance. This is so because when you die, you have to begin at the beginnning of the level, and, as it is not that easy, doing the same over and over again can be tiresome. The other slightly negative point with this title is partly the multiplayer. As such, it is fine, and, even more, it offers a backstory to the single player which is well-done. But this is also a problem because you can obviously, but unfortunately, only play it with somebody else, and apparently only with a local player (not via internet). The only workaround seems to be using a programme which allows you to simultaneously control two players at the same time, such as, GlovePie.
In general, this is a masterly produced and designed game with excellent playability and art style, so I give it an 85 % rating.

Shank is a 2D brawler. Shank tells the tale of a very angry man who was left for dead while his girlfriend was kidnapped.
Shank has been wronged , and you set out on a quest to fix these injustices by slaying every person who dares to stand in your path.
You job is to kill everyone involved until come to the man behind it all. Boss of bosses. This reminds me of movie Kill Bill.
And so you fight, and fight, and do a bit of jumping, and fight some more.
You're not chasing loot, or levelling up your character; you're merely slashing, shooting and chainsawing everything that gets between you and the right-hand side of the screen.
Every few levels you're presented with a new weapon, and it's fun to see how a machete handles differently than a katana or see how things change when you switch from a pistol to a shotgun.
The high point of the single-player adventure is the boss fights. These fights are all pattern based, and though they are fairly easy, they are still quite entertaining.
Each boss has a specific weakness you must exploit, ranging from knocking one thug into a roaring fire to tricking a butcher into lassoing a hanging pig.
Shank singleplayer mode is 3 hours long. Aside from the single-player campaign, there is a separate story mode to play through cooperatively. This is a prequel tale to the main event, and you are restricted to teaming up with your buddy locally as there's no online option here.
Despite that combat is simplistic and repetitive I still did find this game entertaining.

Klei is far and away my favorite developer just for the majesty that is Invisible Inc, but they have a plenty impressive catalog outside of that. Shank goes way back to their early days as their second title, and while it carries their distinct style it definitely feels like a sophomore effort. I love a good beat-em-up and Shank is packed to the brim with blood and combos, but it makes a few of the common mistakes that games of the genre often do.
Have you seen Desperado? Good, you know the plot to Shank. Dead lady, three henchmen, one big bad. Your headlining character comes armed with knives, pistols, grenades, and a chainsaw to work his way through streets and rooftops full of thugs. There's a bit of climbing and swinging between fights but the bulk of your time is going to be spent comboing mooks to death and chugging 40s to get your health back.
Keeping enemies corralled while you hack them to bits is key here, because Shank is a full 2D beat-em-up with no Z-axis movement. Your foes are a diverse bunch, with spry stick fighters, machete-wielding psychos, gun-totting troopers, lumbering brawlers straight out of Fist of the North Star, and more. The further you get in the more the groups are mixed, causing plenty of chaos and headaches when you have to manage melee, ranged, and explosive threats.
Early on the slick combo system provides an easy hook for the game. Everything you do combos beautifully, no matter how you mash your light, heavy, and gun attacks. If you can turn that button-mashing into strategy you should be able to hang with the game pretty well, but by the time you get on the third minion's trail the challenge starts to get a little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tty. There's more than one sequence with random explosives raining down on you, and a major late-game street brawl has four waves of foes capped with a minigunner who can easily stunlock you to death.
You have plenty of tools besides just your three attacks, including two kinds of grapples and some very useful grenades. While mixing things up can help you get out of unfavorable brawls, it won't help you much against the bosses. Each big bad has a gimmick that must be exploited to beat them, unless you want to whittle their health down a sliver at a time. It's not always obvious what you should do but dying once will pop up a tip straight-up explaining the gimmick, which is a heavy-handed but effective way to address the difficulty.
There's a lot of combat in this game over the two to three hours it'll take to beat, so minor aggravations can easily weigh Shank down. Even with all the enemy types it gets repetitive after awhile, playing out across sprawling, linear levels with no secrets or items to find. If you're just here to kill people, though, you'll get plenty of that in lavish comic book style. The game's cutscenes are a highlight, rendered like everything else in Klei's signature look, though the voice acting lacks the impact to really sell the scenes. Overall Shank is a bloody good time that drags in a few places but gives you more than enough action to make up for it.

Im waiting for some friends to get the game before I buy or host a proper server for us. So this review is based on my game time as solo mode.
Dark and Light has so much potential, but remember it IS early access and that means its unfinished. So if you're OK with that, and you've played other survival games (ark, conan, ect). You're in for a treat.
Imagine if Skyrim and Ark met in a club and had drinks and then had a fling and they had a baby. That baby would be Dark & Light.
I love how the EXP system works. Rather than spending points to unlock what you want, you have little sub-exp bars in various skills that unlock as you do things that those skills will need. For instance, you unlock ranged combat and bows by collecting wood and twine, two major components in making a bow. This is a really neat way of tailoring your character to your play style.
The game uses Unity, and so if you're familiar with Ark you will see a lot of the fingerprints of that game on this. It's also of note that the company behind this game bought Ark's developers. So, while some are calling this "the new ark", it's really just the next progression in the genre.
I've had fun so far, and I recommend it at the 25 dollar price. It's got enough to keep you playing for a while, and it's going to get even better over time.

A nicely done sidescroller brawler with revenge story.
Common problems, complaints with the game and their fixes:  the updated game removed some cutscenes because they retroactively changed their minds about what's beneficial to the game and what looks decent, removing the more bloody/aggressive parts for whatever reason (blood flows with every landed hit anyways...) ---> you can rightclick on the game in library, go to properties, then betas, and activate [shank classic]. You'll get achivements, everything works, and you'll get back the original cutscenes.  Also, if you play a game on a windows account that has non-english characters in it's name, the game won't be able to save. The fix is simple, create a new win login on the pc, it takes only 2-3 minutes.
And then about the game: the game goes roughly one (or two) normal levels, then a bossfight, unlocking new weapons as the game goes on. I played with a controller and the controls are absolutely on the point, easy, well-flowing experience. The story is alright, the main charm of the game is the fighting, managing a group of enemies with different attack styles and patterns and the game does a good job at it.   Normal difficulty's campaign is roughly 3 hours long, the game has a local coop story campaign (different one), with the use of joytokey or similar programs you can bind P1 and P2's controls to the same buttons, so it's even playeable alone :)  The game is a nice brawler-like game, with the bosses being focused on dodging and counterattacking a lot - I think normal mode offers a pleasant challenge and nice story for everyone, as checkpoints are forgiving, always spawning again with 3 granades.
extra about the hard difficulty:
It's a slightly negative aspect how much of an overkill hard difficulty is - having no checkpoints on whole levels while doing considerably less damage, while punishing super-hard for buttonsmashing / not dodging in time. They ocassionally stunlock you, and dropped health is extremely inconsistant (Big Guys drop hp, sometimes after fighting two I got 0, 1 or two health potions) and one of the later levels features a constant rocket barrage that was a pain in the butt even on normal...  so if you'd like to try hard difficulty, it's *really* hard compared to the normal, a real challenge, maybe a little more than it would be necessary.

As a former CoH 1 veteran and fan of competitive multiplayer strategy games, I finally found the game that will fill both aforementioned roles.
When CoH 2 was out, I refused to buy it after being frustrated by the inglorious end of CoH 1. Veterans of CoH 1 will understand... abandonment, bugs, imbalance, NAT connection issues, too many exploits and lame stuff that would ruin your fun in the long run.
I grabbed it on sale 2 weeks back together with Western Front Armies and I can say "well spent money".
For quite some time, I have been on the look out for a modern era strategy game that has deep tactical gameplay combined with an excellent multiplayer service; the one that you can just click automatch and start playing (ranked or not) against someone of equal skill. Something that games like "League of Legend" do very succesfully. And it gets better, as with the newly launched observer mode, you can now watch games live from other players.
As for the game itself, it exceeded my expectations. Graphics, voice overs, mechanics, the vaulting feature, the cold and much more are of superb quality. So much improvement over CoH 1 that I can sit here for hours listing every single one of them.
As for the balance I have yet to see any. From previous threads, I can see there were some issues but from what I have seen so far, most of them have been fixed. I believe you can expect to find a well balanced multiplayer experience.
-To CoH Veterans: Do not be as reluctant as me, BUY IT. It is not the pain we all remember as seen in CoH 1. It actually exceeds expectations. Hopefully, you will be as surprised (in a good way) as I am with it.
-To newcomers: I definitely recommend it. However, don't expect to find a game that plays like age of empires, starcraft etc. Remember it is a TACTICAL strategy game. A lot of stuff need to be done to achieve victory apart from training soldiers&tanks and blobbing them all in a single attack. My recommendation: Watch replays and live games! preferably from top players. This is the method I used to become better at this game. Watching how other players go around the battlefield can be an invaluable lesson that will only make you better. If you cant be bothered watching it all, just use 2X, 4X + speeds. You can still learn stuff even on Fast Forward.
The only negative that I want to mention is the great number of trolls and whiners that are present within the community. Unfortunately, that is something that wasn't adressed properly from CoH 1. If you take a look in the forums, you will see people whining, screaming over balance, trolling etc etc.
I believe there will always be small or big issues with balance with games like CoH2 due to the nature of the game itself. However, crying, cursing and screaming like a spoilt 10 year old "OMG OMG OP THIS OP THAT NERF THIS BUFF THAT ♥♥♥♥ NOOB, WTF RELIC, STFU OMG OMG", even if you have a legit point, it does not make it any better.
As with the first CoH, there were REAL issues with balance. Indeed! however, this was the excuse for people to start whining about everything. even for things that weren't broken. From my experience, most of the whining comes from L2P (Learn to play) issues. People that expect this game to be like age of empires. Sorry guys, this is NOT AoE. Learn to play well first then cry about balance. You will see that the things you call OP, UP or Broken are actually lack of experience and skill. Both Experience and Skill comes from playing and LEARNING from your mistakes.
Thats all!
9/10 Keep at the good work guys ;)

This is, by a long shot, my favorite sci-fi game of any genre, and it is probably my favorite singleplayer strategy game of all time on top of that. I'm a huge strategy fan, and I like games that present an interesting challenge. FTL is both interesting and challenging for many reasons.
It's interesting because it's a game about piloting a ship in space, but it's not 100% about combat (even though the combat is core to the game, and a lot of fun). You get to choose how you want to play. I've never really done a lot of traditional role-playing in games before, (where you pick a type of meta-personality you're going to stick with before you start a game) but it's a lot of fun to do in FTL. I once piloted a self-proclaimed pacifist ship from beginning to end without engaging in a single fight. I got my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me in the Last Stand, but I still completed my goal. I was able to talk my way out of fights, take bribes from pirates not to interfere in their hijackings, or keep my defenses powered up until I could jet away to safety. You can choose to be full defense, full lasers or missiles, full drones, or focus on stealth, hacking, mind control or a boarding party. Whatever you want.
When I say it's challenging, I mean it. I've played almost two dozen ship lives now, most of them on Easy, and I haven't beaten the game yet. I've gotten to the last phase of the Last Stand more than a handful of times, but I haven't sealed the deal. It just hasn't gone my way yet, but I'm not worried about it. I've had a ton of fun losing and unlocking new ship types and layouts. I just unlocked two ships that I haven't even tried yet, and the game remains fresh because of it's procedurally generated world and encounters. I have plenty of reasons to keep playing. Also, the soundtrack is ♥♥♥♥ing good!!

It's a "forum in game's clothing". Meadow has a wonderful map, the biggest one yet in any of the Shelter games, and you can explore it at your heart's content. You don't need to eat, you don't need to drink, you don't need to protect your cubs or fight for them.
This is also an online experience. There's no singleplayer, there are three different servers with three groves each where you can choose to hang out. Whether alone or with friends, Meadow makes for a unique experience you may or may not enjoy depending on your personal tastes.
Do you prefer a game with quests and npcs basically telling you to fetch their hat? Nope, not for you.
Do you enjoy a story-driven experience with a lot of plot? Nope, not here.
Do you want to roleplay in text chat? Absolutely not.
Meadow allows you to choose from a set of animals (which animals you have will depend on what you own from the Shelter catalogue) and each of them has its own quirks, skins and emotes.
That's right, emotes. Communication happens through the good old non-verbal channel: you can express your thoughts and objectives through a set of emotes. Body language and calling out is also a part of how you can express yourself.
After all, you're playing as an animal and that's exactly how animals communicate, and really, you don't need a text chat to say hi when you've got an adorable little emote just there. Personally this is one of the features I enjoy the most and I think that not having a text chat available really improves the experience, along with the fact that there's no tutorial. Tutorial ruins the immersion sometimes and immersion is what you need to enjoy this game to the fullest, you learn how to play by simply playing.
After all this is an unique experience. If you're looking for in-depth gameplay or complex plots then Meadow simply isn't your cup of tea and you can move along. If you've played "The Endless Forest" before you'll probably enjoy Meadow as well.
Then, on a side note: M&D is a great team of developers. For just 2,99 there's a nice amount of content, and more to come~

As much as I love this game, I simply cannot in good conscience recommend this to anyone but avid 40k fans. For more in detail about the mechanics of the game, look to other reviews, I'm mainly going to be covering my gripes about the game.
Heres why I think this game isn't worth 40$ in its current state:
This game is lacking some very basic features and has made some questionable design decisons at this time.
-Formations
--This is massive. For a 2d space game this should be one of the core things you impliment. Especially when positioning is so dreadfully important. The lack of it at launch reeks of heresy, and is extremely annoying.
-hotkey tooltips
--for a game thats so fast, hotkeys are incredibly helpful. However, no hotkeys can be seen upon the skill menu on the bottom right, making it very difficult to reliably remember all the different hotkeys for each individual ability.
-Glitches
--many more glitches were prevalent in the beta, and to their credit they have done a pretty good job stomping them out (although very very slowly). However, it should be noted on launch there are still a few annoying ones.
-Custom matches
--Yes its coming later apparently. But its not here now, and considering developer track record, it should be noted. I will edit the review once its added.
-Major balance issues
--The developers have the mindset of the big nerf hammer as compared to the small tinkering changes. In the beta they have drastically changed around abilities, added in new weapons, and entirely re-wrote abilities (forgetting to change the tool tips of course). This indicates a lack of forsight and gentle balance touch by the developers, making me worry for the future of the game between the 4 factions.
-Major missed opportunities.
--There are some really basic things they could have done to make this game much more thematic, but chose not to. For example, naming your captain of your vessel. Even if it didn't have any in game effect, putting a name to a captain makes it much harder to execute them in battle, and would have been a♥♥♥♥♥♥easy change.
-Lackluster campaign.
--This is the hardest of all for me to say. A almost XCOM like campaign defending the gothic sector from the enemies of the imperium and managing your planets in a slow downfall, barely winning against the odds? Count me in! However, the campaign is like a little nugget of fools gold. Amazing when you initially look at it, until you realize theres not much there beneath the surface.
First of all, its notable to say that only the story missions have voice overs of ANY variety. What would have been a nice addition of basic voice lines at start/end of battle is lacking, and when the voice actors are SO good for a 40k game, it really stands out when they arn't there considering how prevalent they are in the story missions.
Second of all, all non story missions use the same mission types as multiplayer/skrimish, with no variety/changes/campaign only modifiers. Not bad if your a new player, but if you play the multiplayer beta, or do skrimish/multiplayer alot and then come over to campaign? Very annoying, and gets repetative.
And third and most aggregious of all... The planets your fighting for feel meaningless. Names on a starmap with no context.
Its impossible to interact with any planet other than ones that have current defense missions on them. You can see a little tooltip next to them seeing what incredibly minute "bonus" they provide to you (its more of a "keeping a negative modifier from applying").
There is absolutely no fleet movement mechanic. You get a set number of deployments per "turn" to defend your systems. Most of the time, if you suceed in every mission, you'll keep on top of things. I've heard it gets quite difficult if you start failing, but on hard I personally am not having too difficult of a time.
The lack of a fleet movement system makes it ever more prevelant that the starmap is a fancy exel spreadsheet your trying to manage with your victories. No context or reason to fight in anything but the story missions.
All this combines to make you feel less of a admiral defending the systems against all odds, and more of a basic rts campaign of loosly related missions disguised under pseudo-random xcom style defense.
With all the gripes out of the way, I want to make this very clear:
This is a good game, bogged down by missed opportunities, glitches, and lack of basic RTS functions.
These are not unfixable by any means, save my gripes with the campaign unless they do a overhaul.
And there are plenty of good things about the game.
The core combat is satisfying, although a little fast.
The campaign is pretty decent, and the story missions with all the voiceovers and cutscenes are especially good.
The multiplayer is pretty fun, although lots of cheese fleets are currently hammering slow imperium/ork fleets.
But the question becomes this:
Are you willing to pay 40$ for a game that doesn't even have formations in a fleet style game?
If your a huge 40k fan, why are you even reading this? Buy it.
But if your not... I'd recommmend patience and watching the update cycles. If they fix the non-campaign issues, it would be worth buying. Otherwise... wait for a sale.

If you want Dead or Alive 5 just as a fighting game, and can wait patientily and practice for the next 3 months for the release of the online mode, then this is definitely worth getting as it now stands as probably the best 3D fighting game on Steam. We have no Tekken (yet), SoulCalibur, or Virtua Fighter, so as it stands the competition is near non existent. That is unless you count games like Naruto, which while good, are not really what I would call true competitive fighting games.
Dead or Alive 5 as a 3D fighting game is more than competent. It's fast. It's flashy. It's just fun to play. Nothing wrong with that.
Sure, this being Team Ninjas 2nd game to be ported to Steam, they are still showing they have a LOT to learn. I mean as far as ports go, this one is far from perfect. But it is not as broken as some say. It is missing some stuff. But the core gameplay is at this stage is excellent.
What is missing?
The Danger Zone and Crimson stages which are PS4/XBOX One exclusive
The Soft Engine
Some PS4 particle effects
Online mode (coming in the next 3 months)
Support for keyboard configuration
The only 2 things in that list I find a bit unacceptable would be the lack of online, which IS being patched in, and the keyboard configuration. Hopefully the KB configuration will be patched in later. Though I find for a 3D fighting game, that a controller works much better. And this game has controller support. But the other 3 things? I'm not going to whine and say this game sucks because of the lack of those things, like some people are doing. Why? Because I actually have enjoyed the game so far. And is that not what matters?
As for the game itself, Dead or Alive 5 is like a much faster and flashier Tekken and Virtua Fighter. A game that focuses mainly on hand to hand combat. It includes a basic fight system that consists of a punch, kick, grapple, and reversal button. It allows movement in all directions, with a basic side to side 2D movement as the primary, and an easy sidestepping as the alternate. Each of the 30+ characters has a wide array of moves and combos, and varying styles of fighting as to not have too many "duplicates" among characters. One of the big features of the DoA series is the reversal button, in which if you time and aim it right can reverse almost any move. But timing is the key. So people who master this move will obviously have a major advantage. The nice thing is that DoA very easy to learn. But DoA is also hard to master. It's a game you can play both casually and competitively and have fun either way.
Stages are the next big draw for the DoA series, as DoA is one of the first 3D fighting game seires to include multi-tiered fighting levels with breakable walls, or other hazards that knock players into new parts of the stage. And it looks absolutely fantastic when doing this. Like starting the fight on top of a balcony and knocking someone over the edge into a courtyard below, or smashing someone through a wall into the next room, and more like this.
And of course, the absolute biggest draw (though some will be ashamed to admit it) for DoA is the costumes. And there are tons of them. If you did not preorder the game, you still get a massive assortment of costumes to select from for the 30+ characters. Yes, the costume DLC at this point is ridiculously overpriced, but I guess fans are going to pay what fans are going to pay. But none of it is required to get the most enjoyment out of the fighting portion of the game.
Anyways, this is not really a review, but just me rambling, and looking for a way to give a thumbs up to this game. This game has a lot of potential. I have highly enjoyed even the single player gameplay all week. I highly recommend single player, at first, just to get your bearings. Once you figure out what you're doing, going to a hosted server and throwing PvP into the mix will make the multiplayer gameplay a very different experience than single player. There really is just so much to see and do in this game, I can't even begin to list the postive aspects. I don't think I've even explored more than 1/3 of the map, even with the 100+ hours I've already put in.  I'm really very pleased with the game, but I'm going to focus on reviewing the negative aspects of gameplay for the sake of Early Access development.
Some of the issues that really irritate me are:
Almost all mobs currently get stuck in trees. Makes them very easy to tame, though.
There are a lot of little villages that are currently unpopulated.
The 3 main cities could use quite a bit more attention to appear more alive and bustling.
There needs to be a few scripted boss events of some sort.
Crafted armor sets are not complete, most sets seem to lack an item for at least 1 slot.
Items like tier 2 and 3 water and air spells, as well as the iron greatsword cannot currently be crafted.
When ordering tamed mobs to "Wander" they should keep within a proximity of the location you gave the command.
The Bestiary UI seems like something they should've easily completed by now - it's a highly inaccurate mess.
There is an unbound/nonfunctional Keybind setting for "Defecate." Seems like overkill on the survival features aspect.
There is no way to clear the crafting queue on workstations like the Workbench or Magic Altar.
Mob density is way too high in most areas, they could cut down 50% of the population and still have too many mobs.
There should be a way to break down or disenchant items into base components from the inventory.
There needs to be much more variety of magic spells and skills.
Holding the block button should, directionally, block undefinitely at the espense of shield durability.
There needs to be a way to disable the quest/tutorial window for more experienced players.
The giant transport dragon gets stuck in one of the tower ruins on literally everyone's server.
There is no trade interface between other players.
Something else about tamed creatures that really irritates me is that all of the flying mobs follow you by flying in a circle that paths directly over you. They constantly path right over you at high speeds, and if you're trying to harvest things, you can very easily accidentlly kill them. They should just follow behind you like the ground mobs and not circle you. Their circling behavior is ideal for assisting you in combat, though. The ground mobs should try to circle enemies in combat, like the flying mobs do, so that you can use tactics to actually fight with your tamed ground mobs. Currently, either you attack the mob, or use your pet to attack it and watch. Any of the ground mobs will just charge the enemy and spam attack it as closely as it can get to the enemy, meaning if you try to attack an enemy with a tamed ground mob attacking it, you're just as likely to kill your pet as you are the enemy mob.
There are a lot of temple ruins/structures in the game, and you can't build on any of it. I was really dissappointed because I was expecting to see some sort of mini-boss, or something that drops some kind of special material or loot at each of these locations, they really seem ideal for it.
I haven't found any of the dungeons yet, but there are supposedly at least a few of them. So far, though, the only attainable items are either gathered or crafted. There aren't even any rare materials, dropped spells, dropped items, or any kind of traditional loot. I can't imagine the dungeons will be useful for anything other than exploration if they don't add any bosses or loot - very dissappointed. I would at least like to see some kind of specialized material drops like dragon scales, cyclops eyes, sacred griffon feathers, or just some items that make for some really fancy stuff if you put some real effort into attaining it.
As expected for an early release, there are quite a few bugs, and the game appears unfinished in some areas, most of which they've explained properly in the Early Access disclaimer. This game really shines with cooperative group play, and House (Small Guilds) PvP battles. A properly run server with a good community of solo players and rival Houses and I'd say this game has the potential to be better than any MMO ever released (it's not exactly an MMO).

As a former CoH 1 veteran and fan of competitive multiplayer strategy games, I finally found the game that will fill both aforementioned roles.
When CoH 2 was out, I refused to buy it after being frustrated by the inglorious end of CoH 1. Veterans of CoH 1 will understand... abandonment, bugs, imbalance, NAT connection issues, too many exploits and lame stuff that would ruin your fun in the long run.
I grabbed it on sale 2 weeks back together with Western Front Armies and I can say "well spent money".
For quite some time, I have been on the look out for a modern era strategy game that has deep tactical gameplay combined with an excellent multiplayer service; the one that you can just click automatch and start playing (ranked or not) against someone of equal skill. Something that games like "League of Legend" do very succesfully. And it gets better, as with the newly launched observer mode, you can now watch games live from other players.
As for the game itself, it exceeded my expectations. Graphics, voice overs, mechanics, the vaulting feature, the cold and much more are of superb quality. So much improvement over CoH 1 that I can sit here for hours listing every single one of them.
As for the balance I have yet to see any. From previous threads, I can see there were some issues but from what I have seen so far, most of them have been fixed. I believe you can expect to find a well balanced multiplayer experience.
-To CoH Veterans: Do not be as reluctant as me, BUY IT. It is not the pain we all remember as seen in CoH 1. It actually exceeds expectations. Hopefully, you will be as surprised (in a good way) as I am with it.
-To newcomers: I definitely recommend it. However, don't expect to find a game that plays like age of empires, starcraft etc. Remember it is a TACTICAL strategy game. A lot of stuff need to be done to achieve victory apart from training soldiers&tanks and blobbing them all in a single attack. My recommendation: Watch replays and live games! preferably from top players. This is the method I used to become better at this game. Watching how other players go around the battlefield can be an invaluable lesson that will only make you better. If you cant be bothered watching it all, just use 2X, 4X + speeds. You can still learn stuff even on Fast Forward.
The only negative that I want to mention is the great number of trolls and whiners that are present within the community. Unfortunately, that is something that wasn't adressed properly from CoH 1. If you take a look in the forums, you will see people whining, screaming over balance, trolling etc etc.
I believe there will always be small or big issues with balance with games like CoH2 due to the nature of the game itself. However, crying, cursing and screaming like a spoilt 10 year old "OMG OMG OP THIS OP THAT NERF THIS BUFF THAT ♥♥♥♥ NOOB, WTF RELIC, STFU OMG OMG", even if you have a legit point, it does not make it any better.
As with the first CoH, there were REAL issues with balance. Indeed! however, this was the excuse for people to start whining about everything. even for things that weren't broken. From my experience, most of the whining comes from L2P (Learn to play) issues. People that expect this game to be like age of empires. Sorry guys, this is NOT AoE. Learn to play well first then cry about balance. You will see that the things you call OP, UP or Broken are actually lack of experience and skill. Both Experience and Skill comes from playing and LEARNING from your mistakes.
Thats all!

Mero 2033 delivers a very interesting story and gripping gameplay. Metro 2033 is a First person shooter but unlike Call of Duty, the game changes pace from constant shooting to intense stealth segments. You will find your self slowly moving and looking around every corner when you hear a sound and/or when your searching for supplies.
Aside from the gameplay, the storys premise is quite facinating and its depiction of a dead Moscow due to the effects of nuclear weapons is truley remarcable. When the nuke hit, about 40,000 people made it into the metro system to survive. You play as a survivor named Artyom who has to travel to a distant section of the Metro system to deliver important imformation regarding hummanitys new enemy. The journey is not easy as you will have to fight or run for your life quite often. The story also contains themes about the threat of nuclear power on the environment and the dangerous aspects of human nature.
Metro blends action, a hint of science fiction, and a hint of horror. Deep silver also put in a lot of attention to detail such as having to switch filters for your gas mask or having to wipe your masks glass to see better.
There arent anythings that particularely bothered me other than very miniscule nitpicks such as the main character never talking except in his journal entries. so all in all this game is definetaly worth buying for retail price.

Metro 2033 Redux is an improved version of Metro 2033 that improves much in terms of graphics, new interaction, less loading screens, new guns, and more. The game takes place in post-apocalyptic Moscow, which looks great. The deepest, darkest areas in the game look good and are spooky. The Metro stations are believable and immersive, and the war going on between the N@zi and Communist parties is quite captivating and exciting. I also really enjoyed the dialogue in the game. Up above, in the streets of Moscow, ruin lies in the streets and the snow and buildings (both near and far) look great. The people who live in the Metro are likable and you will find yourself appreciating their presence. The gunplay is perfect, the guns can be upgraded, and there are weapons to suit everyone's needs (stealthy, close-up, distance). The enemies you will encounter are believable and diverse, although often only one type of enemy is dealt with in each area.
There are a couple of problems I would like to point out:
Some of the areas are frustrating, to say the least. At one point I completely ran out of ammo and had to run around while a NPC fought the Dark Ones in order to dodge and survive.
Do not try to kill the librarians- kill one to get the achievement, and sneak around the others. They are too strong.
The D6 area is a pain and made me almost want to quit. This is because I ran out of air filters at the beginning and had to rush around the D6 in darkness trying to find new ones. I spent many minutes trying to succeed and almost thought it was impossible to move on in the game.
The Tower has some QTE moments that I was not even aware of at first. Make sure to press E when you climb the ladder.
Back to the good:
The game is like all other good games; it is an experience, not at all just a way to pass time. I recommend Ranger mode because I often do not like HUD and it is grittier. Also, this game looks great on all graphics settings. In all, this game is a little world that lives and breathes, is interesting, and provides hours of entertainment. It is a time you will always want to remember.
Not much to say about this game. It's unique and fantastic. GREAT replay value and it's a game you can put down and come back to over and over again.

This game is complete with a great soundtrack, humourous commentary, comprehensive city building, and despotic policy making. You can opt for a totalitarian, militaristic government that executes any dissenters, with no media outlets, and where wages are low and offer jobs only in agriculture and mining. You can also choose to educate your citizens, provide electricity, and have a diverse source of labour with various industrial and professional sources of income. Creating your own city and managing it for fifty years will have you playing for hours; however, don’t overlook the campaign because it is both hilarious and captivating. This game is substantially better than both its predecessor and its successor. Tropico 3 is another great game, and Tropico 4 took everything good in that game and expanded it. Tropico 4 is essentially a more comprehensive Tropico 3. Tropico 5 forfeits much of the hands-on city building aspects that are present in Tropico 4 in favor of some strange combat engine. Tropico 4 is the gem of the series and is worth the price.
10/10 would recommend.

Fighting games are usually for a certain majority of players that like to improve their skills instead of having mindless fun, which isn’t a bad thing. It’s just that a lot of people are not going to enjoy it as much as DOOM or F.E.A.R in the long run. This happened to me as well.
However, Shank manages to be a part fighting game with platforming elements to give it enough variation for replayability to make the game memorable and last longer. There’s even enough charm in the game that makes the game gritty and laws of nature defyingly funny in looks which took me by surprise the first time I played it. The gameplay and art style is what the developers put thought into and not the story, so If your
thinking this game is for the deep and meaningful, then look somewhere else.

The mechanics of the game is more of a simplified, yet well-made fighting mechanic that manages to be easy to learn but hard to master. You have your only light weapon the shives, your heavy weapons, your ranged weapons and your limited throwable. You can combine these attacks to deck out massive damage on your enemies with time. The first time you play this you will die, A lot. But with time you will get better and that just brings up the next mechanic.
, you will love the grab move in the game because of the many things you can do to the thugs when you get your hands on them. Each weapon and move has a different variation on what you can do to the them and the others around you, especially throwing them against other enemies. The light attack with grab must be my favorite and my god is it brutal, anyone unfortunate enough to be in this situation will turn into a human ragdoll.
Then we've got platforming, what do I have to say, meh. It’s not bad it’s just easier than it looks. They're so contextual and smooth to go through that it makes a super meat boy stage as hard as a boss fight for the protagonist. But their short and a nice change in the game that somehow fits the setting well with all the impossible leaps of faith and the ability to
.

Basic enemies in the game are varied little in their shape, but what they make up for is in specialty. Any weapon that their holding will be used at the best of their abilities that fits the character’s movements. The light guys will usually use one handed weapons and numbers, the massive guys will mostly use two handed weapons and cover a large area, and the nimble girls will use light weapons and their movement. Even what weapon their using can dictate their health depending if they are ranged or melee. The variation is so large that even the enemies without weapons act differently, depending on their shape, which is quite impressive.
There are only two kinds of boss fights in the game, one that acts like more of a puzzle to defeat, and the ones that require you to remember everything you did when you encountered specific enemies. The latter is the hardest because the only way to deck damage is to attack normally, because the puzzle enemies take as much damage in their weak points, as a light, ranged guy. This is more of a mixed thing because some of them I liked and some of them I just didn’t like.

The art style in the game looks like a cartoon network version of “machete”. It’s well animated and entirely hand drawn. It doesn’t have hand drawn frames like “Skullgirls” but it looks good enough to be eye candy. The story fits the art style well with visceral violence mixed with bright colours to fit the theme. The story isn’t a timeless classic of our age, but is still good enough for the theme. The game story is about a guy “ironically” called shank and the story is unfolded to us about why he is taking vengeance against a group of organised criminals. It may sound serious but when you get to the point that you fight guys bigger than a house, why bother.
The cut scenes look good, but the dialogue is purposely asinine at best. The story is mostly told through the cut scenes with the character interactions being forgettable, but the way it’s given to us is its strength making character building and storytelling good. I would be lying if I said that I didn’t like the protagonist and some of the characters. It’s dark, it’s scary, and that’s what it just wants to tell us.

Now when you begin the game, one of the first things it shows to you is “recommended with controller”. Now you can play the game with the keyboard, it’s just that its layout is awful. The key binding scheme could have been laid out better, it just that the first time I played I assumed it was made without testing. It’s not a bad thing because you can bind the keys in ways to fit your style and you can play the game.
An even bigger complaint is balancing. There’s so many weapons and enemies given to you that balancing can be a hard thing. Some weapons are overpowered, whereas there are weapons that do sod all damage, a good example is the ranged weapons. The shotgun can pierce through enemies and the charge attack with it can literally mostly clear out a room of hostiles, where the submachine gun does less damage than the pistols and it's only good trait is it’s grab attack variant that does the more damage than the shotgun.
Certain enemies can be a pain, especially the dogs that tackle you and bite you to death. This wouldn’t be so bad if there wasn’t one attack you could do when you grab them and is just throw them, which does♥♥♥♥♥♥poor damage.

“Shank” has been recently overshadowed by its more smart and agile sister “mark of the ninja” which is probably a shame because it’s quite a good game. It manages to be a good 2D platforming fighting game for anyone who likes “F.E.A.R” or “DOOM” or generally feeling like a badass. If you want something to last and for something to show to your kids when you get older, buy this. You’ll like it, your kids will like it and you’ll probably bore your husband/wife to death when you talk about it.

IMPORTANT NOTE: BEFORE YOU START PLAYING THE GAME, MAKE SURE TO RIGHT-CLICK ON THE GAME (WHEN INSTALLED), THE GO TO PROPERTIES, THEN BETAS, AND MAKE SURE THAT INSTEAD OF CHOOSING 'NONE', THAT YOU CHOOSE 'classic'. When done, the game should say; Shank [classic]. The classic version includes all the cutscenes, while NONE is missing most of the cutscenes, so make sure to opt into the classic version under Betas.
Shank is an amazing, bloody 2D beat em up game that every indie fan should take a look into. Even though the story may seem a little cliche, it's still very enjoyable. The art and soundtrack of this game complement the story very nicely, but the soundtrack isn't something you'd listen to outside of the game. The gameplay is the best part of the game. Even though you only get a few weapons, it's nice to be able to switch them while in combat, so it can help when situations change very quickly. The AI isn't too bad either, they're not dumb, but they aren't hard to the point where it's impossible, at least on Normal difficulty. The boss fights are better than I expected. Some of the fights are really boring and way too easy, while some are challenging and exceptionally fun, especially the last fight. I actually played the last boss fight a few times over and over, so the game does have some replayable value to it. The only issue about the boss fights is that they aren't spread out evenly. What I mean by this is that sometimes you'll fight one boss after the other, and because most of them are pretty easy, it kinda throws you off a bit, and you can get bored sometimes. And then sometimes you'll have to complete another 5 levels to get to the next boss, so it does feel a bit weird to me personally.
Otherwise, overall, this is an exceptional indie game. One that will take you a bit of time to complete on Normal, and then a couple of hours to finish on Hard. The gameplay is superb, the art and soundtrack is beautiful, and the story is a tad bit cliche, but it is still enjoyable. A must pick up for any fan of indie games! :)

Pros:
+ We finally got a CoH2!!!
+ The Eastern Front setting is a fantastic change of scenary from the over-used US vs Reich D-Day scenario
+ Great visual design and performance on mid-range systems
+ Theatre of War game mode is a nice addition that sits somewhere between campaign and straight-up skirmish modes
+ Campaign is just as good as the original game
+ Small tweaks and additions to the CoH formula are welcomed
Cons:
- The removal and later selling of other "factions" is a bit questionable (i.e. shipping with two and later selling the American and a second German faction)
- There are supposedly issues with online balancing (though personally I'm not a MP kind of player so...)
- Rubbed some Russians the wrong way...so...if you're Russian you probably won't take kindly to the Soviet bashing (though it's completely justified...)
Bottom Line
It perplexed me that it took this long for a CoH2 to come out. The original game was highly popular and still being played by many people and it was a little worrying that this IP was seemingly going nowhere. While the game's release was a little bugged and there are supposedly still some issues with the MP, from a SP/campaign perspective this game is fantastic and should be a must-have for any WWII or military strategy gamer.
The narrative/campaign is just as strong as the original game's and the choice to move out of the over-used Western Front was an effective and intelligent one in order to ensure the game felt like a fresh experience. I also applaud the game makers for taking a risk in portraying the Soviet Union/Red Army as it was as opposed to how it's painted in overly nationalistic/romantic Soviet history books. Undoubtedly COH2 didn't make many Russian friends but hey...sometimes the truth hurts...

Company of Heroes 2 is a fantastic, albeit it slightly rage-inducing multiplayer experience. The singeplayer - i.e, the campaign and the mission packs that go with it in Theatre of War mode, is pretty lacklustre with not much to show for itself other than a narrative storyline driven by a relatively novice approach to the Eastern Front and some interesting cooperative missions for the Case Blue ToW mission series.
Multiplayer is where CoH2 really comes into its own. I feel the game is in this respect vastly superior to its predecessor, but it doesn't come without flaws. As an Ostheer player, the game breaking nature of the British Forces addon often results in boring, repetitive gameplay, wherein a British player need only establish a collection of mortar emplacements and Bofors guns to hold strategic locations, making them impenetrable without the right tools. In many cases you'll end up having to field medium tanks such as the Panzer IV to make any progress against these positions as the hitting power of the 8 cm Granatwerfer 34 (standard German mortar) is not sufficient except in large numbers to quickly get rid of the British mortar emplacement, which is static and fortified, and fires quite rapidly.
If you want this game to provide a realistic experience of the Second World War, or a balanced multiplayer, don't bother. Both the Ostheer and Oberkommando West require a decent level of skill on the part of the player in order to function correctly. If you're relying on someone you don't know - either in 2v2, 3v3, or 4v4 setups - you might find yourself losing games repeatedly, which can be extremely frustrating if you feel you're doing well. Allied and Soviet units such as the SU-85, Jackson, and IS-2 are big threats, since their build can more or less carry even the most incompetent Allied or Soviet player in the mid to late game. As the Ostheer, you'll find yourself commanding skilled but in many cases inadequate units against hordes of American riflemen with BARs, Tommies with their green cover rapid firing bonus, or just Soviet conscripts in large numbers. To counter this you have to be quick off the ball, with an effective reaction time and an understanding of which units trump their counterparts, and so on.
All in all I enjoy the game, and I would recommend it, though it does have an abundant capacity to make you utter every naughty word under the sun.

Metro 2033 Redux is an excellent remodel of Metro 2033, which I received during a free game promotion on Facebook. It had been sitting in my backlog for nearly a year now until I decided to finally pick it up based on the amazing reviews my friends have been touting. Now when I was deciding which to play, the original Metro 2033 or go ahead and pick up the Redux, I was stuck between a rock and a hard place. Many review sites just copied and pasted their original reviews without adding any additional input on the game's updated graphics. Like a true Steam sale connoisseur, I went ahead and purchased the Redux at the lowest price with the intentions of playing, eventually.
I will admit, the first couple moments into the game were quite boring (and dull to say the least). It felt like a generic FPS based in a Fallout environment, however, moments into the storyline, once you are flashed back into your Metro, home stations for the surviving human population, the game really showed it's true colors, a dark, decelent game with little hopes of human survival. From the underground conflicts between the rival groups, Red and the Naiz, and the cruel irradiated monsters that now walk (and fly) in the streets of a nuclear Moscow, you aren't looking at a walk in the park.
I HIGHLY recommend Metro 2033 Redux to anyone that enjoys post-apocalyptic games like Fallout or Wolfenstein: The New Order.

Wow. Can I just say that I had no expectations for this game. I saw it advertised to me, and it look interesting. All I knew going in was it was about exploring as an animal and one review said it was a "walking simulator". It's so much more than that.
I spawned into the beautiful world as a Badger Cub with just some calls to make and 3 emotions to show. I quickly found a group of badgers and we used our emotes to group up and explore the world with eachother. Our objective, collecting flowers and essences and essentially looking for treasure and beautiful scenery.
My adventures brought me through dense forests where relics can be found and several animals are required to be present for it to break open and present its treasures. We found a few of these and continued on before entering beautiful cave system. After emerging from that, it seemed much of our group at scattered and gotten lost or broken out into their own groups. Nevertheless, we reach the crest of a hill and my badger cub buddies, a long with a graceful deer and a happy little frog happened upon another large group. We quickly joined forces and were off on our adventure.
Now, I noticed there was a set of beautiful waterfalls to go towards, and because I obviously can't type (I'm an animal) I couldn't convey to this large group there may be something worth checking out. Afraid to leave my new friends, I followed them in the opposite direction. After getting their attention because I happened them upon some treasure, I made them follow me all the way back to the waterfalls.
We arrive, and break into the cold waters where some icebergs are floating and we can stand on them. In the excitement of this new beauty, my group splits off and starts following what I beleive to be a mountain lion. I'm standing alone on my own iceberg, while everybody is heading away. I'm crying, because I see them leaving but there is an amazing cave system to explore behind the waterfall that they didn't notice.
I continue crying, and they cry back, but it seems nobody is turning around for me. I accept that they are long gone, and I enter the caves by myself. What I uncovered I can only explain as the most beautiful cave system. It must of spanned a mile tall with 3 waterfalls coming from what seems like heaven. I make my way up around the outer walls on a path, sad because my previous friends are not experiencing the beauty of this all with me.
I eventually exit the cave and come to accep that I am by myself. But I am okay. Because it doesn't matter what other people think, I know what I did.

To be clear from the start Race 07 is a simulation game. That means to play it, it is recommended to have a gamepad or wheel. Trying to do anything without one of those is a waste of time.
To start off with there are lots of annoying things, the control setup is tedious (but it works), the settings are sometimes overly complicated, people online can be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥(if I had a cent for every first corner accident...) and the AI opponents are mentally challenged.
However once you've set up everything correctly and connect to a multiplayer server (preferably with some friends) the game is great. For people who like 'real' racing the gameplay is great. Cars handle like they should and once you know what you're doing close racing is very much possible.
Also because of the driving aids people with different skill levels can easily compete with each other for fun racing sessions.
From there on there is a myriad of tweaks and settings to change to get that extra bit of speed out of your car, I am not interested in that but for the simracing enthusiast it is great.
To conclude, there are some small issues with Race 07 but on the whole it is the best sim racing game available on Steam, period.

I used to love to play this game as a kid, and when I heard that there was a downloadable version, I had to get it. It's everything I remember and more.
Gameplay is very simple. You're a dino, and you're trying to avoid the impending apocalypse, all the while collecting eggs and munching critters. By collecting the eggs and critters, you get upgrade points (DNA) to make your dino faster and stronger. It's a very simple system, although it can take quite a while to get all the DNA you want for the last few upgrades.
There's also two main gamemodes, the campaign and speedruns. The campaign has you move through several levels with limited lives. The speedruns have some gimmick attached, and you get one try or you're forced to restart. This version has more than the original browser game, and removed some that were somewhat unfair/boring.
The multiplayer works relatively well, and can be done with traditional gameplay or can be treated as a sandbox to mess around in. I haven't done too much of it but it works.
Controls are tight. You can run, jump, and crouch. You also have a activatable speed boost. The boost can upgrade depending on how much DNA you get, allowing the player to make some harder jumps or get up a hill faster. The difficulty is well balanced in all but a few speedruns on Intense difficulty and Intense Campaign, but if you're a good player and playing with a maxed out dino, it's managable with either a good seed or game knowledge.
There's plenty of achievements if that's your cup of tea, and the really catchy soundtrack can be unlocked by collecting a secondary currency called "Bones" (that also unlocks the speedruns).
The only complaints I have is that the game doesn't make the boost apparent to you unless you read the instructions (silly I know, but some people just skip by it assuming the game to be simple). Additionally, the physics engine can be a bit wonky. Sometimes some jumps get gimped because the slope is slightly angled, and there are a few spots in a few select seeds and levels where a rock or an enemy dino can push you through the floor (don't worry though, if you do, the game will let you fall for a while and you'll teleport to the top of the world).
All in all, this game is a great runner. With great gameplay, great music, functioning multiplayer, and lots of vanity options, it brought me back to my childhood playing it on the web. I can guarantee you'll be having a great time escaping the apocalypse, just like I did.

Braid is a brilliant game that gives you a rich, satisfying experience.  The surface mechanics of the game are very similar to the old Super Mario World, but the twist that makes it fundamentally different is the ability to manipulate the flow of time either forwards or backwards, which makes for some truly ingenious puzzles.  In addition to being able to move backwards and forwards through time, each of the five main worlds of Braid introduces a new element to the spacetime manipulation that keeps the puzzles fresh and intriguing.  While the storyline has a distinct stream-of-consciousness style and can be hard to follow, the artwork and the soundtrack make for an aesthetically pleasing ride through the game.  All in all, one of the best and most memorable games I've yet played.

TL;DR
