Hey everyone. So I jumped on EA for Dark and Light and even amidst all the hate I have some positive things to say about it. What I don't get in today's day and age is people who buy a fantasy themed Ark in early access the second it comes out and then complain that it's a fantasy themed Ark. Like, with so much info at your fingertips, why? Anyway.
So some caveats. I love Ark, I have 650 hours in it and it's one of my favorite games. In the right conditions. I play with a small group of friends, we play PvE Coop, and it's all about the story, the adventure, building together, working together to achieve something in a fantasy world. We don't do PvP, we don't do public servers because they are toxic, we don't do mega tribes and we add things like Structure+ and accelerated rates because we have lives, kids and work. So if that's not you, then this review probably won't mean much to you because I honestly don't know how the other stuff is going. I couldn't tell you about alpha tribe faction based PvP and voting for king or any of that jazz.
So with that in mind. I really enjoy Dark and Light. Is it an Ark clone? Of course it is. I mean the engine is basically Ark, we all know/knew this so I'm ok with that. Does it have some of Ark's issues? Yup, but not enough to make it ragequit. Now I enjoy Ark's setting but man Dark and Light just oozes high fantasy. I can be an elf throwing fireballs at goblins riding a dragon? Yes please! Check out my screenshots and drool!  Granted the goblins are creepy af right now with their sorta tooth grin shudder. And the little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s can knock you out and steal all your stuff! Kill them from afar! Anyway. Setting wise it's right up my alley. I love how you have starting citadels with NPCs and guards! You can sell and buy stuff! There's even a tutorial quest line to teach you the game!
The mechanics are familiar with Ark players but instead of leveling up and unlocking engrams you unlock recipes by doing stuff in that tree. Want to be the house builder? Keep building stuff and unlocking things in that tree. It also means you don't have to grind narco for 3 hours because you really want a saddle. Just play the game like you enjoy and unlock what you use and do. I do like that a lot.
LOVE the magic stuff. A spell to give you more weight? A spell to lessen the weight of stuff in your inventory? Heal? Light without holding a torch?? Fireballs? Drain resources without a pick?? Oh man, again I'm a fantasy buff but I love love the magic stuff. And I'm only getting started! The downside to the magic though is this focus concept. Basically as you cast magic your focus goes down and you need to rest to get it back. That part was confusing because you need a bedroll which is a one time rest, and eventually a bed. But without "healing" focus you die. Now that I know it's not an issue but that part was a little odd.
Taming is challenging. Instead of knocking something out and then feeding it it's more of a shoot it with arrows with ropes until it tires, then build a trough next to it to feed it. Took me some time to adjust from Ark and of course there are different types of creatures and some can only be tied down with bigger ropes etc so that's just a learning curve but once I figured it out it sorta made sense. There's also no concept of perfect tame, that I can tell, so you end up shooting the tame a few times midway to keep him tired.
I had no crashes, only a few bugs like the quest line and random mobs poofing from in front of me. I also built my base on a "meteor site" which is a loot drop, and now with loot drops come skeletons or wraiths, so that's fun inside your house :)
All in all, really really enjoying it. If you hate Ark or survival crafting this is not the game that will change your mind though.  So keep what I said in mind as for how I like to play and don't believe all the hate. I also play 7d2d and Empyrion so I love the genre and this is a pretty good entry. Needs some work? Of course. Have I experienced it all? Not by a long shot, but I'm excited to get back into it.

Pros:
+ We finally got a CoH2!!!
+ The Eastern Front setting is a fantastic change of scenary from the over-used US vs Reich D-Day scenario
+ Great visual design and performance on mid-range systems
+ Theatre of War game mode is a nice addition that sits somewhere between campaign and straight-up skirmish modes
+ Campaign is just as good as the original game
+ Small tweaks and additions to the CoH formula are welcomed
Cons:
- The removal and later selling of other "factions" is a bit questionable (i.e. shipping with two and later selling the American and a second German faction)
- There are supposedly issues with online balancing (though personally I'm not a MP kind of player so...)
- Rubbed some Russians the wrong way...so...if you're Russian you probably won't take kindly to the Soviet bashing (though it's completely justified...)
Bottom Line
It perplexed me that it took this long for a CoH2 to come out. The original game was highly popular and still being played by many people and it was a little worrying that this IP was seemingly going nowhere. While the game's release was a little bugged and there are supposedly still some issues with the MP, from a SP/campaign perspective this game is fantastic and should be a must-have for any WWII or military strategy gamer.
The narrative/campaign is just as strong as the original game's and the choice to move out of the over-used Western Front was an effective and intelligent one in order to ensure the game felt like a fresh experience. I also applaud the game makers for taking a risk in portraying the Soviet Union/Red Army as it was as opposed to how it's painted in overly nationalistic/romantic Soviet history books. Undoubtedly COH2 didn't make many Russian friends but hey...sometimes the truth hurts...

Company of Heroes 2 is a fantastic, albeit it slightly rage-inducing multiplayer experience. The singeplayer - i.e, the campaign and the mission packs that go with it in Theatre of War mode, is pretty lacklustre with not much to show for itself other than a narrative storyline driven by a relatively novice approach to the Eastern Front and some interesting cooperative missions for the Case Blue ToW mission series.
Multiplayer is where CoH2 really comes into its own. I feel the game is in this respect vastly superior to its predecessor, but it doesn't come without flaws. As an Ostheer player, the game breaking nature of the British Forces addon often results in boring, repetitive gameplay, wherein a British player need only establish a collection of mortar emplacements and Bofors guns to hold strategic locations, making them impenetrable without the right tools. In many cases you'll end up having to field medium tanks such as the Panzer IV to make any progress against these positions as the hitting power of the 8 cm Granatwerfer 34 (standard German mortar) is not sufficient except in large numbers to quickly get rid of the British mortar emplacement, which is static and fortified, and fires quite rapidly.
If you want this game to provide a realistic experience of the Second World War, or a balanced multiplayer, don't bother. Both the Ostheer and Oberkommando West require a decent level of skill on the part of the player in order to function correctly. If you're relying on someone you don't know - either in 2v2, 3v3, or 4v4 setups - you might find yourself losing games repeatedly, which can be extremely frustrating if you feel you're doing well. Allied and Soviet units such as the SU-85, Jackson, and IS-2 are big threats, since their build can more or less carry even the most incompetent Allied or Soviet player in the mid to late game. As the Ostheer, you'll find yourself commanding skilled but in many cases inadequate units against hordes of American riflemen with BARs, Tommies with their green cover rapid firing bonus, or just Soviet conscripts in large numbers. To counter this you have to be quick off the ball, with an effective reaction time and an understanding of which units trump their counterparts, and so on.
All in all I enjoy the game, and I would recommend it, though it does have an abundant capacity to make you utter every naughty word under the sun.

I came into this game as both a long-time RTS fan, and someone who's never really played a Warhammer game before. This review is for people who have no nostalgia about this game or franchise.
Honestly, I can't really recommend it for RTS fans. It's pretty simplistic, especially for something coming from the tail-end of the golden age of RTS games. It has a few interesting mechanics, such as the ability to enlarge and customize battalions on the fly, but mostly this just leads to trying to have a bigger army than the other guy.
I didn't really see a lot of ways to mix up your tactics, you'll mostly be trying to capture and hold control points and just putting a lot of resources towards buying more basic infantry squads. Vehicles take a good deal of extra time and resources to build, and aren't really worth it when you can just spam grunts and turrets to win.
I can see the appeal of this game, it's much faster than most RTS games, but it's just not for me, and I can't really recommend it for someone who isn't already on board with the franchise.

Battlefleet Gothic: Armada is the RTS videogame adaptation of Games Workshop’s classic tabletop game, pitting the Chaos, Imperium, Eldar, and Orks against each other in visceral space-battles.
Developed with Unreal Engine 4, Battlefleet Gothic: Armada offers deep management of every ship composing the player’s fleet, both during and between battles. From the fastest frigates to the gigantic, miles-long battleships, the player will customize all aspects of his ships: weaponry, defense and support sub-systems, but also crew, captains, and more... each customization affecting the very performances of the ship and the special abilities available during battle. From battle to battle, the admirals and crew of surviving ships will gain experience and promotions, improving the battle-readiness of the ships for future, bigger and more dangerous battles.
Additionally an extensive multiplayer mode with persistent fleets where up to 4 players can battle simultaneously, Battlefleet Gothic: Armada also features a big story campaign, taking place during the 12th Black Crusade and putting players in the middle of the Gothic War that raged between the Imperium and Abaddon the Despoiler. Players will be at the centre of every fight, commanding fleets of gigantic ships as the Chaos unleash a sequential chain of surprise attacks on Imperium worlds – the start of 20 years of warring in the sector.

In my opinion, this is a good, solid fighting game, and if you've played any of the DOA games in the past, then you'll feel right at home with this. Granted, I'm not much into fighting games, and the last one I really played was DOA3 on the original XBox. Playing this feels just like that. The fight controls are smooth and responsive, the different fighting styles of the characters require you to learn them rather than just button mash (assuming you want to progress beyond Easy difficulty), there are a lot of characters to choose from, and they are well designed.
And it has all of the trademark fan service you would expect from a DOA game, so if you aren't into that sort of thing and can't ignore it, then this game may not be for you.
I'm aware that the game isn't as feature complete as the PS4 version, but frankly, I couldn't care less about that. It is still a good fun fighting game, or at least it is from the point of view of the casual player of fighting games. My only real disappointment in this game is the lack of Steam achievements. A game like this is practically begging for achievements, the the lack of them is glaring (let's hope they include them in a future update).
Otherwise, it plays great on my machine (MSi GT60 2PE Dominator Pro, 2.8GHz, 24GB RAM, 8GB GeForce GTX880M graphics @ 1920x1080) with my plugged in XBox 360 controller (I have nothing to say about KB/M controls, as I haven't bothered to try it, and frankly wouldn't really consider playing a fighting game like this with KB/M). The lack of complete controller support (no controller vibration) is a minor disappointment, but not a dealbreaker.
So, if you have liked DOA games in the past and are itching to play one on your PC (for example, if you are like me and haven't owned a console in a long time, and so haven't been able to play a DOA game for a long time), and if you aren't worried about the fact that the console versions do have some more features, then you'll probably want this game. Just be aware of what you are getting into; read the DOA5 FAQ first to see if the game will be enjoyable with your set up and play style, because my personal experiences with the game probably aren't generally applicable across all of the various hardware and play styles out there:
And for one final big HOWEVER, you may want to wait a bit for some future updates to bring more promised features like online play, as well as wait for a sale price, as it may not quite be worth full price for you right now (Here in Thailand, the price has more than doubled on release day from the pre-order price; I payed 652.10 Baht for the game, and now the price is showing 1431.00 Baht! Definitely wait for a sale).

So, what can I say about Double Action:Boogaloo? A lot, that's what! This exciting, over-the-top Action-movie styled shooter is something of a unique design. It was derived off the mod for Half Life, The Specialists. While Double Action is made on the Source engine, rather than the old Goldsource engine, the game lacks the graphical touch that a lot of modern Source engine games get. However, if there has ever been a game that shows that a game doesn't have to have realistic graphics to be enjoyable, let it be this one. Double Action carries many unique traits that I have not yet seen in any other shooter. The feature that sets it apart from most shooters is the brilliantly fun Stunt system. This allows you to press right mouse (by default) to leap through the air, and even slide for several metres across the ground! Or you can use this to unrealistically and rather painfully slide up stairs, whatever you prefer. Not only this, but it has many other uses. You can use it to leap off walls, or effectively double-jump, the world is your oyster! The Stunt system isn't the only part of this shooter that makes it truly unique. While playing this game, you will find the game repeatedly slows down. This is for dramatic duels between players, and it allows you to make your moments of glory last that second longer. This leads to epic James Bond  (sorry I couldn't be more imaginitive!) movie-esque duels between players that never get dull. I could ramble on a bit longer, but for a man with only 3 hours into this game (at the time of writing this review, I plan to play many more!), I've bored you quite a bit. Here's a list of pros and cons of the game from my experience:
Pros:
+ It's free!
+ The Stunt and slow-motion systems are unique to this game, and really add to the exiting atmosphere you're in when you play the game.
+ Weapons are *fairly* balanced, none in particular stand out as 'overpowered' to me.
+ Maps are strategically-well-designed.
+ Bots seem to be fairly sensibly coded AI-wise.
+ There are no in-game purchases.
Cons:
- There aren't many maps (albeit, as said above, they are well-designed).
- The player base is fairly small, but I've never failed to find a server with a decent amount of people on it (I'd say 10 people is the minimum for a fun game, a lot less than the likes of Team Fortress 2).
- Graphics could do with touching up a bit.
- Updates from the developers are sparse, and there appears to be little communication between the developers and players as of late (the last update was in October of 2016).

Warhammer 40k Dawn of War
This game, and many of the games in the series meant more to me growing up than I'll never be able to express. Dawn of War came out in 2004 and it was revolutionary, a game from that time with mechanics and graphics that blew a lot of things people were used to out of the water, rich in lore and immersive as all hell. I'm sure I don't have to go into detail about all the ways this games core mechanics were astounding, or how the Campaign was magnificent, I know for a fact there are many people who can explain all of this better than I ever could.
Many people review games based on their nostalgia, and their own experiences, so I'll make the honest attempt at explaining just how much this series has meant to me growing up, and why I can't recommend it enough.
When I was quite young, I had experienced quite a few traumatising incidences that would make me a very ostracized child growing up, I was given Dawn of War by my parents and this game helped me find an escape from a lot of the turmoil I'd felt daily, and it offered me a bit of respite where I could find none in sleep.
I've had Post Traumatic Stress Disorder for as long as I can remember, and through this game I actually managed to meet some of my first friends in school as they were very like-minded with Warhammer, and I was even able to get through my days easier.
Dawn of War had given me an outlet for a lot of my grief and anger, and allowed me to find some form of relaxation in a time where I was nearly always debilitatingly anxious, I even played it to the point of falling asleep, something I'd often struggled with as I had, and still have quite terrible nightmares.
I'd proceed to buy every Warhammer 40k or Warhammer Fantasy game that came out on sheer principle alone, and while the games changed drastically, I've always been a steadfast fan, to the point that my next tattoo is going to be Warhammer related.
This game series meant a lot to me from Childhood up til now, and because of this Warhammer 40k will always be my favourite franchise.
I do wish they'd have listened to their fans, and stuck with the direction their game had started with. Dawn of War 3 was fundamentally disappointing, but the first game, and the ones up to Soulstorm will always be the closest and most true to what the Warhammer 40k Universe is. Grimdark.

Great improvement over SR3. It recycles basically all the assets from that game, so there isn't much in the way of new environments or vehicles, but it seems to have allowed the developers to make use of their time in developing and polishing the storyline and characters, which was desperately needed after the trainwreck that was 3.
The gameplay is just about the same as all Saints Row games, with the addition of further weapon customization (stats and appearances). And, of course, super powers, which are refreshing and greatly enjoyable, but which make the vehicles completely redundant. There is also greater variety in the types of activities and missions, mimicking various other gamestyles.
The story is a mix of "They Live" and "The Matrix" with a tiny touch of "Bill and Ted," and assuages your conscience by turning those pedestrians you're always running over and blowing up into just simulations (even inside the game). The story makes great use of the science fiction setting to explore the characters' (admittedly limited) personalities in fun and usually silly adventures.
On the negative side, they've decided to maintain their obsession with the increasingly disappointing and vacuous character of Johnny Gat, going so far as to retconn his recent past in a way that feels primarily masturbatory. The story itself also basically retconns itself right at the end. The DLC missions are also pretty big disappointments, one being a recycling of basically the whole game, and the other adding new material but not doing much with it. Finally, there's as much gratuitous infantilism as always, so be prepared.

Metro Redux is not your typical fps. The gameplay is dark and unrelenting, and it gives a feel of horrible dread between each obstical. Ammo conservation is a lot harder in this game compared to the original, and so are all the levels. Completely using stealth tactics (throwing knife, etc.) throughout the game is incredibly difficult due to the stealth system being as glitchy as ever. This game has a developed plotline that goes through most of the metro system, where humanity flocked after World War III. You have to make your way past communists, nazis, weird mutants, and a highly evolved type of human. The game is difficult wether you have it on the easiest difficulty or not. Some stealth sections are outright infuriating after a while. This isn't a horror game, more of a very intense action fps. It's scary in the way Left 4 Dead is scary. It's all about stress. Hoo boy. This game...
I desperately wanted to like this game, I really did... It's not a
game, but it's just so mediocre. I mean everything about it is just mediocre. For the sake of ease and for my own sanity, I'll try and explain what's wrong with this game by breaking it down into sections.
The differences from the free version of this game are:
Personally, I don't think this constitutes tacking on the moniker "DX" to Dino Run. There simply isn't enough here that differs from the orignal to justify marketing it as the delux version of the game. At least not at it's current price tag, but I'll get to that later...
This game's controls are unresponsive at best and fighting the player at worse. The floaty movement of your dino combined with the wonky physics make for a thoroughly frustrating experience. Perhaps this was an intentional choice on the part of the developer, as it is highly reminiscent of the flash version. Maybe it's just me, but giving the player poor controls feels like a poor substitution for difficulty. It's one thing if that's one of the main selling points of the game (Titles like
for instance) but this never struck me as one of the definable characteristics of Dino Run.
What you can do:
What you can't do:
To be perfectly honest, the lack of ability to toggle video options or framerate does not bother me. This isn't a particularly processor-heavy game. That being said, neglecting to include a key mapping option irks me. Your movement choices are WASD or the arrow keys. Spacebar/escape is pause. Shift to occasionally speed up. What if I want my speed boost to be the "E" key? What if I want to move with the "r" "j" "q" and "b" keys for some silly reason? This may seem nitpicky, but neglecting to include this one little bit of agency for the player reeks of laziness.
I want to stress that in listing the differences between the Deluxe and flash versions of this game I stated that there were UI changes
UI improvements. The most noticeable change is in character customization. Rather than having to cycle through different hat choices and colors via clickable arrows, there are now 6 pages of icons to cycle through; it's not perfect but it's significantly more user friendly than it was. My favorite option of this customization menu is the auto-match feature; this matches the hat you select to a specific matching color combination for your dino. This is what was done right.
Now for what was done wrong:
None of the outfits have names listed, as such you can't search for anything by keyword. Apparently I've unlocked the
and
hats. Which ones are they? I have some guesses, but I couldn't definitively tell you. So apparently the hats have names, the player just can't see what they are.
The list of hats can be organized into three possible categories: Classic, Indie, or Halloween. These options serve to sort the entire collection of hats in a different order depending on your category of choice. Where does one category end and another start? I couldn't say, as there are no descriptions. Also, I hope you like the hats, because once you pick one, you're wearing a hat. You can no longer go hatless. Maybe my dino's scalp is especially susceptable to sunburn or something.
It's a ghost town. Multiplayer essentially doesn't exist.
It's short and quickly gets boring. Yeah there are other worlds but the Halloween world is short (albeit a fun 7 minute romp through crazy) and Planet D is unplayable without having full stats.
Challenge or speedrun are your choices. Challenge follows the harrowing journey the harrowing journey that your Dino must undergo to reach shelter facing the end of the world. Speed run lets you choose between a selection of 24 levels with different weird twists to run through. Does one game mode sound more robust than the other? That's because it is. Speed run is a fun gimmick for maybe 20 minutes. Challenge mode has a life span of a few hours at most. While neither is packed to the brim with content, the challenge mode brings a bit more to the table.
You can choose to upgrade speed, jump, acceleration, and strength. This is identical to the flash version. There was so much potential here. The developer could have expanded this upgrade tree and allow the player to go for different builds.  Maybe there would be more of a multiplayer community if the ability customization was a third as robust as the appearance customization options. Right now, its just a battle of numbers (assumming stats factor in, when playing multiplayer; I don't know since I can't find an opponent). Also, there is nothing to indicate what these different attributes do. I have a pretty good grasp of the first three (speed, acceleration, and jump), but strength? I think Boulders knock me around less or something? Like the other area of customization, the options lack explanation and make the players choices lack meaning
DNA and bones. DNA lets you improve your stats and bones are currency...I guess. Bones allow you to purchase the levels in speedrun mode, so that you can actually play in speedrun mode. To be blunt it feels like forced content, but that's kind of how I feel about Speed Run mode as a whole. DNA is slow to come and a grind to get. There are a few achievements [called milestones] that award the player with DNA, but the big boons for DNA are finding the various Super-eggs strewn across the levels. Even with collecting these milestones and collectables, the player is still required to run the same levels over and over to try and improve their dino before they can even think about playing on higher difficulties. This gets old quickly. Even though things are "Procedurally generated" some two runs certainly feel the same, despite what the game claims. Different screens may be strewn together to create levels, but the choices feel limited and tend to blend together, regardless of which portions of a level spawn and regardless of sequence. I have a sneaking suspicion that "Speedrun" may be a glorified level select with some added wonky game features.
I have more that I could say. A lot more, but character limitations prevent that. The worst part is, I'm a fan of Pixeljam! I've had a lot of fun with Gamma Bros, Rat mazes 1 and 2, and the browser version of Dino Run. I just was expecting more from a title with a $5.99 price tag. Six bucks may not sound like a lot, but I don't necessarily
a lot to throw around. If this game were $1.99, I'd be more forgiving. I made this purchase because I wanted to support Pixeljam and I had high hopes for how they may have improved this game. Unfortunately, I'll have to file this one under "regret." I'll return to it and play it some more, but it's sad to see my Dino exist in a perpetual state of mediocrity.

Do I recommend this game? I think I neither do or don't. But if I was forced to pick one over the other, I'd slightly lean more towards yes, because it is the ONLY BFG game out there. Now, Battlefleet Gothic has plenty of great experiences don't get me wrong, however there are some experiences that are not so good. Let me tell you all about it.
The game is based on small fleet management where you can upgrade your vessels one by one at the cost of renown. To get renown, you win or lose battles by playing a match. However if you lose, there will be a cost at the same time rewarded (rewarded by failing? I like!). Eye and ear candy is everywhere to be seen. However, your brain will hurt at times as this game requires too much thinking and upgrading your ships from the shipyard is actually not how it should be. Dive into semi decent gameplay where half of the controls are missing, but it's ok as you just watched epic cutscenes. Popcorn required.
Visuals/art/animations/graphics: - 12/10
Immersion: 10/10
Voice Acting: + 1 (bonus)
GINORMOUS EFFORT! Mind blowing wows with extra points. Just throw a trailer into that intro ALONE. HERE! TAKE MY MONEY! By the love of gawd epic. And the cutscenes throughout the campaign maintains same level of quality. Skippable. Voice acting is god.
Campaign: 10/10
Tutorial: 3.5/10
Now here is why the campaign is almost perfect. You can die and still be rewarded. The campaign is tough, tougher than side missions, and if you fail them, you'll pay the price and don't need to start over at the same time. You don't need to replay anything. You can continue with your failures or load up the last game where you succeeded. On top of this, the devs included both failure and success cutscenes for dynamic plot. And you can choose where to attack or what planets to save. If you fail, you get one more chance to succeed! I'm not done with the campaign, but I see me finishing it in the future.
So the campaign is great except for this one little catch: An unskippable tutorial! The tutorial in this game is scary. "You must complete this mission to move on. Or else, you will never... ever experience the campaign, MWA HA HA" It holds your hands forcing you to do this and this and although it has voice acting which is good to lower the learning curve, the tutorial is boring. "Well, all tutorials are not supposed be fun." you may say. Again may I say it is not skippable. If you played the beta, you'll feel my PAIN. You'll need to play the campaign over again. And believe me, if you die in this mission (which is really EASY), you will need to start over and repeat steps 1-death. It is frustrating.
AI: 8/10
Balance: 10/10
Feels very balanced. The costs of things you purchase versus the how they compete is well done. AI is well done. However, haha, you gotta work on how they move through asteroids. On "Destroy Convoy" missions, the AI sends their convoy through asteroids, blow up, and I don't have to do anything. Easy victory.
Gameplay: 5/10
Mechanics: 3/10
Replayability: 6/10
Ship Customization: 7/10
Learning Curve: 9/10
Here is the part where the game feels like it is falling apart. I played so far 17 matches (campaign + skirmish). Gameplay is only average. Through the aesthetics, sounds, and what not, gameplay in this category is hidden by the sheer masterpiece of aesthetics and sound. It is only slightly better than Star Wars: Battlefront, where this game has a similarity with it. The game feels like it is trying to hide the gameplay because the coder can't come up with better ideas to make it more fun (no offense). And here is what I mean by this: Do you ever feel like something is missing from PLAYING the game? How much fun do you actually have battling other ships every single match? It's immersive, but slow. And no I do not mean "Cogitators" slow, I mean there is boredom in gameplay. There is no large fleets, there is no massive battles. It feels like you are forced to micro or you WILL lose.
Mechanics, there are a lot of things missing. Control groups are missing. Queued moves? Missing. Shift key irrelevant. Hotkeys are most likely missing. No way to select all ships, no way to attack move, and reliance on tactical gogitators 24/7. To get massive fleets will take ages, tons of dedication. Where are your controllable fighter units? Why do you have to micro everything?
Replayability, besides the campaign, leveling up to get the best stuff, there is ok value of achievement. You do not become god, though, and like I said, fielding massive fleets in this game is impossible or at least stupid as you have to micro EVERYTHING. Throughout time when you get better stuff, your enemy will too. And the progression, the difficulty only gets harder and harder as you go up in rank as your enemies do as well. Though there are options to choose how many ships you want to field, and the bonus of renown. But overall the game needs work as I kind of feel tired of playing this game over and over again.
Ship customization is good, but could be better. I would like it better, if I can choose how many upgrades I want to upgrade at the cost of renown, instead of waiting level after level to get this and then that. Feels wonky. And, and, where is my true ship customization? I want lasers fired out from the sides or give my ships more guns! Like lascannons, meltas, plasma batteries, whatever weapon I want. Not there. You cannot customize your ship visually. Instead, you have to choose between a bunch of ships and you can't scrap any for renown or get more slots whenever you want.
Learning curve is good. However, I sure would like to know a better way to navigate around the map or select units outside of my camera.
OVERALL: 7.8/10
It's good. Could be better, but still a good game. So I recommend it. However, do not kill people over this game. If you have a lot of money, and you want to have a nice Battlefleet Gothic experience, then this game is for you. But do not expect to be playing it 24/7. Watching it on youtube let's plays is also recommended to get you the feel of the game before buying it. Overall this game was well made, but I hope there are mods out there and/or patches to fix what is missing. GJ.

I've used Blender for about four years now, and all throughout my academic career, often to the chagrin of my tutors. I stuck to my guns throughout all the debates, and whilst I can use stuff like 3DSMax, prefer Blender for my workflow. The biggest criticism of open source stuff like Blender is that it is simply not 'professional' enough.
What utter trash. Anyone who brings this up in a debate is someone you should politely smile and nod at, because its obvious they know tupenny about 3D. Being good at 3D is all about understanding the fundamentals, and constantly pushing yourself to learn and implement said fundamentals in new ways.
Blender is a one stop shop, housing a variety of tools with everything from box modelling and sculpting (though I would suggest sculpting in other apps like 3DCoat or ZBrush), to unwrapping, and rigging and animation. Across the entire suite, all of the contextual hotkeys and layouts apply, it is a universal design approach to UI which is really intuitive and that once you get a handle on makes creation very quick.
Other applications, such as 3DS to me personally, feel bloated as a result. And in fact, in many cases they simply are, including everythign from the install size of said application, to the save files. Blender is efficient, compact, streamlined and compact. Setting up Blender on a new computer takes all of ten minutes, which is the amount of time it takes to just boot up Maya.
There are downsides to Blender, and Im not a fanboy by any stretch, but all 3D programs have their strengths and weaknesses. The major strength to Blender is the open source nature of it, with updates coming thick and fast. The progress Blender has made in the last couple of years is staggering, and it just keeps getting better.
For students, and ESPECIALLY indies, Blender is a lifesaver. It is a free licence but an incredibly professional product, with really no limitations except your own ability to make cool stuff. The only issue you will ever really have with Blender is if you are working in a team with other artists doing animation who use another application, and you need to rig in said program, as rigs and animation data do not export. This could be said for anything though, and its important to be flexible.
All of that said, its all about the fundamentals, a polygon is five edges, is two tris, is four verts. That will never change. If you learn how to model well, how to unwrap well, how to rig and animate well, you can take this knowledge into any application you are required to use; all it takes is learning where the tools are.
TLDR: Blender is pretty great.

neo scavenger is a game that comes out of the blue in the steam indie market. Some games are good, because you remember the time you met that NPC that you felt engaged, and connected too, and of how believable they were, and because of the epic landscape that makes you feel like you were living an alternate reality then a program installed onto your computer. And then there are some that have unecesary and game breaking mechanics that is more of a nusciance and a story that fells like it was put together with no thought and imagination making the experience into an endurance test. so where does Neo scavenger come in, it is a role playing, post apocalyptic survival game with a top down perspective on a map that closly resembles to a board game. The game in my opinion is one of the most emmersive games i have played for awhile and i have considerably played enough to know the positives and negatives and heres why:
if you watched the trailer of the game, you would have noticed that it has still images and is text based, thats because it is. It is a turn based game simmilar to the rpg genre but unlike most turn based rpgs, your actions are in sync with the npcs. whenever you talk to someone in a confrontation you could be at risk at being shot with a range weapon because, when were about to talk, that person blasted your head off because it was their intention. you can sneak up to npcs and kill them but the problem is that you dont know who your sneaking up to. you could end up killing a harmless scavenger then a raider makeing confrontations even harder. the game does a great job at making confrontations meaningful and difficult to handle without felling cheap and half fasted.
you woundering what the story is about like what most games have, well NEO scavenger has a story which is unique and enagaging. The world has many factions that has changed the world in their own ways, but it more happens in the background and what you do have little to no affect on them. Because you cant be a force of nature saviour or villian, it is because you are human. You do not have any special superhuman skills that games secretly slip into your character and instead make random events and point of locations intense. you instead have to think through things because if you don't your going to die, alot. Did i mention that when you die, you die for good and that you have to restart the game. This is the level of detail simmilar to darksouls, only more soulcrushing as the world is belevable and you are quickly reminded your human because you tried to play hero against a healthy dogman.
The survival mechanic has been thrown around recently in alot of indie games because game developers impiment this, but end up copy pasting and being bland because they forgot what makes survival fun. The developers have managed to make the survival genre good in their game as it makes you feel like your recovering from wounds and actually hunting and cooking food. Whenever you attempt to patch yourself up or feed yourself you have to do it manually and organically, you have to think whats right and wrong theres no indicator except for the multiple bars on the right that can be summed up as your health bar. Even fighting feels visceral and brutal. The game uses text to explain what part of the body you hit on an npc and that npc can be   also knocked out through pain (the same can happen to you).
The game has its annoying nitpics that i have witnessed throughout the game like, why do i have an imaginary pocket for my cash and, why can i reload my gun and patch myself up in ONE TURN like im the flash (whenever you acsess your inventory the npc can now have a prolonged turn because you were busy BUT ONLY THIS as you can manage your inventory for as long as you want and the npc can't do anything about it). There are the problems with the limitations of the flash engine as sometimes your save file could be deleted (this only happened to me twice).
skills can be a mixed bag. You can be a tough, melee botanist but end up dying because you didnt have the athletic attribute that can help you outrun the dogman or a feble, frail survivor thats good at hacking, electronics, mechanics with eagle eye and tracking but died to a good punch to the face from a raider skilled in melee. I managed to stop this with a mod called big bad cheater which give you a defect called mega human that gives you all the traits and still make you feel human without turning you into a god. Go to the blue bottle site and search it up, instaling is dificult so go to youtube to get help.
I remeber having fond moments with i fight i had with a crazed, infected man with a loaded bow, got shot, pulled the arrows out which caused him to beg for mercy after what he witnessed, and killing him with multiple hatchet blows because he would have killed someone or infected them with a disease simmilar to the plague (the hatchet is not in the game it is a mod called Mighty Mini Mod of Doom which adds more equipment and an extended story line. It also works with Big bad cheater, i highly reccomend it). Neo scavenger is a game that may not be for everyone so in summary do you want:
*be emmersed in a believable world
*feel more of a human than a walking tank
*get into fights with bloody detail, simmilar to manhunt
*organicly complete tasks and naturally survive with a permadeath system
*actually care about your actions
if this interests you, buy it you will never experience anything like this. The developers have done a great job at making a game true to their genre and i hope that they make games in the future with this much thought and imagination put into them like this simply made but absorbing game.

Wellll, it's really hard for me to give a thumbs-up to this game, considering I think Saints Row 2 is the pinnacle of the series.  Saints Row 4 is lacking so much in both story and game features that made the previous games, even SR the Third, compelling, interesting and fun.  Many other people have said much the same before, though, and so much better and more thoroughly so I'll just keep this fairly brief.
SR4 feels like a mere retrospective, a fond looking-back at the glory days of the series, lots of "Hey, yeah, remember when THAT happened?  That was cool." callbacks.  As much as I admire Volition, I feel sad that they've basically painted Saints Row into a corner with no way back to the heart and soul of its early days.
Totally coincidentally, the one thing I discovered that SR4 is totally GREAT for is allowing me to re-experience that heady super-hero "feel" that I've been missing since NCsoft shut down City of Heroes.  The super-jumping alone gives me flashbacks to CoH like crazy, and that's really really hard to object to.  Running up buildings is stupid-fun too, as is the huge feck-off powerstomp.  :D
So -- SR4 isn't all bad.  It's funny in enough places and sometimes really fun to play, but it's a shell of what it used to be and it didn't let me shoot Matt Miller in the face, so it gets a big fat thumbs down from me.

Most of these servers kick players with ping over a certain limit, so your options are limited as far as multiplayer.
However, even when this game was in its prime, the multiplayer wasn't all that great anyway, unless you were playing on LAN. This is especially true in space battles. The netcode is really basic, buggy and there would be latency even if all players had great ping on the server.
Recently though, there is an issue with the latest Crimson drivers where there are extreme artifacts and discoloration, making the game almost negative colors and virtually unplayable.
I believe there is a time when a game finally has to die, and I believe that time is now. I'm not recommending this game for the sake that people on newer systems won't be able to experience the full gameplay experience as it was when it was in its prime.

For the last few weeks, I have dedicated my life to Meadow. Sleep, food, job and even family became less priority and only water kept me hydrated so I could survive till the final release and tell you a story you may or may not enjoy. Are you ready to spend few minutes of your life, yes? Very well, brave badgers and devious lynxes, buckle your seat belts, because 'Shelter' is going bye bye!
So what's this Meadow is all about you may wonder. Let's cut all the 'woo woo' stuff and dive deep into it.
It's not a survival game. You don't have to fight for food and water to keep your kids alive. You don't really have your family around any longer. There are no predators, no real danger. Story? Not a bit of it. End goal? Ain't gonna happen. So, what do you do in Meadow, you may wonder?
Well, you can walk. And walk a lot!
So, are you all alone in the wilderness, with nothing left to do? Not really.
Meadow is an online project, thus you cannot start a single player/offline mode. Not yet anyway. At least some internet connection is required. Being socially oriented, exploration still plays a significant role here. Despite the lack of usual activities, you can lose yourself in the big, open and quite beautiful world where you can find four different seasons collapses, from foggy swamps to snowy mountains, filled with chillaxing (and sometimes terrifying) ambient music and sounds. You can spend some good amount of time just wandering around, filling your eyes and soul with that beautiful scenery. You will have these 'yay!' moments quite often.
Only recently I have come to realize what's 'A forum in games clothing' actually means, the description line you read first on Steam page. Basically, the world of Meadow, that big floating island in the middle of nowhere - a social playground, where your main purpose is to collaborate with other people, be social and have fun. The world itself is so-called interactive 'forum' in gaming disguise, a forum without text/voice chat system, and it's actually very cool! The lack of any modern communication brings the benefits and the core immersion into the wildlife. After all, you're part of the natural habitat. You can use your body language, emoticons, self-awareness and care about other people around you. Primitive yet innovative at the same time. You won't hear shouting, swearing, chat spamming messages - you have a bunch of emoticons and your body to express yourself!
So, except being super social and stuff, how do you play?
You can pick from a different type of animals. Just a few from the beginning, but you can unlock more while you play. If you're a passionate collector as me, you will be pleased with the amount of things you can gather. Flowers, crystals, and of course, achievements are here to keep you productive :) While unlocking animals, you can also get new skins for them or new emoticons to use, including special 3d and sound ones. There are also black obelisks you can break with the help of other players, so being in the pack may be handy, and it's more fun of course. Oh, and by collecting all the shiny things around you will receive essence, main resource of the game that will determine your place on the leaderboards, in case you want some competition.
As of my review is coming to an end, few worthy things to mention:
I felt like a child, to be honest, when I met my first people in Meadow. It was a baby badger and then momma badger appeared nearby so we acted like a complete family (I was a little badgie as well), screaming, jumping around, smiling with emotes and it was as cute as embarrassing, but who really cared. I was very excited! After some time lynx joined the party so we traveled together for a while! It was joy!
Be active and embrace the possibility to meet new people. This is a social playground, so most of the time your level of fun/boredom will depend on what you do and what company you keep. Play around with things, find collectibles together, organize some event like making a pack of badgers, crawling around under strict look of caring momma, do some role-play. You can even have a sleeping party on that big rock (thank you, Sass), all kind of animals invited!
What language do you speak? French, Spanish or perhaps Norwegian? Doesn't really matter, as you will use common emotes to express yourself and communicate with pretty much any person in the world. No more lost in translation.
Meadow already has awesome and friendly little community, and I can say all the people I met on my journey are very very nice. I've made some friends I enjoy chatting and playing with and I'm sure I'm not alone. And you can say the same about developers, Might&Delight. Very nice, responsive and kind people, ready to help and even play with you :) I remember such behavior from my time with Paws when Jens and Co responded to my every single question and made sure I enjoyed my time with the game.
Will you like Meadow depend on your personal preference and what you're looking for. Keep in mind, this is relaxing, slow paced, exploration-socializing type of game experience first and foremost. Yes, there are things to do, like collectibles and achievements, but you will get bored pretty soon, as all the activities depend on the cooperation and communication between players, rather than actual action. If you are a Shelter fan and heavily into survival, killing, hunting things, better keep playin' something else (another Shelter 2 playthrough perhaps?)
I will update my review later on, listing all the pros and cons. Thank you so very much for reading, I appreciate you all!

Without a doubt, this game is on my top 5 "zombie survival" games list...and i've played almost all of them...even the ones in development. This first-person shooter has a great "intro" story (which always helps you understand why you are where you are in any game) and the controls are great. Even though there is no sand-box environment in this game, the co-op feature more than makes up for it but you have GOT to stay on your toes because this game will "end" you, at the drop of a dime, if you aren't paying attention. Not all of the zombies "announce" their attacks so you have to be aware of where you are, what you're ready to do next, and (like my best friend says) "ALWAYS have an escape plan".
This is one of the few games with real "flow" that allows you to be that bad-a$$ and do it with some grace. Using the bow on this game is pure bliss because you can silently take down a zombie or you can blow it to smitherines. You can dive off a MASSIVELY high bridge into the water or you can vault your way to a better position...this game is majorly "parkour" inspired and that also makes it fun. Heights are irrelivant IF you know where to land :)
Night time is tough in this game because the masses come out, in force, and hunt you down if you can't make it to a safe zone and there are settings (even then) that allow them to attack if you want a challenge.
Like i always say: If YOU like it...PLAY IT. Don't ever let something someone else says convince / dissuade you on playing any game. A review is simply one person's take (their view) on the game and by NO means makes them any kind of "authority". And this is WHY i've wondered (from day ONE) why there is a "comment" option on a review. No one person's take is written in stone and comments only serve ONE purpose, to allow a person to be "attacked" when others don't agree...because a review isn't a test, it's someone's own take on something.

Pros:
+ Game does a REALLY good job at being an open world zombie survival game. You have to craft things, weapons break down after a while, guns are scarce, ammo is scarce, zombies are attracted by loud noises, they attack you in hordes, they don't die easily, etc.
The game reminds me a lot of the Walking Dead: Survival Instinct PRE-LAUNCH. All the things we were promised in the game that either weren't there, or weren't as good as it was in the final release, you can guarantee are in here. There is a strong emphasis on using your environment to aid you in killing zombies. There's scattered spike traps you can lure zombies into, there's puddles of oil to ignite, oil barrels to explode, so on and so forth.
You also get to kick enemies. This can help you knock down enemies, and you can also kick zombies off of anywhere. The ragdoll is pretty damn funny, and boy is it amusing to knock a zombie off a 6+ story high building.
Also, if you've played Dead Island, then this will definitely be very familiar. Only difference is: this is actually a good game.
+ Free running was a brilliant idea
The game has its fair share of fetch quests, but they are much less tedious due to the method of travel which is the free running. Every surface, ledge, window, balcony, is all climbable. It's pretty much a first person Assassin's Creed game in this particular aspect.
You also unlock a grappling hook which is awesome. There's also cars in the DLC.
Getting from point A to point B is pretty funny, and not tedious like I mentioned.
+ Skill Tree is pretty good
There are a lot of abilities you can unlock. You can unlock more stamina, health, faster health regeneration, the ability to slide, jump over zombies, curb stomp zombies, being able to roll after jumping off of high places, etc. It's seperated into three different categories: Agility, Survivor, and Power. They each have their own levels and XP progression, so doing specific actions only count towards that specific category of skills.
For example, you level up Agility by doing free running. You will gain a certain amount of XP for every jump, climb, etc. For survivor, you earn more XP for doing quests, side quests, picking up care packages and delivering them, and what not. Power levels are earned by killing and hitting enemies.
If I had to complain about it, I would definitely say there's quite a few skills missing that should've been in the game.
+ The game changes the setting half way through the game.
You go from a beach resort/urban city looking place in the first half, to an old Roman inspired looking city in the latter half. What I love about this is it offers a breath of fresh air to the game. I don't know too many open worlds that do something like this, but they need to do it more often.
I started getting tired of the first city (Harran), and the second one (Sector 0) was refreshing to explore for the first time. I don't know, props to the devs for doing this.
+ Enhanced Edition has a lot of value
For $30 (or $23.99 on sale), you get the game, and the Following, which is like another game in of itself, and some other crap that's neat I guess lol.
Cons:
- Hard Mode is sometimes unfair
I probably would not recommend Hard Mode for this game. I selected it thinking it would just be more challenging and require more strategy, which it DEFINITELY DOES, BUUUUUUUUUUUUT, it is pretty damn unfair a lot of times, and it's genuinely frustrating.
You will lose surivor points everytime you die. Not sure if that's only in Hard Mode or not, but even if it's not, you die more often which will make you lose the points a LOT. As a result, I was half the survivor level as I was for my Power and Agility level.
One good thing about it though, I found myself using the spike traps more often. Same with the oil barrels and puddles. Also, dodging is necessary for a lot of enemies. Get it ASAP!
*Then let's talk about whether it's a good port or not*
Overall, yes. Completely good port. If I had to complain, maybe not a whole ton of graphics settings, and not a lot of in depth one's (for example, there's just an on and off setting for Anti-aliasing instead of FXAA, MSAA, SMAA, etc.)
The performance is good for the most part, but the bad part is understandable. A lot of zombies can be on screen at once which drops the framerate a bit. Sadly though, lowering some settings didn't really ease this by much (maybe 5 FPS more when I turned some stuff down.)
Overall, it's good. Good controller support, yata yata.

I'll split my review into two sections, the game itsself and the PC port.
Game:
For anyone who hasn't played DOA games before, this series and the Soul Calibur series are by far my favorite fighting games.  However, the only problem I have with DOA is the excessive amount of fan service in the form of costumes.  They can make the game look rather juvinile to onlookers at times, which is annoying.  Ignoring those, DOA has a very deep, satisfying, and fun fighting system that strikes the best balance between being button mash friendly for new comers, but also accomodates a very high level of advanced play for those who put in the time.  The moves and graphics are really flashy as well, makes you feel like you're part of a movie.  As for DOA5 in particular, from my experience every entry in the series is clearly superior to all the entries before it, and DOA5 is no exception.  Some fighting game series' aren't so fortunate, and their effort to appeal to a broader audience sacrifices the gameplay quality at the high level.  DOA5 somehow dodged this pitfall, and remains a great game.
The PC port:
Contrary to what many reviews here have stated, from my experience the quality of the PC port is actually quite good.  It runs very smooth and looks amazing, even on old/slow hardware.  My midrange AMD laptop from 2011 plays the game perfectly at 60fps and that says something.  I haven't noticed any bugs or crashes either, which often happens with poor port jobs.  I know there are some features missing from this version, but all of them except for 1 really aren't a big deal at all.  The game is still tons of fun and looks/plays great.  The only glaring feature that I think may impact a purchase is the missing online multiplayer.  However, this will be added within 3 months, and I'd rather play the game offline now and get multiplayer later, than for the entire game to be delayed 3 months.  Thinking of this as a preview release of the game helps things in my mind.
I absolutely recommend this game to both newcomers and veterans of the series.

Shank is a 2D side scrolling action game from Klei Studios. This is the first in a series of two games and while the second game is a far more refined experience, the original is still fun in it's own way, even if it is a pretty simple game.
I have to confess I played Shank 2 before the original so I am slightly more negatively biased towards the game as the first is missing a lot of improvements added in the sequel. This doesn't mean the game isn't fun, it just means it's relatively simple and superficial when it comes to mechanics. In Shank 2 you were almost required to have the proper load out to complete certain levels. In the first game, you have the option to switch weapons on the fly, but you probably won't need to as the two starting weapons (chainsaw and double pistols) can get you through the entire game pretty easily (hard mode included). Additionally there are only three enemy types (medium, large, dog) with a few variants. Once you know how to take down one variant, you can take down all of them with relative ease.
I don't mean to say that Shank is a bad game, just one that needed to be fleshed out a little more. In terms of content it's a very short game and I was able to get all the achievements under 10 hours. There is a co-op campaign but it's local only which is very unfortunate because I found it to be pretty fun to double up with a friend and run through some missions. I actually prefer Shank's co-op to Shank 2's co-op (which is a really difficult survival mode). Shank's co-op (although local only) actually fleshes out the story a little more. There is an achievement for completing local co-op so make sure you've got a buddy and an extra controller if you plan on getting all the achievements.
Overall Shank is a great looking 2D beat 'em up/shoot 'em up with a great soundtrack and fun bosses. The game may be relatively easy and simple and could use a little more content but it's still a blast to play.

This is by far one of my favorite games of all time.  It has this vibe that almost no other game has matched, at least for me, and you love it as soon as you click the play button. -Several hours will pass while you think you've played just half an hour.  As they say, time flies when you're having fun, and time certainly flies here.  This game is extremely immersive.

Bad
-There's a bit of a lack of customization (I would like to emphasize that this is a VERY minor issue), but hopefully with modability in the future, this can be fixed.

I'm amazed that there are no reviews for this game. Unless they're all blocked until the beta is over.
This game is fanatastic, while I haven't played the multiplayer, and stuck to the solo skirmish, I can honestly say that the mechanics are solid, I haven't experienced a single bug.
The ship customisation is solid, with numerous upgrades to the ships performance; although a limited number to each ship, forcing specialisation, but hey, no ship should be the ultimate upgraded beast form which you can deliver the Emperors Light in a competitive multiplayer game that also has a fully fleshed out campaign much like dawn of war 2's and dark crusade.
The ships, and the races (Imperium and Chaos as of the beta) are true to the lore and TT game for the most part, and they certainly have different play styles.
To win a battle you need strategy and tactics, as well as a good understanding of each ship in your fleet, and playing well to it's role. The battles are surprisingly fast, and hectic, a lot can be going on, and you need to keep track of it all. Which comes to point, the "tactical cogitators" the ability to slow down time, of course, during multiplayer, if one person slows down time, everyone goes slow mo, until the initiator turns it off, leaving room for potential trolls.
One thing I MUST point out is the AI, it's fantastic, the guys behind this AI needs an applaus. It thinks, it plans, it reacts. Example; Whilst playing a round of Data Extaction (I think that's the name) a sort of, hold the "ball" and GTFO game mode. I managed to get the data on my ship, as I'm running away, and about to GTFO via warp, just as my ship jumps to warpspace, they steal the data, and in the midst of the cluster**** I thought I'd won, then the ship warped out immediately after taking it, and BAM! game over, I lost.
So the AI, saw a situation, planned an action, queued commands, and thus won the match. In a way I simply could not have forseen or countered. You could say this was dumb luck, but I've seen it do this exact tactic, twice since, and my god does it make me rage every time.
Also, the Orks are immense fun, just throw everything you have at the enemy face first and bash them with you big red button. Whilst the Eldar are extremely diffcult to play as, due to them being hard hitting fragile speedsters. They outrun every other race, but you never want to get rammed. Ever.
TL;DR The game is solid, the gameplay is solid, the content is solid, and the AI opposition is incredible.

Game is really good to start with as Team Ninja's first PC game. It plays well, as always, no FPS drops, slightly CPU intensive, nice and colourful, stages were reworked to match the PS4 versions, and it's all good: TONS of costumes, BEST tutorial in any fighting game, and classic music. The game looks about as good as the the PS4 version, as the "soft engine" is just a placebo for jigglier boobs. I compared the PS3 version to the PC, and the PC to the PS4. Here's the cracker, right. Even without the Soft Engine, the game looks about the same as the PS4 version, minus the amazing particle effects, the characters' skin and textures look the same, we get the hairstyles such as PS4. This thing about the port being the same as PS3 is not even remotely true. It's because in the source table it said for effects that it was PS3 equivalent, and everybody went off from there.
But here's my gripe with this Game:
As much as I love DOA, there is always something that I don't like with it, or a mistake that Team Ninja makes.
No New Stages - Wtf? Why? Stages are one of the key features in a DOA game, and they were cut out. For what reasons? Because it's not a playability issue. The port is decently "optimized" as it is. I hope they are added in during the online patch. That would be a smart thing to do.
No Online Until 3 Months - I don't really play online on DOA anyway, but having the option in this day and age should be there DAY ONE. It's kind of silly that they did that, as that is what people do now, and not adding online day one is risking sales. Nonetheless, I don't mind. I can wait.
No Particle Effects - Needs to be in ASAP. It makes the game look better than it is, and in 4K, it will be amazing...
TN "MAY" (I say may because it is not official yet) be working on adding the missing features in a later period of time, but however, the damage has already been done, but things will get better and the clouds will clear up. Just god dammit TN, do it, and do it fast. This could be better.
I recommend this game, but get it AFTER the Online patch. You won't be disappointed. OK? Ok. It's a deal.

Edit #2: I left a comment but maybe putting it in the body of the review will help: I'm seeing a nearly even split between people considering this review helpful and not. I'd like to see comments responding who can tell me what about my review is helpful and what's not so that I can improve it and other reviews, both those that I will make in the future and the few I've done in the past. This lack of any sort of verbal response otherwise leads me to believe that people are voting "helpful" on my review because I liked the same game they did and recommended, and others are voting "not helpful" because I liked the game and recommended it and they hated it; this being perfectly counterintuitive to how helpful vs. not-helpful reviews should work, I'd like to be proven wrong.
Edit of below: I just wanted to add, to clear up any possible confusion regarding what I said about "not having a beast of a rig," this link:
This is a link to the CPU-Z validator page for my current build. In my opinion a good machine but not a game-chewing monster. The fact that I have no problems running this game won quite a few points in my book.
All of the pre-order hate can stop now. I pre-ordered this game and I regret nothing.
The internet would have me believe that this game will require a beast of a rig to run and not look hideous. I do not have a beast of a rig.
I cranked it as open as I can: 1080 (can't do 4K), full AA, maximum shadows. Jumped right into a fight. Despite a very active background and the pace of the fighting, the game never dropped under 59 FPS for me and otherwise stayed solid at 60. I only noticed the frame drop on account of clocking it with FRAPS.
Appearance wise, the game is gorgeous. The details are there--fighters get sweaty or dirty as the matches go on, and there's plenty of destructible environment for you to smash your opponent into and through, just as expected. Soft engine? Don't need it. Maybe it's just my eyes, but the skin looked pretty skin-like to me.
And finally, the core component of it--the experience. I haven't played a DOA game since DOA2 Hardcore on the PS2, and this game perfectly captures that same feel of a high speed, incredibly intense fight that I had from that. I never played the original DOA5 on other consoles, but if it played like this? I can see why it was so positively received. This was exactly what I expected for and hoped for out of a Dead or Alive game.
In short, KOEI delivered--this game is exactly what I wanted when I pre-ordered it for myself and my friends. And when the multiplayer component is added in, I will gleefully let myself get the snot beaten out of me on the internet in enjoyment of this game.

There is nothing more anger inducing (To me) than missing a 99% chance to hit shot, because the game just decided I did and then the Thin man gets a critical on my best solider. The whole campaign becomes forfeit as the rest of my soldiers fall one after another.
With that out of the way, I’ll keep the overall review short.
Pros:
Graphics are nice to look at with a unique style to them.
Random generation of solders from all over the world is nice. It adds to the us vs them mentality that you need to fight aliens.
The music sets the tone for the game. Every mission could be your last. (THIN MEN!!!!!)
The base building is fun and really requires you think everything out. (On harder difficulties)
Researching is self-explanatory. You research to better your resistance, I like it for what it is, but it could always be better.
Cons:
Gameplay is fun, but can be buggy and game breaking at times. Save often.
Customization of individual soldiers is lackluster. Not horrible, but not great either. I think it needed quite a bit more to give that feeling of uniqueness to every person who got recruited. I would have been way more attached if I didn’t think to myself “Eh, I’ll get another spikey haired assault trooper at some point.”
Inbetweener:
Upgrades are okay. It’s the usual worst to best.

I said last time in my Poker Night at the Inventory review that I was going to review more of the premium games I have in my Steam Library. For me, Poker Night was a very well done and the first premium game I had. So I bought more paid games after that and I got Braid for $2.75 during a sale and...well, I had mixed feelings. After revisiting it I can finally give my opinions on it, and man, do I have some problems with this game.
I will begin with the plot but I will make it vague so I won’t spoil anything. The protagonist Tim is looking for a princess he apparently had a close relationship to and he goes on a quest to rescue her. However the reason this story is so intriguing is the fact that before every set of levels there are storybooks lying around and you can read them. The stories are more like clues and they are very distant to boot. We find why the princess is missing and what Tim is actually like. But if you aren’t in the mood for a deep story, you can just skip them and have a simple rescue the lady plot.
And now on to the gameplay which I can safely classify as pretty damn good. The game is a side scrolling platformer with minor enemies there just because. I will admit that this game from the outside is very similar to Mario. You are after a princess, just like Mario. At the end of every world a grey dinosaur comes to Tim and says that the princess is in another castle, just like Mario. And this game is a 2-D platformer, just like Mario. But this is NOT the same as Mario. However, Braid’s Tim has a very sneaky trick under his belt. He’s a time thief. By pressing the SHIFT button (assuming you’re playing it on Steam), Tim will reverse time so your error will have never accrued. Died by an enemy? Reverse time and stomp on him. Miss a very important jump? Reverse time and try again. Want to manipulate the stage to solve a puzzle? Reverse time and press on. This is what makes Braid so different from other games because the time tinkering feature is so well implemented. This system makes puzzles clever and very creative. There are things like enemies to bounce on and locked door puzzles that use the time mechanic very well. On the other hand, you technically have no deaths, but trust me; soon I will tell you why this game is so hard.
The music in this game is totally awesome. I love the violin pieces so much and the small amount of piano is good, too.
However, the problems I have in the game start to arise in the puzzles. Every level has a few puzzle pieces to find and putting them all together will make a portrait. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ These puzzle pieces become ♥♥♥♥ing annoying! All of the levels in the game are puzzle pieces either out of reach or requiring you do something really ♥♥♥♥ing specifically hard. It took me so goddamn long to find a few puzzle pieces in the FIRST WORLD! I hate, hate, hate the puzzles.
OK, so putting my personal rage aside, the puzzle pieces make up the game and while you might want to go through the game without searching for them, then the game has no purpose. Levels in platformers like Mario and Kirby are different because they are lengthy levels with some optional collectables that are yours should you go out of your way for them. In this game however, levels are a quarter the size of most Mario levels and the puzzle pieces are just there because you feel like it is a must to get them. Not going for the puzzle peices with shorten the game alot and even if you DIDN’T know you would have to get them, they would still be there in the level, bugging you and saying “C’mon! Try to get me!”
Look, I tried as hard as I could to NOT trash this game, but the problem is there are dozens of other 2-D platformers that I would consider to be of better quality. I will still say this game is worth your time, but unless you are a challenge craver or a Sherlock Holmes for puzzles, this is a game you’re better off liking if you get it as part of a sale. The $10 price tag (or more I’m not sure) might be worth it if you like hard games, but if you aren’t buy it during some kind of a sale.

FTL is an exceptionally good and innovative game - you have to manage the crew and systems of a starship travelling from sector to sector, exploring and fighting your way to the final showdown(s) with the enemy flagship. On the way you can recruit more crew members from several races, upgrade your ship with better weapons, upgrade your systems to be more effective, scavenge fuel and scrap from various combat and non-combat situations you find yourself in, as well as the occasional quest you may come across.
Combat can get pretty hectic, although you can pause any time you need to, as you can have melee battles going on in both ships, robot invaders, fires raging through your ship, oxygen depleting due to a broken atmosphere scrubber, repairs needed on your shield system, a large hole in the hull, and even in some systems asteroids or solar flares periodically making things worse for everyone. And then the enemy ship warp countdown completes and they fly off with your boarding party still on board, never to be seen again...
This leads onto the key aspect that makes the game work so well - you will almost certainly lose crew members during each game, but each game only last a few hours, and while experienced crew members are more useful, rookies are capable enough that while losing crew makes things harder, it is usually recoverable as long as you don't keep losing them.
Due to the procedurally generated (roguelike) nature of the game, you aren't guaranteed to find any particular crew members at any point, or specific types of weapons, augments or extra systems - so you have to adapt to what each game throws at you, rather than just follow the same formula each time, which combined with the very different ways each ship type plays, plus the different abilities of your crew (based on their race), two games are rarely very similar and the game is very replayable. The downside of this is that a series of bad luck results at the wrong time can completely mess up what seemed to be a good run up to that point, but it is best to try and treat these things as a learning experience and it makes the victories that much sweeter when you know you can lose almost at any point if you aren't careful.
Adding to the replayability is the extra ship types and variants that can be unlocked for future runs - in the end you will have 9 ships to choose from, and if you achieve certain things in them you can unlock a second layout for each of them - some of which play quite similarly, but others play very differently in terms of how defendable certain key systems are, where the medibay is, where the external doors are located, etc.

NEO scavenger is a tough as nails survival game that will make you hate it so much you'll either kick it off a window or end up loving it.
It's a turn based tabletop-RPG-of-sorts that starts you waking up in a cryo facility in the middle of the post apocalyptic ruins of Detroit. It is sorta RPG because despite having almost no character progression to it you'll pick up a bunch of traits at the start and both skill checks and inventory management will be paramount to your survival, and sorta tabletop because you'll move across hexes using said abilities and items to gather, fight and resolve the situations you'll find yourself in.
The graphics are reminiscent of the DOS games of the early 90s and the sound design is minimalistic but effective.The player model will reflect equipment changes and every item has it's own art, and hexes have varied art that will let you know what to expect from each. Everything is functional, but the real star of NEO scavenger is it's gameplay and game design, and its biggest make or break factor.
The most important part of the game is undoubtedly the RNG, since it dictates how successful you'll be when scavenging, what you'll get, how combat will go, or whether you'll catch one of the many incredibly deadly diseases that plague the wasteland. There are some things that the player can do to nudge said rng one side or the other trough their abilities and gear, but make no mistake: take a whiff of blue rot or drink from the wrong water and you're pretty much done for, without being able to do much else about it.
The beginning of the game is the toughest and most frustrating part of it, because you'll start out virtually naked and extremely vulnerable, to the point that an idiot with a frying pan will be able to do you in. Avoiding confrontation is without a doubt the most effective way to play the game, but the implacable entropy will eventually force you into taking risks be it food or gear. Combat can be equally frustrating since being in the wrong place at the wrong time can earn you being 1 shotted by a hick with a rifle, although I gotta admit when that happens to you killing an enemy with just one bullet feels badass and satisfying as hell.
When you finally reach Detroit Megacity things get substantially easier. You'll be able to scavenge the surrounding areas and sell the loot for money, and you'll basically be doing scavenging trips while way better equipped and with better fallbacks. You'll be given missions regularly that will take you to stupidly dangerous places so you'll have to still stay on your toes. But having access to DMC is a far cry from scuttling around in a hospital garb praying to make it without ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ yourself to death due to cholera or freezing to death inside an abandoned building. You'll likely have to retry the first weeks over and over again, but once you manage to get a character rolling it gives you a great sense of accomplishment. Of course the game includes a full compliment of biological needs to take care of, but ironically those are one of the easiest parts of the game with the right perk or once you get some of the very early gear.
In closing NEO scavenger is a very long, hard and replayable game that you'll either hate until you love it or just plain hate it. Regardless, it's cheap and if you like survival and a challenge you shouldn't be afraid to pick it up. 7/10.
