BEGINNER REVIEW(Long review incoming)
I have played quite a bit of MMO's out there and I won't say something like "Oh this takes the cake" or "Best game I have ever played" or even "This game sucks so bad." Instead, this will be my initial thoughts for my first 2 hours of playing. I won't lie, I love the classed and races. Cosmetically. I don't see any class or race to be more OP than another class or race. If you would rather be a distance fighter, go for it. You like to be up close dishing out damage, have at it. Classes have been reworked and they seem to be all pretty balanced. The game first was released in sometime in 2011 so they have had quite a bit of time to rework a few things let alone more additions to the game. Originally it was also owned by gPotato and is now owned by
and made it an international game. Enough with the boring stuff. My first class, was an Inventor, which is the Arisen race I believe. Also known as an Engineer classes. With this class I am ranged equipped with a gun. Send out bots to help aim you in battle. Looking through the skill tree I seen this class can be DPS or Healer. I'll admit, I'm having a bit of fun with this class and has it's advantages. My health is on the low side of the spectrum but having the ability to move and cast a skill at the same time makes it better for me to keep my distance from enemies.
Quests, quests, quests. That seems to be all I'm doing at the moment. Tons of sides and of course your main quests. In the beginning I see that there are quite a variety of enemies and you encounter all of them through quests. Whether you need the items they drop or just the kills. My suggestion, if you want to level faster as well as do your main quest line, accept all quests you see. You never know if your main quest will cross over with those side quests giving a bit more experience and money, with just a little extra time spent completing the objectives for the side quests. The quests, so far, are pretty easy. Now the quests for your crafting on the otherhand, not so much. Make sure you have the money to even start the first quest because you will need to buy the items to complete the quests from the quest giver. I noticed I need to complete a few sides just to get the money. That or sell old equipment but I even did that and didn't seem to be enough for even one item.
As of this date, November 5th, 2016, I had received a few complementary items in the Boutique tab in my inventory and it really helped to get started. I don't know if they are just doing this for the time being because of their New Order update, but if not, it is definitely a great way to get players to stay. You get a few items to help you level, as well as points in representing a faction. You get a couple of item chests that contain other beginner items, such as armor, to help you get started. So the game does give you a quick head start to enjoy the game. It may take a bit to get farther into the game if you are new but more experienced players know ways to get to the top fast.
All in all I would recommend this game to any MMORPG gamer. It can be pretty fun as well as a relaxing game. I have not got the full experience of this game yet but when I do I will release another review as well as my progress. I do enjoy the game features it has to show and feel that with more and more time spent, it can be a pretty good game. Give it a try, put your first 2 hours into and see what you think, I hope this review helps your decision and thanks for the read.

Metro 2033, as well as Last Light, are based off of novels. That being said you don't need to read them to get into the game, but it doesn't hurt to be further educated on the subject matter.
The game is a survival horror in every true sense of the word. You live underground in Moscow, where the city has been destroyed by nuclear warfare and the surface can only be bared with the proper equipment. Mutants roam the lands and Metro tunnels 24/7 and you must stay alert if you want to survive. However the mutants aren't the only threat in this game. There are more than one civilization of humans; factions, if you will. You will have encounters with them as well.
Every. Bullet. Counts.
You will scavenge high and low for every bullet, every health pack, every grenade...
Each one found is a little hope instilled in your soul.
Not only are bullets for use in the obvious way; shooting. They are also your currency - making you decide - Do I save it to shoot or do I use it to buy supplies?
Every decision is crucial.
Redux is the definitive version, adding two distinct playstyles: Survival & Spartan.
Survival is the way it is meant to be played - low ammo, high damage and smarter AI.
Spartan is more in the spirit of Last Light, giving you more ammo and supply pickups.
Ranger Hardcore mode erases all HUD, hints and interaction buttons from the game.
I highly, highly recommend playing the campaign on Survival: Ranger Hardcore.

I make it no secret that the Dawn of War series is my favorite RTS (one could argue the later ones are more rpg) series, StarCraft coming close second and followed by the Command & Conquer.  …I think I just named all the big RTS series out there to begin with so that may have just been mute.  Regardless, it’s a great game though struggles to remain relevant due to some quality of life and less than stellar story.
Respect Your Elders:  I really enjoy this game and it shows an amazing stepping stone from early RPGs, yes I’ll easily admit it doesn’t hold up as well as I’d like.  The bare game (without mods) is from a previous generation in both graphics and functionality.  It has most of the quality of life components you’d expect:  Shift Clicking, Queuing Orders, etc but lacks a lot of the expected polish, especially in the realm of pathing.  In many ways this game was the cornerstone of future amazing RTSs.
Some Assembly Required:  The game really needs certain mods installed to work correctly, specifically the zoom out mod and the higher screen resolution mod (both of which can be easily found via google) but once these are installed the game runs just as well and is just as fun that I remember.  Another thing that adds to this game (including the rest of the series) is a massive quantity of mods provided by the community, from Grey Knights to Tyranids and new campaigns you can find it all.  Though not as numerous as games like Fallout there is much here to provide years of content.
I’m not here to tell you a story:  To be fair the story isn’t all that amazing, it’s more of the cliché ‘kill the enemies attacking you only to find that other enemies are there as well but oh! I got backstabbed by my best friend’ kind of story and the book isn’t terribly better either.  With that said, it does get the job done and is more or less on par with a lot of other RTS games out there.  It doesn’t hold a candle to the story in DOW2 or SC (period) but it is enjoyable and begins a long narrative for the sequel to expand on.
Overall, this game is highly recommended, though it may not hold up to modern standards I greatly enjoy the game and feel that it continues to live up to and (with mods) keeps pace with the modern RTSs out there.  I’d argue it is one of the greats and a game that I constantly go back to every year or so.  Highly recommend this game.

Dino Run DX (and the Dino Run series in general) is a surprisingly beautiful 8-bit, 2D side-scrolling game that has been near and dear to my heart since I first began my fateful escape from the Doom wall around August of 2010, when the game was a free Flash game found on various sites on the internet.  The player controls a customizable velociraptor using the arrow keys or WASD (along with other keys for other various functions) to run away from a Doom wall following behind, all while gathering the eggs, bones, and little critters that you encounter to gain DNA points to later boost your stats.
The dino can be customized with many different skins and hats, with a large surplus of options available immediately.  Want an entirely pink velociraptor with Boba Fett's helmet?  That's 100% possible.  Ever fantazise about being a pixelated Optimus Prime dinosaur?  Wait no longer!  Or, how about a blue dino with a dot on its back wearing a top hat?  Perfectly acceptable.  With over 38,000 different combinations of hats and skins from the get-go, you CAN'T go wrong!
Besides the given Challenge mode, there are a few other game modes to choose from, as well as a multiplayer mode, each with a unique style of gameplay and insanity that is survival of the apocalypse.  (
)
Overall, even without a gripping story, Dino Run DX is a very enjoyable game with simple yet compelling gameplay, yet filled to the brim with intense challenges, wacky achievements, hidden gems, and secret areas that will have you coming back for more.  Its 8-bit graphics and retro-style music give the impression of a classic- a title Dino Run DX fits into quite well.

The African Kingdoms is a small expansion compared to The Conquerors or The Forgotten, but it definitely makes up the lack of quantity in quality. With its great campaigns and interesting, balanced civilisations, it showed us that there is still massive potential in this game.
If the previous Age of Empires 2 HD expansion was more like the monetisation of a fan project, then The African Kingdoms is like a serious attempt to show us that this team is capable of delivering a high-quality DLC.
Although AoAK brings quite a few balance improvements and some new universal elements, it is more subtle with its additions, including the four fresh civilisations (where funny enough, one is actually European). Whereas The Forgotten created civs that specialised in all new areas, African Kingdoms veers towards balanced ones, where players may find them comfortable on most maps, including the new random map types.
The more polished feel is especially strong with the campaigns (one for each new civilisation). As expected from a proper RTS, the levels emphasise base building, while also introducing fresh, exciting ideas in both mission objectives and map design (although some are borrowed from other games).
The resulting package is so good that I would go as far as stating that African Kingdoms has probably the best campaigns in the entire game, making this DLC a must-have for any AoE2 player.

NEO Scavenger is something of an oddity among survival games, in that it is extremely good. It's an intriguing mashup of genres - take The Road crossed with The Mist with a little dash of Blade Runner and throw in a sprinkling of cryptozoology and Unsolved Mysteries and you've got NEO Scavenger in a nutshell. It works extremely well despite this hodgepodge of influences, and the world at no point feels contrived or artificial.
In any case, I'm getting ahead of myself: at the beginning of the game, none of this concerns you. Waking up in a deserted cryo-facility three-quarters naked and knowing nothing but your name, your most immediate priority is survival. You have several routes to achieve this, but all of them involve the same basic points: eat, drink, sleep, stay warm, don't get sick and don't get wounded, and if you do get wounded, take care of yourself promptly.
You accomplish this basic survival through two main methods. The first is scavenging, which involves travelling across the hex-based overworld map, choosing a tile to scavenge, and then choosing a specific location within that tile to scour, and at last choosing what abilities and items you'll use in the process. The yields are seldom all that great, but this is the game where you will feel exuberantly grateful for plastic shopping bags, worn flip flops, plastic bottles and old pots - where an intact shopping cart by comparison is an unimaginable score. Most of these things you use in crafting, in which you turn things you find into marginally more useful things.
If it sounds easy, believe me when I say it's not. Comestibles are scarce, and there's only so much nutrition you can get out of 50-year-old bags of chips and snack cakes. The pressing threat of starvation can lower you to the point where you're wandering across the land eating every little thing that seems the least bit edible to buy a few more hours of life, a threatening prospect when your character lacks the botanical skill to identify poisonous foodstuffs.
What to do when you run into a stray feral dog thus becomes a no-brainer. When pressed enough, you might even contemplate the unthinkable. Encounters with both animals, people and
are both somewhat rare and appropriately tense. You most often can't judge a person's intentions by sight alone, and trying to talk things out can leave you extremely vulnerable if they turn out hostile. In some cases, if you stumble onto a face-to-face encounter with someone, you may not even try to talk, given that even that moment of hesitation would be enough for them to stick a meat cleaver in your skull.
The combat in this game is a little bit of an odd duck. It's a bit similar to the original Wasteland, turn based, highly abstracted and without a tactical map - every enemy has a number representing their distance from you, and you have a number of options - advance or fall back, charge or run away. If your target is within range of your weapon, you can attack, and you can pull various special maneuvers or defensive moves depending on the circumstances. It can get a bit mechanical if you know what you're doing and are fairly well kitted, but when you're more down on your luck it can be fairly exciting in an 'oh god please let me live through this' sort of way, as playing it safe can become less justified if it means prolonging an encounter where every moment threatens death. Altogether though, the combat lacks dilemmas, in that there is almost always an objectively optimal action to take in each given situation. Not that it doesn't still have interesting situations - enemies with guns are an interesting example, as you have to weigh the possibility that they're bluffing with that of them actually having bullets and plan accordingly, and this is after all a game where you can win the fight but die slowly and painfully in your camp of an infected cut, huddled up in a sweaty sleeping bag and shivering with fever.
Death, I should mention, comes easy and takes many forms, if that wasn't already clear. If a scavenger stumbled onto your camp while you sleep, there's little you can do. Even if you manage to wake in time, you might be better off running blindly rather than risking a fight in the dark. But you don't need to fight to die. Cholera, food poisoning, diarrhea, infection, hypothermia, exposure to chemicals, yet more exotic diseases - there's plenty of ways to die and none of them are pleasant. One of my bigger problems with the game plays into this - there's certain encounters where you're given choices that can kill you instantly. On one hand, this makes every choice feel grave. On the other, it's kind of a cheap shot, and you can suffer immense penalties from consequences you had no way of foreseeing.
One of the things that I found immensely interesting as a possible consequence of the above is how the wasteland comes to warp your sense of morality. Whereas in other games you might be inclined to do good because you think you're a good person, here, the stress of constantly looming starvation, predation by other humans and the ease with which death comes can make you rather disinclined to stick your neck out for others. Even if you throw a good deed or two out now and then, putting yourself in harm's way for someone else's benefit is not something that the world encourages. If you find yourself in a state of pressing enough need, you might even find reason to screw an innocent over for your own benefit. Once you're put in that situation, you kind of start to sympathize with all the people trying to kill you for your stuff. At the very least, you can't really blame them any more, not when they're in the same ♥♥♥♥♥♥ situation as you. In that way, the game is an excellent illustration of how irrelevant morality becomes when survival is at stake, and the horror that results from that.
The game does have story, I should mention, and even a vague sort of plot. The writing is very good, the world building is great and the atmosphere is amazing. I should warn you that this game is incredibly bleak - it's not the sort of wacky post-apocalyptic amusement park of the more recent Fallout games, or even the relative optimism of the originals and FONV - it is a world of misery, starvation, murder, cannibalism, despair, negligence, scarcity and extinction. It isn't actively malicious, the depiction of suffering is not gratuitous - the world is callously indifferent, and this comes across in the writing marvelously. The world doesn't center around the protagonist, and for most purposes you're just another wasteland ragman whom nobody gives a hoot about. Some locations and encounters could have used a little more fleshing out - in one particular instance I imagined that my character could have the opportunity to finally get some answers about the state of things in the world, but to my disappointment I couldn't even ask about even the littlest point of interest. Incidentally, I found that the odd bits of old newspaper offering scattered details about the world's backstory far more interesting than the plot involving the protagonist's past.
In that vein, one of my bigger problems was a relative lack of content. There's plenty for the price, but a few more locations, conversations, quests, NPCs, cryptids to encounter and supernatural horrors would have done wonders for a relatively small investment. In the course of my first successful playthrough, I've seen just about everything there is from one point of view. There's still time to start new playthroughs and see how things turn out for different choices and to explore bits of missed content, but overall there's still less than I'd have liked, in an ideal world.
Ultimately though, NEO Scavenger was one of my favourite video game experiences of recent memory. It's engaging and atmospheric, and weaves gameplay and narrative seamlessly together. More games should try to be like NEO Scavenger.

Loving it so far, minus a few crashes and bugs with matchmaking. The detail is excellent though i had to manually go to my nvidia control panel to enable the GPU, game was using my integrated card by default. The detail on the strike craft leaves something to be desired and fighters/assaultbarges/bomber squadrons feel tacked on and lacking in visual creativity. the real star of the show, ive found is the maneuvering of your ships. your weapons will for the most part auto engage, leaving it to you to set enemy priority and target subsystems in the crucial seconds before a battle, (unless you have early intel from probes, which give you additional time) but steering and turning your ships to bring weapons to bear, engage the brakes/speed boost to avoid torpedo volleys and bombs, and ramming smaller ships feels weighty and solidly done. The metagame which involves customization of your ships and ship and crew leveling in multiplayer encourages sound tactical moves as opposed to blind rushing by punishing you for losing ships to a (temporary) extent, this sees players attempting to judge whether they should commit their ships final seconds to a last ditch effort attack, or a tactical warp-jump retreat from the field to preserve their favorite capital ship and captain. The depth of customization is varied enough as it is, that when seeing an opposing fleet for the first time, it is difficult to judge what special abilities the opponent may be fielding so every battle feels different even if the ship lineup is currently a little anemic.

XCOM: EU was my first game of the XCOM series and it just blew me away. It's my first turn-based tactical game and I never thought the genre could be as much fun as it is.
XCOM: EU is a reboot of the main series and thus a perfect candidate to get into it. XCOM in short is an Alien Invasion simulator where you are the commander of a military organization, which was created and funded by 16 nations from all around the globe to defend Earth against extra-terrestial threats. The game includes a vast tech-tree, base building, detailed soldier customization, detailed loadout selection, different soldier classes with specific perk-trees, air combat simulation and of course the main part of the game: grid-based, 3d maps of different locations such as buildings, forrests, alien spaceships, bases and more where your troops fight the aliens turn by turn.
The DLC (or rather expansion) Enemy Within adds another three mechanics to the game: Covert Operations, MECs (mechanical exoskeletal cybersuits) and gene modification for your troops.
The base game itself is very entertaining and the expansion adds enough content to make another playthrough of the campaign viable but honestly if you play on Normal you're looking at just a couple of days or 1-2 weeks of playtime until you're through with it. That's certainly not how I gained 700 hours in this game.
You probably heard it a thousand times already but XCOM:EU + EW truly shines through the Long War mod. I have yet to beat the campaign with the Long War mod on Normal/Ironman difficulty. It's absolutely brutal and you will hate yourself for ever starting with this mod but once you do there is no going back to vanilla. It's addicting!
If you are unsure whether to buy XCOM 1 or 2 I'd say it really doesn't matter if you're just after the vanilla experience. XCOM 1 is absolutely not outdated in terms of graphics or mechanics in any way or form so don't miss out on it if you see it on sale. On the other hand though if you really want to see how good you are at turn-based tactical games, there's no way around XCOM1+Long War. Play through vanilla once and then add the LW mod and find out if your assessment of your skill-level is correct.

A wonderful expansion to the base game. This DLC adds 4 new fully voiced campaigns as well as 4 new civilizations (the Portuguese, Berbers, Malians and Ethiopians. Definitely get it if you enjoyed the campaigns in Age of Empires and want some more.
I played all the campaigns from start to finish and really enjoyed them. The first campaign is the Umayad Berber conquest of Iberia and includes naval battles as well as a very tight narrow corridor style level of getting through a winter in the Pyrenesse. The second campaign, with Sundjata of the Malians is also interesting having the player explore the African plains, hunting elephants and mastering a new type of fighting (infantry and fast axe throwers). My favourite campaign was the Portuguese campaign. In this one, almost every level starts with the Portuguese in a small highly defended fort with walls. You can not win by only fighting on land since your enemies are many but you have the advantage of Caravel ships and cannon ships to wrestle the African coasts. I really enjoyed this one since you have to fight like a small naval power and defend your walled stronghold and then send ships to do battle in the seas and then raid the coasts. The last campaign, Yodit presents the Ethipian civilization. It is also an enjoyable campaign with interesting levels which include a level where you need to protect caravans in the desert as well as a level where you progressively open up a city for conquest.
For me, this game is great for the story and the campaigns. Unlike the Forgotten Empires campaigns, these campaigns are fully voiced and the level design is simple and interesting. If you are looking for a campaign set like the originial Age of Kings and Age of the Conquerors, this is it. They are even better.
The new civilizations are also interesting, The Portuguese have advantages while fighting on the seas and have a unique unit which can attack multiple ships as well as an unique building which can provide a constant flow of resources. The Malians are an infantry civilization, with all barracks units receiving a pierce armor bonus. The Berber are a cavalry unit with interesting support units such as an anti-archer cavalry as well as a unique unit adept at defeating cavalry archers. Lastly, the Ethiopians are an archer civilization who can progress through the ages more rapidly, have archers with a faster rate of fire as well as a good raiding castle unit. The new civilizations are very welcome addition in my opinion.
An expansion which is definitely worth it if you enjoy playing story campaigns as well as interesting for the new civilizations and the unique take on African history. Somehow, although it has come out many years after the original campaigns it really feels like an integrated experience. It feels right at home. :)

This game is so exciting and no doubt one of the most difficult simulation game I ever played. I haven't managed to finish the Normal difficulty though (maybe it's just me), and there so much surprise on your adventure to the final sector (from vanishing of the crew due to huge monolith to the crew zombified and turn against you—and you have to kill him with your own crew).
The permadeath feature is essential to the constant tension and managing your encounters with different ships and dangers, to the final sector which you have to fight the Rebel mothership which evolves after you beat it in the first place—and not to mention the huge amount of replayability due to diverse randomly generated worlds and scenarios (and the recent updates add tons of additional content, from ship, story, to alien race).
However, as good as a game might be, there's always a room for improvement. Though this game features Cloud Sync, the game save file is NOT compatible cross-OSes (I played on Mac and Windows) which is quite a drawback for people who constantly use different OS on everyday basis. The achievement is saved in your save file too, which means it's not saved on Steam and again—it's not compatible with cross-OS save files. I really, really hope the dev will address this issue pretty soon.
However, those issues is quite minor compared to the fun you gonna have from this game. Sim-fans and Sci-Fi-fans who want a taste of their intergalactic adventure from the comfort of your home (with retro graphics), this game is a must buy.

It's good.  Runs like a dream.
Just a note:
I've been using a XBOX360 Controller as my input device and my System hardware comfortably exceeds the recomended requirements;  so as far as I can tell, the game runs perfectly.
As for the fight engine, you can't really fault it.  It's the same formula that's been refined and tweaked ever so slightly from its inception, so whether you played since DOA2 or just now picked it up, you'll be pleased to know that you are getting the same classic DOA experience.  So re-acquainting yourself will come very easily.  If you are new to the game, it's easy to pick up, and can be challenging to master.
As for the things the game lacks, 2 stages and a soft engine.  Hardly deal breakers IMO.  36 stages are already a lot, and most of them are quite dynamic with environmental hazards and multiple tiers.
If I were to make a criticism it would be about the lighting, but it would be from a perspective of design choice.  The devs wanted the game to look, feel and play like something fantastical, but somehow the characters always look like they are apart from the environments they are fighting in, rather than immersed in them.
As always, the story is non-sensical, but that is the hurdle that most fighting games fail to surmount.  Fighting is the mechanic, so of course when you throw individuals from the largest DOA cast ever, into situations that can only end in a fight, their reasons for doing so vary from whimsical, farcical and... well, typical.
The stock game comes with heaps of costumes, which is already more than most fight games of its genre, but if you want to purchase more, be prepared to pay a premium for them with Tecmo Koei releasing 2 sets of DLC which already exceed the cost of the game.
Finally, once you beat the game, all that's left is to polish your skills on the various game modes until they release the online component; but in the interim, just have your friends over and play with them - zero lag and the purest experience.

A wonderful expansion to the base game. This DLC adds 4 new fully voiced campaigns as well as 4 new civilizations (the Portuguese, Berbers, Malians and Ethiopians. Definitely get it if you enjoyed the campaigns in Age of Empires and want some more.
I played all the campaigns from start to finish and really enjoyed them. The first campaign is the Umayad Berber conquest of Iberia and includes naval battles as well as a very tight narrow corridor style level of getting through a winter in the Pyrenesse. The second campaign, with Sundjata of the Malians is also interesting having the player explore the African plains, hunting elephants and mastering a new type of fighting (infantry and fast axe throwers). My favourite campaign was the Portuguese campaign. In this one, almost every level starts with the Portuguese in a small highly defended fort with walls. You can not win by only fighting on land since your enemies are many but you have the advantage of Caravel ships and cannon ships to wrestle the African coasts. I really enjoyed this one since you have to fight like a small naval power and defend your walled stronghold and then send ships to do battle in the seas and then raid the coasts. The last campaign, Yodit presents the Ethipian civilization. It is also an enjoyable campaign with interesting levels which include a level where you need to protect caravans in the desert as well as a level where you progressively open up a city for conquest.
For me, this game is great for the story and the campaigns. Unlike the Forgotten Empires campaigns, these campaigns are fully voiced and the level design is simple and interesting. If you are looking for a campaign set like the originial Age of Kings and Age of the Conquerors, this is it. They are even better.
The new civilizations are also interesting, The Portuguese have advantages while fighting on the seas and have a unique unit which can attack multiple ships as well as an unique building which can provide a constant flow of resources. The Malians are an infantry civilization, with all barracks units receiving a pierce armor bonus. The Berber are a cavalry unit with interesting support units such as an anti-archer cavalry as well as a unique unit adept at defeating cavalry archers. Lastly, the Ethiopians are an archer civilization who can progress through the ages more rapidly, have archers with a faster rate of fire as well as a good raiding castle unit. The new civilizations are very welcome addition in my opinion.
An expansion which is definitely worth it if you enjoy playing story campaigns as well as interesting for the new civilizations and the unique take on African history. Somehow, although it has come out many years after the original campaigns it really feels like an integrated experience. It feels right at home. :)

XCOM: EU was my first game of the XCOM series and it just blew me away. It's my first turn-based tactical game and I never thought the genre could be as much fun as it is.
XCOM: EU is a reboot of the main series and thus a perfect candidate to get into it. XCOM in short is an Alien Invasion simulator where you are the commander of a military organization, which was created and funded by 16 nations from all around the globe to defend Earth against extra-terrestial threats. The game includes a vast tech-tree, base building, detailed soldier customization, detailed loadout selection, different soldier classes with specific perk-trees, air combat simulation and of course the main part of the game: grid-based, 3d maps of different locations such as buildings, forrests, alien spaceships, bases and more where your troops fight the aliens turn by turn.
The DLC (or rather expansion) Enemy Within adds another three mechanics to the game: Covert Operations, MECs (mechanical exoskeletal cybersuits) and gene modification for your troops.
The base game itself is very entertaining and the expansion adds enough content to make another playthrough of the campaign viable but honestly if you play on Normal you're looking at just a couple of days or 1-2 weeks of playtime until you're through with it. That's certainly not how I gained 700 hours in this game.
You probably heard it a thousand times already but XCOM:EU + EW truly shines through the Long War mod. I have yet to beat the campaign with the Long War mod on Normal/Ironman difficulty. It's absolutely brutal and you will hate yourself for ever starting with this mod but once you do there is no going back to vanilla. It's addicting!
If you are unsure whether to buy XCOM 1 or 2 I'd say it really doesn't matter if you're just after the vanilla experience. XCOM 1 is absolutely not outdated in terms of graphics or mechanics in any way or form so don't miss out on it if you see it on sale. On the other hand though if you really want to see how good you are at turn-based tactical games, there's no way around XCOM1+Long War. Play through vanilla once and then add the LW mod and find out if your assessment of your skill-level is correct.

Took me a bit to get into this game coming from being such a huge Company of Heroes one fan, but once I got the hang of it and they got some of the balance and bugs worked out, this game has proven to be a very enjoyable experience. The graphics are very detailed, the sound is excellent, the combat intense and the strategies required to win are never set in stone. It is a difficult game to fully grasp if you've no experience with an RTS like it, but features like destructible environments, cover, dynamic line of sight, and even things like armor facing make this an incredibly unique RTS with no equal.
Don't expect this game to go easy on you - every little second and ability counts just as much as the units you pit against your enemy and your strategy on how to combat them. You must be able to multitask and micromanage very well all while understanding the dynamics between each unit. This is a game that is all about how you are able to deal with the cards you are dealt, not the kind of deck you build before the fight. In other words, its not so much about build order and timing as it is about positioning, reconnaissance, micromanagement, reactions, and being able to think on your feet. If that sounds like an interesting challenge to you, then I HIGHLY reccomend this game.

Let me preface this by saying I play on my
account and NOT through Steam.  I only downloaded the steam version to write this review.  Originally, I was a little skeptical, but figured it was F2P so I'd check it out.  I have since rolled a character on the P2P server and am loving the game.  Allods Online is a Solid MMORPG from top to bottom.  The gamplay would be classified with those of WoW, EQ2, SWTOR, or FFXIV.  It's your classic tab targetting system.  The skill point system is very in depth and lets you make the character you want to play.  The graphics are better than WoW or EQ2, but not quite as good as FFXIV.  I would classify the quality of graphics close to that of Wildstar, but it is not as cartoony.  It does have stylized graphics, but much less cartoony than any of the forementioned games.  The characters, mobs, and environments look solid.  The story is really well done, and holds your attention, but you will have to read some quest text in order to follow it.  The setting for the story is unique; this is not your typical fantasy setting.   THis is mor of an MMORPG, than most of the newer F2P games coming out that are MMOGs at best.  This is a throwback to the old school mentality of what a good MMORPG should be.  If any of this sounds intriguing to you, than I suggest you are the perfect target audience for this game.  I recommend rolling on the P2P server where there is no cash shop.  It's a sub based server and has absolutely no P2W options.

This game is so exciting and no doubt one of the most difficult simulation game I ever played. I haven't managed to finish the Normal difficulty though (maybe it's just me), and there so much surprise on your adventure to the final sector (from vanishing of the crew due to huge monolith to the crew zombified and turn against you—and you have to kill him with your own crew).
The permadeath feature is essential to the constant tension and managing your encounters with different ships and dangers, to the final sector which you have to fight the Rebel mothership which evolves after you beat it in the first place—and not to mention the huge amount of replayability due to diverse randomly generated worlds and scenarios (and the recent updates add tons of additional content, from ship, story, to alien race).
However, as good as a game might be, there's always a room for improvement. Though this game features Cloud Sync, the game save file is NOT compatible cross-OSes (I played on Mac and Windows) which is quite a drawback for people who constantly use different OS on everyday basis. The achievement is saved in your save file too, which means it's not saved on Steam and again—it's not compatible with cross-OS save files. I really, really hope the dev will address this issue pretty soon.
However, those issues is quite minor compared to the fun you gonna have from this game. Sim-fans and Sci-Fi-fans who want a taste of their intergalactic adventure from the comfort of your home (with retro graphics), this game is a must buy.

I wrote an earlier review not recommending the game, but am now revising it. My main issues were with PvP, but I was unaware of the ability of users to create private servers that can disable PvP. Without the threat of three days of work being demolished by someone else while you sleep, the game is far more enjoyable. This does mean I do not recommend any of the official servers, as they are all PvP as of this writing, but if you can put together a private server with a more cooperative setting, the game is far more fun if you prefer building stuff as oppossed to destroying stuff.
The issues with the game being early access generally didn't bother me much, though for those expecting a finished polished game, this can be a dealbreaker. Melee is, in general still a non-starter due to syncing issues except against mostly stationary targets, but other than that, the game plays fine, if really unpolished (the long loading times when first starting the game is the most major issue I can think of that will probably dampen your play experience).
All in all, for me, if you enjoy the constructive, building aspect of survival games, I would recommend this game played on PvE server. I can't address for those who enjoy the marauding, raiding aspects of such games, but for the all too long a period of time I spent on a PvP server, the high level players seemed to be enjoying themselves, so if that's your cup of tea, you'll probably enjoy the game as well.

The grotesque and rather terrifying mutants known as The Dark Ones have now invaded your home station, Exhibition. It's up to you to defend the many survivors and factions (who have immensely detailed culture and lore) in the Moscow metro. Equip yourself with obscenely powerful and customizable jury-rigged weaponry held together by duct tape and ball bearings. You're also gonna need some gameplay features such as a gasmask with scarce filters, a manually rechargeble flashlight, and military grade bullets that have the potential of either trading currency or devestating damage to enemies. It's a game of choice really, it's up to you if you have a stealthy or aggressive journey to the philosophical conclusion of whether the mutants are the next step in evolution or if humans can truly have a second chance. Either way, good luck, кролик.

This is the best thing you can get for free! There's almost no reason anymore to spend money on 3DS Max or Maya. Just download this, learn it, and use it!
I've written two guides on how to use this to create objects for games (specifically Space Engineers and Blade Symphony) and it works great. The only thing slowing it down is some game developers are stuck on using max and maya, and some of them use crappy proprietary tools that are plugins for only those packages. But usually there are workarounds and I think the gaming industry is starting to realize that if they want to support modding they need to support Blender for modding.
I highly recommend the CGCookie video tutorials to help you get started. This stuff is complicated and video tutorials help a lot. Don't get discouraged if it seems to complex at first because once you get used to it it becomes second nature to use.
Also, please consider joining the Blender Foundation if you use Blender all the time. Even if you only donate $2/month via PayPal then it's worth it if you use Blender all the time!

Dying Light is a game developed by Techland and published by WB Games
This game runs super smooth with everything maxed. Everything from textures, animations, and lighting look great. Even the facial animations are above par which is one of the more difficult things to get right
The gameplay is solid. Most of it will consist of melee combat but there are bows, crossbows, and guns. But all of those pale in comparison to the things you find to beat over the head of zombies
There's a huge variety of melee weapons and the parkour really is what makes this game awesome. The combat seemlessly flows into running up and onto walls. This makes for a very unique experience
There's also a fully fleshed out perk system that adds to the combat, crafting, and parkour
The only thing I don't like about Dying Light is the shift it takes in the second half. You change settings and personally I prefer the first area to the second, but that's just my opinion
Even with my one tiny problem I still think this is a great game that shows us why the zombie genre is an interesting genre and after the terrible Dead Island series, I have faith with Dying Light and Techland's other games
I'd definitely recommend buying this whether it's on sale or not

Quick recommendation: If you want the 100% Dawn of War 1 experience, get Dawn of War: Soulstorm + Ultimate Apocalypse mod, instead. But if you want to really introduce yourself slowly to the Warhammer 40000 universe without clotting your head with too many stuff at once, play this one first.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Yep. It's old, but it's one of the most defining RTS during its time.
I used to own all of the DoW games once, pirated. Being used to Warcraft and Starcraft as pioneer RTSes, I thought, ya why not. Another space-sci-fi RTS. Recently I bought all DoW titles on Steam, just to remind and appreciate how Dawn of War introduces me to an uber-awesome sci-fi universe which is WARHAMMER 40000.
This game opened doors for me. It introduces me to the dark, grim and hopeless Warhammer 40000 franchise. From there I get to know that GW miniatures are a thing, and am hooked to collecting and painting the minis now. And Warcraft and Starcraft actually are inspired by the Warhammer and Warhammer 40000 franchises, respectively.
Back to the game, this is one of those innovative RTSes where you can control an entire 'unit' (or squad) of up to 9-10 soldiers instead of training them one-by-one a la War/Starcraft. This allows bigger battles with more units on screen. Other innovative things are all units can engage in either ranged or melee combat. Why melee in a sci-fi universe, you ask? Well melee is a big feature in the Warhammer 40000 universe, where combats tend to get up close and personal.
So within those melee combat, they will sometimes have 'sync kills' where some of your/enemy's troops will execute a brutal melee kill animation that's really fun to watch. Other innovative things in this RTS is certain bigger units like walkers and monsters will be able to mow down and toss smaller troops around, and this really brings the battlefield alive.
Am really excited Dawn of War III, the third installment of this franchise that is coming soon. And if you really are interested in delving into the universe without purchasing the overpriced models, codexes and books, this game is a must play to get you the general feeling and atmosphere of the Warhammer 40000 universe/franchise. It is a very good entry point to the overly complex universe.

Dawn of War was my introduction to the Warhammer 40k universe and thanks to it I am now very interested in this series and it's lore. Dawn of War is a dated but charming strategy game with nice stylized graphics that still hold up relatively well. The story is lackluster and didn't really engage me full force, however it did invest me into this universe. I still played through all the 11 campaign missions which took me roughly about 10 hours, and that was at a leisure filled pace exploring every corner of the map I could. The missions are very linear and repetitive offering little to no variety, forgetable characters, limiting maps, restricted troop types. But the missions isn't what the game is based around. And what is it based around you might ask? Well in my opinion two main things, first is the design of troops and locations. They are amazing, the world is so stylized and really cool looking. The gameplay however is without a doubt the main and best part of this game, the combat is so fun and engaging offering a variety of troops and weapons. It's awesome having an army of Space Marines all equipped with upgraded weapons, varying from rocket launchers to plasma guns running into battle while screaming, "For the Emperor!" As their bodies fly in every direction yet they still push onto the enemy, brutal killing animations begin as they tear apart their foes. From hand held chainsaws tearing open a man's chest to a giant robot throwing a man hundreds of feet away this game does not lack brutality or style. Overall this is a very fun strategy game and I look forward to playing this game's standalone expansions and sequel(s).

A nonsensical plot atop a mind-bending puzzle game. I won't describe the plot anymore than saying it does not make any sense and when you think you've got a handle on it, it quickly flies away.
As for the gameplay, its pretty damn fun if you're into this kind of puzzle game. By that I mean really hard ones with no hint system whatsoever. You can rewind time, and must use this skill and some platforming to collect jigsaw puzzle pieces. This isn't strictly necessary but, given the terrible storytelling, the puzzles are the only fun this game offers. Oh and the game often adds very interesting wrinkles to this time mechanic. The design is fantastic. But this is also an extremely hard game. There is no smooth difficulty curve. I tried to get each puzzle piece myself and only looked up a solution after reaching peak frustration. I was able to get the majority of them myself, and more than a few times found the solution to be something I never would have thought of.
I'm happy to have played Braid, mainly because I wanted to see why critics love it so much. But while the gameplay was definitely novel and very clever, the difficulty felt like poor design to me. (Full disclosure, I'm NOT a fan of very hard games.) And I HATE the story. So I'm glad I got t for cheap in a humble bundle.

Roguelike permadeath meets somewhere between Zork Zero and Return to Zork.  Only there doesn't seem to be a set storyline.  Therefore, expect alot of roaming around in the dark until something interesting happens.  Also expect to die alot including rerolling a new character each time.
You start out as a survivor of a disaster, you wake up basically naked and unarmed with no items.  Now go wander around scavenging so that you don't die.  You will find lots of good loot that will go to waste because you just don't have anywhere to put it so you leave it on the ground and hope you can find your way back later if you find a use for it.  It can be  a real bummer sometimes.
If you don't find clothing right away you basically are gonna have to start again until you do.  Finding clothing is totally randomized.
It has the feel of sifting through trash can after trash can looking for something you can use while hiding from monsters in the dark.  Hence, the name NEO Scavenger.
I have yet to live past day 2.  Difficult game it is, but if you give it a little time, you might have a different experience than most hack and slash survival games.

11/10 would shout "KAMIKAZE" before crashing my V-Wing into the enemy cruisers bridge and surviving while being launched out of the battle area again
Beyond that, I remember playing this game on Playstation 2 at my friends house. The three of us would sit down offline, like the squeakers that squeakers call squeakers we were, and from my own perspective had a blast every time. 7 or 8 years later, I found it on this workshop, and needed to have it. And, for only $3.00, it was like Jesus Christ himself had come down and hended it to me for free, because, even after 11 years since release, this game is just as fantastic as ever. The game AI represent a real obstacle to the player, mainly because there's so damn many of them, all of whom have about 3/4ths the skill of the average player, and I cannot tell you how many times during the excellent campaign(which we'll ge to shortly) I lost a mission because of a stubborn swarm of defending AI. And battles with 32 Ai on a team with maxed reinforcements on Polis Massa, Dagobah, the Tantive IV, or Felucia can be intense, with conquest points constantly changing hands(I don't realiy play much else, except the space battle assaults), or just being forced to sit at one capture point or risk having the AI driven back to a point they may not be able to hold without losing more men than the opposing team. The gamemode conquest, as I mentioned, is your typical conquest mode, not all that different from Battlefield conquest. Then, there are the space battles. Oh, I love these so much. You can fly from your cruiser to the enemies, engage other ships, destroy the enemy cruiser's systems from without or within, as well as their escort ships, all while defending your own. Fly in four different ship classes: Generic balanced fighters(all around good ship that can be brought to most engagements with a chance of success), a bomber(particularly good at destroying the enemies sustems and escort, but not the best choice for ship to ship combat, but it is outfitted with a second seat with either a gunner position or remotely guided missile to aid in such engagements), the... well, let's call them interceptors(pretty damn good against other fighters and such, fast with effective guns, but low health and poor weapons for assaulting the enemy criser and such), and the transport(land one of these suckers inside of the enemy cruiser, and you have a spawn point in the hangar until it is destroyed. Lots of health and effective missiles make this a good ship to assault the enemies shields as you approach their hangar, and with a whopping four seats, each with their own weapons and purpose, this can make quite the effective tank when fully manned by players), or you can stay aboard your own ship and man a turret to fire at the enemy ships. Ground battles have 6 classes for each faction. Four universal ground: Rifleman(pretty damn good for a generic class, with an automatic riifle, a pistol, and four grenades), Heavy weapons(Not my cup of tea, equipped with an RPG of sorts, a pistol, a few grenades and one or two mines), the CQC(This is my baby, equipped with a shotgun, a repair tool, 3 packs of explosive charges, and 5 health and ammo drops), and a sniper(Semi-auto sniper rifle, pistol, 3 grenades, and an auto-turret, this is what I choose for those long, narrow choke points with wall ribs), two unique ground classes varying by faction(usually a paladin type of guy with allied buffs and a powerful primary and a pistol, and also a light assault units, with a grenade launcher or a fancy-doohicky that scares me too much to use, and a pistol, or, in the case of a Bothan, active-camo, and some grenades and another piece of equipment that I'm blanking on right now, and half of these are Jetpack units. Bear in mind, I'm not the best source for either of these classes, as I don't play as them often), and hen two space battle classes: The pilot(pistol, repair tool, four grenades, and automtically repairs ships while inside them) and the Marine(automatic rifle, RPG, and 3 timed explosives). Tanks and lighter vehicles can be found on the ground as well, and also some defensive turrets. A great number of maps makes gameplay very different each time, seeing as how the two eras make the gameplay different already on their own, although there are only about 8 space maps. Heroes based on what faction and map can provide a much needed diversion, or become your worst nightmare(In Jabba's Palace, Aayla Secura can force back a force of 20 odd troops on her own in the narrow corridors, which can be a blessing or a curse based on which team you're playing as), but also lose health over time, which can onlly be regained by killing enemy troops. While the official multiplayer was taken down in 2014, another option does exist: Gameranger, your free way to play this game online. You can set up private lobbies to play with your friends, or public lobbies, or join other peoples lobbies(just make sure you don't window into the game itself until after you X out of the add that inevitably plays blaringly loud and cannot be canceled after the game is launched). It's easy to setup and download, and I've had good experiences(bear in mind games hosted on your own PC may lag a lot for you or for other players, depending on where you are in relation to one another) playing with my friends. There is also a campaign mode, where you play as a veteran of the 501st legion, starting with a tutorial on Geonosis, then really starting on Mygeeto, and ending on Hoth 14 ground assaults and 4 space battles later. As I mentioned before, these can end in losses if you're not careful. It plays out in CTF, assault, conquest, TDM, and hunt(CTF and TDM are generic, and hunt is something like eliminate a species), and is pretty damn good. If you really do need to ask yourself if this game will run on your computer, then you probably need to get a new one, since it would need to be at least a decade old for this game to not run properly. In other words, this game runs great, and it has good graphics for it's time period. There's a larger than you would expect selection of mods out there, some of which add maps, and others graphic enhancements, but they may cause crashes or not work properly. When running Gameeranger, it would probably be best to just play the vanilla version so as to avoid the inconvenience.
So, this game, which I probably do have some level of nostalgia glasses and foavoritism(as it is my favorite game), is not only worth the ten dollars it normally takes to buy it, but is still worth more than that price over a decade after release, as well as being a better game than the reboot, which has half the game in DLC, whereas all of this game's DLC ws either free or extremey cheap.If you're thinking about buying this game, do yourself a favor and replace that thinking about with a going to be. If you don't enjoy, well it's only ten dollars, at least you didn't buy some other half-released, more expensive version of it, right? Unless you already did, in which case, you have my condolences. I mut also apologize for how all over the place this review is, and for any speling errors(it's 1 AM for me rn).

Not a worthy sequel at all. In fact, much of what made the first game great is completely lost in this game. There's an absurd amount of cutscenes that drag on endlessly, not only boring you to death but also making the silent Freeman seem extremely out of place. The tutorials scattered throughout the game coddle you and expect that you have no idea what you're doing. Also, the pacing is completely mangled and horribly inconsistent. For example, ravenholm initially sees you yawn your way past basic enemies and basic level design,
finding one of the several gimmicks interesting, then sees the second half of it throwing enemy after enemy at the player, which are pointless to attack with anything but the shotgun, all culminating in a rather anti-climactic "final battle" that left me laughing from how absurd
was. Weapon balance was improved in some ways (the SMG isn't
garbage now) but mangled in others (Max ammo for the shotgun and revolver, etc.). You can expect to keep getting fed pistol ammo throughout the game even though it becomes useless at highway 17, you will go for long stretches of time without any resources only to be flooded with them later (and no, this isn't a test in ammo conservation, it's just bad planning as evidenced by the gameplay). One gunplay problem that was present in the first game as well is the weapon inaccuracy. Most of the time, whether or not you lose health in long-range gunfights boils down to whether or not your gun wants to work. Many of the game's concepts of gameplay fall flat and actively detract from the game, such as the horrible, completely worthless driving segments (if it weren't for ABH I'd skip highway 17 onward) and the god-awful storming of Nova Prospekt, where you're forced to swtch away from guns to use a tool that in reality is almost complety worthless, and where you're forced to make a one-man assault on Normandy Beach to simultaneously fight off two gunships, all the while gunners are tearing you apart with mounted guns (at least during the gunship battles you can actually retaliate).
At many points during the game, I was totally lost on what to do. The biggest downfall of this game's world is that Valve tried to be what
was while being
and failed miserably. Pointless, boring, incredibly simple puzzles block progress to exploration and combat, and most of the time you're thrown a puzzle you'll spend five minutes looking for the stereotypical "door that you open to move on" before realizing that you first have to walk back and forth from point A to point B 6 times before you're allowed to move on. In a similar vein, the writing for this game is some of the worst storytelling I've ever seen in any game. In the first game, you had to travel to a seperate wing of Black Mesa since the way in couldn't be used as the way out, learned that the US military wasn't there to help you, you had to fight your way through that wing to open the blast doors outside and start moving towards another lab to close the portal you opened, you had to take a rail system (which was the worst part of the game and the only part of the game to "make" you use railcarts, which isn't a coincidence) to a rocket launch station to put a satilite up into orbit, got knocked out and left for dead, traversed an underground sewer system to get to the Lambda Complex, teleported to an alien world, slayed their overlord, and was greeted by GMan himself and given an ultimatum. In this game? Go to point A, watch a cutscene, oh no, an unexpected attack! Go to point B, watch a cutscene, oh no, an unexpected attack! Ad Nauseam. Even
has a more interesting and cohesive plot.
Perhaps worst of all is that the movement system has been totally and completely dumbed down. Unlike the first game, where you held shift to walk and moved normally otherwise, in this game you move slowly unless you hold shift to sprint, itself on an "aux power" limit that slowly regenerates and severely slows you down. Perhaps this was a move to get you to "appreciate the atmosphere" or some other bs devs like to ramble about. In any case, it's a stupid mechanic, especially considering it shares the same meter as your flashlight and oxygen (I get that tying how long you can hold your breath to sprinting may be a bit more realistic, but flashlight? come on now). Worst of all in this category is that they disabled bhopping. The very mechanic that defined the Goldsrc and Quake engines has been phased out in this game, and the only reason I can actually tolerate the game as-is is that the team responsible for banning bhopping did such a backwards job of it that they made Accelerated Back Hopping a thing (which is indicative of how every other aspect of the game works).
So, to sum it up, Valve took everything that made
an extremely successful title, tore it up, threw it out the window, and proceeded to make a "sequel" completely detatched from the first game in every single way, left the ending a horrible cliffhanger to get you to buy the episodic trilogy, then left the trilogy unfinished in order to feed off of the hype for all of eternity.
Seriously, don't buy this game.
P.S.: The flashing light effect of the gravity gun's primary fire gave me a migrane that put me out of action for the next day. Thanks for that, and the several other obnoxious particle effects. Will not be attempting "Zombie Chopper" again.

Very good brawler. Tight controls, interesting moves, decent weapon variety, and a nice artstyle. I personally found it enjoyably challenging, and a bit frustrating at times even on Normal difficulty, but I'm not really much of a fighter/brawler player so your experience may vary. The story was somewhat interesting but truth be told it was nothing revolutionary imo.
It's not without flaws, of course. Enemy variety is frankly not the most impressive. Also be warned the singleplayer story mode is very short. First playthrough only took me about 2 to 3 hours. There's some replayability if you want to try hard mode or unlock all the costumes, but frankly after you settle into a pattern of attack that you like, beating up very similar goons already becomes somewhat repetitive in the first playthrough so I'm not sure how many more I'd be interested in doing. There's a multiplayer campaign I haven't done yet, so maybe there's some meat to be had there.
Also the save system is automatic and stage based, and it's not always completely clear what the stage start and end points are. So if like me you decide you want a break after reaching a checkpoint and exit the game, you might find yourself having to repeat some content.
Around 2 hours of my play time were actually alt-tabbed because I was getting a bit salty and wanted a break, but didn't want to redo the whole stage thanks to the limited autosave system.
It was an enjoyable experience and I would recommend it, just be aware that this can indeed be a game you beat in one (short) sitting.

As of April 2015,
The Good:
- Load time on startup is less than 4s and stages practically don't have loadtimes (SSD + 4770k @ 4.2ghz)
- Very respectable performance
- "Support" for 4k resolution
The Bad:
- Controller binding issues.
- Keyboard 1p ONLY or Controllers 1p-4p ONLY.
- No keyboard remapping.
- No custom resolutions without mods.
- Missing content from equivalent releases.
- No online play.
This game is a port of the respective vesion on PS3. "Last Round" contains several DLC costumes that have been released since 5 (eg. Cheerleader, Kitty, Naughty Girls). Massive bundles of even more DLC costumes are available, and ninja costumes are expected to be released as well.Yet the developers have announced that some features are missing and yet to be released with the base game: ONLINE multiplayer support.
To add on to the list of "what this game could have" (compare the equivalent Last Round release on PS4 and XB1) are: soft engine, two maps, and full controller support. If you're using an x-box controller with triggers, you may need a workaround to bind those as buttons. Furthermore, the game will only detect 1 type of control input, determined on launch with priority for controllers. If you want keyboard, you'll have to do without controller (and vice versa).
If you've always been a Team Ninja fan and you love DOA, you'll buy this game anyway.
If you're a fan of the 3D fighting genre and have been dying to get one on PC for a long time, I can't promise satisfaction.
For the rest, you'll wish you'd have gotten more out of what you paid for. Save your money and check up later if the game sorts its issues out... or maybe just buy another game that isn't full for false promises.

Before you look at my hours played, I should point out I played this a fair bit back in 2012, so what I say is based on my time with the game back then and from the changes I've seen so far.
Anyway to start it's definately WoW clone, but it's a WoW clone with enough of it's own identity to stand out. The setting is actually quite unique, with cyborg space zombies to a cold war Soviet city (Lulz Russia) all set on a 'Burning Crusade' floating island world. Combat is typical tab targetting and classes are pretty stock standard. We have dungeons, raids, and all the typical group activity dressing you find in most theme park MMOS.
End game is where the game shines in my opinion though. To describe it in a sentence.... Take the Gunship Battle from Icecrown Citadel, add a player pilot who controls said gunship and fly around landing on islands for loot while fighting off other player gunships to protect your bounty, all set on the backdrop of the 2001: A Space Odyssey LSD trip David takes at the end of the film.
And now the bad. As others have pointed out, playing for free is the epitome of p2w. It's a cash shop full of everything that makes this model bad. We have EXP boosters, gear and costumes with stats, mounts, pets, potions, end game currency, crafting supplies, anything you can think that's ever existed in a cash shop you'll find here.
Despite that, I'll be giving this a recommendation. The game itself is great. It's suprisingly polished considering it comes to us from Russia and if you're a fan of theme park MMOs it's definately one of the better ones. There's some interesting aesthetics here and while gameplay is a bit more old school, it's solid. The p2w cash shop will leave the worst taste in your mouth, but that's completely washed away if you subscribe.
TL:DR Good game if you subscribe. Good but pointless if you play for free.

The permadeath feature is essential to the constant tension and managing your encounters with different ships and dangers, to the final sector which you have to fight the Rebel mothership which evolves after you beat it in the first place—and not to mention the huge amount of replayability due to diverse randomly generated worlds and scenarios (and the recent updates add tons of additional content, from ship, story, to alien race).
However, as good as a game might be, there's always a room for improvement. Though this game features Cloud Sync, the game save file is NOT compatible cross-OSes (I played on Mac and Windows) which is quite a drawback for people who constantly use different OS on everyday basis. The achievement is saved in your save file too, which means it's not saved on Steam and again—it's not compatible with cross-OS save files. I really, really hope the dev will address this issue pretty soon.
However, those issues is quite minor compared to the fun you gonna have from this game. Sim-fans and Sci-Fi-fans who want a taste of their intergalactic adventure from the comfort of your home (with retro graphics), this game is a must buy.

Civilization V was my first experience with the game series.
I was a little overwhelmed, at first, but much of it is intuitive and there are great guides out there for any questions you may have.
I prefer the single player, to the multiplayer, because people frequently leave and it’s rare that you’ll finish a game with all the players you started with.
You can set the win parameters by time, as in whoever has the most points by turn ___ wins the game, but I usually remove that type of win as it’s easy to points and win with little effort this way.  However, it’s a nice option if you have little time to play.
Otherwise, there are wins by; science, culture, diplomacy or domination.  There are also many difficulty levels to choose from, and countless parameters to choose from in order to set up your perfect game.  You can choose; map type, map size, map layout, number of city-states, number of civilizations, number and type of barbarians, auto selecting pieces, auto attacks, auto moves, map terrain, time period to start in etc… etc…
With so much customization, it would be impossible not to find a set-up you enjoy.
At the lower difficulties, the A.I. will make poor choices and a win is rather easy to achieve.  At the highest difficulty, the A.I. gets good at blocking your wins.  They also start with more advantages depending on how high you set the difficulty.  There is a challenge level here for anyone.  It could be that veterans of the series, who are good at memorizing patters, could find a way to exploit the A.I. but my guess is that this is rare, and not, what the average player is looking for.
As a newcomer, I experienced the game as a multi-layer chess match, yet far less dry.
There is great ambiance and music and the music changes for each civilization and for each city-state.  You also get to meet and see the pictures of the leaders you are playing against, as well as see their expressions change from friendly to guarded to warlike, depending on your relationships.  You will hear the music created in your civilization, see the art, and get a quotation for any writing works.
One thing to note is that games can take a long time if you start at the beginning of time. At the start, my games would take several days, usually ending after 12 hours.  Even after hundreds of hours of playtime my games can take up to 6 hours.  You don’t have to play it all at once, of course, there are both auto saves and manual saves to continue games.
The only con I found is that the mid-game can be slow, and at high difficulty, you can find yourself without a way to a win midway after taking much time to set up.
Regardless, I absolutely love this game.

Braid is a time-altering side-scrolling platformer.
In a story that seems to mirror that of the Mario series (find a princess), but there's more at work than just that, if you carefully read and think through the story blobs told when you walk over books. Personally, this wasn't really to my tastes.
The gameplay in this game is, in my opinion, a much more important aspect than the story, Given that it's a side-scrolling platformer. The aim is not to finish the level quickly, but to get all of the puzzle pieces. The puzzles to do so revolve around the use of time-altering powers. Slowing Time, reversing it etc. And provide some nice tricky challenges and a good feeling of success when you complete them. But you will inevitably do so, as the game doesn't take an extremely long time to complete.
This game can be controlled via. Either the keyboard or a controller. I tried using both and they both work well.
The graphic stylings of this game are very nice. The art gives a sort of "painted" look to the game, and changes as you utilize time travel powers. Despite it being a "painted" look, do not think that it will be static sprites. The game looks and feels very fluid.
The graphic setting themselves are set on-launch, and cannot be changed in-game. A tad annoying, but once you figure out the best settings for you, you won't need to worry about it.
The music is very intriguing. As you utilise time travel powers, the music changes accordingly. Be it moving in reverse, or even in-step with your movement.
As I previously mentioned, this game doesn't take  a very long time to just run through each level. Finding every puzzle piece and assembling them takes a bit longer. If you do want to speed-run it, once you complete the game you can select this option from the main menu, which adds an extra level of difficulty.
This is a well polished game, and given all the bugs that could occur with the "time-travel" mechanic, it had no bugs that I could see.
Overall this is a great game to play if you're a fan of side-scrollers, or puzzle games that involve a time travel aspect, which I feel is somewhat hard to come by in a well-made manner.

Shank is the first game in the Shank franchise by Klei Entertainment, the wonderful people behind Mark of the Ninja. Shank and its sister sequel Shank 2 were developed before Mark of the Ninja and does not focus on straight stealth like Mark of the Ninja did, but full on action with the same art style and same bloody action
The story basically shows us a guy named Shank who was tasked in killing his wife but was followed by some other gang members of Cesar where they kill his wife and leave him left for dead, this storyline made me say that it is something roughly around Quentin Tarantino's Kill Bill volumes (which I highly recommend watching!)
The game is exteremly short, homing in at around 3 hours. But it does have its good and bad sides. Bad, because it is extremly short but good because it does get repetitive after a while. Shank 2 apparently suffers with the same length problems homing in at around 4 hours long (checked via
, thankfully Shank does offer a New Game+ mode as well as a multiplayer campaign... but sadly, I don't have any friends to try it out :(
The graphics are beautiful and made me remember playing Mark of the Ninja (I played Mark of the Ninja before Shank) as well as Disney cartoons, only Disney's cartoons are less bloody than Shank is. The animations are also really good, from the sword play to the gun fighting
The controls are very annoying on PC and it shows that Shank was originally developed for Xbox and then horribly ported onto the PC, it is impossible to play it on a keyboard, so much so that I had to plug in my controller to play it properly, and if you do happen to have a controller, I highly recommend playing with it as soon as you start. No wonder the game highly recommends playing with a controller when you boot up the game, it wasn't joking...
The music and sound effects, are okay but nothing memorable
You will die, a lot, thankfully there is a fair checkpoint system in the game. The voice acting was okay but nothing special, it does suffer like Mark of the Ninja's voice acting, some good, some bad...
I had fun playing Shank, even though it did have its fair share of problems here and there, but on the whole, it was a really good action game. Hopefully, its sequel would have ironed out most of the problems Shank had... hopefully...
Additional civilizations, voiced-acted campaigns about real historical events, defiantly worth a buy.

I have mixed feelings about this one.
I did not even care for the plot. 1stly it seems, like, you need to know what happened in previous games, but either way it seems... Well, a bit over the top and ridicolous to me. So I started skipping very soon. But, let's be honest, when did fighting games had an actually good plot? I do not remember such.
Graphically it's ok, even thouhg it's PS3 port, rather than PS4 from what I understand. Although, to be honest, in terms of looks, I like only Mila and Tina. They seem most "real" to me, despite Tina having bigger boobs, than what she would have had IRL. Others seem too plastic and dumb-faced, IMHO. Generalizing a bit, maybe, but still. I like Mila and Tina as characters, too. Well, again, they seem more "alive" and "down to earth" somehow compared to others.
Music seems good, which is also important to a fighting game. Maybe not the best OST, I could think of, but my ears does not bleed and some of the tracks do really suit the mood of the fights.
Now... For the most important thing: gameplay. Well... As usual I started with playing tutorial. I know, that most fightings have same basics, but tutorials can give hints on some more complex technics. I exited tutorial on the last part of Critical Burst or something. The one where you press Punch and Kick simultaniously. The one where you need to "follow up the Critical Burst". I thought I had to do the same thing as in previous tutorial, where I do Critical Burst, than a combo, than Critical Burst again, but... Either it did not register or something entrely else was meant. EIther way, even up to this point, Iive been noticing some issues with registering directional keys when they are required to be input inbetween punches\kicks. For example when you press Punch, Punch, Right, Punch it's oftren registers as Punch, Punch, Punch, Right. I'm using XBOX ONE controller and.. This frustrates me. Even stranger, that if I try to recreate this without touching the opponent it gets recareated.. Most of the time, but not always. Like 75% of the times it's done as expected. While with opponent odds are reversed.
But ok. That may be a rage quit. I checked the following tutorials simply by names and there seem to be some more advanced technics in there. Instead of trying those, though, I decided to start the story mode and return to tutorial, if I feel AI too strong to handle withouth finishing it. Well... Button mashing. Maybe not exactly, but it works. I mean in Mortal Kombat, for example, you needed to do complex combos and use skills to finish AI opponents. Here - just punch and kick randomly, while using directions to switch High\Mid\Low attacks to break through guard. That's it. Drive opponent into the corner and just use quick jabs and uppercauts (when opponent is down). That is it. Maybe it will become harder closer to the end, but so far difficulty seems to rise up mainly because the new opponent has different body type and you need to get used to his\her animations.
But suprisingly it felt... Fine. The kind of fine, that you can get from DMC games, if you just mash the buttons. You still get through, not artistically enough, but you disable your brain for a moment and just let it out. It does give some satisfaction. Primal one, very simplistic, but still - satisfaction. And again, there are more advanced moves in there, that are quite hard to master, so you can up your own game.
So, I will mark it as recommended. It is a quick fix, just to blow some steam off and watch some jigglies. After all animation is pretty good (although boobs seem to jiggle too much even with "natural" settings. And characters do have different body types, seem to have different speed and thus do actually feel a bit different when playing them.
But, my advise: wait for a discount. Like 50% or more. And do not bother with those costume packs, which cost evenmore than the game itself. If you have that much money to waste - better give it to me ;)
