Allods Online is not really 'free' to play.
Oh I know, they offer that as an option, but the unfortunate fact is that this game can't be played without spending money, even on the f2p server. You will not be able to make it past lvl 20 unless you have a full group of friends playing with you, have a high level guildie running you through content, or you pay money to buy whatever those blue gems are called to buy incense to get your deity buff. It equals a 50% increase to damage and healing, and all content is scaled to where this buff is necessary. Even as a pure DPS class, you will notice around lvl 15 that enemies take 2-3 times longer to kill, and therein lies the draw. You NEED that buff, AND the Speck of Life consumables that trickle in from drops or that you can buy via the cash shop because they both increase DPS and survivability substantially.
Similarly, you need money to buy megaphones for global chat, to buy mount feed to raise a mount, to buy an item to let you raise your crafting ability past a certain point. Everything you want to do costs money. And don't let the 'can be bought on AH' fool you...the prices for even the simplest item are so astronomical it'd take you grinding for months at cap level to be able to buy them.
Allods is a fun game. I like the asthetics ( especially the Empire ) and the classes and skill trees are nice and robust, but the "f2p" server and greedy paygating are among the worst I have seen, and have been since this game first came out in the West ( I played then, too...even subbed a bit ). If you have no problem buying a subscription with third-party currency ( I refuse to ) to play on the 'fun' server, or don't mind a game that was designed to overlay a dollar sign over every in-game mechanic, then have at it.
However if you are looking for a real f2p MMORPG with optional cosmetics to spend money on, I'd look elsewhere.

I preordered this game, but I'm not upset. It's a good game series that I'd like to see come to PC. They've told us for over a month now that multiplayer wouldn't make it in on release. I'm fine with that. I'd rather have single player now than have them delay the whole game another month. I don't begrudge them for not having multiplayer working yet. I really don't mind them not wasting the effort to have keyboard support. Trying to play a 3d fighting game with a keyboard is like trying to play an fps with a controller. They told us about not having the soft engine. I looked up videos comparing the game with and without it; I couldn't tell the difference. The game still looks great. It's not just a port from the old console versions. They have a pretty decent graphics options menu for a first time port. It's right here:
It's not a bad port either. I have an i5 3570k, a gtx 970, and 16 gigs of ram. I can play on Max settings and never go below 60 fps. I can understand why some are upset. They are releasing the game among a sea of bad console ports. Many are very wary of any delayed or cut features. I'm saying it's not as bad as many would like to think it is. The only real loss is needing to wait for multiplayer. After not having access to a dead or alive game for a good 10 years, frankly I could use the practice before heading online.
That's not to say it's a perfect port, but it's not nearly as bad as everyone makes it out to be either. If you want to play Dead or Alive, this is by far the best version.

Seems to be a decent port. I have the PS4 version as well, graphics are a little different on both platforms. PS4 has a better skin shader and a few extra particle effects while the PC version has supperior anti aliasing and texture filtering.
The lack of online is an issue for people, I like the convenience of having quick access to it on my PC for practice however if  you don't own it on another platform with multiplayer it's certainly limits the playability until they patch it in later. I see people complaining about the lack of steam achievements, however the game does have it's own achievement system built in which people display them in multiplayer matches when they add them.
Performance wise I have no trouble, the game does depend on a single CPU core so it is only influenced by clock speed, in some cases i3s and older AMD chips will out perform i7s in a laptop. I can't get it to drop frames on a 3.6ghz AMD cpu, so I would imagine any intel core series over 3ghz is safe.
It's pretty easy on GPUs, I can easily run 4k with 4x SSAA on a single r290x gpu.
It's sort of difficult to review it as they have yet to release the multiplayer part. As is it's probably mainly interesting to existing players who want quick access to the game on PC, it does load a lot faster than the console version if you're switching around training modes and characters. It might have been a better idea to use early access for this game, I can see how people could accidently buy it assuming it has muliplayer running, however they were upfront about multiplayer being added later in the description.
***********
Updating review as multiplayer patch has been released.
Multiplayer does function to some degree however basic features from the PS3 and xbox 360 versions are missing.
The majority of content released for the game post release does not work with the PC version, no attempt was made to inform customers that if they purchased the PC version that they would miss out on upcomming content and functions.
DLC does not function the same way as the consoles, if you buy any DLC it will not be visible to people in multiplayer unless they bought the exact same DLC.
It's unclear if development will continue but at the moment the game is incomplete and not what any reasonable person would expect to get based on how it is advertised.

I guess I should mention that the music is awesome though.

REVIEW UPDATED 4/11/2016 to "Not Recommended" after the lack of real love from Tecmo on the PC version.
The fact that they have not figured out how to give us the new stages that the PS4 and XBox One have received makes me extremly sad.  Also, a good portion of the costumes that are released recently have battle damage options on console, and not on the PC.  Tecmo has had plenty of time to figure out how to give the PC DOA fans these features, but now I am certain that they devs do not care about giving us what they have delivered to the PS4 and Xbox One.
I really wish that my review could stay as it was.  I have kept the original review below:
========================  Below is the old review from when the game first launched =======================
I am extremely happy with this port of the DOA5 Last Round arcade game.  It is better than the arcade version, with the ability to run shadows at an incredible resolution.  Also, the 4x anti-aliasing makes the game actually look better than my PS4 version.
Of course, there are some missing features, such as the two extra stages and the over-the-top particle FX... but after playing a bit, I did not even notice they were gone.  Also, the SoftEngine stuff is missing, but to be honest, the difference is not even noticeable.
Another thing I want to point out is that I was able to play the game on my 3D TV as well with my 970gtx.  I was able to tune it up and make it look pretty amazing in 3D, and it was a lot of fun.  Game runs at a solid 60fps, even with 3D enabled at 1080p and 4x anti-alising with 4k shadows.  You can even set the game to run on a 4k TV at full native resolution, but unfortunately I do not have the TV to test it on.  Online will be coming in a few months as well, and I am looking forward to it.  I have not had a chance to try my Xbox360 fight sticks, but I have a good feeling they will work, since my XB360 pads work fine.
For the current $35 price tag, I definitely would recomend this game to anyone that enjoys fighting games.
My system is currently running Win7, Intel i5, 8 gigs of ram, and Geforce 970gtx.  One last thing I would like to mention is that load times seem almost non-existant when running off of my SSD currently.  I have not tried it on my normal HDD, but it may load pretty fast from them as well.
Happy gaming, everyone!

It's a great game and will keep you busy for some time, especially with co-op. Humor's well done, the actors are all superb and the way the devs made it a point to show how the simulation can occasionally "glitch" is a really nice touch.
Uuuuunfortunately there were some bugs that weren't only intentional, but were very annoying at best and required a restart of the game at worst:
- The dubstep gun (DLC) would continue to play music even after you stop firing it,
- A lot of the quests I did did not sync up with my co-op partner. Really, the only ones that did consistently were the story quests and the DLC
- some quests had to be restarted multiple times in order to trigger the cutscenes properly, and even failed outright because of this.
- there were multiple instances where me and my co-op partner were stuck in a loading loop, forcing one of us to disconnect from the game.
And the one to break the camel's back for me was that I was unable to complete the final main quest with my co-op partner; when doing the second free fall with the power armor, I glitch out, ragdoll, and die. This happened three times in a row, and after all the crap the both of us have had to put up with during our campaign I said screw it, the game is not worth finishing in single player or in co-op.
I could very possibly forgive all of this if this game was just released to the public in the last month and the devs said that they were working on a fix. But no, this game was released almost two years ago and the devs have done absolutely nothing to address these problems despite other players complaining about it to this very day. If it weren't for the fact that I spilled almost 30 hours into this game and my partner gifted me SRIV I would have asked for a refund.
If you want to get this game and fly solo, sure, go right ahead. But if you intend to get yourself and a friend a copy, don't bother, because there are plenty of other games out there that won't give you a massive headache when dealing with co-op, even if both computers have entirely different specs

Civilization V was my first experience with the game series.
I was a little overwhelmed, at first, but much of it is intuitive and there are great guides out there for any questions you may have.
I prefer the single player, to the multiplayer, because people frequently leave and it’s rare that you’ll finish a game with all the players you started with.
You can set the win parameters by time, as in whoever has the most points by turn ___ wins the game, but I usually remove that type of win as it’s easy to points and win with little effort this way.  However, it’s a nice option if you have little time to play.
Otherwise, there are wins by; science, culture, diplomacy or domination.  There are also many difficulty levels to choose from, and countless parameters to choose from in order to set up your perfect game.  You can choose; map type, map size, map layout, number of city-states, number of civilizations, number and type of barbarians, auto selecting pieces, auto attacks, auto moves, map terrain, time period to start in etc… etc…
With so much customization, it would be impossible not to find a set-up you enjoy.
At the lower difficulties, the A.I. will make poor choices and a win is rather easy to achieve.  At the highest difficulty, the A.I. gets good at blocking your wins.  They also start with more advantages depending on how high you set the difficulty.  There is a challenge level here for anyone.  It could be that veterans of the series, who are good at memorizing patters, could find a way to exploit the A.I. but my guess is that this is rare, and not, what the average player is looking for.
As a newcomer, I experienced the game as a multi-layer chess match, yet far less dry.
There is great ambiance and music and the music changes for each civilization and for each city-state.  You also get to meet and see the pictures of the leaders you are playing against, as well as see their expressions change from friendly to guarded to warlike, depending on your relationships.  You will hear the music created in your civilization, see the art, and get a quotation for any writing works.
One thing to note is that games can take a long time if you start at the beginning of time. At the start, my games would take several days, usually ending after 12 hours.  Even after hundreds of hours of playtime my games can take up to 6 hours.  You don’t have to play it all at once, of course, there are both auto saves and manual saves to continue games.
The only con I found is that the mid-game can be slow, and at high difficulty, you can find yourself without a way to a win midway after taking much time to set up.
Regardless, I absolutely love this game.

I picked up Metro 2033 Redux and Last Light Redux on the recent bundle sale. Being a veteran FPS player and pretty hardcore fan of Fallout 3 and S.T.A.L.K.E.R I jumped into Metro 2033 feet first by going in on the Ranger setting. (Something I strongly recommend for any 'serious' fps players)
It only took me 16 hours or so to beat it dispite going in on one of the harder difficulties but I liked it and got a good feel for the series as a whole, im looking forward to my playthrough of Last Light. But as I am writing a review for Metro 2033 Redux I'll cut to the chase and give some insight into the things I felt most notable be it a pro or con.
Cons: Clipping, enemies can run right through you and vice versa making it pretty difficult to melee Watchers or Nosalis - I even had human character I had snuck up on turn around clip through me so my sneak attack missed and shot me in the face for my trouble.  The save system runs on a Trigger and Timed method, meaning it can e brutally punishing I had to restart a couple of chapters because the timed save went off when I was nearly dead or choking to death from a lack of air filters. While STALKER was inspired by the same book Metro was based off of, Metro 2033 lacks the open world feel of STALKER and is pretty linear. All the children sound like russian versions of Gary Coleman, very creepy.
Pros: Does  the 'post apocalyptic world' very well, the story is interesting (if a bit hard to swallow at times). The VERY limited (on ranger at least) time that air filters last in toxic enviroments means you must resource manage between stealth and time factors, I snuck through a building stealthily killing every human enemy then choked on the roof for half a  hour before giving up and restarting the chapter.
The weapons are mostly very believable, cobled together from the remains of mundane items into deadly weapons and bullets are a reasonable form of currancy, even if the exchange rate on some of them is terrible. The monsters tend to be quite terrifying, especially the Watchers and dealing with multiples of them in waves can be quite troublesome (especially when they clip through you and scratch your back). Stealth kills and throwing knives are a lot of fun, later in the game I found myself using throwing knives against Watchers quite effectively and even stabbed a Flying Demon to death at a pivital moment in the story, cause I had no ammo, no throwing knives, nadda....was fun.
Final Verdict: Enjoyed myself, Recommended to anyone that likes FPS, survival horror, and post apocalyptic settings.

I recommend this game with some reservations. I commend the developer's brutal commitment to total realism that make this game an extremely tough experience. the intriguing game world, and attention to detail. The game truly does make you thankful for objects as trivial as a shirt or even a worn out shoe. That being said, the game is hard enough that sometimes it feels as if it is unfair. On many occasions I would sit down for a session and be having fun until a single dog or man with a gun kills me and ruins hours of progress. The permadeath system creates a feeling that you've wasted your time whenever you die from something you can't avoid. I feel as if a progression system, saved games, or a checkpoint, perhaps at the end of each day, could go a long way to combat these issues. If you are looking for a turely brutal survival experience with immense attention to detail, this may be the game for you, provided you are able to deal with some of my previously mentioned grievances. The game has a few major flaws but has enough redeeming qualities for me to give it a recommendation.

CoH 2 shares the same meta as the older CoH. It handles in a similar manner. For some reason, people find this to be a negative thing, which I don't really understand.
Either way, CoH 2 still has substantial changes which makes it's experience quite different from the previous title. Different capping system, territory arrangement ( you have much more strategic points now), population arrangement ( isn't linked to the amount of territory owned), Commanders, Realview mechanics ( Viewrange is affected by the unit's surroundings), etc etc. These things, small on their own, mage a big impact when bundled together.
Also, due to how maps are usually designed ( and defensive stuff Factions can get non-doctrinally) CoH 2 is much less campy than CoH. The lack of a faction like the Commonwealth helps to counter the campiness.
Another issue usually perceived: DLC's. People think that DLC's = Win. Well, let me tell you something. It isn't precisely like that. While it is true that some DLC's commanders are a relief in certain situations, they aren't going to win you a match. A player with "stock" commanders can still beat somebody with these add-on commanders. To be honest, there are basically six commanders which are really worth it, out of all the ones available. Soviet Industry Tactics, Tank Hunter Tactics, Mechanized Assault Doctrine, Elite Doctrine, Rifle Company, and Scavenge Doctrine. The rest are cool, but not really needed. Some of them are unique but mostly a hinderance in actual competitive matches ( I own every single available Soviet/Ost commander, and Scavenge, Rifle Company, and Elite Armor Doctrine. This is a sincere opinion of somebody who's shelled more money on DLC's than the games themselves).
Basically, if you're on a budget, go CoH 1. If you have money to burn ( not precisely get DLC's. They're not needed), get CoH 2. Both are awesome.

+Nice UI

I've been having huge fun with this game.
BFG: Armada is a tactical RTS that focuses on a limited number of units moving on a 2D plane that have a wide range of capabilities, weapon systems, active skills that you need to employ at the right time, strengths, weaknesses, maneuverability profiles, firing angles and so on.
Like the tabletop game, it uses age of sail combat doctrine as its foundation with many of the ships having their firepower concentrated for broadsides, though there’s obviously no wind and then there’s quite a few exceptions to that with prow mounted weapons, torpedoes, bombers and the like. Pushing this further, we’ve got 3D graphics, but it's a 2D plane where the ships move like ocean going vessels on just the X-Axis – the Y-Axis is not a gameplay consideration and is only interacted with from the perspective of viewing angles. your ships will level up and they can become quite individualized with specific crew improved, passive enhancements or active skills that can be quite decisive when used at the correct moment in battle. Even ships of the same class with the basic same armament can end up being very different from one another after a while depending on how you upgrade them.
The combat itself – which is really the foundation of the game – is something that I find quite satisfying and doctrine varies a lot based on the race you use. The base characteristics of the ships are very intricate with the idiosyncrasies of their assorted elements between hull strength, shields, weapon types, optimal ranges and weapon firing angles which comes to life during the combat. Ships are probably a bit more maneuverable than one might expect for capital ships, but they still labor through their turns and have the inertia and momentum that’s requisite to give them weight and separate the gameplay from a dogfight.
The gameplay would be totally overwhelming for many players with the need to micromanage things if you had to play at full speed all the time, so thankfully there’s a tactical slowdown which is not the same as a tactical pause, but its pretty close. This is also available in multiplayer at the time of this writing and its probably true that this stutter-stop-start aspect detracts from the flow, but the game would be really frustrating for the majority of players without it.
There’s three main components to the game, which is campaign, multiplayer skirmish and singleplayer skirmish. The campaign hasn’t been finished as of now, but it seems really promising from the teaser missions that I’ve tried and is structurally very similar to the Dawn of War 2 campaign. There’s a stratmap-lite narrative sort of component and then really nice atmospheric cut scenes as well as good over the top 40K voice acting for the Imperials, though I have no idea how big it will be.
The other two elements – multi and solo skirmish - are mirrors of one another and in fact have something of a campaign feel to them compared with one off skirmishes; the reason for this is that your fleet is persistent between missions and develops in a sort of RPG level up type manner.
You start small with a couple of light cruisers and access to a pool of replaceable escorts and then go off on missions for fame and glory. Your line ships will level up individually while each class of escort can be improved (ie. you could increases the hull armor of all your Cobra class destroyers and it doesn’t matter if one is destroyed because any Cobra you deploy will get the upgrade). Your Admiral will also level up which opens up more ship slots on your roster, both for extras of ship classes you already have as well as unlocking larger vessels.
Edit - April 29th, 2016: The developers have put out a Roadmap for future development which looks absolutely fantastic.
I think if you’re open to tactical spaceship combat with an emphasis on micromanaging, you’ll have a lot of fun with this one. The replay value is looking very good with lots of variety between the factions and specific doctrines within factions.

Ok, real review time.
Issues this game has; Lack of Co-op, Simplistic AI, Multiplayer is iffy, and unintuitive.
The lack of co-op is a big hinderance on this otherwise solid game. Custome game lobbys exist where you can play vs AI, but without being able to add friends, its a rather limited feature.
The AI is quite simplistic. They use their ships skills, take into account range and some basic tactics, but ultimately they just run at you. Due to that, you can easily cheese the AI and find an win.
Multiplayer is where the game seems to be aimed at for its lifespan. However, any sort of matchmaking system they use is rather unreliable. You dont know if you will get a first time player, or a person whos broken their fleet down to a science. That aside, there are a lot of reports of lag.
The game is overall unintiutive. You have to learn how to play the game, how to use the UI and just what all the little things on your ships do. Because of how the games combat system works, you dont really know a lot of whats happening. Is the next volly going to do damage? How much will it do to this target? When is its next volly? Those are all questions that are manditory, but the games system make damage a chance and you need to keep track of attacks mentally to know when the next attack will hit.
But to get more in depth about that, I'll need to get into the positives of this game. So, here they are.
High learning curve, quick games, satisfying campaign and a good representation of Warhammer.
The high learnin curve is one of the main aspects thats good, but also bad. Going into the game from a non-Warhammer 40k fanboy, theres lots of weapons ships and names of skills and effects that will need to be learned. This can be daunting at times. However this same depth also ensures that the better you know the game, the better you will be able to perform.
Matches typically last between the 5-10 min mark making its widly available. Get home from work/school, play a game or two, then get on with your life. Or you can sink in hours at a time and fully enjoy quickly learning the ins and outs of various ships and fleets.
The campaign is satisfying. Wont go into details about it for spoilers, but it clearly wasnt a patched together story.
It is the 40k universe (not really, but essentially is) and you do feel it. From the races to the "Factions" that you can have your ships represent, you can clearly see the the iconic visuals of the 40k universe. Names and skills are also very 40k, like the auto naming of your ships (that can be changed) that give them a very uniquely sounding 40k name.

Let me start with saying that the PC version of DOA 5: Last Round is indeed inferior to it's console counterparts. Yes, the extra stages are missing, and the keyboard layout is horrible.
However, you do not buy a fighting game to play it with a keyboard. It is a genre that is best played with a controller or arcade stick, and is, as the genre describes, about the fighting. Just like the other versions, is the fighting fluent and flawless, and a lot of fun. The game is far from lacking in the fighting department. I also have to mention that the game works fine when working with a controller. And despite it using the PS3 engine, the game looks very good to me.
The fighting maps are appealing, work like they're supposed to and bring the element of environment interaction to Dead or Alive. It´s a lot of fun juggling your opponent, only to have his face smacked into the ground by a giant Buddha statue. This is only available to the Solo fighting however, which is a real shame. Combo's can be pulled off, and chaining attacks is so much fun! Unlike a seeming majority of people, I think DOA 5: last round is still a fine fighting game, even on PC. Although it is inferior to it's console counterparts.
Now with the plusses out of the way, it´s time for the negatives. Oh boy, this port has a lot of them.
A minor flaw, since fighting games never had a solid one, but the game doesn't have a great story. You can breeze through it in a few hours, and it's not exactly an appealing one. The story simply feels like a way for them to show off what the engine can do. You go from one random location to another. Very poorly done.
First of all, now more then a year after release, the game still doesn´t have proper multiplayer. The only thing provided is a very laggy, poor ranked system, that not a lot of people use. DEFINITELY DON´T BUY THIS GAME IF YOU WANT TO PLAY ONLINE WITH FRIENDS. As mentioned before, the only thing available here is a poor ranked system, that is laggy and not fluent in the slightest. Pulling off combo´s has been proven to be impossible for me online and I have never been able to play the game with friends. There is no invitation or friendly match option. The only thing you can do, is qeue for ranked, stay in the same region, and pray to the gods that you qeue up against one another. 90% of the time this won't be the case however. Absolutely awful.
Aside from the multiplayer, this game never feels complete with the amount of DLC that is being released. The DLC is, with the exception of 1 character, only a collection of costumes, or a few scenes you can visit. The price they are charging for it, is outragious. DO NOT BUY IT. You will regret it.
If you only have access to a PC, I can't say I would recommend buying this game. You can't buy it for the online functionality, and the DLC is impossibly expensive and worthless, unless you want a quick fap. This game is a lot of fun playing on the couch however. If you have just a PC, I would say it's worth getting to play against friends at home. Definitely with the possibilities of Steam link nowadays, you can have a lot of fun playing the game around the house or on a big screen. I can say the same for people that are a fan of fighter games, and would like a challenge in the AI. The AI can be quite cheap however.
However, if you also have a PS3, PS4, Xbox One or Xbox 360, buy the game for your console. This game is not worth getting on PC if you can get a superior version.
TL;DR:
Pros:
---------
- Fighting mechanics
- Game is (in core) the same fighting game as it's console counterparts
- A solid fighter (single player or ON COUCH multiplayer) for PC
- Bouncing boobies (and jigglephysics)
- Still one of the graphically appealing fighters
Cons:
----------
- No extra stages
- Not a great story
- Graphically not as good as it's console counterparts
- Keyboard mapping is AWFUL
- Terrible online multiplayer (read barely any)
- No way to play with friends online
- DLC WAY TOO EXPENSIVE
- Barely any steam support
- A very strong NO MOD Policy on PC?! SERIOUSLY?!
It is a shame that there is barely any steam support on the game, and the DLC prices MUST be adressed. I'm not paying 50+ euro's for just a couple of costumes, no matter how many there are in a pack. Even though this is the same story on it's console counterparts, TECMO MUST ADJUST THE DLC PRICES.
The controls for keyboards play fine for me, although a possibility for changing your controls must be implemented. If you want a solid fighter for PC (whatever your reason is), the base game would do fine. I recommend the game for anyone not able to play on consoles, but play the base game only. there is no need paying an additional 100+ euro's to unlock just a couple more costumes. Either they cut their packs into smaller DLC packs for individual characters (for a fraction of the price), or the DLC is not worth getting.
Final verdict:
-----------
4/10

6/10: Brutal light-speed chase through unforgiving space. Outrun the rebel pursuers while optimizing your ship, but one unlucky decision, arrival, or purchase can spell your doom.
At the outset, FTL feels like it will be a cosmic journey. The ship and the crew setting out to race back to their allies and defeat the rebellion, making deals with pirates or saving the distressed as the case may warrant. Trying to mind the line between getting away and finding enough resources to stay alive and moving provides a great tension along with a challenge. All of this, presented as little more than the layout of a spaceship amid a galactic background.
Even so, this game can be unforgiving, and you will die countless times even as you switch between ships and builds. Arriving someplace new can find you in an asteroid field, by a flaring sun, or straight up boarded and fighting off an enemy ship all at once. The money spent on repairing and fueling the ship always threatens to leave you without the funds necessary for crucial systems, all of which must be mostly upgraded by the time you reach the last part.
While the challenge involved makes victory that much more satisfying, it is nigh impossible to fully prepare for the variety of problems that await even with more than 4 crew members and a reliable build. It's all too likely that you will just throw your hands up in the air and curse to the skies. All before restarting and giving it another go, because this time you'll be ready for it. Or die again. Probably.

Let me start by saying that I've played Allods since day one open beta, for around 4 years (over 12k hours of actual play time). I've stopped playing the game for nearly 2 years now, but I do still lurk the forum and occasionaly log in the game to check what's new, In case the game had a 180º turn, as well to keep in touch with some good old friends (the very few that haven't quit by now).
I was for the most part an hardcore player, purely free to play, part of some of the best endgame guilds (Invalid, 3rdFaction, WarSong, MInc).
With that being said, my review is from a vet endgamer point of view, that went through multiple updates, server merges and even publisher changes (gpotato/webzen, Mycom).
Allods as a game, is a great mmo, it has plenty of content to keep your enternained, leveling was never so easy (those who were around during gipat update as well the lv47 24k gold cap, can relate). There's a very good amount of zones with different aspects to it, and the endgame can be fun if you play for fun and not to solely outperform the guy next to you in hope that your epeen will stretch a tiny bit more.
However the Allods curse is the "free-to-play" model it has. It's the worst piece of crap you can possibly find in a game. The company is utterly greedy and will make sure the cow is milked to its bones.
So unless you have very deep pockets or are willing to spend ridiculous amounts of time farming in circles, just to stay competitive, this game is not for you and you should avoid it at all cost.
The fact there is a currency exchanger where you can trade ingame currency (Gold) for Item Shop currency (Crystals) becomes meaningless when you take a look at the racio. All the best and must have items comes exclusively from gambling. Radiant Strongbox sales EVERY SINGLE WEEK, just to make sure you don't stack too much gold, and spend money to stay afloat. You can technically buy it from other players with gold, but the prices are off limits to most people.
And when I say "must have", you realy must have those items or you won't stand a chance in PvP and PvE. I'm talking about scrolls that give extra talent points, stat points, rubies, unlimited build reset and stats reset, combat mounts, trinkets and many more.
Even worse, there's different qualities on most those items (green, blue, purple, orange, fable) and they stack up, giving those that have all these Pay-To-Win items, a ridiculous edge over Free-To-Play, new comers and occasional buyers.
And don't even make me talk about runes. Basically, there's six of them, three offensive, three defensive, it goes from lv1 to 13. To make a lv2 runes you need two lv1, to make a lv3 you need two lv2, and so on... Bare minimum to stay competitive shoud be full lv9 by now.
Then there's patronage that increase your damage a lot and costs too much as well. It's just too many things you need to spend your money or huge amount of time on, and the worse part, they keep adding more with each new update.
The community in the game keeps getting smaller and smaller, after a month you'll already know who is who. I won't say it's a toxic community, but I have to say it's demanding and there's barely any room for mistakes.
The truth is, Allods always had a lot of potencial, but due to poor management, greediness above all, it never went past the hopes and dreams we, the players, had.
If you're still brave enought to waste your time in this mess, you better make a bank loan and keep in mind you're going up against many players that literally spent so much money by now, that they could have bought a new car or two.

I'm a bit of a graphics snob.
The way I see it, there's a reason why we're updating our computers every few years, there's a reason why developers are pushing the boundaries of what the technology can do ..
.. because the perfect game - well, it's visually beautiful, engrossing, realistic, immersive.
SO
FTL .. it's not the perfect game.
I tried it on a whim, and I really don't regret it.  If you park the retro graphics to one side, it's an interesting and addictive game.  Just like plugging away your money in an old school arcade when you're a teenager, every time you lose at this game, it just makes you want to try it again.
As you command your starship, you are -not- Jean Luc Picard, sitting back, tenting your fingers as you study the situation with a calm mind behind a chrome dome.  You're not even Captain Kirk, banging every female alien you can find, contracting god knows how many interstellar social diseases.  You're on the run from a massive enemy fleet, and there's every likelihood you will die.
(probably in an inglorious way)
Even so, it's a good, fun game.  When you get everything right - a good crew, balanced systems, good strategy, you really feel like you're on a space adventure.  The random situations and variety of ships you can earn really make the replay value on FTL very strong.
So .. even from a graphics snob ... this game is *good*.

Well... This game is basically a modified Russian-themed World of Warcraft with auto-run features.... Everything will feel familiar if you are a World of Warcraft player. You will find many similarities like Humans(Kanians + Xadaganians), Elves (Also known as Elves), Orcs (Just Orcs), Undead (Arisen), Werewolves(Priden) and the Gnome replacement (Gibberlings who are Tiny Furries). However, the problem is just that. What's so special about this game? What does it have that World of Warcraft doesn't? Also, it's Pay To Win, it's 100 Euros for 10,700 Crystals (cash currency). With Crystals, you can buy Mounts, Buffs and even remove Curses on powerful weapons. If you don't have Crystal, it sucks to play this game.
1. Auto-quest
My favourite part of the game. Don't know where to go? Press auto-quest, it will bring you to wherever you need to be. The only thing that World of Warcraft doesn't have.
2. The Beginning (Arisen)
2 Guild Ships duking it out while a giant Astral watches. So cool.
3. Gibberlings
You control them as a group of 3. Very unique.
4. The Beginning (Gibberlings)
June Ruins with the floating bubble. The flying ships which resembled the transport boat system in World of Warcraft's Booty Bay.
5. Crafting Mini-Luck Game
There's a tiny mini-game if you try to craft items. It's purely luck based.
6. Quest Markers
They have little markers on the mini-map that highlight other quests in the area. If you scroll over them, it tells you what you need to collect or do. This is very useful.
7. Less Aggro Range
Majority of creatures are Neutral (Yellow Circle). This makes it less annoying to run around and is more thematic.
1. Bad Story
It's not a gripping story, it's just not the way the Warcraft lore unfolded.
2. Level Limiters
If you're 3 Levels below a boss monster's, you're dead. There is no way to deal it any damage. Gain 1 more Level and suddenly he's feeling the pinch.
3. Fetch Quest
Haven't most MMORPGs understood this by now? You shouldn't need to make a return journey to turn in the quest. Just comms it in. There are no generic speed-up spells so you'll have to play a tedious game. If you forget to collect a quest from a NPC, get ready to run back and forth.
4. Pay To Win
You can actually pay money to get stronger in this game. Horrible business model. 100 Euros for 10,700 Crystals (cash currency).
5. The Game Engine Technology
For a "$12 million" game, this game has really old technology. It's like time stood still and locked it in the World of Warcraft engine, which FYI is over 10 years old.
6. Lamp Post Issue
All NPCs and creeps just stand and patrol the same area. There is nothing special about them. They don't "live or breathe".
7. No Flying or Fishing
All the little things are missing. There is swimming though I've yet to experience it.
8. Grinding
The max level in this game is 70 but it takes a long time just to grind past level 10.
9. Professions
Similar to World of Warcraft, 1 profession at any time. You can get a max of 2 if you get a certificate. Tailoring, Leatherworking, Blacksmithing, Disassembling, Alchemy, Mining, etc
10. Classes
It's really similar to World of Warcraft. There are 10 main types with differnt names for different races but they are all the same.
11. AI is pretty silly
You attack a Mutineer ship to get 3 treasures. They are all aggressive. Don't worry, you just need to attack 3 or 4 Mutineers and the rest won't take heed of who you are.
12. Talent Point System
You gain Talent Points to put into your Talent Tree at a really slow rate of 1 Talent Point per level. However, you need a cumulative amount of points for each additional skill level. E.g. Level 1 Bee Swarm needs 1 TP to upgrade, Level 2 needs 2 TP to upgrade, Level 3 needs 3 TP and so on and so forth.
Man, that finale willpiss you off. But once you do finish it, you will ejaculatex1000.

What can I say about dark and light? I wish there was a middle thumb button but ill just give it thumbs up.
Some people compare it to Ark, because to a certain extent some of the systems of the same. But there are some key differences too that no one likes to mention.
No more engrams, you simply gain whatever type of recipe you get for leveling up certain specialization trees. A cool concept that needs polishing.
Factions and races. Ark has never had this and this concept is one that is a great addition, is it polished? No, its EA so get over it. Based on the faction you choose you get that race, either dwarf, human or elf. Not a bad system in my opinion.
Character customization is ultimately so much better than ark was, since basically every male or female fundamentally looked the same but now with this you can have keen differences, between race, stature, build, structure. Theres alot there for early access.
Now I've only played the first 10 or so levels and decided the game wasn't for me but I don't believe it is truely a garbage game. It just needs polish. And if you're looking at these reviews looking for a comparison between this and citadel they are two findamentally different games so comparing the two would be like apples and oranges. Citadel being cheaper and not having "survival" type of gameplay, that might be for you. Dark and light having a better taming system, and fleshed out skill trees etc. that might be for you.
I found that Dark and light was too slow early on for me is all, within the first 10 or so levels it feels like it doesn't bring anything too different to character depth until the later or much later levels, and while that may be fine for some, I've played survival games, I'd like to see my first damage spell or something given to me at level 2-5 just for something in terms of different variation in combat, not only learn my campfire schematic.

Tropico 4 is a good and bad game at the same time. It's really hard to rate, because it's a very enjoyable experience yet it manages to be very lacking in some aspects which are basically a norm in other 'tycoon' games.
The game's visuals are great, even 6 years after release. The texture quality of buildings/rocks/vegetation is sweet. Can't lay a finger on a bad thing about the sound either.
But when it comes to the mechanics and gameplay it feels like game is either not giving you enough information to properly manage your city or everything is cramped inside unintuitive menu. Sure, I can build plantations, destilleries, cigar factories farms, fishing huts but nowhere in the game can I find information on how much of each resource I currently have. I have no numbers on how much sugar I'm producing and how much is being taken to produce alcohol, why the factory is not doing well, how much food is currently being consumed etc. I can't see which part of the production chain is lacking. This is a huge downside for me, after games like Anno. There are some clues in the 'book' but it's a simple information that im currently producing enough food, welp.
You can produce power plants and yet there are no charts about consumption, production. You have to manually click on the power plant/wind turbine to see how's it doing. It starts getting obnoxious after you reach populations of 500+ where there is no time for such micromanagement.
The game allows you to allign your island towards some political views, yet there's no visual differences and anything special about doing any of the paths. Your island looks the game and people mostly behave the same whether you're full time commie or a capitalist. I wish I could distinguish communists/religious people/nationalists, not only read that they belong to these groups after clicking on them.
Yeah, each citizen has personality, political views, belongs to some group yet I can't see some more important information - how many people are unemployed, how many people work at selected education levels. I have no idea why selected citizen left his job as a doctor, priest.
Simple tutorials/information displayed when hovering over on option or more advanced charts could solve most of these problems. Yet, this is one of a kind game, and it's generally enjoyable (sometimes too easy) so I'd give it a go if you can get it at decent price.

The other day I played one of Capcom's "Dead Rising" games -  I forget which one since they are all sort of the same anyway. I generally enjoyed the large open world and huge hordes of zombies, but disliked the zanier aspects of the characters and plots. I wonder if Techland - the developers of Dying Light - felt the same way because their game is essentially a Dead Rising clone with the wackiness stripped away. In some ways this made the game more enjoyable, but at the same time Dying Light felt characterless and flat in comparison.
Functionally, the game is quite impressive. It has a huge open world - made even larger with the addition of "The Following" DLC pack. Given their size, I was rather astonished by how fast the maps loaded, even on a slow mechanical hard-drive. The frame-rate was silky smooth, even with settings maxed and on an older GPU. The parkour-focused combat is slick and easy to learn, and the move-set is impressive; I was very quickly doing slide-kicks, grapples and vaults as I hacked my way through the undead horde. The actual gameplay-loop was less exciting; Dying Light takes its cue from Ubisoft's open-world games, littering the landscape with side-missions and collectibles that aren't individually very exciting but at least offered a reason to free-roam the game's giant map ("The Following" DLC at least added a useful alternative in the form of driving challenges with the addition of a car).
A major downside of the game for me were the weapons; variety was largely mechanical in nature, and it utilized a common/rare/unique color-coding system similar to Diablo (or Techland's own "Dead Island" games). Technically, the game features thousands of weapons but in actual gameplay it pretty much boils down to "blade", "hammer", "pistol/rifle" and "shotgun", with the major differentiation being how much damage was inflicted. More concernedly, weapons only have limited durability, and break after too much usage. Although I understand the idea behind this mechanic - having your best sword break during a fight can be a terrifying adrenalin rush - in practice the weapons broke far too quickly, making the constant scrounging for new gear a dull grind which artificially extended the game's length.
As much as I enjoyed the melee combat, I was less enthralled with the first-person parkour; the perspectives never quite looked right, and never felt as fluid and natural as, say, the third-person platforming of the Assassin's Creed series. It didn't help that climbing down was far more difficult than going up, and too often I fell to my death instead of lowering myself down level by level. While games like Mirror's Edge and Dying Light show that first-person parkour is possible, it still isn't my preferred method of in-game acrobatics. The game's strengths are its exploration and combat, not its platforming. Unfortunately, certain missions of the game stress the latter, to their detriment. The final mission is especially terrible in this (and it doesn't help that the end-boss is defeated in a series of dull - and completely unexpected, since its a mechanic that isn't used anywhere else in the game - quick-time events).
When it stuck to its strengths the game was largely enjoyable, but it was not a very memorable experience. While it is a striking improvement over its predecessor - the Dead Island Franchise - it still has a number of shaky bits. Hopefully the developers will learn as much from Dying Light and their next game will actually be something I can whole-heartedly recommend, but its not something I can honestly do with this one.

Although I have less than 5 hours logged in this game, I can already tell it is a work of art and should be revered.
The artwork is beautiful, and really adds an enchanting quality to the game. The theme fits very well with the other aspects of the game. It is a game about making mistakes, and really makes you think, not only about puzzles, but about life, consequences, and regret. It is always said that mistakes are essential for learning, but this ideology never seems to be upheld. Instead we are punished and berated. This game brings a large question. What if none of that happened? Your goal is to progress through the stages, collecting puzzle pieces. It would be like any other platformer, except for the fact that pressing shift causes the entire game to run in reverse, effectively undoing any mistakes you made, so you can learn from them instead of being punished for them. Throughout the stages, the game shows several other time-twisting game mechanics that really make you think. It is fantastic.
Now, although this is the essence of a great game in my mind, I know others may not like it. That being said, if you don't like thinking, questioning, or solving mind-bending puzzles, Braid is not for you. This game requires serious thought. I have sat at my screen for at least half an hour trying to figure out a particularly tough one multiple times. I say again - This is not for those who want to relax their mind. I requires strenuous thought on many occasions.
Now, games that expand the mind are my favorite kind, so this is a big yes in my book. I would recommend this game to anyone I meet. I can think of nothing wrong with it at all. It seems to be the perfect puzzle game. 10/10.

I picked up Metro 2033 Redux and Last Light Redux on the recent bundle sale. Being a veteran FPS player and pretty hardcore fan of Fallout 3 and S.T.A.L.K.E.R I jumped into Metro 2033 feet first by going in on the Ranger setting. (Something I strongly recommend for any 'serious' fps players)
It only took me 16 hours or so to beat it dispite going in on one of the harder difficulties but I liked it and got a good feel for the series as a whole, im looking forward to my playthrough of Last Light. But as I am writing a review for Metro 2033 Redux I'll cut to the chase and give some insight into the things I felt most notable be it a pro or con.
Cons: Clipping, enemies can run right through you and vice versa making it pretty difficult to melee Watchers or Nosalis - I even had human character I had snuck up on turn around clip through me so my sneak attack missed and shot me in the face for my trouble.  The save system runs on a Trigger and Timed method, meaning it can e brutally punishing I had to restart a couple of chapters because the timed save went off when I was nearly dead or choking to death from a lack of air filters. While STALKER was inspired by the same book Metro was based off of, Metro 2033 lacks the open world feel of STALKER and is pretty linear. All the children sound like russian versions of Gary Coleman, very creepy.
Pros: Does  the 'post apocalyptic world' very well, the story is interesting (if a bit hard to swallow at times). The VERY limited (on ranger at least) time that air filters last in toxic enviroments means you must resource manage between stealth and time factors, I snuck through a building stealthily killing every human enemy then choked on the roof for half a  hour before giving up and restarting the chapter.
The weapons are mostly very believable, cobled together from the remains of mundane items into deadly weapons and bullets are a reasonable form of currancy, even if the exchange rate on some of them is terrible. The monsters tend to be quite terrifying, especially the Watchers and dealing with multiples of them in waves can be quite troublesome (especially when they clip through you and scratch your back). Stealth kills and throwing knives are a lot of fun, later in the game I found myself using throwing knives against Watchers quite effectively and even stabbed a Flying Demon to death at a pivital moment in the story, cause I had no ammo, no throwing knives, nadda....was fun.
Final Verdict: Enjoyed myself, Recommended to anyone that likes FPS, survival horror, and post apocalyptic settings.

I think there are only slightly more redeeming qualities to this game than there are bad ones, so this is only a "recommend" because "meh" wasn't really a choice.
The game is very tedious. One thing that survival games tend to forget is that survival is a very tedious business, and they compress the timeframe a bit for emphasis of that particular aspect, but that just tends to make it even more tedious. This tends to detract from exploration or story-telling: you can't care about those things if the only priority you can possibly have is just making it to the next day. NEO Scavenger seems like it has a very rich and detailed story behind it and a setting that has the potential to be deeply immersive, but none of that matters if you simply die within the first week most of the time.
It doesn't help that the game is somewhat obtuse about a lot of extremely important mechanics, such as the combat system, or health, or that drinking unfiltered water pretty much guarantees that you get cholera or are poisoned. Sure, that last one is pretty obvious in retrospect, but what that implies is that a decent portion of the time you have is going to be spent sterilizing all your water, and hoarding water, etc., which is just about as fun as it sounds.
Item durability is also a terrible system. I don't think it was ever fun or strictly necessary in any game in which it was ever implemented. Yes, on some level, it intuitively makes sense, but it's overly simplistic in its implementation and just keeps forcing you to obsessively hunt for more junk.
The skill system is interesting at face value, but your choices are limited from the start, and since they're fixed this drastically limits the options available to you (particularly at the start of the game) and you are always made painfully aware of it whenever you craft or interact with anything. It doesn't help that some are incredibly useless or situational.
Permadeath is a good thing, I guess, but it also discourages the player from taking risks. There is always an element of risk in everything, but if you're dealing with an unknown and don't know how to assess the risk, you will eventually come to the conclusion that chancing it isn't worth it in most situations, which, again, runs counter to the player's natural drive for exploration. If you're gonna have permadeath in a game, that's great and all, but you gotta throw the player a bit more of a bone here.
I think this game certainly has potential so I'm not gonna trash it utterly. But it is a very very lukewarm recommend at best, at least for now.

EXPLAINING MYSELF
Before I start my review,I will say that I played the first Company of Heroes with all its expansion packs(Opposing Fronts and Tales of Valor) and that I had a rather enjoyable experience.The factions were diverse and unique and the campaign had some challenge in it.The multiplayer was the epitome of multiplayer strategy.
ONE OF THESE THINGS IS NOT LIKE THE OTHER
So,what does Company of Heroes 2 offer that its predecessor doesn't?Well,the setting is different.Eastern front in the center of the game,therefore Ostheer(East German army) and the Soviet Red Army are the available factions to play as.The Germans have smaller squads but are generally superior in equipment and training(e.g.the Panzergrenadiers can be upgraded with Panzershreck to eliminate armor,none of the Soviet infantry has any upgrade to do so).The Soviets have larger squads,which gives them better chances to survive and reinforce(except the Engineers who have 4 and Sniper team who has 2,the rest of the Soviet squads have 6 men).
NICE,BUT HOW DO YOU PLAY IT?
The gameplay is the same as in the last game;capture point to get resorces and don't let the territories get cut off from your main base.However,instead of some points offering munitions,fuel or manpower, most points offer both munitions and fuel(in a smaller amount) with some offering just fuel or munitions but in a higher amount.Those that offer both may be secured to either increase their munitions or fuel output(but not both).Tactics such as taking cover,flanking,suppressing and vehicle positioning are important to win battles,since a heavy tank can be defeated if engaged with a AT gun while the bazooka team flanks and attacks his weak back armor.Overall,it's the same game,but...
LET IT SNOW
The snow ain't just for aesthetic purposes.Heavy snow can slow down both infantry and vehicles,and in some situations your men will freeze to death if they are not in a building,vehicle or near a fireplace.Blizzarrds may occur at random(you will get a warning and a timer telling you how much is left before it hits).It lowers the sight range of all your units,while freezing the men,forcing you to take care of them.Vehicles and men leave marks on the snow so you know if someone passed there and where he went.
YURI,WHAT DO YOUR BLUE EYES SEE?
Tue line of sight is implemented in this game.In simple terms,your units cannot see behind walls or through trees,making ambushes a potent tactical solution(the first game didn't have true line of sight).It is a very fun mechanic that I haven't seen since the games of Stormregion(Codename:Panzers and Rush for Berlin).It makes scouting a neccessary maneuver to your strategy and smoke screens a life saver from artillery and machineguns(my Soviet Shock troops saved a lot of my men with their smoke grenades).An excellent addition to the game.LOVE IT!
WANT TO GO TO A THEATER?
Theater of War is and addition to the singleplayer portion of the game.You have solo challenges and coop scenarios.These can vary from officer assasination,holding a position,eliminating a armoured column during the blizzard and so on.It extends the life of the game and if you have a friend,some of the scenarios you can play with him.
COMPANY OF FUN
The multiplayer is so fun I don't know what words to use.It's immersive and action packed,but smart action.You need to make decisions fast and smart to win.The user interface really helps here;on the bottor right you can select the production buildings,set a rally point and order a unit to arrive.this is important in the early stages of the game,when deployment to the frontline is crucial.The various maps also help in this,considering that they are different in sizer and terrain.
SINGLE IS COLD
I played the first three missions of the campaign and didn't continue because I ran out of time(I played this during the free weekend action).The campaign is inferior to that from CoH1.Whil CoH1 displayed the Americans,British and Germans as normal people doing their duty,the Soviet army men are portrayed as cowards who shoot their own men in the back.True,attrocities were made by the Red Army and the methods they used were brutal,but htere must have been some heroic moments.Sadly,the campaign doesn't show that,and the way the story is presented doesn't help.It is told via a flashback,which makes it feel detached from reality.Add in that the focus is on the bad side of the Red Army(and that the Germans are nothing more than obstacle,rather that a force),while showing nothing bad about the German army(they did attrocities,no army is safe from that) adn you get and rather empty and almost surreal story that is hard to believe or take serious.
COMRADE,WHAT IS THE CONCLUSION?
Company of Heroes 2 is an excellent strategy with excellent multiplayed balancing,a sizeable singleplayer content and a dull campaign story.If you're buying it for the multiplayer,you won't be dissapointed.If you're buying it for the challenges,missions and scenarios in th Theater of War you will get a kick from it.If you're buying it for and interesting story then you will get dissapointed with it.

NEO Scavenger is a hard-core survival game that takes place in a dystopian post-apocolyptic future.  The interface is simple and the graphics are basic but this masks a game that is flush with choices and possibility.
You awaken with nothing on you and no knowledge of what has happened to the world.  From the moment you are revived at the beginning of the game until you die due to exposure (or starve to death...or get torn limb-from-limb...or...) you are constantly pressured by the environment and your characters own survival needs to move ahead.  Death is far more likely than survival and the options to keep yourself going can get pretty deep and dark (for example, eating the flesh of other humans is a perfectly acceptable way to go...if you don't mind a growing ravenous hunger for the flesh of the living).  To be completely honest, I've yet to get anywhere close to the end of this game but  never stop revisiting it because the sheer diversity of options always leaves me feeling like there were other choices and that any of those other variations might have led to a profoundly different outcome (IE - death by some new lurking horror or contraction of an unexpected disease).

I have this game on my 360, PS3, and PS4, along with every single costume DLC on one platform... the so called missing features that so many of you are dissapointed at ain't all that to be honest. This PC verison is essentially DOA5 Ultimate Arcarde port + Last Round updates. There's no controller vibration because the arcade joystick doesn't vibrate either xD, no key mapping because there is no keyboard at the arcade, stereo sound instead of 5.1 because that's how the arcade machine is, and no achievments because the arcade doesn't have it either. Team Ninja took the easiest port because the arcade machine they used for Ultimate is 100% a PC. Why would they waste more resources porting PS3/360/PS4/XBO version which are proprietary formats. Sure, the latter two are x86 architecture but they are still more proprietary than the readily available arcade version they spent time and money developing couple years ago.
As someone whom already owned pretty much every console version there is, I did not hesitate to get it for the PC simply because it's the very first DOA game for the PC and I can install it on portable systems to play it anywhere I go. If you enjoy the core gameplay of the DOA series, there's no reason not to buy it. The so-call missing features are just icing on the cake, not manditory and does not affect gameplay one bit.
About the delayed online modes, if you are already a DOA player like myself, we can easily wait. If you are a new DOA player or PC is the only format you have, it's actualy a good thing because you can take the time to pratice before heading out to the wild on day 1 and getting owned by veterans. :)

The first proper Dead or Alive game on the PC. How does it fare? It's actually a pretty good port. A lot of reviews are... I'd have to say "whining" about two stages being cut and no achievements. The latter may be added later for people that like to get those things.
As for the game itself. It looks pretty. The characters, which are arguably the most important asset in the game, all look fantastic even if they're using PS3 textures, the shadowing makes up for it imo. It's the same trick used in the past two Dynasty Warriors games Koei has ported to PC: Dynasty Warriors 8: Xtreme Legends Complete Edition and Dynasty Warriors 8: Empires. This does indicate that perhaps Koei just doesn't know much about PC porting in general, whether it's Team Ninja or Omega Force, but it gets by. If you're looking for eye candy, the game's like a light version of something like Dragon Age: Inquisition. The game is pretty stable, I'm running a budget build at 1080p with 2k shadows and full AA, it looks great. I did get one crash in Story Mode but ever since then it hasn't given me any problems.
As for the gameplay if you're just a fighting game fan or just semi-interested in the genre, the gameplay's pretty solid. Nothing too hard to get used to, no knowing of any strengths to punches and kicks, but do note that everyone can counterhold almost any attack you throw out. However this comes with a rock-paper-scissors type of mechanic where a Strike wins over a Throw, a Throw wins over a Counter, and a Counter wins over a Strike. You can freely move around no problem with most characters and can side step, making defense in this game very easy to get into. As for offense, every character has an assortment of moves that can extend combos depending on circumstances such as stun and critical stun. The game itself has an extensive tutorial mode that delves into the deeper mechanics as well.
The music is very mood setting, it gets you into the fight. The sound effects are satisfying. Nothing seems to be downgraded at all in this port, though you do hear a change in quality if a Virtua Fighter character talks but that's something minor.
The controls are decent. Keyboard warriors may have a tough time, even if this game is incredibly accessible to a keyboard user by design. For a controller, I don't know if anyone's had this same issue, but the XB360's left analog stick seems to register a bit too sensitively with the game, slightly tilting it to left or right on the character select makes it cycle too fast so if that bugs you, just use the D-pad, there's not many intricate movements or combos where you'd want the stick anyway.
I like the game myself and for the price, I'll be honest I think even WITH an Online mode later, it should remain at $35.99. While there is cut content (not essential at all, but hey it's still missing content) and the game uses shading trickery to look better, it'd fall between the pricing of Blazblue: Continuum Shift Extend and Ultra Street Fighter IV/King of Fighters XIII. It's a great game, easy to pick up and play. If you somehow like fighting game stories, the game's story mode isn't like Mortal Kombat 9's even though it tries to be, you'll be done with the story mode in a couple of hours, the rest of the game itself is great. If you want a nice 3D fighter on PC, this is a safe bet and if you're a DOA fan that hasn't been able to play a DOA game since DOA2, this has a lot of things carried over with some new moves and new mechanics. Hopefully the later Online patch will show if the game was well balanced.
On a numbers scale, I'd rate this a 7/10. Definitely get it if you have the spare money but only if you want a good 3D fighter or are a fan of DOA, otherwise do snag it when it goes on sale.

I remembered playing Dino Run when it was a flash game on Newgrounds, so when I saw the deluxe Steam edition on
for cheap I had to pick up a copy for old time's sake.
Dino Run DX is every bit as fun, silly, and frustrating as I remember. The mechanics are simple: run from one end of a chaotic obstacle course to the other, avoiding the wall of imminent death chasing you down. Along the way there are secrets to find (if you have the time and the skill), pickups and little critters to devour to improve your dino (and for achievements), and challenges and speedruns to complete on several different difficulties (for kicks). And before I go any further, there are hats. If you play Team Fortress 2, Dino Run DX is right up your alley.
The speedruns aren't that bad on higher difficulties (except for Nobody Likes You). For the most part, they're just
. If you can pick up the gameplay fast enough there's no reason to do the lower-difficulty runs if you're after the achievements, since completing on Hard or Insane will also count as a completion on Medium.
Speaking of achievements, Dino Run DX has some bugs related to the them and to the leaderboards. Like
I was unable to get the Bronzed and Silverado achievements unlocked until I got all the gold trophies for the Goldie achievement. I was also able to get the Easter Bunny achievement without finding all the large eggs just by grabbing the Bronto Egg in
. Lastly, I had a similar problem to
during one run, and an instance where I fell through the world and was able to make an insane time on another. Between these two buggy runs I was able to boost myself to #20 on the overall leaderboard, which I don't actually deserve.
There were a few times when I managed to glitch my way into walls and couldn't escape, destroying an otherwise perfect run, but with the exception of weird world geometry there are very few problems with the gameplay. If it's cheap, why not? Even 100% completed Dino Run DX is a great time waster.

EDIT: This review is now outdated, so lololo.
Quake Live is a continuation of Quake 3, which started in 2010 as a browser version of it, with beta period before that. It's like Q3 but cleaner, online only and being Free-To-Play, with abilit to subscripe for some features. I think it's great to be able to get into game in just a few clicks - Carmack (if I am not mistaken) said something like that while game required you to register and download plugin and such. In 2014 it became a standalone game and was ported to Steam, not being in-browser anymore.
This is where Q3 veterans went. Community is still alive. I found no players on Capture The Flag and Variety Pack though, strangely, at least from few tries. And there currently aren't enough players for ranking to work properly, be ready to be thrown into matches full with really good players and that one super-players who wrecks everybody else.
So, in nutshell, it's like Quake 3, but with continued support. Balance updates, other stuff, small changes. It dropped offline campaign though, those silly progressive bot matches. You don't miss them. It also doesn't support mods or such, but that's okay. It also has much mroe cleaner astethic. Mostly comes from not being able to have gore and gibs due to low rating, but it still looks great on an eyes this way too. I even think it's overall more colorful and prettier.
It also still has Duel, Deathmatch and Team Deathmatch modes of Q3, with Capture the Flag and some others. Most important new additional mode is Clan Arena, which is like Team Last Man Standing and shows the best of Quake 3 weapon balancing, where you better use weapon according to situation to stay alive. You can't respawn, everybody starts with 200 health, with all weapons. And in teams. And no damage on rocket jumps. Though, it does remove Arena Control, since there are no items on arena itself in this mode. But still great addition.
It also added quite a controversial Loadout system feature. You can spawn with a select additional weapon out of six with low ammo for it. Mostly people hated it because of Call Of Duty stereotype, without thinking. It's not applied to Duel and Clan Arena. What it means is that player doesn't spawn as defenceless, which is quite a problem in more massed gamemodes like Deathmatch where one can spawn right in front of another player. And yea, weapons are still balanced around each other, so good players will still want to stock up on arenas for more, running around. It's just that they have some chances to survive. Well, and to kill. It also gets annoying when everybody on the map has rocket launcher or railgun with no care. But it's still not as horrible idea as it's made out of.
So, yea, Quake Live is pretty great, being able to play Quake 3 styled arena multiplayer shooter once again. For free and with a click of "Play Now!". Some may find it outdated, not having fancy leveling or such, while others may be put off by high skill of current community. But hey, still feels more fair and fun than Counter-Strike.

So if you want to watch with good resolution (and why wouldn't you) you may be forced to watch a few minutes, take a break, watch a few minutes, etc through the whole thing like I did.  In my opinion that spoils the experience quite a bit, so I recommend finding another way to watch it.
Of course, if you have blazing download speeds and the servers are humming along nicely you might have no problem.  And Steam may eventually fix the buffering issue.  But I would have appreciated a warning in the reviews I checked, so I'm taking time to write one.  Cheers!

Pretty solid game. Is it the best Early Access survival game I've ever played? No, it's not. But it is certainly the most unique.
There are some solid features this game has, making it stand out to me from others.
1) Free class leveling.  You aren't locked in to being a mage, warrior, or scout. You can put the work in to level up any skill you want, to create a true jack of all trades if you so wish.
2) The building. Yes, of course, it is similar to ARK. But it's better. Pieces are more unique and decorative, and there's a lot more that's interactive. Nice day out? Open your windows! Starting to rain or get a little cloudy with dragons? Close them back up!
3) The art style. Not too demanding on the computer, playing on epic setting doesn't seem to slow me much. And the world is charming. There are some jaw dropping landscapes to see and explore in this game world, and the creatures are wonderful to gaze at.
All in all, I definitely recommend checking this game out. For being in early access, it sure seems like there is plenty to do and the world is quite big. You definitely won't get bored any time soon, and I have yet to come across a game breaking bug.

I personally really enjoy this game! Its very remenesent of original fallout titles, but I feel like this game expands on Turn based actions and combat. (for example, the tough ability, since it gives you the ability to headbutt someone.)
I find that the abilities and flaws you can choose from give the game a lot of replay ability, and can be either incredibly angering, or extremely useful.
The difficultly makes you really try to find good ways out of a situation, and plan ahead, but even if you plan you could freeze, dehydrate just a hex before a river, or find a pack of feral dogs/Looters. IT makes you actually panic when you see your character in danger, since you know that if you take one small step in the wrong direction, you have to restart.
the random situations in the cities make you feel as though you really are helpless at times, becuase sometimes no matter what you do you wont be helpful, It paints a grim picture on how far humanity had fallen, and really helps set the scene.
I've gotten to the DMC around 4 times, though its hard to last long after that for me! After finding out that strong + trapping the wolfman in the beginning of the game gives you a warm coat, Dehydration has been the worst for me.
The only issues I've found with the game is that the "New game" and "save and quit" button are the same, so if you don't pay attention, you'll press new game by reflex, and I've lost 2 DMC saves to that.
Another is that there's no setting to turn off permadeath, I know some people who would love to play this game, but the difficulty and permadeath keep them away(like a lot of people with dark souls, haha)
A large glitch I've found is where you will be able to see the "scavenge" button, but it refuses to activate scavenging, though its available in the area (you are notified of scavengeable area's with a glass icon) and you have to turn your game off and on again to fix this. People have talked about this glitch for a long time now, but it hasn't been resolved.
In short, the game is one I'll be recommending to a lot of people, Since I really enjoy it. (at the time of this review i've had the game for 2 days, and played 28.4 hours)
If you like challenges, survivals, permadeath and looting, this is a game for you!

The other day I played one of Capcom's "Dead Rising" games -  I forget which one since they are all sort of the same anyway. I generally enjoyed the large open world and huge hordes of zombies, but disliked the zanier aspects of the characters and plots. I wonder if Techland - the developers of Dying Light - felt the same way because their game is essentially a Dead Rising clone with the wackiness stripped away. In some ways this made the game more enjoyable, but at the same time Dying Light felt characterless and flat in comparison.
Functionally, the game is quite impressive. It has a huge open world - made even larger with the addition of "The Following" DLC pack. Given their size, I was rather astonished by how fast the maps loaded, even on a slow mechanical hard-drive. The frame-rate was silky smooth, even with settings maxed and on an older GPU. The parkour-focused combat is slick and easy to learn, and the move-set is impressive; I was very quickly doing slide-kicks, grapples and vaults as I hacked my way through the undead horde. The actual gameplay-loop was less exciting; Dying Light takes its cue from Ubisoft's open-world games, littering the landscape with side-missions and collectibles that aren't individually very exciting but at least offered a reason to free-roam the game's giant map ("The Following" DLC at least added a useful alternative in the form of driving challenges with the addition of a car).
A major downside of the game for me were the weapons; variety was largely mechanical in nature, and it utilized a common/rare/unique color-coding system similar to Diablo (or Techland's own "Dead Island" games). Technically, the game features thousands of weapons but in actual gameplay it pretty much boils down to "blade", "hammer", "pistol/rifle" and "shotgun", with the major differentiation being how much damage was inflicted. More concernedly, weapons only have limited durability, and break after too much usage. Although I understand the idea behind this mechanic - having your best sword break during a fight can be a terrifying adrenalin rush - in practice the weapons broke far too quickly, making the constant scrounging for new gear a dull grind which artificially extended the game's length.
As much as I enjoyed the melee combat, I was less enthralled with the first-person parkour; the perspectives never quite looked right, and never felt as fluid and natural as, say, the third-person platforming of the Assassin's Creed series. It didn't help that climbing down was far more difficult than going up, and too often I fell to my death instead of lowering myself down level by level. While games like Mirror's Edge and Dying Light show that first-person parkour is possible, it still isn't my preferred method of in-game acrobatics. The game's strengths are its exploration and combat, not its platforming. Unfortunately, certain missions of the game stress the latter, to their detriment. The final mission is especially terrible in this (and it doesn't help that the end-boss is defeated in a series of dull - and completely unexpected, since its a mechanic that isn't used anywhere else in the game - quick-time events).
When it stuck to its strengths the game was largely enjoyable, but it was not a very memorable experience. While it is a striking improvement over its predecessor - the Dead Island Franchise - it still has a number of shaky bits. Hopefully the developers will learn as much from Dying Light and their next game will actually be something I can whole-heartedly recommend, but its not something I can honestly do with this one.
