I have to painfully admit defeat.  Metro 2033 Redux, is a visually impressive, story rich FPS that faulters on the technical side.  A look into the forums show the problems that this game has had since it launched and there doesn't seem to be any relief from the developers in the future.  Sadly, for my part the game becomes unplayable.  I get Framerate stutters every so often regardless of what settings I am using (low, High, PhysX off or on and so on).  For reference I have a i5 2500k running @4.4 ghz, a GTX 780ti, 8 gig of ram, window 8.1 64 bit and so on.  I can be running at 100 to 120 fps then all of a sudden drop to the 30 then it goes back again.  This happens constantly, and it is enough of a distraction that, for me, takes away the fun of playing the game.  I have looked around for workarounds and most of these work arounds do not work for me.  Even if they did, I shouldn't have to mess around in a Bios, or do anything that extreme to get one game to work correctly.  If you sense frustration, it is because I want to enjoy the game.  Between stutters, I did enjoy it, but it happens to often to ignore.  Perhaps in the future there will be a fix in the game and it will be playable.  But for me, at this time, I have a hard time recommending it to anyone.

I think intriguing plot and characters are very important in video games, as well as in other forms of entertainment. There are exceptions in games, such as Pac-Man or Space Invaders, where there isn't any dialog, many any "events," or much implied character personality, etc., but the gameplay compels the player in and of itself. For some players, Tropico 4 might compel them to play, just based on the gameplay. However, for myself, the gameplay in it doesn't immediately grab ahold of me, and when a game's gameplay isn't an immediate hook, the game needs other means of getting players to want to play it. If the gameplay of Pac-Man doesn't appeal to you, there's not much else that could convince you to want to play it.
Now, real time strategy isn't really a go-to genre for me, but Command & Conquer Red Alert 3's zany over-acting and setting got me into its campaign a bit, while Starcraft II's characters and story got me to buy and play through all fo it with a great thirst for more each step of the way, despite not even really being into that genre. I understand those are combat-oriented and this is about building a city/nation, but the premise is the same: I wasn't into the genre, but the story and characters got me on board with those other games and I like them as a result.
With Tropico 4, you are in charge of growing a city/nation, and that's it. As with my Pac-Man example, if you aren't immediately sold on the gameplay, there weren't story and characters making me want to play this game and give it more of a chance. I was turned off, and the game made no efforts to appeal to me. If growing a city sounds addicting to you, you might like it, but if it just sounds "okay," there isn't much else here to make the experience something you will enjoy.

Take everything I say about Shank with a big ol’ spoonful of salt; I don’t like platformers, I generally don’t like 2D side scrolling, and I hate brawlers and fighting games. So what is Shank? It is a 2D side scrolling brawler with comic book aesthetics and short elements of reactionary platforming.
Needless to say I started off the first level with a sour taste in my mouth and my judgments pre-rendered. After all of that, I’m not going to make a 180 and say Shank is great, but I got WAY more enjoyment out of it than I ever expected. The fighting felt to me like a run-and-gun adaptation of the combat found in Mark of the Ninja (a game I actually am quite fond of). While the platforming certainly picked at my nerves, the sections were short enough that I was able to push through them and keep playing. Helping matters was that Shank is an absolutely gorgeous game from an aesthetic standpoint. The animations are clear and well fleshed out, the cut-scenes are very rich and capture that comic book vibe, and the colors - while a bit muted for my tastes - are varied from level to level.
In the end, Shank is still a brawler. I don’t like memorizing combos and I don’t like how any fighting games handle. But I think in the end, that just says a lot for the quality that this game brings to the table. I’m not about to hand out my game of the year award, but Shank is pretty alright.

This remaster is excellent! I played the original through once, and absolutely loved it. But I found that there were a few things that could have been done better, such as the view through your gas mask which became hard to see through after a few minutes, and the UI and inventory seemed a bit rough around the edges. With this version, they basically used the UI from Metro Last Light and applied it here. It looks like a slighty refined Metro Last Light, but with the 2033 story and setting, which is exactly the same as the original. I believe they used the Metro LL engine, and basically revamped the lighting and texture detail a bit. The graphics are of course incredible as is Last Light, and is hugely better than the original 2033, especially in the texture side of things.
On the performance side, the game runs very well. 4A really, really knows what they are doing in the optimization department as well as the eye candy department! Framerates are smooth and steady and there are enough visual options to tweak so that lower end systems should also run this well (Another complaint I had about the original 2033 was the lack of options to tweak). I set it exactly as I had the original Last Light settings and it runs pretty much identically as that game did. I'm running an FX 8320 @ 4.2 GHz and an R9 280X @ 1170MHz with 8 GB DDR3 1866 RAM. I run all settings maxed except Tesselation, which is set to high. V-Sync is enabled, too. I'm not sure of my exact average FPS but there is no lagging or glitching and it looks very smooth. The game has not crashed or showed signs of any problems at all.
4A did an excellent job with this remaster. I am very happy with this game and also happy to support a top notch developer like them. This game was worth every penny! If you enjoyed the original, you'll enjoy it even more in this form, definitely worth a replay. If you haven't yet played it, then don't hesitate to grab the Redux version!

Shank is similar to a side scrolling God Of War.  Lots of enemies and lots of blood, with some sexual themes here and there, so it is not for the kiddos.  If you are going to play this game, you better make sure you have a controller, because the keyboard layout requires Mr. Fantastic fingers to use.  But if you want a larger challenge, skip the controller.  Shank begins his quest with just a few weapons, but more are obtained as he progresses.  Here is a weapon break down.
Duel Pistols: have a good firing rate and good distance, but do not do a lot of damage so the larger enemies and bosses will barely notice them.
Shanks: Primary attack.  Don't do much damage but are fast.
Chainsaw: Does a lot of damage but is slow.
Shotgun:  Does a lot of damage but is slow and does not have good range.  Is very effective against large enemies.
Machetes: Faster than the chainsaws, but does less damage.
Uzi: Fast firing rate and good distance, but not so powerful.
Chains: Slightly slower than the mahetes but do more damage.
Katana: Fast with good range and does some decent damage.
Grenades: Shank starts every level with three but can hold up to five.  A throwable explosive that can damage or even kill enemies at a distance.  Should be used wisely.
The game can get challenging and sometimes can get boring.  It is reccomended that Shank is played in spurts.  On normal mode, when Shank is defeated, he respawns nearby with full health.  But in Hard mode, there are no checkpoints. which means that every death sends Shank back to the start of the level, and the enemies are tougher than before.
The bosses are fun to fight and have a stragety on how they are to be defeated, but some bosses feel like more powerful copies of previous bosses.
Overall, if you like a beat em up, are okay at the sight of blood, and know how to get tactical in battle, Shank is a good game, but should be bought on sale.

Edit: Single player is a good bit of fun. Each turn has a set number of deloyments (each fight counts as a deployment). Although prone to repititon, you are in a constant battle to keep the gothic sector from being overwhelmed by orks, eldars and chaos. I haven't played the board game that this is based off but I'm guessing this is a lot more fun :D
Each race has its own set of unique looking ships starting from transports to destroyers, light cruisers, cruisers, battlecruisers and battleships (each class a set point value).  All of them pretty and intricately designed.
Depending on the kind of mission you load into (nope can't choose your missions in solo skirmish) i.e. cruiser clash, assassination, convoy escorts etc. you will be given a point cap. You will have to decide your fleet composition according to the opposing enemy race.
The battles are super fun, quick (lasting about 5 mins on average) and are visually stunning (pwetty explosions and sweet sound effects). You are expected to fight within a limited tile set or boundary (in real time) and use your races advantages to secure victory. Each race has its own specialty which allows for different play styles.
However, some mission types favour certain races, for example, one such mission type requires a ship to approach a randomly spawned marker on the map in order to bombard the planet below. The eldar have the upper hand in such missions are they are fast and agile and difficult to catch even after using your ships abilities to slow them down.
As you win battles you can upgrade each ship class within a limited number of slots available for upgrades (passive abilities) and special orders (active abilities). You may even adopt a favour by paying renown (in-game currency earned for both wins and losses) which attaches special abilities to individual ships. One such example is the inquisition favour for the imperial fleet which grants +1 crew points to all your crewmen (yup, you will have to upgrade your crew) as well as grant you the ability to reveal an enemy ship from infinite range (which would otherwise be hidden or masked as a blip).
Get the right combo going on for your fleet and you can turn those frustrating losses into wins.
The races are not so balanced in my opinion. The orks and imperials have the upper hand, i'm not very fond of the Chaos fleet, and they are average in every way. However, the eldar are super powerful (yet fragile) and are tough to catch, this can be hard to counter even with stasis bombs that slow ships.
The biggest selling point is the ship navigation. Depending on the race, your ship will have x number of prow mounted weapons (torpedos, lance cannons) and starboard & port mounted cannons. To get the most damage done, you'll have to line up your attacks in way that you would expose the most weapons at a single time towards the enemy (kind of like an old school ship battle). A combination of tactics can be used: lining up a perfect torpedo salvo (prow), a quick swing to the port side for a burst of macro gun fire followed by a frontal ship ram is extemely statisfying to pull-off when done right. You can even set up ambushes in gas clouds which will hide your ship from radar detection.
I'm not sure why you can't pair up with your friends in 2v2 games as opponents (private matches). I hope they implement that soon.
Other than that, expect more races, space marines are coming soon with the promise of another race (no idea which one yet, seems like necrons are getting the popular vote).
To summarise, get it, there is tons of replayablity. You'll feel like a proud father once you see your entire fleet put together, each with its own favour and colour scheme. Be prepared to get your♥♥♥♥♥handed in multiplayer. It ain't easy but it sure is fun.

Being the wrong side of forty, cough cough, and having played the original GW game all those years a go.  I bring ancient, ahem cough, wisdom to this short review.
Spaceships and factions are all very well rendered with the unreal engine bringing them to life in very dark and atmospheric ways.  The various missions conform for the most part to the original game.  The campaign cut scenes are engaging and moving.  Unlike the turn based original,  all the action occurs in real time, with a bullet time option to slow things down giving you time to zoom in to the action and behold the carnage.  Of course this also gives you time to issue new orders when things get crazy and put together tactical plays.
The empire ships feel spot on and just as I imagined from the original turn based game.  Slow but purposeful with strong fire power good armor and exceedingly slow speed.
Chaos seem a little weak on long range firepower relying heavily on lances and suffer from weaker armor but have faster speed than the empire.
The Orc ships are well presented but are heavily reliant on micro warp jump and taunt to close with faster more manuverable ships ie everyone else !
If you love pressure and extreme micro management then the Eldar are your fleet of choice.  They come with some very strong firepower but lack armor and are extremely fragile.  The holoshields their ships hide behind require that the player keeps them on the move.  The faster they go the harder the eldar corsairs are to hit.
With space marines just around the corner and another yet to be announced new fleet in the works this game is full of potential and so far goes a long way to realising that BFG itch that resides in the hearts and minds of the GW faithful.  It's also a pretty fine two dimensional ship to ship combat game.  What more can I say ?  WAAAAAAAAAAAAARRRRRRGGGG !  Blood for the Blood God ! and in the name of the Emperor enjoy !

This review assumes you are buying this with all the DLC; I did not play this without the DLC, and all of my friends who DID play it without the DLC said it was awful or at least not nearly as good as it is now.
There's a lot to love about this game. The single player games can be as long or as short as you'd like, really, and you can quit or start new ones whenever. I did that a lot, honestly. Some of them I'd finish just because, but others I felt like after 100 turns I needed a change of pace. I also spent a lot of time playing games with my friends; it was what we'd look forward to every week. We'd play for 3-4 hours a week, and we'd finish the game in a month or so. Loved that.
All that being said, this game isn't perfect. The AI can be really, really dumb. The difficulty scaling, despite having a bunch of difficulties, is still chaotic and jumpy. The beginning of the game can really drag, and war I think could still be improved (heard it wasn't really in Civ VI). Overall, though, probably the best strategy game I've played aside from the ol' Axis & Allies on PC from the early 2000s, but that was a childhood favorite. This one is a true keeper for years to come.

ARK, for me though, always seemed out of place mixing dinosaurs with guns and never really finding a good balance for them, whereas this game is set and a fantasy world and truly feels like a fantasy world. The AI right now in incredible dumb, however, and there's definitely some improvements to be made for those who want to PVP, but this game is fun right now as it is, and I can only see it getting better as it gets more polished closer to release.

You're a skilled Botanist, and you find castor plants, smearing yourself with them and making your scent toxic to drive the beast away. You make your way towards the glow, picking up a mismatched pair of shoes and dragging around two grocery bags filled with twigs, kindling, and empty water bottles.  You're close to hypothermic, but just need to survive until the next day so you can focus the sunlight to start a fire to warm yourself.  As dawn approaches, you slip into oblivion...
You wake up in a cryo facility... Good luck!
NEO Scavenger is a brutal game where you'll die often, and in horrible ways - even once you understand all of the mechanics, the random number generator will seal your fate if you're not very very careful (and sometimes even if you are).  There's surprising depth in the crafting, combat, and survival aspects for a game without any animation.  You need a tin can, a lighter, and some twigs to make sterile water to drink.  You need the same things plus a dirty rag to make a clean rag.  If you get hurt and are bleeding, you need to wash the wound with sterile water (or another antiseptic) and then bandage it with a clean rag.  I died of massive infections twice by the time I realized how to properly care for myself after a fight.  I died several times in combat before I realized how to play defensively and wait for openings.  I still die just through bad luck, but I'm getting further and further into the game each time.

If you're looking for an intense, unforgiving turn-based isometric strategy surivival game with perma-death I recommend you give this a try, although I do recommend picking it up when it's on sale, $15,- seems a bit of a steep price in my opinion.
You start off the game by creating your character, selecting strenghts and weaknesses, after which the proverbial♥♥♥♥♥♥immediately hits the fan.
You find yourself just awoken from cryo-sleep in a facility when you notice a strange-looking beast approaching you. You can deal with this using strenghts you've previously selected, after taking care of the wolf-like creature you start to wonder where you are, or who you are, you remember next to nothing, and as you set foot outside the facility you notice everything has changed, buildings are in poor condition, and there are no signs of life to be found.
You must scavenge for survival, your first order of business is protecting yourself from the elements, finding clothes is your #1 priority. After getting yourself warmed up and safe from hypothermia, you should probably find a way of protecting yourself, and scavenging for weapons can be a tedious task, but the excitement you get from finding a mint-condition rifle or shotgun is more than worth it, I won't spoil any more of the game, but I will say this: it's extremely unforgiving and I myself have never survived for more than 25 days, unraveling quite a portion of the story, but not close to all of it.
TL;DR
NEO Scavenger is an unforgiving and exciting survival game, and I'd definitely recommend it if you're a fan of the genre, but you will die. A LOT.
Happy scavenging ;D

Rating 6.5/10
OVerview: 2d Action
The Good:
+ Great graphics and animation.
+ A good combat system, you have light and heavy attacks, ranged attacks, grapple and leap attacks. You mix this all together to create fun and fast combat mechanics.
+ A variety of weapons to fit your playstyle
The Average:
The boss battles are mostly the same. Each boss has similar attack patterns making each encounter feel more like a chore rather than a challenge
The Bad:
- Its main failing is that the game is very very repetitive. There is very little variety in the level design, thus every level has you beating up enemies, moving on to the next screen and doing it all over again.  The game is short clocking in at roughly 2-3 hours on normal and by the time you reach the end you pretty much had enough anyways.
Conclusion
It is a good first effort from Klei Entertainment, they have a unique artsytle and animation to their games which make them stand out but this game is a bit on the shallow side.

Honestly I can't reccomend this game, this is due to the very heavily re-used saints 3 aspects. It's painfully obvious. They did try to spruce it up with a new storyline and some new vehicles. But beyond that nothing new added except some parts where you're on a spaceship (for about 6 minutes) and then on your own spaceship, otherwise it's the exact same steelport. Not only the re-skin bugs me, what also bugs me is that you're this gigantic super powered god that is VERY hard to put down. You're so over powered in this game it's a joke. I did learn you can active a cheat to turn off superpowers so you have a bit more of a challenge, but honestly it's pointless because it disables achivement progression.
Pros (New things I enjoyed)
-Some new vehicles and the gun customization is great
-Space themes are kinda cool
-The Cops morphing into aliens looked neat
Cons (Where for me the game suffered a big blow)
-Very heavy re-skin of 3 (This means Steelport, clothes, vehicles, and some weapons)
-Neon lights everywhere means play in a well lit room or your eyes will start to hurt (mine did)
-Too overpowered, even for a simulation you're a god that just can't die
-Superpowers can sometimes be a burden
-Not much added that was new besides DLC clothes/vehicles and some new concepts
Final Verdict: Not for me, way to much of a re-skin, might play more since I bought it and will get my use out of it, but really only buy if you're a die hard fan.

ARK, for me though, always seemed out of place mixing dinosaurs with guns and never really finding a good balance for them, whereas this game is set and a fantasy world and truly feels like a fantasy world. The AI right now in incredible dumb, however, and there's definitely some improvements to be made for those who want to PVP, but this game is fun right now as it is, and I can only see it getting better as it gets more polished closer to release.

I downloaded it as soon as it was launched on Valve's Steam and been playing it ever since. I own both the XboxOne and the PS4 editions of this title but, to be fair, I really like this edition of the game the best for the following reasons:
- the graphics, o.k. so it doesn't use the 'latest' technology in comparison to the latest gen consoles but I am sure I can see pores on the characters' faces, the beads of sweat are gorgeous, personally, I even think they are better than the PS4 edition!, and on my rig (Pentium i5 4460, Nvidia chip), I find the stage detailing really gorgeous again (you can see far into the distance on the Sky Tokyo stage, the water effects are SUBLIME and although on my rig it tends to judder it still can clip by at a good enough pace!) + the costume detailing is also really effective i.e. muslin looks and feels like muslin, crêpe-de-chine looks and acts like crêpe-de-chine, silkenwear, again, looks-and-acts like silkenwear would!
- the DLC extras, to anyone who didn't pre-order this title on Valve's Steam, I would feel slightly sorry for you as I am so glad they added a lot of costume DLC to this release at the pre-order stage as I like most of the extra imaginary threads A LOT almost to the point of it being unhealthy (I believe it was 31 costumes all-in-all, if my memory is serving me rightly)! Personally, I think they look awesome as rendered by a decent P.C., I even like Ayane's 2014 Hallowe'en costume A LOT and the Aloha costumes, again, look AWESOME on a P.C. setup, so-much-so even that I have no intention of EVER purchasing any DLC content for the Xbox One edition from henceforth and would only ever consider expanding my DLC experience on solely the P.C. when on sale, though! In fact, I think I will only ever keep on purchasing further iterations of the series now on ONLY a (gaming) computer, that's how much I enjoy gaming on the computer these years!
So, to sum it up, if you have never tried the series before then definitely give the title a go as you are in for a treat, it will be the best version of the game graphicswise anyway of the lot; trust me, I should know as I really like this version even compared to the PS4 version running on a Full HD t.v. 1080p at 400 Hz! If you can holdout, get it in the sale and splash out on some costume DLC at the same time, you shan't regret you did as the imaginary threads will look stupendous and add some much needed variety in between scraps! Don't get me wrong, I am in NO way a Tecmo fan these years as their DLC pricing is simply ATROCIOUS and a MAJOR buzzkill but some of this iteration's downsides aside, I am just hoping that they will eventually add extra stages (the Crimson being one of them) as they did the Zack Island stage as a titular update to DeadorAlive5 out-of-the-blue and as they are going to do with this title's online functionality thus greatly improving this title's expandibility for the p.c. 'community' on Steam. Fingers crossed they will 'cause otherwise they are adding another great blemish to the DOA series and subsequently to Valve's Steam. PC MASTER RACE!

"A Warhammer Wonder.
When I first heard about a potential Space-based Warhammer game, my thoughts went immediately to Homeworld, I hoped so much that this would be to that scale. Let me start this off by saying that I own this game for both the XBox360 and the PS3.  While a lot of people are rating this game negatively, it is not because of the aspects of the game itself.
So, first of all, Dead or Alive is a long-standing 3D arcade fighter hailing from the original Playstation.  It's claim to fame was filling a gap left vacant by a lack of Battle Arena Toshinden titles on that generation of consoles, and it's primary competition was Tekken, which was very mixed as to whether it was considered good or not.  What drew most people's attention back then were innovative features.  The first was battlegrounds that responded to the actions of the character.  Knocking an enemy into a mine in a minefield or into a laser fence did extra damage.  The second feature of note of the original game was boob physics.  This was actually its primary selling point, at the time, because no other game had done it at this point (that wasn't a hentai game on pc, at any rate).
Fast-forward many years and DoA has gone through a lot of changes, but has been relatively true to its original concept and has even managed to expand on it.  Make no mistake, this is a fan-service title in every respect of the term.  Men have rippling muscles, women have beautiful aesthetics, skimpy outfits for both genders (as well as some silly ones); even the scenes and battlezones are right out of an otaku's wet dream.  But underneath all of this is, actually, a very solid fighting game with a very good understanding of the martial arts used by the characters.  For those of you who are looking for the more mature aspects of this title, there's plenty of 'barely there' outfits for botht he male and female characters.  The characters also sweat and get dirty as you fight, affecting both clothes and skin.
Where this game excels:
This game benefits greatly from the hardware available to it on a good pc.  While the specs are a little high, you will be rewarded for the fantastic visuals of this title.
The fighting mechanics that drive the game are very fluid and solid.  Motions look largely natural aside from the clearly impossible wire-fu attacks of some characters, and the battles will just about always be intense and worthwhile.
A wide variety of genders, fighting styles, and character costumes will give most people plenty of replay value and time.
Where this game is lacking;
The AI for the game is notorious, across all of the series and every platform, of blatantly cheating, and this is no exception.
Timing for counters is very unforgiving.  While the AI has the capacity to do this flawlessly, you will probably be far less adept at this.
Stun locks and air juggles are a bit too common for my liking, but this is no different than the console version, and has been something that has become increasingly 'unfriendly' about this game since DoA4.
This game is a little heavy resource-wise.  You'll need a fairly decent computer to run everything smoothly, but if you've got that system, you will be richly rewarded with a beautiful game with beautiful men and women.
Things that people complain about that aren't really a thing:
No multiplayer:  Granted, this is a bit of a pain, but this is something that will be patched into te pc title a few months after release, so it's not really that it has no multiplayer as much as it simply does not have it, yet.  We WILL have multiplayer, just not right out the gate.
Not using the render engine of the XBOne and the PS4:  Once again, while this is true, this is a relatively minor issue.  We don't know what technical issues there were during the port, but I'm going to assume that the developers were having too many issues with the engine for the consoles and decided to go 'tried and true' to make sure that everyone on PC would have a good and solid experience.  Therefore, since this is saving headaches and ensuring playability with minimal loss of performance, this is not an issue.
Missing extra content:  This is something that is going to be patched in over time.  Some of the features not included had things involved in them that used the features of the 'Soft Engine' that caused the delay of the port in the first place.  As they work out these issues, that additional content will be patched back into the game.  They may even, eventually, release an overhaul of the game using the Soft Engine at a later point, but we don't know for certain what will and won't be patched in.  Even still, grand scheme of things, we are missing two stages....whoopedy doo.....   This is a very minor issue considering that you have a completely playable game otherwise.  We even have some costume content that the console users didn't get, or at least don't get for free.

So far I'm not having the same horrible issues being reported widespread, but maybe I'm lucky or tempting fate by saying so.
>The controller works just fine for me so far, though it's true there's no vibration.  Kind of weird nowadays, but that's okay.
>I tried changing my name after unlocking something and restarting the game.   My save seemed to be intact.
>There's no online yet, but we knew that going in.
>There's a pile of expensive DLC on day one, but it's Dead or Alive.  What did you honestly expect?  And it's just costumes, so it's by no means required to enjoy the game.
Now, onto the game itself.  I played this first on PS3 so I already went into this knowing what to expect.  Just like previous iterations, Dead or Alive 5 is a solid fighting game that will kick your♥♥♥♥♥ but has difficulty settings that make it playable for noobs like me.
Yes, it's full of bouncy T&A which objectifies the hell out of the women in the game.  Again, it's Dead or Alive.  What do you expect?  It's eye candy amid a solid, good, intense fighting game.
Dead or Alive is more about punching and kicking than flinging fireballs and smearing blood around.  You will find very little of that here, so if you must have blood, gore and sorcery to have fun, you won't find much if any of it here.  (Not that there's anything wrong with blood and sorcery, I love MK, Soul Calibur, and the rest of 'em.)
All this being said, if you're a DoA fan, go ahead and grab this.  It shouldn't disappoint.  If you like fighting games, go ahead and grab it too.
If boobs and panty shots, or a lack of blood and fireballs, REALLY bother you, then don't get this game, but that's not what the core of the game is.  It's an absolutely solid♥♥♥♥♥kicking fighter, which occasionally decides to get a little weird, pull down its pants and tell you to kick it harder.
I look forward to getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked by you all when the online mode launches.  If I run into any problems, I will edit this review.

TLDR:  I only play on private dedicated servers. The game is a fun, but clearly is in early access. If you are a fan of sandbox, building, exploring and fantasy theme you will enjoy this game. If you understand what "Early Access" actually means, and the caveats that come with it. Then there is no reason to not buy this game if it interests you.
The game has a lot going for it. As many have compared it to Ark it has a lot of those elements. This didn't bother me at all. I loved Ark and have played it for many hours. The big draw to this game for me was the Fantasy theme. I enjoy sandbox games a lot. I also only play them on local or private dedicated servers, and mostly just enjoy exploring the world and experiening the game. I don't play on official servers and I don't deal with the PVP aspect of these sandbox games.
Things I think the game has going for it currently.
- Fantasy Theme
- Building works fairly well
- Magic Is fun
- Creatures are interesting
- An intro to the game with basic quests
Things to be aware of that will effect your experience. Most of these are related to Early Access.
- Terrain collision needs polishing. You find lots of spots you should be able to move past but can't
- Some of the spells, skill, schemas you can unlock aren't actually in the game even though you can earn them
- Leveling / Skill up system is a bit restricting. If you want to focus on a specific area sometimes you find yourself constrained due to levels. I hope this changes over time and they let you focus on what you want regardless of level cap restriction.
- Lots of misc Bugs.
I am really excited to see this game evolve over time. I went into it expecting it to have many flaws due to early access. As you can see I had enough fun to put almost 40 hours into the game up to this point,  despite it being Early Access. I can say I have just about reached the limit of what the game has to offer me at this point. Due to things just not being in the game that are required to continue progression and exploration.

Braid was floating around Steam for quite some time before I gave it a second look. I had heard many great things about Braid and knew there were some great reviews for it. Still, I wasn't as attracted to the game as I had hoped to be. Eventually it went on sale, and I thought, "Why not?" That weekend, I gave Braid a try; it blew me away.
Presentation: 9/10
The game starts off with a simple notion and subtly nudges you along, presenting you with simple concepts and well-written segments at the beginning of each world. The exquisite literature within these "books" help lay the foundation and reason for your journey, and as you progress through the game, you'll continuously find yourself connecting to our hero and his ambitions and goals.
Graphics: 9/10
Simple, yet elegant, the artstyle brings about a strong aura of innocence to accompany the story and its protagonist. The amount of detail put into the game's artistic world is stunning, and you'll often find yourself pausing for several seconds to admire its beauty. The artwork resembles that of some paintings and really gives you the feel of a game crafted with love.
Sound: 9/10
The music is calm and wants to lull you into its world. Soothing and conveyance of innocence in Braid, the soundtrack meshes well with the artistic representation of the game.
Gameplay: 8.5/10
Thought provoking at times, the puzzles were never made to be impossible and required a little perserverence and patience to complete. The basic concepts shown in the beginning of each world quickly expands and tests your intelligence with different situations that require some "out-of-the-box" thinking. This is what metro 2033 should have been at release. I enjoy the updated visuals for sure but the true testament to this redux is the upgrade to controls and playability. While stealth combat was absolutely useless in the original, you can ACTUALLY use it in this game. New takedowns, game levels expanded with new paths, intelligent rather than black and white AI, this game truly is what the designers have hoped to achieve. Im not gonna lie, in the previous title I HAD to use brutally cheap tactics to advance in the game. I have not had to resort these measures in this game.
There is some small problems though, I have found points in the game where the 2033 game and the Last Light playability have clashed with each other and take it out on the player. For instance in 2033, demons just swatted at you from the sky, while in last light they could carry you and throw you. Seeing how 2033's levels were not originally designed for this, there were points where demons came into play and i found myself being thrown off cliffs, or being repitively picked up as soon as i landed when there were 2 demons.
There were some good additions too, like extra rooms or a safe, which required you to explore the level to find the key to open it, rewarding your exploration. in stealth areas, new stealth friendly paths have been added as well. new guns and attachments also make an appearance.
All in all, this game is a prettier, playable version of metro 2033, which doesn't sound like much but believe me it makes all the difference in the world. Metro 2033 grabbed me on the immersion but brutally pulled me out during its unplayable combat and stealth. now that Redux has fixed those issues, I look forward to finishing the game.

Purchased for 24$. AMAZING GAME! LOVE IT! :)
+Beautiful design
+Amazing graphics

+Gameplay is superb
+Characters are great. There are two brothers in the game that are hilarious.

+Decapitations are super satisfying
+Best gore I have seen in a game. Period.
+Music is pretty good and matches the mood / setting / events. One particular song was fantastic when paired with chopping the limbs off of bad guys
+Killing is satisfying
+Guns are overpowered, as they should be, so I only used them when I was in a fire fight. Loved the fact I could sneak up on enemies with my rifle/pistol drawn and force them to put their hands in the air and plead for their lives (moments before having their skulls blown off)
+One emotional moment that made me a little upset
+Environment is fun to parkour in and pleasing to destroy
+Most missions are unique and have little stories built into them, so you actually enjoy doing side missions. Don't worry about tedious fetch quests.
+Looting is done well. Same with crafting and the level system
+Cool, but unoriginal (for the most part), enemy types. Mostly the same from other popular games
+Just the feeling you get when you are walking down the city with the shine shining and the beautiful lighting effects raining down upon buildings, cars, and more
+Markers are only on screen when you press Q, so if you enjoy strictly the scenery and are not a fan of having a vomit of HUD effects everywhere, Dying Light has you covered
+Runs like a dream. I heard it was hard to run, but I was getting 80-90 fps in open areas of the cities and 100-144+ fps everywhere else with an R9 390, i5-6500, and 16GB of RAM
+Checkpoints are well done and you never get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off by spawning 10 minutes earlier in a level like most games unfortunately do
+Main game is 30-35~ hours of content. May update after finishing the DLC and completing bounties, which are short little challenges you get after completing the game to help achieve max rank
-Story was nothing to brag about
-The main villain was pretty cliche and there are moments in the story that just make you scratch your head or laugh at how bad it was
-Quarantine missions are boring and frustrating. They are OPTIONAL, so you can skip them (which is what I did). The one that I actually completed had zombies spawning infinitely, so I ended up rushing through the mission spamming medkits
-The perk called "Tic-Tac," which was supposed to make you be able to climb up a wall and jump off of it to evade enemies, but instead only serves the purpose of forcing your character off of buildings when you are actually trying to climb (leading to your death and irl rage)
-There are 2-3 missions that required me to look up a tutorial on Youtube due to them being "find this" missions without any markers.
-Final boss was a QTE and an annoying one at that

This is one of those games that makes you hate life and everything about it, but you get moments of amazing experiences that keep you looking for more.
The RNG will make you want to die, but instead of you dying it'll be most of your team.
One game I ran my shotgun guy to kill a unit, he had a 96% shot to hit the enemy was the last one on the map, he missed and then promptly died the next turn.
The Good
Gameplay wise, it's a great time. It's simplistic enough that there isn't any intense learning curve to sway away people that are trying to get into strategy games, but there's enough mechanically so that you have to think about positioning, and utilize every ability that your troops can obtain, suppression is probably my favorite because I'm really unlucky and that really drops the rate to hit.
On top of all of that you have to manage XCOM itself and make sure that you keep every area around the earth safe, or people will lose hope in XCOM and stop funding, if everyone leaves you lose the game.
Other things I've really enjoyed so far about this game are all of the different classes, and the different weapons and abilities they can use. It adds variety to combat, not every single average Joe can grab a sniper and use it you have to balance your team so you can quickly take out targets as well as make sure you can suppress and heal your guys.
The Bad
There are two big issues that made it really hard for me get into the game at first, the RNG can be really deterring and has also left me feeling more wronged by the game than anything. Nothing feels worse than having all your guys behind full cover with height advantage, and the one surprised enemy manages to hit one of your guys and kill him. It's a part of the game but it can get really frustrating, and it happens a lot.
The other really big issue I had with this game is the moving interface, there were too many times that I would try and tell my solider to move inside a truck, or a small encased area only to click outside of the truck, this ends up moving the right in front of the area I told him to go, putting him into a bad position and usually getting him killed.
Summery
Overall, this game is really good and well worth the price tag but I HIGHLY suggest that you get the Long War mod it adds a lot of missing weapons and items to the game, and just overall improves not he feel.

These kids clearly need to track down some OLDER films - not to mention read some comics (y'know, those things they used to make with PAPER) - and generally catch up on their "grindhouse" and "exploitation" history a little.
First of all, before Robert Rodriguez got involved with Machete, there was Grindhouse, in which there was a fake PREVIEW for Machete.  Before that, he directed a little film (which bears an equal amount of similarity to this game) called Desperado.  THAT was a sequel-of-sorts to his very modest FIRST film, called El Mariachi.  We could then go on to mention that some guy named Quentin Tarantino started making (by-and-largely BETTER) films around the same time of somewhat same-ish ilk, and if we REALLY wanted to get pedantic we could acknowledge that there have in fact been DECADES full of movies directed by guys with names like John Woo and Sam Peckinpah without whom, let's face it, NONE OF THIS would have existed.  Oh, and then there's comic writers and artists like Frank Miller, who not only co-directed the film adaptation of his Sin City comics (with a certain aforementioned Rodriguez character), but whose distinctive silhouetted-action art-style (which he's been doing for decades) is co-opted more than once in the course of...THIS VERY GAME!  Which we should probably start talking about, in all fairness (since this is supposed to be a review of it an' all).  SO ENOUGH WITH THE MACHETE REFERENCES ALREADY, OKAY?!  The SEVENTIES were FULL of movies which could just as readily be cited as influences to this game.  And action anti-heroes were rapidly firing twin pistols back in the EIGHTIES, boys and girls, in ASIAN movies no less!  Anyway, enough geriatric ranting, on with the review.

Shank is good.  REAL good.  And kinda hard.  Sometimes REAL hard.  But is it unique?  No.  Just as its INFLUENCES (see last paragraph, just in case you missed it) aren't exactly brand-new, neither is the gameplay.  But is there anything wrong with this, when the game is by-and-largely good old-fashioned 2D side-scrolling beat-'em-up FUN?!  OF COURSE THERE ISN'T!!  I mean, I don't play many of these games these days, but just 'cause an idea is OLD doesn't mean it's inherently "bad".  Sure, it adds some SEMI-modernisms, like oodles of bloodshed and endearingly cartoonish visuals, but it's basically the same-old, same-old, albiet done WELL.  And there ain't nuthin' wrong with that in MY book.  Apart from some slightly ♥♥♥♥♥♥/awkward platforming bits and a baffling inability to assign any of the buttons to the mouse if you choose to play with keyboard, there really isn't that much to complain about.

Well, okay, one thing.  I actually got the ♥♥♥♥♥ and threw in the towel on the chapter immediately preceding the final boss battle, because I honestly do lack the patience these days to keep fighting the same twenty-seven guys over and over and over again in order to yet yet again reach that one bit where I keep dying, and the game's sudden, stubborn lack of check-points was forcing me to do just that. Guess I should try the sequel some time, too...

Dino Run or Escape Extinction: The original Dino Run (also titled Escape Extinction) was released on the 30th April, 2008. In that time the game has been played over one hundred million times making it one of the most successful flash games ever developed.
The original is still widely available… for FREE!: Although Pixeljam promises that DX has made significant improvements over the original it’s a hard argument to justify purchasing this over playing the original flash games. There’s additional game play options, more levels and more hats in the DX version of the game. Of course, Pixeljam have taken complete advantage of what Steam can provide for players – achievements, full screen mode, Steamworks integration,
But what exactly is it? Dino Run bills itself as one of the first ever runner games. It’s certainly the first ever prehistoric runner game. The objective is to take your dino to the end of each level before the dreaded doomsday beats you to it. Once completely engulfed by doom your round is over. However, if you beat it to the end you get to continue. Of course, there are bonuses and traps along the way that will either aide you in your journey or hinder you. At the latter levels these traps can become immediately deadly. In the earlier levels they can still be deadly but you are given a little more leeway than you are later on. One of the best things about the game is that the levels are randomly generated. This avoids the pitfall that games can feel repetitive.
Multiplayer: One of the major selling points for Dino Run DX is the addition of multiplayer and the level sharing feature. The latter, especially, gives the game a much needed shot in the arm and extends the potential of the game almost limitlessly. Of course, when you have a daily peak of just 8 players and an all-time peak of 74 you really need to increase that for the title to see the best that it can be.
It really boils down to the value proposition: Are you a fan of Dino Run? Then this is a no brainer for you. You’ve likely already got the game or you didn’t know that it was on Steam – in which case hopefully I’ve brought it to your attention. If you haven’t played it before then I suggest you give the free flash version a try and if you like it by all means jump into the game and purchase it off of Steam. The value is there for fans of the game.

Pros:
* Authentic-looking, kilometers-long, badassfully manly space churches
* Immersive and destructive space battles
* Free DLC once for early adopters
* Customizeable ships (aethetics/appearance, abilities, skills, upgrades and crew)
* Gripping prologue and characters with excellent storytelling and voiceovers.
* Constant flow of events in battles require second-by-second change in tactics and inevitably develop ships and captains with their own colorful history.
* Responsive devs (hoping this will continue since this WILL BE a crucial selling point)
* Satisfying AI and control layout (shortcuts, pathfinding, auto-activating abilities available, engagement possibilities and tactics)
* Races (four currently: imperial navy, chaos, ork pirates and eldar corsairs) feel individually unique with potential for personalized warfare.
* Rewarding combat especially for truly brilliant tactics and strategizing; losing doesn't even feel bad.
* Great multiplayer potential
* Campaign holds excellent replayability potential and losing battles does not necessarily mean game over but rather tougher battles in the future.
* Key points in the game along with accomplishments in certain battles will allow Spire to change the whole course of the 12th Black Crusade and change certain details in the original storyline of the tabletop game lore.
* Can run with high graphics even on mid-level specs
* Great price, especially with 10% pre-order discount
* Fun classic ship-of-the-line battling and tactics: tacking and ramming (in space) amongst other things.
* Clear sense of multi and singleplayer segregation. Players have separate single and multiplayer fleet profiles that are progressed exclusively from each other. You don't need to be online 24/7.
Cons:
* Controls could use some user specialization and customization while some annoying problems occur. Abilities and commands have hotkeys and shortcuts but are not displayed even on tooltips, requires constant returns to the control options menu unless you memorize it all. Minor, but very tiring.
* Game modes may get repetitive depending on map variety and story content.
* Ships will blaze through minefields if you have overriding move orders.
* Current maps are cookie-cutter: space with random asteroid, station and cloud layout and background though this is to be expected, space isn't always necessarily creative.
* Soundtrack is fine, but nothing memorable so far (personal opinion)
* Lack of map/scenario editor reduces replayability (devs could've saved some funding since players would've done their job and uploaded new maps, themselves)
You won't find the word in the title but this is the universe of Warhammer 40000. The only constant is war, compassion is weakness and red things 'go fasta'. You are Captain Spire, the soon-to-be admiral of your own fleet. Danger looms over the endless horizons of space as duty calls for you to lay down your life for your Undying God-Emperor on His Golden Throne. You are but one of many, but yours is a role that will send waves and tremors across the vast reaches of the Gothic Sector. Your crew look to you for orders. They will not find you wanting. They MUST not find you wanting. Welcome to Battlefleet Gothic, admiral.
Now, for an in-depth detailing of pros and cons, I am deep into chapter 4 and have seen enough to give some solid feedback. Take note, however, that their may be a spoiler or to in here. First, characters, scripts, gameplay and storytelling remain outstanding. Cutscenes are used sparingly and, much like the exterminatus you will see in-game, are exacting, powerful, well-timed, grim and very, very, badass. Elements remain true to the grimdark machinations of the Warhammer 40K franchise. Battles can get tiring, but in the way that you must constantly adapt and counter every move your foes may make, lest you suffer crucial losses, or a decisive defeat. Pathfinding could use some fine-tuning, such as ships ramming space debris without care as well as an annoying problem were I can use the 'S' and 'D' keys to scroll across the map but leave the 'W' and 'A' keys unresponsive, though this may or may not be an isolated problem.
With regards to replayability (possible spoilers) certain game choices will allow you to alter history and deviate from the original warhammer lore. An early point comes whether or not you are able to keep two certain artifacts (mentioned at the beginning cinematic with abaddon) from chaos forces. You can also defy typical Imperial behavior and actually heed an eldar's warning. Then again, it is entirely up to you. Take note, that this will have crucial impact on enemy strength and races you go up against. Siding with eldar, for example, will ease their attacks and may stop them entirely.
For more cons, while game modes remain repetitive, there are enough variation and randomization that it doesn't get all that tiring, though objectives remain boringly linear: keep x from reaching y, go to a, keep b from stealing c, and so on. Ultimately, the battles main selling point is not the end of the journey, but how you get there, namely how you're gonna triumph against enemy fleets whilst keeping yours intact, on the way to accomplishing your objectives. The maps could use some more loving, but it's space, and other than some fancy looking backgrounds, you're not gonna find anything more besides rocks, space debris, and giant space cathedrals.
On the multiplayer side, most of the campaign experience carries over, save for the lack of a story and general direction. Ultimately the goal is to have fun, pitting yourself against human foes in, at most, 2V2 fights, though that experience in itself may see its own hiccups as automatic match-making can never really gauge tactical skills in order to truly pit a genuine novice against his own breed. You may find yourself fighting a strategy veteran, despite the fact that your levels are the same. In hindsight, though, that should be fun in its own way and trust me, 4 people against each other will be complicated enough. Still here's hoping for bigger fights, bigger maps, and even more ships in the future.
So, final thoughts, the game is spectacular considering its price, and while the campaign is as well told and as manly as they come, BGA's real attraction lies in human player pitted against human player. I honestly think you'll be spending the majority of your time in the multiplayer lobby while the campaigns potential for replays offers a substantial distraction. Progression in both multiplayer, random skirmish and campaign is linear, with branching elements restricted to individual ship specialty (maneuverability, firepower, etc.) with corresponding choices in terms of crew and upgrade loadout and distribution. And the real question: is it worth the price tag? By the Emperor, it is. Now if we could just take care of those minor cons.
Verdict: 40K/10 will ram with space cathedrals again.
P.S. The issue of the space marine DLC is in the end a matter of perspective, but comparing it to the fact that the first Dawn of War game had a basic four race selection (Space marines, chaos space marines, orks and eldar) it certainly seems fair enough by my standards. Ultimately, naval engagements are predominantly left to the imperial navy in canon warhammer lore, though that does not necessarily mean the space marines are pushovers (there's a reason they have 'space' in their name), it's just that the imperial navy are the space posterboys and would have a priority in being included first. Again, that's purely my opinion, so perhaps we should just be grateful the space marines WILL be coming soon, and with no extra charge at that, provided you buy the game soon.

This game....Wow. If you love 40K and love space battles....then you will love this.
In Battlefleet Gothic: Armada, you take command of a fleet of one of 4 races. As you do battle, your commander levels up, unlocking more ships with different abilities and loadouts. Not only does your commander have levels, but each of your ships have levels as well. Which each level, you are able to select improvements to the ship, whether it be active abilities, passive increases, or more guns! Each ship has a loadout that can be directly affected by what you choose to improve. So not only is the strategy in the battlefield, but also in fleet composition as well.
Now onto the battles...This is where the game really shines. Before the battle starts, it has a Total War deployment phase. You place your ships how you want, select their firing options, optimal firing range, and start the match. When playing, the enemy ships aren’t shown, but their location is. So if you decide to head to a target and it ends up not being their flagship, you may have to watch your flank for them, because if you are caught out of position, you could be in trouble. Each of the races’ ships have different attributes and skills which changes your strategy depending on which race you are in battle with.
This is definitely a fun and challenging game!

I'm mainly posting a review to combat all the negative attention this port is receiving.
Here's my impression so far: The game runs perfectly, the graphics are good, and I have experienced no issues at all. The gameplay feels spot on (which I'm assuming is what should matter in a fighting game) to me. Overall it's been a blast playing it so far. It's been years since I've played a DOA game, but this brings back fond memories of DOA2 through 4.
It doesn't have online play yet, which may influence your decision to buy, and it's missing a couple of minor graphical upgrades that the PS4 version has. Otherwise, it has the same textures and the same character roster. To be honest, I would never have noticed a difference if I hadn't gone and watched a video that outlined the subtle differences.
So, if you have a PS4, I suppose you could just get that version. But I'm assuming that many people who are looking to buy on Steam don't have a PS4. So in that case, this version is pretty great, despite a few quirks (no achievements, rumble, etc.). However, to be fair, those quirks are pretty much all laid out in writing on the game's Steam page anyway. And hey, can you play the PS4 version in 4K? A PC does have its advantages.
So, overall, it's been a great experience. The actual fighting and roster of characters are great. The only problem I have is that the game's sexuality is kinda ridiculous and I could personally do without it. However, I know some fans dig it. To each their own.
DLC prices are asinine, but I'm not planning on buying any of it. I actually hope no one does, at those prices.

The game itself has changed since it was first being developed, I heard the developers (previous developers) had worked on a weather system so dynamic and wonderful that it beat everything in the competition and even to this day is the best weather system to exist. Well, I'm not entirely sure If they are still using that system since last I heard someone told me the developers were doing some work for the military or something. Thus, new developers moved in on the project and it's now using the same template as ARK and it's quite different from what it used to be. That being said, the game doesn't necessarily need to turn into a piece of garbage, it can still be redeemed and become something rather enjoyable but some major changes need to be made. For starters, why am I barely hitting 30-40 fps on a GTX 1070? That's the recommended card so I'd expect to at least be above that, the reason I'm bringing this up is precisely because it's the using the same engine as ARK (we all know how that turned out).
The movement of the animals seems to be clunky, they'll walk into walls and even somehow get stuck inside of them which I can't even fathom. You'll spend most of your time waiting on the loading screen contemplating why you even bought this game in the first place, and when you finally get in you'll probably just get slapped by a character creation bug which prevents you from even making a character. But, I don't want to dog the game too much simply because it's literally ARK with a makeover, the game can be enjoyable and the vast amount of magic you can learn certainly could bring joy into the game. You can shapeshift, shoot fireballs and even tame some unimaginable creatures (some ripped straight from ARK iirc but not a lot) but the combat in general does need work, especially combat with melee weapons since that is just straight up crap.
If the server is PVP then players will just kill NPC's so you can't progress with that tutorial lady at the start, and you can't buy or sell stuff which is just annoying. Another thing you'll find on PVP servers is people just being slayed around the starting area, you'll honestly be hit by a fireball to the chin before you can even take your first step into the world.
I'm insanely skeptical about the game simply because of ARK, I bought that on day one and remember keeping it because I believed in the game getting future optimisations which never actually happened. I couldn't play it, and was unable to get a refund because I had waited too long. I was stuck with a game I couldn't play properly, and with developers who spent more time on DLC that wasn't needed than fixing the game they made. Such a shame really, because ARK was also a game I really wanted to enjoy.
Do I want to play this game? Yes, I really want to enjoy it but for now it's going to be refunded until further optimisations and updates come but I'm doubtful they will considering ARK's current state.
Do I recommend this game? No, I can't recommend the game in it's current state, all I can say is keep your eye on it and see what happens in the future.
My review may turn into a positive in the future, I'll probably buy it when I hear about an optimisation patch and update the review with the current state of the game during that time.

Despite the mixed reviews I decided to go ahead and make this purchase. I'm a huge fan of ARK Survival Evolved and figured this would at least be worth the initial price of $25. I played about 4 hours in single player and found the game to be a lot of fun. As with any survival based game, the first few hours are the most difficult and frustrating as you learn your way around the game and how to work with the mechanics and interface. However, despite the challenges starting out I think it is definitely worth playing.
The graphics are amazing and apart from a few instances where loading was occurring in the background I had no problems with stuttering or hitching. I think most of the "lag" problems people are complaining about are due to playing on one of the overly crowded official servers, or overestimating their gaming machine's ability to handle newer technology. Overall the gameplay itself has been smooth and seamless, and I have no complaints there.
Being early access there are obviously going to be bugs, and I found several already. But purchasing an early access game means you accept the fact that you are paying to alpha/beta test a game, and you WILL experience bugs and gameplay issues. You knew that going in, and to complain about bugs in an early access game is honestly a bit childish. Expect bugs, expect wipes, expect savegame corruption. These items all go hand in hand with testing an early access title.
In summary, I think Dark and Light has some amazing potential, and I look forward to seeing what the developers end up doing in the long run. I'm eager to keep playing and discovering what the game has to offer, and I think it was definitely $25 well spent!

I have this game only for a reason. I grew up with The Bluecoats ("Les Tuniques Bleues") because it was published in my country. The comic is narrating the story of Chesterfield, a sergeant who is fighting in the cavalry for the Union (and whose cousins chose to fight for the Confederates), Blutch, a corporal that searches to avoid the fights and the best friend of Chesterfield, Stark, the mad captain whose war cry is well known ("Chaaaaaaaargez"), etc..
Set in a comedy mode, this game is a strategy one, like I don't like them: a map where you're moving your units. Here, the aim is clearly for children. Because there are no real parameters to take into accounts apart random attacks from Mexicans or Native Americans, the thunderstorm moving from a state to another - and you can disable them. Some states have forts, linked by railways. When you connect two forts between each other, a train with gold will travel. Thanks to that gold, you can add units or use other items.
For a battle, you're in control of your calvary, infantry and artillery: it's up to you to destroy or frighten the enemy... or to be destroyed or to retreat. If you have to capture/defend a fort, you have to shoot enemies hiding and aiming at you, in a shooter mode. And if the train has to get through an enemy state (whether it's the South Train in one of your state or your train going into enemy territory), you have to reach the steam wagon to steal the gold if it's the enemy train, by avoiding obstacles or shooting bad guys and if you have to defend the train, you just click on the arrows to make your guys jump on the enemy.
You can choose your difficulty and the AI one. You can also choose a year: the map will be different. And also, the two players mode can allow you to play on the same computer. But well, I use this mode to train too.
Anyway, it's a perfect game for a kid... well, make sure to set the AI to the easy difficulty. If I understood well other players, it seems that the AI is quite the "cheater". I can attest that at a moment, despite being the strong one, I thought that it was the end for me. Thanks god, I've managed well with the minigames.

Blender is one of, if not the best free program I've ever used.
It's a 3d modeling program, kind of like the famous 3Ds Max, except it's not ridiculously overpriced. It just costs two easy payments of free. Despite not having some of 3Ds Max's advanced features, Blender still has several neat things you can do with it. It can be used to model 3d objects and create 3d animations. It can render realistic lighting and shadows with its built in Cycles rendering engine. It can be used to create simple or complex games with its built in game engine. And it can be used as a video editor and compositor, as an alternative to After Effects and Adobe Premier. One complaint I've heard quite often is that Blender has a very steep learning curve. There are plenty of tutorials that can be found through YouTube and Google on how to use this program, and all you have to do is watch them and learn.
If you have any interest in 3d animation, game development, video editing, or vfx compositing, then you might want to check out this program. You won't regret it.

A challenging, clunky, and surprisingly deep survival sim.
Best:
Atmospheric, procedural game world interspersed with story events and areas
Brutal but fair survival sim keeps you coming back, learning new tricks each time
Perks grant new info about the sim mechanics (eg playing Medical allows you to see your health bars)
Modding to allow saves or grant more perks adds greatly to already high replayability
Worst:
Not a lot of explaining done, only partial visibility of what's happening under the hood, mechanically. If you're the kind of optimizing player who needs to know how many units of hunger a gummibear diminishes, you'll be stuck spending some time on a poorly-maintained wiki looking for clues.
Awkward UI for a modern game
Unpredictable responses from game engine (ie autosort ground inventory when away from camp) discourages late-game experimentation
Inefficiency makes for a time-suck
My strong recommendation for NEO hinges on the opinion that the simple mechanics support a compelling emergent narrative. Repeatedly clicking the "kick when down" option in combat, each time seeing your fallen opponent gain increasingly grisly status conditions, packed a surprising emotional punch. And that's what this game is going for: drawing engaging story moments of wilderness and post-apocalyptic survival from austere gameplay elements. Never in a game have you been so happy to find a plastic bag, so afraid of a lone dog, so desperate for a drink of clean water. The very central crafting system, while inefficient, is fairly intuitive and visually interesting. After I'd played for a while, a central occupation became setting up camps decorated with the bones of my enemies. The story was interesting, though you'll have to play hard or get lucky to see all of it. Modding to allow saves broke the game in that it destroyed the haggard, roguelike grind for survival. How quickly, failing to plan ahead, you'll find yourself surrounded by a pack of dogs or caught out in the open at night makes every decision important, and the longer you survive the more is at stake. Without saves, however, I wasn't able to gather the resources necessary to explore the hacking and electronics mechanics, or to wholeheartedly play the story encounters, which are often deadly, without being afraid of losing my entire enterprise to a single bad decision. Then again, that's exactly what NEO is all about.

This is one of those games that makes you hate life and everything about it, but you get moments of amazing experiences that keep you looking for more.
The RNG will make you want to die, but instead of you dying it'll be most of your team.
One game I ran my shotgun guy to kill a unit, he had a 96% shot to hit the enemy was the last one on the map, he missed and then promptly died the next turn.
The Good
Gameplay wise, it's a great time. It's simplistic enough that there isn't any intense learning curve to sway away people that are trying to get into strategy games, but there's enough mechanically so that you have to think about positioning, and utilize every ability that your troops can obtain, suppression is probably my favorite because I'm really unlucky and that really drops the rate to hit.
On top of all of that you have to manage XCOM itself and make sure that you keep every area around the earth safe, or people will lose hope in XCOM and stop funding, if everyone leaves you lose the game.
Other things I've really enjoyed so far about this game are all of the different classes, and the different weapons and abilities they can use. It adds variety to combat, not every single average Joe can grab a sniper and use it you have to balance your team so you can quickly take out targets as well as make sure you can suppress and heal your guys.
The Bad
There are two big issues that made it really hard for me get into the game at first, the RNG can be really deterring and has also left me feeling more wronged by the game than anything. Nothing feels worse than having all your guys behind full cover with height advantage, and the one surprised enemy manages to hit one of your guys and kill him. It's a part of the game but it can get really frustrating, and it happens a lot.
The other really big issue I had with this game is the moving interface, there were too many times that I would try and tell my solider to move inside a truck, or a small encased area only to click outside of the truck, this ends up moving the right in front of the area I told him to go, putting him into a bad position and usually getting him killed.
Summery
Overall, this game is really good and well worth the price tag but I HIGHLY suggest that you get the Long War mod it adds a lot of missing weapons and items to the game, and just overall improves not he feel.

This is a 50/50 recommendation from me.  The dumbed-down AP mechanics and total lack of stealth really hurts the strategy.  Combine that with the absolute crap aim of your soldiers until they have ranked up quite a bit and you have a game that is about as "tactically satisfying" as winning a coin-flip.
+The destructible environment is great.  The EW expansion adds a few much-needed features (MEC troopers and gene mods are awesome) to the vanilla EU game.  It's XCOM - shooting aliens is fun.  I like the side-view base layout.
-The aim of your soldiers in the early-game is terrible.  You can plan great manuvers only to die terribly to RNG giving you the feeling that planning is pointless (which is bad for a strategy game).  There is no stealth : Once the enemy sees you, they get a free move into the best cover nearby.  The 2AP system means you get one attack (until you rank-up) and if it misses or doesn't kill, your soldier will die in the following turn (reinforcing the coin-flip feeling).
Overall, playing this game feels disappointing compared to its predecessor.  The game can be fun when it's not stomping on your best laid plans.  I feel like this is one of those so-so games that could have been great.

Ich bin ein riesiger Fan vom alten Original North&South.....ich habe das Original gespielt ohne ende. Mit meinem besten Kumpel damals. Stunden voller Spass.
Dann dieses Remake. Voller Hoffnung und noch mehr Vorfreude.......und nach 10 Minuten die totale Enttäuschung.
Wie kann man einen Klassiker so zugrunderichten?
Die Steuerung ist eigentlich nur noch der blanke Horror. Auf der Strategiekarte kann man seine Armeen nicht bewegen solange man im Vollbildmodus ist. Das ist echt kein Scherz.  Man muss in den Fenstermodus wechseln um seine Armeen bewegen zu können. Traurig, einfach nur traurig. Aber kommt noch besser.
Der taktische Kampf......seufz....wie kann man nur....heul.
Hier mal ein kleiner Tatsachenbericht von einem Gefecht:
Kampf beginnt. Tastatursteuerung? Fehlanzeige. Alles mit der Maus. Also Einheiten anklicken, aufs Ziel klicken, rest machen sie automatisch.........Ja, sollten sie zumindest. Ich nehme meine Infaterie, klicke auf den Punkt wo sie hinsollen. Wähle dann meine Kavallerie und geb ihnen die feindlichen Kanonen als Ziel. Will wieder zu meiner Infanterie wechseln da sie gleich einem Angriff ausgesetzt sind durch die gegnerischen Infanterie. Also draufgeklickt und....nichts. Meine noch immer ausgewählte Kavallerie bewegt sich plötzlich in Richtung meiner Infanterie, die grad niedergemetzelt wird durch den Beschuss der feindlichen Infanterie. Meine zurückballern? Häh, wieso auch.....pazifismus yeah! Meine Kavallerie fällt dem Kanonendonner zum Opfer und meine Geschütze wurden eh gleich niedergeschossen. Alles in allem hat das Gefecht nicht mal ne Minute gedauert.
Vorbei die Zeiten wo man beim original Klassiker die Cursortasten nutzen durfte um seine Soldaten selber zu steuern nur um dann die Leertaste zu vergewaltigen. Achja, was waren das noch für herrliche Zeiten wo Spiele genauso funktionierten wie sie sollten.
Selbst für 50 Cent würd ich das Spiel nicht mehr weiterempfehlen. Behaltet lieber die Erinnerungen an das Original, als sich die Hoffnung auf ein gutes Remake mit diesem Mist zu versauen. Der Name eines guten Spieles wurde mit diesem DING regelrecht durch die ♥♥♥♥e gezocken. Schade
R.I.P.

I played Dawn of War to death when it came out more than 11 years ago. I had just started work, and I had convinced my boss into letting me use a company discount to buy a computer. And then Dawn of War came out, and just blew me away.
This was the first real-time strategy game I'd played which was completely 3D. It was the first that seemed to reward an aggressive play-style, what with the capturing of resource points. It was also my first introduction to the grimdark Universe of Warhammer 40,000, and all of the myriad stories of the setting. Never mind the SEGA logo, this was THQ and Relic's baby, and we owe it to them to remember who was responsible, the good and the ill.
There have been a number of expansions (one dependent on this, and two standalone) and a very good sequel series that changed things around. There's been a lot of ♥♥♥♥♥ing about rule-changes and Eldar-favouring (I can't imagine why anyone would want to favour those pansies, but I guess it takes all sorts), but this game was great, and this was where Dawn of War started.
The story is, in hindsight, fairly typical of the Warhammer 40k Universe; human world faces threat, Space Marines arrive to kick♥♥♥♥♥ Eldar skulking around being cryptic and mysterious and whoops! It was a Chaos plot all along. But it's well-acted, with Gabriel Angelos being grim and dark.
You do owe it to yourself to play through all of the games (except maybe Soulstorm, though I have bought that as well) because the earlier games are solid RTS with multiple unique sides, and the later games are fairly fun squad-based tactical RTS games. Though I would recommend waiting for a sale to buy them all up.
The only real "problem" I have with Dawn of War is that it doesn't scale well to widescreen (though Dark Crusade and Soulstorm don't have that issue). However, the game is old enough that I can run it using the Intel video graphics rather than the NVIDIA, and I can run it windowed (which is better I think, for a game that came out before Full HD).

This is a good game let me tell you why as I recall the last moments of my last life:
I had kept this character alive and well for a good 15ish days when suddenly in the middle of nowhere he began vomiting. I was worried but I had some Antacids on me so I swallowed them and kept going unknowing of what was happening. about a day later I saw I had a disease called 'blue rot' it was stage three. Having no clue of what this was and fearing for my characters life I looked it up on the wiki. Turns out naturally I only had a 30% change to survive it but If I found a certain NPC in a certain place (I wont tell you here) Then I could be cured and immunized. the problem was that in 72 hours there was a 70% chance I would be dead. Panicked by this I began to search the map frantically to the point where I was running through a forest at night when something approached me... I searched and searched but couldn't find anything due to the low light conditions I was stuck in. Then suddenly I was slashed in the stomach by what was revealed to be a dogman (think of a werewolf with no human form.) Startled I took my equipped crowbar and smacked it in the face stunning him. This didn't come without a cost however as the dogman swung again causing my leg to start bleeding profusely. I saw that the beast was stunned took my opportunity and ran while I could through sheer luck I lost it.  Wearily I continued my search for this illusive NPC well into my second sleepless night when I saw them. My dogman problem had tripled. Three dogmen 20m away. I didn't want to use it but I saw no other option. I took out the only item of value I had (a pistol with a full mag) from my bag and began to shoot knowing that running was out of the question due to their speed. 6/7 of the shots hit the pack but they were starting to close the distance. I took my bow from by back dropping the pistol and began to unload all five of my arrows into them. One of the dogmen had collapsed due to the pain I had inflicted but that still left two. There was now only 5m between me and them, my two sleepless night had left me on the verge of collapsing and even if I somehow survived this the blue rot would likely kill me. I wanted to die a hero at least. I dropped everything but my trusty crowbar. I braced for impact then swung with all my might at their leader. I was immediately slashed, battered and bruised but I had nearly got the leader at least. It was then that my sleepless nights  combined with effectively a marathon got the better of me. My battered body unable to continue collapsed of sleep deprivation and there unconscious I was torn to pieces and devoured by dogmen.
This was only of of the epic moments of this life. From this game I have so many stories I could tell from wandering out of the cryo chamber for the first time to reveal the ruined world I was surrounded in to hunting a deer for an entire day with a single spear to turn its skin into a bag of which I hauled around the best cuts of meat I could get from it. This game is an experience and I recommend trying unless you don't like to read because to become really immersed then you need to read all the text they present to you.
