I'm amazed at the highly critical reviews around every triple A game to be released on steam. I'll put forth my two cents.
This game is my favorite 3D fighter. I own at least two dozen fighting games, mostly on console, including DOA5 for PS3. The gameplay flows well and looks incredible, with even counters looking fluid and realistic while other fighting games just implement general combo-breakers (nothing wrong with that, but the amount of fluidity speaks measures for the work and detail put into the game.)
The cast is wide and each character has a highly impressive selection of costumes, as well as the ability to make minor adjustments to each costume after choosing your character (Hair style, glasses, etc.) Everyone will be able to find costumes they like and are comfortable fighting in. If you're like me and are turned off by skimpy outfits and overly sexualized costumes, don't be scared off by the game's reputation, you'll find costumes that don't bother you, trust me.
While I recommend it highly in general, I do have to make a few warnings.
This game is gorgeous and as such, is incredibly demanding on your rig. I see a lot of people complaining about it not running well. The game runs perfectly for me as well as a friend of mine who plays on a laptop, but if your computer has trouble running some high-end games, this one probably won't run super well.
The online isn't up yet. Much like Resident Evil: Revelations 2, the online is disabled at launch, presumably so Tecmo-Koei can keep tabs on performance issues and patch in fixes before optimizing online play for the Steam servers. If you're a hardcore fighting gamer who plays online only, maybe it'd be best to wait, and then read some reviews on the netcode, as fighting game netcode can make or break a fighting game in the long run.
If you're looking for a new 3D fighter and have a very good computer, though, this one was a huge pleasant surprise for me when I first tried it on console, and I still enjoy it on PC. Some have complained about not liking the controller bindings, but please- you can adjust that in game. Options menu isn't that hard to find, people.
As of right now, there are currently some issues with saved games if you change your profile name. I'm expecting this to be fixed in an upcoming patch so I didn't mention it, but be warned, if you like to change your name a lot I suppose. I'll edit and remove this note when it's fixed.

I am a huge fan of the DOA franchise. That being said, my fanboyism in me is disappointed. However, I'll try to be fair here. My experience thus far with this pc port has been fairly positive.

Rig is as follows:
i7-4790
16GB ram
GTX 770 SLI
Windows 7 64 bit
I've suffered no framerate issues. Game runs just fine at a solid 60 fps with max settings.
My controllers have worked fine. I've used my Eightarc Fusion fightstick and Xbox 360 gamepad, both used the same control scheme as the console versions.
This is far from the worst port I've ever played. Everything has worked fine for me. (minus the online which who knows when that will get here). The gameplay is the solid fast paced fighting I know and love from the franchise. For those who have never played DOA before, it's a 3D fighter with a 3 button control scheme, much like Virtua Fighter. It's one of those easy to learn, hard to master sort of games with a pretty deep combat system. I have over 100 hours in ps3 version, and I can promise it's worth the effort you put in. The single player in this game isn't terrible, but you will begin to wish you were playing with somebody else. The story mode is basically a huge tutorial. It teaches you everything you'll need to know to get started. However, and I know this is subjective, I did not care for the story at all. So to keep yourself busy when you're not in training mode learning the 90+ moves every character has, you get the options of versus mode, arcade mode, survival mode, team fight, and time attack with tag team options. Survival mode is for those who really hate thier fingers. Arcade in my opinion is lacking, theres no character specific mini story to keep you going, just fight till you win and unlock those costumes. Time Attack is for speed freaks. Versus is one on one. And team fighting allows you to pick multiple characters to form a team, and then fight a team of the same size. And thats really all you get in this version, besides a replay function. Is that enough to keep yoiu satisfied? Well that's up to you. Oh, you also get breast motion options, which is pretty awesome.
I will now let my fanboyism talk about what I'm disappointed with. I wanted this to be the superior version of DOA. I wanted it to look the best, run the best, and just be total eye candy that took advantage of more powerful rigs. Well, I learned my lesson there. Delayed for a month for no real reason as far as I can tell. Also what's with goofy thing of not being able to save games if you're username has something other than letters or numbers in it? REALLY??? I'm really upset about the missing stages, which are awesome. Lastly, either I read it wrong somewhere or imagined it, but I was sure this version came with all previous DLC. And no it does not.
So to finish off, I hate to say it, but I cant recommend Last Round. At least not yet. When the online gets patched in, then yes, I say go for it. But for now, I would just play the waiting game and see what happens.

Dark and Light is the experience that I wanted from ARK but never got, finally being the game that properly merges survival and fantasy genres. The game is tough and forces you to work hard to fight the environment, unlike a lot of survival games that have a negligible PvE experience resulting in rampant KoSing just to have fun. The skill system is much improved over ARK's, with no skill points to spend you can truly master everything if you put the time into it. The map is huge and beautiful, teeming with diverse fantasy wildlife. Personally, the game runs great for me. Everything set to high/ultra and staying above 60fps
There are issues with the game. Namely, many people seem to be having serious performance issues. There is also some lag when harvesting resources which makes the game frustrating at times, like when you just want 1 wood but have to spend minutes waiting for the server to catch up. The game also suffers from the experience gap that ARK had where if you're a high level, you can just easily stomp over everyone lower than you due to having flying mounts, way better armor, and top-tier spells. Luckily, it seems like because of the difficulty of the game compared to other survivals, high level players are more willing to help you than hurt you. Overall, I highly recommend Dark and Light if you enjoy survival or fantasy games; it had a solid launch and is full of content, but still suffers from many of the problems that Early Access games tend to have (server lag, optimization).

Slick, varied and downright fun combat is really all this game is about. Sure, it has an attractive art style and an enjoyable (if somewhat cliché) soundtrack but its core is the 2D beat-em-up gameplay. Be sure you have a controller you can play with as I can't imagine playing this with the keyboard (I used a PS2 controller).
For me, the highlight of Shank is its boss fights. Each one has a unique weakness that you can take advantage of. However, if you want more of a challenge or can't figure out the weakness, you have the option to whittle them down with normal attacks. While there isn't a huge variety in the grunts that you'll fight, I never grew tired of them because you steadily unlock new weapons that reinvigorate things and quite simply, the game isn't long enough to start getting bored. It also helps that you have 6 different attacks, a dodge/block button and jumping at your disposal as you combo your way to victory. There are some platforming bits that got tiring but fortunately the developers were smart enough to keep those sections short.
The story is a very simple tale of revenge that is entirely forgettable but serves its purpose to drive the action forward. The voice acting is equally adequate without being distractingly bad nor anything noteworthy.
Given Shank's short length it's hard to recommend at full price. But on sale or packaged in something like a Humble Bundle it will surely entertain you for an afternoon or two.

I have discovered my true calling as a hobo, fighting off feral dogs to scavenge post-apocalyptic ruins for anything remotely valuable.
This game is quite good. It's actually very short, which is probably a good thing because it's so difficult. However, despite the amount of random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that seems to kill you in this game, I never had a death where that I couldn't see why it was my fault. The world is extremely harsh, but you'll mostly find out about the stuff that kills you early in the game, or it's common sense, so you won't get to the endgame only to be insta-killed unless YOU do something stupid. Just be aware that the minute you DO do anything stupid, you will probably die. This, together with the core gameplay around surviving, is what kept me coming back to the game, even after ragequitting in frustration and deciding to never play it again. The different systems around survival -health, scavenging, combat, crafting, character creation, bartering, and inventory - work together extremely well. I have a weakness for survival and sandbox games, especially rogue-like survival games, but I'm also very harsh on them. I have a lot of problems with games like Minecraft, Rust, Ark, Terraria, DayZ and more. NEO Scavenger has been the perfect survival experience for me though. It's not something to spend hundreds of hours on, no. Based on my playtime so far and the playtime of other reviewers, 70ish hours seems to be the cap before interest dives. That's when I felt like I had thoroughly learned how the game worked. What makes this an engaging experience is going from knowing nothing about the game to being able to take on any challenge it thows at you. Amazingly, it succeeds in being an experience both fantastic and realistic.
It's not perfect, of course. The story events and random events have some problems, but even though these choose-your-own-adventure style events can kill you, they're actually surprisingly lenient compared to the core mechanics of the game. You usually have to screw up pretty bad to get killed, and most frequently you just get a slap on the hand if you didn't choose exactly the right path through event. Since I died so much outside of the events, it was pretty fun to see how different paths and different character builds affected the outcome. Other than that, I personally couldn't care about the story and events very much. It's interesting, moderately good quality, and original. I normally love narrative and world-building in games, but in NEO Scavenger it took the backseat to the core gameplay. The only negative thing I can say about that is it could just use MORE. The art style, while flat, is exactly what it needs to be for the game, but everything definitely looks the same after only an hour or two. If there were a few more hex-types and some variation in textures, and especially if there was some physical depth, as in changes in elevation, to the terrain, it would be much more visually interesting. The item count is decent, but if there was just a bit more customization possible it would be awesome, and then every single npc wouldn't look identical. The map is actually quite large, and it can take a long time to get across it when you're looting everything that's even slightly lootable and fending off all manner of dangers along the way, but it could really use a few more unique locations with events tied to them, even though I said that's not what I'm here for. The character building is great: it really does feel like original Fallout and it totally determines what you can do and how you play, but for a system so deep it just feels so small. The world NEO Scavenger takes place in is very interesting, but outside of vague newspaper articles there's not actually all that much to explain it all. With a more cohesive and expansive lore, I could really get into this world. The story, like I said, is very short, and I frankly don't care that much about it; it's good enough for me. But it does have this interesting problem that unless you explore everything you can easily "complete" the story in just two "quests". It's pretty hard to tell what kind of story NEO Scavenger wants to tell, and how. I don't think it needs to be longer. With multiple paths and endings and the difficulty of the game it benefits from being short. But it does need a few more storytelling mechanics, and probably a better, more dense distribution of the story throughout the gameplay. As is, you play the core game and progress for a long while, and then you get a big chunk of wall-of-text story.
All in all, if you want a solid survival role-playing game, this is what you want. I think that for the type of people who enjoy this game you can expect as much as 70 hours of extremely engaging time with this game, which is definitely worth $15. Enjoy!

Did you enjoy the old browser game Dino Run? Dino Run DX is the latest game in the franchise.
In Dino Run DX you play as a dinosaur that is trying to avoid extinction. You must keep running in order to avoid the killer cloud of dust that is approaching quickly. I had some fun with Dino Run DX. At first I found the game to be kind of boring but it started to grow on me. Dino Run DX will mostly appeal to people that enjoy runner games. If you really enjoy runner games I think you should enjoy Dino Run DX and should consider picking it up. Otherwise I would maybe wait for a sale on the game.

I was and am a huge fan of the Age of Empires franchise. Their expansions always have been particularly good- Rise of Rome, The Conquerors, The Warchiefs, Asian Dynasty. I bought this game for one reason. To kill zombies. And this game gave me plenty of them to kill. The storyline was "ok" but the ending seriously sucked.
Then the DLC came out and I bought it as well. The dunebuggy is fun as hell to roll around in. But once again, the story was "ok" and the ending is total crap, either you become a zombie or you nuke everyone. But as far as fun and neat ways of killing zombies, this game is pretty good.

Note: I bought and played mostly on the GOG version of the game, hence why I have less than 2 hours in Steam. I probably logged over 100 hours.
Anyways...
What this game does right is giving you lots of options when it comes to survival. Too often survival games feel limited, like things you should be able to do easily in a real life situation just aren't available in game. A couple examples that come to mind:
- Need to boil something but don't have a cooking pot? Use a tin can!
- Need to make fire but don't have a lighter? Rub two sticks together or use sunlight and a piece of glass!
- Need a container to carry items but don't have a backpack? Use a plastic shopping bag!
- Need bandages? Rip clothes, get rags. Need clean bandages? Boil rags.
- Need string? Rip rags.
Nice features include:
- 'Building' your camp: pick an abandoned building with the appliances you need, place traps, leave a sleeping bag... Not a whole lot of options but you do feel like you have your own personal secure spot you can come back to.
- An engaging storyline that makes you want to find out about what happened to the world and yourself. An interesting lore as well.
- Lots of crafting options to get the stuff you need to survive.
- Skills that give you special abilities
- Pretty good learning curve: you'll have to keep trying at first until you learn the basics. Then you'll manage to survive fairly well, and you'll still have many more things to learn and discover. There's lots of stuff you'll have to figure out on your own (or you can use the wiki).
- Overall, enough content to keep you engaged for many hours.
- Low hardware requirements. Will probably run on that $200 laptop you bought to take notes in class (check the specs to be sure though).
Cons:
- The game is text-based with a graphical interface. Nothing is animated, few things are drawn, most is just described through text. The combat system especially takes some getting used too as well. It's very playable and some people like that style, but for some people it's a deal-breaker. So be warned.
- Only one save/permadeath (although you can easily circumvent that).
- Not being able to pick all skills can make the game feel limited, forcing you to play again to explore other things (you can mod the game to get all skills though).
- The randomness can be harsh sometimes and force you to restart many times before you'll get lucky, have a good start and actually get somewhere.
- Many random encounters don't have a "good" resolution to them, sometimes making you feel like the game just ties your hands excessively and won't let you try hard enough, or making you feel like your skills are useless. Some encounters can actually punish you severely, with no way for you to predict that your decisions will lead to a really bad outcome. This is in deep contrast with the rest of the game where you have so many options to accomplish what you want to do.
Overall I recommend it to people who enjoy the survival genre, have the patience to fail, learn and try again repeatedly, and who can overlook the game sometimes throwing you in tough situations without you being able to do anything about it. People who aren't so hardcore can just mod the game a bit to make it easier and can circumvent the one save/permadeath feature.

HOARD is a fun arcade-style game about building your loot hoard as a dragon. It's played from an overhead view on maps that look like that they are built on a tabletop. As a dragon, you fly around destroying structures and enemies, collecting gold, and returning it to your hoard. As you collect more gold, you can upgrade your dragon's stats. There are several game modes but they are all essentially based on this mechanic and all about obtaining the high score.
While this is all enjoyable, HOARD was clearly built around multiplayer (with both co-op and competitive modes) and playing by yourself to get a high score on the leaderboards gets boring very quickly. Unfortunately, there is no local multiplayer option and I was unable to find any games to join online. As a result, my wife and I couldn't play together and I had essentially experienced all the fun HOARD has to offer after just 15 minutes or so.
Overall, there's nothing wrong with HOARD. It's a good concept that's executed well and seems like it would be fun to play... if you could actually play it with anyone. But with a dead community, lack of local multiplayer, and a complete lack of support from the developer (which was bought out by Kings), there really isn't much reason to play this one. I can only recommend HOARD if you pick up multiple copies so you can play with friends.

This port is not finished, it's lacking content, and it's very buggy at the moment. I'm *hoping* that Team Ninja will get the PC port up to speed, at which point I will re-review. I'm really, really, hoping that patches are forthcoming (and soon). This is very sad for me, as this is my all time favorite fighting series and despite the over the top clevage bouncage, it's one of the smoothest fighters I've ever played.
Negatives:
- Not sure how to advance without a controller from the main screen
- If you tab out of the game (while in window mode), your controllers stop working (wired XBox 360 controller AND PS3 controller via motioninjoy) when you tab back in
- Visually it looks to be about the same as the PS3 version (which I own, and contrasted on the same display)
- No steam achievements
- No controller vibration
- Missing content (2 stages)
- Obviouslly it's missing online play
- Missing the engine used on the PS4/Xbox One
I did notice one review that stated you could not remap your controller. That is FALSE. You have 3 different schemas to pick from, and you can define your own custom scheme if you want.
Positives:
- The gameplay on this is silky smooth. It's much smoother than the PS3 version in both action and pro setups.
- Load times are almost non-existant, and they flow into one another very quickly (the biggest gripe I had with the PS3 version)
- The input lag seems to be much lower on the PC version vs the PS3 version, so a lot of the moves, combos, and juggles are much easier to pull off or rather, more accuate and allows you to actually pull them off now.
- Local multiplayer works flawlessly. Had 3 people playing at a team match locally, all with their own controller and we didn't notice so much as a hiccup.
General Information
- The gameplay is capped at 60fps
- The cutscenes are capped at 30fps
- To configure the game, right click on the game in the Steam client and choose config. That let's you set all the visual options.

Last year I decided I'd be a wise man and pre-order this undoubtedly top of the grade PC port of Dead or Alive 5 Last Round. I hadn't really played a Dead or Alive game since I was a lot younger, last one I played being 3 I think. The idea of owning the game that had some of gaming's most attractive character design and elaborate scenery enticed me very much. Essentially I'm a sucker for good character aesthetics.
Now, it had been a while since I actually played a DOA game. Most of my knowledge came from videos of other people playing and I bought this because I really... REALLY liked the look of it. Then I decided to hang around the community hub. There was outrage and intrigue, people were attacking each other about what features would be in and what wouldn't. "They'll make a crappy port" "Surely TK cares!"... Well, it only took the first delay of the game's release for me to raise my eyebrow on the whole situation.
Then it appeared. Only a few days after my birthday. I was excited, I stopped caring about all the features that were lost. Only... I didn't realize how much there actually was missing. My first thought was "Oh no" when I saw that the default use and enter command was "M" on the keyboard. I went straight into options and tried to go to the controller option but I instead got a very rude "RRRR" noise. I felt like I answered a question wrongly on a family panel show. It denied me access to the "change your bindings" menu. Of course, this didn't sink in at first. Only after about 12 attempts at pressing M on the damn thing did I realize that it was impossible.
I got my controller, plugged it in and restarted the game (because you have to restart in order to change controller type). I was going to try and play this safe. I hadn't played a DOA game in ages so I went into the training section and started the tutorial. Fairly straightforward. Then the combos happened...
OH MY ♥♥♥♥ING GOD THE ♥♥♥♥ING COMBOS HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥ I don't think I've ever been this angry with a game. I actually started swearing out loud at this ♥♥♥♥ing thing. Every single little movement on my controller was picked up. One of the combos needed me to go diagonally down so I tried. GUESS WHAT!? It went down, diagonal, right in a split second, breaking the combo. After a good 10 minutes of trying this I unplugged my controller and restarted the game... again. I thought to myself that playing with the keyboard has to be better than a glitchy controller. I started the tutorial from the beginning to get used to the new key bindings which were horrible. I felt like a goddamn T-Rex.
Combos... Back to this. With my keyboard, movements register more accurately so I tried. And tried. And tried.... Well it didn't matter that I perfectly produced the combo as it displayed, it still didn't ♥♥♥♥ing work. Realizing that this was near impossible I decided to go with the controller again... Plug in controller and restart game. After ages of swearing to myself and cursing the gods, I finally did it. Bliss. I did the ♥♥♥♥ing tutorial for combos.
Then came the test "Follow up with a critical burst"... Uh huh... Okay... ♥♥♥♥... This took 3 ♥♥♥♥ing tries because of how glitchy the controller input was. But I did it. I beat the enemy... Then came more combo tutorials... Yeah no, I quit out of that straight away. At this point I was so damn mad that I felt my blood pumping. One of the other kickers was how the stupid thing went down to 30 FPS every time a cutscene appeared. WHY!? I seriously don't get why it's capped like that for cutscenes. This is an issue present on the consoles versions too.
I decided to play the story and while it was very hard to follow, I, believe it or not, had fun. I didn't even need to button mash. The graphics, while not as good as the PS4 version (can't believe I actually said that) still were pretty good. The music the gameplay the everything... was actually great.
I guess what I'm trying to say is despite it's faults as a game and its faults as a port, there is still fun to be had.
At the end of the day, this is a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥port. The developers/publishers don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the PC audience but, hey, it could be hell of a lot worse...
So...
So...
So much worse...
But yeah I like it. Can't really recommend it for the average gamer though. It's like trying to knit a motherboard with wire.

Cons:

As owner of the original Dead or Alive 5 on Playstation 3 I was a little upset when Team Ninja announced DOA5 Ultimate and then when they announced Last Round since they did not give any options to either buy at a lower price/upgrade to the people who purhcased the original one. However, seeing that Last Round also came to PC and considering the fact that I did not purhcase Ultimate, I decided to give it a go and pre-order.
So far the game has run smoothly and I have encountered zero issues. The biggest problem right now with this game and all the negativity surrounding it is that it was not ported from either the Xbone or the PS4 versions and I still do not understand why Team Ninja made this decision. However, the game looks incredible and I've seen comparisons between the PS3/PS4 Xbox 360/Xbox One versions and the graphical change is barely noticeable, as well as the soft engine. Sure it'd be nice if TN would give us a port comparable to the current consoles as the PC is more than capable of running the game at the highest settings without issues. I hope that TN realizes this and gives us those missing features. I'm against practices like this as it was false adverstising on their part and shows how little effort may have been put into porting this game to PC. Online is not available and that really is a shame. For a game like this, not having online can really hurt. I don't really play online so the fact that it doesn't have it yet doesn't impact my enjoyment but I know that most people who play this game will want online multiplayer available asap.
That aside, the game is highly enjoyable, the fighters look incredible, the gameplay is smooth specially at 60fps/1080p. If you did not buy DOAU and your PC meets the minimim requirements, I say go for it and buy it, it is not a bad game by any means and the negative reviews seem to be more aimed at the fact of how the game was ported to PC. I for one will be enjoying the hell out of this game, the new fighters, the stages and the costumes (won't buy any DLC though, those prices are a joke). If you want a good fighting game on PC, go for it. Hopefully modders will enhance the game and TN will eventually patch it so we get what's missing.

This game while obviously early access, has many clear design problems which are not likely to be revisted in the polish phase. Let's make a quick comparison to ark, especially the early game portion. As survival games, your main early game goal is to set up a simple base with storage and a respawn. With a foundation this is only 3 structures, simple stuff right? In ark this is very easy to accomplish which lets you quickly move on to more entertaining challenges, such as dinos trying to eat you. In dark and light, this very basic setup instead of taking maybe 15 minutes, is going to take you many hours, as you have to grind much longer to even access these basic necessities.
The grind is obviously also not fun currently due to the complete lack of any polish, such as rabbits and sheep being almost impossible to hit with melee weapons. This means that most everyone who tries this game is going to drop it really fast. The horrendous spend 12 hours to tame this thing mechanic also got even worse, as now you need a location where you can build a feeding trough in order to tame creatures, and you can't build near other people's buildings. The ark style primitve equipment and the high power magic don't really mix thematically either, and I'm going to count that as bad design.
Right now all you are buying is a promise.

I've heard some people say they don't like FTL because it's too luck based but I can reliably win even on hard by knowing what to do. DISCLAIMER!!! Though I LOVE the DoA franchise I'm very definitely a casual fighter. Also this is my 1st DoA 5 game. I played a little of it on my friends 360 but this is the first 5 I've owned. Previously I've owned DoA 3 and 4 as well as the Xtreme games.
So lets start with the game play. It's as fluid as it's ever been. I'm not quite a button masher but I definitely don't know all the fancy moves. But so far the characters behave exactly as I'd expect and VERY similar to DoA 4. All the characters feel very different and so far the rock paper scissors game play works perfect. If you're a casual fighting fan like me this is definitely "pick up and play" fun.
For modes DAMN are there a ton of options! I've completed the story and played a little versus and tag yet I feel like I've really only just scratched the surface of what this game offers. The cutscenes are very entertaining and filled with action and intrigue. The characters are colorful and sexy and the dialog is fun. Versus has more pre-fight options than I've ever seen in a game. I love choosing between the hundreds of costumes and the many hairstyles. There are plenty of difficulty levels so you'll be able to find the exact challenge you want. You can deselect characters and maps from being used when you select "random" so you're always playing something you want. Just TONS of different ways to play this game.
Graphics are damned pretty as well. They're far from mind blowing but they are more than good enough. The art is fantastic and more than makes up for the lack of fancy visual effects. I'm running this game on max settings (1080p) with a GTX 760 and a AMD 8 core 4.0GHz CPU with 8 gigs of RAM and I easily get 60 FPS in matches with absolutely no dips at all. However the main menu and ALL cutscenes are capped at 30 FPS and the transition from fight to cutscene is jarring. Also I have experienced a crash.
There are LOTS of little things to unlock as you play the game such as titles and costumes. I'm not sure about the costume unlocking criteria but I've looked at some of the titles and they're very diverse and will make me play the game in different ways. To me this more than makes up for no Steam achievements and such as I'm unlocking stuff in game... the way it's supposed to be. That said there's really no reason they couldn't have costumes and titles as WELL as achievements like they do on consoles.
So far the game controls brilliantly with my 360 controller no setup or tweaking necessary. The menus and gameplay work all as expected but there is no rumble which is really disappointing.
And now for the unfortunate part which has been said a million times by other reviewers. The developers/publishers are greedy mother ****ers. They call this game the best experience yet it's lacking WAY too many features the console versions have including quite inexplicably many graphics features. Then they charge more than the freaking game itself for DLC that has absolutely NO impact on gameplay. No extra characters or maps... just costumes and that will run you over $90. Insane. And to top it off they've been VERY secretive about the PC version giving us nearly no info until the last second and absolutely no gameplay footage. Simply put they have been blatantly disrespectful and have lied directly.
My review is going to ignore the terrible way they've treated customers and focus completely on the product they shipped. And that product is simply freaking amazing for a long time casual DoA fan who hadn't purchased DoA 5 until this release. HIGHLY recommended.

The game is still just as fun as Quake Live before steam, and more importantly Quake 3. There is a bug with this game being "launched" even after you close out of it with steam, and connecting your Quake Live account with Steam is an irreversible process *see edit*; so if you're fine with the standalone client, then use that. But for those new to the game, you dont really have much to lose; the game is free, first of all. Fast-paced, adrenaline-fueled fun with a high skill ceiling is all this game is, and if you want that, there is no excuse to not download Quake Live. It also, being that the game runs on Idtech 3, can run on the oldest of computers. Definitely worth a shot for fans of the FPS genre.
Note: While I don't necessarily prefer the loadout system added to Quake Live, I do feel that it was a change needed to expand the audience of the game.. Does it benefit us that have been playing the game for years? Hell no. Does it allow newbies to have a much stronger foothold when first getting into the game? Hell yes. More players to frag is always better, IMHO.
Edit (5/22/2016}: So, they made the game pay to play. The game still has a healthy playerbase of about 1000 players during peak hours, and 450 during off peak. That makes Quake Live the most popular aFPS on Steam. If you're looking for the most populated aFPS, this is it. I still have very few complaints about the game, other than the lack of GNU/Linux support (understandable, but kind of a dickish move considering past support). It's also worth mentioning that there is no actual standalone client anymore, its Steam or nothing. As much as I enjoy Quake Live, I can't exactly recommend it to people that have never played an aFPS before. If you happen to have never played an aFPS before, then I would recommend that you try Warsow, Xonotic, or Cube 2: Sauerbraten (all freeware) to see if you like the subgenre. But if you know you like the subgenre, or you have tried one of the previously listed games and found yourself to like it, then do buy Quake Live. New players are always welcome.

SHANK! Shank shank shank!  Whenever I see this game I think of Borderlands and Moxxi's second husband and leader of the prison gang. The game pays homage to the Double Dragon/Streets of Rage style of gameplay, but ramps it up a notch to awesome.  This a solid beat-em-up with a variety of weapons at your disposal.  The fighting, after you beat the game, almost takes on a zen-like quality as you mash 'n slash your way through to the the final showdown with Cesar.
Graphics are hand-drawn style animations that are sharp, crisp, and fluid.  The game is fun to watch and even gives picture-in-picture style display to peek in on the action somewhere else.  The music is appropriate for the mood and will push along the story in a poignant but not overbearing way.
My only real complaints come in the controls department.  I find the handling to be a bit sticky, not as accurate as I would expect from the genre, especially with the wide range of moves at your disposal.  For example I would pounce on a person and start beating the hell out of them and while I'm on top of them I will either aim left or right and shoot to take out others nearby, but I have to be extra deliberate with the button presses for him not to shoot in the wrong direction.  The same could be said for dodging, juggling, and shooting up or down.  I hear they totally revamped the controls for the second and that fact alone is enough to drive me to play the sequel.
I managed to beat the game in under four hours, but with the achievements, modes and unlockables, you could easily spend a whole weekend with the game and get your money's worth.

Metro 2033 Redux is not merely an HD cash-grab. Far from it. There is simply no other way to enjoy this, admittedly already great, game. It would be wrong to even say that the biggest improvement over the original game is the visuals--though they are significantly better. The Redux version has a vastly improved stealth-combat system which makes playing as a 'ranger' with little ammo much more entertaining. Additionally, if you have a PC that can handle most of the games coming out these days, you will find there is a shocking performance improvement from the original game. Gone are most of the frame-skips which plagued combat and movement in the original game, it runs far smoother just as you may have experienced playing Last Light. I would assume Nvidia players will also experience even better visuals and particle effects with PhyX, but I cannot comment on that, owning an AMD card myself.
I must also disagree with those reviewers who have said the emphasis on lighting in the visual improvements makes the game less scary. For one, games are never quite as scary the second time round or thereafter. But more importantly, Metro was never scary for its abundance of pitch-black places. You always have a flashlight available within a second or two even if it needs recharging. The atmosphere of the post-apocalyptic Moscow Metro made the game 'scary' and gave it the mood so loved by the fans--the Redux's visuals only add to the level of immersion and therefore help to build the franchise's unique atmosphere. As somebody who has also read and very much enjoyed the novel by Dmitry Glukhovsky, I can also say that the contents of Artyom's 'notes' and a few other features in the game actually bring it much more in-line with the progress of the novel.
In short, the Metro franchise has become one of, if not *the* best FPS franchise on the market currently. Metro 2033 Redux brings to the original game the polish of Last Light while still maintaining so much of the atmosphere that made it seem the better game of the two. Now there is no doubt which of the two is superior. This is a must-play for fans of the original as well as people trying it for the first time--aside from perhaps the hardcore fan, there is no point in playing the original after this release. 9.5/10.

I figured with the Redux version that 4A games would bring us the game that they wanted to originally put out along with all of the enhancements, lessons learned over the years and new features their engine could bring to the table. Boy, this was not what I was expecting...
It’s surprising how many bugs still made it through to release. I encountered my fair share and also read about the others encountered on the forums. For example, in the original Metro 2033, the “Trolley Combat” level had a game-breaking bug where the scripted sequence could get completely broken. This required you to restart the level as you couldn’t progress forward anymore. Now, take the Redux version in the same level. There is a bug where if you entered the previous scripted sequence before the level with your night vision goggles on, the game will force them on before you enter the cart, making it nigh-impossible to kill enemies. Only solution to fixing this? Restarting the entire previous level all over and making certain to not put the night vision goggles on before the scripted sequence that causes the bug. I am baffled how these bugs (among others,  as the same script-breaking bug apparently exists in Trolley Combat. Nice.) made it to release. Especially when it involves the same level that was reported to be very buggy the first go around.
Sure, I’ll give them some credit. The graphical atmosphere is improved with more special effects and post-apocalyptic textures compared to the original. That’s pretty easy to see from the original with entire rooms made to look more decrepit and affected by the nuclear fallout. Texture texture quality is also significantly better than before. Facial animations don’t look so odd and dated either, though at times the characters look...look like they were transplanted poorly into new bodies. The Physics engine is also better and far less sensitive compared to its predecessor. UI also looks more modern and up-to-date though it gives less information than the previous game did. Not sure how they managed to pull that off.
I do disagree with their assertion that the lighting system, AI and weapon handling is better. Mutants feel far more bullet-spongy (even at Ranger difficulty levels) and there’s been some reports that hit-boxes aren’t as good as they used to be. I noticed how headshots at point blank range with a shotgun wouldn't kill the easier mutants. How it handles secondary weapons is a 180 in the wrong direction. Instead of your grenades, knives and other related weapons being easily accessible from keys 6-9, they stow them all away in a single key that is changed by holding tab and moving your mouse in the direction of the weapon you want to use. What. The. Heck. Doing this during combat is overly difficult. This is a consolitis change and I absolutely hate it. Additionally, the AI seems extremely random and unfocused in its thinking. I’ll have some attempts at the level where the AI will completely ignore me and go for the other NPCs around me. Other attempts will result in the entire horde of mutants zerging and overwhelming me. It feels extremely schizophrenic and if this is truly Last Light’s AI engine, I’m not looking forward to playing the sequel.
The stealth system is probably the worst change of the bunch. Instead of having a nuanced three-level stealth system, that at least gives you a chance to recover from almost being seen, it throws it all out for a binary in-stealth and no-stealth system. One little touch of light on you and you will be immediately spotted by the AI. Due to this, it seems like they had to dumb down the AI so that even if a human guard is five inches from your face, they won’t see you so long as you’re in the dark. It’s hilarious and sad at the same time.
This remake/redux is an avoid. If you want to experience the best of Metro 2033, the original is the better way to go. The graphics are better, sure, I can agree to that and the optimization is much better than the original. I can definitely agree with that assertion. But the downgraded stealth system, same amount (if not possibly more?) of bugs, less enjoyable combat and quirkyness caused by the port to the new engine doesn’t make it worth it. There are a other changes that I didn't talk about that don't fit well or bring the game down. I was willing to overlook some of these problems until I ran into the game crashing bugs. At which point, I figured I was better off investing my time into finishing the original rather than dealing with this port that could have used a few more rounds of QA and playtesting.

The good:
- It's atmospheric as sh*t.  You feel like you're in a city full of scary dead things.  It's scary when they swarm you for quite a while and nighttime also feels meaningful (if you get sloppy).
- Zombie combat is pretty satisfying.  And that's what we're all here for, I think.
Middle ground:
- Parkour'ing around is fun, but I wound up disabling fall damage because it doens't feel right to continually die to a missed click if you can all-but-fly around otherwise (once you get the grappling hook).  And since this came from console-land, I feel it's not quite as easy as it should be to do certain things.  Also, the grappling hook desperately needs its own keybinding, since it's shared with some other things you really want to use and you wind up constantly doing things like throwing a molotov cocktail at the point on a wall that you wanted to grapple to.
- The UI comes from console-land.  It's workable but mildly annoying.
Oh, come ON!:
- You have to solo the start of the game, so if you're just interested in co-op, like I was, prepare to do something else for a while.  This wasn't the end of the world, but at the END of the game, they did it again!  The final fight area is solo, so even though you were playing for tens of hours with your buddy, you won't get to finish it together.  Even worse, the finish is made up of a lot of "interactive cut-scenes," where you have to hit the right key at the right time as it flashes on the screen, for example.  You wind up dying a few times as you memorize it.  It's just so out-of-place from the rest of the game.
- The story and voice-acting are BAD.  I didn't believe my own character for a minute.  Certain things that I knew were going to happen at the start took painfully long to unfold.  I'll mention that the story is fairly bleak (lol), but I know a lot of you emo f*ckers are into that :p

I made it. I finally had made it big, and was loaded for bear.
$1,000 in my pockets, with bullets to spare. I was making my way back to the DMC, happier than you could even think. I had made plans. I was going to sell these spare bullets, and buy a real gun and maybe some night vison goggles. I was going to be unstopable, moreso than I already was. Hell, already people were running as soon as I got in the same area as they were.
Like a fool, I traveled at night, with nothing out to help me see. Suddenly, I was attacked. I took cover and laughed. "Probably some Bad Mutha trying to kill me, I'll show him," I thought as I readied my new-found bow, and fired into the night mist. The arrows wizzed by, missing anything that could possibly be near. Suddenly, a fist slammed into my face, and in that second I was able to make out my attacker. I wasn't lucky enough to get a Ba Mutha or a random looter, but instead my attacker wore a hospital gown. A Blue Frog.
I wasn't able to ready my crowbar quick enough, and found myself on the recieving end of a beat down. I managed to crack my crowbar on the man's head a few times, which would normally kill anyone else. At one point, the man went down, and I had a choice. I could have run, and possibly gotten out fine, but I was a fool.
"I've gotten so far. This jerkoff won't be the end of me," I thought to myself, as I readied the crowbar, intending for it to pierce the man's skull. Instead, I found myself back on the ground, the crowbar and bow out of my reach. The man had somehow gotten the advantage again, and as I found myself slowly losing my wits, blood, and for that matter my life, I only had one thought.
"I was so close. Why did I have to die like this?"

Just to open if you love strategy games you should already own this title, otherwise continue reading. XCOM is by far one of the best turn based strategy games on the market with a fantastic story that can be lost at any point adding an epic sense of urgency to your play through.
Graphics – The game sports a very smooth shell shaded look with an almost cartoonish feel somehow still keeping its dark tone and creepy atmosphere. There are a few buggy areas now and then with some textures not looking proper but they are few and far between and won’t effect your enjoyment at all.
Gameplay – Just as one would assume the game is played out in turns between yourself and the enemy. Actions are carried out by your squads whom are all fully customizable offering a deeper attachment to your team. On the battle field all sorts of things can come into play from cover advantage to target distance, armor, gun type, skills, and so on. You will need a good understanding of the way the game is played to stand a chance on the harder modes since the game can have a very steep learning curb if you’re new to the genre.
Story – Keeping spoilers out the game story is pretty simple with no crazy twists and turns. Invading aliens are out to get earth and you are called upon to spearhead the charge to fend of the oncoming threat. You won’t be alone though as the world’s best and brightest are at your back not to mention just about every country with money to back you. However if you aren’t up to the challenge key support countries can be lost permanently causing the games difficulty to increase, lose to many and the story is over for you.
Recommendation – Overall this is a must have even at full price especially if you’re the strategy type. Playing the game on an easy difficulty along with the full customizability of your squad, game changing options, and a good versus mode will keep you playing for plenty of hours.

A fantastic city builder with a good sense of humor revolving aroung Cold War Era politics. Tropico's Latin American flair and soundtrack make for a shockingly relaxing experience even as your island falls to chaos and poor management.

Be it communist or capitalist, progressive or strictly theocratic, Tropico allows you to build your nation as you please. The game is easy enough to make sure even new players are having fun while simultaneously giving vet players a challange with a variety of sliders and options to make your nation, economy, and poltiical scene more unstable. Combine that with the hilarious banter of your faction leaders as your island grows and Tropico is a game you can play over and over again.
Also, as a quick note, people seem to be especially angry about the login requirement. It should be noted this was an old relic from when the game had online features like downloadable custom scenarios and scoreboards. Despite them being no longer active (the game is fairly old as of this review) the game still stands the test of time as one of the best city simulators of the 2010s.

Dino Run is a simple to play, hard to master, very polished racing-ish game with simple but quite pretty pixel graphics!
The game has two modes: single player and multiplayer, and they have some differences.
In single player mode, you have 4 difficulties to choose from, which take you through a set of levels trying to race away from the apocalypse and to the safety-cavern at the end of the last level.  You can find secrets and achieve goals to earn DNA (exp), and at the end of a level you can increase your raptor's stats.  Those stats persist between runs, so you can keep strengthening your dino's acceleration, top speed, jumping height, and strength (to move things around) to better succeed at the levels.  You can also collect bones which count as a sort of currency, letting you buy a neat handful of unlocks such as wallpapers and the game's soundtrack.
Multiplayer pits you in a race to safety against other raptors.  It plays similarly to single player, but without the stats upgrading.  Instead, you have points you can gain, levels you can increase, which let you host higher-level races which give more points.  You can also unlock hats as you go!

If, like me, you played and enjoyed the original Tropico then this game needs no explanation: go out and pick it up. Tropico 4 takes everything good about the original, updates it and makes it even better.

If you’re new to the series then this game needs a little more explanation, although it’s similar to other city-building sims like SimCity. What makes Tropico unique is that, instead of playing as the mayor of a city, you’re the dictator of a small Caribbean island (mostly) during the Cold War. As such, there’s less managing the sewer or transportation system (although there is a little bit of that) and more balancing of relations with global powers, keeping your citizens happy and crushing revolutions.

What I also found refreshing about the Tropico series is it’s humor: this isn’t a game that takes itself too seriously, and in an age where so many games try to be funny, and so few succeed, that’s a huge plus. The only “downside” to this is that gamers looking for a really challenging, hardcore, city-building sim will need to look elsewhere.

Before any review of this game, people should be aware that it is being sold at the Playstation 4 price, but with less content. Here is a full list of what is missing/broken at the moment.
That's quite a bit to swallow... and should be enough reason for most people to avoid this game unless it's on sale or Team Ninja fixes it. Given the publisher track record with Dynasty Warriors though, it is doubtful anything missing is coming... except the promised online.
With that said, the game looks nice and runs very well. Anti-aliasing and higher resolutions go a long way visually... and the game has yet to lag or stutter for me during any matches (although the occasional cutscene will drop frames). If you have an Xbox controller, you're going to have problems. Using several different Xbox 360 controllers I was not able to map anything to the trigger buttons, and start is mapped to the right analog stick... there's currently no way to fix this. Using a PS3 Mad Catz Fightstick I was able to map any button though... so that means the game has full DirectInput support... but Xinput is busted right now.
I'm sure by now most of you have heard of the Dead or Alive series and know what you are in for in terms of characters and gameplay. I figured with the Redux version that 4A games would bring us the game that they wanted to originally put out along with all of the enhancements, lessons learned over the years and new features their engine could bring to the table. Boy, this was not what I was expecting...
It’s surprising how many bugs still made it through to release. I encountered my fair share and also read about the others encountered on the forums. For example, in the original Metro 2033, the “Trolley Combat” level had a game-breaking bug where the scripted sequence could get completely broken. This required you to restart the level as you couldn’t progress forward anymore. Now, take the Redux version in the same level. There is a bug where if you entered the previous scripted sequence before the level with your night vision goggles on, the game will force them on before you enter the cart, making it nigh-impossible to kill enemies. Only solution to fixing this? Restarting the entire previous level all over and making certain to not put the night vision goggles on before the scripted sequence that causes the bug. I am baffled how these bugs (among others,  as the same script-breaking bug apparently exists in Trolley Combat. Nice.) made it to release. Especially when it involves the same level that was reported to be very buggy the first go around.
Sure, I’ll give them some credit. The graphical atmosphere is improved with more special effects and post-apocalyptic textures compared to the original. That’s pretty easy to see from the original with entire rooms made to look more decrepit and affected by the nuclear fallout. Texture texture quality is also significantly better than before. Facial animations don’t look so odd and dated either, though at times the characters look...look like they were transplanted poorly into new bodies. The Physics engine is also better and far less sensitive compared to its predecessor. UI also looks more modern and up-to-date though it gives less information than the previous game did. Not sure how they managed to pull that off.
I do disagree with their assertion that the lighting system, AI and weapon handling is better. Mutants feel far more bullet-spongy (even at Ranger difficulty levels) and there’s been some reports that hit-boxes aren’t as good as they used to be. I noticed how headshots at point blank range with a shotgun wouldn't kill the easier mutants. How it handles secondary weapons is a 180 in the wrong direction. Instead of your grenades, knives and other related weapons being easily accessible from keys 6-9, they stow them all away in a single key that is changed by holding tab and moving your mouse in the direction of the weapon you want to use. What. The. Heck. Doing this during combat is overly difficult. This is a consolitis change and I absolutely hate it. Additionally, the AI seems extremely random and unfocused in its thinking. I’ll have some attempts at the level where the AI will completely ignore me and go for the other NPCs around me. Other attempts will result in the entire horde of mutants zerging and overwhelming me. It feels extremely schizophrenic and if this is truly Last Light’s AI engine, I’m not looking forward to playing the sequel.
The stealth system is probably the worst change of the bunch. Instead of having a nuanced three-level stealth system, that at least gives you a chance to recover from almost being seen, it throws it all out for a binary in-stealth and no-stealth system. One little touch of light on you and you will be immediately spotted by the AI. Due to this, it seems like they had to dumb down the AI so that even if a human guard is five inches from your face, they won’t see you so long as you’re in the dark. It’s hilarious and sad at the same time.
This remake/redux is an avoid. If you want to experience the best of Metro 2033, the original is the better way to go. The graphics are better, sure, I can agree to that and the optimization is much better than the original. I can definitely agree with that assertion. But the downgraded stealth system, same amount (if not possibly more?) of bugs, less enjoyable combat and quirkyness caused by the port to the new engine doesn’t make it worth it. There are a other changes that I didn't talk about that don't fit well or bring the game down. I was willing to overlook some of these problems until I ran into the game crashing bugs. At which point, I figured I was better off investing my time into finishing the original rather than dealing with this port that could have used a few more rounds of QA and playtesting.

If you haven’t played the original Metro 2033 then you will probably enjoy this Redux.  However anyone who’s played the original will be disappointed in this Redux.  The Redux incorporates all the bad parts of Last Light and turns this into a more linear shooter game that the original.
First of all, as pointed out by others, the lighting system is different.  The original colouring was mostly in brown tones and bathed in a soft yellow light which is what one would expect in tunnels where the artificial light sources are mainly incandescent and gas lights which tend to produce a strong yellow caste.  This yellow caste created a sombre mood and helped to provide a more intimate relationship between Artyom and his environment. Redux uses Last Light’s colouring scheme which creates an unnatural “blue” light as if the tunnels were bathed, not in incandescent lights, but harsh LED lights.  This blue caste looks unnatural and unconvincing and makes everything appear slightly brighter and therefore lessens the mood established in the original.  Also, similar to Last Light, is an over sharpening of all detail which tends to “delineate” everything making objects seem less natural.
The gameplay was too similar to Last Light’s gameplay, and to me, Last Light played more like Call of Duty game than a Metro 2033 game.  If anybody thought that the original Metro 2033 was too linear then the Redux is even worse.  You will notice this most when you are topside on the surface.  The Winged Demons play a much bigger role in the Redux and are constantly swooping overhead.  They are used to keep you on very short leash meaning you have to get from point A to point B quickly and I found that I couldn’t really explore the surface as much as I wanted to because of them.  It seemed to me that there was less exploring and stealth encouraged in this game and more fighting like Last Light (I played in Survival mode which was supposed to play like the original Metro 2033 so that was a surprise).
The character models are redone and they seem to have more of the plastic, mannequin look that the characters had in Last Light.  The Khan character is the Last Light version (the goofy Pirates of the Caribbean wannabe) not the original designed character.  Unfortunate, the superb, original voice for Artyom has been replaced with the same crappy, read directly from the script, Last Light version.  The Nosalises are the same hairy ones from Last Light and they always looked goofy to me.  Also making an appearance in the Redux are the sonic emitting Winged Nosalis from Last Light.
On the plus side the Redux is not entirely a scene for scene remake, there are minor differences and you will be exploring a few expanded areas.  Many of the original areas are slightly redone (landscape slightly different and rooms and buildings slight different) usually incorporating more detail or a redesign from the original.  So even if you recall the original quite well there will be some variation here and there.
Is the Redux worth the purchase? Because I owned the original I was able to pre-order the Redux at half price, so it was worth it.   If you never played the original the Redux is worth the full price.  There’s a lot of gameplay for your money and the graphics are top notch.  Besides nobody creates apocalyptic games like the Ukrainians (i.e. Metro 2033, Last Light and the S.T.A.K.L.E.R. series).
***Update***
I have just replayed the Redux months later and my opinion hasn't changed.  I will say that if you’re a Call of Duty fan or even Resident Evil fan (there's a big gloopy, slimy, bubbly monstrous thing near the end of the game that's right up the alley of Resident Evil so those fans should feel at home at that part) and like blasting things then the Redux is for you.  Also, for you Call of Duty and Resident Evil fans your AI partners that often accompany you on your travels actually fight alongside with you.  As a matter of fact I've sat back and let the AI do a lot of the shooting and killing of the creatures.  So you actually get useful companions.

As the game loads each time, you are instantly presented with a warning that you should be using a controller to play the game. This is unacceptable, as I've purchased it for PC, and I expect it to be played as such. Despite this misplaced excuse of a warning, Shank can be played and enjoyed with the keyboard. The controls and combinations aren't too pitiful, and you will be able to execute most of them as soon as you get used to how the mechanics work. The artwork is well done, in a comic book style setting. The voice acting is okay for what it is, but you should not expect them to be excellent. Even though the game is violent, the overall atmosphere is quite mild and cartoony. The story isn't very original nor is it interesting, but it does fit fine with the overall presentation and game play style. Even though Shank attempts to go back to the glory days of early to mid 90s Beat 'em ups, it comes off as unpolished and sometimes inadequate in some forced platforming elements. There is very little variety between the levels and enemies, and once you get acquainted with the moves, Shank gets increasingly repetitive in all aspects, and you will be hoping for a quick finish to the game. After a very short while, it all looks the same, feels the same, and plays the same. The unlocks don't add much at all, and there is very little to be gained with the weapons the game makes available to the player on a permanent basis as you progress through the story. The boss battles can often drag and do not offer any true challenge or difference in game play in comparison to the rest of the enemies. There is very little charm in Shank, in comparison to games of the same genre from earlier generations. It's button mashing without any skill or strategy whatsoever. The music and setting are akin to stereotypical Southwestern United States, and this provides the player with slight immersion to the theme, albeit a basic one. The general concept would have been better suited for a short animated film instead of a shallow and slightly subpar game. Tedious fight mechanics coupled with poorly designed boss battles makes for a forgettable and passable gaming experience.

This game reallhy isn't good gameplay-wise. The graphic style is nice. The vague story is a bad ripoff of Tarantino type revenge films. A mixed blessing is that it only takes 3 hours to beat. If it wasn't one of the cheapest games i've played since I had a NES, it probably only would have taken an hour and a half. The shortness of the game meant that I dealt with the frustration because I knew the end was in sight. If it was a 5-6 hour game, I probably would have quit after the first hour.
The combat system is just plain boring and too random. It feels like luck is almost as important as skill; sometimes regular hitting combos turn into grapples when you don't want them to, which gives other enemies an open shot at you. Different weapon combinations don't really have much effect other than a couple just being generally worse than others. Pretty much all difficulty comes from the game just throwing tons of enemies at you that throw grenades and shoot assault rifles rather than actually making the enemies smarter or requiring more skill.
Honestly, it feels like they prioritized the look and style and added the actual combat as an afterthought with no actual idea behind it other than it should look cool. Kung-fu on the NES has much better combat IMHO because it's 100% skill-based. There aren't any unavoidable deaths, your character reacts predictably and it's never cheap.
Certain levels have missles come at you from offscreen and pieces of ceiling fall on you, much too fast to be able to react to, which adds nothing but frustration and random deaths.
Pretty much all of the boss fights are glorified quicktime events. They all involve dodging and getting in the occasional hit that does next to no damage until the flashing "grapple now!" QTE graphic pops up, at which point your character does a specific attack animation. Each boss requires going through 4 of these QTE's to win. The devs got lazy, because even if you don't have a chainsaw or pistols equipped, your character wil still always use them for the QTE attacks.
To top it all off, the developers made the huge mistake of adding a bunch of terrible platforming, with a few notable areas where trial-and-error is the only option. The missles from offscreen appear in one stretch that is super frustrating, and at one point you actually have to shoot your guns at an offscreen enemy to prevent him from killing you mid-jump.
Anyways, I LOVED Mark of the Ninja, with a similar visual style by the same devs, because at it's core it's a great stealth game, but at Shank's core is a random button-masher of a fighter mixed with a horrible platformer.

This game is the closest a game has ever gotten to being "perfect" in every measurable standard.
It's so heart pounding that you won't even realize it's a turn-based strategy. Seriously, if you are turned off because it's turn-based, just give it a chance. When you sit there with 4 guys left, surrounded by 5 enemies, and you are sweating trying to think of how to fix it, the adrenaline surpasses any fast-pace scale Halo, CoD, or BF match. It's the crossing you fingers and sitting at the edge of your seat when you end your turn, hoping that you survive the alien's assault, that makes this game so invigorating. On harder difficulties you can really only play this game a few hours at a time or you can get burned out.
The game perfectly balances base management, combat, and nation relations in a way that they don't feel micromanaged and tedius, but feel like you are an actual commander walking around a base shouting orders to best affront this war. The things you do in combat actually impact the research you can do at base, which in turn impact your effectiveness in combat. It's all so perfectly intertwined.
Yes there are the occasional glitches, the camera does get a little annoying, and the UI does take some getting used to. As for a lot of complaints about it being Dark Souls level difficulty, I have one thing to say: if there was an actual alien invasion, do you think they'd go easy on us?

I would love to love this game. It has a fantastic presentation with a Mexican desert flavor, great animation, big boss fights, a plethora of different looking enemies and it is a 2D beat em up published EA (but people think its indie). Its just not fun. In an era full of Metroidvanias beat em ups such as Guacamelee, you will find Shank is more of a basic left to right sidescroller with very few ups and downs. There are no secret areas or even breakable walls with meat in them. If the original Castlevania had secrets, why not Shank?
The game has great controls, a quick melee button, strong melee button, a gun attack, a pounce button, grapple button, grenade button, block button and even a jump. It has everything that you'd ever want in a 2D beat em up. With all of that being said, it feels so monotonous. Your attacks feel very weak and each enemy takes an exorbitant amount of hits. The enemies are pretty smart, they'll block and roll through you to sandwich you between enemies. If they have enough distance, they'll pull a gun out and shoot. While there are a lot of different looking enemies, they all pretty much fall into a few categories. Standard foot soldiers, big brawlers, weapon users and dogs.
The game is very forgiving on normal mode. There are no lives, you just respawn pretty close to where you died. It is a welcome decision to do so. Of course, there is a hard mode too.
The problem with the game is that it gets dull really quick especially when you have the same attacks from start to finish. You gain no new abilities to keep things fresh. There are a few extra guns and strong melee weapons that you can use, but nothing feels like an upgrade, just a sidegrade. The bosses boil down to finding a weakness to exploit, pouncing on them and stabbing them.
There are light traversals to break up combat for a mere two seconds, such as climbing a brief fall, briefly hanging from a pipe or jumping platform to platform, but it just needed more of a break from the monotony of combat. It is so odd that there can be so much diversity in combat, and yet you can still just button mash your way to victory. Also what does it say about Shank's combat when the next game the creators made after Shank 2 was a stealth game? Another issue with the game is the blah music.
There is co-op to improve the experience, but having a friend around can improve any experience. I'm from an era of Nintendo and Super Nintendo beat em ups that have less combat options, but more enemy diversity. I just couldn't get into Shank.
Finally, there will be plenty of sales if not game bundles with Shank 1 and 2. Just wait for the combo pack sales with $5 for both.

So, I see a lot of negative reviews here, but I don't think that's entirely fair and here's why: this is a good game and should be viewed on its own merits rather than the behaviour of its publisher.
Graphics:
Generally nice. Fluid 60fps gameplay which isn't too demanding on systems. The high resolution options and the availability of super sampled anti-aliasing make this game sharper looking than any of the console versions. Admittedly, it would be nice to be able to select an arbitrary resolution, so hopefully this will be patched in. The texture work is pretty solid all round too, although, being a last gen console titile originally, it doesn't compete with the latest games.
Controls:
Quick and responsive. The game plays well, but it does have mapping issues with some controllers and could really benefit from the ability to remap all button, e.g. start and back.
Gameplay:
It's a Dead or Alive game. Fast, responsive fighting has always been the trademark of this series, and this version appears no different. It also has the largest character roster in the series history, with a mix of new characters alongside stalwarts from the DoA and Virtua Fighter series. If you're a fan of the series then you can't really go wrong here.
Caveats:
The game is missing features from the PS4 version. Two stages are gone and so is the "Soft Engine", i.e. the enhanced boob physics. Also not present at launch is the online multiplayer mode, which Team Ninja have promised to patch in and is the biggest flaw at present.
Overall:
While not quite as good as could be hoped, and despite Tecmo's woeful lack of communication pre-release, this is a solid port of an excellent game. It has plenty to recommend for fight fans, if you can overlook the missing features.

Pros and cons and then a full review:
Pros
+the same fun combat that has been in DOA since the beginning with new stage interactions that can be turned off
+Runs well (on my machine, others seem to be having problems)
+A decent enough story for a fighting game
+Plenty of modes such as survival, story, arcade, vs, etc.
+Several costumes for each character at the start and many more to  unlock through gameplay
+Great graphics on the fighters, chlothing and shadows
Cons
-No online multiplayer at launch, and its not scheduled until June/July when the playerbase will already be gone
-The subserface scattering added in the ps4/xb1 versions is not here
-2 stages were cut from the game
-The textures on the arenas and in story cutscenes can be pretty low res
-graphics options are done through a launcher and not in-game
-the pause/menu button is mapped to pushing in the right stick (on game pad) and can't be remapped.
And heres an actual review
tldr: The game is great but has no online mode.
Almost all of the negative reviews for this game are because the game is a port between the graphical quality of the ps3 and ps4 version, not a prettier version of either like it should be. While this is true, I feel that this game should be viewed in its own right and not compared to other versions of itself as it is the only version available on pc. As such I won't review the practices of the developer or continue comparing this game to versions on other consoles.
DOA 5 is, at its core, a great fighting experience neutered of the life and soul  of what makes many fighting  games have staying power: an online mode. This is a shame as the game is very fun, and in my opinion is the best of the series. It has a large character roster, each with many costumes to unlock (I believe there are 500 or so costumes split between 30 or so fighters). It has a decent enough story mode that pushes you from fight to fight, a great tutorial and practice mode, and all of the other offline modes you have come to expect from fighting games these days.
Each of these modes shows off the excellent fighting mechanics and engine of the game. There really is no other game that plays anything like DOA. For those unaware, the game gives you four main buttons:punch, kick, hold and grab. Rather than being a game about mashing in combos or learning how to throw magic like in many other fighters, DOA is about timing your strikes and reading your opponent. You won't make it past easy in the arcade without timing your combos with throws and counter-grabs. And this is not an easy  game to master. In fact, it is probably the most difficult fighter to get truly good at, because you aren't just using muscle memory to toss combos, you are actually trying to read your opponent and do a proper counter.
Ultimately I feel this is a great game, though  slightly incomplete. I give it a positive review because I like it, and would reccomend it to anybody who wants to play alone or locally with another player (which this does allow); However, some may not find this worth the money without an online mode, so I cannot reccomend for all. Even when the online is patched in, there is no telling if it will be laggy or if there will be anybody playing it still.

So tired of reading the negative reviews on this game.  At the end of the day it is EA, you buy the game (at a reduced price) knowing you are supporting its development and knowing that there are going to be bugs and issues with the game that are going to make some aspects unplayable.
To compare to other games and complain about it being a clone of this game or a clone of that game is absolutely ridiculous, it's a frigging survival/sandbox multiplayer... Newsflash, they all require gather resources, craft equipment/weapons/bases etc.  You get hungry, you get thirsty in all of them, so basically they're all the same thing with individual tweaks.  As for it being a clone of ARK, good frigging job, Ark is a sound and very enjoyable game to play.
As for a review of D&L, on official servers the game is struggling right now with lag issues and the standard 10 year old griefers out to cause as much hassle as possible.  As a pretty computer illiterate old man, I've been able to set up a private dedicated server and am currently having a blast with my youngest son.
Although the quest system is currently bugged with a certain earn gold quest holding up progression, on review of the task lines, thing look to have some decent depth and are not resorting to the kill x amount of this creature, rinse and repeat quest lines of some MMO's, what quests we were able to follow were intuitive and brought on knowledge of the game nicely.
Yes the tutorial popups, pop down way too quick, however by using a couple of brain cells you realise you can open the task menu and read the text you missed in there, not sure if that's the case for every pop up, but it certainly ios for the important stuff.
The graphics are magnificent, vibrant and full of depth, I'm running at a sound 50-60FPS on high settings with a rig that is about 18 months old, so by no means the best processor or gpu, my son's pc is my old hand me down and is about 5 years old (one of the first Aser first i7 models released) and although it has a 1070 gpu installed there is very little else upgraded and it runs the game just fine.
In summary, keep away from official servers for now until a few more patches get the game optimised, play with friends as it certainly makes for a more enjoyable experience and finally play with an open mind knowing that it is an EA game in its first week open to the masses (regardless of how long it has been in development).
If I could leave you with one final thought, can anyone give a true review of a game if they've played it for less than 5 hours? I think not.  People can be to quick to criticise and throw negative reviews around which damage a games reputation and stunt its growth, the game in its current state is worth every penny of the £19.08 I paid, and I look forward to many more hours of adventure and discovery in the near future ENJOY!!!
