TLDR: If you've got a sour taste in your mouth from Mighty Number 9, this is the fix for you.
The best thing I can really say to get this review started is that if you're a fan of any sort of Mega Man styled game, you can't go wrong with this one. The general premise is that the Robot Masters are witches, there's a mysterious plot that has to do with a great magician's soul from long ago, and... Well, this is the sort of game that doesn't really -need- a plot. By all means, it's here and translated to English, but you can pretty much get right by without it as you can choose to play either with the text and cutscenes, or without in an Arcade Mode.
The game itself is easy to pick up and play if you know how the old Mega Man games worked. Eight bosses, eight stages, pick whom you want to take down first. The controls are rather simple, with two primary buttons for jumping and shooting, a Previous/Next weapon swap, as well as MM1-6 pause-selection. However, keep in mind that pressing Escape at any point resets the game akin to an old NES reset button, so be aware. Each boss has their own special weapon which can be super-effective against another, yadda-yadda. Seriously. It's classic Megaman here. Once you clear the eight primary stages, the Castle stages open up, and you go through a gauntlet where your special weapons don't recharge after each stage and careful management becomes key.
If I had to really pick one highlight, it's going to be the soundtrack. I remember quite a few of these tunes are the type that you'll be humming occasionally, and even years after I played the original I still had some of the final boss themes playing out in my memory rather vividly. You can't go wrong with that type of catchiness.
If I had to point out a major flaw in the game, it would have to be the difficulty curve. Some stages and bosses are very clearly more difficult in nature, especially if you're going in blind unlike myself. While the curve does even out once you hit the Castle stages to be somewhat more predictable in nature, it's still going to be a bit jarring. The stages themselves are for the most part vastly easier than the bosses.
There's a good bit of replay value here as well, for those whom worry that the somewhat short game might have one hesitant to purchase this. A Saved-Replay feature lets you watch your own runs, encouraging you to learn from mistakes and get faster at the game. There's also a second campaign featuring one of the boss characters that you can play as, but you get told how to access it only once you defeat the final boss after the credits roll. It even has a bit of humor about itself with Game Over screens customized for each stage, usually a jest involving another game or franchise, so even if you fail you can still grin about it. Honestly, this game was great a few years ago, and it's still plenty of fun today.

Gameplay 5/5: A Mario-inspired puzzle platformer with a rewind mechanic that changes enough from world to world to stay fresh, but always remains intuitive.  Creative puzzle design makes the most of the game mechanics to require both clever thinking and precision maneuvering.
Art 2/2: Beautifully designed worlds, backgrounds with multiple layers of depth, and a score of gorgeous Celtic folk string compositions that distort along with time make this game atmospherically engaging as its gameplay.
Story 1.25/2: The elements of the story are creative, but are divulged in an overwrought and cryptic manner that is more pretentious than poetic.
Technical Support .25/1: Game is forced in 1280x720 fullscreen mode.  Supports XBox 360 controllers and keyboard, but   no support for other controllers or rebinding keys.  The keyboard controls also lose the unique buttons for using doors or the magic ring, making any workaround with Joy2Key or Xpadder imperfect.
Total 8.5/10: Minor problems can't detract from what is one of the most beautiful indie games to date.  Highly recommended.

Disclaimer: don't be fooled by the 1.2 hrs play time. I played the game while having no internet connection but logged in on steam on another pc during that time, so steam seems to have messed it up a bit but I finished it after about 10 hours. Also I didn't play the original Metro 2033 game so I won't refer to it in this review. On a side note, I played the game on non-hardcore ranger mode.
Overall I had a pleasant experience and the gloomy atmosphere pulled me in for several hours straight (I tend to get bored easily, so that's a good thing).
Technical stuff: I think I don't need to say much about the graphical fidelity... 4A Games did a fantastic job here. High res textures, incredible lighting and well designed, detailed environments. They also optimized the game quite well: I was able to play it on maxed out settings on an i5 2500K with a Radeon 7950 OC and had 40-60+ fps depending on the scene. The audio was done very well: music and ambient tunes always fit, weapons sound great and monsters scare the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you with their howls and screams. I decided to play the game with russian voiceovers because the english voice actors are just awful. Not just in this game but the Stalker series suffered from this as well. Be warned though: the game has no subtitles for ambient chatter, which kind of removes some of the immersion while spending time in the populated metro stations.
Story: Without having read the book I can say the storyline is pretty decent but nothing too special. Even though it offers a very unique setting, I think there is some wasted potential. The characters are rather bland: Khan for example plays a large role as the mysterious, spiritual guy who helps you reach your destination but at no point did I feel the urge to know more about his background or personality. Other characters such as Hunter, Ulman or Bourbon are pretty much forgettable.
The game does have a mysterious, even fantastic touch to it but they should have put more effort into fleshing out those characters and add more notes and recordings to find and people to talk to.
Gameplay: overall it was a smooth playthrough with some minor hickups. For example there were some parts in the game where I had a hard time knowing where to go next (this might be due to the missing hints as part of the ranger mode). Don't be fooled by this notion though, the level design is rather restrictive and does not leave much room for exploring but there is usually an alternate route for sneaky players.
Which brings me to my next complaint: the AI of humans leaves a lot to desire. They don't react well to their surroundings. You can knock out or stealth kill enemies just a few feet away from their comrades, remove light bulbs with no reaction whatsoever or sit behind cover without them making use of grenades or flanking maneuvers. It's not game breaking but makes firefights much less fun than sneaking even though that's way too easy, too. Throwing knives kill all but heavily armored enemies instantly as well as melee attacks (even from the front).
Fighting mutants is more challenging as you can't sneak past them most of the time. They are fast and unrelenting and really keep you on the edge.
The weapons are well designed and customizable and go beyond your typical generic military shooter crap. They really are what you'd expect to see in a post-apocalyptic world without being over the top.
To wrap it up, I reccommend this game to anyone who missed out on the original. It has some flaws but those are easily forgotten while crawling through the dark and filth ridden tunnels of the metro.

The game feels like a cross between half life and the stalker series, Half life for its linear storytelling nature and atmosphere. And S.T.A.L.K.E.R. for its combat style and setting of the game.
But even that doesn't fully describe how pretty and immersive this game is, oftentimes inbetween levels you'll walk through a metro station filled with people that live there. And it feels like they actually live there, farming pigs and living their daily lives out under the aboveground wasteland. It really pulls you into the game world.
One thing this game does very well is the sound design and the AI, I highly reccomend playing this game alone with headphones for best effect. Oftentimes you're alone on the surface with nothing but the growl of monsters nearby and the sound of your gas mask ticking its way down to expiration. And then out of a hole in the wall behind you jumps a dog sized rodent creature to bite at your heels and then run away the second you turn to look at it. Or you'll be sneaking your way around bandits hearing them talk idly unaware of your presence as you attempt to line up your sights for one silent shot.
I would like to note that the level design is incredible it feels like a real destroyed world and avoids the use of invisible walls. There are even places where it looks like the development team built a normal building and then destroyed it to make an interesting level so there are all kinds of places where its clear there WERE other ways to go but they've since been destroyed or broken. I feel that lends a lot the credibility of the world at large.
I like this game a lot, the shooting is fun, its open ended, you can even get through some parts without killing anybody. Or you could stealthily snipe out people from a distance, or just go rambo on em. Its really up to you and thats what I like the most about this game it leaves it open to replayabilty to find the things you've missed.
However the redux isn't without its problems, most notably it doesn't give you a tutorial on the Metro Last Light control scheme and thats important because you may never know that you can wipe off your gas mask or switch throwable objects, or burn spiderwebs with your lighter(that last one can actually get you stuck ingame if you don't know how to do it).

Random chance will dictate the path you will take and the experience you have - making most of your sessions unique from each other even if you become familiar with all the game's content out of sequence.

This game is one of the finest RTS games ever to grace the genre. The game truly holds well even to this day, well over a decade afters its initial release. The game offers an interested and very fun singleplayer campaign where you play as the  Blood Ravens Space Marine chapter as they fight against a massive Ork force on an imperial planet. It's up to you to use your brain and tactical sense to destroy the Ork menace. But as time goes on the forces of Chaos arrive as well as the elusive Eldar and the stakes only begin to rise. The gameplay is solid. From the army commands as well as base building and management. Unlike other, older, RTS games the way you gain recources is by capturing and holding points that are around the battlemap making those areas complete hotspots for some epic large battles. You get to command large armies and pit them against other large armies, unique units and buildings per factions (four factions are available in the game), an army painter (very basic, but still fun to use custom armies in skirmish), and overall the game has a lot to offer. There are some downsides sadly, but these are more in the technical side rather than the game itself, the game does not support 16:9 resolutions, but with some mods you are able to force a 16:9 resolution in the game, but the mini map tends to bug out. The unit path finding can be a bit wonky at times as well and artillery units can be a real pain if you don't know how to properly use them, but overall nothing too serious, just minor inconveniences. This is a great game for both RTS fans and Warhammer 40k fans or if you're a fan of both, you're doing yourself an unjustice by not owning and playing this great game.

If games like Civilization and Endless Space suffer from the 'one more turn' obsession, XCOM one-ups that notion with the 'one more operation' syndrome.
You, commander, are tasked with leading a multinational secret organization created to thwart an alien invasion of the Earth, just like in the old games. You hire soldiers, scientists and technicians, build up a secret underground base and set out on missions all over the world to manage crisises and keep the aliens in check. It's a damn tense and fun game of cat and mouse.
Tip: name all your soldiers, at least the first ten or so, after your friends. It really adds to the excitement of the game to see which ones survive and what they become as the game progresses.
Thee turn-based combat, while fairly simplistic, feel tactical enough to be considered an interesting puzzle every time, and the varying enemy unit compositions that evolve throughout the game keep you on your toes. In fact it is this progression and escalation that makes the game so very exciting. You start off competent and capable, then get overwhelmed by a more powerful opponent only to scramble to improve yourself so that you can overcome the ever-greater challenges on the battlefield.
It is great! I love it!

Neo Scavenger is a fantastic indie turn-based, survival, strategy, roguelike game played on a hex map.
The game is very punishing and largely based apon RNG but also requires a lot of pre-planning strategy and skill to complete. Every playthrough randomizes many locations in the game and enemy spawns, allowing the game to be very replay-able. The learning curve may be steep at first but once you have the basic mechanics down it's just a matter of playing it safe, but the game can be very deep with a great skill system opening up many different ways of surviving the post apocolyptic wasteland.
+ Fantastic survival mechanics ranging from your usual hunger/thirst to illness , fatigue and comfort.
+ Challenging turn based battle system based around your skills and condition.
+ A large variaty of items.
+ Randomised loot, enemy and location spawns on every playthrough making it very fresh.
+ A good story with lots of hidden treasures and ways to complete.
+ Great stealth mechanics.
+ A hidden reputation system.
- The RNG can be absolutely infuriating sometimes, but that's the way of the roguelike.
- There are very limited animations, the game is mostly text based.
- At first the game is not very user friendly and the UI may be difficult to navigate. ( particularly campsites )
- Extremely difficult to complete on your first few runs, requiring you to playthrough once or twice to learn which options to avoid.
- Limited options for character creation.
- Very limited building options for shelter / bases.
All-in i would deffinitely recommend this game if you are into hardcore roguelikes, there is a lot of depth beneath the surface and the randomization and character skill system brings a variety of ways to play the game. If however, you are looking for an easy survival game to build up your own haven and sit back surviving the nights i would stay clear as NEO Scavenger can be very punishing at the worst of times.

Brains are basically the supports, they can place down health "generators" and ammo "generators". as well as some traps to help out in base defense which makes them more suitable for defense, but they're not bad at all in offense as well.
This game is without a doubt worth a try, but it needs some balancing with the heroes.

There were words I had for this game. Once, years ago, I could tell how much I love this game with several paragraphs. I've since lost those words, but the feeling has stayed.
I've loved megaman games for a long time; I didn't get to truly play one of the classic games until I rented the Megaman Collection on the gamecube through gamefly, but what I played I very much enjoyed. Somehow I was never able to complete 1 and 5...
But still, this was over 10 years ago. I've since tried and loved the X games, and Megaman Zero 3 was actually my first game I played that had Megaman in the title. Or was that Battle Network 3? Either or.
So, I loved these games. and I can happily say, with very few words, that Rosenkreuzstilette, its extra mode, and its sequel, are all still as good when I first played them all those years ago, as they are now to this very day. It's a beautiful love-letter to megaman fans while also weaving its own interesting world and a setting that is very different and unique to the origin series. Especially with the apparent disappointment brought about my Mighty No.9 to the fanbase, This game getting a true localization was exactly what Megaman needed.
As a note regarding difficulty; RKS is not easy. It's harder than a good portion of the original megaman games. You'll need to figure out the boss order to have a relaxing time with the game. And that's just the base game...
Rosenkreuzstilette is a game that offers old fans of the series a bit of nostalgia, and a side game for those who loved the X and Zero games as well. But to me at least, RKS still feels fresh. I, personally, think it's aged quite well since its release in about 2007 or so.
And as an aside, Congratulations, Darksquid Media. I can only imagine how it must feel, to be the original Fan Translators of something like this, only to be approached by the man himself responsible for the game to be tasked with its official english release. Congratulations, seriously.

This game is absolutely amazing. The art, the music, and especially the narrative. In 2007 when Braid was first released on the Xbox store, it gained mass popularity, and I never really understood why, until now, after seeing the fantastic ending. Before seeing the ending, I thought it was okay, but not deserving the popularity it had. But the ending is a massive twist, and presented amazingly well. I won't spoil it, I urge you to play this game and see it for yourself. It is definitely worth finishing one of the most difficult puzzle games I have ever played for this ending. It's a great end to all the effort put in. Really.
The game's controls were very creative, I loved being able to manipulate time. The controls (forgetting about the epic twist at the end) brought a lovely fresh of breath air to the cliche story of 'catch a princess'.
The game is a puzzle-platformer, and it's puzzles were good. Extremely good. Each puzzle took me quite a while to finally solve, and they were each very clever. The layout of the levels makes it seem like they are easy to solve, but in reality, each level takes about 30+ minutes to solve each.
Each world brought new game mechanics, and taught each mechanic very subtlely, and not in your face. Some of the puzzles were re used, but the change in game mechanics changed the re used levels almost completely. For example, there was a world 3 level used in world 6, but because of the different game mechanics, it was much, much harder to solve in world 6.
Some people dislike the re-use of levels, but I, personally, liked it. I think it's cool to see how different game mechanics work on the same levels. Also, the reused levels were used as mechanic tutorials, making the player think "Ahh! Well I've done this before, so I can do it again easily", before realising that they can't solve the puzzle the same way due to different mechanics. As I said before, very clever.
The games graphics and sound track were utterly beautiful. I love the comic book style the game has, it looks amazing. The classic music style matches the theme of the game perfectly. However, I would have prefered a couple visuals to go along with the storybook narration. I think the lack of visuals whilst being given a narrative is a turn-off for some people, myself included. This is a shame, since the story is sensational.
I give this game a 8/10, missing two marks solely because of the lack of visuals during narration. Easily reccommended.

While the theme meshes very oddly with the gameplay - you are less of a mighty dragon and more of a fragile, sneaky wyvern - Hoard still provides excellent, arcadey action gameplay.  Burn the things, don't get hit while doing so, and ferry the treasure back home for points.  Simple, but effective.
Individual sessions are quick, and replayability is provided in the form of several diverse modes, along with the heavy emphasis on high scores.  Coop is quite fun, but unfortunately there's no community to speak of, so you'll only get to enjoy it if you have friends.  Competive mode is even more fun, with the ability to convert towns to your side!
Unfortunately, the scoring system is very arbitrary on a map by map basis, with some gold medals being easy to get and others nearly impossible.  The scoring system also is critical to a fault, and will ruin an entire run if you make the mistake of getting hit even once or twice in a ten minute session.  However, these minor flaws don't detract from the overall experience too much.
This is a fantastic game for what it is, even if it's not what people were expecting from it.  Don't go into this one for a power trip fantasy - you are a glass cannon through and through.  Hoard can, perhaps, be blamed for choosing a theme that is not entirely matched perfectly with the style of game it is, but it's still a blast regardless.

This game is one of the finest RTS games ever to grace the genre. The game truly holds well even to this day, well over a decade afters its initial release. The game offers an interested and very fun singleplayer campaign where you play as the  Blood Ravens Space Marine chapter as they fight against a massive Ork force on an imperial planet. It's up to you to use your brain and tactical sense to destroy the Ork menace. But as time goes on the forces of Chaos arrive as well as the elusive Eldar and the stakes only begin to rise. The gameplay is solid. From the army commands as well as base building and management. Unlike other, older, RTS games the way you gain recources is by capturing and holding points that are around the battlemap making those areas complete hotspots for some epic large battles. You get to command large armies and pit them against other large armies, unique units and buildings per factions (four factions are available in the game), an army painter (very basic, but still fun to use custom armies in skirmish), and overall the game has a lot to offer. There are some downsides sadly, but these are more in the technical side rather than the game itself, the game does not support 16:9 resolutions, but with some mods you are able to force a 16:9 resolution in the game, but the mini map tends to bug out. The unit path finding can be a bit wonky at times as well and artillery units can be a real pain if you don't know how to properly use them, but overall nothing too serious, just minor inconveniences. This is a great game for both RTS fans and Warhammer 40k fans or if you're a fan of both, you're doing yourself an unjustice by not owning and playing this great game.

Took me a bit to get into this game coming from being such a huge Company of Heroes one fan, but once I got the hang of it and they got some of the balance and bugs worked out, this game has proven to be a very enjoyable experience. The graphics are very detailed, the sound is excellent, the combat intense and the strategies required to win are never set in stone. It is a difficult game to fully grasp if you've no experience with an RTS like it, but features like destructible environments, cover, dynamic line of sight, and even things like armor facing make this an incredibly unique RTS with no equal.
The campaign is a bit lax in terms of how fun it is, but if you are buying this for the single-player experience, you are buying the wrong game. Playing against and/or with others is what makes this game what it is - and adrenaline driven, fast paced, high action RTS.
Don't expect this game to go easy on you - every little second and ability counts just as much as the units you pit against your enemy and your strategy on how to combat them. You must be able to multitask and micromanage very well all while understanding the dynamics between each unit. This is a game that is all about how you are able to deal with the cards you are dealt, not the kind of deck you build before the fight. In other words, its not so much about build order and timing as it is about positioning, reconnaissance, micromanagement, reactions, and being able to think on your feet. If that sounds like an interesting challenge to you, then I HIGHLY reccomend this game.

I have had this game in my library for quite some time and figured that now would be a perfect time to review it as well as I think it sort of deserves it because this was the very first game I got on steam a couple of years ago thanks to my brothers. Originally, I saw it on PS3, but for reasons I can't remember I got it on here, thus starting my life as a PC gamer. However, that is a story for another time, for now it is time to say I would whole-heartedly recommend this game for those who don't have the time to play full games, yet it is quite challenging for those that want a bit more in their small games.
You are a dragon and have to collect gold for your ever-growing pile back at your nest. Sounds simple enough, the difficulty comes in when you start to capture princesses, take down towers, defend your treasure agains thieves all the while raiding the villages around the map. There are many different mods, along with a nice tutorial which isn't all that helpful. How it works is you basically have to hit certain events in order to trigger more information about it. Once you've learned all the game has to offer, it lets you play a full game and offers you a gold if you can complete the challenge.
It is very beautiful looking, I love the table-top aesthetic that is given to all of the boards. It runs really smoothly and the controls work alright for what it's worth: WASD for movement, mouse to aim. The only problems I've really come across was that the AI is extremely basic, which is difficult when you're doing Co-Op challenges trying to get gold on everything. Multiplayer is also wierd, but there isn't much else I can say about it.  Another thing to note is that it does tend to get very repetitive by flying around destroying villages, protecting your stuff and upgrading every time you reach a certain gold limit. The final thing I want to mention is that the enemy AI is RELENTLESS and will more often than not kill you more by sheer numbers than actual difficulty.
You can also customize your game by modifying a few things, but not that much, if you want a quicker game or easier. If you have friends who are on the same network as you, there's a LAN feature that allows you to play together. For what it's worth, I say it's worth at least checking out if you're the type of person that enjoys grindy games and wants something to play for a few hours at a time in the same league as Fortix. Not really much else that I can say about this game without going into pointless details about the options, which there are a fair number of if you're the person that likes fiddling with menus.

One thing anyone will notice when first looking into playing a Jagex game is some form of complaining, whether that be nostalgia whining (once was extremely prevalent with RuneScape but thankfully has calmed down in recent years), entitlement, conspiracy theories or something else. That's an inevitability about Jagex's games for whatever reason. However, the one upside to that is that Jagex's games actually tend to be pretty amazing (even though their reputation for abandoning games is unfortunately often accurate). Sure, they're not quite AAA quality, but they do well for being a studio that -- despite being the company behind the world's largest free MMORPG -- is relatively unknown.
Block N Load is no exception to that. One of the rare cases where Jagex got back into a game and reworked it to try to reboot it, this game started off enjoyable but has really only gotten better with age. Reaching a unique middle ground between modern team shooters like Team Fortress 2 and the more nostalgic older feel of classic arena shooters that I grew up on (such as Quake or the original Starsiege: Tribes) while tossing in Minecraft-esque building mechanics, Block N Load is THE shooter to go to when you're sick of the standard shooters out there and want something new. It allows you to play however you want, though there are strong encouragements in the mechanics to try to make you WANT to work with your team. Want to run-and-gun and completely ignore the building mechanics? You can do that, but your team may not like you too much and you have a higher chance of losing. Want to only build and babysit the base? Again, you can do that, but you certainly have a better chance of winning the round if you work with your team to see if they need you to defend or attack. But if you want strong team mechanics with both solid shooter gameplay and building gameplay, that's where this game really shines.
Of course, it all depends on whom you get in-game with. If you get a bad team, it will inevitably be less enjoyable if you're aiming to have a good team experience. However, when you get with a really good team, you'll find yourself enjoying every moment of the experience. At first glance, the game doesn't look too high-adrenaline, but when you're in a match, it really does get your adrenaline pumping. It's quite a bit of fun, especially when it's a close call, as you really can only do so much to stop the enemy from winning.
See, that's one advantage to this game. Where other shooters tend to be rather see-through after a few matches, this game has a lot of variation to it tactically. You CAN just invade from above ground by charging in or building a bridge around to the other side. However, there are also virtually unlimited paths and tactics that you can add in by digging underground and attacking the enemy from underneath. Much of the time, even with several radars, it can be difficult to predict where your enemy is coming from. This unpredictability makes each match pretty evenly unique and fun.
What's nice about Block N Load in terms of the shooter mechanics is that it's not like your modern shooters where people can quick-scope cheapshot you all the time. You don't have to be an FPS pro to play this game. Instead of the modern FPS approach, Jagex and Artplant developed this game in a more classic arena shooter way where you can take several hits before dying, with headshots and torso shots dealing more damage. This, combined with the building mechanics and encouragements towards team play make the game feel unique, but not foreign.
The game isn't without faults, however. There are many situations, particularly when getting in-game with a team that lacks cohesion, where frustration rears its head. The way the game is developed helps to deliver a more fair experience (often shooters make me feel like I've been cheated when I get killed by cheapshots or at the very last minute). But despite their attempts to keep frustration at a minimum, it's inevitable with any competitive online game. Other than that, however, the game is really solid despite how people are probably going to start review-bombing the game because they introduced completely optional lootboxes.
Ultimately, one signature of Jagex's games that I've experienced over 13 (nearly 14) years of playing their games, is that every one of their games has this certain something to them that makes your experience FUN. Video games are meant to be fun before everything else, and Jagex knows how to do that. Whether you play RuneScape 3 or Old School RuneScape, Block N Load or Chronicle: RuneScape Legends, Transformers Universe (when it was a thing) or the catalog of games on FunOrb, all of their games are soaked with fun. I don't know if it's the fact that the games never take themselves TOO seriously, or if Jagex's developers are just brilliant (maybe both), but their games have always felt fun and memorable to me. I highly recommend pretty much everything they release. They're not a perfect studio (there isn't such a thing), but they do maintain a great consumer-friendly business ethic along with great company culture that allows for them to develop fun games while also maintaining a very strong connection to their communities. Block N Load is a pretty good example of that, if we're being honest.
All-in-all, I'd give this game a solid 9/10. It's genuinely one of the best shooters I've played, possibly my second-favorite one after Planetside 2.

This is an open world zombie apocolypse game with rpg progression and parkour integrated into its core. I know, "great, another zombie game cashing in on the zombie craze". Trust me, I have been and am still there with that mindset. This actually does deserve your time though. It is actually a good game that was made how it was, becasue that was the vision. It wasn't made because "oh zombies are cool in COD now we need zombies too."
Pros:
+Some pretty top notch graphics
+Voice work
+Parkour traversal
+Weapon diversity
+Loot
+Both Zombie Types
+Progression trees
Cons:
-Plot
-Lack of a sniper rifle(personal grudge after loving the two in Dead Island Riptide)
-Character differintiation
Dying Light is Dead Island improved in almost everyway with an added parkour element added in. The graphics are leagues better. The skill trees are actually useful. The exploration feels more fleshed out. The zombies are more fun. What makes this even better is how Techland has been with the community, from their twitter, updates, events, and just overall care they seem to have with this game and it's players.
This game puts you in the shoes of an operative trying to find answers on an island. What follows is you slashing, smashing, cutting, crafting, and killing your way to your objective. There are tons of weapons, from swords and hammers and planks of wood, to pistols, bows, and grenades. On top of that, you also have mods to boost certain attributes like damage and durability as well as status effects you can apply such as poison and fire. You have your slow and stupid zombies, your super fast running ones, and then a handful of special types you can discover on your own. All the basic ones are fun to fight as you witness their arms and legs seperate from their body, or their torsos falling off their waist. The gore is very very satisfying. Then, you have your cities. The 2 you get to explore are wonderful to be in. Slice up some zombies, then climb up the side of a buildinf Assassins Creed style to safety.
Could this game be better? Yes. The story could be better. The sense of fear and desperation could be improved. The fact that every player is the same guy with sometimes different clothes could be improved. Other things worked on would make for a better game, but this is a terrific game as is and is a solid foundation that Techland can make great things from. If you liked Dead Island, you will for sure like this. If you want a more realistic zombie game than a lot of what is out there, you will like this. If you just want a good game you can play with friends, I am sure there is joy to be had in this game for you.
Try it out, see if you like it.
Good night and good luck.

Here's how I picture the Team Ninja PC team: few guys in a small room with little knowledge or resources to port anything properly, paid way too little to care about the end product. Chain smoking and gloomy, shaking their heads while editing the lines of code. One guy leaves, never to return. No one notices.
The game doesn't have achievements, no Steam Cloud support. Hell, it doesn't even support controller vibration. All the effects are PS3-based and if your Steam ID has non-standard characters then the game won't save your data. The "Last Round" edition was advertised having two new stages and both are missing, obviously. Online modes will be patched in indeterminate future. Get this - the official FAQ says that if you're getting any visual problems you should set your desktop resolution to match the game resolution. Did I travel back in time to 1995? Am I expected to edit MemMaker again? Maybe change the Soundblaster IRQ? Nah, there's no surround sound here, only stereo is supported. Maybe it is 1995 after all...
Team Ninja says this port is based on the arcade version of the game like it would explain all the problems somehow. It's a disaster on par with Deadly Premonition or Devil May Cry 3 on PC. I could excuse the former for being kinda niche and the latter for getting released in 2005, way before Capcom learned that PC gaming is an actual thing. None of these excuses work for DOA5 though, this is a major title in 2015, the same year when Steam hit 125 million users and even MGSV is getting a stellar PC port. How is it possible that Ikaruga got a perfect version with achievements and Steam leaderboards while a huge company like Tecmo can't spare a dime to put one of their flagship titles on PC properly? And they will probably use the bad reviews as proof that they should not bother with PC audience. Because hey, bad sales of Ninja Gaiden Z mean there's no reason to port Ninja Gaiden Black to PC, right?
DOA5 is still a fun game with lots of content even without the online component. It's also one of the most casual-friendly 3D fighters out there but this version is a travesty. I paid $12 for it before Steam region locked everything and stuck with it. Don't buy it now, wait a few months before it's discounted heavily and keep your expectations low.

Blender is a brilliant software, and the creators behind it are damned gods. I would like to write this professionally and as formally as possible, but I feel that is actually impossible because how good Blender is. Of course you can't come into the 3D Art business looking at an easy start, starting out making a AAA M1911 and to make a remedy art style of games like Battlefield and DayZ and all those fun games that have absolute graphics. However instead, you will most likely start with archaic graphics, maybe like the early 2000s games, or even similar to Unturned style blockyness. Truth is, that's completely OK. That's how it's supposed to be, because once you start developing things that are damn close to AAA studio style, you will look at old models you made and compare them to now, and it's an incredible sight to see truly. On top of that, all these models are made with a thousand dollar software by professionals, where Blender is completely free and you can become a self made professional if you have the determination, and the will too!
The GUI is professional, however I changed my theme because I prefer a darker color, I feel it's easier on my eyes while working later in the night.. The controls seem quite wacky at first, but you will get the hang of them, or even change them.. I've done both of that, and I do prefer the controls I have (which is more like 3DS Max) but I like Blender quite a bit more than 3DS Max.. Mainly because of simplicity yet power, as well as the small download too :D
The heaps of tutorials will attend to senses also, you can literally go on YouTube and find almost anything, the harder things to find in my honest opinion is probably making houses for game engines, but the best way to do that is modular + assembly in-engine, because you can use one wall to make probably like three different styled houses. Larger, smaller, and you don't need to re-model a whole new house just to get a bigger house! I also feel Blender really appeals to every engine that's currently assessible, that inclues Unity (as much as I dislike it..), Unreal Engine 4, CryEngine, and whatever else there is to use, as long as you can import some form of .fbx or .obj, it'll work out great!
Almost concluding this review, I also can say I have experience modeling things for Runescape private servers also, as bad as it sounds, it's quite fun to make really cool swords and put them into a game where players can find, use, become rich off of, so Blender has endless possibilites, and it's development pipeline is good too, I don't need to take my model from Blender to Maya or something to do animations, I can do it all right in Blender.
Brilliant software Blender Developers! Good luck to all you future developers!

Hoard is hard to pin to a particular genre, but I’d call it a mix of real-time strategy and action arcade with more focus on the latter.  Players will assume the role of a dragon whose goal will be to score the most points.  Players can go it alone, compete against the AI, or invite up to three friends into a multi-player match.

In Hoard, there are four modes: Treasure, Princess Rush, Survival, and Co-op.  Treasure is the main mode in which players will be competing to earn the most gold.  The map will evolve around them as gold carts make their way from building to building.  Cities become more populated, castles become stronger, and the human NPCs become more vicious.  Players will be attempting to burn down whatever they can to collect gold and bring it back to their base, though they are free to attack each other.  If a dragon loses its health completely, it is forced back to its base to regenerate health and loses any score multipliers or gold that it may have been carrying.

Therein lies the strategy element to the game…players can go about their business and just concentrate on collecting gold for their stash, but will miss out on resetting an opponent’s score multiplier by draining all of their health.  Allowing another player to keep a 3x score multiplier throughout the game can be disastrous.  Multipliers are earned by staying alive and continuously funding the stash, but can be lost in a number of different ways.

Another neat aspect of the game that I find to be a great addition is that you can level up your dragon.  The more gold you stash, the more you can level up.  You’ll be able to increase your dragon’s speed, fire strength, armor, and carrying capacity.  Will you spec your dragon to be a slow-moving, but powerful tank…or will you opt to be Speedy Gonzales, stashing gold like no one’s business?
All in all, Hoard is a fun diversion in fifteen or twenty-minute spurts.  It’s not something I’d play for hours on end, but it’s a game I come back to every so often when I need to fill time.  I’d recommend waiting until it was on sale (Steam does this often) and pick it up then.

Braid is a simple puzzle platformer, or at least at the first glance. Gameplay is incredibly smooth and well done along with all the time tricks you get to experience throug the levels. You'll love the relaxing "classical" music and overall soft and chill appeal in whole design.
The trick is the first glance of simplicity wears off quite fast and you are going to get stuck. Often. Braid is by far the hardest puzzle game I've ever played. This is truly going to test how patient and clever you are. You are going to be frustrated at times, but at the same time each puzzle is going to give you a great feeling of accomplishment if you are patient enough to solve it on your own. None of the puzzles are dumb or repetitive and each brings a new pattern to uncover and understand.
About the story - I must say I enjoyed the sentimental style and slow uncovering of it, but most of the time I was quite confused and had no idea what it was all about. Well, I definitely experienced better storytelling in games, but this game won my gaming soul just by its crisp gameplay.

I'm going to be honest: I didn't expect to enjoy Shank.
However, Shank is now one of my favorite games, and is a a game I recommend to any friend with a few spare bucks.
Shank is a 2D sidescroller with wonderful comic-book style graphics, an amazingly satisfying combat system, and unique parkour mechanics.
The combat system is stunning.You have three weapons at any given time: your heavy weapon, your gun, and your shanks. You can switch out each of these on the fly (there are 4 heavy weapons and 3 guns), though they have to be unlocked progressively. The game gives you new weapons seemingly the MOMENT you get used to the previous ones. Combat is ridiculously fast paced: the game constantly throws enemies at you, and you have to block, pounce, shoot, stab, and slice through your opponents at light-speed.
Movement is equally well done: you can run up (nearly) any wall by climbing with your shanks, you can swing off of lamp posts and other hanging objects, you can slide down inclines, and other parkour game staples. Seeing this in a 2D space may seem like a horrible idea, but trust me, it's great.
The story is kind of cliche, but it's seriously unpredictable. You really don't understand what's going on until halfway through the game, as the backstory is slowly revealed through flashbacks, and the final flashback isn't until the final stage of the final boss of the final level.
In short: it's a Mexican drug cartel action-romance-tragedy-mystery.
Shank also includes a separate local co-op campaign and controller support (in fact, the game works better on a controller.)
If you have 10 dollars to spare, or want to play a 2D game, or just want a hell of a good time, pick up Shank.

Some things that'll give you a flavour of Tropico 4:
Make sure to keep the different factions of your citizens happy (capitalists, communists, environmentalists, etc), otherwise you may lose the yearly vote. No fears if not though, rigging the elections or declaring martial law is always a plan B & C. Who needs an democracy these days anyway!? Alternatively, once you've installed the secret service into a public hub of your choice, the local opposition may "have an accident." Or just send a soldier to gun them down in broad daylight. Slightly cheaper, stirs up the locals a little mind. Don't be surprised if a few turn rebel if you take this route, nothing a strong military won't deter though.
Trade with all different countries from around the world who want the valuable resources foraged and industrialised from your island. They are all goofy, over exaggerated versions of the current world leaders of the time the game is set in. If you fulfil the quota for Smoked Beef for the Middle East, the representative may sent you their favourite camel as a present! :) If they are unhappy, he may ask for $7,000 for difficult times (how else is the Sheikh supposed to finance all his wives birthday presents - great calamity!).
Plan your island to have the rural hubs, with farms producing crops of your choosing, mines digging for the ore you've set them to, littered with run down tenements and small clinics, pubs and churches to keep the local populous ticking over. Once this has financed your treasury, use the monies to open up a new urban district where your newly established school can train educated factory workers, teachers, policemen and firemen (etc) who can live in their apartments amongst the cabaret, cinemas and dining restaurants. Finally, for the best of the best who require college education: your generals, ministers, bankers, foreign aid workers; build lush homes or mansions coupled with cathedrals and hospitals with running electricity. Or don't and have everyone live in shacks and fend for themselves, mix it up so the poor live amongst the rich. Set the wages so their is no divide between poor and rich. You choose.
So the intellectuals are getting you down? Enact a book burning decree. Sorted! Want to increase your population and keep the church happy? Ban contraception! Want to keep the rebels second guessing their next attack? Enact the military modernisation policy. Want to keep the communists happy? Free housing for all! There's approximately 30 different edicts which issuing/denying will change the way your island runs. For good or for bad? Well, that depends who you're trying to keep happy, your people or your treasury.
TL;DR: In my opinion, the best strategy/simulation builder to date. If strat/sim is your sort of thing, you should find this easy and fun to pick up and play, but pleased with the learning curve that you'll follow to find it can be very challenging at end-game.

Saints Row 4 is an open world, action adventure that has been receiving positive feedback for quite sometime...luckily not from me. Saints Row 4 was supposed to be a DLC for the previous installment of Saints Row 3. This game was a cluster of boredom and repetiton... I understand the Matrix vibe that the game brought to the table but once you obtain the powers all vehicles and weapons become unnecessary, eradicating the fun. This game had a fair share of amusement but only for the writing... not the gameplay. The gameplay is explosive and fun at first but the mission's are always repetitive. The side quests are down right horrible, receiving useless junk as your reward. Main mission's are even worse, hardly expanding the possibilities the game could've made. I also didn't enjoy the simulation, the city doesn't amuse me and it's very bland. A collection of lights and skyscrapers surrounded by a tangle of dim roads and dull houses... that is a perfect representation of a city and this game executed that nicely but a collection of mission do not involve the center of the city, they involve the boring and quiet sections. I just wish there was more interacton with the actual city..maybe a building falling, a bridge collasping or clinging on to a fire escape attempting to hide from Zinyak's minions. I want the environement to not only change from my actions but I also want it to change the gameplay. Something that also pulls my strings is the stupidity of some of the activities. Crashing myself into traffic for super speed and destroying♥♥♥♥♥♥is fun but pointless... like they didn't know what else to do....AND DOING IT MULTIPLE TIMES DOESN'T HELP. And even after all that they still screwed something else up...the villain....the antagonist.. Zinyak was terrible, having hardly any character development. He exploded into action during the first mission, then you hardly even see him for the rest of the game. Of course you hear him at times and he is included in some missions but there were moments I forgot he existed.. I didn't hate him or feel any emotion towards him and his character. How am I supposed to be eager to kill someone when they only appear a few times in a game that is approximately 20 to 30 hours long!? This game was not only a disapointment but it even failed at being a fun and enjoyable game. 4.3/10

I've played Quake Live years before it was released on steam, and i need to admit the steam version takes some of the classic Quake feel to it due to the developers adding loadout options and even adding a heavy machine gun. Back in the older days this game was basically the same thing as Quake III Arena where you start off with the Machine gun and the gauntlet and then find all of the other weapons around the map. The game itself is still a lot of fun to this day, the combat gameplay is still the same as it was years ago, Just my only complaint goes to the loadout options where you can start off with an overpowered weapon and dominating all of the other opponents which makes the combat less of a challenge. My reason to that is back when you started off with the machine gun, the combat was more difficult when someone with the lightning gun would spawn kill you in the matter of seconds. With all of that being said, the game is still a whole lot of fun. I will recommend this game to the players who like free-for-all or CTF combat without the constant raging like in CoD(I'm not comparing this game to CoD). If you're a huge Quake fan like i am then you will be very confused at first with the game mechanics but the combat is still pretty much the same as in Quake III Arena.

I remember looking this game up before buying it. The game, and seemingly its developer, takes itself way too seriously. The game, as well as its advertising, seemed to be full of the worst kind of indie pretension: the one that judges everything else to be crap, and seems to pass judgement on those who complacently consume said mediocrity. Braid touted itself as an experience in a league entirely of its own, that the big bad AAA titles could not touch.
And, wouldn't you know it, as much as I hate to admit it, they were absolutely 100% right. Braid is in a league of its own. It makes almost every other puzzle game in existence seem cheap, insipid, repetitive, uninspired. I think it's most incredible feat is that, while it is far from easy by any means, it is neither complex nor is it frustrating. I've never seen another puzzle game achieve this most delicate of balances.
Every puzzle is delightfully simple, requiring you to discover some novel new use of the mechanics you've learned so far. You are not expected to pick apart intricate constructions, and spam a few techniques you've applied dozens of times already until the solution falls out. No, for practically every puzzle in Braid, you will do something new, something you haven't yet considered. And when the solution does fall out, it's often beautiful, and you will feel AMAZING.
Speaking of beauty, the whole game is extraordinarily beautiful. The music, the art, the story, the puzzles: all of them are exquisite. Looking at screenshots does not do the game's artwork justice, as the backgrounds shift and breathe in a most serene yet breathtaking manner.
Basically, this game ends whatever remnants of the "Are video games art?" discussion. In every conceivable way, this game is a master-class in game design. Highly recommended.

Braid is one of those games you have to play once. You may never play it again unless you decide to speedrun it, and that's fine, but you do have to play it once.
What sells this game is the gameplay: simple platforming with a time-reversal mechanic that turns the genre on its head. It's more of a puzzle-platformer than anything else, though some of the sections that require you to move quickly are more action-based and they both mesh together quite well. Every world has a different gimmick to it - and I don't use that word negatively. Each new level offers a unique experience and the game teaches you how to use your new powers quickly and without shoving it down your throat. When you know how the rooms are solved, the game goes by very fast, but for a first time player it lasts a good amount of time. The build-up to the final level and the climax of the game are well worth the effort.
Story-wise, it's not the best. Most of the plot is conveyed by text boxes that you read before the levels and while they are nice and poetic at times it's not straightforward in the least sense. The rest of the story is told through the levels themselves, and the final level is a shining example of gameplay driving story.
Visually, Braid is nice. It's not blow-your-mind amazing but the art design is very smooth and colourful and it fits. The soundtrack to this game is great and the sounds of the world mesh well with it.
Overall, Braid is a great game. If you haven't played it yet, do so.

I am happy that I bought this game for only $2.50. This is one of my first experience with a rogue-like game. For those, that don't know, a rogue-like game does not let you save, you will die often and most likely not "win" until you master the basics.  This game is very punishing, you can go from a full crew and upgraded ship to a breached hull, damaged oxygen tanks, and a teleported intruder destroying your ship.
Pros:
It is the games difficutly and procedurally generated world that keeps you replaying. Every time you play the sectors are different and new events occur randomly.
I love how the ship systems are all interconnected. If you have a fire you can send your crew to fight the fire and get hurt, or just open an air lock. However, you need to provide power to your doors to open, and power to your oxygen tanks to refill your rooms. Generally, power is limited and you have to juggle what systems are priority. The different species/races you crew your ship have interesting and unique abilities. Engi are robotic like and can repair your ship quickly, Zoltan are energy based and can self power their assigned system. There are also rockmen, slugs, mantis and humans. Each race has their own ships with three different layouts, all of which are unlockable.
Cons:
***To be honest if this was not a rogue-game, it would receive terrible reviews for its very short story line.*** Not that this game is limited, but the content is very short. You have roughly eight sectors to clear and only one boss.
I personally like to roleplay my gaming experience, especially one so rich in races, starships and encounters. I like to get attached to my characters and build them up. I expect to lose a few crew, but not totally lose everything and start over. This game will let you personally name your starship and your crew, but why bother. It took me 15 hours to beat the game on easy, and I probably lost over a hundred star ships.

Shank is a great side scrolling beat em' up game, much like the olden days of Double Dragon, Final Fight or Streets of Rage except no 3rd dimension.
The game is over the top violent, which makes it oh so wonderful.  I found myself mashing buttons together just to see what crazy combo he would pull off next.  Some but not all of the environments are interactive, for example while on a train you can throw bad guys off of it.  I found that incredibly entertaining.
The game is a side scroller which means at some point you're going to have to jump through obstacle courses.  The developers did this step right though, for instance if you're sliding down a slope and you need to make a life or death decision in the next few seconds, the game will go into slow motion until you make that decision.  It's an excellent system, but this feature goes away in the final levels, which is a bummer because then you have to memorize the next few steps, or die and restart from the last checkpoint.
Boss battles are actually fun, as each one has a tick, similiar to Punchout, and no two boss battles are the same.
Overall a very good game that deserves a play through if you enjoy side scrolling beat em' ups.

The original Metro 2033 was an amazing game that was oozing with atmosphere, detail and personality and it's still fun to play to this day.
As great as the original was, it felt a bit clumsy to me at times, the interface was somewhat confusing at times and certain animations looked really unnatural, but now we have the Redux which just blasted me back into the amazing Metro universe, it holds onto all the great things Metro 2033 offered and just updates them to look/sound/feel better and it also offers different playstyles; Spartan offers a more forgiving type of gameplay, while Survivor is more about stealth and resource management.
All of the original difficulties are back, including Ranger mode which luckly isn't paid DLC this time around.
All in all, Redux is what a remake should be, it does not mess with the core game but just adds some little things to make the experience even better.
If you're looking to get into the Metro universe, I would heavily reccomend playign this version.
However, if you loved the original Metro 2033 and want to enjoy it again, I would also reccomend getting the Redux, you are paying the price for a new game though and that might put some people off.

I've played this game for fifteen hours now, not very far into it. I can make a few assertions about the game quality however. First allow me to state this fits into my desired game "style" very well. Turn-Based and Survival and two of my favorite types of games - this has both. Perma-death is also another great feature of the game. Namely, the sense if you die you have to start over is a great motivator to be extra careful while scavenging.
The combat mechanics take a bit of getting used to, but once you have them down it's fairly easy to "manipulate" the encounter to be in your favor. Naturally you don't want to attack everything you see, sometimes it's wiser to stay hidden and let the group of guys with guns walk past you.
The crafting system is great, it's very well thought out. I love having the ability to make a tarp shelter and after I'm done sleeping breaking it down and collecting my tarp and string to be able to move along with a smaller load.
Scavenging for supplies is well done, the mechanic is both rewarding and frustrating at the same time - mainly when you're looking for something specific and keep getting trash.

You will learn what hunger is. You'll find yourself starving, losing energy, panicking. Maybe you'll trap a squirrel for a snack. Or beat a feral dog to death for some real meat. Maybe you'll take a step back and wonder how things got this way - huddled in some burnt out building, greedily eating packets of ketchup and saltines, washing them down with questionable river water. You might even find yourself in an unthinkable situation. You might manage to hold your own against a bandit. He came upon you while you were sleeping and tried to loot your camp. You woke, and he punched your head in a panic. You stand and brandish a crowbar. He turns to run, but he trips. You seize the opportunity. You strike. Again and again. Soon his blood rushes from his crushed head. And only then do you realize how hungry you are.
tl;dr buy it.

Overall, an excellent game. The meat of the game is turn based tactical combat where you control up to 6 squad members of varying classes. There is also a large strategy element outside of the combat, where you decide what base buildings you need, what research you need, what countries you need to save(you can't save them all unless you are on easy mode), and how to spend your precious resources. It is quite difficult at the start of the game, if you aren't familiar with the game you will get utterly destroyed a few times before you start getting the hang of it. Once you get toward the mid game it gets much easier though. Endgame is pretty easy if you know how to position you units and get the best weapons and armor built, though Sectopods are still OP to the extreme. Some of the decisions for when to give players specific stuff is a little confusing. For instance, late game you get access to a base room that tells you what species of aliens are at the mission locations. Early game, this would be INSANELY useful. Late game, it doesn't really matter because you are probably just going to stomp them anyway.
Graphics are pretty good. Music sets the mood well in my opinion. There is a large variety of hand crafted maps, but if you play long enough you will see repetition. It was rather buggy for a while after release, but it is pretty stable now. Some weird stuff does still happen, but it's mostly just funny stuff like a sniper facing the wrong direction and still headshotting his target.
I highly recommend getting Enemy Within. It adds a human enemy faction, which is interesting as they use different tactics than aliens. They can be irritating as they will steal money and research from you if you don't attend to them regularly. EW also adds Meld, a resource used to genetically modifiy units and build MEC troopers. Genetic modifications are a lot of fun, though a little overpowered to be honest. For instance, you can get Mimetic Skin for snipers, which allows you to become invisivble when moving into high cover from somewhere enemies can't see. Snipers get a perk that makes all cover high cover, so you can almost indefinitely stay invisible. MEC troopers are really fun. They can't take cover, and they can't equip a secondary weapon or a tactical item. They get special utilities from their mech suit, like AE medkits or mines. They also get access to special perks, lots of which make them very durable.
I would highly recommend this to anyone who likes turn based tactical combat and strategy. I would recommend it to people who don't know if they like that sort of stuff but are willing to try it, this is a very good example of this sort of game(play on normal mode first).

Braid is a perfect example of how to take something good and make it better. The classic platformer has been around since before Super Mario Bros., and Number None has made their own wonderfully puzzling take on the genre. Braid will make you think in ways you would never expect. In each section of the game you play with time as you platform, and in each section there is a new obstacle/method to master. The story is intruiging as it is mysterious, the gameplay is smooth and intuitive, and the mechanics are mind-bending in the best way possible. Braid is a new take on an old classic and it deserves its spot as a treasure amidst Indie games. It may not provide the same experience that a AAA title may be able to achieve, but it more than makes up for any lack of fancy graphics and massive world with its creativity and uniqueness. Try out Braid if you want a challenge, just make sure you prepare to be surprised.

I really want you to play this!
In fact, I can't be totally objective about it, because this game is one of my absolutely favorite ones, but I'm going to state that this the most well-made game in the whole universe.
I mean, not a single component is out or feels weak, everything is how you want and expect it to be, or maybe even beyond your imagination.
I'll try to give a clue about what the game is...
It's a looking-like-Super Mario Bros.-platformer with a deep thrilling storyline and amazing mind-blowing puzzles that that require various manipulations with time.
Our hero is able to turn the time back to the any point after you entered a stage without any limits or restrictions. Basically, you use to switch the time back if you die, so there're no game overs or anything in that kind. You don't have to restart a level when you die, you can just switch back the time to the point you can fix your faults and just move on. But what's more - in this game you use time switches for solving puzzles.
The game is separated by worlds and every world has it's unique features, like time-resistant objects; shadows, that repeat your moves, which were previously recorded by you; a ring, that freezes the time in a little range around it and more. All these things will help you to solve the puzzles and save the precious Princess...or not. The difficulty of some puzzles is pretty challenging, it can require some great patience and irregular way of thinking. Also, the difficulty doesn't really change gradually. Every world has some relaxing and insane puzzles, they're just different in the way of solving. So you won't get bored nor annoyed.
Every world has it's own atmosphere. Fantastic soundtrack and drawn game art will make you shiver every time you touch this masterpiece. Plus the storyline.
Actually, if you play through this game quickly - you might not even notice it, because the whole story is written in the books which you may just skip. But you shouldn't, really. I spent an insane time playing this game before purchasing a Steam copy. Maybe to discover its' secrets, beat all challenges, etc, or maybe just to be in-game, in this gorgeously-made world. But the best thing that I've discovered over time is a plot. It made me look at this game at the absolutely different point of view. I found out that every single world, every single piece of a puzzles that you collect, world's atmosphere and their features - everything is related to the plot, which is rather ambiguous, full of metaphors and sense.
I won't pretend to spoil about it, so just try this out yourself, it's an absolutely unique experience in the wold of games, so don't miss it and play this game right now!

Playing a dragon and doing what dragons do best (kidnapping princesses, burning villages and farms, and taking all the gold you can) is a blast. I've had a lot of fun and a lot of laughs playing this game. It is overall simple, yet it contains some complex elements. You can destroy towns and farms regularly or you can leave them alone and let them prosper, making farmer carts and wagons more valuable. You could even choose to make a town fear you and send you tribute instead of destroying it, but enemy dragons could destroy it or even make a town fear them instead. You can upgrade your dragon to suit the situation. The dragons change visually depending on how they're upgraded, which I thought was a nice touch.
Hoard is at its best when you have friends to play it with. I still have fun in single-player, but the AI is not a challenge and has not been polished. I can easily end a round with more than 200,000 treasure while the enemy computer-controlled dragon has about 1,000 treasure. The AI is prone to flying straight through enemies without trying to dodge. Computer-controlled dragons will also sit on top of powerups for long periods of time in an attempt to pick them up, yet they can't because they already have a powerup that's ready to use. I've also had problems with computer-controlled dragons just hovering in random places for very long periods of time, causing them to get killed. You can play with up to four friends, but if you don't have enough players, the game will fill in any extra spots with computer-controlled dragons.
I don't like the game's current music. It is too serious and doesn't match the fun, light-hearted nature of the game. I would recommend downloading and installing the old music. It really improves the game's atmosphere.
I think the game is a bit pricey, but I'd recommend getting it and the DLC when it goes on sale. Definitely try to get friends to play it with if you get this game.

Purchased this video on sale awhile back. Wanted a video editor and the price wasn't bad so i gave it a shot. I don't do anything to fancy but for what i do this program does a pretty good job at it. With the program I'm able to edit out parts of the video i don't want. I'm even able to make several edits in one go and the resulting video is always solid.
Another great feature is the ability change resolution (ex..720p to 1080P) and to set quality levels within each setting, low to ultra. Also a very important feature is the ability to take mulitple vidoes and turn them into a single vid. They can even be different resolutions. You can set an overall resoltion and quality when you merge them together.
Now for the not so great parts:
First, the final output file and be huge. I know this has to do with the quality settings but honestly after using this program i run the video through handbreak. I've litterally turned 8gb videos into 2gb ones with no noticable drop in quality. But thats more of an inconvenience really.
My second issue is one of efficency. I'd like to be able to add video to the queue while its working on something already, can't do anything else with the program until its done working on the job. Also it be great if i could add a video where i'm editing out parts and add it to a queue of other video's so I don't have to wait till its start just so I can set up the other projects to run.
Finally this is my biggest grip with the program is that when I add video's together, espeacilly large ones, the audio can fall out of sync with the video. This again requires handbreak to address.
Final thoughts:
The program does enough right to make it worth it. The reality is that there is no single free/inexpensive video editing program that does it all or is flawless. The ones actually do it all are either really expensive or requre subscriptions, liquivid requires niether.  In the end the program does enough right and is priced well enough to be a decent buy. You may need another program or so to get the perfectly edited final product but you'd have to do that even if you went with another program to be realistic about it.

The original Metro 2033 was an amazing game that was oozing with atmosphere, detail and personality and it's still fun to play to this day.
As great as the original was, it felt a bit clumsy to me at times, the interface was somewhat confusing at times and certain animations looked really unnatural, but now we have the Redux which just blasted me back into the amazing Metro universe, it holds onto all the great things Metro 2033 offered and just updates them to look/sound/feel better and it also offers different playstyles; Spartan offers a more forgiving type of gameplay, while Survivor is more about stealth and resource management.
All of the original difficulties are back, including Ranger mode which luckly isn't paid DLC this time around.
All in all, Redux is what a remake should be, it does not mess with the core game but just adds some little things to make the experience even better.
If you're looking to get into the Metro universe, I would heavily reccomend playign this version.
However, if you loved the original Metro 2033 and want to enjoy it again, I would also reccomend getting the Redux, you are paying the price for a new game though and that might put some people off.

NEO Scavenger is a very different game. I haven't played many like it, and certainly not any that I have enjoyed as much. It's a complicatedly simple game. It nearly masters survival against the elements, finding and cleaning water to drink, gathering plants for food or beating a deer to death with your bare hands for food.
It's style will put a lot of people off. It is a text game at it's descriptive and story core, something I am absolutely fine with, coupled with a hex based pixelated landscape. The controls are entirely mouse based or a combination of mouse and keyboard, and while it can seem strange and complex at first, a few playthroughs and you'll master them.
Another thing that will put people off is it's genre. It is that, no common, "rouge-like." When you die, you're kaput for good, and you start another play through. I liken it to Faster Than Light, in that aspect. Not just for it's art style and rouge-likeness, but for how you can upgrade your character, or ship/crew in FTL, and progress in the story only to die horrbily.
One great thing about NEO Scavenger is it's story. What is its story? I can tell you that you play as Philip Kindred who, after some odd years of cryo-stasis, wakes up in a world vastly different from what used to be. Kindred doesn't know that, of course, since he's conviently lost his memory. That's what you learn at the start, and that's where the story can end for you.
You can spend all of your time in NEO Scavenger simply getting better loot and surviving for as long as possible. The only way to advance the story is to seek it out activly. On the surface, it's a great survival rouge-like, but under the surface lies a vast and complex story filled with multiple branches, characters, challenges, and intrigue. There is an ending to the game. I didn't even know there was one, and I've been playing since early access. Honestly, I die or screw up before I make it far in the story.
The storytelling is all driven by you. You see a strange glow at night, follow it for a few days, and suddenly you find yourself surounded by life at the Detriot Mega City. What is this strange DMC? Ask some people, read some newpaper scraps you find while scavenging. Or don't. Go somewhere else, advance the story in a different way. I've found three ways you can "start" the story, and all of them require you to think and act proactivly.
The enemies and lore behind them is also great. I won't spoil what they are, but this game is supposed to be a realistic survival sim-like thing while also having deep roots in the supernatural. If you wonder to yourself," Oh my god, what the hell is that creature from the bowels of my worst nightmares," then google it and you'll likely find an real urban legend from Michigan that the enemy was based on.
NEO Scavenger is one of the best games in existence, in my opinion. Unlike a lot of other games, it has a demo! If you're on the fence, play the demo. If you think you like it, buy it without a doubt and get into it. I don't rate games, but for the sake of this review, I give it a 9.5/10. Why a 9.5, you ask. Because I'm super biased about this game, but I admit it's not perfect.
So go play the demo, fall in love, and buy this game. Throw yourself full heartedly into the world and lore that surrounds NEO Scavenger. Explore the DMC, find awesome old-world loot, investigate strange amusement parks, derilect cities, and even face otherworldly horrors in the pursuit of Philip Kindred's epic story.
Or don't. It's up to you, but be warned: you'll likely freeze do death anyway. Seriously, Michigan is cold and it rains a lot. I'm talking ALL the time. ♥♥♥♥ rain.
Oh, and go ahead, take off that talisman. Seriously, it's no big deal.
Just don't lose it. Ever.

Have you played the original Metro 2033 game? If not, get this one. If you want to know why or if you answered the question with yes and want to know why I like the redux version - look below:
- Graphics: The most obvious one, yes. But besides the looks itself, the Redux version runs more smoothly than the original one did.
- Atmosphere: The levels are more detailed, the characters (and enemies) have been adjusted to the designs from Last Light, especially the important ones - Miller and Khan to name the most obvious ones; also the reich troops, who got upgraded from Hobos with Nazi helmets to actual combat troops with unique gear. This makes both games feel more consistent and also looks better in all cases. Also there are more than two different faces for NPCs now, which is a huge and obvious improvement. (and you can wipe your gas mask now, which is more useful than you'd think).
Some people might not like the brighter lighting effects from last Light; I liked it and therefore don't care. It is however brighter than the original game, imo this doesn't change the atmosphere though (since you don't even notice that in most levels).
- Items: All the weapons from last Light and its DLC have been built into the levels and storyline and are accessible at some point through the game. These are the AKSU-74, the Bigun (Shotgun made from Bicycle parts) and the portable flamethrower and maybe some others.
- Level Design/ Story: Well the story is the same. Same goes for the basic level design. But apart from more details I already mentioned there were some minor changes: In every level you can find at least one safe with items in it, but you have to find the key first (Metro veterans may recognize this from last Light). Also, at some point in the game, a short part of a level has been redesigned for a new kind of enemy that veterans may know from - guess what -  Last Light.
- Gameplay: Well, apart from the new HuD (you guessed right - like in Last Light) there are two game modes (besides the different difficulty settings): Survival and Spartan. Survival is like the Original Metro game; Few resources, harder enemies - A more horror oriented approach. Spartan is more like last Light - More ammunition and generally more action oriented.
All in all, pretty awesome.
