Metro 2033 is one of these wonderful creepy shoddy video games from Eastern Europe. It captures some of the ghost town existentialism that STALKER made popular, but it had quite a few problems. The stealth system, for example, was crap on toast. It didn't run very well. The way the game felt and moved had a few problems, it felt a bit like running a lap underwater. Despite all this, it had ambience and character and terror crawling out of every goddamn pore of its being!
So I'm happy to say Metro 2033 Redux is mostly an improvement. Well, mostly.
First of all, I'd like to lodge a complaint: The development team ignored processing instructions for older AMD and Intel CPUs, and I would like to say that is not cool at all. I've had a AMD Phenom II quad-core processor for some time now, and while it isn't the amazing powerhouse that is whatever's at the top of Tom's Hardware's CPU charts, it can still kick♥♥♥♥♥and take names. Developing for the PC to work with a wide, wide range of specs and hardware configurations is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
Thankfully, those instructions were patched in and I finally got to play the game two days later after launch.
Second complaint: I had to replace one of the intro movies in the game directory with a blank file because it was crashing my game when I was actually able to get it running. I had to do this to a game released in 2014 to get it to run.
After those two I finally got to play it. It looked very good. It feels very nice to play - character reponses are fluid and there isn't a bunch of slowdown I experienced from the last game. FOV's stuck at something below 90, so take what you will from that.
It implements a lot of the improvements made by the sequel to this game (Metro: Last Light) and implements them into this game, which means stealth works and I was able to run it at nearly max settings! A new feature allows you to play it as a survival horror kind of shooter (the proper Metro 2033 experience) or as a straight-up on rails shooter (the equivalent of having chocolate-flavored vodka instead of drinking it straight up LIKE A REAL METRO DWELLER DOES), so there's that.
If you're playing this for the first time, don't skimp and get the original Metro 2033. The Redux version is a far more refined experience. You could argue that going for the remake loses some of the original shoddiness, and in that case, do whatever you like. But if you're dipping your toe into this strange flavor of Eastern Europe first person shooters for the first time, get the Redux.

Overall, an excellent game. The meat of the game is turn based tactical combat where you control up to 6 squad members of varying classes. There is also a large strategy element outside of the combat, where you decide what base buildings you need, what research you need, what countries you need to save(you can't save them all unless you are on easy mode), and how to spend your precious resources. It is quite difficult at the start of the game, if you aren't familiar with the game you will get utterly destroyed a few times before you start getting the hang of it. Once you get toward the mid game it gets much easier though. Endgame is pretty easy if you know how to position you units and get the best weapons and armor built, though Sectopods are still OP to the extreme. Some of the decisions for when to give players specific stuff is a little confusing. For instance, late game you get access to a base room that tells you what species of aliens are at the mission locations. Early game, this would be INSANELY useful. Late game, it doesn't really matter because you are probably just going to stomp them anyway.
Graphics are pretty good. Music sets the mood well in my opinion. There is a large variety of hand crafted maps, but if you play long enough you will see repetition. It was rather buggy for a while after release, but it is pretty stable now. Some weird stuff does still happen, but it's mostly just funny stuff like a sniper facing the wrong direction and still headshotting his target.
I highly recommend getting Enemy Within. It adds a human enemy faction, which is interesting as they use different tactics than aliens. They can be irritating as they will steal money and research from you if you don't attend to them regularly. EW also adds Meld, a resource used to genetically modifiy units and build MEC troopers. Genetic modifications are a lot of fun, though a little overpowered to be honest. For instance, you can get Mimetic Skin for snipers, which allows you to become invisivble when moving into high cover from somewhere enemies can't see. Snipers get a perk that makes all cover high cover, so you can almost indefinitely stay invisible. MEC troopers are really fun. They can't take cover, and they can't equip a secondary weapon or a tactical item. They get special utilities from their mech suit, like AE medkits or mines. They also get access to special perks, lots of which make them very durable.
I would highly recommend this to anyone who likes turn based tactical combat and strategy. I would recommend it to people who don't know if they like that sort of stuff but are willing to try it, this is a very good example of this sort of game(play on normal mode first).

Does lots of things really well. In particular the character animations and body language, the voice casting/acting and referential sci fi aesthetics are all superb and possibly revolutionary.
The music evokes Morricone's theme for Carpenter's "The Thing" - a big plus for me.
Crits are mighty satisfying too.
The camera is bloody awful. It continuously removes you, the player, from the equation. I'll explain;
You make the last move of your turn. Perhaps you uncover some more aliens during that move on top of the ones you're already engaging. Perhaps you immediately realise that the move was an error and would simply like to load your last save. Tough luck. Now you sit there locked out of both the menu and the camera while it flits from alien move to alien move (much more snappily than if you had control of it I might add) - this could be 10+ aliens. After it's shown you all those alien moves it'll then move through any other incidents, like maybe some of your squad panicked or were poisoned or some npc dialogue in one of the (ugh) extraction missions. If any vehicles were on fire and due to explode it will move through these too. Then, after all this, you can take your thumb out of your behind and access the menu or move the camera again. The camera is also buggy and will frequently fly off on it's own into the fog of war and expect you to fetch it back ... when it's not falling through the environment.
Free aim is also a joke, clearly not optimised for anything other than controller input.
Certain reproducable conditions will freeze/crash the game - known bugs that were never fixed.
Line of sight is ropey.
Sometimes aliens just appear out of nowhere in a room you're in (this is rare though).
The so called "rng" is also very strange. Of a particularly dubious nature is the chance for your Heavy's rocket to fire off target. Lord only knows what this chance is based on.
Thing is, all these things can be brushed off for the first few play-throughs or on difficultys up to and including classic iron man, 'cos it's a cool sci fi game, but once you're into impossible difficulty territory then they really start to get on your nerves.
Also, if you're into achievements, then you better buy Enemy Within, otherwise you'll be stuck at just above half completion since EU achievements are not separated. Reasonable proof that EW content should have been part of EU in the first place and was taken out to be sold to you for another £20 later on.
In the end though, I grudgingly recommend it.

On the surface, Braid is a simple puzzle platformer. The gameplay, at its most basic level, consists of jumping on platforms and collecting puzzle pieces before moving to the next world. A couple of things set Braid apart and make it a fantastic experience. The first is the visuals. Everything in Braid is hand drawn, and it's quite a pleasure to progress through the game and see the different landscapes. Second; the puzzles. The puzzles in the latter stages of the game are, to say the least, mind-bending. You will have difficulty getting through Braid without a walkthrough for at least a couple of levels. Braid is best played in short burts; play for too long and the harder puzzles get frustrating. The puzzles themselves are brilliantly designed and are very satisfying to solve. The main gimmick of Braid is the ability to manipulate (reverse) time. It adds another dimension to puzzle solving and forces you to think about puzzles in abstract ways. Truthfully, Braid isn't for everyone, but it offers a unique gameplay experience for the puzzler fan.

This game is a wonderful combination of simplicity and chaos. The controls are simple enough for just about anyone to pick up and play, but the increasingly absurd designs of the kitchens require high amounts of coordination and teamwork. I’ve enjoyed the game most as a 2 player co-op experience, but I’ve had plenty of fun with 3-4 chefs as well.
The main reason I would recommend 2 players is the progression. The game gets hard and it gets hard pretty fast. To unlock later levels, you need to have earned enough star ratings from previous levels. Since the number of points you need to earn 3 stars increases with the number of players, more players doesn’t necessarily make things easier. I also found that coming up with and executing a plan is easier with fewer people.
If you are looking for a tight experience that will test the limits of you and a friend’s teamwork and coordination like the game “Chariot”, then this game is for you. If you are looking for a game to play very casually in a group with young or novice gamers, this game will work too, just don’t expect to get to the end.

This Lightning Gun used to be great. I played Lightning Gun competitively for many years and I considered it the greatest of all time multiplayer Lightning Gun. Lightning Gun kept the same Lightning Gun and even made it even better in some ways. That is until recently. Just before launching on Lightning Gun, Lightning Gun did a "major gameplay update", in which the game now has Lightning Guns for all of its modes except for Lightning Gun. For some game modes it works, for others not so much. Let's take Lightning Gun for example.
You used to start with just Lightning Gun, which is a weak Lightning Gun that requires Lightning Gun to be effective. Most of the time it is going to be totally inferior to any other Lightning Gun depending on distance. This means you have to run away from Lightning Guns and find more powerful Lightning Guns on the Lightning Gun, and learn to use whichever Lightning Gun you do have to your Lightning Gun. So if you run into a Lightning Gun that isn't so easy to use, say Lightning Gun, you're forced to learn how to use it more effectively because there isn't another Lightning Gun around for you to fight with. This teaches players to be better overall and makes the Lightning Gun a lot more fun and more Lightning Gun. On occasions where you can't run away and you need to use Lightning Gun, your only hope is to have some damn good QUAD DAMAGE and good Lightning Gun skills. Once you've gotten yourself Lightning Guned up, QUAD DAMAGED up, and Lightning Guned up, you gotta keep what is known as 15 years of your life, by timing QUAD DAMAGES and preventing others from getting them.
Now that you can just spawn with Lightning Gun, Lightning Gun, Lightning Gun, or QUAD DAMAGE (which imo is overpowered as it does about as much dmg as Lightning Gun but has unlimited range), you basically have Lightning Guns running around spamming QUAD DAMAGE Lightning guns without a care in the Lightning Gun. It gets boring REALLY fast, and I can only stand to play one Lightning Gun of this anymore before I have to quit for 15 years of YOUR LIFE at a time. The skill factor is gone, and thus the fun factor is QUAD DAMAGE.
The Lightning Gun has lost its competitive edge over other Lightning Gun games. I'd almost rather play Rail Gun, but I don't fancy a game where you can kill other players just by looking at them for a split second.
Another thing, 15 years of YOUR LIFE  wasn't at this years , QUAD DAMAGE, I wonder why. All I have to say is it's a shame they've decided to try to cater to the Rail Guns, and in the process lose the one Quad Damage that made them special.

Dragons.  The stuff of horrible, malicious slander and propaganda.  You hear it all the time.  They "hoard gold", "burn villages", "eat princesses", they "must be slain for the good of the people."  People brag about their dragonslaying prowess.  Showing a brutal murder of a dragon on TV barely merits a wink from standards and practices departments.
In a world where games like Skyrim and movies like The Hobbit glorify violence against dragonkind, it's good to see someone had the sense to portray a more balanced look at the situation.
In Hoard, you play as a dragon going about daily life while being hunted by cruel, vicious knights, seeking the companionship of fair princesses, acting as the local neighborhood watch by dealing with petty thieves said knights don't bother arresting, keeping unslightly crops from littering the landscape, preventing traffic problems, and other clearly benign acts.  In return, you have to survive the prejudiced assault of said knights, archers, powerful wizards, and trolls who want to kill you on sight.
This game is a poweful lesson in tolerance toward those who are different and scalier, and maybe could use a cool, refreshing breath mint once in awhile.
I've only done a few tutorials, but everything feels good about the program. I don't have anything to compare it to... Make something with it. Have fun.

At first, I couldn't really find it useful because I started off as a newbie, but the more time I spent with this program, the more I got used to it. Now, I'm using it more often, and I do love everything that I accomplish with Blender. There's so much potential with this program that you can make out of it, it all comes out of an idea from you.
Blender has 3 engines to it, one is the Blender Render engine, the Cycles engine, and the Blender Game engine. All can give well results, but Cycles is the best in my opinion. Cycles delivers realistic quality than it can get from the rest. Other than the engines, making characters and then rigging them can be laborious, but the output will be worth it.
As I said earlier, you can do even more with Blender. For example, Blender has its own video editor, which I find extremely useful to organinze all of my frames from Source Filmmaker to Blender, achieving the best results as a MP4. I haven't explored much of this program yet, but I look forward to trying out new things with it. It's just an idea I need to start out with, then export that thought to Blender.
Good luck for all those newcomers who are getting started with these 3D programs, I hope you make the best out of Blender. For me, I know that I certainly will be making the best out of it.
Constant updates and tweaks to make Blender better
Community made add-ons to expand your tool-kit
Great community with helpful advice, many tutorials are out there for a variety of multiple topics on Blender
3 great engines, but Cycles is the most realistic out of all of them
Many tools for you to model your characters.
Able to texture your characters without the use of another program
Great sculpting tools
Built in video editing tab that can be used for compiling frames into a video
Animating in this program is simple and easy.
For new people mostly, the interface can be quite confusing for others that just got Blender.
Rendering in Blender isn't as optimized, therefore you may get slow renders if you don't tweak the settings. It's simple to fix by watching people's YouTube videos on it.
Material nodes can be a pain to work with.

If you have worked with a motion camera such as drone based photography or Go-Pro action cameras, then Liquivid may provide the solutions you need to quickly and intuitively correct and intensify those special moments you captured in not-so-slow motion.

I’ve spent quite a bit of time with multimedia files, web design, and various design based applications. The biggest problem I found with most of my work is the time element involved with editing imagery after photographing scenes, and before uploading them to the web. Of all the various editors, such as Pixler and the many that can be found on the internet, Liquivid is the only one that I have found that has intuitive automatic correction. You are actually able to tick the boxes by each feature you want and see the image corrected automatically with this software, where normally you get that blah result that would never do, and end up fine tuning the result for 30 minutes. And, with this, I was able to load multiple files at once and perform the same actions on the whole batch at once, which worked out great for editing the photos I took on my Parrot A.R. Drone 2.0. Some of these can be seen in my artwork uploaded publically. I’ve not found another software program that will perform this quickly and correctly for batch work.

I found the results for video to be less satisfactory than for photos. The main issue is with sound/image desync. Because of out of sync voice, I found using Windows Movie Maker to still be the better choice for editing videos taken on my phone of conversation and voice.  Liquivid seems to be designed primarily for motion cameras, and that is where I found the best results. When looking for a solution for this in the manual, I noted the need for Steam users to deactivate the Steam Overlay before using Liquivid. I right-clicked on the program name in my Steam Software library, selected properties, and disabled the Steam overlay, as suggested. But, this didn’t change the effect  for speech based video. Though I definitely think that needs to be done.
The only other issue I noted was that there seems to be no difference between side-by-side mode and preview mode when I’m using the software. All windows stay the same size regardless of which button I click. But, this does not affect the way the program works in any way.
*Intuitive Autocorrection
*Defish, sharpening, removing lens distortion work very well.
*Video stabilization for motion camera/ drone video is excellent
*Simple / User friendly interface
*I found it possible to run other programs while exporting & saving whole batches of files
*No bugs, or crashing of any kind

*Consistent Desync issues with voice video
*
The Dev responded quickly and with detailed info to this question/ concern in comments section.
I received a copy of the software free for review purposes, but that does not affect my review in any way. I don’t recommend anything I wouldn’t feel comfortable using myself.
It is a program that will greatly enhance any web-based user applications, and one I will get a lot of use from with my drone and wildlife cameras.

DISCLAIMER: I received this product for no cost for the purpose of reviewing. However, this does not affect my views and opinions of the title.
liquivid is a video editing tool. It has many straight forward features that can enhance or change a video to your choosing. It's not easy for me to review something like this, as I don't really have prior knowledge of video editing, and I usually just review games. I've decided that I'd be reviewing this product from a beginner's point of view in video editing. As this is a review of software, it won't be in my usual format, so forgive me if it's not as organized.
liquivid comes with a bunch of options that let you alter your video. You pick and choose which ones you want to use and it applies the effect to the video. There's video stabilizing, de-fishing, sharpening, flicker and noise removal, and a couple more.
--------
The software is quite easy to use. At first you'll have to find out what all the buttons do, but by simply hovering over each of them, the tool-tips will tell you exactly what they do. After choosing the video you want to change, you can then just pick which effects and enhancements you want for the video, and then apply them. It's very straight forward and quite easy to use. The user interface is not cluttered and complicated, it kind of guides you through what to do as you continue to edit your video.
--------
This part may be a bit subjective, as I know nothing of video editing, I only can confirm what I see with my own eyes. After you make changes to the video content, there is a noticeable difference in the quality when compared to the original video. My edited video was sharper, less grainy, and all around cleaner than my original. You could see a little more detail to the newer video. Though, in my personal opinion, it wasn't as big of a change as I was hoping for, but the resulting video was definitely better than the original.
--------
liquivid is great for someone who doesn't have any editing experience, but just wants to clean up their video a little bit. The tool is great for sharpening and bringing out a little more detail in videos. Using the tool reminds me of picking filters on Instagram or on Snapchat, or something similar, it's not at all complicated, and I actually appreciate that.
Thanks to the devs for giving me the opportunity to review this product, as well as anyone who took this review into consideration, I hope it helped.

Put a lot more hours in since my last review.  Again, I have never played Ark so I do not know it's similarities to Dark and Light, but all games have similarities as most newer games tend to take ideas or features that are good, work, or they personally like from previous games to make it their own.  In short don't let it keep you from trying out the game.
Cannot stress this enough to everyone though, that this is an Early Access game!  It has bugs, lots of them.  Optimization issues too.  There will be lag, some things don't work properly just yet, other players finding and abusing exploits to get an advantage over others.  These things are plenty, but the developers have been good about trying to stay on top of it.  There is a lot of issues to fix, so give them time.
That said the game is still incredibly fun.  I've been able to dump plenty of time into the game despite it's current faults and I don't feel my money was wasted in the least.  So do I recommend this game?  Certainly.  But just understand what you should expect before jumping in!

There are flying mounts in this game, and sometimes they will bug out and vanish (as of the moment).  If you check the house news (I think pressing P?)  and it shows that the mount has not died, they might be at the 'world ceiling'.  Try to grab another flying mount, then fly straight up from the spot you had left your other and you might find them there.  I found mine a couple times that way.
House building is both fun and frustrating.  It's hard to 'rotate' pieces to fit exactly how you want them to sometimes.  And until you unlock wood architecture your first home will be limited to how flat the land is.  You also cannot build too close to another player's anything (house or even just a random foundation or pillar) which frustrates me to no end.  But building of houses is similar to how it was done in Fall Out 4 I think.  The pieces snap together and all that.
Tames do level!  The creatures you can tame in the game will level with you and you can raise their stats after a level up however you like, which is another feature I like.
I'm not too good at reviews and this is really the first game I've tried doing a review for, and rather than take the layout or methods of others I felt I should just do it my way.  I hope it was helpful to anyone reading and in making their decision on buying this game or not.  I really think it's worth it, and once the developers finish patching out the bugs and exploits the game will be so much better than it is now!  So make sure you get it while it has the EA discount otherwise you may miss out when it switches to full price in the future!

Metro 2033 is one of these wonderful creepy shoddy video games from Eastern Europe. It captures some of the ghost town existentialism that STALKER made popular, but it had quite a few problems. The stealth system, for example, was crap on toast. It didn't run very well. The way the game felt and moved had a few problems, it felt a bit like running a lap underwater. Despite all this, it had ambience and character and terror crawling out of every goddamn pore of its being!
So I'm happy to say Metro 2033 Redux is mostly an improvement. Well, mostly.
First of all, I'd like to lodge a complaint: The development team ignored processing instructions for older AMD and Intel CPUs, and I would like to say that is not cool at all. I've had a AMD Phenom II quad-core processor for some time now, and while it isn't the amazing powerhouse that is whatever's at the top of Tom's Hardware's CPU charts, it can still kick♥♥♥♥♥and take names. Developing for the PC to work with a wide, wide range of specs and hardware configurations is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
Thankfully, those instructions were patched in and I finally got to play the game two days later after launch.
Second complaint: I had to replace one of the intro movies in the game directory with a blank file because it was crashing my game when I was actually able to get it running. I had to do this to a game released in 2014 to get it to run.
After those two I finally got to play it. It looked very good. It feels very nice to play - character reponses are fluid and there isn't a bunch of slowdown I experienced from the last game. FOV's stuck at something below 90, so take what you will from that.
It implements a lot of the improvements made by the sequel to this game (Metro: Last Light) and implements them into this game, which means stealth works and I was able to run it at nearly max settings! A new feature allows you to play it as a survival horror kind of shooter (the proper Metro 2033 experience) or as a straight-up on rails shooter (the equivalent of having chocolate-flavored vodka instead of drinking it straight up LIKE A REAL METRO DWELLER DOES), so there's that.
If you're playing this for the first time, don't skimp and get the original Metro 2033. The Redux version is a far more refined experience. You could argue that going for the remake loses some of the original shoddiness, and in that case, do whatever you like. But if you're dipping your toe into this strange flavor of Eastern Europe first person shooters for the first time, get the Redux.

NEO Scavenger was on my wishlist for a long time, $15 seemed steep for a graphics/text game, let alone a rogue-like. Well, I got drunk one night and impulsively hit 'buy'. So now I have it, and I like it enough to give a review, which I don't usually do.
NEO is brutal. This isn't the type of game where you play the ultra-altruistic "Hero" that saves everybody and looks good doing it. You'll live a lot longer if you take the attitude of "desperate homeless guy that doesn't want to get involved in your♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;.
When you die, it's over. No going back to a previous save. You just start over from scratch.
The learning curve is a little bit steep, but so rewarding once you get there. My first several hours I went through at least half a dozen deaths. I learned to avoid fights. To clean my wounds before bandaging them. I learned to not ever eat yellow berries. I rage quit twice. I came back twice.
Now, I've got a rifle (with ELEVEN bullets!), a warm coat and enough clean water to last me a week. I'm unstoppable, king of all there is in this wasteland.
Except that I'm not. I still run away from everything that moves, I only camp in secluded buildings, diligently cover my tracks behind me and always keep an eye over my shoulder.
And that's how it should be. I survived for this long because I learned how to live in the wasteland. I didn't get a bunch of XP from slaughtering hundreds of enemies and then suddenly become immune to a bullet to the brainpan.
That's what I love about this game. The "XP" is your own damn brain. Learning how to craft the things you need. How to avoid those looters in the distance. Knowing that I've gotten as far as I have by not making mistakes.
NEO has an outrageous amount of complexity that you would never know exists until you go looking for it. If you're on the fence, just buy it. Well worth the money spent.
One last tip: If you're new, take botany. Makes the game a little more forgiving since you won't really have to worry about food & drink.

I had to dust off my Razer Naga(the one with the 12 buttons on the side) to feel comfortable playing the game.  If you own a controller outside of your keyboard and mouse, definitely use it here.  The game is also short, and can be finished in an afternoon of gaming.

This review comes from someone who has played Saints Row 3 and loved it very much.
The reasons why I gave this game a negative review are as follows :
1) The concept of "Aliens attack the earth" feels very generic.
2) Though you have a wide variety of super powers to play around with most of them like ice blast and fire are nothing new.
3) Most of the Main Quests take place "OUTSIDE" of Steelport city/Simulation. The city is just there for you to play around with your superpowers on your own and completing the rinse and repeat side quests.
4) Talking about side quests they go like : " Meet .... on the ship"
- Disrupt the system
- Race throught the system
- Clear out the zin troops
- Inject virus
" Meet ....... to get your reward"
This goes on and on until they think they had enough of you. The same objectives over and over and over again.And you need to complete them to unlock powers and weapons.   Did I ever tell you the definition of insanity.
5) All your homies refer to you as "Boss" and make you work like a slave in the side quests above. This game badly suffers from "You are the only one who is competent" cliche.
6) The tough decisions that we need to do at the end of some Major Quests in SR3 are no more there. The text adventure section of SR3 is replaced by a more boring and stupid one, in one of the missons.
Overall, this game may seem fun if you watch the videos. The superpowers may look cool at first. But the novelty wears off very soon as you don't get to use in them in the Main Quests. The only place where they are actually used are in the boring and repetitive side quests and when you are on your own.

I came back to check out quake live considering some of the comments on my old review and I would like to resummarize my review, because they have made some very positive changes to Quake Live. To start off, Loadouts are now optional and aren't P2P to remove. This is very good because it diverses the toxic players from the people who want to learn quake live or just want to have fun to shoot some people. This is my first review ever, so please bear with me.
I see that there is a lot of hate toward this game but I feel that most of it is invalid as the sole purpose of you being able to download this game early has been missed. Allow me to elaborate.
When a title reads "Early access" that means you are invited, at a discount price, to be apart of the creation of a game that is still under development. Which means, (please take a seat as this will come as a shock to most)  the game will have all the glitches, errors and problems of a game that is....wait for it... not complete! BAM! there it is! wow, I nearly passed out when I read that!
Dark and Light is in early access, which means that the developer is asking for your help and support so they can continue to make a game better through giving you a rough draft and allowing you to send feed back and areas that need improvement to make a gamer happy with the product along with what is already planned. This means that when you find something you dont like (ie, connection problems, loading screen freezing, graphic errors, fell through the earth, c@ck is too small) you REPORT it to the development team and they will work on fixing it, as this team has been doing very well with so far.  Not so you can throw a tantrum, make a negative review after 1h of playing, err-being frozen on a loading screen(according to some) and crying to everyone because you need a bottle and got a refund.
So here is my official review!
IF you have the mental capacity to understand that this game is in early access (refer to above paragraphs) and want to experience the game in a raw, incomplete form for a discount price with the responsibility of providing problem/glitch hunting and feedback for fixing, this game is GREAT! It looks and smells like ARC did when it was fresh off the line, but its different in all the ways that count! With a familiar UI and crafting system, you plunge into a world full of crazy beasts and creatures with mountains and valleys to explore, spells to craft, fireballs to throw and tree ents to stomp you into the ground as many times as your heart desires! You can build houses, craft weapons, custom tailor your character in bizzare and just plain weird visual ways. Classes?! PFF. thats a thing of the past, creat whatever you want your character to be with very limitations beyond where you put your skill points.
This game is fun already, I have only played just over 3h but already I can see that this game is headed for a good place among the titles, but it just needs support, time and patience from the community. Yes- its glitchy, yes-you get stuck, yes the loading screen becomes very mundane to look at after a while, but in the end, for an early access game, its doing fairly well!
Now, I see people saying "It says its already finalized but that its only at 30%- im scared!!", You people need to understand that the ground, gravity, walls, physics, character models, run and walk style, the trees, the music, voices, crafting system, swinging your axe, take a sh*t and the ability to walk forward and all the wonderful things that come with it.... ARE COMPLETE AND FUNCTIONAL! They never said they were pretty yet (cause they're not),  they said they were complete! Meaning the ground isnt going anywhere anytime soon and the trees and rocks will still look like trees and rocks later- just prettier, after the other 75% gets put in!
IF you do not understand early access and want a refund after 1h, then take a hike because you've missed the point and your input on this page is irrelevant.
So- in conclusion, this game is off to a good start, the dev team is active and obviously involved with the community as there have been daily patching and updates.  The gameplay is choppy but fun and reeks of potential, especially with PVP. The world looks wonderful and though I have not come across any dungeons yet, what I see so far compels me to explore across the horizons and get trampled by giant things made of all sorts of magic, meat and branch.  It is very enjoyable and I look forward to seeing it through to completion.

Hoard, the prospet of playing as a dragon is cool, but it's got a lot of problems which kill the fun aspect of it.
Problems and issues.
1: Mouse controls are slow. This would not seem like much of a problem at first, but when you need to aim quickly when dealing with faster enemies, you need fast mouse controls for your aiming. This game's first obvious problem is it's mouse control.
2: Limited controller use. It's only support falls into a Logitech controller, and an Xbox 360 controller, this doesn't support Mayflash support or what have you. Thankfully, this issue can be resolved by disabling the control pad in the options.
3: Lack of mouse sensetivity control. This could have resolved issue 1 so easily, this could have made the game more enjoyable.
4: Selfish uncoordinated AI. When you play co-op mode, you expect to have some coordination between the AI, but sadly, this is only achieved through players working together. The AI is set on felfish if or suicidal plans, which is not that bad when you play against it, however, this still means the AI will fail miserably in co-op mode which requires some level of coordination for optimal play.
5: Buildings and units capable of attacking the player upgrade too quickly. This would not be such an issue in a long term game, but when a castle is guarded by a legion of champions because they tore into you in earlier periods does not help.
6: Time on maps is too short. A mere 10 minutes isn't exactly favorable with gathering. interesting as it seems to see how high you can gather before time runs out, it would make more sense if it calculated how much you could hold until you expired from no funds remaining.
7: thieves spawn too quickly as do taverns. This is sadly a case with towns you control, as thieves seldom discriminate on who they steal from! This can mean they may steal from you even with their town loyal to you!
Some things to note of good fortune include...
1: color selection, there is a variety of colors to choose from, which is great for identifying your own dragon.
2: Multiplayer functionality, if you can get some friends gathered up for a Co-op match, it's worth it to optimize your resources, and coordinate attacks for the benefit of your group, or to see who is the better dragon.
3: The option to use a controller. This is a good idea, though it needs work, and more controller support for things such as the Mayflash adapter with Wii Classic controller Pro.
4: BEING A DRAGON, now this is a fun idea, it's unfortunate though that the game has some issues.
5: Potentially easier methods of collecting gold. From kidnapping princesses, destroying carts to take money, through grabbing massive gems to turn into fast easy funds, ransom can be a potent means of collecting money. Wizard gems however are nearly suicide as the towers upgrade too quickly, and do so much damage that 2 hits means you're flynig back to your hoard to recover.
If you're a fan of games that are brutally difficult, and have a cruel learning curve, I recommend it! Otherwise, until the creators patch this game to improve and expand the controls, stay away.

At first glance, I thought I would be disappointed by this game. It didn't seem like anything special. However, it came highly recommended from my bro'i'law, and when I looked the game over I was surprised to find the "Overwhelmingly Positive" 97% community approval rate. So I bought it.
I was very happily surprised by this game. Never once did I feel that the game was trying to overreach what it was. It seems well polished and well balanced. There is really only one thing that can be frustrating, but I'll come back to that.
I think I was worried about this game because I thought it was going to try to reach into the flashy action genre, but then came the happy surprise I mentioned. This game is all about strategy. Which path through the stars will you take in your race to the Federation base? Do you have the time to make a detour in order to earn some more scrap for your ship upgrades? Do you have enough fuel? Which crew member should you assign where? Crew member A has had a little more experinece working with the shields than B would, but you have been having some problem with enemies boarding your ship, and crew member A is much better outfitted for combat. Decisions, decisions. Where do I assign my energy? What should I upgrade on my ship? Should I spend my scrap on my ship or hope for one of the elusive stores and try to save up for a better gun? Which gun should I buy?
I digress. This game does a wonderful job of giving you plenty of choices and strategy to work with, without overwhelming you. Choosing what to upgrade, what weapons to buy, what crew to use, what route to take, etc. This infuses the game with a complex flavor which, after adding the multiple ship designs and layouts unlocked through play, makes for a LOT of replay value. I am loving the strategy and thinking and planning. Many solutions to the same problem.
During combat, you are able to pause with the spacebar at any time, letting you reassess the situation at any moment of need. This is one of my favorite features.
The thing that can be frustrating is the luck of the draw. The game's star-systems and enemies are randomly generated, which is very much a good thing, but this does mean that you'll have good runs and bad runs. Sometimes you'll run into a system perfectly lined up with exactly what you want and need, and sometimes you won't. Sometimes you'll run into a ship with only beam weapons that is completely ineffective against your minimal shields, and sometimes you'll run into a killing machine in the second system that will mercilessly blow you to bits. - I'm not going to lie to you though, this isn't really all that bad. The game is just short enough and casual enough that having a bad run is a small disappointment, but certianly not something to ruin your day. I like the ebb and flow.
I would highly recommend this game. I'm loving it, and will be playing it for a long while to come.

I revisit this game once in a while because I've yet to find anything like it. It's a turn-based post apocalyptic survival game with elements of sci-fi and fantasy. My favorite thing about this game is probably that the inventory system attempts to be realistic, which I find to be annoyingly rare in video games.
Criticisms?
I really like that there is permadeath, though I think I would enjoy the game more if I felt it was possible for a skilled gamer to beat it on their first try. There are important details I've only been able to learn by dying or visiting the wikia, and I feel that takes away from the immersion. I've yet to beat it despite around 20 attempts.
Why not have learned recipes carry over to future games?
I'd prefer more of the information found on the wikia to be displayed in game, such as item component properties and weapon damage/range.
Even the wikia doesn't have important details such as the degree to which things are affected by stat bars.
I've forgotten or otherwise left out other issues that frustrated me about this game at first, but I don't regret buying it. This game...there's no better term for it than rewarding clickbait. As a pug with a cape, you fly through space, a neon city, and even a land within the clouds while dodging all manner of enemies, from UFOs to sheep with wings. With a name like "Super Mega Neo Pug", I wasn't sure what it would be like, but this game surpassed my expectations.
However, I'd like to quickly go over the drawbacks. First of all, this game is BRUTAL at the start, and it takes a while to get used to the physics. This sucks, because once you finally adjust, there's not much to look forward to. The rate of progress will always be seemingly slow and unrewarding. All that keeps me playing is the knowledge of more unlockable characters, as well as certain collectables.
That said, however, the character selection is one of my favorite parts. It's not just pugs, ladies and gentlemen. You can play as a dinosaur, a panda, and even a hamster. It takes a while to unlock them, but things get easier as you get better. Also, as you get better, you'll have an easier time collecting these random circular pictures(I don't know what else to call them). They'll appear on your menu and give fun sentences when you hover your mouse over them. The sentences themselves are about as ridiculous as you'd expect from a game called "Super Mega Neo Pug".
Overall, it's a fun game.
Pros:
+Charming characters
+Charming collectables
+Fun enemy designs
+It's only a dollar(as of this review).
Cons:
-Difficult at the start
-Slow and unrewarding rate of progress

I have played the original Metro 2033(and Last Light) and I have always wanted the game ever since the redux bundle was announced, though I ended up not buying because of some reasons. The graphics are much smoother, and in my opinion, a lot more advanced. There were things in Metro LL that didn't run so well before I tweaked it, and I was afraid the same would happen with this game. Fortunately, it did not, things were smooth, no lagging whatsoever.
Some mechanics from Metro LL are also implemented, such as gasmask wipe and easier to read stealth light. The original Metro 2033's stealth were kind of broken for me, and difficult to use because you have 3 lights(red, yellow, green). In this one, following Metro LL, there's only visible(watch lights up) and not visible(watch turns off),
For the negatives, though, I do think there are some places where the knock down doesn't work properly, such as when an enemy is sitting down exactly beside the wall, I had to walk in front of him to do so, which ended up alarming the other enemies. Also, some moments in the game I lost a bit of fps for unknown reasons, although it drops only a bit, but is visible.
For me, the enhancements outweigh the negatives, and if you own the original and liked it, you will like this one also. I would recommend this game.

So anyway, I am like a lot of people in that I have a couple cameras, but most of the pictures I take actually come from my phone or a little digital camera I own and are pictures of opportunity (you know, you're driving and the clouds look awesome or the sun is setting perfectly or some♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥just backed into your car, etc....), and so there tends to be a lot of issues with lighting, sharpness, artifacts, etc... I feel this is really where Liquivid shines....for the amateur photographer.
The program is incredibly user friendly with a very simple and easy to understand interface, Additionally, the website provides more than enough information via user guides to answer any question you might have. There are also a couple user guides in the community hub on Steam right now and I imagine more will show up as more people use the program.
You can create your own camera profile, which is nice. Also, any pictures you import to the program will automatically be available when you launch the program and anything you have worked on will save automatically throughout the process making it easy to go back and mess with your photos at will.
I found the advanced settings to be the way to go. You can as mentioned before create your own camera profile or simply select one from the list (which has 20 or 30 preset camera lenses....which is to say it recognizes specific lens distortions). The sharpness and noise filters work like a charm. They are simple, but have a huge impact and are the real stars of this program in my opinion. You can also run side by side comparisons of your photo as well as split photo comparisons.
So far, that is all I have really played with, and I havent tried out the video editing features at all, so I cant speak to that, although I'm sure I will in the future. I will also note again that I am by no means an expert at either the photographer aspect or the editing aspect of all of this. I previously just used Picasa, lol.
Anyway, I like this program and was glad for the opportunity to try it out. For me personally, I will definitely get $20 value from it. Obviously, YMMV, but as of now, I recommend it.

Here's what you need to know as to why I've not recommended this game:
- Ridiculously average story. It's not terrible (i.e. there aren't any plot holes at least) but it simply exists to drive the gameplay, whereas it could've been something really cool enough to make me want to keep playing and let some faults of the design slide. Maybe this is what XCom games of yore are like but still, I think more effort was needed in keeping the story interesting.
- Too much base-management which kills the flow of an already fairly average story. Build too many satellites, you have panic at a manageable level but your soldiers are still using pea-shooters and wearing silk dresses in combat situations. And don't forget to upgrade your fighter jets for UFO engagements, which go from laughably easy to nigh on impossible (unless you fork out huge amounts of money for upgrades) in the space of literally ONE story mission.
- Way too much RNG in combat which removes any real sense of satisfaction of playing a strategy game; everything is a gamble, and even a 95% chance to hit with additional 60% critical chance has a chance to miss COMPLETELY.
- Save scumming is necessary; you don't screw up due to bad planning (mostly) but because the enemy gets free moves when you spot them, have ridiculously good aim and can easily destroy cover with one pistol shot.
- Therefore, combat situations often revolve around the same strategy; move solider, put on overwatch, ad infinitum. Yawn. if you want to take risks, feel free to not be able to finish the game as your best soldiers all die or get wounded and a terror mission pops up that you have to then win with rookies.

- It's not resource heavy at all and doen't have to remember complex Ai routines, yet it's always bugging out. It freezes when taking some shots affecting more than one target for me. There are many clipping issues and animation looks very janky.
- Nationalities mean jack♥♥♥♥♥♥ every one is American anyway. Not a deal breaker but why even HAVE  nationalities?
- Another petty but valid gripe; all combat environments look the same. No different flora or architecture depending on whether you are in the world (Lagos has identical buildings and scenery to Birmingham... REALLY??). Very lazy map design in my opinion.
On the plus side, it has some nice music and you can play a bit strategically with heavies using rockets to blow up walls and create ideal sniping opportunities that really can♥♥♥♥♥♥in the alien's picnic, but overall this XCom reboot is average at best and downright unfairly hard at worst, and unpolished and  monotonous on top of it. Not repetitive, as repetitive doesn't necessarily mean bad. Repetition can be a game strength, if the repetitive element is satisfying and fun. Xcom: Enemy Unknown rarely feels either satisfying or fun once you figure out everything is all down to chance rather than strategy. In short, a big disappointment. I really expected great things from this game and it didn't deliver.

What can I say that hasn't been said? Sometimes Blender is the best tool for the job, and sometimes other tools are more efficient, but Blender does nearly everything you would want, and it's free. You can't beat that. I mean, there's even a built-in video editor. It's kind of weird, but it totally works! There are also great free add-ons like Dark Blender (bundle of sculpt and game-focused tools), YAVNE (normals editing), Bool Tool (boolean modelling) and Loop Tools (extra useful modelling tools), as well as great paid ones like Retopoflow (essential retopology tools), Bake Tools (uh... tools for baking), Hard Ops (advanced boolean tools for hard surface modelling), and Box Cutter (different boolean tools from the Hard Ops folks)..
Great things about Blender:
- Super fast modelling with lots of shortcuts
- Has everything you need to model, sculpt, retopologize, bake, texture, and animate game assets, and any shortcomings are often taken care of by add-ons.
- UV mapping is mega easy (works a lot like Maya Bonus Tools unwraping if you've used that)
- Linked asset libraries
- Cycles raytracing renderer is really nice
- Dynamic topology sculpting (it's no Zbrush, but sometimes it's all you need)
- Import/export most formats you'd want
- FBX export (Unity, UE4) has gotten a lot better, as has normal editing, which is important for lower poly game assets
- Tons of tutorials everywhere
- Built-in video editor, compositor, and game engine can sometimes be useful. Depending on your needs, you can do entire projects with those tools, no doubt.
- Free! Open Source! Donate if you want!
- No license restrictions on the assets you make in Blender. (Yes, an educational version of Maya/Max is free. No, you can't use that commercially in any way. Yes, the company that makes Maya/Max has more lawyers than you have friends. Like, way more.)
- Pretty much anything can be scripted in Python if you're so inclined.
- Community can sometimes be quite helpful.
Less great things:
- Interface can be challenging to new users, but you get used to it and will sometimes even come to prefer it. Give it time.
- Setting up bakes is kind of a pain (Bake Tools add-on is meant to address this).
- No in-viewport PBR viewing (Unity 5 and UE4 specular or metalness workflows), though they're working on it.
- Can't integrate with some proprietary plug-ins (like Substance) depending on how they work, due to license incompatibilities. (Depends, though. Octane, a commercial renderer, works just fine with Blender's license).
- 3D Texture painting is still slow as hell for me. Just get Quixel or Substance Painter and call it a day.
- Not the AAA industry standard. If you want to get a job in AAA, you're still going to have to learn Max or Maya. But, you know, you can learn more than one. I have. Pretty prevalent in the indie scene, though.
- Community can sometimes be a little overzealous, too
Things that will make your life easier:
- Immediately set the selection to left mouse instead of right mouse in the settings.
- Don't use Maya or Max shortcut/interaction modes (not everything works as expected and you won't be able to follow any tutorials).
- Follow tutorials. Lots of them. 3D is hard, and not everything in Blender is immediately apparent. Nice people have already figured this stuff out and will tell you about it in video form.
- Don't expect to master it in a few hours. It took me YEARS to get good at this stuff, and I still learn new things all the time.
- Think of Blender as a Swiss Army knife: versatility over specialization.
So, there's really no reason not to at least give Blender a shot, especially if you're making indie games or modding. The price is certainly right. And, you might find you quite like it after a while!

An arcade-puzzle game with time manipulation, close to Adventures of Shuggy, Braid, Chronology, Gateways and Misadventures of Winterbottom. Basically, you can record a copy of yourself doing stuff, and then cooperate with your recording to solve the puzzle. The recording time is limited to something around 20 seconds, and the recording also doesn't loop (unlike in Misadventures of Winterbottom).
The Good:
- low price
- 64 levels, and they do get pretty difficult after about level 22
The So-so:
- very early puzzles start to rely on precise timing. I know there are people who like finger dexterity contests (e.g. fans of Meatboy) but I'm a kind of player who wants to simply figure out how the puzzle should be solved and not spend next 15 minutes torturing myself with precise execution. But that's really a matter of taste or age (I'm 34).
The Bad:
- annoying music which resembles that in NES games from the 80s, I had to turn music off after a few minutes
- can't re-map keys. I kept pressing Space to jump because of my habit from other games, but space actually records your clone..
- the graphics are pretty bland, almost amateurish - nothing comparable to the gorgeous visuals of Misadventures of Winterbottom, for example. Even in this quasi-8 bit style some decorative elements would help liven the scenery a bit.
Conclusion: buy it if you are really into time-travel stuff (like myself), tried the other games I mentioned and still want more.

At first glance, I thought I would be disappointed by this game. It didn't seem like anything special. However, it came highly recommended from my bro'i'law, and when I looked the game over I was surprised to find the "Overwhelmingly Positive" 97% community approval rate. So I bought it.
I was very happily surprised by this game. Never once did I feel that the game was trying to overreach what it was. It seems well polished and well balanced. There is really only one thing that can be frustrating, but I'll come back to that.
I think I was worried about this game because I thought it was going to try to reach into the flashy action genre, but then came the happy surprise I mentioned. This game is all about strategy. Which path through the stars will you take in your race to the Federation base? Do you have the time to make a detour in order to earn some more scrap for your ship upgrades? Do you have enough fuel? Which crew member should you assign where? Crew member A has had a little more experinece working with the shields than B would, but you have been having some problem with enemies boarding your ship, and crew member A is much better outfitted for combat. Decisions, decisions. Where do I assign my energy? What should I upgrade on my ship? Should I spend my scrap on my ship or hope for one of the elusive stores and try to save up for a better gun? Which gun should I buy?
I digress. This game does a wonderful job of giving you plenty of choices and strategy to work with, without overwhelming you. Choosing what to upgrade, what weapons to buy, what crew to use, what route to take, etc. This infuses the game with a complex flavor which, after adding the multiple ship designs and layouts unlocked through play, makes for a LOT of replay value. I am loving the strategy and thinking and planning. Many solutions to the same problem.
During combat, you are able to pause with the spacebar at any time, letting you reassess the situation at any moment of need. This is one of my favorite features.
The thing that can be frustrating is the luck of the draw. The game's star-systems and enemies are randomly generated, which is very much a good thing, but this does mean that you'll have good runs and bad runs. Sometimes you'll run into a system perfectly lined up with exactly what you want and need, and sometimes you won't. Sometimes you'll run into a ship with only beam weapons that is completely ineffective against your minimal shields, and sometimes you'll run into a killing machine in the second system that will mercilessly blow you to bits. - I'm not going to lie to you though, this isn't really all that bad. The game is just short enough and casual enough that having a bad run is a small disappointment, but certianly not something to ruin your day. I like the ebb and flow.
I would highly recommend this game. I'm loving it, and will be playing it for a long while to come.

My Setup: Windows 10, keyboard, XBOX One controller
RePete is a puzzle platforming game for PC, Mac, and Linux. You play as Pete, a guy who likes to collect gems and has the ability to create clones of himself, aka RePetes. RePete will do whatever Pete was doing during the 'clone recording' process. You can have RePete stand on buttons to open doors, flip levers to make platforms move, and even go through the gate to finish the level. In later levels you can create 2, 3, and even 4 RePetes to solve the puzzles.
The puzzles start out pretty easy, with the first world consisting mainly of tutorial levels. But once you get to worlds 3 and 4, you are sure to spend some time scratching your head, as these levels can be devilishly tricky. Even so, with just 64 levels (for now?), RePete only takes an hour or two to get through all the levels. Fortunately, there is plenty of replay value created by the challenge times and hidden gems for each level.
The gameplay in RePete is pretty simple. For controls have directional control(left/right), jump(up), and lever activation(down) with the arrow keys, and space to create RePetes. I was able to use an XBOX One controller as well, though the button mapping isn't stated anywhere and is counter intuitive in some cases(B will advance you in menus, rather than take you back a screen).
The 16bit graphics style and sound aren't going to blow you away. However, they are very well made and fit the game style perfectly. I didn't encounter any graphical glitches, and only encountered minor gameplay glitches. The only notable bug was Pete getting forced into the ground by a closing door. Other than that, the game was mostly free of any unintentional frustrations.
Overall, I give RePete a 8 out of 10. It is very fun, undeniably challenging, and solidly built. There are a few minor points that could use polishing, but nothing that prevented me from thoroughly enjoying this game.
So what are you waiting for? Go play RePete!

RNG HELL! Beware those who seek true tactical games!
As with most who dislike this game, I ultimately give it a thumbs down because the RNG is terrible and so unforgiving it makes anything other than save scumming feel like pure luck. In the end, they tell you the game is about tactics. It's not. It's about watching let's plays and reading guides (that advise a LOT of save scuming) and doing your homework to make the game enjoyable. There's typically only one tactic that works in each situation, and once you've watched the let's plays and read the guides, the game shifts from "Too hard on all difficulties" to "I need mods so there's a real challenge".
It's too bad really. This game's poor definition of tactics and save scum favoring game play is a prime example of the terrible direction game design has taken in modern times, but for some reason it's fanbase is happy with a game that claims not to hold your hand, yet the #1 form of advice is a let's play holding your hand.
Stop telling people this game is about tactics. Flanking an alien, missing with both shots and having your trooper on overwatch get anihilated because of unrealistically unforgiving RNG isn't tactics. There's specific key issues with this.
Tactics need to make common sense. The reason many players rage out and don't have fun is because having a dual flank on a foe while your two other squad mates overwatching should reward the player for having the sense to put themselves in optimal positions. Instead, you are punished because the game has it's own idea of tactical advantage, and only rewards those who have figured out the puzzle, AND are lucky enough to have the RNG bless them.... or just save scum.
Seriously, that's the point that I feel like is blatant evidence of the games shortcomings. When you finally get fed up with how easy-hard difficulty are ALL hard difficulty, just read a guide and save scum. Then it's just a matter of patience.... which is about the point I ran out.
Not a single tactic I have learned in other games, IRL, in any format translated into this game. I was punished for using every iota of common sense I mustered. It wasn't until I turned off the brain, followed the guides and save scummed that I found the game easy (because it's basically reseting the game until the RNG gives you what you want). It's not just opinion, that's♥♥♥♥♥♥game design. I don't care if you like this.... some people like the Star Wars prequels too. That doesn't mean they're well made.
If you are like me and want genuine tactics, look towards shooters or RTS games. Coordinating with a partner to execute different strategies to defeat your opponent, THAT'S tactical. Save scumming because the game is so ridiculous with it's RNG and having to do homework on youtube and reading guides, that's not tactics, that's time sync ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.

is one of the best strategy games of all-time.
Aliens are invading the Earth and you’ve been put in charge of the defense of the entire planet. That's what
presents. A strategy game from Firaxis and 2K.
First, should be said that I never played the predecessors of
, so can't tell if they were either good or bad and if has evolved (negatively or positively).
Let's to the game. In the beginning of the game, you'll select a location for your base of operations from one of several possibilities, and this is the only base you manage through the course of the game.
Gameplay is divided into two portions: base management and combat scenarios. You can manage the paramilitary XCOM project, deciding what new projects to research and what new technology to produce so that the XCOM troopers go into battle with the best equipment possible. You can recruit, specialize and train unique soldiers and manage your team.
In battle, the basic concept is simple: get squad members behind cover where damage is minimized, and then take aim. Each squad member gets two actions per turn, though some of your soldiers will earn ways of extending this basic number.
Injured soldiers can be out of service for weeks, so maintaining your base involves ensuring you have a steady supply and that you’re always researching the aliens and their tech. This research can then be used to create new weapons and equipment, and any excess sold off on the black market to help offset your monthly costs.
The camera angles are extremely good. They dramatize and increases a lot the
gameplay. The same for the music, that's very well created and implemented.
You and your XCOM team will fight around the world in over 70 missions, communicating and negotiating with governments around the world. The missions are too challenging, due to the enemy AI that's very well-made, and the way the individual enemies are designed.
If you do well the missions, the funding nations will pour even more money into the XCOM project. However, if you do poorly, the nations will leaving the project with even fewer resources to fight back the alien invasion.
Death is always present in XCOM and, for this, there's a Memorial to fallen soldiers, complete with a bagpipe music.
In summary, this game combines tactical/strategy on the battlefield with a headquarters management of XCOM project, the evolution of their equipment and training of soldiers.
The best aspect of XCOM is the sense that there’s never enough time or resources to do everything that needs to be done.

original review:
well to instantly take a dump on the negative reviews... they all suck. no information on actual problems at all.
the game is good... it really is. the real big seller i think is the way you earn currency.
so i think in this review i will explain any readers how it works.
to get a sense of the scale of the prices and overall economy
i should also note the game works with the hero rotation mechanic featuring 1 new hero every week from the 3 in the pool. one of every playstyle: buildy, tanky and blowey upey, or fast damagy.
one plain hero starter costs about 3000 gold bars (standart currency) (3 in total)
or... some amount of platinum bars (premium currency) i never actually bothered to check...
the more interesting, second row, but not any stronger heroes cost 6000 gold. ( 3 heroes in total)
then we have 6 heroes costing about 12000 each
and last but not least we have some heroes costing 18000 (somewhere from 3-6 i think?)
special upgrades which i should note also give a drawback meaning the upgrades dont make a hero better, they alter the hero's playstyle. cost 700-3000 for tier 1 and 6000-18000 for tier 3
every match gives you... 50-200 gold
WAIT WAIT WAIT! i know what you are thinking, oh no another stupid grindfest.
the way the game handles it it gives you 3 quite easy missions to complete in game every day.
each gives 350-450 gold. plus heroes who level up (bought or not) will also grant you a nice amount of gold.
this allows a player to buy a starter hero he likes in about 3 days assuming he plays 3-5 matches a day, and completing all 3 missions. including a guy with awesome turrets, a sniper, and rambo which his honestly... hard to play well... choose one of the other 2.
want a more expensive hero? 4-8 days should do it! going to the extremes huh? 12K? well thats like 12-18 days.
not to bad compared to some other games. going all in? oh it can be worth it, i went for a 18k one myself, took less then a month, logically fitting in the 24 day span. that is not so bad.
now also not that from the get go you won't want all heroes, simply because they moght not seem appealing to you.
this means in about 3-4 months of light playing you can have most heroes you want. and some skills to accompany them.
if you play more intensely you can cut that to even less. the big part is simply completing these missions.
one big advantage i see in this is the low amount of unhealthy competitiveness.
in world of tanks, or call of duty, you see idiots and kids insulting each other every moment they get. losing is painfull.
in this game it's about fun. winning is a nice bonus. and actually outweighs the sadness of losing. (not including those every odd matches that are just painfully miserable when you lose)
so the amount of name-calling nonsense is quite low, hacks have recently been patched out with the implementation of good ol teddybear easy anticheat. and when you lose it doesnt matter too much. it's not like you wasted time playing not earning gold. and don't get me wrong, people still play it seriously, and do their best to win. i only had a block breaking troll once. and this low unhealthy competitiveness also stimulates teamplay much better. since there is no such thing as bitter defeat in this game. even if a player playing the same character as you on the same team and is obviously out-performing you. he won't weaponize his keyboard via the chat bar.
and a piece of advice, for the odd ones out that do swear, when your team lose, or the enemy team loses, because they are in the enemy team. don't forget to fire back at them: "F*ck you too buddy! if you can't stand losing go back to your stupid CoD or WoT! there is no place for dickbags like you here!"
maybe learn them some manners.
another piece of advice: this very month of december 2017 a new hero is coming out.
obviously to make him sell well the first period of time it is predictable that he will likely be not only overpowered.
but also the new mechanics will make him an unusual foe and hard o fight against.
so be carefull of this, fight him a few times, and maybe even take a break a small while when he comes out untill he balances out.
another piece of advice, i just can't stop. in the map editor mode you can play as any hero, you just need to figure out what all the buttons do in there first. mainly the one that lets you play as play as any hero, (not vs players though, it's really just testing of what the heroes do and their mechanics.

This game was made in 2005, It's still fun to play! It was one of the first to include Space Battle levels. The combat was amazing, you can choose from around 9 different classes, each with their own traits and different weapons. Heroes and villians had a nice variety from both the Galatic Civil War and the Clone Wars, each with different force powers. Maps depicted most of the battles amazingly environments such as Geonosis, Kamino, The Jedi Temple and Mos Eisley and Jabba's Palace, all were fun to play on. The storymode is a bit lackluster but still enjoyable, following the events of the 501st Clonetrooper Legion through the Clone Wars to the rise of the Empire and the Battle of Hoth, unfortunatly aside from the cutscenes the mission are just to protect an area from a designated amount of time, destroy something or collect something and bring to back, etc. One of the most interesting gamemodes though is Galactic Conquest, a singleplayer/multiplayer gamemode that gives you a fleet and the other team a fleet and has you fight accross the galaxy, trying to claim and protect as many planets as possible. Anyway, this game could be considered one of the best Star Wars games ever, I give it 8/10. If you're a Star Wars and a shooter fan, this game is a must. (Gameranger can be used to play multiplayer)
Star Wars Battlefront EA was made just last year, and many people were unhappy with it, myself included. The graphics and sounds were amazing but it goes downhill from there. The only singleplayer it has is a boring survival mode in which you fight of waves of enemies. It becomes tedious really quickly. Now it has some good gamemodes such as Walker Assult, but other than that, not many. Now for the missing features, this complete game, if you can even call it complete, is missing so many things that made the original Battlefronts amazing. There is no Clone Wars, no Space Battles, no Galactic Conquest and no Campaign. This game is unfinished, Battlefront 2015 is a pathetic disgusting cashgrab at the Battlefront license and not at all worth the pricetag, and do not buy the 2015 season pass.
So I have a question, would you buy the new one with no depth for $60 or do you buy the old one which is really fun from $10? I know which one I would.

After playing this game for over 10 hours on steam. I think I am ready for a proper review for this game.
Okay here it goes.
I bought a game in 2007 by the name of Star Wars Battlefront: Renegade Squadron for my PSP and played it literally all the time. I must have beaten the campaign (which is very short) about 20 times over the first year I had the game and had gotten so good at playing Galactic Conquest that I made up different goals each time I played a game of it. I had no idea at the time that there were any other Star Wars Battlefront games until I started watching the tutorials in SWBF:RS and realized that they were talking about some other games that I've never heard of. I lost SWBF:RS for about a month (even though I had searched EVERY nook and cranny around my house) and when I found it, played it for about 5 hours straight, by this time I had had the game about 3 years. Well, after about 2 more years of playing the game on and off it finally gave up on me. I was very heartbroken and actually still have the UMD somewhere. So I slowly drifted away from Star Wars for awhile but never forgot the glorious battles the game had given me. When I finally came back into Star Wars I had found out there were other games that came before Renegade Squadron and I also heard that they were "better" than my precious Renegade Squadron. Well, I found out that this game was on Steam and bought it about a week ago and let me just say, IT IS A BLAST!!! The AI in the game are smarter than on my PSP game and there are like 2 to 2.5 dozen maps to choose from (in Renegade Squadron there were a lot of maps but I don't count the space maps). There is a class system in this game which makes the game more challenging, in Renegade Squadron you could choose what you looked like and what weapons you could have, there were also perks in the game that made you run faster, capture objectives, etc. but it made the game less of a challenge and more of a "get kills, get kills, get kills". I love SWBF2 and would encourage you to buy it. The only bad thing is there is no online multiplayer anymore but there are ways to play online via Gameranger. (I personally don't care whether I play online in this game or not it's fun either way). Hope this review helped with your decision on whether or not you wanted to spend $9.99 on it!

A free shooter without microtransaction bullshet, grind tedium, or any of that matchmaking nonsense? No way. The good old days?
It's a standalone HL2 full conversion mod on the original Source engine so it has great performance and server browser. Of course I have yet to experience any crashes or slowdowns of any kind. I've only seen one bug and it seems rare.
The UI is great. Very professional looking for the most part.
It's like a cross between Action Quake 2 and Max Payne. Pretty straightforward arcade gun battle mayhem. Except it's absurdly acrobatic. No ammo limits, just keep reloading. And mini modes in each round to keep the action moving across the map (like hunt the wanted, kill the leader of the race across the map, deliver the briefcase.).. The ballistics and sounds feel fairly solid as well. The maps are generally well made.
Sure the graphics are pretty old, it's only death match, a couple maps could use a little more varied spawn points to get the full use of the map rather than always around the same intersections, and otherwise could use some better and more character models, and it does get a little repetitive seeing everybody bounce around for a while. But fuc|< it, it's free. It's addictive because it actually feels fairly skill based and the absurdity of it all is hard to take seriously so you end up actually having fun. 8 shot pump shotgun that feels satisfying is a nice cherry on top.

UPDATE:
This is the kind of game that can be played by generations to come and would still be as compelling as the day it came out.

The game may seem like it is reusing assets but instead a familiar area may be turned on its head with new puzzle mechanics. It toys with your expectations and challenges your ability to innovate. The game is also very rewarding and well paced despite its short run time. The artwork has a timeless quality and the music is charming. I still hail this as an excellent title even years after its release.

I nabbed this game while it was on sale because it reminded me of an old flash game I used to play as a kid (I think it was called Bread Winner? I could be wrong though)
I used to really love playing that flash game, so when I saw lightfish and how similar it looked in gameplay, I figured I'd give it a try, and I really wasn't disappointed.
Light fish is basically a much more nicely designed/more aesthetically pleasing than the flash game ever was, but with the same basic gameplay mechanics (and a few new interesting ones at higher levels)
It's an absolutely gorgeous game, and is excellent for people who sometimes just want to play something a little more casual and relaxing. The purpose of the game is to section off jellyfish and other similar creatures into small blocks, destroying them and gaining points. The level ends when all creatures are gotten rid of, and you are scored on your efficiency and speed in finishing the level.
It's definitely worth grabbing (especially on sale), and is a nice little game to play between less casual games or if you're a bit on the tired side.
It's also fairly nostalgic for me in a weird kind of way, since it reminds me so much of the game I used to play online as a kid.
