TL; DR: This is a good game - buy it.
This game is a well made Rogue-like permadeath (something we seem to be blessed with at the moment). On initial plays it drips character through well narrated choices (which may have good or bad outcomes each time) and you will die as you struggle to work out a ship setup and strategy which gets you past the first few sectors.
After a few playthroughs you begin to learn which narrative choices are best avoided unless you have a blue option (signifying a ship upgrade or crew member you have guarantees you a good outcome) and get enough of an idea how to play that you get up to the final boss who trounces you.
A bit later you hone your strategy and begin making informed choices and finally beat the boss - elation! Then you try it again with the other ships which offer distinct challenges (in the opening sectors at least).
After a long time you've beaten the game with each ship and have probably found a strategy and ship setup which works for you and converge on it every game. At this stage you can play the game without much thought and don't read anything in depth and know exactly what to buy when. This takes out some of the fun but - in the game's defence - this took me ~100 hours to reach (fantastic value for money) and, talking to my friends, each of us had a different opinion on the optimum strategy which speaks of the game's balance and depth.
The free update was great and added loads of content even which made using a specific strategy more difficult (a blessing a curse simultaneously) and the new hard mode is unreasonably difficult. This is the only time the RNG-driven mechanics cannot be overcome by good strategy and experience and many restarts are needed to make progress. Normal difficulty is well-balanced so you will win sometimes and lose others (often through your own mistakes or calculated risks). However, there is always the risk of running up against a ship early on that can destroy you and you cannot harm as you haven't had time to patch up your ship's starting weakness yet. This is frustrating but is rare unless you've selected game setting which are meant to be difficult.
So this ia good game. Buy it. Enjoy it. For your first game start on easy and consider diasbling the extra content so the number of modules you need to understand is limited.

The low metacritic score for this game is an utter crime. It is a simple game, but one that is simply fun.
Horde is a party game at it's core, to the point where the ascthetic of the game is one of a boardgame assemebled on a table top. When played with friends it has all the hallmarks of a great board game to, diplomacy, backstabing, the frantic strugle for an edge to eek your way ahead of the competition as the countdown timer approaches zero... Though that last one is rare in actual board games.
For such a simple game it is very well thought out. Every aspect of dragon culture has been carefully included to make a highly dynamic, well balanced, cutthroat multiplayer game. There is no deep story or plot. Just some well developed game mechanics for lighthearted frantic fun. If you enjoy hunting for achievements the single player will offer a lot of replayability as well as they are well designed to actually require some skill and practice to achieve and collect... And that skill and practice will come in handy when it later comes time for you to torch your friends so you can take their precious gold for yourself.
Heres what you need to know. You are a dragon, you live an a fantasy country side in which the local peasants are trying to amass wealth and power, and you being a glorious dragon much more powerful and worthy of that wealth are going to take it from them.
The games consists of a serious of 10-15 minute matches. In those 10-15 minutes, farms and villages will grow, send trade caravans to one another, build watch towers and defences... And you will burn them all to the ground, take the gold that is left from the ashes, terrify the villages into sending you tribute and kidnapping their princesses for ransome all to grow your hoard, because that's what dragons do... All dragons... Those other dragons on the map are not your friends... They are cutting into your profits... You see them eyeing your hoard... Turn your back and they will steal from you just as happily as from the peasants. You can't let them. Because to a dragon the size of your hoard is status, it is power. The more gold you amass the stronger you become. Rush to accumulate wealth the fastest so you can put those other upstart dragons in their place... The timer is ever ticking down, whoever has the largest hoard when it reaches zero wins!
My longest run so far was almost 40 minutes long, got slaughtered in 5th sector. Money well spent, I can't wait till i'll get destroyed again.

is one of the best strategy games of all-time.
Aliens are invading the Earth and you’ve been put in charge of the defense of the entire planet. That's what
presents. A strategy game from Firaxis and 2K.
First, should be said that I never played the predecessors of
, so can't tell if they were either good or bad and if has evolved (negatively or positively).
Let's to the game. In the beginning of the game, you'll select a location for your base of operations from one of several possibilities, and this is the only base you manage through the course of the game.
Gameplay is divided into two portions: base management and combat scenarios. You can manage the paramilitary XCOM project, deciding what new projects to research and what new technology to produce so that the XCOM troopers go into battle with the best equipment possible. You can recruit, specialize and train unique soldiers and manage your team.
In battle, the basic concept is simple: get squad members behind cover where damage is minimized, and then take aim. Each squad member gets two actions per turn, though some of your soldiers will earn ways of extending this basic number.
Injured soldiers can be out of service for weeks, so maintaining your base involves ensuring you have a steady supply and that you’re always researching the aliens and their tech. This research can then be used to create new weapons and equipment, and any excess sold off on the black market to help offset your monthly costs.
The camera angles are extremely good. They dramatize and increases a lot the
gameplay. The same for the music, that's very well created and implemented.
You and your XCOM team will fight around the world in over 70 missions, communicating and negotiating with governments around the world. The missions are too challenging, due to the enemy AI that's very well-made, and the way the individual enemies are designed.
If you do well the missions, the funding nations will pour even more money into the XCOM project. However, if you do poorly, the nations will leaving the project with even fewer resources to fight back the alien invasion.
Death is always present in XCOM and, for this, there's a Memorial to fallen soldiers, complete with a bagpipe music.
In summary, this game combines tactical/strategy on the battlefield with a headquarters management of XCOM project, the evolution of their equipment and training of soldiers.
The best aspect of XCOM is the sense that there’s never enough time or resources to do everything that needs to be done.
is a fantastic strategy game, combined with an engaging atmosphere well achieved.

For those who played the originals, Firaxis's X-Com is an interesting and worthy homage to the original game.
For those who didn't, X-Com Enemy Unknown is a nerve-wracking reboot of the classic tactical RPG that is tons of fun to play, once you get past the rather steep learning curve and understand how to play the game - safe, in other words.
Firaxis did a very good job not only at the tech/research/building tree mechanics in the game but also overall with all of the games systems. If you don't throw your neck on the chopping block to save X-Com council member nations, not only do you lose all control of those countries and they become infested enemy strongholds where you're likely to fail even with a unit full of colonels, but they withdraw from the council and your strength will dwindle. You will pay the price for playing it safe, sooner or later, and this game WILL kill your soldiers. Start save scumming, or, git gud basically.
The X-Com underground base gives you several different "buildings" to work with, each of which has their own unique functions and is crucial to surviving the game - be it the foundry, research lab, engineering, power generators, satellite uplinks, the grey market, the hangar or others. There's a level of micro-management I didn't expect to be involved with the meta game, and once I discovered I was playing wrong, the game became so much more fun.
For a 4 year old game it is still quite pricey on Steam, but this is on sale frequently enough. It will undoubtedly be on sale during a holiday or 2K sale for less than $10. If you like sci-fi like Stargate, or Independence Day, or X-files or just anything aliens-related in general, and if you like tactical RPGs, or games like Commandos/Silent Storm, you will find value in this.

This is the ultimate version of Metro 2033.  If you don't own the original, get the Redux without question.  Those who really loved the original should get Redux as well, especially on a sale.  Last Light's engine really increases the visual quality and performance of Metro 2033 Redux, and it benefits from having Last Light's mechanics and some of the new guns as well.  Stealth is also much better than the original.
The biggest improvmenets have to be in the level design.  Pretty much every level was modified, some more heavily than others.  Dead City and Frontlines in particular offer a lot of new, amazingly detailed areas, following in the footsteps of Last Light.  This increases the length of Metro 2033 Redux to closer to 15 hours (opposed to 10-12 for the original) for those who play on a harder difficulty and really like to explore every inch of every map.  Several short chapters were also combined into one larger chapter.
Be sure to play on Survival mode, on either Ranger or Ranger Hardcore difficulty.  Unfortunately Ranger Hardcore still has an invisible inventory which is just silly.  A few other things stand out as being awkward, like the new voices for children (which sound more like old women), glitchy textures that sometime appear abnormally low resolution, and the forced battle music which the original didn't have.  Also, the cinematic cutscenes are gone, in place of first-person ones so that the game is entirely in Artyom's POV like Last Light.
So some small changes aren't desirable for everyone, but as a whole this is the ultimate version of Metro 2033.

I had a good time playing this game, but I think the mixed reviews I've read are understandable. It's one of those games that's "not for everyone". I don't mean to say that many players won't get it or whatever. I just don't think the gameplay, the themes and the story will appeal to everyone.
That the plot is told backwards will become obvious eventually, but most of what you read will be cryptic and vague until you get to the very ending of the game. In order to get to the ending, you are basically required to solve all the puzzles in every level which require quite some thinking. They're definitely not the first grade level stuff that most games throw at you and some are fairly frustrating even. Personally I appreciated the challenge and had fun tinkering with time, but I can imagine players who are only looking for a fun platformer game will quickly lose their patience. I can't really blame them. I find it hard to argue with the statement that games should be enjoyable above all else and "the reward" you get for making it to the end of Braid might not be satisfying enough to make it all worth it if you're almost losing your sanity over the puzzles.
As for the story, I liked it too although the philosophical way in which it was presented did not really work for me either.
and all the ambiguity seemed to be implemented only to confuse players rather than that it actually adds anything substantial. I think I have an idea why the developer came up with the ambigious narrative, but it is again something I don't think every player will appreciate.
In any case, I still had a good time playing Braid. It was a refreshing experience for me and beating it felt quite satisfying. I would recommend it, but only to people who are particularly interested in it and have sufficient patience to solve tricky puzzles. To those who are merely looking for a fun and simple platformer game, I would suggest you ignore this one.

An amazing rogue-like that blends modern post-apocalyptic modern societal downfall with urban legend and the occult for a very unique setting.  While the game is not without its flaws, I still think it was very worth playing.
The problem with a review like this is that it is hard to recommend the game without exposing story or gameplay elements that are in a lot of ways crucial to the game experience.  As with many roguelikes, game knowledge is crucial to success.  Unlike many, NEO is on of the few roguelikes that uses fixed story and locations and events.  The random elements come in the form of items found from looting and NPC encounters.  The game does not require any combat to complete it, and much of the items lack the progression and semi-uniqueness found in fantasy roguelikes.  There are shotguns, but no +3 shotguns of ammo conservation.  Skills are chosen at the start of the game and do not improve, and you cannot level up.  Thus a large part of the experience is in exploring the unknown of the map, the story, and the game's mechanics rather than the depth of its progression mechanics.  This is both a unique appeal of the game and a flaw.  It fits the setting and feel of the game with the player as a normal person and lends to a stronger story, but further playthroughs are not so meaningful when you know where to go on the unrandomized map and what dialogue options to choose and what items to craft.  If you want a Binding of Isaac, Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup, or Tales of Maj'eyal, this is not the same game.
The story and setting deserve a special mention before I talk about the gameplay.  The content that is there is a good amount of content that allows for diverse approach, good for someone exploring the game for the first time.  However, by the end my feeling was there wasn't nearly enough of it.  The game map is large but a certain portion of the map is lacking in almost any of the game's unique elements.  While the game does indicate the location of a major world feature near the beginning, by chance a new player could decide to explore in the wrong cardinal direction and end up wandering around finding nothing but RNG encounters and generic locales for many many hours.   There are a few locales given extra detail in presentation but with no story attached to them nor reason to revisit, and given the fixed nature of the game's events at this locations it would have been nice for the developers to make more of them.  These and some various 'random' events are presented in a Choose Your Own Adventure book style with events presented in text with a few choices for action.  The fixed events are well written and choices can be very meaningful, but in the random events the choices dont reflect outcomes very well or nearly at all thus making those outcomes feel mostly arbitrary.  Compared to how good the fixed locale events are
, the random ones feel like low-effort filler at best and an excuse to abuse the player character at worst when things turn out badly for no good reason.
Additionally, it is bizarre to me that while the game is a permadeath one it doesn't delete your save after giving you a you a time-limited info dump at the end of the game.  When game knowledge is so crucial to the experience and the story, why freely let the player reload the game at his last save and ask different questions at the info dump?  I'm not against the info dump in principle, its just strange.  This ties into my discussion of game mechanics next as it is important to note here that once you finish the game it becomes apparent that the main thing preventing the player from progressing to the end of the game and rolling the credits is just not knowing where the location for that event is the first time they play.  As I said before, game knowledge and first time experiences are the meat of the game here.
Mechanics wise, the game is very solid when it comes to combat and health as well as how it treats item management.  Its a nice unique spin that doesn't just use HP and stat points like most, has some good surprises, and gives the player plenty of incentive to pick any of the skills at character creation.  Hunger, sleep, and weather are important more than just their immediate lethality from running out and triggering a game over.  Combat has a great mix of options and interactions as you play out whether you attack or wait for a good moment, or space yourself and try to run.  The only real disappointment I had with the game's item selection is that there wasn't MORE to pick from!  I wanted more cool things to find from poking around city ruins and by the time you finish the game you will very likely see every item the game has to offer with no +3 shotguns to spice up the mix.  Item crafting is slightly clunky but useful, but again only game knowledge prevents you from crafting one of the best melee weapons in the game two minutes in.  The game even has diseases but
, which makes for a very odd check of the player's skill.
Lastly, the permadeath nature of the game is a strong contributor to the feeling of being a very mortal normal person that the game tries to present.  I clocked in 46 hours into the game, most of it in a fairly exploratory playthough where I spend a fairly good amount of time hording supplies and  preparing for unknowns with caution.   This felt appropriate, and I still died quite a few times despite my preparation.  I engaged in a fairly modest amount of savescumming for this one playthrough. and it is only apparent afterwards that the preparation wasn't so necessary and that the unique locales and events therein are not required to finish the game.  Again, the wonder of the game is in your first time experiencing what it has to offer.  Either I was supposed to learn to be more YOLO and careless and suicide rush to find new unexplored content, or I was expected to make an even larger time sink than I did from my cautious play.  46 hours is a lot, so seeing a sort of soft-death (such as saving only every 3 in game days or the like) might have been nicer than permadeath or savescumming.
All in all, I loved the game's mechanics and the genuinely emotion invoking experiences it provided.  Absolutely worth the full $15 in my mind.  I would highly reccomend it to those wanting a story and setting focused roguelike, less so to those not experienced with the genre.  If you play, don't feel too bad if you have to savescum a bit.

After playing this game over the weekend with some of my friends i think it's time for a opinion on what i think about this game.
Would i recommend to try it out: yes and no
i will also have a answer for both sides for what my reasons are
Yes side: When i first started out the game there was 3 factions to pick from along with character customization, for laughs i ended up making my character on the human side into a midget dwarf.
When i go into a server and looked around, the graphics all that were pretty good considering the game was just early access, started out by leaving the town spawn and begin punching the flowers to gather flowers, next thing u know meteor comes down and some grim reaper aka dark wraith chased me and i ran like hell to town so the guard would be my meat shield but he eventually killed him so i was safe.
the game itself has all of the hardcore survival stats, like hunger, thirst, focus/tirness etc etc and as u level up from gathering, killing or whatever u do you can have stat points to increase those.
skills are all there for your survival like building houses, cooking, crafting blah blah blah build your strawhouse and be safe inside while there are big dinos and other monsters chilling outside your house.
My first time getting killed or not exactly been killed but knocked out was a bloodly wild goblin robbed me and ran off with my loot which was a life struggle, but the dinos animals etc are pretty awesome considering dinos are like from ark survival (which mind yous i've never played ark once, i was more a reign of kings player).
No side: for a early access game it is to be expected like lag, glitches, bugs you name it, but when it comes to getting into the game can be hard at times.
when you log out and come back in theres a chance that u may spawn back over your retraces when you originally didn't log out there and if that happens it can cause you having hard time gathering like trees or stone overtime.
the combat system is what needs to be looked into whenever, due to the fact melee combat is so glitchy and buggy like doing a power attack and you get that recoil/knockback and the times you actually hit something it does occur but the game thinks you missed.
Range and magic does have their problems but not as worst compared to melee style fighting.
PVP however and i've tested this by jumping on people outside npc town they run back to town thinking their safe but really they're not, i keep attacking them by throwing knives and the guards just look the other way unless if one of the guard or npcs have been hit.
So even that pvp is fun and been a bully, but the fact is that the new players don't feel safe anywhere unless if the town guards get patched up and retaliate when a player is getting attacked by another player.
For parts like having issues gathering, retraced logged in etc, atm only way to fix it is usually triggering death on yourself, (which you shouldn't have to do that in general)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This is what i think of the game, and i will continue to support it, i do however see great things coming along the way.
So if you want to give this game a try to experience ark and skyrim then i say of course and try it out for a epic world.
but if you're the sort who can't stand the glitches bugs lag etc then i suggest don't buy the game yet until later on in the future where it's in a more stable condition.
Happy Gaming steamers.

Mostly clever, mostly good, a stone's throw away from perfect, but hampered by one single glaring flaw; there is no hump.  The game lacks a difficulty curve once you've learned the mechanics.  That is not to say it is as easy at the start as it as at the finish.  No, no, that would be f(x)= 0*x + C.
The difficulty is derived almost entirely from the random number generator and, while that is an element inherent to roguelike games, most of those I've played had a point after which the player can feel comfortable in their position, their build, their methods.  The only constant in this game is the fight at the very end, for which you will need one of a few fairly specific loadouts in order to win, but achieving those loadouts is, again, a matter of luck.
You might not find stores carrying the items you need when you have the cash to pay for them.  You might be taking the Rock B cruiser out for a spin and run into a random event that drops five Mantis boarders on your ship, three of which blew up your medbay before you could show up to duke it out inside.  You could be flying through a nebula and fleeing a losing fight when you find a stray mine, fail the option to steer out of its way, fail the option to disarm it, and take the last five points of hull damage necessary to blow up your ship.  Or you could find three scrap recovery arms by the end of the second sector and every shop in sight is selling exactly what you want and you breeze through the final fight with an eye closed and a hand behind your back while alien hotties massage your temples and ears.
It's for exactly this reason, the psychotic and completely unpredictable chance of getting smeared across your deck plating or invited to the pleasure cruise to paradise, that I can not recommend this game to most people.  I feel no sense of accomplishment when I win, and I feel no sense of failure when I lose, because it all feels like my success is based on whether my mother bribed the referee before the big game started.
If you can get past all that, though, there's a great deal of variety in ship layouts, weapon loadeds, crew tactics, for a simple and fairly inexpensive game.

Lightfish starts out as a pretty fun and basic puzzle game but quickly devolves into a confusing, chaotic mess. In later levels the screen becomes cluttered with obstacles and enemies, making it difficult to focus on a winning strategy. Since there are certain enemies that are completely unpredictable it is simply easier to brute force your way through a level by being cautious rather than cunning.
Major grievances include: poor enemy spawning, sometimes an enemy will spawn right on top of you and kill you without warning; imprecise controls which caused a number of lava related deaths or by getting stuck on geometry; no restart button, somewhat of a necessity to let the player quickly restart the level if they are going for a top score.
You won't get much play time or challenge out of Lightfish and the lack of variety in mechanics and level design leaves a lot to be desired.

Metro 2033 was easily one of the best games I've ever played, even with it's bugs, poor optimisation and difficult stealth. The immersion was incredible. One of the things I remember most fondly was the gas mask. How it could crack during combat, how you had to remember to keep applying new filters, everything right down to the droplets of water. The scarcity of ammo was another thing. You couldn't just spray away or else you'd be left with nothing but a knife, or you could decide to essentially start shooting money, which was the only way to purchase necessary equipment.
Now we have the Redux version. Which has less to no bugs (I haven't encountered any yet), the optimisation has improved drastically and stealth is now not only viable, but often the best way. The game levels are also a lot more interactive. It's great to shut off all the lights, stick on my NVGs and get away with no one aware of my presence. Apart from the lack of an FOV slider (seriously? I thought this was guaranteed) the game is now more or less flawless in my eyes. I've been lucky enough, as I've said, not to run into any bugs. For those who are, just know that when you do get it working properly, it's one hell of a game :D
Make sure you have a 64 bit OS before purchase, and you shouldn't have any issues.

Ok, strap in boys and girls 'cause this is gonna be a fairly long one(I think).
The game is about a secret task force, the titular XCOM, that has to defend Earth against an invading alien force with unclear motives. You need to help various countries that are invested in the XCOM project, as your lose condition is losing too many countries to the alien threat.
Let's get the main flaws out of the way first. The game doesn't exactly feel entirely complete without the Enemy Within expansion which along with the base game makes the price a bit high at first glance for a 3-4 year old game. However, it could be that the expansion adds so much that it's hard to think of the game without it.
Also, the Normal difficulty feels much too easy after a certain point in the game, to the degree where I could aggro 3 enemy squads/pods(something which is very stupid, you should only aggro 1) and take them out easily. To get a better experience of the game, to really immerse yourself in the atmosphere of the game which asks you to take on an unknown enemy, you have to play on the harder difficulties.
Another complaint, albeit a somewhat subjective one, is that weapons don't really have the variety that is present with the different types of armor. There is an armor type that grants extra HP, another 2 that amplify your soldiers mobility, one that grants the ability to turn invisible, so on and so forth. With weapons however, all classes are limited to having one type of weapon(with the exception of Assault). All new weapons that you develop are incremental improvements over their previous iterations. Perhaps it would've been nice to add some abilities depending on the weapon itself in order to make them more varied.
Another thing is that the soldier customization is disappointingly bare-bones, it's hard to make soldiers distinguishable from one another without giving them something ridiculous(my favourite soldier was Guile Theme, named so due to his fabulously ridiculous blonde hair). This is probably fixable with some mods though.
Lastly, the game is fairly buggy. Crashes are pretty infrequent, but I've had more than too many situations where the game would get stuck in one animation and I would have to restart it in order to continue or when the movement UI wouldn't work properly and I would accidentally expose a soldier.
Enough with the downers, now with the positives.
The gameplay is INSANELY fun. XCOM: Enemy Unknown is turn/squad based and you have to use cover smartly in order for your soldiers to survive and you have to think of ways of defeating enemies that are (most of the time) in solid cover themselves. It is amazing trying to outflank or flushing them out of cover with explosives, not to mention a large variety in enemies and tactics to handle each. The basic formula is extremely simple, yet it proves addictively fun.
The variety in soldier classes is also a strong pro. There are 4 basic classes with 2 others discoverable later in game(provided you have Enemy Within installed). That might not sound like a lot, but there are numerous combinations of classes that you can try in a squad. What's more, each class has various abilities that have a mutually exclusive alternative and those make the soldier play differently from one of the same class, but with a different selection of abilities.
Lastly, the game has plenty of time/money value, warranting multiple playthroughs on different difficulties, with Second Wave settings that also change the game and after that you can also try the Long War mod which is supposed to overhaul the game entirely, though I cannot say more on this since I did not try it. However, just one playthrough of the campaign took me more than 30 hours with a lot more to try left.
Some mediocre aspects of the game now.
Story. It's mysterious at first, becomes increasingly meh in the mid to late game and becomes interesting again at the end.
Basebuilding outside missions. Crucial to your performance, but dull.
Slingshot DLC is meh.
That's about it, overall a definite recommendation for any strategy game fan and a good way to get non-fans started on the genre.

So I have to say that the release of this was a mess. Missing lighting that arrived in a patch on day 1, 1.7GB or so in size, that added terrible over-done lens flare that makes every light source look like a small sun in some places.
I couldn't even run the game for the first day, because it just returned to desktop after the intro movie. A LOT of people had this issue.
It was fixed quickly, but it's still not acceptable.
However saying all this, it IS metro. The new difficulty mode, survival, works great alongside ranger hardcore to make a real challenging game. Even though I already knew the game inside out, I have died a few times already, and failed stealth at least twice before I am even halfway through.
I expected it to be last light levels of difficulty. Which is to say, NO difficulty even on ranger hardcore.
This isn't the case. It is still a good challenge.
The only problem brought forth by the last light mechanics integration is that you never come close to running out of ammo or filters, which is a shame since metro is supposed to be about resource management, and scavenging for every bullet and every second of filter time should matter to you. Missed opportunity there, I think.
They have however added some nice new areas for people to find. I have found about 3 or 4 of them, and a couple of them are very memorable, such as a watchmen mother protecting her babies in a nest.
At the end of the day, this IS metro 2033. It's changed in some subtle ways, but it is still the greatest game ever made in my opinion.
I still prefer the original. It felt darker and more dangerous to me, even after multiple playthroughs I am on edge in certain levels.
This has more of that tension than I expected though, enough new stuff to keep it feeling fresh.
I have to mark it down for the lack of effort put in on the graphics, because in some ways the original looks a lot better, such as floor textures in many areas here are very low res, and some items on table tops, like papers and such, just look like part of the table texture.
I also have to mark it down for the poor execution on release. Terrible way to release a game. Maybe it should have been kept back a couple of weeks or so, and then it would have been the game that the franchise and its fans deserve.
But all in all I love it. I can't deny that at all.
It's still easier than the original, but it's much more challenging than last light was, and when I finish this and move on to the last light redux I hope to find that the survival difficulty setting in that makes it a better game. Because with better difficulty and challenge, last light would have been the better game of the two.
If you are thinking of buyin this, or both of the redux versions, I would hold off if you already own them. Wait for a sale. I got them for around £8 for both. That was half price on top of the 50% pre-order discount for owners of the originals. So they should have cost me £16, I got them for half that, which was a great price.
If you can get both for around £15, then that's not too bad. If you can get both for £10, that's excellent value for such great gaming.
If you don't own the originals, I still recommend metro 2033 original release, as it is still a better game, but not by too much. Since you can get it for like £3 now, I would get that, and maybe get the redux later if you feel you enjoyed the original enough.
Last light is a better value buy for people who don't own the original though. For the extra difficulty, and the fact that it contains all DLC (which was underwhelming and overpriced for the most part), getting that for around £15 is very good value if you don't already have it.
I have to give this a thumbs up in the end, purely because they spruced it up some, changed it enough for people who already played it, and kept the challenge (mostly) of the original. It's metro, so it has to be thumbs up, regardless.
But thumbs down for the full price, it's just not worth that when you can get the original for £3.
But judging the game itself, thumbs up all the way.

Pretty much everything there is to say about this game has been said, though I'd like to throw in my two cents as well as address a couple issues I've seen people comment on in some of the reviews. First of all, the game is out of Early Access and is feature complete(to my knowledge), and does have an end-game scenario. It's just not that easy to do. 195 hours in the game and I have yet to "beat" it. Ususally for me the story comes second to the survival gameplay. The story is unique and interesting from what I've uncovered(and read about), though some things can take a long time to complete, and usually I'll die before I come close to completing my objective.
This brings me to my second point. The game is hard, yes, but it's not as impossible as some people make it out to be. Jumping right in to the game with no prior knowledge, like I did, will be tough. You'll die quite often until you start to make some sense of the mechanics and gameplay. You will also get unlucky at times and be woken from a dead sleep by a creature which can mess you up bad. But, like I said, it's not impossible. You just need to try new skill combinations and ways of going through the world. Taking the strong/tough perks will allow you to wreck NPCs that you come across, but when you're faced with a life or death story scenario, you may not be as well equipped to deal with dangers as you may have thought. At the time of writing this, I've been playing a no-combat-skills build. I've taken Hacking, Medic, Botany, Lockpicking, Eagle Eye, Tracking, Athletic and Electrician, along with Fragile and Insomniac for the extra points. I've been playing this character for three or four real life days now, and I've gone through at least thirty in-game days. Without dying.
Playing like this forces you to reconsider everything you've been doing. Before, I'd walk right up to that feral dog and turn it in to a pin cushion with my bow. Now though, I'm fragile and unskilled at any combat. All I have for protection is a war club, which, in my hands, is about as deadly as a shoe. If I even see a feral dog, I'm headed in a new direction. I've also found out that running away
. I may not be able to kill that guy and eat his body, but I'm alive for another day. And I didn't even need his man meat. I've got the botany skill and can just forage around some forests and fill up on berries. In this current game, I've also not used any noise traps when I sleep, because I don't have the room. I get burdened easy, and only carry a couple small backpacks. Still, I have yet to die.
You just need to think a little before commiting to an action. Before I try to get some rest, I hide and wait for a few turns to see if anyone's in the area. If no one has wandered into my camp, I sleep. And since I have insomnia, I usually wake up before anything gets too close to me. I know there's a terrible and unfortunate death waiting for me in the future, but until then I'll keep scouring this wasteland, looking for the RFID spoofing software I need in order to advance a story encounter I have yet to complete.
This game isn't for everyone, but for me, it's definitely in my top 5. It's easy enough to pick up and play for 30 minutes of down time, or I can spend hours in the game, completely immersed and elated when I find a text file worth nearly $2000 in a laptop that's been sitting in a building for years, and which would have been useless to me were it not for the hacking trait.
If you're undecided, just play the demo or watch some videos. There's quite a bit of content missing from the demo, but you'll get the gist of things and be able to make a more informed decision on whether or not this is your type of game. To anyone buying this game, I sincerely hope you like it, as it's like no other game I've played before, and absolutely one of my favorites. Thanks for the amazing game Daniel, and I am looking forward to your next endeavor.

As of the time of writing this, The game has been in early access for 3 days. Each day so far, I have woken up to a new set of patch notes of bug fixes and quality of life improvements. The team has adresssed issues they know about, but have not been able to fix yet, such that players experiencing these issues know it's not a problem with their computer. Of all the waays to do early accesses and open betas, this is the correct way. They are actively improving the game and fixing errors uncovered by community play testing and feedback. The game does feel like somewhat of a shell at the moment, with some content that is very shallow or not implemented. There are bugs, including one that will prevent you from progressing through the guided questline pretty early on (like an extended tutorial, not really a storyline from what I can tell). There are balancing issues, Server issues, and Obscene load times (15 to 20 minutes to start the single player mode on medium and high settings, I have not seen the game load at all on epic settings, though I didn't try for all that long) brought on by a lack of optomization. BUT. This is a very good framework, and so long as the developement team continues working at the pace they are, I could see this very easily becoming a truly incredible game. The sandbox survival genre is already oversaturated enough with games like Rust, ARK, and Day-Z and all their clones, but this one seems to have a different play style and some unique mechanics (though I will admit, it's similar in places to what I've seen of ARK). The game so far is very fun, and even just the single player can give you a few hours of fun (and anger, damned Panthers won't leave my stuff alone). I'm looking forward to seeing the skill system being filled out with more buildables, weapons and armors, and all the other bells and whistles. I also hope the developers are able to drastically cut down on loading times, especially for single player games, where no server connection is required. There are clear plans to continue expanding the game much more, with a huge map layed out which will hopefully contain very many unique and memorable locations. This game truly seems to have been released in its earliest playable mode, so the game could be developed with as much community feedback as possible.
TLDR; Game suffers usual early access problems and unusually long loading times. Dev team is very active so far in attempting to fix problems, and lets the playerbase know when a problem is encountered that they won't be able to fix right away (see 7/23 patch notes regarding 100 gold quest). Huge promise, Keep an eye on this one whether you plan on buying in early access or not.

Mostly clever, mostly good, a stone's throw away from perfect, but hampered by one single glaring flaw; there is no hump.  The game lacks a difficulty curve once you've learned the mechanics.  That is not to say it is as easy at the start as it as at the finish.  No, no, that would be f(x)= 0*x + C.
The difficulty is derived almost entirely from the random number generator and, while that is an element inherent to roguelike games, most of those I've played had a point after which the player can feel comfortable in their position, their build, their methods.  The only constant in this game is the fight at the very end, for which you will need one of a few fairly specific loadouts in order to win, but achieving those loadouts is, again, a matter of luck.
You might not find stores carrying the items you need when you have the cash to pay for them.  You might be taking the Rock B cruiser out for a spin and run into a random event that drops five Mantis boarders on your ship, three of which blew up your medbay before you could show up to duke it out inside.  You could be flying through a nebula and fleeing a losing fight when you find a stray mine, fail the option to steer out of its way, fail the option to disarm it, and take the last five points of hull damage necessary to blow up your ship.  Or you could find three scrap recovery arms by the end of the second sector and every shop in sight is selling exactly what you want and you breeze through the final fight with an eye closed and a hand behind your back while alien hotties massage your temples and ears.
It's for exactly this reason, the psychotic and completely unpredictable chance of getting smeared across your deck plating or invited to the pleasure cruise to paradise, that I can not recommend this game to most people.  I feel no sense of accomplishment when I win, and I feel no sense of failure when I lose, because it all feels like my success is based on whether my mother bribed the referee before the big game started.
If you can get past all that, though, there's a great deal of variety in ship layouts, weapon loadeds, crew tactics, for a simple and fairly inexpensive game.

Despite its aged graphics and less than perfect UI this is a real gem of a post apocalyptic survival game. It can be truly unforgiving, but that to me was one of the things that drew me into the world of NEO Scavenger. The survival aspect is a lot more engaging to me than most other survival type games I've played, and you quickly learn to pick your battles very carefully. Just like in reality, a single wound can end up killing you if you're careless and don't have access to modern medicine, and nature itself can be equally lethal. This is something I've found to be missing from most other survival games.
The story is fairly interesting as well, but some of the choice based encounters are a bit harsh. And losing a character that survived for a long time in one of those is rarely fun. Still, the game kept drawing me back in until I had beaten it, and I'm looking forward to what the developer has in store for us next.
If you want a challenge, love the roguelike aspect of dead is dead in a post apocalyptic setting and can look past the graphics then you can't really go wrong with this game.

Fans of the originial Metro 2033 game will find that this the the same game that they've come to know and love. But, with enough different to make you fall in love with it all over again. There's new stashes to find, new switches to flip, and new buttons to press. All while keeping the things that were in the original there, too. So, if you've played the game before, you'll remember exactly where everything is, but you'll still be just as excited to explore for things you've never seen before.
They did a very fine job with the engine overhaul. It runs more smoothly on my machine than the original and looks the part, too. There were parts of the scenery that made my jaw drop in awe just like when I played the original for the first time. Which I found to be a pleasant surprise.
In my review for the original, I talked about how you had to unlock the good ending by earning "Good Deed" points or "Moral" points. That is still the case but, in the original, all you could do was earn points. I was both shocked and impressed when I found that there are now bad deeds you can perform that take those points away.
This game series is known for paying a lot of attention to detail, and this installment is no different. But, not only does the game pay attention to detail, but you have to as well. For example: You will get a more wholesome experience out of this game if you take your time to listen to people's conversations. They may reveal to you a better way to complete a level, or just give you some insight as to who they are.
The story is just stellar. Albeit linear. But, it doesn't fail to leave you wanting more. I found that I just could not put this game down. I had to keep playing until I got it done. And I will certainly be playing a couple more playthroughs.
Bottom Line: A great game on its own merit and a phoenominal remake of the original. If you've never played a Metro game before, but enjoy the dystopian genre with in-depth stories, great characters, and detail, you will love this game. If you're picking this up after having played the original(s), you won't be disappointed. Absolutely worth the full price.

This game was made in 2005, It's still fun to play! It was one of the first to include Space Battle levels. The combat was amazing, you can choose from around 9 different classes, each with their own traits and different weapons. Heroes and villians had a nice variety from both the Galatic Civil War and the Clone Wars, each with different force powers. Maps depicted most of the battles amazingly environments such as Geonosis, Kamino, The Jedi Temple and Mos Eisley and Jabba's Palace, all were fun to play on. The storymode is a bit lackluster but still enjoyable, following the events of the 501st Clonetrooper Legion through the Clone Wars to the rise of the Empire and the Battle of Hoth, unfortunatly aside from the cutscenes the mission are just to protect an area from a designated amount of time, destroy something or collect something and bring to back, etc. One of the most interesting gamemodes though is Galactic Conquest, a singleplayer/multiplayer gamemode that gives you a fleet and the other team a fleet and has you fight accross the galaxy, trying to claim and protect as many planets as possible. Anyway, this game could be considered one of the best Star Wars games ever, I give it 8/10. If you're a Star Wars and a shooter fan, this game is a must. (Gameranger can be used to play multiplayer)
Star Wars Battlefront EA was made just last year, and many people were unhappy with it, myself included. The graphics and sounds were amazing but it goes downhill from there. The only singleplayer it has is a boring survival mode in which you fight of waves of enemies. It becomes tedious really quickly. Now it has some good gamemodes such as Walker Assult, but other than that, not many. Now for the missing features, this complete game, if you can even call it complete, is missing so many things that made the original Battlefronts amazing. There is no Clone Wars, no Space Battles, no Galactic Conquest and no Campaign. This game is unfinished, Battlefront 2015 is a pathetic disgusting cashgrab at the Battlefront license and not at all worth the pricetag, and do not buy the 2015 season pass.
So I have a question, would you buy the new one with no depth for $60 or do you buy the old one which is really fun from $10? I know which one I would.

Lightfish copies in the style of classic arcade game as you try to slice and contain an area of enemies.
This is very much an arcade game clone, and you may well have played something like it before. You control an entity and try to move it around the map, slicing it up and "locking off" certain areas. Lock enough off to complete the level.
The gameplay progression in this game is good. The enemies become progressively harder, and this is aided by certain environment "blocks". There are 5 'worlds' of 9 'levels' each, so it does not take an extremely long time to complete the game but these are available in both timed and score-oriented modes. One issue however is that navigating the map can at times be imprecise. E.g. It can be difficult to know just how far away you need to be from lava to avoid being harmed by it.
As this game has a very arcade feel, I would definitely recommend using a controller.
The graphic stylings in this game are extremely good. Enemies have a sort of warped look on the environment, and everything is in a consistent outlined and glowing style. Given the name of the game, the art style really does match what many semi-transparent bioluminescent sea creatures look like.
The music in this game has a very calm "aqueous" feel to it, and is definitely well composed.
Something rather annoying in this game is that the menu is hard to navigate. It will always select the highest uncompleted level, and if you have already completed the game it will simply skip to the end. Meaning that every time you want to play a previous level, you will need to re-navigate the entire menu. This is not an issue unless you are re-playing it however.
Lightfish is a good, if short game, with  fairly well polished gameplay and if you like arcade-style game is definitely worth a buy.

As the sequel to one of the best strategy games of all time, this installment certainly merits a look. The game, as expected, is well fleshed-out, superbly animated and in general covers all the same bases as the original. The graphics are top-notch too, and the general level of work that has gone into the title is impressive.
However, a few notes should be had. The game certainly has a few flaws
- Massive Graphical Demand - I have a pretty beefy machine and this game forces me to run it on medium graphics, where it looks about as good as the original, and still has frame drops
- Balance - There are clearly a few strategies that work far better than others, and the meta is ridiculous
- Realism vs Gameyness - While all the units are certainly realistic, massively changing how units function, such as the tank-hunting StuG III assault gun, just to fit how the faction's roster should look is somewhat irritating. In a war where massive varieties of weapons abounded, surely they could just use a different one?
- Somewhat limited rosters - The unit selection is fine for an RTS, but the WW2 theme practically begs for more units in each nation's roster
In these points don't break the game for you, just buy it. Its worth it.

I really would like a "Neutral" rating, as it's neither bad nor is it amazingly good. But let's start off on a good foot and note the positives:
-Good parkour:
Parkour is very smooth and works as expected, though there isn't a real 'climb down' button. To do that you need to first fall and quicky hold space to get into the climbing position. Then you need to hit c to drop down, after which it will automatically hold onto the next available ledge. It would have been great if they actually had a proper ledge climbing like AC.
-Good skill tree:
I normally hate unlocking things in a B2P game, but this one is alright. I like how there's enough diversity to not feel like it's all just "do 10% more damage". Each skill tree levels in a different manner but when combined together allows you play more of your style.
-Great gore:
I'm really astounded by the detail they put into all the different skins of zombies you will encounter. It really feels as though each person was infected in a different way under a different situation, not to mention how scary it would be if you saw one in real life covered in open wounds and blood. And when you kill them, they break apart really nicely giving you satisfying visual aftermath.
-Great atmosphere:
Whether you're stuck inside a claustrophobic hallway surrounded by zombies, or on the highway seeing a flood of them, it really stirs a whole heap of emotion within you seeing these different scenes.
-Good voice acting:
I really enjoyed hearing Crane talk as well his conversations with the other main casts.
Now for the bad which prevents me from really recommending it:
-Bad combat:
For a game that relies quite a lot on melee, it's actually quite lacking in depth. There's no directional attacks nor blocks, which makes the combat really tedious and boring. You basically have two things that you need to worry about in melee: Your weapon and stamina.
Your weapon determines how hard you hit and you have to ensure that it isn't broken so it actually deals its damage. As for stamina, that's pretty straight forward, if you run out, you swing much slower. Now with these two combined means that you have a fairly one dimensional combat gameplay: keep hitting left click while you have stamina. You can bypass the stamina problem by drinking a stamina booster which gives you infinite stamina, but then you basically just get stuck with left click mania.
The other really annoying thing with combat is the grabbing by the normal zombies. A lot of the time, the zombies will just ignore your attacks on them and lunge through it, grabbing onto you and biting you. At other times they might stagger but still continue forward, knocking your camera all around. The only way to interrupt them is with a kick (which you will most likely also be spamming). So from tedium and boredom, it also turns into an annoyance when you're trying to combat a bunch of them.
Then there's combat with human NPCs. The combat feels similar to combating zombies but with more RNG. They will occassionally be able to block/dodge all your attacks and once you're able to hit them, they'll enter this 'unstoppable' animation where they will counter attack regardless of what you're doing to them. So the only quickfire way of killing them is with the bow or guns. Once again, tedium due to the lack of melee depth.
What would have been a great addition to the melee combat is directional attacking and blocking (like Mount and Blade). Not only would this shake things up a bit, but hopefully also remove the RNG from attacking humans.
-Bad 'special' infected:
It'd probably be a bit more boring without them, but most of them are so badly designed that I'd rather just have a larger pack of normal zombies attack me instead. Let's start off with the biggest offender:
Bomber:
This is probably the worst designed special infected of them all. They basically just a 'lose some survivor points' zombie. In the open, they're a bit better as you have more opportunities to run away. But it's when you round a corner or just open a door and they blow up instantly that makes this infected an absolute nuisance. Their damage radius is also atrociously huge, where even if you're 5m away, you'll still take some slight damage. They really shouldn't be in the game and wouldn't be missed if they were removed.
Goon:
Basically tedious combat incarnate. They have high health, a slow attack and slow movement. Combine this with the melee combat and you've basically got cat and mouse for several minutes. They're not really dangerous, but you'll often be found having to kill them to get to an objective. And the process of killing them is basically hit them a couple of times to trigger an attack, dodge back out of range, wait for the attack and repeat until they are dead.
Toad:
Not as bad as the other two, but just a minor nuisance once again. Tends to annoy you when you're trying to do an objective.
-Overall
It isn't a bad game, but it isn't an award winning game from me either. If they do make a sequel, I hope it'll only be a spiritual successor so they can redo the combat to make it much more interesting.

In short, the best comparison I can think of off the top of my head is an amped up Oregon Trail in space, and I mean that in the best way possible.
You do your best to make it from point A to point B while gathering what you can to survive later dangers, being careful not to waste too much time, should the always approaching enemy fleet catch up and rip you apart.
You will find yourself constantly trying to gauge risk/reward as you make decisions. Should you gas up, or should you buy this new weapon? Or maybe you need your shields. Do you have enough time or is your ship in good enough condition to attempt this quest? Should you send your crew down to help these people against giant spiders? What to do about these slavers? Etc.
The combat is also loads of fun. Trying to delegate who does what, whether they are your pilot, shield operator, go-to repair man, weapons operator, etc. What's that? You are boarded? Well you could fight all of the enemies...or...you could open all of the air locks and suffocate them.
Just as a heads up, as fun and fantastic as traversing space with all sorts of different ships, crews, and tactics is, the game can be pretty unkind. One minute you are acing through everything it throws at you, the next minute one of your crew members was eaten by giant alien spiders, you are being attacked by like the millionth pirate or rebel, your ship is on fire, has holes in it, and you have enemy robot drones shooting your ship on the outside while robots board you and tear you apart from within.

-There are ways to protect your base from offline raiding after you hit level 20 with a House Seal. I hate offline raiding, so this is a BIG plus for me. Players need to delcare war on you and you must accept beforee any kind of raiding can happen. Before level 20 though, you and your shabby♥♥♥♥♥hut are going to get repeatedly looted.
- Looks great. Some players seem to have difficulty getting it to look nice though, not sure why.
- Feels RELATIVELY polished for an early access. I think it's def in a much better state than Ark was at release, or for months afterward. I was expecting much worse, honestly.
-Lag on the unofficial server I'm on is almost non-existent. Not sure about officials.
- The magic is really fun to use.
- The monsters are awesome and terrifying.

- The map is REALLY fun to explore and really dangerous.

Maybe Pros, maybe cons depending on your perspective:
- Very grindy. Pretty slow to skill up.
- If you're not playing PVP, you are mssing out on a core element of gameplay, imo.
- There is no map til you craft one, then it's a consumable resource.
- Wiki is pretty minimal at the moment. Don't expect too much help for mid/end game things.
- Much of the map is locked due to being incomplete.
Cons
-Melee hit boxes are broken. this is a HUGE problem that nees to be fixed asap. Like. Today.
- Early game can be REALLY hard depending on your luck and how fast you figure out the game.
-Updates and server down time are not announced in advance (if you're in the middle of a long tame, this can be a big issue)
There is a very unprofessional message on the loading screen that says "game is 30% complete. Believe us, we are going to make it great." Not really the most inspiring message I've ever read...

- You will probably die a lot in early levels and lose all your stuff repeatedly to players, goblins, reavers and panthers. Travel light and don't get attached.
- Jumping on rocks is buggy. I'm often afraid I will get stuck (haven't yet!)

- There is A VERY annoying hit box bug that basically makes melee useless
- Walking up hills is unncessarily hard. falling down hills is like sliding down on ice skates.
- Hunger and thirst and rest are ridiculously difficult to manage in early game while you are trying to learn.
- Unlocks don't work logically (level ranged crafting by mining stone!) Very unintuitive.

After playing this game for over 10 hours on steam. I think I am ready for a proper review for this game.
Okay here it goes.
I bought a game in 2007 by the name of Star Wars Battlefront: Renegade Squadron for my PSP and played it literally all the time. I must have beaten the campaign (which is very short) about 20 times over the first year I had the game and had gotten so good at playing Galactic Conquest that I made up different goals each time I played a game of it. I had no idea at the time that there were any other Star Wars Battlefront games until I started watching the tutorials in SWBF:RS and realized that they were talking about some other games that I've never heard of. I lost SWBF:RS for about a month (even though I had searched EVERY nook and cranny around my house) and when I found it, played it for about 5 hours straight, by this time I had had the game about 3 years. Well, after about 2 more years of playing the game on and off it finally gave up on me. I was very heartbroken and actually still have the UMD somewhere. So I slowly drifted away from Star Wars for awhile but never forgot the glorious battles the game had given me. When I finally came back into Star Wars I had found out there were other games that came before Renegade Squadron and I also heard that they were "better" than my precious Renegade Squadron. Well, I found out that this game was on Steam and bought it about a week ago and let me just say, IT IS A BLAST!!! The AI in the game are smarter than on my PSP game and there are like 2 to 2.5 dozen maps to choose from (in Renegade Squadron there were a lot of maps but I don't count the space maps). There is a class system in this game which makes the game more challenging, in Renegade Squadron you could choose what you looked like and what weapons you could have, there were also perks in the game that made you run faster, capture objectives, etc. but it made the game less of a challenge and more of a "get kills, get kills, get kills". I love SWBF2 and would encourage you to buy it. The only bad thing is there is no online multiplayer anymore but there are ways to play online via Gameranger. (I personally don't care whether I play online in this game or not it's fun either way). Hope this review helped with your decision on whether or not you wanted to spend $9.99 on it!

As I said, this is better than the original version in almost every way, making it the truly great FPS that it had the potential to be.

Fans of the originial Metro 2033 game will find that this the the same game that they've come to know and love. But, with enough different to make you fall in love with it all over again. There's new stashes to find, new switches to flip, and new buttons to press. All while keeping the things that were in the original there, too. So, if you've played the game before, you'll remember exactly where everything is, but you'll still be just as excited to explore for things you've never seen before.
They did a very fine job with the engine overhaul. It runs more smoothly on my machine than the original and looks the part, too. There were parts of the scenery that made my jaw drop in awe just like when I played the original for the first time. Which I found to be a pleasant surprise.
In my review for the original, I talked about how you had to unlock the good ending by earning "Good Deed" points or "Moral" points. That is still the case but, in the original, all you could do was earn points. I was both shocked and impressed when I found that there are now bad deeds you can perform that take those points away.
This game series is known for paying a lot of attention to detail, and this installment is no different. But, not only does the game pay attention to detail, but you have to as well. For example: You will get a more wholesome experience out of this game if you take your time to listen to people's conversations. They may reveal to you a better way to complete a level, or just give you some insight as to who they are.
The story is just stellar. Albeit linear. But, it doesn't fail to leave you wanting more. I found that I just could not put this game down. I had to keep playing until I got it done. And I will certainly be playing a couple more playthroughs.
Bottom Line: A great game on its own merit and a phoenominal remake of the original. If you've never played a Metro game before, but enjoy the dystopian genre with in-depth stories, great characters, and detail, you will love this game. If you're picking this up after having played the original(s), you won't be disappointed. Absolutely worth the full price.

a fantastic and thoroughly challenging adventure game/exploration RPG hybrid unlike any one thing you'll've experienced before. NEO Scavenger's mechanics are constantly intriguing, but more than anything, it shines with the world it presents and the judicious exposition thereof. while it certainly fits in the post-apocalyptic genre, it's a stranger catastrophe that's befallen this world than the usual nuclear or ecological disasters we see; the rules of the universe seem to be in drift. setting is dripped out in tantalizing paragraphs fished up out of scraps of newspapers from before and during whatever disaster it was that set things askew. the frustrations of a challenging narrative roguelike make things that much more intense: unlike a Stone Soup or a Binding of Isaac that can more or less be set aside at any point, NEO Scavenger demands the exploration of its mysteries, keeping the player coming back in the face of annihilation because of the raw power of the strangeness of the world that it depicts.

In a word, this game is lacklustre.
Although I can't say it's a terrible game, I certainly can't say that this is a good game either. I felt that it was visually overstimulating, with too many flashy graphics making it difficult to see everything that's going on. Basically it's full of substanceless flashy graphics which actually hinder gameplay instead of enhancing it. It's quite a short game and it's by no means a challenge. The few instructions that exist in the game are poorly written (or translated), which says to me that no one really cared too much. I found the lava walls a little questionable when the controls aren't precise enough and a safe distance from them a matter of trial and error every time.
The objective of the game is to capture areas of the game screen. You are safe from most creatures on your baseline (though not all). You dash out and try not to get hit by enemies, and once you capture 75% of the original area, you win the level.
If you're looking for a game of this sort, then I would strongly recommend you consider Fortix2 instead (which also has a section that includes the Fortix original levels in the Fortix2 artwork). The Fortix games are more challenging (if you play on hard), more engaging, have more levels, are better thought out, and last but not least, they're a whole lot more fun than Lightfish. Also, I think that the Fortix games on an easy difficulty setting are easier than this game because the controls and game mechanics are better.
I've enjoyed the game for a few hours, but I'm not sure it was worth it. Depends on what $5 is worth to you, how bored you are, and how much you love this sort of game. It also will not work on my Mac.

This is an incredible game.
I always seem to love the free roam games like Skyrim, Zelda, and Super Mario 64. This game is no exception. The level of freedom in this game is beyond that of any of those games. You see a place where you want to go? You can go there, unless it's out of the playable area. The massive variety of weapons and tools that can be used in the game are wonderful. If I had anything to recommend to the devs, it would be to add more tools that affect the player.
The story is pretty cool, too. It might seem a bit overwhelming if you're not paying attention your first playthrough, but it's easily understandable if you get into it. Crane as a character is pretty realistic as he changes his mind throughout the story based on what he knows.
The graphics are beautiful. Positively breathtaking in some areas. There are details in places you wouldn't expect them. NPCs have animations for everything they say, as well as a variety of idling animations. Lots of interesting and entertaining visual effects for different events. It even includes a trippy psychadelic scene for people who are into that kind of thing. Framerate is consistent if you have a good computer.
Multiplayer is great. Love playing online with other people and seeing the unique weapons they found and what they do with them. Racing challenges are the best. I love competing with other players to see who can get to the next point the fastest.
The DLC is nothing short of incredible. The amount of time it took to make something like this implies that these guys are obsessive. Some parts of the story really tie together certain unexplained parts of the original game. The buggy is so much fun. Love running zombies over, and of course racing friends. The plot is so crazy, especially at the end. ***small spoilers*** There should be a sequel to both endings of the game. ***end spoilers***
The developer secret weapons are one of my favorite parts of the game. These guys made a serious game, but have all kinds of silly secrets that are totally unrealistic. It's a game, why not include some random button that teleports you to different parts of the map, or a chicken on a stick that does more damage than most swords?
Seriously. If you play first person games, I can't recommend this game enough. It's worked its way up to the top of my list of favorite first person games. I kid you not.

LightFish is a pleasant clone of Qix/Fortix-styled games, where you attempt to claim sectors of a map by drawing lines to fill in areas while enemies flit about attempting to destroy the line trailing behind your character, which in this case is a glowing fish. Claim a certain amount of territory, and you clear the map and move on to the next one.
LightFish is pretty basic - and maybe a bit shallow - but it works well enough: the controls are responsive, and the graphics and music are quite pleasant. The "Story" mode (such as it is) can be completed in a couple of hours, but maps can be replayed at any time if you want to improve your score. There's also a time trial mode which is pretty challenging, and there are 18 Steam achievements too. Both of these things add replay value to the game.
LightFish isn't as good as something like Fortix 2, but it's still a respectable casual game.

Pros:

Players need to delcare war on you and you must accept beforee any kind of raiding can happen. Before level 20 though, you and your shabby♥♥♥♥♥hut are going to get repeatedly looted.
- Looks great. Some players seem to have difficulty getting it to look nice though, not sure why.

-Lag on the unofficial server I'm on is almost non-existent. Not sure about officials.

- The monsters are awesome and terrifying.
-  Players can take over NPC towns and be mayor! Definitely a lot of political stuff to do.
- The map is REALLY fun to explore and really dangerous.
- Ark players will feel very much at home.
- Base building is snappy like legos but is not entirely without its frustrations.
Maybe Pros, maybe cons depending on your perspective:
- Very grindy. Pretty slow to skill up.
- If you're not playing PVP, you are mssing out on a core element of gameplay, imo.
- There is no map til you craft one, then it's a consumable resource.
- Wiki is pretty minimal at the moment. Don't expect too much help for mid/end game things.
- Much of the map is locked due to being incomplete.
Cons
-Melee hit boxes are broken. this is a HUGE problem that nees to be fixed asap. Like. Today.
- Early game can be REALLY hard depending on your luck and how fast you figure out the game.
-Updates and server down time are not announced in advance (if you're in the middle of a long tame, this can be a big issue)
There is a very unprofessional message on the loading screen that says "game is 30% complete. Believe us, we are going to make it great." Not really the most inspiring message I've ever read...
-There were no PVE servers at first. (I think there are some now?)
- You will probably die a lot in early levels and lose all your stuff repeatedly to players, goblins, reavers and panthers. Travel light and don't get attached.
- Jumping on rocks is buggy. I'm often afraid I will get stuck (haven't yet!)
-People running unofficial servers don't have all admin tools they need to customize the play. I assume this is coming.
- There is A VERY annoying hit box bug that basically makes melee useless
- Walking up hills is unncessarily hard. falling down hills is like sliding down on ice skates.
- Hunger and thirst and rest are ridiculously difficult to manage in early game while you are trying to learn.
- Unlocks don't work logically (level ranged crafting by mining stone!) Very unintuitive.
- No IP locks mean that you get all kinds of unsavory sorts on the offical servers (Chinese mega guilds etc)
- The UI needs work. Everything is too big and texts end up on top of each other.
- Solo play is really hard. You want to group up.
- Players new to survival games are going to have a rough and possibly rage inducing time.
- Building Collision limits your ability to get your base EXACTLY how you want it.
Tips for beginners:
- Craft a bow. Kill all the things. Melee is gimped at the moment.
- Night time is not a joke. You are not safe.
-Eat flowers to regain focus. Gather flowers by swinging sword with rmb on bushes (esp red bushes).
-Play on an unoffical server with some kind of multiplier. 3x seems good imo. Unless you have something to prove by playing on the grind and grief-fest that is official servers...
- Get away from the starter town asap. You don't need♥♥♥♥♥♥there and all the resourcs are depleted and no-lifers like to hang out there and grief (yes you can be killed in NPC towns)
- Make berry jam. Never need water again.
- Hold down LMB when you are walking and just collect EVERYTHING.
- to get around the gathering bug, press ctrl (crouch), left click, repeat. don't spam them too fast.
- learn which tools get you which type of mats.
- Craft fairy lights to level light magic easily.
- use knives to get fur.
If you are choosing between several games, I would say DnL beats out Ark, Rust, Miscreated, and DayZ and definitely beats out Citadel (played beta yesterday).

A good example of a game that started off what I thought horrible and buggy, but months later made up for it with it's changes. I remember pre-ordering this game like 7 months before it was was out and was incredibly disappointed when I played it and left it out for a few months. I came back to it later and really enjoyed the game because of changes. But the question you may be asking is what is it like now?
Well, now after a year and a half of changes and updates, this game is simply amazing and is one of the best RTS games around today, if you are willing to spend a lot of money that is, for the DLCs. Here's some good and bad points to sum it up:
Good:
.Lots of faction variety and all are interesting with different playstyles given.
.Good balance at the minute. It's not perfect, but is damn good.
.Plenty of unit variety. Every unit has its use in my opinion.
.The doctrine system. People may not agree on this, but there is near 20 doctrines on two factions from the vanilla game and 6 at the minute for the western front armies. Compare that to the COH1 doctrines which had 3 doctrines per team eith 2 paths to toake.
.Snow graphics. The winter atmosphere and detail are unmatched in any RTS game. Even though the winter maps may not be very fun.
.The game is still alive with updates and has a couple of years plan so the devs not done yet! Lots of more stuff is to come.
.Most of the community. The game has a good community up at
always discussing balance and replays.
The bad:
.Winter maps with blizzards slow down the gameplay and are unnessaccary in my opinion. Just the blizzards and cold though.
.Some of the community. There are always those people that moan and complain about things or generally take the game far too seriously that leaves you having no fun and possibly annoyed.
.DLC. I wouldn't blame anyone if the DLC put anyone off buying this game. There's alot to catch up on. DLC includes commanders, vehicle skins, faceplates, Digital collectors edition and the Newest but recommended DLC, the western front armies.
Performance problems. This game is not even the best looking and requires a MONSTER PC to play on the highest graphics. These are not fixed and probably will never be.
My verdict: 8.5/10
