Metro 2033 is an atmospheric first-person survival-horror shooter, and it has been recrafted in it's sequel's far superior engine.
If you've never played Metro, now is the perfect time to jump in, as both 2033 and its sequel, Last Light have been re-released for the PC, PS4 and XBOX ONE for a discounted price.
In the past, Metro 2033 was a largely masterful if wonky study on atmosphere, with some odd design decisions that kept it from being a great game. While they are a market step up, the improved visuals are not the main draw of this remaster. Rather, the shooting mechanics are far tighter, the field of view and screen effects in general are not as immersion-breaking and the audio experience is rebalanced and much improved. The stealth mechanics are lifted wholesale from Metro: Last Light, and therefore both improve and hinder the gameplay. The stealth in Last Light was too forgiving, and 2033 Redux cannot escape this gameplay rebalance. Even with 2 separate modes to choose from, Survival (closer to the original Metro 2033 release) and Spartan (Balanced with a focus on action a la Metro: Last Light), Metro 2033 Redux is noticeably easier than the original. Having said this, the original release had a series of half-baked stealth mechanics that were entirely broken, so having playable stealth is a first for 2033, and a welcome addition.
This should not be taken as a negative review. The nitpicks outlined above are just that, and Metro 2033 Redux is worth every discounted cent of its asking price. Just play it in the dark with a good pair of headphones on Ranger mode with the dialogue in Russian. You can thank me later.

You can check your inventory using your journal now, and important decisions do have hud overlays to make sure you don't accidentally click the wrong button. The visual fidelity has been lifted up quite a bit, and many of the small gripes with the original game are now gone. The only issues I have had so far is that the game uses Last Light's AI and Stealth system. This sometimes does not fit very well, but that really only applies to one level. If you enjoyed either of the Fortix titles, or other games in the vein of the classic Qix, Lightfish brings more of this type of gameplay, and adds a visual style that is reminiscient of games like flOw.
There are some interesting enemy types and obstacles that set this title slightly apart from its brethren.
Fire walls are obstacles that you have to maneuver around. Stray too close and you're crispy-fried.
Ice walls slow your movement, but if you can break your way through them, they fall apart entirely. Watch out for enemies that aren't slowed by the ice.
Exploding jellyfish try to reach for you if you get too close, and their area of effect explosions can catch you in the blast if you don't keep your distance.
These are but a few of the innovative mechanics that Lightfish has to help separate itself from the pack and provide a fresh experience among Qix-inspired titles.

Lightfish.  It's Qix, but dressed up in fancy vector-looking graphics and set in a computerized looking acquatic environment.  As such the game doesn't have the abstract power of the Qix presentation, but the mechanics are exactly the same and so you'll find the same sense of enjoyment as the venerable old arcade game.  The new updates involve some different types of opponents which exhibit different behaviors (one will explode near you, another will seek you out when you draw your lines, and another just floats around getting in your way).  There's also different elements that you traverse when drawing out your territory which can slow you down, block you, or kill you if you touch it which add to the variety of the task.
I like it, but it's a very slight game and not one you're likely to pick up and play a whole lot unless you just happen to be in the mood for Qix action.  I thought the music was okay although it's very much Amiga old school mod music.  I tend to like that sound...

I came back to it later and really enjoyed the game because of changes. But the question you may be asking is what is it like now?
Well, now after a year and a half of changes and updates, this game is simply amazing and is one of the best RTS games around today, if you are willing to spend a lot of money that is, for the DLCs. Here's some good and bad points to sum it up:
Good:
.Lots of faction variety and all are interesting with different playstyles given.
.Good balance at the minute. It's not perfect, but is damn good.
.Plenty of unit variety. Every unit has its use in my opinion.
.The doctrine system. People may not agree on this, but there is near 20 doctrines on two factions from the vanilla game and 6 at the minute for the western front armies. Compare that to the COH1 doctrines which had 3 doctrines per team eith 2 paths to toake.
.Snow graphics. The winter atmosphere and detail are unmatched in any RTS game. Even though the winter maps may not be very fun.
.The game is still alive with updates and has a couple of years plan so the devs not done yet! Lots of more stuff is to come.
.Most of the community. The game has a good community up at
always discussing balance and replays.
The bad:
.Winter maps with blizzards slow down the gameplay and are unnessaccary in my opinion. Just the blizzards and cold though.
.Some of the community. There are always those people that moan and complain about things or generally take the game far too seriously that leaves you having no fun and possibly annoyed.
.DLC. I wouldn't blame anyone if the DLC put anyone off buying this game. There's alot to catch up on. DLC includes commanders, vehicle skins, faceplates, Digital collectors edition and the Newest but recommended DLC, the western front armies.
Performance problems. This game is not even the best looking and requires a MONSTER PC to play on the highest graphics. These are not fixed and probably will never be.
My verdict: 8.5/10

Dying Light is honestly one of the best zombie open-world games I've ever played! The parkour system is simply amazing and so much fun to traverse the awesome playground of Harran. Combat is very visceral and uses a good melee system that really feels rewarding the more you level your character in the game. The skills are all very useful in this game and the amount of content this game offers is insane. I adore the land to explore, find material to craft best weapons, and get blueprints/newer weapons. Quarantine zones are great and the atmosphere of the game is vastly improved when trying to survive at night. This game really has it all and I haven't touched the DLC yet and already have played the game this much just exploring, leveling legend levels, and finding the best possible weapons.
The game does have its setbacks though. The main quest/story is rather meh and has one of the worst, most pathetic boss fights I've ever been a part of. The side quests are simply terrible as every single one is a fetch quest but if you want to level they're worth doing but out of 44 side quests, only one was memorable for being good. Not a single likeable or well written character is to be found in this game. No fast travel is a problem too and the constant failing to grab railings leading to unwanted deaths. Rhais is also a try-hard Vaas rip-off and I can't take him seriously at all. There's a bunch of other problems with the game but the positives far outway the negatives.
Overall, if you see this game on a steam sale, this  is a must purchase if you enjoy melee combat, a good open-world, zombies, and a damn good parkour system that will keep you addicted for hours on end. Keep in mind side content is very bad but everything else will keep you hooked. Can't wait to actually start the Dlc

I was NOT a fan of Ark.  It had run fine for me but the way raiding worked, the simple 'hold left click until whatever is in front of you dies' combat and the lack of challenging PVE to compliment the PVP were all things that kind of killed it for me.
Pros:
-Combat is still simple but it's a bit more than just smashing buttons until♥♥♥♥♥♥dies.  I've noticed different creatures take different amounts of damage depending on if it's fire, ice, lightning, etc and different amounts from arrows vs sword vs magic.  I'm not sure if this is a built in resistance system or not but it made choosing arrow types, magic, etc a lot more interesting.
-The creatures are interesting, seem to have a food chain and aren't locked into leveled areas.  Meaning you can run into dangerous creatures right out the gate.  I think it needs to be tuned up a bit because running into a level 100 griphon three steps off the spawn area is kind of silly, but I like that there's a challenge.  Maybe add some 'safer' zones for us to get started in where high level enemies can't spawn?
-Really promotes group play.  There's a lot of skills to level and unlock starting out so having friends to specialize right off the bat is a good idea most likely.  The Clan/House stuff works right now.  You can make your stuff and share it between clanmates.  Not a huge deal but I've known a lot of these games to release without this feature.
-The world is fairly large and it's quite pretty to look at.  There's ruins, a massive volcanoes, verdent forests, etc and it's all pretty nice looking(depending on your rig)  I'm running a little above medium settings atm and I have no complaints so far.
-Individual creatures and especially large monsters have special attacks.  Boars charge, Dark Wraiths spin into haymakers with their scythes and griphons dive bomb.  Wolves roam in packs, panthers in pairs.  You get the idea.
Cons:
-Crafting lacks variety atm.  Specifically regarding weapons.  There's one bow.  There's one crossbow.  Three Staves.  The differences in stats are nil too.  I crafted my rank 2 stave and it made literally no difference to my damage, cast speed or anything else.  I assume this will change in the future but it's there currently and should be addressed.  Armors on the other hand, there's a fair few of them and they for the most part function as solid upgrades.  I'd really love to see some side grades featuring elemental resistances or damage type(piercing, blunt, slash) though.
-Some pop-in at long distances.  Nothing other engines don't struggle with but it's still pretty ugly when it comes around.
-Really promotes group play.  To the detriment of the solo players.  I really can't imagine playing this game solo.  There's so many encounters just in dealing with the PVE elements that can wipe your progress seemingly randomly that I don't think it would be fun.  Our group had a pack of wolves roam up to our base and kill all our livestock.  Panthers, wolves, griphons coming at you on a frequent basis that required our group to fight them off.  As a solo player you will get downright F'd in the A by these pack animals early-mid game.  Throw in PvP too?  You're going to have a hard time.
-There's a severe lack of tool-tips and in game documentation for a lot of the game's systems.  This will come about eventually either by the game devs adding the tooltips or wikis popping up.  It does make trying to figure out building or ranking requirements a bit of a pain though when the game tells you to do one thing but means another.
-10 minute loading screens.
All in all I do enjoy the game.  It runs smoothly when in game and is fun to play with my group.  You can definitely see the spirit of Ark here but it's a different enough experience for me to enjoy it.  I think if they keep what they have and expand+bugfix the game will be even greater.  As a solo player you'd best wait for now unless you plan on finding a clan though.

Perhaps the first point of reference for reviewing COH2 should be its predecessor, Company of Heroes. In many ways, people who played the original will find many aspects of COH2 familiar (the cover system, many game mechanics and a few units). That being said, the sequel does also include a fair amount of impressive new content (interactive scenery, dynamic line of sight, and increased unit abilities). Considering these issues, I would strongly advise buying this game.
The only fly in the ointment is the balancing issues. Anybody who has played COH2 would have to acknowledge that there seems to be a strong Axis bias (which is reflected in the people searching for a game as those factions; 80:20 Axis to Allied ratios are not uncommon). I freely admit that on paper, the Allies have many good units, but in my opinion their reliance on micro-management makes them far less attractive than their relatively a-move-ish Axis equivalents.
In short, there is still room for improvement such as tinkering with the balancing, and new unit abilities (sniping drivers out of light vehicles, etc) and in-game voice chat, but overall I would say that this is a game that, with the right attitude, will keep you entertained for years.

The game is riddled with bugs and mechanics issues.  The expansion is even more buggy and pretty much unplayable.  However, the original without the expansion, despite its numerous issues, was a lot of fun, and I certainly got my $ worth out of it.  Replayability is pretty low, once you do everything it's not real engaging after that.  The expansion almost is enough to offer some more play through, but then it's so busted the frustration takes over, especially after you lose your game due to crashing.  So yes, I recommend the core game, you can see the hours I got out of it, but here are all the problems so that you're aware:
You have to save nearly every round to ensure you don't lose 30 min of play to a crash, and to change your strategy due to the game mechanics failing.
Despite having a high ground clear line of sight on an exposed side, an enemy often gets full cover bonus from something on the other side so you're at 20% to hit.
The RNG borders on cheating some times, there is no way all 6 units should miss on a reaction shot when something drops in at point blank range.
Movement is quirky and requires a lot of camera rotation and elevation change to be able to move where you want on more complex maps.  Some times there are places you simply can never click because of layers being in the way.  Some times you click one place and go another.
AI pathing is idiotic.  Troops run right through poison clouds, and yet will climb up a ladder and jump down the other side instead of walking around something.  And, you simply can't pick your path, there is only one choice, so if the path is a problem you have to go somewhere elese instead.
The tutorial leaves out some vital information, like the fact that you need to focus all resources on getting up satellites as fast as possible or you will lose badly, and that launching a sat needs to be done strategically 5 days before the council report to reduce panic.
Overall pace is a bit broken, you go from struggling to survive the first few months to swimming in resources, sweeping maps with no issue.
Some enemies have greater than sniper distance and crit with high accuracy with the same weapons you can only use as short range assault weapons.  This includes being able to shoot at you from out of visible area locations which should be impossible.
Sometimes you have no target despite the target being right in front of you.  Like, in the adjacent square.
The game mechanics appear to be set up to "prevent cheese", which is all hit outcomes are determined at the start of the turn before you move.  As such, you will ALWAYS miss that target at 75% no matter how many times you reload.  Yes that's fine, I get it, but the result is some really weird combat mechanics and outcomes.
Enemies routinely fail to trigger overwatch reaction shots and just pick you off while you stand there and watch instead of shooting.

You grind for the star blocks which is the only currency in-game, it is used for everything like:
- Character unlock
- Dungeon/Place unlock

It's rather daunting to speak about a legend like Braid. Many credit it as the reason the indie game Renaissance kicked off in the first place, and whether you believe that's a fair read or overreaching a bit, there's no question that Braid played a formidable role in the advancement of the indie game market, and the role of indie game as "art film," not "demo album." Braid succeeded financially and critically. Braid opened people's eyes to the idea of the indie game as a form of expression, and the validity, and necessity, of games that don't follow a formula or sort neatly into a category. To call Braid merely a "platformer" is to miss the point entirely.
Most of what I'd like to say about Braid falls under the realm of spoilers -- it's a very hard game to talk about, without not only entering spoiler territory, but asserting one's own theories about what happens in it, what the player is seeing, what the events depicted in the game really mean. Braid is a game to be interpreted, to be meditated upon...not a game to be engaged with blind forward momentum. Speedrunning through Braid would be a terrible waste of the experience, at least until the game's events are well known to the player. Let me try to delicately walk the line of preserving Braid's many secrets, while sharing enough of the game to help demonstrate why it shines.
From a mechanical perspective, Braid is a sidescrolling platformer. Your protagonist Tim runs, climbs, jumps and falls in a manner immediately familiar to the player. Upon his first death, however, we learn that we have the power to reverse time, and by holding down a key, rewind the game back to the point of decision and try again. We can do this as often as we like, reverse every mistake made, every mistimed jump, every unsuccessful stab at a puzzle, if we wish. Indeed, the game makes clear that this is not only our power as player, but Tim's own power, and that he's done this, over and over, in his own life. The puzzles encountered begin to incorporate Tim's power, requiring one to play with the flow of time to solve them, at this point.
The puzzles are clever and fun, and finally figuring them out is quite rewarding, but they are, like the puzzles of Thomas Was Alone, merely a macguffin to draw the player into Tim's world, into his head, and into his way of thinking. The game is a philosophical reflection upon what it means to be Tim, to have this power, and to look at the world the way he does. Braid engaged by its mechanics is a clever and interesting experience, but Braid engaged in the context of its meaning, of what it might be saying "between the lines" -- that's what makes it a must-have game. Enter Braid with the idea that the game is just an excuse to have a very interesting conversation with its creator about human agency, mistakes, regret, and the nature of interpersonal relationships. Be ready for the game to throw you some ferocious curveballs, and for you not to be satisfied with its story as a story in itself -- rather, for the story to be a vehicle that brings you to a new vantage point, from which to examine your own ideas of human agency, cause, effect, and meaning.
Braid left me with a head full of thoughts about the way memory fails us, and the places in which wishful thinking seeps into the jars of our memories we thought were watertight, and spoils the things we imagined were well-preserved forever. It asks us, at the beginning, to imagine a world in which forgiveness is absolute, where mistakes can be erased, leaving no mark upon the future. Trial with ever-mitigatable, never lasting error sounds lovely...but the game will, eventually, force you to confront the consequences of such a world, and to the temptation to mistake uncomfortable truths and reality for "mistakes."
Surprising narrative power, for a cartoonish platformer with liberal nods back to the Super Mario Brothers franchise.
If you're looking for a clever platform-puzzle game, Braid will fit the bill...but you'll be missing so much of what makes it special to engage it simply as a platform-puzzle game. Braid is a story, an inner journey, into the meaning of human agency, of love, loss, mistakes, lessons learned, and the nature of why time and causality work the way they do, told through a deceptively simple run-and-jump game with unlimited continues. If you're the sort who wants the game to applaud and cheer you for winning, you're exactly the sort of person Braid wants to meet...but you're going to be disappointed, in the end.
That's okay. Weather the disappointment. Braid is talking to you; let it speak. Embrace your own discomfort with the things Braid has to say. Listen, and stop rewinding time to see if it'll say what you want to hear. Its message is not a "mistake" to be "fixed."

“How long can you survive the post-apocalyptic wastelands of NEO Scavenger?” Asks the developer.
To be more precise, It’s a game that will make you cherish plastic bags more than anything else.
At one time I did carry three plastic bags at once: One in each hand and one put on the shoulder. Inside these an assortment of the finest junk ever seen by man: Empty bottles, cigarette lighter, a t-shirt, twigs, a sauce pan and even more crumpled plastic bags, in case the current ones rip apart. Let me tell you, plastic bags are the superior container for almost anything you might want to carry at some point in the post-apocalypse.
Oh and don’t drink unboiled water – I did and it was a mistake. A few days later while trying to sneak up to a sleeping stranger at night (To rob him, obviously; I needed a pair of new shoes), I got diarrhea. Uncontrollable stomach cramps made me fall down and curl up into a ball. The moaning woke up the stranger who’s been in a very bad mood. I started to bleed from my nose – probably from a virus like cholera I’ve ingested by drinking the water from a pond days earlier. I was indeed particularly thirsty the last few days.
The stranger sprinted towards me and a few moments later, without asking questions, he clubbed me to death with the butt of his rifle – not because of my pain, but to conserve ammo. I think it was for the best, I would have died from internal bleeding anyway. My life was over before I even knew it.
The interesting part here is that all of this did not feel “unfair”; I made a mistake hours before (drinking contaminated water) and could have prevented it (by boiling the water). Even after the fact, the symptoms of dehydration gave an indication that something was wrong: I could have ingested medicine immediately, but I didn’t.
It’s great that games like this are made.

This is an incredible game.
I always seem to love the free roam games like Skyrim, Zelda, and Super Mario 64. This game is no exception. The level of freedom in this game is beyond that of any of those games. You see a place where you want to go? You can go there, unless it's out of the playable area. The massive variety of weapons and tools that can be used in the game are wonderful. If I had anything to recommend to the devs, it would be to add more tools that affect the player.
The story is pretty cool, too. It might seem a bit overwhelming if you're not paying attention your first playthrough, but it's easily understandable if you get into it. Crane as a character is pretty realistic as he changes his mind throughout the story based on what he knows.
The graphics are beautiful. Positively breathtaking in some areas. There are details in places you wouldn't expect them. NPCs have animations for everything they say, as well as a variety of idling animations. Lots of interesting and entertaining visual effects for different events. It even includes a trippy psychadelic scene for people who are into that kind of thing. Framerate is consistent if you have a good computer.
Multiplayer is great. Love playing online with other people and seeing the unique weapons they found and what they do with them. Racing challenges are the best. I love competing with other players to see who can get to the next point the fastest.
The DLC is nothing short of incredible. The amount of time it took to make something like this implies that these guys are obsessive. Some parts of the story really tie together certain unexplained parts of the original game. The buggy is so much fun. Love running zombies over, and of course racing friends. The plot is so crazy, especially at the end. ***small spoilers*** There should be a sequel to both endings of the game. ***end spoilers***
The developer secret weapons are one of my favorite parts of the game. These guys made a serious game, but have all kinds of silly secrets that are totally unrealistic. It's a game, why not include some random button that teleports you to different parts of the map, or a chicken on a stick that does more damage than most swords?
Seriously. If you play first person games, I can't recommend this game enough. It's worked its way up to the top of my list of favorite first person games. I kid you not.

Plays like Fortix.  You're a fish who starts at the edge of a rectangular map and swims in straight lines to clear off sections of the map until about 75%, after which you're scored and given 1-3 stars.  You increase your score by capturing (destroying) enemies and powerups within your rectangles, clearing off larger sections of the map with one move, finishing the level more quickly and by playing on hard difficulty where enemies are faster and respawn (recommended for a challenge and high scores).
While in the process of swimming from one safe point to another you leave a line behind you and are vulnerable, so If an enemy runs into your path you die. New enemies and obstacles are introduced at a fast enough rate to keep things fresh and the campaign will last 2-3 hours.  In addition there's a time trial mode and online leaderboards, though I didn't see a filter for friends unfortunately.  Looks nice, good music, easy achievements.  Worth it on sale.

The way I see it, JRPGs should be judged on three things: Story, gameplay and functionality.
Story, which would would include characters, dialogue, plot, etc, is pretty average. The characters are great, and can be funny, but the plot is nonexistant. Granted, I haven't finished the game, so I'm not really holding that against it too much in my judgement... but it still bothers me I'm five hours in and the plot of the game is "do sidequests!" If that's the plot, that's fine... but I still don't like it.
Gameplay, is also extremely average. It's your basic JRPG battle system, but not interesting at all. This cheap, rpgmaker niche that has appeared on Steam has shown it can have interesting battles... just look at a game like Cubicle Quest. In that game, you basically must figure out what the foes weakness is, and rearange your party to combat it. But in this, the all your party members basically fit into two categories: those who spam basic attacks, and those who spam their strongest spell. Weaknesses and resistances don't really fit in much, since they only affect the latter group, and even then, if you have a tier two level spell that is resisted by the foe, it will do more than a tier one level spell that has an elemental advantage.
Plus, the inclusion of MP is useless in this game. Your MP pool is so big, and you level up so fast, you never run out of it, so there's no point.
Oh, theres also this half-a$$ (did I mention that instead of swearing the game just puts symbols in? Because they do that, and it makes me think their target audience was nine year olds) active time battle system which seems like its probably a public script you can find on the rpgmaker forums. It's useless, too, since your characters are going to move in a certain order anyway. All it does is add breaks in the gameplay.
But I can excuse this, because I love myself an average jrpg, sort of turn based battle system.
But functionality just flops. I inlcude graphics and audio in this... and they both suck. Basic rpgmaker graphics, which, while not gamebreaking, do stop me from saying "Daaaaaaang this place looks nice" or "holy crap this battle theme sounds great." But I can excuse this.
What I can't excuse are the glitches. There are quite a few, and while most are pointed out by the "Glitch Fairy", and you're shown how to avoid them, there's one that is consistent and not pointed out: the fact that, for some unknown, god-forsaken reason, certain battles will crash your game. You will lose all your unsaved progress. But it's okay, right, because they just tell you to save every three seconds, and promise to fix it in the remake on the new version of RPGmaker. (spoiler: it's not okay.)
Theres also the price. 5 dollars. That's absurd. This game is worth 2.50 at best. So I don't recomend this, unless its on sale for half off or more. But that's fine. Because when it goes on sale, they usually put it on super sale (I got it for less than a quarter of a dollar).
Buy it.

Very fun game. Choose a ship, jump between stars, manage your ship systems and crew for maximum efficiency in combat or crises, customize your ship and crew, and stay ahead of the enemy fleet until you get to the end!
The main mechanics in the game are managing your power to systems to keep vital areas active as your ship becomes damaged or doesn't have enough power for every system at once. In addition, you can get more efficiency out of your systems by having the proper crew manage each system. You also get to target which enemy systems you can target with your weapons. Choosing wisely in any of these areas can mean the difference between victory and becoming a loose association of floating debris.
Each playthrough is relatively short, but the replay value is immense! You only start with access to one playable ship and you unlock the others by progressing in the game or by finding hidden quests. Each ship has several different designs available, if you can unlock them.
The game can be quite unforgiving at times with a random number generator. Do yourself a favor and start out on Easy until you figure out how it works. Don't let a little bad luck discourage you, it makes you better when you learn to prepare for it as best you can!
Good luck, and stop the rebel fleet!

I rather enjoy RPG Maker games; you can usually detect the investment of time and energy in a game within the first hour.  If this remains true, the ALBINO HUNTER registers as perhaps, the most lazy and uninspired RPG Maker game I have ever encountered.  While story is prominent, and none too bad, the actual mechanics are horrid.
Controls were via 360 Controller, and were terribly unresponsive; especially when tasked with speaking to someone.  Dreadful...
No interactive elements in the environment; those you would think to offer riches were met with a repetitive phrase no matter your location.  All crates, "This crate is heavy"...etc.  "Logs have insects" or some other nonsense.  The story seemed great, but it went from zero to nowhere fast; bugs kicking me out during a fight....  the capper was having to sit through APG regeneration at EVERY attack, bringing combat to a boring standstill...
While I support the RPG Maker community wholeheartedly, it is truly sad that such a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥effort would be introduced under that tag.  There is little gameplay, and virtually no passion introduced as a game element, other than a cool introductory story.  I was with you at the beginning...too bad you couldn't deliver the game to meet the story.

I enjoy the game, XCOM is a great game to play in a group or alone. Alone is fairly straight forward, it's just you, all alone, maybe talking to someone while you play with full control over everything. However, upon an event I joined in with my group a few years ago and had a blast with, in a group we all sit with sight or voice as to the game plan in game and when we go into a mission everyone who wants in on the mission gets a person and we each take turns playing our character and doing team things in the mission. What I think would make this game better is a co-op option or even DLC if it must be made that way where you can play with a friend doesn't matter how far away you are and you both play together. Purchases must be agreed on, as with selling items or completing requests, same goes for improving the base. When it comes time for abduction missions you can have a choice of going together or splitting the team to take out two missions (seems a bit broken but it means the max people you will have is 3). Saves would have to only be doable from HQ, this I'm perfectly okay with, means you have to take more care on the mission! Your girl has been slain by those you once called comrades, and now, one by one, you will have your revenge. Sweet, bloody revenge. All of this, of course, is just an excellent excuse for some clever, enjoyable platforming and delightful strategic combat.
There's something fascinating about charging at a thug with your chainsaw drawn, and flicking him into the air with a satisfying growl of its engine, then juggling his body with a blast from your shotgun. And because you are driven by REVENGE, then leaping into the air and manifesting your titular shanks into his prone body, before hurling him into the crowd.
As Shank continues on his vengeful quest, he adds machetes, katanas, machine guns, and much more to his arsenal. For, if nothing else, Shank is multi-talented.
And then there's co-op mode, where Shank's good friend joins him on his quest for revenge. I don't recall what his name is -- I just always call him Danny Trejo.  So there you go.  You can play as Danny Trejo.

Curently doing a Spartan playthrough of 2033 and a Survival playthrough of Last Light both on Ranger Hardcore both are absolutely excellent games and up there with my favourite of all time. 2033 has seen a vast improvement and visually looks as good as Last Light to me even though my GTX 770 can't get it smooth maxed out it still looks great with a few settings turned down. Defintely one of the better looking games to come out in recent months. The brighter lighting in 2033 may take away some of the atmosphere but the excellent sound design and sheer immersion ensures a wholly terrifying experience regardless. The Spartan mode is defintely fast and fun as opposed to the original Survival although its still very hard on the hardest difficulty. The slightly clunky intro to 2033 seemed much smoother this time with a few new links in there too. The throwing knifes particularly are thankfully the same as in Last Light a big improvement on the original although without a hud aiming gets pretty tricky. All the little improvements detailed in the above trailers really do help to bring it up to par with modern games.
Its been a flawless playthrough other than that I had to replay through one mission again because at the start of the next I was locked into a sort of cutscene with my gasmask on even though it should have not been necessary. My filter kept running out during the cutscene meaning everytime I suffocated - I think I recall it happening on the original Last Light as well but its a weird little bug. To be honest though I'm such a fan of these games nothing would stop me enjoying them.
Its very neat as 2033 was pretty rough but still managed to be one of the best story driven fps' out there, now its much smoother and still absolutely brillant.
I'm looking forward to continuing my journey through the Metro (although definitely dreading the Library!).

XCOM is the best kind of strategy game. It's the kind of game that makes you second-guess nearly every choice you make. Throughout the entire early-to-mid game, you have way more options available than you have resources with which to invest in those options. Do you research plasma weapons or hover armor? Or, if you've researched both already, do you BUILD plasma weapons or hover armor? That's just when you're at base; when you're on the battlefield, you have an entirely different set of options to constantly second-guess. You WILL, at some point, spot a group of aliens during your last action of the turn, and they WILL get first dibs on retaliating. Sometimes they'll rock your world, sometimes they won't, but the mere threat of them rocking your world is enough to make you load your last save.
Fortunately, on the default difficulty setting, the game is quite forgiving of mistakes, because the AI is intentionally dumbed down, sometimes to the point that enemies do literally nothing on their turn. You can still complete the game even if you make several "wrong" choices. Especially because, as implied in the last paragraph, save scumming is an integral part of keeping the game going. Save early and often. (It baffles me than Ironman mode even exists...and further baffles me that people have completed it.)

TL;DR: This game is 7/10.  But! old original game that this is ramake of, was 10/10 because it had much much richer tactics. Why?!
This game compared to original:
- lack of inventory screen of unit during battle (and also at all)
- related: can not freely have any loadout, e.g. 3, 5, even 20 grenades, or 3 nades and 7 indenciary nades, and 3 pistols, or riffle and pistol and rocket launcher... it's all dumbed down to few classes plus few "buffs"
- less weapons/items in the entire game
- can not pick/drop/throw/pass to other teammate things in battle
- can not do any combination of actions in turn, it's dumbed down to 2 actions usually walk, then shoot (sometimes 3 with some buffs)
- I prefereed grid map more, in isometirc view, it's less cool maybe, but better for tactics
- less advanced stats of each unit
- less advanced shooting: usually just shoot, instead of aimed/snapshot/auto fire (some units can have buffs to do cover fire or snipe, but not all)
- less advanced management of items in base
- especially: there is just ONE BASE, so no way to have several bases, move squads between them, move items, aliens
- can not destroy all map terrain !! :(
- can not so nicelly set thing on fire and watch the fire spread
- can not mine the terrain (put down trap mines at places where you expect enemy to come through)
- line of sight of units is not shown, this is a very serious tactical problem! Does the guy cover this door with his sight or not? (In original it was more of fog-of-war thing, but it usually got that job done, because aliens are in undiscovered terrain - and also isometric map, and top-down map helped)
- movement is done in 1, at most 2 steps. Instead of walking the say 15 meters step by step and seeing with each one what parts of map do you exactly see
- missing map of entire battle (with marked units)
- game chooses classes of your teammates, they are a bit random (e.g. small girl -> Heavy, bad aim guy -> Sniper, etc) and you can not change them or "multiclass"
- aliens are spawned when you trigger a waypoint. it's a bit lame.
But there is good too, just not in the areas that I wanted the most from this game:
+ it is not Dos pixelart game (like original) + cool 3d graphical effects and♥♥♥♥♥♥br>+ another xcom based game, yey
+ the dumbed down version will appeal to some players that are a bit more casual and would not play the game otherwise
+ the "I hear noice from this direction" idea is good... but it replaces the missing "motion scanner" and longer range spotting enemies
+ maybe seeing this game will convince you to look for the old game (and it's modern free open source re-write OpenXcom) and you will get to see the best game ever :)
Quite good modern version of best game of all time [for me] the UFO: Enemy Unknown game from 1994 year (also known as "X-COM: UFO Defense" on USA market).
But the original game from 1994 was much better, and it's modern free version OpenXcom is even better and free to download (I highly recommend).
...
So if you have a friend who must have neat 3d effects in his tactical/strategical game, or if you want to see modern take on same story with 30% of original gameplay capture - play this game.
In origianl - you could destroy all terrain in any way, build base in any way, arm units in ANY WAY (inventory screen), do any kind of actions on teammates in any order, there was only action points per turn limit.
You could e.g.: prime a grenede, walk 3 steps, throw it to teammate, step back, drop pistol on ground, arm rifle, kneel down and take aim and guard the door.
Or you could fire 3 random shots to set a barn on fire, deploy smoke, go in, pick up your unconcious teammate, and carry him outside.
All in one action turn.
You could there build any layout, usually a team unit had 5-10 items on him plus armor.
How ever, it's still a game more interesting then other modern tactical squad shooters... 30% of experience of best game ever [imo] is still fun. You could buy it, but I can not honstly recommend it seeing the lost potential to be excellent.
If you prefer deep tactical games and want all the options, or if you come here because you played the original 1994 game - well then you will notice how this game is dumbed-down in comparsion. But you can always get the free remake "openxcom" game, and buy this one here too.

NEO Scavenger is a really intense survival game. You can make a character based off of different skills and survival tactics. Depending on what you chose, your experience with the game will change. If you take Medical Knowledge, you can tend your wounds faster, or if you take Melee, you will be able to fight better.
It's a very brutal and unforgiving game. If you mess up, it could cost you your life. Perma-death is a thing so you really want to be careful.  The descriptions of what you do in combat is very descriptive and really helps with immersion.
Pros:
- It's very fun
- Rewarding if you come across some good gear
- Very realistic in the mechanics
Cons:
- no animations or visuals during combat
- Purely text based (could be a good thing if you like that, I do)
- near impossible on your first few lives.
- UI takes some time to get used to
Over all, it's a very brutal, but fun survival game, and I am really glad that I got it. If you enjoy wilderness survival games, this one will not dissapoint you.

This is a surprisingly fun and addicting game. I can't really stand those Bejeweled and other Facebook/mobile type games, but when you add the RPG elements it becomes a really clever puzzle game that offers more gameplay rewards than just bumping up your score. Instead of getting pointless points, performing combos allow you to do more damage and show you the extent of how strong whichever character you're using really is. It's a bit  roguelike, it can be very challenging in later stages and each playthrough is unique. Whenever you start a new playthrough you pick your character, your level and whatever bonuses you can afford (with starblocks, no in-game purchases in here. Not sure about the mobile version though) and start fresh. It has a decent difficulty progression, though the game tends to "seem" like it randomly spikes in difficulty.  I haven't gotten too far with the game because like I said earlier, the later stages of the game get pretty damn hard, but in all the time I've spent playing I've never been bored and I've had a lot of fun with it. I'm not the only one though, I've showed it to some off my family that like those mobile-type games and they all really like it after explaining to them how the RPG mechanics work.
Overall this is a pretty fun "matching game." It's really fun to play but if you're going to buy the Steam version I really recommend a tablet laptop or anything with a touchscreen, this game really needs a touch-screen to avoid that there carpal tunnel syndrome. If you don't have one I'd recommend getting the mobile version, preferably on a full sized tablet but it could work just as well on a cellphone. Get this game if you're looking for a fun and challenging puzzle-RPG.

The Witcher is an action role-playing hack and slash video game developed by CD Projekt RED and published by Atari.
The game is based on the book series of the same name by Polish author Andrzej Sapkowski. The Witcher takes place in a medieval fantasy world and follows the story of Geralt, one of a few remaining "witchers" – traveling monster hunters for hire, gifted with unnatural powers. The game's system of "moral choices" as part of the storyline was noted for its time-delayed consequences and lack of black-and-white morality.
The game utilises BioWare's proprietary Aurora Engine. A console version using an entirely new engine and combat system, titled The Witcher: Rise of the White Wolf, was to be released in Autumn 2009 but was suspended due to payment problems with the console developers, Widescreen Games.

Screw that I'm writing a real review.
-
FTL Is a game where you play as a captain on a ship which is loyal to the Federation, with your ultimate goal to destroy the Rebel Flagship, after travelling through the first 8 sectors and powering up your ship overtime to try and have a chance at beating this final boss.
Story -
The story is rather barebones, however, it's just enough to get me atleast invested in destroying the evil rebels and being a good guy on the way, or trying to be more of a pirate myself with the mods that the game offers.
Art -
Ahh, the art. The art of FTL is quite spectacular, really. With mods that enhance the quality even further, it's hard not to wonder how they manage to do that in the first place. The game really captures a coherent theme and makes you truly feel like you're in space experiencing what they do, albeit to a lesser degree than say, HTC Vive Elite: Dangerous. The sound design I'm lumping with the art because they're both fantastic. Immersive songs that really get you invested into the outcome, or get you wondering about the lore of this incredible game. The songs are very distinct, and definitely worth listening to on their own.
Gameplay -
In my opinion, the frantic, fast paced real-time-yet-inevitably-turn-based combat constantly keeps you on your toes. One minute you're charging up your beam weapon to finish off the rebel ship you've gotten to low hull points, with your weapon systems guarded by a nice shield to prevent their destruction, and the next they've either hacked your weapons, or more likely, shot a massive missile at you that hit & destroyed your weapons in their entirety and also caught the room on fire and also caused an air leak and suddenly you're thrown off of your position of power in that fight, and onto the back burner as you scramble to extinguish the fire whilst getting rid of the oxygen leak and also fixing your weapons back up before the enemy ship launches another one.
The mechanics of the game are extremely elegant and well designed, and while I'm sure many prefer real time combat to turn based combat, trust me, you will be using the pause button more than you've ever used it in your entire life, because the friendly zoltans turned on you and they have a mark 3 anti-bio beam that will cut through your crew like a knife on butter, or that the seemingly useless mantis with no weapons actually has a 4 man teleporter that you didn't notice because you didn't bother repairing your sensors and now there are 4 combat ready scissor monsters all named Nathan sitting in your shield room ready to ♥♥♥♥ your♥♥♥♥♥♥up. So, you pause, think long and hard about your life choices, and decide the best course of action is to lure the Mantis into your medi-bay 3 at a time and kill them while you've got the upper hand via constantly regenerating life. Or maybe you destroy their teleporter and cowardly man your doors to lock them all into a room with no oxygen while you hide like the totally awesome space faring captain you definitely are. I won't judge.
Replay Value -
This game primarily gets it's intense levels of replay value out of unlocking new ships, trying on harder difficulties (good luck), and mods. First off, ships. Unlocking new ships is an interesting process. There are 10 ships in the game, 8 of which can be unlocked by beating the game with the last unlocked ship, 2 of which are special snowflakes and only unlockable through special means, and all of which have at least 1 alternate form, 2 alternates for the 8 basic ships. However, as it is unlikely you'll beat the game 7 times with 7 different setups each time any time soon, some of them have special conditions you can unlock them under. Take, for example, the Stealth Cruiser, who can be unlocked by finding a specific quest in a specific (randomly generated) sector type, going to the proper beacon, and defeating the boss that awaits you. I won't make an entirely new section for difficulties as they're quite simple. There's You're going to die (Easy), You're going to die sooner (Normal), and good ♥♥♥♥ing luck (Hard).
Mods -
Mods however deserve a section to themselves. Mods will fall under two categories for most players. Either completely overlooked, or completely integral to their experience. I fell under the latter. Mods add so much replay value to the game it's insane. Take, for example, FTL: Captain's Edition, CE Infinite, and CE Endless Loot. Captain's Edition alone adds so much content to the game with new weapons, enemies, and an entirely new lore friendly story behind your campaign, with brand new events and gameplay mechanics. CE Infinite takes this and allows you to traverse the universe potentially forever, by allowing you to stay in whatever sector you're currently in under a new randomly generated map, and CE Endless Loot overhauls the weapon and drones of the game with a sort of MMO type of attribute system, allowing you to find incredible variations of base game or even Captain's Edition weapons.
Oh and did I mention the entire experience is permadeath.
Overall -
Overall, I would give this game a solid 9/10. I know I haven't discussed the negatives of the game quite yet, so here they are. I do not factor mods that fix negative aspects of a game into a review score, as they are not the game itself and are therefore not part of the score, though I do mention them in reviews themselves. Negatives wise, while it does have amazing replayability, it can get quite stale without constantly changing your mods to be doing the same thing over and over run after run, and even during individual runs. After all of that, I would definitely give this game a buy if anything there sounds good to you.

First stage: Confusion
Your first impression is "pretty neat game, it will be fun". After first few missions you cannot understand how aliens manage to kill your troops in full cover from large distance, but you try to enjoy the game.
Second stage: Anger
Missed shots with percentage of success over 70% are starting to annoy you, as well as a bunch of aliens waiting behind a door to rush and obliterate your troops at the moment you open the door. You are questioning how is that possible, yelling at incapable soldiers and quitting the game during the mission.
Third stage: Adapting
After not playing XCOM for several days, you get calm and think of new tactic how to lead sloppy troops into victory. Even after carefully developed tactic and units positioning, swarming aliens manage to crawl out of every corner getting critical shots at your troops.
Fourth stage: Depression/Frustration
You are losing hope in this game, your troops and your life. Finally you understand that everything is in vain. You accept inevitability of death and failure.
Fifth stage: Acceptance
You understand this game isn't supposed to be fun nor make any sense. You start laughing whenever an alien takes critical shot on your soldier. You don't question or worry anymore, you have accepted this fate. There is no hope nor victory.
Good

I rate Warhammer 40K: Dawn of War (this game still doesn't explain why this game is called 'Dawn of War') Game of The Year Edition 3/5. Ok.
Well this game was probably pretty good (3.5/5) when it first came out but like movies, games can age and often not in a good way. By today's standards I'd have to say this game is fairly bland and, particularly during single player campaign, somewhat boring. This is partially due to the relatively drab graphics but is also partially due to the gameplay itself which is, sadly, a little too repetitious, Regardless of whether you play multiplayer, in the single-player skirmish mode or on the main campaign, the game's battles are primarily focused on the need to capture and control certain victory control points. Capturing and holding these control points primarily give you the ability to requisition more soldiers, equipment and vehicles or allow you call for more buildings with which to reinforce.
Unfortunately, this kind of tactical battlefield gameplay gets old pretty fast as, regardless of which side you play (they are all pretty evenly balanced against each other), the underlying tactics one must employ change relatively little. Essentially you must build units, capture points and then build more units, reinforce and upgrade your current units and capture more points. The single player campaign attempts to spice things up a bit with story-oriented objectives which require you to do things like eliminate every enemy building or kill a particular enemy. The multiplayer and single player skirmish modes also includes settings which allow those matches to be won and lost if similar objectives are achieved. However, regardless of how victory is to be declared, control points must be captured to get more battlefield resources.
Limiting the potentially creative tactical possibilities even further, the gameplay is heavily focused on the deployment of infantry. (Some sides use more light, faster-moving infantry and other sides use heavy, slower infantry but all sides mostly use infantry organized into individual squads which you can individually attempt to control). In the main campaign you can only play as the Blood Ravens Space Marines. There are no air units which you can control while there are a few tanks and other armored units you cannot assign a squad to specifically guard and accompany a particular tank (this has to be done in a more manual fashion), though the game mostly just treats different tanks as merely different types of artillery support for your infantry squads (for example, you cannot use tanks to run over infantry unfortunately).
Different units have different roles and are absolutely prevented from working outside of those roles (unless their roles change due to being upgraded). Only infantry can capture control points. Oddly, tanks and armored walkers cannot. The gameplay often feels oddly inflexible as a result. You can assign Heroic units to certain squads but you cannot tell a squad to automatically guard another squad and so forth. I remember back when I played Homeworld I ways setup complex, interlinked guardian roles for all of the units I had so each unit was ultimately protecting (and would automatically reinforce) other units. As in most other tactical games, can't do anything approaching this level of complexity here. This game isn't very subtle. The gameplay is mostly about reinforcing units fast (by clicking on buttons on the lower menu as fast as you can) and selecting different buildings and ordering them to produce ever more units while telling your workers to construct more buildings while telling your infantry to take control points while telling your artillery direct their fire at certain high-importance enemies. Sometimes you get to do flanking maneuvers but sometimes not. There's not a lot of ways to think outside the box in this game. Mostly you just have to try to be fast.
In terms of graphics, this game can seem a bit bland by today's standards. The complexity of the textures which this game uses have not aged well. However units have a fair number of animations but the stuff they automatically say when selecting them or giving orders becomes really repetitive really fast (I was happy the game has an option to turn off this particular part of the audio) This game depicts some brutal combat situations with bodies that sort of stack up on the ground (a nice graphical touch) but the characters themselves look, well...cute. They look really, really really CUTE. LIKE OH MY, THOSE SPACE MARINES LOOK SO LOVABLE with their big feet and big shoulders and relatively little heads! The Space Marine Dreadnoughts are even more cutesy and funny. They look like cute walking garbage dumpsters (and they have the deep metal garbage dumpster voices you'd imagine a walking, talking garbage dumpster to have). To be fair, the Chaos forces and the Eldar forces and the Orks generally look a quite a bit less cute though (and this game lets you zoom in to an amazing degree to see each individual close up if you want to though you won't possibly be able to be an effective commander if you try to play the game like from such a view as individuals run into and out of your zoomed-in field of vision). The cuteness might be intentional but Warhammer 40K characters BEING CUTE IS NOT TRUE TO THE WARHAMMER 40K UNIVERSE. Unfortunately because of the extreme cuteness ineptly combined with the seriousness of the dialogue and its suitably heavy-handed delivery, the main campaign's movie scenes are a laugh riot. It is commendable that the designers of this game tried to use the same graphics as the game itself to do most of the cutscenes to advance the plot, but when shown up-close the characters all run like marionette puppets (like in the movie Team America), don't move their lips remotely in sync to the dialogue and well,, LOOK ABSOLUTELY TOO CUTE TO BE BELIEVED!!! If you like inadvertent humor, look up the between-missions scenes. WHAT WERE THEY THINKING?! After a while I started wondering if a Hello Kitty Space Marine was going to show up to perform exterminatus on the planet.
The AI does more than adequate job, but then, given the terrible lack of potential tactical options which this game presents you, I'd expect nothing less. The sound is adequate. Although I liked 2 of the pieces of music used in this game the vast majority of it is boring. I got so bored with the music I played music from a media player on my computer while playing several of the larger battles. This game has very few outright bugs and no bugs which are game-breaking. The final boss is not overly difficult though the AI is far more aggressive in the skirmish mode than the main campaign. The main campaign effectively acts as a sort of long tutorial of sorts. The ending of the game is a disappointing cliff-hanger although I suppose I should expect that given the world of Warhammer 40k.
Ultimately, given all this, do I recommend this game or not? I'm not sure. I think, in the light of newer games that have come out since which eclipse this one, I do not recommend this game. This isn't a bad game but it is beginning to age badly.

text:
First of all: if you paid $15 for this game, you've underpaid. Sunk more than 90 hours in this game (online and offline) and I STILL can't see half of the content and this is just vanilla. I made the mistake of adding a mod to this game and holy crap...still can't see past 10% of the content without either dying, getting completely wrapped up in a spawn and exploration run and enjoy the hell out of simply trying to LIVE long enough!
NEO Scavenger's one of those games that no matter how much you die, live, fail, respawn, mix your talents up and roll again...you want to play some more. I've clocked almost 20 hours in the DEMO alone and when I bought the game, I bought copies for friends and sat many a night down in Teamspeak and we've compared survival times and setups and this game suceeds in making you declare "One...more...game..."
I turned this into a serious review just because I've joined the forums, added input and done a bit of bug submission as well and even the community is together despite it being a lone-dev game.
PROS:
-A very good "One more game..." setup.
-A lot of the in-game recipes are common sense based. Combine...and see what happens.
-The turn-based battle system with different movesets depending on your talents is functional and efficent. That feeling of satisfaction when you stab a feral dog to death with a wooden spear crafted by your own hands and sharpened with a glass shard.
-The storyline so far is intriguing and you get this sense of "Where am I? Who am I? What is going on?" constantly.
-Because of the game's setting and environment, finding so much as a shopping bag to hold your stuff feels like the greatest success. You'll know what I mean when you play.
-The idea of drinking water straight from a pond is hazardous at best.
-Eat berries, dog flesh, human flesh, cooked food, soup, scavenged snack cakes. The world is your buffet table!
-Josh Culler's submissions for the soundtrack of this game are short...but VERY, VERY suitable.
CONS:
-The game is programmed for Flash. Depending on your PC and stats and some measure of bad luck-you ARE going to get some frustrate-level crashes. Save often and make sure the game doesn't bug out randomly because it pretty much means you're going to lose your progress. It doesn't happen often but when it does...damn. Hard luck. TIP: run the game in fullscreen and set your cache for Flash at 10MB to prevent random lockups.
-The game tilts itself against you unfairly sometimes, especially when you decide to settle down in an area for extended time and the enemy spawn rate tends to increase. Not exactly fair when you're someone who likes having a "base" to call home but the gameplay is meant to keep you mobile. Not stuck in one spot. Explore at will but know that if you hang around somewhere long enough, the game WILL start pushing you out to go do something else or go somewhere.
-The amount of enemies that can populate one tile per battle sometimes goes a little overboard. Nothing more rage inducing than getting strangled to death in your sleep by 4 enemies, 3 of whom took apart your noise traps and the other strangled you to death with a pounce. Not sure if this is intentional but it still is frustrating when it happens.
-Not all the recipes work seamlessly. Sometimes you HAVE to check your recipe book to see if you've learned it by accident and you need to click the RECIPE to craft said item in the first place.
-No way to repair items CURRENTLY at the time of this review without mod assistance. It's pretty annoying to have to play vanilla, find a backpack on 3% and lose it the next turn to decay, go play a mod and then come back to find out that there are still some minor frustrations.
The reason I approve this game is because the community contributes ideas, help, bug reports and helps design its own mods. So far there's 3 main stable ones that are available at the website forums and they add SO MUCH to the game already. You know you've succeeded with a game when people are climbing over themselves to add content and mods to your game, free of charge.
VERDICT:
Buy this if you like roguelikes, turn based and making decisions via micromanagement of inventory and move turns. You'll spend a good few hours with this game and still find yourself coming back for more. The gods help you if you add a mod. Might as well quit your day job while you're ahead! :D

This game is advertised as a puzzle/JRPG. Its an alright puzzle game but I’m not quite sure it fits any JRPG elements. Lets first start off with the puzzle aspect of this game. There’s very little skill involved between battles and the game constitutes of clicking on matching blocks to attack enemies, heal and defend. There’s only 6 block types: treasure chest, gold, attack, magic, defend and heal. When you aren’t fighting enemies attack blocks transform into experience until your next battle.
In essence the puzzle aspect of this game is more of a roguelike / time trial. In between facing foes you’re basically making a mad dash to match as many blocks as possible to level up. And the blocks you get are random with very little ways to influence them. There are a few items that might get rid of a certain block type or change one block into another but overall items are pretty random and not at all easily accessible as item costs are fixed and show up randomly. So you’re very likely to reach a store selling a high priced item when you just start out on your journey.
There is also equipment available for purchase but it’s awkwardly done in that you don’t get to equip your item right out the store. It goes into your inventory that can be accessed in your next playthrough. While we’re on the concept of price and purchases you are given random quests that you gain star blocks through. Star blocks are used to buy items, characters and stages at the start of the game. You can earn them mostly by doing side quests or defeating section bosses. Remember the various equipment I mentioned that you can purchase during your quest? Well when you start a new game you now have the option of… purchasing it AGAIN with star blocks. So technically purchasing equipment in the field unlocks it. You have to purchase it with star blocks every time you start a new game if you then want to equip it. And note that you can only have one item and equipment at a time.
I feel like these crippling in game cost mechanics are leftovers from the app side of this mobile to PC game. It’s not a freemium model but sort of acts like it. The game never asks you for real money but the way the in game economy works it’s definitely a lot harder and less enjoyable not being able to purchase stuff.
Now on to the RPG side. RPG to me has the impression that there’s going to be a story in there somewhere. You start the game and you just keep breaking blocks. You only see NCPs to buy stuff from them and that’s pretty much all the interaction you have with the residents. There’s no dialog to speak of, no characters to get to know. You do have HP, MP and gain experience but that’s the extent of any RPG elements present in the game.
I will say I enjoy playing this game for what it is and not what it’s pretending to be. It’s a grindy, casual tough as nails puzzle game where luck and speed play as big a role as any skill you might have for these types of games. It won’t appeal to RPG fans but if you want a bit of a time killer then this will suffice for a short casual playthrough when bored.

I want to say that I love puzzle games. From Tetris to Adventure of Lolo to Talos Principle to Tetris Attack to Yoshi's Cookies to Puzzle Quest to Monkey Island. I love puzzle games from PC to console to mobile platforms. I've played more than I can count.
Now, I own this game on both Windows Phone and Steam so don't let my play time fool you. Also, the Windows Phone version has beem broken for months with no update in site.
With all that out of the way, I can say that this game is just not fun. There are two elements to this game and I will cover them in the following two paragraphs. Those elements are "RPG" and "puzzle". Frankly, neither work and I will explain why.
The RPG elements are bare bones and might as well not exist. Im not just talking about the experience and leveling system either. I'm talk about the entire "RPG" experience that's presented here. The story is non-existent.. literally. There is no dialog or NPC interaction besides stores. No, you can't buy weapons or armor or accessories either. You fight monsters in random battles but there is no depth to the monsters. There's no elemental element or monsters that are weak against such and such. Nothing. In fact, you will almost never even take your eyes off of the puzzle field to look at the monster. You CAN level up and when you do so, you get one point you can put towards your stats and that's really the only RPG element you will experience to any meaningful degree in this game.
The actual puzzle game is another barebones mediocre experience. I thought about writing a huge paragraph here detailing why the puzzle aspect of this game doesn't work and I really thought about comparing this game to some of the greats like Tetris Attack or Puzzle Quest but then I realized I can sum up the entire puzzle experience. All you do in this game is click blocks. You don't get to manipulate the board like in Puzzle Quest or Tetris Attack and you don't need to plan your moves and think ahead like in Tetris, Puyo Puyo, or Super Puzzle Fighter. Do you see two of the same blocks next to eachother? Click them. What next? Hope the blocks that spawn in, spawn in your favor. That's it. It's a surprisingly empty experience. Fighting monsters means clicking sword blocks or magic blocks as they appear and fighting bosses means clicking any blocks as fast as possible. You'll generally lose on boss fights because you take more damage faster than the right blocks can spawn in.
It's a hollow and utterly pointless experience. No aspect of this game feels competent enough to keep your attention. I really really REALLY wanted to enjoy this game. This game should have been made by looking through the DECADES of puzzle games we have and influences should have been taken from a dozen games. The reality is that what we have here is a game that feels like a mobile game that came from 2004; like something you would have played on your Razer phone.
I'm sorry for my harsh review but I really wanted this game to be good.

- Escalating costs to every unlock in the game. For example, unlocking a character would first cost you 9 star blocks. Then 12, the 35...it just seems to keep going up. This is made worse by the fact that...
- You only earn one star block per boss you best in battle. You can get others by completing quests, but depending on setup, this could be doomed to fail because most of them rely on sheer dumb luck if you complete them or not. Even then, the most I’ve gained from a quest thus far is 3 at a time. There is the enemies which test your nerves, but a little later.
- You know how it most, COMPETENT RPG’s you can have a weapon AND armor? This game makes you choose one or the other. You can only hold one equitable and one consumable item at a time.
- The enemies are also a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Their scaling is awesome compared to how poorly you scale. The bosses scale EVEN HARDER (like they should), but the problem comes in when eventually, you will reach a point where you are unable to keep up and you WILL DIE. The fact that the previously mentioned one piece of gear at a time thing only makes the worse.
- There is no real feedback when you go to use items that destroy rows/columns. When it comes to consumables, you click on them, click the OK button and they go into play. Nothing else changes to show that you’re in the midst of using the item, like the cursor could change, or the row/column could change color as you’re moving over the blocks.
- This last one is just a knit pick, but why are their tablet/smartphone terms like “swipe” in a game that is on the PC!?
I could go on. But this review is getting long, and if I go further, I will have officially put more work into this than the developer put in the port of this game.
Block Legend DX is a legend alright. A bad one. I’m usually one to give a smartphone game a shot on the PC, but this time my faith was misplaced. In short, the port is terrible and the developer should feel terrible.

I would absolutely recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the RTS genre or interested in WW2 in general. Unlike popular RTS games like Starcraft, this game relies heavily on unit preservation and tactical thinking. Resource income is determined by territory you control across the map rather than the classec builder/resource collector of the CnC/Warcraft era.
Battle is intense and commanders are rewarded by correct tech decisions as well as when to stay and fight, and when to retreat to fight another day with veteran units. The numer of units available to each faction is excellent and each commander will be able to appreciate the unique nature of the force at their command. There is essentially very little overlap betwen the 4 factions at present and the game feels well balanced*.
As with all games balance is a contentious issue and it's not entirely perfect in this game, however Relic (the developer) have been very good at interacting with the community and updating the game regularly (1-2months on average). I feel the balance is currently in a very good place and would only recommend minor changes.
This game is a challenge but will reward dedicated players with satisfying victories as well as high fidelity combat and exciting sequences. I would recommend this game to anyone that has the slightest interest in RTS games. If you're still unsure - check out youtube and lookup "the propagandacast" or "generals gentlemen" for shoutcasts of top players. Alternatively have a look at
for the number one fan site and take a look at popular streamers. I recommend Siberian or Stephenn JF as streamers to watch.

Very fun game. Choose a ship, jump between stars, manage your ship systems and crew for maximum efficiency in combat or crises, customize your ship and crew, and stay ahead of the enemy fleet until you get to the end!
The main mechanics in the game are managing your power to systems to keep vital areas active as your ship becomes damaged or doesn't have enough power for every system at once. In addition, you can get more efficiency out of your systems by having the proper crew manage each system. You also get to target which enemy systems you can target with your weapons. Choosing wisely in any of these areas can mean the difference between victory and becoming a loose association of floating debris.
Each playthrough is relatively short, but the replay value is immense! You only start with access to one playable ship and you unlock the others by progressing in the game or by finding hidden quests. Each ship has several different designs available, if you can unlock them.
The game can be quite unforgiving at times with a random number generator. Do yourself a favor and start out on Easy until you figure out how it works. Don't let a little bad luck discourage you, it makes you better when you learn to prepare for it as best you can!
Good luck, and stop the rebel fleet!
