Overall: 9/10, Don't bother if you already have Metro:2033, unless you NEED graphic updates. If you havent expirenced the series yet DO. NOW. GET TO IT.
So before I begin, I want to say that this series is my favorite, and for many reason ( which you get to hear ), so I may be a bit biased. Also, almost everything I say here can also be atributed to the original. So, as previously stated, I love this series, and when I heard about the redux, I was scared, as I didn't want it to be shamed by what is basically a next gen console port by things like new voice actors, or possibly streamlining for "wider appearl". I also feared that Ranger Mode would be cut off and sold seperately, as w/ the original Last Light. Thankfully, since THQ desolved into the ether, neither of those things are there. Instead, we have good 'ol Metro:2033 but with better graphics, and other devolpers need to realize that this is how you do it.
Gameplay: 10/10
The original's gameplay (i.e. gunplay/stealth) was just fine and it hasnt changed a bit. This may sound like a criticism, but its not. While some games try to innovate and fail and some try to innovate at the behest of everything else, Metro games try to instead set the bar by good atmosphere, world building and of course, good gameplay by using what works and results in a bar that is only raised in my book by Half Life. The guns feel good, and especially in Ranger Mode, the games hardcore playthrough mode that remove almost all hud elements ( you have to count the bullets left in your magazine by looking at it) and increases damage to enemies and the player (it also makes resources more scarce, but we'll talk about that later). If you prefere a stealthy approach, you are in luck. While the levels where stealth is encouraged are extactly Thief 2 big, the are nicely sized and have multiple access points and little secrets to discover. Also, it takes the idea of Thief's Light Gem (a little gem at the bottom of the screen that displays how visible you are) and incorporates it into a watch that you can see when holding your weapon out. Overall, I liked the gameplay, my only annoyance that a lot of guns were REALLY quiet. The Duplet, an icon of the series, (a double barrel shotgun made out of pipes) is no louder that an slightly miffed cat coughing. But worth it and im sure the modding community can fix that issue.
Enviroment/World: 10/10
The Metro Series has the advantage of being based off of a book, and even more of one by being by a Russian author. (I'm not being biased against all but Russians, but the Russian side of a nuclear apacolyplse is rarely touched otherwise, especially in games.) Books have much better world and story that most games The idea of the Moscow civilians in the underground metro being the sole survivors is just genius to me, and lavely to play in. When you aren't sneaking through the underground section, you are on the surface, sneaking by or just fighting off mosters and enemy factions and that is really quite fun as well. Since most of the game is in dark, claustrophobic enviroments, it is very welcome to walk around the surface. When you are on the surface, you need a gas mask to survive. You also need filters, which you find in the world. These filters have an alloted amount of time before they run out, the more you have, the more time you have. This I find an espicially nice touch, adding to the Survival-horrow aspect. The enviroments however, at least compared to its successor, are quite linear. On the surface, you have wide open spaces, but a rather set path to travel them. In Last Light, you have wide open spaces that were, wide open. This made you want more filters, so you could explore more, and get better weapons/ammo or other gear. A similar problem is underground. While Last Light had more exploration in its tunnels, 2033 has a bit less so, but it isnt really noticeable. Also, in the metro stations that serve as towns, often you are immediatley rushed through, with little time to breath. In Last Light, these are calm areas, with little things on the side to do, be it help a child find his teddy bear, or watch an old man tell children about birds and green trees. However, all these are made up for by the facts that A)The sequel didn't exist yet, so it really should not be compared to it, and B) The setting is so unique and instantly interesting that it completely makes up for it.
Story/Characters:
As I said earlier the fact that this is based off of a book gives it an advantage story wise. The entire draw of books are stories, not filling Nazies and Communists with bullets and then stomping off to the surface for a quick irradiated run through the wastes. And it really shines through to the game.
Summary:
You play Artyom, a child who grew up shortly after the war ended in the Metro station known as Exhibition. When your station is threated by the Dark Ones, irradiated mutations that seem to be superhuman, you begin your odyssy to Polis (another station) to take the message of your missing friend and save your station.
Ok, that sounds cheesy, especially with the inclusion of communist and Nazi factions, but it is made up by the character of Artyom himself. In gameplay, he never speaks, but on loading screens, he writes in his diary, and reads it aloud, so you hear his voice, which is nice, since silent protagonists annoy me, and ones who voice opinions i disagree or annoy me with their character (see Booker DeWitt) I dislike even more. Also, if you find paper throughout the level, Artyom writes notes in his journal which shed more light on the situation and also don't do the Mass Effect thing of huge exposion dumps via the Codex.
Some thing that annoys me, once again taking cues for Thief (not that its a bad thing, I love the first two of those) is that no matter how much Artyom tries not to care, he still gets embroiled with the factions.
I didn't do a X/10 rating for this section because I don't know what to thing of it. The mark of a good story is that you think about it afterwards and on my first runthrough of the original, the story really did stick with me, especially the ending MINOR SPOILER
END MINOR SPOILER. The ending was also good as it rounded out the story with no sequel hook, but still was open enough to have one. However, they're was a lot of little things that dragged it down, especially the beginning. It begins en midias res with you fighting monsters close to the end of the game. Then it jumps back 8 days to when you are in your metro station, meeting w/ the guy who goes missing. Then, finally he goes missing and your journey begins. This made it feel drawn out, and results in lowered expectations. But i guess I liked it
Nice little touches:
You can wipe your gas mask to wipe blood and grime off it
You have a lighter which clears away cobwebs
You have a notepad that displays objectives and it has a compass that points the way if you are lost
All of the above remove the need for a hud (more immersive)
Flashlight needs charging
Military grade rounds are the currency, so shoot'em or spend'em
Feels like an odyssy as the camera almost is never outside the players perspective and the story is continuous
Good weapon and character design
Annoyances:
When picked up by Demons (really big mutated bats) and then dropped, the animation is buggy (might be fixed later on)
Sometimes switches to military grade rounds without saying so
Depending on the order which you collect paper, Artyoms notes are sort of out of order
NOT SURVIAL HORROR- NOT SCARY
Spartan mode has resources up the wazoo
Assorted minor bugs
Overall: 9/10, Don't bother if you already have Metro:2033, unless you NEED graphic updates. If you havent expirenced the series yet DO. NOW. GET TO IT.

An interesting mix of rogue-like and puzzle game, you take a character on a quest fighting monsters and bosses and earning stars to unlock more stuff.  This is a great and well-thought out, simple game that is incredibly addictive.  This game is small and will run on just about anything.
And for all of those people who are complaining about how the game isn't engaging and all that other nonsense....it's a casual puzzle game.  It's not meant to be played for hours and hours on end (even though I sometimes do that as a distraction to other thigns).  It's a short and simple game, meant to be picked up, enjoyed, and put down before moving on to other things.  I don't really understand why this is such a hard thing for people to understand.
A few tips:  The DX doesn't only refer to this game as a port from some other console, new features were added to it. If you scroll down to the bottom of the character list, there are some extra characters down there.  If you are having a particularly hard time with things, try using Unity-chan.  She starts with a very high vitality stat, doesn't need to be unlocked with stars, and will probably give you a higher survivability.
Stars aren't meant to be something that you just get constantly to unlock stuff.  They aren't particularly hard to get, but you don't get them in large quantities.  This is done as a simple 'effort and reward' system.  If you spend the effort to unlock something, you will most likely enjoy how that changes gameplay for you.  It's not a part of microtransactions or other nonsense, it's just something to reward players who play the game long enough to unlock stuff.  Quests are easily cycled through in most cases, and if a quest is proving too hard to fulfill, you'll eventually come across an npc who can change it for 100 gold.
Lastly, items have a huge impact on the game.  You unlock things as you purchase them in the game for coins.  You can then start with those items for a guaranteed advantage on your next playthrough at the cost of stars.  If you are having trouble getting through something, don't be afraid to buy items and experiment with them so that you can use them later.
Worth the £8.49 that I paid for the pre-order,  runs a lot smoother and I mean a LOT!

By creating WH40K:DoW, Relic Entertainment has brought into existence the best Warhammer video game adaption up to date. Dawn of War is a title which doesn't just simply entertain, it takes a special place in the player's memory, and it does so due to two reasons. The first and the more considerable of these two reasons lies in the very fact that this game is set in the grim future of the 41st millennium, a future where there is only war, death and the laughter of thirsting gods. However, in order to adapt such a brilliant setting to the screen of computers, experienced, devoted and skilled game designers had to take matters into their own hands. This is where the second reason for the titles success comes into play - the developers. Relic Entertainment had the right framework to build their RTS upon from the very beginning, but even with such a great basis as the WH40k universe, talent and thoroughness were required so as to make a good quality game. Before DoW, several WH40k titles were already developed for the PC, with most of them being released in the 90's. While these predecessors were usually of good quality, certain factors prevented them from being as accomplished as DoW, graphical limitations being one of them. Relic Entertainment utilized the technology which was available in 2004 to implement the best possible graphics into their RTS, and graphics are indeed one of the most remarkable attributes which Dawn of War possesses, even to this day. The gameplay mechanics are also unique and exceptional, as are all the other aspects of the game.
In Dawn of War, Relic Entertainment employed a semi-innovative resource control system. Unlike in some older, well known real-time strategies where the player had to directly gather resources which fueled his armies growth, in DoW the economy revolves around control over strategic points that are scattered all across the battlefield. The amount of the strategic points controlled is crucial since they directly affect the players requisition income, thus forcing the opposing combatants to constantly fight for the control over territory. In addition to strategic points which play the primary resource role and grant requisition, DoW also has a secondary resource called power. This resource is just as essential as requisition, since power is required for researching or upgrading technologies and abilities, and is also spent when deploying advanced units and vehicles. In order to gain power resource points, the commander must build power generator structures either near his base of operations or at special slag deposits which grant more power income. By the time Dawn of War was released, the requisition control system was new but not unheard of, since there were already games that utilized a somewhat similar concept. Massive Entertainment's Ground Control II for an example, which was released approximately three months before DoW, used a system called acquisition in which points were earned through the capturing of victory locations. Later on, Massive Entertainment used the same system in their well acclaimed RTT World in Conflict. In fairness it must be said, that even though Relic's resource control system was at that time both original and well designed, it wasn't actually their invention. They did, however, put this system to good use, because in terms of economical balance, DoW is a perfectly designed RTS. Missions in-game usually alternate between jungles and ravaged urban ruins, with Fog of War being persistent in those areas of the map which either have not yet been uncovered or were abandoned by allied forces. In battle, the environment plays a minor strategic role as well, on account of that in Dawn of War, certain types of terrain can provide troops with either good cover, granting them a protection bonus, or harmful cover which exposes the troops and makes them vulnerable to enemy fire. In general, terrain and the surrounding environment both contribute to the tactical detail of the game, with infantry traversing faster over certain terrain types, while treaded vehicles will move slower. Infantry squads all have morale that affects their combat effectiveness. An infantry squad with broken morale will be much less effective in combat, and will need to retreat in order to replenish their fighting spirit. Squad leaders also give each squad a significant morale boost. Enemy infantry has morale as well, and certain weapons, such as for an example a flamethrower, can break it faster, rendering enemy formations broken and in a state of moral dismay. In Dawn of War, there are four different factions which are anything but similar and are all driven to annihilate each other. All four of these factions have their own distinctive units, structures and strategies. Units can be divided into infantry and vehicles, with infantry groups usually being versatile and possessing the ability to capture strategic points, while vehicles often take an assault force role. Dawn of War provides the player with an immense arsenal of weaponry, including artillery, tanks and walker vehicles. Unlike some RTS games where opposing armies often have visually different but functionally identical units, in DoW units which are exclusive to one certain faction are unique in the sense that they rarely have a counterpart amongst the three other factions. Therefore, all units in DoW are not only distinguishable by their appearance, but also by their abilities and properties. The Tech-Tree in the game is well developed, each faction has numerous types of infantry, vehicles, skills, technologies and upgrades. The player can also upgrade his primary and defensive structures to go higher in the tech tree, further benefiting his fighting force. In the single-player campaign, the player will have the opportunity to play as the Space Marines Blood Ravens chapter, taking the role of Force Commander Gabriel Angelos. Throughout 11 bloody missions, players will first fight against the Ork menace, will struggle against the mysterious Eldar, and will then finally engage against the traitorous Chaos Space Marines. Most of the missions are focused on elimination of the enemy base and army. Dawn of War offers three levels of difficulty, with the "Insane" difficulty level being the most entertaining and challenging one. The gameplay in Dawn of War can be described as balanced, intense and loaded with ceaseless combat action.
Dawn of War has detailed, beautiful graphics which appear terrific and well modeled even up to today’s standards, regardless of the fact that the game is over 11 years old. The palette in DoW fits the WH40k's universe perfectly, with darker tones overshadowing the brighter ones. The colors in game are full of contrast, all is dark yet by no means monotonous. Also, the darkness which pervades in the game by no means makes it faded or bleak; the game is rich in color, and everything has it's unique shade, from crimson blood spilled over the crusted earth to the smeared paint on war-scarred vehicle armor. In my opinion, the graphics in DoW are beyond any criticism, and were obviously created by competent individuals. The UI was elaborately designed to resemble a futuristic electronic panel, whilst the menu backgrounds appear as old parchments (with holy dogmas and aphorisms adorning the corners of these parchments).
DoW isn't merely a well designed, good quality game, it is a game with a soul, and that alone says much, because such games are very hard to come by. It is worthy of staying in your heart, for once you play it, you suddenly acquire understanding of what an RTS should be like. Relic Entertainment has successfully brought a WH40K RTS to the display of computers, and for that they deserve honours. Dawn of War is the definition of an outstanding real time strategy, and whoever plays it can be fully confident, that his expectation won't be ruined.

This is my first attempt at a review, so I figure I might as well use this game for practice.  I'll be focusing more on design aspects than typical reviews, so keep that in mind.  Also, note that my hours played aren't accurate.  I've finished the game and complete nearly all of the side quests, but was forced to launch the game outside steam to avoid a lag problem.  (Windows 10/defender freaks out and devours CPU resources when the game is launched via steam, but not when launched directly via game.exe)
First of all, the pros:
1. It's
a hentai game, although this may be a con depending on why you're looking at this game.  I guess it's just normal fashion for the women in this kingdom to walk around with their boobs nearly hanging out.
2. Great storytelling.  The developers clearly put the bulk of their focus into trying to tell the story, complete with likeable non-mary-sue characters and a few plot twists.   As someone who grew up on SNES-era RPGs, I'm used to and pretty tolerant of mangled engrish, so my expectations with jRPGs are pretty low.  This game only had a few minor grammatical mishaps, but was otherwise quite well written.  It was quite the breath of fresh air.
3. Good quest flow.  Everything was tracked and nicely documented in the quest log.  In fact, I never had a moment of wandering around, wondering "okay, where the hell do I go next?"
4. No level grinding required.  This was likely the result of an inverse difficulty curve though, so see "cons" for more info.
5. No random encounters.  The overworld is completely empty and in dungeons, enemies roam around and only fight if you run into them.  They're slow, stupid, and easily avoidable.  I want to 10/10 this game for this alone.
6. It's a fairly short, bite-sized RPG that only took me about 7 hours to complete, including nearly all sidequests.  This could also be a con I suppose, but to me, 100+ hour timehogging games get tiresome.
Now for the cons, and many of them have to do with combat:
1. Attack magic is literally never useful.  The "warlock" character does more damage with his basic attacks, which is asinine.  His only meaningful ability is a magic debuff (unless grinding his levels past 20 or so gets something I haven't seen yet) which is unfortunate.
2. The difficulty curve moves in the wrong direction.  The game starts out fairly average, but by the end, most attacks just bounce right off you, and as mentioned already, I spent no time grinding levels.  To give an idea, the last boss was only able to kill any of my characters through instant death attacks, but that was easy to counter with a revive spell or item since both of these attacks were single target and he only acts once per turn.
3. The main character is stupidly overpowered compared to the others.  By the time you get her 3-hit attack, most boss fights become trivial, 2-3 round endeavors.  To give an idea, strap-boobs has the highest natural attack power and deals about 200-250 damage with her attack.  Meanwhile, the main character's 3-hit ability does around 700-800 damage total.  Once you learn it, every boss fight is basically going to be the other 3 characters supporting the main character as she grinds the poor boss into pudding.
4. The maps are a mess.  The overworld looks like a hurricane swept through the countryside and many of the dungeons have the same problem.   The layout of the last town is especially atrocious and made me long for an exit spell.
5. The ending feels really rushed.  Despite having a nice, involving story, the end consists of flying to the final dungeon, walking inside, only to find out it's really just a tiny room.  You're immediately thrown into a short dialog, followed by the final boss fight, some dialog between the characters, and then...well that's it.  I guess I was expecting a bit more.
6. There's not really enough character development for the 3 other party members.  Each one had a personal side quest, but these side quests were really just "go to a location, interact with a thing, and that's it."  It would've been nice to see more depth and to learn more about each one.
7. There seems to be a bunch of different art styles going on here and it's kind of off-putting.  This is a common mistake in smaller-scale indie games though, so it's not too big of a deal to me.  Still, I thought it was worth mentioning.
8. The main character smells bad.  No really, she has time to sleep in the spare bed whenever you need to recovery HP/MP, but always complains about never having any time to take a bath?
9. Almost forgot:  There appears to be different damage types in the game (fire, lightning, etc) but I can't think of a single time when they actually felt relevant.
So overall, no regrets.  I got this game on sale for $0.49 and I'd say I got my money's worth.  Thanks developer, keep up the good work. :)

Normally, I'm a sucker for match-3 games.  This one, though, gets a couple of things wrong that push it into unplayable territory.
Firstly, it's very, very clearly a mobile port.  Not that there's anything wrong with that.  But to play using items costs "Starbucks" or whatever, which you earn by doing quests.  Absent in the steam version is presumably the microtransaction store where you can buy more Canadough to unlock them.
Secondly, it's not terribly deep.  After playing vastly more strategic match-3s like HuniePop (which isn't very deep, but vastly more engaging than this), this is simplistic, at best.  The strategy boils down to "match lots of hearts and shields".
Lastly, though, and most inexcusably is the fact that the gameplay is sluggish, unresponsive, and disengaging.  Every time the monster does something, it flashes a huge red warning on the screen and blocks your input.  Given that I play these games with a Wacom tablet and have no issues playing FAST the lockout of input every time the monster does something renders this basically unplayable for me.  Given that the game forces you to match hearts/shields AS FAST AS POSSIBLE, explicitly making it go slow is mindboggling.
Give this one a pass.

Puzzle platformers tend to be platform games with a few easy puzzles. Braid is a puzzle games with some easy platform elements. The puzzle mechanic is one of the most innovative I have seen. It involves time manipulation and challenges you to think in new ways to predict the consequences of manipulating time in various ways and use this ability to achieve your goals. It starts out easy and the difficulty ramps up at a good pace. Towards the end the game is challenging even for experienced puzzle solvers. The game is also non-linear in that you don't need to solve everything in one part of the game to progress to later parts, if you get stuck on a puzzle you can go somewhere else and come back to tackle that puzzle later.
The game has an artistic style that feels completely natural and fits well with the unique style of the gameplay. Graphics and sound contribute further to make the game atmospheric. The story is told in various ways, including texts you can read at the start of each level but also, in a way, through the pictures that you need to assemble to complete a level.
All in all this is the best puzzle platformer I have played (unless you count Portal as a 3D puzzle platformer) and highly recommended to anyone who likes puzzle games.

What is Block Legend DX?
Well, wrong question. The question rather is, what is it not? And the answer here is: "A motivating RPG". And that could be so easy to change...
Block Legend DX is a "match 2" RPG. On your grid of 7x7 squares you click on blocks to remove them, where two or more similar blocks next to each other can only be clicked. Now I am only around half an hour in, but got bored with this.
Around that is some kind of RPG, or rather a fighting and leveling simulation. There is no story that is in any way necessary to enjoy the game. Sure, I don't play Skyrim for the story either, and still would recommend it wholeheartedly, but Block Legend DX has not enough variety here.
The graphics are held in an 8 bit style or early 16 bit style, but clearly distinguishable as retro styled by having several modern elements to them. This can be seen on the screenshots on the store page.
The music is fine, but not memorable.
So let us come to the gameplay itself. With the match 2 gameplay you run your hero or heroine through various levels automatically, use the elements on the 7x7 board to attack enemies, rarely make any choices that go beyond the immediate situation. Yes, it is zen-like in the regard that you live absolutely at the current moment. But this is also where the game fails to deliver: You get not enough rewards to keep you motivated. You collect some stars that you can invest for future runs, but only into items you found on your runs. Also, each time you die your hero is reset to zero. This would not even be an issue if there was any way to prevent your death by grinding or something, but there is not. I would rather call this a match 2 roguelike than an RPG, and that is only if you imagine a Rogue where you progress automatically and have almost no strategy involved.
When you get to a battle, you have a certain amount of turns before your opposing creature deals damage. There is no variety in that damage either, it is on a per creature base. Now that is fine, but I would rather have seen something more RPG like. Maybe not necessarily something even more random like critical hits, but varied enemy behavior. For example there could be an enemy that comes first and runs away but yields high experience if you manage to kill it, just like those blocks in Lufia II. Or maybe some enemy that heals itself completely once per battle at the expense of 2 or 3 of his future attacks. Or, or, or.
Then what could be done to make the game motivating? Well, easy: Let the characters become stronger permanently as you play. When I beat the first level, let me get some weapon or armor I can equip, etc. Just let there be ANY form of progression that makes you feel like "Hey, I played this for 15 minutes, I died, my character is back to the beginning but now I start at least with an additional shield if I pay those 3 stars prior to my run."
Stars are gained very easily, but without much to spend them on after the half hour I played - only a drink that helps me for 2 or 3 rounds - it feels like senseless grinding already.
So what remains in the end is a nice basic concept for a game that has some potential but does not use it. Too bad, Block Legend DX could have been something as enjoyable as 10,000,000. The almost complete lack of persistent progression as well as the partially high difficulty make this game unfortunately one that I can not recommend picking up. Since the fixes are so easy, one can only hope for a patch with a free addon, maybe as a separate game mode even, that gets rid of the complaints I have. If that is implemented, it could be worth even the asking price. Until then, either wait for a cheap sale or for another bundle with it.

(While this review also draws from the time I've sunk into the iOS version, after playing DX I can safely say that what I've written applies to both the original and DX versions of the game.)
TLDR; If you want a game as complex as Puzzle Quest or other similar titles, this isn't what you are looking for. But for $5 (or $2 for the iOS version (minus a few features), you can have a fun experience with a game that is charming, and has more depth than you would think from the mechanics. It also has great music, very charming writing and humor, and a consistent and polished art style.
The Map/"Story" System:
Let's get one thing out of the way; there is no story. Instead, you are controlling a hero who is progressing through a 2D land on a side-scrolling path. Each land has two towns, one boss at the end, and various enemies that pop up randomly based on the area. Each town has three randomly selected NPCs which offer various services. After you defeat the boss, you are taken to a randomly selected land (with the difficulty scaled up with each boss you defeat). More lands can be unlocked to explore for your first run as you earn and spend Starblocks. While there isn't any story, the various dialogues for the bosses and monsters are where the writing shines, and the goal is more arcade-style ("get the best score") than plot driven ("save the world").
Your Hero:
Your hero has a single equipment slot and a single consumable item slot, which start off empty, and you can buy or earn items and equipment as you go. The first two heroes have no bonuses, but as you earn Starblocks you can use them unlock more heroes that have different advantages and disadvantages, and require different gameplay strategies. As you unlock and use more characters, you have to learn how to utilize the right stats and blocks for each one, to suit their abilities. As you level up you can upgrade their stats to make them more powerful, of course, and upgrading certain stats benefits some heroes more than others.
Gameplay and Board Mechanics:
Your board stays consistent throughout the game, from when you begin to when you eventually, inevitably, fail, including during and in-between battles. This is a large part of where the strategy lies, because some blocks change what they do when when in battle versus when out of battle, and you have to make various decisions based on that. For example, when not in battle, the sword (physical damage) blocks turn into experience point blocks. So do you use the time spent between battles to rack up experience and level up quicker, and leave yourself without much physical attack power when the next enemy appears, or to arrange your board to do the most damage? Or do you use the time in between battles to build up your defense, heal yourself, or to earn money and treasure?
Matches are made by tapping two or more of the same adjacent blocks. Racking up combinations ups the benefits of the blocks. The blocks above the ones you cleared drop down and new ones appear at the top of the board. While it seems simple at first, you quickly learn that you need to carefully plan out how to get the largest combinations by chaining the same block groups, or arranging the board into massive groups you can clear with a single move. These strategies quickly becomes necessary if you want to survive past the first boss or go into the hardest dungeons.
There are two meters you fill as well; your defense meter and your treasure meter. The defense meter is raised by matching shield blocks, and reduces damage taken in exchange for defense points. (Example: You have 3/5 in your defense meter, and are attacked for 4 damage. You receive 1 damage and your defense meter is reduced to 0.) There also is a treasure meter, which is filled by matching treasure chest blocks, and gives you a random consumable item to use.
Starblocks:
Starblocks are the main "bread and butter” in the game: what you aim to get. They allow you to unlock new characters, lands, or start off with a previously used item or piece of equipment on your new run. Mostly, you get these by completing various tasks (such as not attacking for 30 turns, defeating an enemy in one hit, etc), and by defeating bosses.
Towns, NPCs, and Dungeons:
In each town, there are three randomly selected NPCs which offer various benefits in exchange for coins, ranging from buying armor, weapons, and consumable items, to delving into dungeons or changing the land you are in. (Dungeons are essentially a gauntlet of several enemies in a row, without any time to arrange your board and clear tiles in between battles.) You can only use the services of one NPC per town, so you have to choose which one has the most benefit to you at the time (such as going into a dungeon to gain more experience before the boss fight, or buying armor to raise your defense, etc).
Aesthetic:
I honestly find this game to be one of the most charming battle puzzle RPGs out there. The music is fantastic, reminiscent of older arcade RPGs. Each character is polished, with unique animations and skills. Each monster and NPC has a catchphrase, which is where the humorous writing comes into play. Overall, the game is consistently well rounded, with nothing standing out as being ill-fitting or poor quality.

NEO Scavenger is an incredibly in-depth survival game with a real throwback feel. It *LOOKS* rough on the edges but is actually incredibly well made.
* TL;DR*
Well made game about making tough decisions to survive a wasteland in a rogue-like setting. Almost a Darksouls/Fallout child with survival and exploration focus. Prepare to die, pretty often, and have fun.
* *
The game is all about making those tough decisions. From the get go what traits you feel you'll need or use best, and what hindrances you're willing to cope with to take on all of those useful traits/skills.
Fairly regular scenarios in which you make decisions based on the items you have, the skills you've acquired, and your environment, whether it be setting up camp in a crumbling building or out in the woods, to drink water of questionable origins, eating berries that may or may not be poisonous (a choice you can ignore with the botany skill), knowing eating said berries could stave your growing hunger a little longer, but also that it may end your game with you sweating and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ your life away... unless you find the right medicines. Was that the red pill or the blue pill (should've taken the medic skill)?
This game pulls no punches. It's hard, it's frustrating, and it can feel like your progressing very slowly... and you will. But you'll learn. You'll find what works for you. If that's a spear-wielding bandit, preying on others, chopping off their legs for a nice roast, go do it! If you want to hide in the forest, hunting game, living off berries and scattering sound and animal traps amidst your domain, go haunt those woods why don't you?
The game's replay value is high. (Mostly) randomly generated, with no real reason to follow the story except personal interests. If you want to make a life for yourself in the wastes, there's nothing (but everything) to stop you. It cannot be recommended enough, and for the price, it's a steal!

Super Mega Neo Pug has some of the most revolutionary gameplay I have ever witnessed and has a story filled with deep philosophical questions that makes me ask myself about my purpose in life and my humanity. Few games question the players actions in a way that weighs what we believe is right and wrong. This game tackles the biggest issues in our society from the racial quotas of institutions to what defines life and the balance between privacy and protection. As you progress through each level, you see the same situations from a different point of view. Can anyone's actions truly be justified? Can different cultures and ideologies coexist or can peace never be reached among these different groups. From the beginning of this game, you are driven forward with an unsatisfiable lust for money. This game is an endless cycle of failure (just like you) with the definition of victory being up to the player. Is it reaching a new high score or is it unlocking a new character. It does not matter because the choice is for you to make. Whether or not a game as complex and intriguing as Super Mega Neo Pug is worth putting time and effort into, is also up to you. Usually these "infinitely replayable" games hold my interest for one full playthrough unless they are mind-numbingly boring or unplayably buggy, but I rarely ever start second playthrough (let alone complete one). I bought FTL at deep discount ($2.49) expecting to play through it once, kill a few hours, and get my money's worth. For once, I was incredibly suprised by a supposedly "replayable" game. I've spent about 30 hours on FTL, beaten the flagship once, and I'm still on the edge of my seat. There is something about the combination of true roguelike RNG and built-in replay mechanics that makes FTL something special. Though I've gotten many unlucky runs where everything seemed stacked against me, each crushing defeat felt truly unique. While FTL can be frustrating, it has never felt unfair. There is always something new to learn or try out. There is a real thrill that comes out of constructing a strategy, trying to implement it, and inevitably adapting it based on the hand you are dealt. STRONGLY RECOMMEND, even at full price.

Alright, after solving the issues and getting to actually play the game, I've revised my review. I would recommend this to friends, but with warning that the loading takes a long time, so if waiting upwards to an hour to get in a server is too much for you, then wait until it gets fixed. The bright glowing rings in the sky are caused by the sky quality. Make sure you have it at max sky quality for them to disappear. The game has quests which helps you understand how to play the game(If you've played Ark, you'll still need it. It's very hard to grasp without it.) which is a very great part about the game. Taming isn't really explained, and neither is what you can or can't tame.(Saddles can help give you an idea of course.) The bestiary absolutely needs work, I find it to be the most useless part of the game right now. Building is very straightforward and almost identical to Ark so it's very easy to do. Magic is a little complicated, but once you start to use it, it becomes easier to understand.
If the loading issues are fixed and the taming/bestiary/magic is worked on, I would easily recommend this game to anyone and everyone. For now, I'd only recommend it to people who love the survival genre and games like Ark.

The beta period for Dawn of War was one of my favorite gaming experiences ever. Believe it or not, there was a pretty long period of time where the general tone of gamers online wasn't overtly negative and troll-ish, and the whole beta was filled with fantastic players who were down to play this new and exciting entry into the RTS lexicon.
That being said, Dawn of War has certainly aged strangely. Since it has been out for nearly twelve years at this point, its kind of a funky game. Video games have grown up and changed a lot since this was new, but that doesn't really detract very much from the overall experience. Widescreen doesn't really work and isn't worth trying to get to work, as a sidenote.
The core gameplay is based more around controlling squads of units than building a base. There are still resource nodes to grab on the map, and you still need to be mindful of the tech tree and working towards better units, but most of the game is army and unit based. Each of the races in the game sort of play similarly, with similar ideas, although some asymmetrical aspects are present. The core design is still fun years later, and games versus the AI can be hectic.
If you have a buddy who is down to do some 2vAI games, and you don't mind clunky early 2000's interfaces, you'll get some good mileage out of this. The campaign is totally forgettable and only features one race, though. Online seemed to be a ghost town when I tried it out, but that also might be a side effect of the confusing naming of the first Dawn of War game + expansions.
You see, the GOTY edition doesn't contain everything, strangely enough. You're still missing the expansions. If you want the complete experience, you'll have to look elsewhere and get the Platinum edition. I got this through a bundle, so I'm not too miffed, but the naming is confusing.
Overall, this was a good bit of time for some nostalgia. I had a blast playing a couple of maps and doing most of the campaign, but there isn't much staying power here if you're not a returning player. You might find the design a bit flawed overall, and there are later Dawn of War games that improved on the formula this game established.

My experience with the Redux thus far has been excellent.  I can't be sure, but I believe there is new/editted dialogue which is more inline with the book, or maybe I'm just understanding what's going on better after reading it.
Engine wise it runs much more smoothly than the original, though some may prefer the original look.  There are pros/cons to both.
I actually wish the game was much darker,  pitch black beyond the lit areas.  In the books it is explained that nearly all the stations are extremly dimly lit, with the exception of places like Polis, which is a virtual metropolis filled with light in comparison, so these people have very poor eye sight and are unable to go to the surface during the day or else be instantly blinded and eventually cooked by intense UV radiation.
The best part is all the new areas. There are multiple new stealth routes which I found to be very well placed and fun to traverse, and extra places to find stashes and such.  More options, more things to do, without feeling out of place with the original.

Parkour + Zombies. It sounds like a naff combination of two topics that are well past their peak, so I wasn't expecting much but ended up very pleasantly surprised by this highly engrossing, game with genuinely scary moments. There are no gameplay ruining bugs and the parkour system is well executed.
The day-night system brings an interesting dynamic to the game - a largely optional, periodic, in-game difficulty boost. During the day, tread with some level of care and you'll be fending off the horde successfully most of the time. At night, you'll be running around in a state of panic desperately trying to get to the nearest safehouse, slip up once and you get ripped to shreds. It would be a frustrating experiecing if the game forced you to play like this all the time, but you engage it on your terms: sleep through the night or go out and double your experience gathering pace - as long as you don't blow it.
The music is a refreshing change to the usual bombastic cinematic stuff - very reminiscent of John Carpenter movies and works well.
The only annoyance I have with the game and perhaps it's deliberate on the director's part, is the incoherent locale. The game is clearly set in an Middle Eastern or North African environment and other than the lead, the main characters speak with an appropriate accent but there's an abundance of characters that speak with regional UK or North American accents, signage is in English, the architecture is a confused mess from various continents and so forth.
It's as if mid way through development they had a change of heart and tried to make the game location neutral or perhaps part of the content was done by a different studio that didn't get the brief. Contrasting this with the stellar job that Ubisoft did on The Division in recreating New York, this is just sloppy.

Company of Heroes 2 is the best game that I have in my opinion.
It's a perfect stragigic game in WW2. It has alot of negative reviews, they are written by kids that think this game is just like COD, but it isn't. It requires real thinking, strategy, teamwork,... . And that's why these kids are whining and writing negative reviews. It isn't pay-to-win, You get some basic commanders and you can also buy other commanders, but none of 'em are that more OP than the other. You have 5 sides which you can chose from. ( 2 you get for free and are developped for the basic game, those are the Sovjets and the Whermacht, they also have a single-player campaign. You also have the Western Front that you can buy, these include 2 factions : Oberkommando West and the Americans, they also have a single-player campaign. The fifth factions that you can buy are the British, they have no single-player campaign.) Every factions is well balanced on one-another. The single-player campaigns are fun and teach you, surely in the beginning, alot of the basics. You can fight vs Ai or vs other players. The Ai is well programmed and are verry difficult to beat on the highest difficulty and pretty easy to beat on the lowest difficulty. The game-developers are still working on making the game even better and are also organizing tournaments, rating mods,... . The game also have an active mod-community.

Xcom: Enemy Unknown is my first attempt at one of Firaxis’ successful
turn based squad and base management simulators. I am years late to the
party with Xcom 2 out and much lauded as the better game in every way.
Regardless though I wanted to give it a shot, the following are my thoughts
on one of Firaxis’ fan acclaimed series of Xcom.
I had initially been dissuaded by how complex Xcom seemed. It always
seemed way to easy to make a mistake, and pay out the♥♥♥♥♥for it. In my
37 hour playthrough on normal difficulty I had many such noob moments.
My first namely in my first attempt at the game that lasted 5 hours before
I ran out of soldiers because too many of them died. My second attempt
proved much more enjoyable and insightful into why people love the Xcom
franchise.
You can manage your soldiers by classes and eventually can command
up to 6 squad members. I ran one to two snipers constantly and it proved
more than effective in bailing me out of countless jams. My heavy could
not hit the broadside of a barn until the last 5 hours of the game thanks to
RNG and my own inability to spec him properly. You can customize what
weapons you research that you can gather from capturing Aliens alive,
or doing autopsies on their corpses. You get to manage your Xcom base,
including its research, hanger bays with your fighters that intercept UFO’s,
engineering projects, building management. To sum it up, there is a  lot
to do in this game. It can seem overwhelming at first, but my goodness
is this game when you get the hang of it.
The game is not for everyone. It requires quite a bit of patience and
a cool head when your 99 percent chance to hit an enemy before he
kills one of your team MISSES and your squad member in question who
should have lived is dead. The game loves to ♥♥♥♥ with you in terms of
RNG. Sometime you will make the impossible shots and win the day,
other times it's like throwing a sure thing into a barrel and blasting it
into space as your whole squad nearly gets wiped in one turn. But that
is only if you really ♥♥♥♥ up :)
If you enjoy turn based games, with customization that allows you to
grow attached to your soldiers, some solid base management and
squad tactics. Xcom Enemy Unknown is probably for you. I am incredibly
excited to play Xcom 2. As I have heard it improves everything about
Xcom EU, and then some. Give Xcom a try if you are on the fence
during a sale. It is a game worth your time, and I myself expected to
hate it, ended up having a blast.

When single player games claim to have "replayablity" as a tagline, I generally roll my eyes. Usually these "infinitely replayable" games hold my interest for one full playthrough unless they are mind-numbingly boring or unplayably buggy, but I rarely ever start second playthrough (let alone complete one). I bought FTL at deep discount ($2.49) expecting to play through it once, kill a few hours, and get my money's worth. For once, I was incredibly suprised by a supposedly "replayable" game. I've spent about 30 hours on FTL, beaten the flagship once, and I'm still on the edge of my seat. There is something about the combination of true roguelike RNG and built-in replay mechanics that makes FTL something special. Though I've gotten many unlucky runs where everything seemed stacked against me, each crushing defeat felt truly unique. While FTL can be frustrating, it has never felt unfair. There is always something new to learn or try out. There is a real thrill that comes out of constructing a strategy, trying to implement it, and inevitably adapting it based on the hand you are dealt. STRONGLY RECOMMEND, even at full price.

Having sunk well over 1,000 hours on PS2, it's very easily my favorite Star Wars game.
The PC version is much better, that's for sure (no dips, full 32v32 combat, mods, etc.)
Pro tips:
1. Rocket / Heavy class is arguably the worst.  Do not use unless you can't take down a vehicle with either Engineer, turret / cannon, or another vehicle.
2. Engineer is arguably the all-around best non-unlock class, because you can 2-shot people and heal yourself; plus you can repair ammo droids for more health packs. Not to mention, two mines can kill most medium-set tanks.
3. Magnaguard and Shock Trooper are probably the best unlock classes, but Jet Trooper is terrible (fun to fly around, terrible at combat)
4. Sniper is pretty poor for singleplayer, because your bot teammates seem to never benefit from your support; in other words, keep plowing as hard as you can and try not to die.
5. Don't let stray enemies pass you, they almost always perform better than your team for some reason and will probably cap points your team is too stupid to have gotten to or defend.
6. The bomber vehicles are hilarious, two-shotting most other aircraft save for other bombers and personel vehicles.
7. For each army, Darth Maul, Mace Windu, Yoda, and Chancelor Palpatine are probably the best Jedi (Darth Maul is OP), while Han Solo can mow down regular troops like no tomorrow.
8. On Kashyyyk, activate speeders while facing the incline and slightly to the side of a tree, and you'll fly upwards.  If timed right, you can land on the platforms that'd normally only be reachable with jetpacks or hacks.  Those are the most epic sniping spots.

So this is my first entry into the Warhammer 40,000 universe and I must say I was very impressed. Simple to understand, excessively violent and nearly a perfect strategy game that marks the pinnacle of RTS games of it's era.
The story, not to spoil a single thing is superb for an RTS. In my opinion, the story is easily better than that of many games today. With it's twists, turns and full stops, it's a rather moving ride. As you complete missions, the story unfolds a little more until it all breaks down and becomes less of a story to do with missions than all out annihilation. Spending 15 hours with the Blood Raven Space Marine chapter tearing apart Ork by Ork, Eldar by Eldar and Chaos by ♥♥♥♥ing Chaos was a blast and even towards the end never lacked for excitement. However that leads me to slight dismay with the game. Even early in the 15 hours I got sick of playing the same units and the same strategy, the campaign never challanged me to try something different. Maybe it was because I was playing on Normal rather than anything hardcore, but it felt that way. The only time it made me do something strikingly different was when I was pushing away at early linear tutorial missions. However despite this, it's still an excellent game - especially for it's time. Relic, the guys who developed this, along with other award-winning and highly recommended RTS games such as Homeworld and the Company of Heroes franchise did an great job polishing it, making it look strikingly beautiful (of course for it's time) and simple but not bland.
Now onto the Skirmish/Multiplayer. Basically the same mode where on varied maps players/AI must battle it out to complete different objectives based on game modes and on many different maps. Map variety is great, even without the expansions and despite not doing much in the skirmish, you could tell that you'd be in for something different just looking at the startup skirmish screen. Whether you play as the Eldar, Orks, Space Marines or Chaos (plus more if you have expansions and use the CD keys on those expansions) you have a varied playstyle and each race is balanced making skirmishes fair each time. However, another point I must bring up, and I've noticed in Relic's other game - Company of Heroes is, that the AI seems to just do the same each game. I may have said the maps make varied gameplay, but mainly against players or if the bots are decently hard. The AI 9/10 do the same thing each time and makes them very predictable leaving them easily destroyable.
If you skipped reading that, you're ♥♥♥♥ing lazy, but I came prepared:
Pros
- Varied Skirmish Maps
- Balanced and different factions to play as on skirmish.
- Great story was it's twists and turns.
Cons
- AI often predictable on skirmishes.
- Campaign, despite fun, becomes rather repetitive towards the end. One term: Annihilation.
Overall I'd rate it easily a 8.5/10.

A good game with several frustrating moments.
I thing that characters are the strongest part of the game; gameplay-wise there are no random battles (all monsters are visible) which is a _huge_ plus in my books. World is small and backtracking is quite frequent but at the end it starts to feel like a home territory which I also consider a plus. With no random battles it is quite possible to sneak thorugh the territories and some of the monsters are not aggressive which is a good addition to a usual formula. Battles are quite predictable but difficulty curve is reasonable, although on lower difficulty I've finished boss battle on level 29 on main character and about 25 on everybody else, and didn't see higher level abilities. Some difficult monsters don't regenerate which is, again, a good anti-frustrating feature.
Frustrating features are mostly related to speech redundancy: for example, if you didn't win boss fight you'd have to sit through long, slow moving final cutscene again; the vendor on beach has to have... that... pause... every time he offers you a rest, which is very frustrating if you go for dream challenges and have to rest often; Vivian stuck on her long dialog etc. Some sidelines (such as Smith and Priscilla; Helga's father) didn't trigger in my playthrough. Some items in shops are redundant as good gear can be found in wilderness or easily earned. I couldn't find how to dismiss one of companions (Quinta) either. Although the dash is present (L.Shift) there is no auto-dash function.
The main drawback for me is a multiple references to other creations from author and fourth wall breaking. They are not badly written and sometimes funny but I feel that due to sheer amount of them the world didn't have a chance to truly reveal itself. The ending also felt rushed: I finished with impression that much was left unresolved (to visit the other drow village, to brocker peace, to see Lazarus' and Vivian's marriage (or a loud lack of such)), to go to Great Beyond. It was a good story but it did feel prematurely cut just as it started to really flow.  I wish it was longer or there was a second part.

Obtaining Saints Row 4 without Steam in my Country (Germany) is pretty much asking for a quick execution of yourself, because it's been censored quite a bit and pretty difficult to get if you don't have something like GameStop in the area. However, i managed to get it now through Steam and playing it, soon i realized that this censoring kind of had a point. If the game wasn't censored like this, it might encourage people to do some insane irresponsible stuff, like shooting fire from their hands, jumping 40 meters into the air or
.
After he (or, in your backward-Universe, she) saves the world from terrorists, the leader of the 3rd Street Saints becomes the president of the United States and starts running the country into the ground so hard that it tunnels through and ends up under China. Then Aliens attack, kidnap you and seal you into a computer simulation of Steelport from Saints Row 3. Very kind of the Aliens to spare the Developers the task of designing a new Sandbox! But it is actually okay, because the game uses the old Sandbox for new Gameplay elements along the lines of Prototype, complete with the ability to make a dive, face front, into a tank and destroying it - along with pretty much everything in the general area.
Whereas the first Saints Row games were silly, but still grounded in some realism, like Saints Row 2 was, Saints Row 4's relationship with Realism is a quick farewell-kiss before drinking drug-infused Fanta out of a clown's shoe and skyrocketing onto the backside of Mars. Within the first half hour, Saints Row 4 managed to parody Call of Duty, Armageddon, Independence Day, The Matrix and Space Invaders without a single breather. But it's still more grounded than Saints Row 3 was. No, seriously, i mean it! Saints Row 3 was always going up and down between Saints Row 2's "silly crime Sandbox" and Saints Row 4's "bats**t-s**tting-bats-crazy drug trip", and as such it couldn't quite decide on a tone it wants to have.
Saints Row 4 now has accomplished the Task that began with Saints Row 2, which is cleaning off the dirt that marked the Saints Row games as a „Subpar GTA Knockoff“. However it is weird that the Game reminisces so much about the stuff we've finally gotten rid of, with characters from each previous Saints Row game. However, the „Subpar GTA Knockoff“ is now completely rinsed off from this game, which now reveals the game's wacky comedy, which can only be judged by whether the game made me laugh or not. Well, it generally made me laugh, simply because of the fun you have by beating people up with an oversized wobbling sex toy, and the dialogue between the characters is, as always, hilarious to listen to, and some of the parodies work. However it does fall flat at times. Entire sections of the game attempt to make fun of popular games nowadays, but fail to understand the difference between a Parody and a Reference, just like Duke Nukem Forever. One brief chapter is entirely devoted to mock Metal Gear Solid, complete with a cardboard box, inside which you hide to then take out guards from behind, but that's not a joke! It's just what you do in Metal Gear Solid. If you mock through imitation, at least put on a silly face while doing so, or, even better, kick them between the legs!
Saints Row 4 also gets a fair share of licensed music! The Prologue is accompanied by that one Aerosmith song from the Armageddon soundtrack, that just about everyone tearfully admits is kind of alright, and there are other examples, usually to positive effect, but i eventually relaized that they only did this because they made a Sandbox with cars and Radio stations, only to figure out that there's no reason whatsoever to use cars. But even this was cleverly solved by having the radio always available, vehicle or not.
The Game gives you those Superpowers i talked about earlier right at the start (kind of), and then spends the entire story mode regretting this, because all the story missions have some weird reason for your powers to not work, making you wonder why you even spend upgrades on them. The Final Boss however is a great Superpower-Brawl that rounds things up well. Another thing i really liked is that you can get health back from killing enemies, which keeps the pace up, whereas in previous games all you could do was duck and cover and wait for blood to fall off your face. But for some reason, this power is removed during the Final Boss, so it goes back to hiding and sucking on your thumb.
Overall, the Game has a lot of stuff, a Sandbox with Superpowers and vehicles, wacky comedy, Sci-Fi-action, game parodies, a lot of Gameplay features being thrown in, used once and then thrown away, and character customization that even Skyrim would be jealous at. Taken as a whole, the Game is a complete mess, but as the end of a series that has always been moving to the point of maximum mess it does its job pretty well. It is a mess, but it's also a lot of fun! This is how all Video Game series' should end: A big, massive, over-the-top roast of itself, and of video games in general, exploding into everything the series does best. Salute it, with the wobbliest sex toy you can find!

Odd little game that is surprisingly addictive.  Frustratingly difficult, I have yet to complete the entire mission through the final boss.  But even so, it's fun to play even though you will probalby lose very often.
It's a turn-based strategy game set in space.  Decide which planetary system you want to "jump" to, and the game advances a turn while you travel there.  Once you arrive, you might fight a bad guy, or meet some friendly traders where you can buy upgrades and repair your ship, or you could be faced with a moral dilema that might lead to further combat, or potentially to a reward for avoiding conflict.  Then you advance to the next turn.
You must balance the abilities of your ship while buying weapons and fuel, and you are constantly being chased by a superior force.  In the end though, you must fight this force, and that's when I get my behind kicked!  (Actually, there are times when I've lost after just a few skirmishes with the locals, long before I get to the final fight.)  But it's still enjoyable.  If you can get it cheap (less than $10) you'll probably get your money's worth out of it.  I know I have gotten my money's worth already, and I have yet to beat it...

It came to me as a surprise that I never ran into the old XCOM game couple decades ago but with little problem I took this game as an entry point considering it was a reboot of a sort. I generally like tactical turn based isometric rpg games. I was thinking this was kind of like Disgaea but more with guns. I had another thing coming.
First off this game is about risk management. Plain and simple, If you hate gambling of any kind, don't like that chance plays a role in your game then turn away this is not the game for you. Random number generator is an integral part of this game, your chance to hit, enemy chance to mis, as well of numerous other factors are generally affected by it. The key is that you are given tools, means by wich you can increase your chance and hence manage your risk. This is not a game of 'luck', you manage your chances, your risk to your best ability. At this the game is superb.
The game is divided into two major components, the tactical squad based isometric turn based combat and the HQ resource management. On the field you have your soldiers, their attributes, class, gear, items, the map you are in and up to you how to get the job done. In HQ you have to manage panic for countries participating in xcom project. If too many reach max by end of the month, they leave, you lose funding (current or future possible) and potential continental bonus. If 8 of them leave, game over. You also manage your money, your air defenses, your research projects, your gear and abilities for your soldiers. All in all it forces you to prioritize things to what you feel is necessary for you to survive. The base building aspect is also rather interconnected so you will have to most likely look stuff up to be efficient.
Now this game gets a reputation for ♥♥♥♥♥♥happens'. Yes it will, murphy's law will♥♥♥♥♥♥you off. Just keep in mind that when crap does happen, so will the opposite. Sure you will get your newly ranked colonel chomped by a Chryssalid around the corner, but you will also get moments where you MEC trooper (EW expansion) burns entire chryssalid pod to a crisp in one go. Learn to cope with loss, manage your loses, always have replacements, prepare for the worst and hope for the best.
Now, this game has some problems. Sigh. My first run was on Classic, since I feel other difficulties shackle the enemies to the point of little challange. That said the difficulty in general is backwards. The hardest part of the game is the start, the early game. It can be nail biting frustrating. Remember how I said you had to prioritize base building and decisions? Well early to mid game there is not much choice. You absolutely HAVE to go for satellites. It gets so extreme that it feel as if I'm playing a satellite simulator. You can spend 8-10h just to realize it is nearly impossible or extremely difficult to proceed your game, making you start over. The game's tutorial in general is not very good, while it may tell you what functions are,  it doesn't to a good job explaining the interconnectivity of base building, funding, research and actual priority. Unless you read up on it, you will end up with the good old trial and error approach. I restarted about 8h in first time because of lack of knowledge. I am ok with that, but some people won't be. It can be extremely punishing.
Another issue is within the tactical portion. Two things really stand out. One is the flow of combat. You start the mission, move around until you trigger a pod. Immediately on sight they get a free move so they scatter. This makes ambushing extremely difficult, since they have terrain advantage 9/10. Later on you can scout ahead with an invisible unit using a certain armor (or gene modification in the EW expansion) but that is further down the line and it still doesn't solve the problem of them always getting into right position while you have to manage according to them. It makes you feel the hunted nearly every case, and it's a bit of a silly way to give aliens advantage. This can be managed however, by inching your way through the level trying to trigger one pod at a time. Though unless you employ a lot of save games you will end up triggering multiple pods as you are dealing with the original one. Again it helps greatly to move slowly but if you are playing expansion it's another form of risk you will have to manage due to time limiting meld resource.
The other combat issue might seem like a minor thing, but it is frustrating nevertheless. Overwatch, your ability to shoot stuff off turn when it comes into sight. You will use it or you won't get far. Well what happens when you have multiple soldiers on overwatch and enemy walks in all their line of sight? They all fire, instantly,, regardless that the first guy killed it. Your whole squad will waste their ammo shooting at a corpse. This is frustrating as ALL HELL. That drone just walked in first and you were hoping for the Sectopod to catch some rounds? Too ♥♥♥♥ing bad. This isn't even a proper risk factor, it is just a game mechanic that was done half♥♥♥♥♥
Anyway, despite the complaints the game is rather addicting. There is an immense sense of accomplishement when your soldiers return unscathed. When your MEC punches a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ though a wall or into a car exploding enemies hiding behind it. When your sniper manages to shut down everything in sight. When that well placed rocket just took out 5 aliens (or exalt), when you capture few Mutons and gear up on Plasma Rifles and so forth. You honor your fallen and you push forward with your living. The game is a phenomenal tactical strategy RPG, despite some of the issues. If you like isometric squad games, if you like managing risk and priorities, if you are willing to take loss and move on, if you are prepared to make sacrifices to win, get this game, seriously. It will abduct your♥♥♥♥♥for many hours.
(make sure to get the Enemy Within DLC expansion, it add MUCH needed variety and content, more than worth the price)
